In many of the <term>faculties<gloss>branches of advanced study, such as law, medicine, or theology</gloss></term> and the <term>liberal arts<gloss>the core academic subjects of a classical education</gloss></term>, Most Illustrious Prince, Most Merciful Lord, great diligence has already been applied by scholars for some years now. Their goal has been that individual treatises and books on specific subjects—worked upon by different authors and published separately at various times—might be gathered into one body and volume to be presented to those who study these individual arts and sciences. This effort seems to have been undertaken primarily for this purpose: that those writings which lay scattered and widely dispersed across the various sciences—and which could not be sought out and read without great trouble and expense—might be brought together into a single volume in this way. In doing so, they provide the entire <term>apparatus<gloss>the complete set of tools, references, or foundational texts</gloss></term> of a whole art, or at least its most important parts, as if in a most beautiful... <note>original: "veluti pulcerrimo quodam." # EPISTLE

*theater, to be looked upon and gazed at with pleasure by students. From this, as if from a well-cultivated and skillfully arranged garden, they might pluck every kind of healing herb, as well as various little flowers and fruits, not only for their own utility but also for their delight. I decided that this very same purpose and use should also be set forth by me in the present matter of <term>Chemical things<gloss>the study of alchemy, metallurgy, and early chemistry</gloss></term>. And since very many outstanding men, endowed with the highest talents and adorned with singular wisdom—both in our own time and in previous centuries—have written many things brilliantly and almost divinely in various places about this art, I have taken care that their works (as many as could be tracked down with great expense and labor, sought from all sides) be gathered into one body and arranged as a kind of* THEATER <note>The word "Theater" (Latin: *Theatrum*) was a common title for Renaissance books that aimed to provide a comprehensive, panoramic view of a subject, much like an encyclopedia or an atlas.</note>. *I am led by the best of hopes that, through this work of mine, I might perform a service neither unpleasant nor unwelcome to students of <term>Chemical philosophy<gloss>the theoretical and experimental study of nature's transformations, often seeking the Philosopher's Stone</gloss></term>. By this opportunity, as they compare various authors with one another, they might more easily gather insights from one to apply to another, and in this way more conveniently reach the goal of their pursuit.*

For this word *Aludel* in Arabic is a *sublimatorium* in Latin, which that Arab <term>Geber Abenhaen<gloss>the Latinized name for Jabir ibn Hayyan, a foundational 8th-century figure in alchemy</gloss></term> (or Ebenhaen, the preeminent philosopher among the Arabic chemists), Avicenna, Rhazes, Hali, Morienus, and most other Latins frequently use. <margin>Geber, book 2, chapter 43.</margin> An *Aludel*, or *Sublimatorium*, is a vessel in which <term>chemical sublimation<gloss>the process where a solid is heated into a vapor and then collects as a solid again on the cooler parts of the vessel</gloss></term> takes place: which is the "elevation" of a dry thing by fire, with it adhering to its own vessel. By "dry thing," I mean the lower elements, or matter. By "fire," I mean one that is gentle, uniform, moist, containing, drying, digesting, and close to the nature of the thing itself. By "elevation," I mean conversion, or ennoblement, and perfection. <margin>Hermes Trismegistus, "Sift the matter."</margin> "With adherence to its vessel" means that which is of the same nature, salty, and in which there is a stone-ma- <note>The text cuts off here at the catchword "pidifica," which completes the word "lapidifica" or "stone-making."</note>

...purifying. For by that <term>sublimation<gloss>a chemical process where a solid is heated into a vapor and then condensed back into a solid to purify it</gloss></term>, repeated seven times or even more, silver (which by its nature is less pure and less perfect than gold) can be made much more perfect than any natural or common gold. And do not think that this perfection and purity comes to it by melting alone. For if you examine it with the greatest diligence time and again by fire, you will not for that reason make it more perfect or purer than natural gold, unless you rightly employ that chemical sublimation repeated seven times or more. For this reason, therefore, that comparison is most true, by which the prophet David compared the true and pure words of God to such silver, cleansed and prepared by the chemical art, rather than to natural or common gold. For although that gold is considered the most pure and perfect among all metals, it nevertheless contains some dregs within itself, however few and foreign. Otherwise, the prophet would have compared the pure words of God to gold rather than silver.

Dearest son, do not be repelled by the name of the stone. For no one has ever been able, nor will be able in the future, to <term>tinge<gloss>a technical term for the alchemical process of changing the color and quality of a metal, essentially "dyeing" it into gold</gloss></term> gold, except with gold. ### William of Paris. <note>original: "Guilielmus Parisiensis"; likely referring to William of Auvergne (c. 1180–1249), a Bishop of Paris and theologian.</note>

The intention of the philosophers is to make a spirit out of a body, namely pure <term>philosophical mercury<gloss>Not common quicksilver, but a refined, spiritualized substance used as the base of the Great Work</gloss></term>. Since, however, it is necessary to compose the stone from two substances, the **volatile** and the **fixed**, it is necessary first to create their mercury from the union of those two before the Elixir is completed.

### John Duns Scotus, the Subtle Doctor. <note>A famous medieval Franciscan theologian and philosopher.</note>

Some say that it is good to move the material from one vessel into another from time to time, but this is not true. Instead, it is enough for the stone to be placed once in its vessel, well-sealed, and not to leave it until the whole <term>magistery<gloss>original: "magisterium"; the entire alchemical process or the mastery of the art</gloss></term> is completed. Moreover, [to do otherwise] is of evil, just as in the generation of a human being and of every plant, the seed is never placed in the <term>matrix<gloss>the womb or place of origin</gloss></term> except once.

For Oldradus and John Andrew prove that art—commonly called Alchemy—to be true and not forbidden, and that it is not improper for one metal to be transmuted into another. For (as they say) we even see that sometimes a living thing is produced from a dead thing, as we see from worms, from which silk is produced, and many other things: and glass is produced from a plant. <note>Refers to the manufacture of glass from the ashes of saltwort or other plants.</note> Much more so from metals, in which there is a greater agreement and likeness. For since it is made as if from the same principle into similar things, the transition is easier in those things having a <term>common bond<gloss>original: "symbolum"; a shared quality or essence</gloss></term>. # OF THE ART OF CHEMISTRY.

...transmutation, no one doubts that all things are made from quicksilver <note>original: "argentum vivum"</note> and sulfur. For we see a worm, naturally and through natural artifice, changed into a fly, which differs from it in species; and a strangled calf changed into bees, grain into weeds, and a strangled dog into worms, through the putrefaction of boiling <note>In medieval science, the heat of decomposition (putrefaction) was thought to "boil" or transform the vital spirits into new life forms.</note>. But we do not do this ourselves; rather, nature does it, which we merely manage. Similarly, we do not change metals, but nature does: for it we prepare the matter according to the craft. Since nature acts by itself, not us—we are truly its administrators. 

Thus says **Geber**. **Abenhaen**, or **Ebenhaen**, and **Augustine** likewise say in *On the Trinity*, book 3: "Just as we do not call parents the 'creators' of crops, even though the internal power of God works to create those things through their externally applied movements." **Dastinus** <note>Johannes Dastinus (c. 1300), an English alchemist who defended the art to Pope John XXII.</note> says in book 1: "For Art imitates nature, and in certain things corrects and overcomes it, just as a weak nature is helped by the industry of physicians." For Art often helps nature whenever it is hindered. **Geber**, book 1, chapter 9: "Artifice completes the defect of nature in many things." There are also those who assert that the hair of women can be turned into serpents. We also see stones and frogs fall from the sky, and stones produced in the kidneys and bladders of men.

**Avicenna** <note>The Latin name for Ibn Sina (c. 980–1037), a Persian polymath whose works on medicine and "the soul" were foundational in Europe.</note> in the book *On the Soul*, first discourse, chapter 1, says: "A man can make a living thing out of barley. For if you take horse dung, which is nothing else than barley, and place it in a suitable warm spot, beasts come forth from it which they call *Abumes*: just as flies arise from the putridity of the air, and lice from the putridity of human humors." Thus says Avicenna.

For thus, by a certain hidden, concealed, and wondrous natural disposition and skill unknown to men, **seminal virtues** <note>original: "virtutes seminariæ" — a concept from St. Augustine referring to the latent biological blueprints or "seeds" placed in creation by God.</note> burst forth into their proper species in ways and limits determined by nature, as Saint **Augustine** says.

> For, as **Aristotle** says: *Not everything comes from everything, but a determined thing from a determined thing.*

And nothing (says **Johannes Dastinus** in book 1) is suitable for a thing unless it is closer to it by its own nature.

The same **Dastinus** says: "Principles are created by nature, and by art they are made into compounds: thus also our **Stone** <note>The Philosopher's Stone, the goal of the alchemical "Great Work."</note> is perfected by art, because it is born fit by nature to be perfected; yet nature does not have the movement to become a complete **Elixir** <note>term: Elixir (a medicinal or transformative substance) </note> unless it is perfected by operation and art."

Furthermore, as **Theophrastus** <note>A Greek philosopher and successor to Aristotle, known for his works on botany and minerals.</note> writes in the book *On the History of Plants*, book 2, chapter 6: "In the genus of animals, natural changes are seen, either by reason of time, or by the change of locations, or by generation. For from a moth comes a caterpillar, then from that a butterfly is born. And it has been noted that this happens in many other things." Likewise, watercress <note>original: "sisymbrium"</note>

# OF TRUTH AND ANTIQUITY

...as the same author says, unless it is restrained by cultivation, it seems to be changed into mint. Thus he says.

**Albertus**, in the *Book of Minerals*, book 3, chapter 2: *The **prime matter of metals** is an oily moisture, subtle, which is incorporated with a subtle earth and mixed so strongly that the greatest part of each is not only combined with the other, but exists within the other.* <note>This describes the "mercury-sulfur theory," where metals are formed from these two principles becoming a single unified substance.</note>

**Aristotle**, in *Meteorology* book 3, chapter 15, says that metals are created from a watery vapor and a dry exhalation, which are <term>quicksilver</term> <note>original: "ar. vi." or "argentum vivum"</note> and <term>sulfur</term>. But to return to the matter at hand: all metals are made from one and the same immediate matter—namely, from quicksilver and sulfur—as everyone asserts. They differ, however, in form—that is, in their purity and their <term>cooking</term> <note>original: "coctio," referring to the natural heat within the earth that matures metals over time.</note> or digestion. Indeed, the stripping away of accidental qualities, or the corruption of the essential forms themselves and the introduction of others, is possible; and among things that share a **symbol** <note>In Aristotelian physics, a "symbol" refers to a shared quality (like heat or moisture) that makes it easier for one element to transform into another.</note>, the transition from one to another is easy. Therefore, the transformation of metals is possible. For just as the generation of the elements is circular, so too is the generation of metals from one another, as **Hermes Trismegistus** and other philosophers assert. *And the elements are generated and destroyed among themselves in turn; they therefore have a common and identical prime matter between them. They differ, however, in form and species.* **Albertus**, *On Minerals*, book 3, chapter 6: *Among things that share a symbol in their matter, and in their natural powers and potencies, transmutation into one another is easy.* The same author, book 3, chapter 6.

Nor should you be moved by what **Titelmannus** <note>Frans Titelmans (1502–1537), a Flemish scholar whose textbooks on natural philosophy were standard in the 16th century.</note> writes in his *Compendium of Natural Philosophy*, book 1, chapter 24, concerning "celestial matter." He argues that because of the perfection and power of the most potent form given to it from the beginning, celestial matter cannot pass from form to form, because a natural agent is lacking that could either impress another form upon it or take away its own. However, he does not conclude that the same happens to lower, natural things. For he says in chapter 25 that they do not have the same situation, since **privation** <note>The "lack" of a specific quality or form that a piece of matter is naturally capable of receiving.</note> is not the true effective cause of transmutation from form to form by itself, but only an occasion and a "cause without which it cannot happen" <note>original: "causa sine qua non"</note>. For unless there were a privation of absent forms in matter, and unless matter were suited to have those which it does not yet have, it would never be transmuted from form to form. He says, however, that the true and efficient cause of this transmutation is a **natural agent**, which, by overpowering the existing form with impressions contrary to it and favorable to the form it wishes to introduce, impresses them into the matter. Thus, by its active power, it makes the matter pass from one form into another.

Let those people come to their senses, I ask, who dare to overturn Nature herself—the most skillful parent of all things—and all of philosophy. Let them stop attacking this **Chemistry**, which is the better, more admirable, and hidden part of natural philosophy, and especially necessary for the human race...

By citing Aristotle and Albertus Magnus, the author explains that transformation is a natural process where a "natural agent" replaces one form with another in receptive matter.</summary>

# OF THE CHEMICAL ART

...an imitator of nature, which is occupied with the natures of things, their causes, and hidden virtues, especially of the mineral kind, those who are ignorant laugh at it. This art the great **Hermes Trismegistus** calls "true without a lie, certain, and most true" <note>This is a direct quote from the *Emerald Tablet*, the foundational text of Hermeticism.</note>; and it is approved by **Plato**, Eustathius, Suidas, Solinus, Strabo, Pliny, and many others, and which **Geber** <note>Geber is the Latinized name of Jabir ibn Hayyan, an 8th-century polymath considered the father of chemistry.</note> asserts is a gift of the most high, blessed, sublime, and glorious God. By its wondrous artifice is composed that **Royal powder**, or fusible salt, the oil, or the **non-burning sulfur of nature**, the earth of the philosophers, the **Elixir**, <term>potable gold</term> <note>Gold in a liquid form, believed to be a universal medicine that could grant longevity.</note> (or the gold of the philosophers), the **Water of Life**, the tincture: the precious stone, the Indian or "Indicus" stone, the philosophical stone, or the **Medicine**, which performs wondrous actions in the three kingdoms of things—animal, vegetable, and mineral—as will be explained to you more fully in the third chapter.

For this reason the ancient philosophers said that the Stone was at once animal, vegetable, and mineral.

Whence **Arnaldus** <note>Arnaldus de Villanova (c. 1240–1311), a famous physician and alchemist.</note> says in the *Rosary*: *Alchemy is one hidden part of natural philosophy, necessary beyond all other parts: from which a single art is constituted, to which there is no equal. For by it, imperfect precious stones are perfected; the sick human body is restored to health; and imperfect metals are transmuted into gold and silver, by a certain single universal medicinal body, to which all the particularities of medicine are reduced and infused.*

**Albertus**, *On Minerals*, book 3, chapter 9. Those who whiten by means of white things, and yellow by means of yellow things, etc.

Against the sophists and impostors.

May God, the best and greatest, grant that you do not fall destructively into the hands and snares of those impostors, who wretchedly waste their labor on useless or perhaps forbidden things—fake white or red <term>tinctures</term>, "augmentations," "multiplications," and "extractions" of gold (as they falsely call them). They knowingly and maliciously deceive the common people everywhere, promising them many things, even mountains of gold. For with various and vain "sophisticated" <note>In this context, "sophisticated" means fraudulent or adulterated, rather than refined.</note> labors they consume their own means and those of others; they spend their lives in false, dangerous, and harmful studies of practice and a thousand impostures. Some of them chase after drink, others after fortunes, others luxury, others honors, and others the most base lusts. Because of them, that true, natural, rare, hidden, and divine Chemical art—indeed, a science so supernatural—sometimes has a bad reputation among many, so that it is held and believed to be an illusion and mere deception.

<margin>Geber, book 1, chapter 7.</margin>

These scoundrels, sycophants, impostors, and sophists you should count as nothing; despise them and keep them far from your mind, for they are truly not worthy of the title of "Chemical philosopher." Instead, you should embrace and study sincere or approved Chemical books and natural philosophy itself for a long time, with great care and diligence—not at all for the sake of profit or glory. Look up to that sublime Chemistry, sent down from heaven by the **Father of Lights** <note>A biblical reference to God from the Epistle of James 1:17.</note>; favoring it, you should consecrate yourself to it and pray well. For that art is kept within the divine power, and it is bestowed upon or withdrawn from whomever He wills, He who is glorious and sublime, and filled with all justice and goodness. To Him thanks must always be given, and praises sung, for His ineffable goodness, and in-

## ARISTOTLE, in the book *The Secret of Secrets*, to King Alexander, chapter 65.

<margin>Aristotle calls it the metallic egg, and Pythagoras calls it the bean.</margin>
> *First, O Alexander, I wish to hand over to you the greatest secret of secrets, and may divine power help you to complete your purpose and to hide the secret. Take, therefore, the stone which is animal, vegetable, and mineral, which is not a stone, nor does it have the nature of a stone <note>A classic alchemical riddle: the substance is "stone-like" in its final form but is derived from organic and mineral life.</note>, etc. Divide it, therefore, into four parts, and each part has one nature <note>Likely referring to the four classical elements: Earth, Air, Fire, and Water.</note>. Then compose it equally and proportionally, so that there is no division or conflict in it, and you will achieve your purpose, the Lord granting. Moreover, the same author says: when you have water from air, air from fire, and fire from earth, then you will have the mastery.*

## ALEXANDER the Emperor, in a certain letter.

> *Our ancient man is our dragon. This dragon eats its own head with its tail <note>A reference to the Ouroboros, the snake eating its tail, representing the cyclical nature of the alchemical process and the unity of matter.</note>. Both the head and the tail are the soul and the spirit, and the soul and the spirit are created from mud, and this comes from the east and the west through the one who expels harms. I do not lie, because what I have said, I have seen in truth.*

## GEBER, Book 3, chapter 75.

> *Now therefore let the sublime God of natures be praised, blessed and glorious, who revealed to us the sequence of all medicines, along with the experience of it, which we have sought out through the goodness of His instigation and the persistence of our labor, and we have seen with our eye and touched with our hand the completion of it, investigated through our mastery.*

## ALBERTUS, surnamed the Great, Bishop of the Church of Regensburg, *On Minerals*, Book 3, chapter 1.

> *Concerning the transmutation of these metallic bodies, and the change of one into another, it is not for the natural philosopher to determine, but for the art which is Alchemy. This is the best and most certain kind of inquiry; because then a thing is known through its own proper cause, and its accidental qualities are least doubted, nor is it difficult to know.*

Mary’s Bath <note>The *Balneum Mariae* or bain-marie; a gentle water bath used for slow, even heating.</note>.

For that [Powder] is produced from the pure substance of quicksilver <note>original: *argenti vivi*</note>, acting as the female seed or the matter, and from a moderate and small amount of the pure sulfur of gold or silver, which is of the same nature and kind, acting as the male <note>original: *maris*</note> or the form and sulfur. This is achieved by an artificial fire—gentle, even, moist, airy, vaporous, able to be exhaled, and close to the workings of nature. This fire subtly and continuously moves, directs, and excites the process only, without overcoming the formative mineral power. Instead, it aids the proportional and natural fire once the ingredients have been joined in the best possible mixture. The foreign dregs <note>original: *faecibus heterogeneis*</note> are first removed gently and with great skill, and the substances are then brought through frequent sublimation, or grinding and roasting, to a state of solution and a melting, stable fixation <note>The "fixation" refers to the point where the substance no longer evaporates or changes when exposed to high heat.</note>. This state is invincible against fires and achieves perfection, or transmutation, to the highest possible degree. In the meantime, while I write more to you at my leisure concerning the *Chemical Harmony* <term>Chemical Harmony: a theoretical framework where alchemical processes mirror the musical or mathematical order of the universe</term>, the natural principles of metallic things and the art, and the works of both nature and art, let these words suffice, and think well of them.

<margin>
Why it is called animal, vegetable, and mineral.

Twofold multiplication.
</margin>
That Chemical Powder—whether you call it the Philosopher's Stone, the melting salt, sulfur, the Elixir, the medicine, or potable gold <note>original: *aurum potabile*; gold in a liquid, drinkable form believed to be a universal panacea</note>—certainly possesses a wondrous power over three classes of things: animal, vegetable, and mineral. For this reason, the ancient philosophers said that it is animal, vegetable, and mineral. Some call it "animal" because it possesses a soul <note>original: *animam*</note> and a spirit; or because water is its soul and life, which brings life to and nourishes the body or the earth. They call it "vegetable" because it flourishes, is nourished, and grows by addition <note>original: *appositive*</note>, and it increases or multiplies either in its power or in its quantity. They call it "mineral" because it is extracted from minerals.

In the animal kingdom: For it restores every animal—whether human or beast, and whether suffering from internal or external sickness—to health in a very short time. Because the primary qualities, or the elements themselves...

...which deviate from natural symmetry. It restores failing actions and offending humors—the causes of imbalances and corruption, whether arising internally from the body itself or falling upon it from the outside—back to their own nature. For this substance is almost incorruptible; it is tempered by the purified elements themselves and separated from the dregs of the four elements, which are the primary cause of corruption. Therefore, it creates a tempered and healthy body, just like the spirit of life. By its power and help, nature digests what was indigestible and casts out everything undigested. It cuts away all excessive and offending qualities; it enlivens the spirit, hardens the soft, softens the hard, thins the thick, thickens the thin, makes the lean fat, and thins the fat. It cools the hot, warms the cold, dries the moist, and moistens the dry. Finally, it strengthens and confirms the natural heat and the substantial moisture <note>Also known as "radical moisture," the fundamental life-fluid in medieval medicine believed to sustain vitality.</note>.

And it is (as many write) like a universal medicinal body, into which all the specific qualities and powers of other medicines are gathered and infused. This is because it is a certain "fifth nature" <note>The *quinta essentia* or Quintessence, a celestial element beyond the standard four of earth, air, fire, and water.</note>, introduced by the ancient philosophers as an essence and a most thin, purified soul. It resists putrefaction or corruption for the longest possible time, and it is only with the greatest difficulty and labor that it can be corrupted. It consists of equality and homogeneity, freed from all mortal solidification—a celestial and simple substance of the elements. It is as if it were tempered from the elements themselves, purified and separated from the coarser matter and the inconsistent <note>original: *heterogenea*</note> superfluity of the four elements by that chemical sublimation. Whence *Eusebius* <note>A 4th-century Christian historian and scholar.</note>, in his book against the philosophers, chapter 44, says that *Socrates* and *Plato* consider "Ideas" separated from matter to be true substances. *Aristotle*, on the contrary, writes of this in Book 1 of *On the Heavens*, chapter 2. For the Elixir—or that powder of the philosophers, or potable gold—is made from a homogeneous, most pure, and most subtle substance of metal, which can be mixed into any fluid. 

<margin>*The Elixir is made from a moderate and most pure substance of quicksilver.*</margin>

What, indeed, could you find under heaven more homogeneous and more uniform, of a thinner substance, a more tempered nature, and less subject to corruption or putrefaction, than the pure substance of metals, or <term>quicksilver <note>original: *ar. vi.*, an abbreviation for *argentum vivum* (living silver).</note></term> itself? For the elements, as *Aristotle* prefers, are at their absolute purest in their own center. Therefore, once the inconsistent parts (which became attached to them by accident) are removed, the most pure and homogeneous thing will remain—acting as its seed, spirit, and soul. There is no reason, therefore, for you to wonder, or in your ignorance dare to deny, that hidden power of the Elixir—known or believed by so few—unless you also wish to wonder at or deny *Galen* <note>A prominent Greek physician whose work dominated Western medicine for centuries.</note> and what is clearly proven by experience. 

<margin>*In the book "On Simple Medicines," book 9, the chapter on Conia. Because of their greatest subtlety, they act more quickly and cause the least harm.*</margin>

In his writings, he introduces the so-called "septic" faculties, which possess a burning heat but, because of the thinness of their substance, they burn without causing pain. Why then do you wonder, and why do you not cease to deny it, when you see <term>quicksilver <note>original: *ar. vi.*</note></term>, as the substance of metal, almost passable through fire, air, water, and earth without harm? Because of the homogeneity of its substance, joined and mixed through its smallest parts, it resists corruption for the longest time and can almost never be destroyed by any injuries...

## ON TRUTH AND ANTIQUITY
->B 4<-

...to be able [to do this], which certainly happens to no other thing of any kind, whether animal or vegetable? Arnaldus de Villa Nova, in his book *On the Secrets of Nature*, chapter 1, says: *Mercury alone is incombustible and airy, which is a sign of perfection.* <note>original: "Solus Mercurius est incombustibilis & æreus, quod perfectionis est signum." Arnaldus was a famous 13th-century physician and alchemist.</note> Furthermore, what should you say about gold? No matter how much it is heated, it is not diminished; indeed, even by the testimony of Aristotle at the end of the 3rd book of *Meteorology*, all metallic things burn because they contain a dry exhalation. Yet gold, alone among them all, is never burned; and as Pliny testifies, the more often it is burned, the more perfect it is rendered, because of the equal meeting and purity of the *argentum vivum* <note>Quicksilver or Mercury.</note> and sulfur in its creation. Michael Scot also says in his *Alchemy*: *Just as all metals are called imperfect if you compare them to gold, and all living things are imperfect if you compare them to the angelic nature and to incorporeal substances separated from matter: so gold itself is more imperfect and impure than our Medicine—which is our Stone—even though it is of the nature of gold. This is because it is more refined and purified from its dregs, and abounding in a uniform subtlety. For simpler things are more perfect than those that are compounded, and they act more strongly and miraculously through their subtlety, just as a sharp point pierces more than a blunt one.* These are his words. For according to Aristotle, the elements are purest at their own center. Therefore, I do not doubt that you will admit that gold itself, when reduced to its ultimate purity and to extreme subtlety and simplicity, is much more perfect and incorruptible than natural gold. When converted into a <term>Potable substance: "Aurum Potabile" or drinkable gold, a legendary medicinal elixir believed to grant longevity.</term>, it preserves the bodies of living creatures from corruption and imbalance for a very long time. Whence Scot says: *Fire takes away the "being" from all matter except the Sun—that is, gold—so that other metallic bodies cannot be preserved in their state, except in a state of being cherished.* <note>original: "nisi in statu fotari," possibly referring to the gentle heat of the alchemical bath.</note> Yet I would not wish to assert that this medicine is entirely incorruptible because it is made from natural things; rather, because it is composed of matter more incorruptible than all others, and has been reduced to the greatest subtlety and simplicity through the separation of the dregs of the corruptible elements. Therefore, if you preserve it correctly, it will remain uncorrupted for a long time, and when administered to sick creatures, it will keep them in health for a long time. For this reason, physicians command that we use food that is less prone to corruption.

<margin>
Why the ancient philosophers practiced Chemistry.
</margin>
Many of the ancient philosophers, inspired by the divine spirit, consecrated themselves to the knowledge, study, and investigation of this supreme medicine—so necessary for the human race. They did so specifically for this reason and end: not so that they might transmute imperfect metals into perfect ones by that <term>Chemical art: Here used in the sense of alchemy (Alchemia), the precursor to modern chemistry.</term> and thus grow rich, but so that they might cure sick men and preserve their lives for the longest possible duration (to the glory of God) and keep them unharmed until the limit predefined by God. For it is more desirable and holier to cure a sick man and keep him in health longer than to grow rich with wealth and perhaps, through an abundance and insatiable desire for those riches, ultimately lose one's soul. Hence it is written in Ecclesiasticus 30: *There is no wealth above the wealth of health for the body.* <note>original: "Non est census super censum salutis corporis." From the biblical Book of Sirach.</note>

<margin>Logical Reasoning.</margin>
Disease (as physicians teach) is a lack of moderation, or an imbalance of the four elements or humors from which the human body consists, by which it becomes sick, and through which it thrives. Yet that <term>Chemical medicine</term> <note>Specifically referring here to "potable gold" (*aurum potabile*), a liquid form of gold believed to be a universal cure.</note> is a substance that is uniform and of a single nature, consisting in perfect equality. It is a most refined soul, separated from its dregs, and like a simple substance of the elements; therefore, it is tempered and very little liable to corruption or decay. For this reason, it balances the elements or humors of the human body, strengthens the innate heat and the "substance-giving" moisture, and restores the sick to health, moderation, and balance. <margin>It is appointed for men once to die. Hebrews 9.</margin> Thus, one will be preserved safe and whole from disease until the life-term predetermined by God, provided that by using that medicine wisely, one does not otherwise injure the strengths of their nature and the <term>complexion</term> <note>The specific balance of humors (blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile) that determines an individual's physical and mental character.</note> of the body beyond measure.

Since, therefore, man is the end of all things, he will also be the end for which that supreme medicine called the <term>Elixir</term> is intended; it is not only a restorer and reformer of imperfect metals, but also of sick and infirm living beings.* For it is a sufficient philosophical argument that the actions of strong active agents work more effectively on subjects that are disposed to receive them than on those that are not. Since this supreme medicine is nothing other than natural heat multiplied in the substance of fixed <term>Mercury</term>, <note>In alchemy, "Mercury" is not just the metal quicksilver, but a philosophical principle of fluidity and spirit.</note> and the power of heat is to gather things of the same kind and separate things of different kinds: this medicine, by its life-giving heat, will necessarily separate things of different kinds in the bodies of living beings. It will preserve the spirits and humors in a man more quickly than in the nature of metals, because a man, through his own natural heat, separates different kinds of waste which metals are least able to separate by their own natural heat, as we understand by the persuasion of experiments. These are his words. For (as someone writes) this medicine is a spirit of life penetrating all other spirits, offering a "tincture" and perfection of life to solid bodies as well as to bodies...

<margin>The marvelous power and operation of the Stone, or Chemical medicine, upon the vegetable kingdom.</margin>
It performs these actions upon the vegetable kingdom. For the generations of trees and plants, as <term>Theophrastus</term> <note>The ancient Greek "father of botany."</note> writes in his *History of Plants* (Book 2, Chapter 1), occur either spontaneously, or by seed, root, cutting, branch, shoot, the trunk itself, or even from wood cut into small pieces; and these often suffer from diseases, either common or specific, by which they perish. Surely, that medicine heals them. For in the springtime, it vivifies all plants, trees, shrubs, bushes, and herbs with its great and marvelous heat, and it strengthens and awakens their generative power. For if you inject some quantity of that medicine dissolved in water into the heart or center of a vine trunk, it will produce flowers and leaves and bear fruit in the month of May. It acts similarly in other plants, because it is nothing other than natural heat, as it were, fixed in its <term>radical moisture</term> <note>The essential life-sustaining fluid believed by medieval scientists to exist in all living things.</note>. And because, as Lully writes in the *Practice of the Testament* (Chapter 27), nature by its own instinct greatly desires and seeks to be in the depths of an elemental body, where it works by strengthening its natural heat and seed-bearing power, because it is able to penetrate all bodies; for this reason, it is called <margin>Hyle</margin> <term>Hyle</term> <note>A Greek term for "matter" or "primordial substance."</note>.

<margin>The marvelous power of the Stone, or Chemical medicine, upon the mineral kingdom.</margin>
In the mineral kingdom: it transforms every imperfect metallic body—namely lead, tin, copper, and iron—and furthermore, common <term>quicksilver</term> <note>mercury</note>, into either silver or gold. This transformation includes every distinction of perfection: purity, weight, <term>fixity</term> <note>The ability of a substance to remain stable and not evaporate under high heat.</note>, color, malleability, and the tests of the <term>ash-cupel</term> <note>original: "cineritii." A refining process where metals are heated in a cup made of bone ash.</note>, <term>cementation</term> <note>A process of refining gold by heating it with salts.</note>, firing, melting, exposure to sharp vapors, mixing with burning sulfur, quenching, <term>calcination</term> <note>Reducing a metal to a powder through high heat.</note>, and the repetition of reduction, as well as the easy reception of quicksilver.

<margin>The power of the same over precious stones.</margin>
Furthermore, it cures and perfects the "illnesses" or imperfections of precious stones, whether in their transparency, color, hardness, or weight. It restores them to their natural virtue—indeed, to perfection—and (as <term>Albertus Magnus</term> <note>A 13th-century scholar and saint known for his vast knowledge of the natural world.</note> writes in Book 1, Chapter 2 of *Minerals*) it transmutes one into another by that antidote of the medicine which the Alchemists call the <term>Elixir</term>. Their illnesses are cured, their hidden qualities are made manifest, or their visible flaws are concealed.

<margin>That precious stones are made from crystal by the Chemical art.</margin>
For by that Chemical art, these stones are most perfectly composed: the Emerald, the Carbuncle (also called *Anthrax*, or commonly the Ruby), the Diamond, the Beryl, the Balas Ruby (or Palace Ruby), the Chrysoprase, the Chrysolite, and others. IT REMAINS, O diligent student of this sacred, rare, and hidden Chemical art, that we provide the reason why the following doctrine, excerpted from <term>Galen</term> <note>A prominent Greek physician whose theories dominated Western medicine for centuries.</note>, has been added to the end of this little book of ours. ### Galen, *On Simple Medicines*, Book 9, chapter on Lye.

<margin>As ashes differ according to the nature of the wood, stones, or other things: so too do the lye-washes.</margin>
> When the ash is removed, <term>lye</term> <note>original: *lixivium*; an alkaline solution made from ashes.</note> is made. The Latins call the remains of burnt bodies "ash" <note>original: *cinis*</note>, whether they be of a stony nature, or parts of trees or animals. Therefore, lye is made according to the nature of that which is washed: that which has an <term>empyreuma</term> <note>a scorched or burnt quality</note>, or a very sharp fiery nature, is itself also very sharp; that which is not of such a kind is moderate. For this reason, it is mixed with so-called "septic" <note>corrosive or medicinal agents used to break down tissue</note> faculties, since it possesses a caustic heat by reason of its proportions, but because of the thinness of its substance, it burns without pain.

And because, as Lull writes in the *Practice of the Testament*, chapter 27, nature by its own instinct greatly desires and seeks to be in the depth of an elemental body in which it operates—strengthening its natural heat and its seed-bearing power—<margin>Hyle</margin> because it is permeable to all bodies, it has therefore been called <term>Hyle</term> <note>A Greek term for primordial matter; the formless substance that underlies all physical reality.</note>.

<margin>The marvelous power of the Stone, or Chemical medicine, in the mineral kingdom.</margin>
In the mineral kingdom: it transforms every imperfect metallic body—namely lead, tin, copper, and iron, and furthermore the common mercury of the masses—into either silver or gold, with every distinction of perfection: purity, weight, <term>fixity</term> <note>The ability of a substance to withstand the heat of fire without evaporating.</note>, color, malleability, and the test or trial by <term>cupellation</term> <note>original: "cineritii"; a refining process using a cup of bone ash to separate precious metals from lead.</note>, cementation, firing, melting, exposure to the vapors of sharp substances, the mixing of burning sulfur, quenching, calcination, and the repetition of reduction, and the easy reception of mercury. <margin>Its power over precious stones.</margin> Furthermore, it cures and perfects the "sicknesses" or imperfections of precious stones—whether a lack of transparency, color, hardness, or weight—and restores them to their natural virtue, or rather to a more perfect state. And (as <term>Albertus Magnus</term> <note>A 13th-century Dominican friar and polymath who wrote extensively on minerals.</note> writes in *Minerals*, book 1, chapter 1), it transmutes one into another by that antidote of the medicine which the Alchemists call the <term>Elixir</term>; through it, their sicknesses are cured, or their hidden qualities are made manifest, or their manifest flaws are covered.

<margin>That precious stones are made from crystal by the Chemical art.</margin>
Indeed, by that Chemical art, these stones are most perfectly composed: the Emerald, the Carbuncle (or <term>Anthrax</term>, commonly called the Ruby), the Adamant or Diamond, the Beryl, the <term>Balas ruby</term> <note>original: "Balagius"; a rose-tinted variety of spinel.</note> or Palace-stone, the Chrysoprase, the Chrysolite, and others. Regarding this formation and Chemical metamorphosis of stones, you may read more in Lull, in the *Theory and Practice of his Lapidary*, and in the practice of his...

### GALEN, *On Simples*, Book 9, the chapter on Lye.

<margin>As ashes differ according to the nature of the wood, stones, or other matter, so too do the lye-washes.</margin>
> *Lye is made once the ash has been removed. The Latins call "ash" the remains of burnt bodies, whether they are stony in nature, or parts of trees or animals. Lye is therefore produced according to the nature of that which is washed out: that which has a scorched or very sharp fiery nature produces a very sharp lye; that which is not of such a nature is more moderate. For this reason, it is mixed with those powers called "septic" <note>Here meaning "corrosive" or "digestive" in a medical sense.</note>, as they possess a caustic heat by reason of their proportions, but they burn without pain because of the thinness of their substance.*

## DE VILLA NOVA.

The <term>Philosophers’ Stone</term> <note>original: "Lapis Philosophorum"</note>, springing from the earth, is perfected or exalted in fire: satiated by a drink of the clearest water, it swells visibly on all sides for at least twelve hours. Then, placed in a <term>stove</term> <note>original: "stupha"; a dry heat chamber used for evaporation and purification.</note> and purified by the vapor of dry air and moderate heat, it attains the solidity of its parts; and once rid of its superfluous moisture, it becomes fit for <term>grinding</term> <note>original: "contritioni"; the process of pulverizing the material to further refine it.</note>. When these things are finished, <term>virgin’s milk</term> <note>original: "virgineum lac"; a metaphorical term for a specific white liquid or solvent produced during the alchemical process.</note> is squeezed from its purer parts. This is immediately placed in the <term>Philosophers' Egg</term> <note>original: "Ovum Philosphorum"; an oval glass vessel designed to mimic the natural incubation of a chick.</note> and does not cease to be nurtured by a "hatching" decoction until, stripped of its variety of colors, it rejoices with its companion in a snowy white color. From that time forward, without fear of danger, it endures the pains of an increasing fire, until, dyed with a purple color, it emerges
->from the tomb with royal<-
->power.<-

*In Padua, some years ago, a wonderful proof of the alchemical art was found. It was a clay urn, marked with these verses:*

> WHAT DO YOU WANT WITH YOUR PRYING EYES?

# GIOVANNI CHRYSIPPO
## FANIANO, TO HIS
## PHILOPONUS, GREETINGS.
<note>Giovanni Chrysippo Faniano was a 16th-century legal scholar and alchemist from Basel. His correspondent, Johannes Philoponus, may be a pseudonym or a reference to the 6th-century commentator, though here it likely refers to a contemporary scholar.</note>

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'M' set within a square frame. The background of the initial features a detailed landscape with buildings and trees. In the foreground, there appear to be figures, one possibly seated at a desk or table, suggesting a scholar or philosopher at work.</image-desc>It is a marvel that a Physician heals an animal pierced by so many and such great wounds, vexed by so many ailments, and restores it to its former health; yet a philosopher is unable to purge a metal endowed with its own defect, which seems a less laborious and much easier task. For who is there who, if they look upon the ailments of inanimate things as they do those of animals, does not see that a far more dangerous medicine is applied to that "casing of the soul" <note>original: "thecam illam animae," a poetic way of referring to the human body.</note> than to that which has nothing in common with the living except for its ailment? And yet that same physician dares to lay a hand upon the sick and wounded with doubtful health, while the philosopher does not dare to approach the metal—as if, forsooth, the danger to the former were not forbidden, but to the latter most of all, and as if it were more permissible to harm a man than a metal. 

But if someone should suggest that counterfeit money could be coined from "injured" <note>In alchemical terms, "injured" or "sick" metals are base metals that require healing/transmutation into gold.</note> metal, why would they not likewise suggest that many homicides could result from an "injured" man? As if, if someone killed a man with impunity, they would not fear to kill many more thereafter? It is a greater thing to kill than to deceive. Or is he not more harmful who, though he promised to heal the sick, nevertheless killed them, than he who gave a poor coin for a good one? In the latter, it is a matter of property or a small part of it; in the former, it must be a matter of the loss of life. Which, truly, is more precious? 

But "Majesty," you will say, "is touched here; Royal Majesty." Is not Divine Majesty also touched there? It is also more in the interest of Royal Majesty that a man be removed from the army than a coin from the treasury. Moreover, is it not a greater thing to save a man than to increase the public treasury? Truly, for one to deceive another, even if the law permits it, is the worst thing: let everyone be more cautious in protecting their own property, and finally in protecting the cause of the Republic. 

We are indignant today if someone happens to use the common faculties of nature, which at last have been made private property not through any society, but through discord—not by peace, but by war. If someone kills another, we look the other way and think they should be spared. We thus neglect the commandment of God, which is that no one should love themselves more than another. Since this is so characteristic and peculiar to friends—and indeed to those such as Pythagoras <note>Pythagoras (c. 570–495 BCE), the Greek philosopher who famously held that "among friends, all things are common."</note> believed, that all things are common—why do we complain today to a friend about something being taken from our private savings? And for this reason, Socrates <note>Socrates (c. 470–399 BCE), the foundational philosopher of Athens.</note> was rightly accustomed to curse the man who first separated utility from nature; for he complained that this was the source of all ruin.

<summary>In this preface, Faniano argues that alchemy is a legitimate "medicine for metals" and defends its practice against critics who fear it will lead to counterfeiting, suggesting that the preservation of human life and the laws of nature are far more important than the integrity of the treasury.</summary>
<keywords>Giovanni Chrysippo Faniano, medicine, alchemy, philosophy, social justice, Pythagoras, Socrates, transmutation, ethics</keywords>

--- Page 39 ---
<meta>This page continues the introductory epistle from Giovanni Chrysippo Faniano to Philoponus. It builds on the analogy between medicine and alchemy, arguing that while both involve risks if handled by the ignorant, they are noble sciences when practiced by the learned. The author concludes the dedication with a date and location: Paris, 1559.</meta>

It is indeed a double evil both to destroy metal and make it worse, and to kill a man, and certainly the latter is more to be avoided than the former. Truly, he who heals does not kill, nor does he who restores destroy. The hand of the physician is placed upon the sick, not upon the healthy and well; likewise, the hand of the philosopher <note>The "philosopher" here refers to the alchemist, often called a "natural philosopher" because they studied the laws of nature.</note> is applied to the base and imperfect metal, not to the precious and perfect. 

Therefore, both tasks must be entrusted to good and skilled men, not to the wicked, nor to the unlearned. If this is done, there will be reason to hope for the health of man and the value of metal. And indeed, for this purpose, that art which we call by the ancient and hated term <term>Alchemy</term> <note>original: "Halchemisticen." Alchemy often faced social stigma or was associated with fraud, which Faniano acknowledges here as an "exosus" or hated name.</note> has been developed since heroic times <note>A reference to the legendary or ancient ages of the world.</note> for the great benefit of the Commonwealth, provided it can be properly understood. For you know what great philosophers, what poets, and even what historians report concerning it. Hardly anyone considers these miracles of nature to be empty and fictitious, or invented for the purpose of deception. 

This is all the more true because the very precepts of the art are daily handled by anyone at all, and are adapted for use especially by those who lack both talent and diligence. It has happened by I know not what fate—unless perhaps because it seems too hidden or incredible—that it has been set aside and neglected by many professors of fine letters. From this it follows that those who have deserved less from the world of letters condemn it, or even despise it; and what in human affairs could be more unjust than this? 

I would have you believe this—as I suspect you already think—that unless one is instructed in the disciplines of the great arts, they can achieve little in this art. For it is assembled from natural, mathematical, and even supernatural precepts. Since these things are well-known and understood by you, they will provide you with a wider entrance to it—if indeed you think this art ought to be embraced, which, besides the innumerable effects of the nature of things, also has this: that he who attains it can crown his knowledge with great wealth and riches. 

But if you follow our rules <note>Or "our laws."</note> with that most acute intellect, keen judgment, knowledge of many things, and most tenacious and capable memory of yours, I do not doubt that you will easily achieve it. And I wish you to consider that this book was written and dedicated to you for this very reason, as I had previously promised in my letters. <note>Lutetia</note> Paris. The 14th day before the Kalends of November <note>October 19th.</note>, 1559.

# GIOVANNI CHRYSIPPO FANIANO SENDS GREETINGS TO MICHAEL, SON OF THE KING OF BUGIA. <note>Bugia (modern Béjaïa, Algeria) was a significant North African kingdom. Michael was likely a royal exile or diplomat in the French court.</note>

WHILE we were together in Paris <note>original: "Lutetia," the Roman name for Paris.</note>, after I wrote to King Henry <note>Henry II of France, reigned 1547–1559.</note> at your request—in such a way that you are well aware my writing was of no small benefit to you—it pleased you to recommend to me, in no common way, that edition which I had received a little while ago from my friend Philoponus, concerning the book on the <term>metallic metamorphosis</term> <note>The alchemical term for the transmutation of base metals into gold or silver.</note>. Following your pleasure, I took care that the book should be released as soon as possible after your departure. I now send it to you published, and published in such a way that it can only be understood by you and my dear Philoponus. If it seems to you to be properly edited in this way, I believe I have satisfied your wish; if otherwise, you may think your excessive severity <note>In this context, "severity" refers to the Prince's high standards or strict judgment regarding the text's clarity or quality.</note> is the cause. Since I did not wish to displease the people in this matter, I could not provide what did not even seem right to share. You yourself followed the path of Alexander, but I—though in very different matters—followed Aristotle. <note>A reference to the famous relationship between Alexander the Great and his tutor Aristotle, suggesting a bond between the royal patron and the philosopher-author.</note> Farewell.

# JOHANNES CHRYSIPPUS FANIANUS
## On the Art of Metallic Metamorphosis, addressed to Philoponus. <note>Philoponus, meaning "lover of labor," is likely a scholarly pseudonym for Michael of Bugia, to whom the work is dedicated.</note>

<margin>The metallurgical art is manifold.</margin>
Meanwhile, among the various teachings put forward regarding metals, nothing is more admirable than the art of metallic metamorphosis <note>Often referred to as transmutation: the changing of one metal into another.</note>, to which two other arts are added, making three arts in this category which we primarily employ. The first is mining (for divine nature would have produced gold, silver, copper, and iron in vain, had she not also taught the method by which their veins might be reached). The second is the smelting of the metals themselves, or of the dross of slag <note>original: "pumices ærugicos"</note>, and the manufacturing of anything desired from them; this is called both the "craftsman’s art" and "Chemistica" <margin>The Chemistic Art.</margin> <note>original: "ἀπὸ τῆς χημείας," meaning "from *chemeia*" or pouring/infusion.</note>. For what benefit would the discovery of the material bring if we did not possess the skill for its manufacture? The third is the art of metamorphosis, of which we have undertaken to speak in this book; it is called "Alchemistice," from *Alchemia*. <margin>Alchemistice.</margin> For the Greeks call salt *hala* <note>original: "ἅλα"</note>, and fusion *chemeia* <note>original: "χημείαν"</note>; and this art is specifically concerned with a certain fusible salt <note>A reference to the "Salt of the Philosophers," a key alchemical principle alongside Sulfur and Mercury.</note>. Thus, alongside the utility that God has granted to men, a specific art is joined through which that utility can be realized. The first two are mechanical and manual; this third one is a part of that Philosophy which concerns the nature and causes of things. For it teaches the natures and causes of both metals and other things joined to them by some natural bond. It is divided into two parts. <margin>Division of the art.</margin> The first concerns discovery, and is called Theoretical. The second concerns arrangement, and is called Practical. Therefore, we shall first investigate discovery, in which we will examine the nature of metals—not all of them, but only those which come closer to the work of metallic metamorphosis itself; afterward, we shall speak of the second part. <margin>The multiple goals of studying metals.</margin> Some metals are mined for wealth, others for luxury, and others out of rash necessity. For gold (with which copper is often found) and silver (where tin and lead occur) are sought for riches, just as iron is sought for war and slaughter, and gems and pigments for the sake of pleasure. <margin>The origin and etymology of metals.</margin> The Greeks call metals *metalla*, either from *metallaō* <note>original: "μεταλλάω"</note>, which means "I search thoroughly" (for we are accustomed to search for metals within the veins of the earth), or from the phrase "found one after another" <note>original: "ἀπὸ τοῦ μετὰ τὰ ἄλλα εὑρεῖσθαι"</note>. Thus Pliny <note>Pliny the Elder, the Roman naturalist whose "Natural History" was a primary source for Renaissance science.</note> believes that because wherever one vein is found, another is found not far off—a trait common to almost all such materials—the Greeks gave them this name. Gold is formed from red sulfur—bright, resistant to fire, extremely fine, and highly purified—combined with quicksilver <note>Mercury.</note> in the best possible mixture; from this, it hardens into a pure and reddish solid. But one gold is better than another. <margin>The choice of gold.</margin> That gold is superior which is more "boiled down" and digested by nature, enduring the flashing friction of the touchstone <note>original: "indicis... affrictus." A touchstone is a dark stone used to test the purity of precious metals by the color of the streak they leave behind.</note>.

<summary>Fanianus defines alchemy (Alchemistice) as a branch of Natural Philosophy distinct from mining and smelting, and provides the etymological roots of metallurgical terms. He describes the composition of gold as a perfect balance of purified sulfur and mercury, emphasizing its physical durability.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Fanianus’s discussion on the nature of alchemy, specifically focusing on the "spirit of gold" and its refinement. Having defined alchemy in the previous pages as the art of metamorphosis, the author now explores the philosophical and physical properties of the "quintessence" or fifth element extracted from metals.</meta>

# ON THE ART
<meta>catchword: tale (This indicates the final word of the previous page was "tale," which likely belonged to a phrase like "the spirit is of such a kind.")</meta>

<margin>
The various forms of the spirit of gold.
</margin>
...once purified, it rises into infinite forms: sometimes it brings forth a plant, sometimes a stone, or some unusual animal; at times a sea, or a pearl, or a gemstone, or a metal. Emerging sweetly from the commanding flames, it immediately shifts into many thousands of colors, and lives forever as a performer and magician of wonders, never tiring of this labor but growing daily in vigor and strength. Since we often struggle to understand what this is, or how it can be freed from its dark prison <note>A common alchemical metaphor for the "spirit" or "soul" of a metal trapped within its raw, unrefined physical body.</note>, we shall explain it next.

<margin>
The power of this art shown by example.
</margin>
For nearly all competition has now shifted to this art, which is most flourishing with great honor and profit. As Suidas <note>A 10th-century Greek encyclopedia of the ancient Mediterranean world.</note> records, it was once the long-time savior of the Egyptians against the fierce and formidable attacks of Diocletian <note>Roman Emperor (r. 284–305 AD) who reportedly ordered the burning of Egyptian alchemical texts to prevent them from funding rebellions.</note>, during a time when no one could be vigilant in the labor of any more honorable or fruitful matter. There are, therefore, those who distribute gold, and in turn make no end of separating the elements from it, until a certain most pure nature has settled, subject to no natural disturbances; this they call the "fifth element" <term>Fifth Element: also known as the Quintessence, a substance superior to the four earthly elements (earth, water, air, and fire) and believed to be the "breath of life" in matter.</term>, or the balance of corporeal substance. 

<margin>
What the spirit of gold is.
</margin>
For it is like that "fifth nature" introduced by Aristotle, which—being loosened, free, and separated from all mortal thickening—is devoid of earth and moisture, and is neither airy nor fiery. Instead, being set apart from these usual and known natures, it is considered a more celestial substance. 

<margin>
The method of extracting the spirit of gold.
</margin>
They use a bath <note>original: "lavacro," likely referring to a "balneum Mariae" or water-bath, which provides gentle, indirect heat.</note> for this purpose, in which the heat of the fire placed beneath is moderated. The impurities of the gold are, as it were, absorbed, and everything passes into an inward cleanliness. The mass of the gold itself—hard and almost like a diamond <note>original: "adamantæa"</note>—is crushed and undergoes an internal liquefaction and destruction without any loss of substance. Let no one think that a metal so complete in every fire could be diminished in any way; indeed, Pliny writes in his books on natural history <note>Pliny the Elder, *Naturalis Historia*, Book 33.</note> that gold is preferred above all others for this very reason: it is the only thing that loses nothing to fire, enduring safely through conflagrations and funeral pyres. The more often it is scorched, the more the material improves in quality. 

<margin>
The excellence of gold.
</margin>
For although that same mass decreases in bulk and weight, it remains constant in its powers and will never fail in anything. Indeed—and this is no small miracle peculiar to itself—it does not become worse, but shines more and more. It departs from its current state to take on a new character for itself: it casts off weight and exchanges it for lightness. To put it briefly, there occurs a transformation of both its hardness and all its other qualities. 

<margin>
Pindar’s opinion on gold.
</margin>
But it also receives back the powers it held before, now ennobled by this transition, much more vigorous than the original ones, and shining with an inexhaustible splendor. "For gold, when it is refined," <note>original Greek: "οὕτως γὰρ ὁ χρυσὸς ἑψόμενος"</note> as Pindar says, "shows all its rays." <note>original Greek: "αὐγὰς ἔδειξεν ἁπάσας." A reference to Pindar's *Fourth Nemean Ode*, comparing the refining of gold to the testing of a man's character.</note>

<margin>
The hidden power of gold.
</margin>
For there is a hidden power within it from the beginning, like certain little sparks, which—having received a gradual increase—finally breaks out to its peak, and even to the "catastrophe" <note>In classical drama and rhetoric, the "catastrophe" is the final resolution or climax. In alchemy, it refers to the successful completion of the Great Work.</note> of the tale, as they say; and then...

<summary>Fanianus describes the "spirit of gold" as a celestial fifth element (quintessence) that can be purified through gentle heat. He cites classical authorities like Aristotle, Pliny, and Pindar to argue that gold is unique because fire does not destroy it, but rather ennobles and perfects its hidden powers.</summary>

### PAGE 37
<sig>C 3</sig>

...is able to do almost anything, just as Plutarch writes concerning Lynceus <note>In Greek mythology, Lynceus was an Argonaut famed for his supernatural vision, said to be able to see through stone, trees, and into the earth.</note>: that he could penetrate rocks and trees with the sharpness of his eyes. Indeed, such a great power of penetration has been sought for it by the sharpness of his own genius that it is, as they say, the <term>extraordinary skill</term> <note>original: περισσοφὴ (perissophe)</note> of <term>instruments</term> <note>original: ὀργάνων (organon)</note> for all metals. 

<margin>
Various opinions of those differing on the Philosophers' Stone.
</margin>
And yet, there are some who require silver dross <note>Likely litharge, a lead oxide produced in silver refining.</note>, or mercury, or the very essence of silver, or eggs, hair, or human blood, or even wine, vinegar, or the herb called Moonwort <note>Lunaria; a plant often associated with the moon and silver in folklore and alchemy.</note>. Truly, these people terrify others by reciting various and horrific names, when all these things belong to one single family; and thus, as the proverb goes, they make "many things out of one." But let us return to silver. 

<margin>
The sulfur of silver.
</margin>
Concerning the matter of gold—since there is no small contention among the greatest authors of this art—we shall discuss it more copiously in another place. 

<margin>
Gold naturally in silver.
</margin>
Silver, therefore, contains sulfur, as we taught above, which is quite oily; this is why it melts in the fire. I said "quite oily," for nearly every piece of silver contains some gold at its center, 

<margin>
The effect of Chrysulca.
</margin>
digested within its pores. Consequently, almost all silver is also gold-bearing. To test this, it is customary to use <term>Chrysulca</term> <note>Literally "Gold-drawer" (from Greek *chrysos* and *helkein*); an alchemical term for a corrosive acid, such as aqua regia, used to separate gold from silver.</note>. For this liquid attacks the silver and draws it away from the gold like clotted blood <note>original: siderati cruoris instar</note>, with the gold emerging pure and incorrupt. 

<margin>
The cause of the ringing of silver.
</margin>
The cause of silver's sweeter ringing sound is the mobility of mercury and the "glue" of sulfur. 

<margin>
A wondrous experiment of the Author regarding mercury and common sulfur.
</margin>
That sulfur consists of a sticky substance can be learned by anyone through practice: if one places common sulfur—which is entirely "glue"—beneath mercury, 

<margin>
The Author's experiment.
</margin>
one will see the purest silver grow together from these two within a month. We ourselves have seen this, having used the proper time and place for the task. 

<margin>
Choice of gold and silver.
</margin>
Gold and silver are more beautiful the softer they are. 

<margin>
The generation of tin.
</margin>
Tin is found to be composed of a thin and subtle sulfur and a very fatty and dense mercury, poorly mixed; for this reason, it is also "shrieking" <note>This refers to the "cry of tin" (*stridor stanni*), the crackling sound produced when a bar of tin is bent, caused by the internal shifting of crystals.</note>. 

<margin>
The generation of lead.
</margin>
It is born with silver and is melted from mixed veins. There are two kinds of lead: black and white; the white is the most precious. 

<margin>
Of what lead consists.
</margin>
Black lead has a twofold origin: it either comes from its own vein or is found with silver and tin. Both consist of an oily, bituminous sulfur and mercury of the same quality. 

<margin>
A wondrous metamorphosis of lead discovered by the Author himself.
</margin>
This is easily judged: when lead was placed on a glowing wick, it vanished into a poisonous smoke, leaving no dross behind. We have learned by experiment to turn purified lead into gold and silver. It is first hammered and softened with a certain liquid in a small pot or tile, and from there it is cast into a glass vial so that it may be sprinkled with its own "soap" <note>original: smegmati; likely a reference to a flux or purifying agent.</note>. 

<margin>
Growth attributed to lead alone.
</margin>
Thus stripped of its scrapings, it emerges bright. It is then given to the wick, and if any impurity remains, it is consumed by the fires, with silver and gold remaining as residue. But some mercury must be added according to the ratio of the material. 

<margin>
Iron. Copper.
</margin>
To this metal alone, Galen <note>A prominent Greek physician and philosopher in the Roman Empire.</note> grants the power of growth: because, as Pliny is the authority, if lead is left alone in the earth, it revives more fruitfully. 

<margin>
The difference between copper and iron.
</margin>
Copper and iron are of nearly the same composition, except that iron has less mercury and more sulfur of an oilier kind, and is therefore extremely hard.

<margin>
The sulfur of copper.
Copper with silver.

Common sulfur.

...and scarcely flexible. This metal alone also melts with difficulty. Copper is less fusible than the others, containing less quicksilver <note>original: argentum vivum; mercury</note>. Its sulfur, however, is very close to maturity <note>In alchemy, "maturity" refers to the degree of "cooking" or "decoction" a metal has undergone within the earth's womb.</note>, and is only a little short of the required decoction, which is what makes copper itself so glittering. When joined with silver, it makes the silver more resonant <note>original: vocalius; literally "more vocal," referring to the clear ring of the metal when struck</note>, and turns it into its own color; this happens because of the abundance of sulfur within it. But so much for gold, silver, copper, tin, lead, and iron; next we shall speak of other metals. And now, first of all, we encounter that common and external sulfur, as well as quicksilver. This sulfur seems to be a terrestrial substance mixed with a certain bitumen, which Virgil also writes about concerning Mount Etna <note>Virgil describes the volcanic activity of Etna in the *Aeneid*; alchemists often linked volcanic sulfur to the formation of metals.</note>, and it is suited to take on the form of lead by the arrival of a quicksilver peculiar to itself, which is present in lead. It is the venom <note>original: virus</note> and the dregs of the sulfur of all metals, reflecting their subtlety in some part, so that by the meeting of quicksilver it is sometimes hardened into a metal—even a precious one—through the action of heat. Indeed, I have experienced this myself with manufactured minium <note>original: minio factitio; here referring to cinnabar (mercury sulfide), though "minium" often meant red lead.</note>, which is forged from quicksilver and sulfur:

<margin>Silver from manufactured minium.</margin>
some call it cinnabar. For from a drachma <note>A unit of weight, roughly 3.4 grams.</note> of it, I drew out—we produced—an obol <note>A small unit of weight, roughly 0.7 grams.</note> of pure silver. Truly, where the greatest abundance of this sulfur lies adjacent, unentangled by any pumice or jagged rocks, it reflects the intense heat of the sun's rays and burns continuously, having prepared that very place for the benefit of metallic generation.

<margin>
Quicksilver.
The power and definition of quicksilver.
</margin>
Sometimes an internal vapor alone ignites this material. Quicksilver also possesses within itself, like sulfur, a certain hidden breathable heat and a vigorous spirit—the seed of gold and silver—when it is moved by an external pulse, which is a beautiful and admirable secret in this art. This same substance wears down, softens, diminishes, and converts into itself gold and the remaining metals. Moreover, quicksilver is, as most are pleased to define it, a very viscous water, and therefore more dry than moist.

<margin>Every water is viscous, by way of example.</margin>
I added "very": for every water is a little bit viscous and sticky; this is shown by the effectiveness of its internal and most deep-seated substance lurking within it. For in the beginning, the earth lies hidden, ground down like powder and pulled apart into certain indivisible atoms <note>original: insectiles atomos</note>, by which it is bound together into a mass that finally hardens as the liquid vanishes. For the surrounding heat, and even the dryness of the earth itself, drives out the diluting moisture of the water, while the "glue" is retained. Otherwise, how could a composite structure remain? If that glue were removed, would it not be powder again, or the wet form of mud?

<margin>The example of orpiment.</margin>
Concerning orpiment <note>original: auripigmentum; arsenic trisulfide, valued for its gold-like color.</note>, pyrite, antimony <note>original: stibio</note>, chrysocolla <note>A green copper mineral used in soldering.</note>, alum, vitriol <note>original: calchanto</note>, and others of that kind (for these follow next), I will say in passing that they contribute nothing or very little to the Stone. Some contribute to outward whitening and gilding, others to soldering and cleansing, and others to the "gold-separator" <note>original: chrysulcam; a substance used to refine or separate gold.</note>. What is the point of describing how these are made? This one thing, it seems, should by no means be overlooked: that orpiment is also a certain vein of gold, but a poor and needy one. Pliny reports that Gaius the Prince... <note>Referring to the Emperor Caligula (Gaius Caesar), who Pliny the Elder records as having attempted to extract gold from orpiment.</note>

...[The Prince] <note>likely referring to a historical figure or patron mentioned on the previous page</note> ordered a huge weight of this to be boiled out, and it made gold; <margin>Pyrite.</margin> but it was not of the highest quality when tested with a probe, and it was of such little weight that it resulted in a loss. Pyrite is entirely mercury <note>original: argentum vivum; literally "living silver"</note> and sulfur. <margin>Alum.</margin> Moreover, they say that once alum <note>a naturally occurring mineral salt used in dyeing and medicine</note> was found, the digging came to an end. For what reason, I am entirely ignorant, since it is the saltiness of the earth that is promoted into mercury, and a white vein of copper was found beneath the alum. 

But since we have proposed a discourse on the metamorphosis of metals, and have shown that it involves a certain fusile <note>capable of being melted</note> salt—from which the name of Alchemy <note>original: Alchemistices</note> is derived—we have furthermore explained, to some extent, the nature and causes of the metals that pertain to this art (for these things are handed down most abundantly from the beginning). Next, we must see what that salt is, or what else produces it, and from where it is best extracted. <margin>Various opinions on the matter of the philosophical salt.</margin> For some profess that it must be extracted from gold and silver; we hold most of their teachings very strictly and firmly. Others say it comes from gold alone, others from both gold and mercury, and these different authors suggest various ways. 

<margin>The opinion of Geber.</margin> For Geber <note>the Latinized name of Jabir ibn Hayyan, a foundational figure in early chemistry</note>, in the book titled *The Testament*, writes that gold and silver are turned into "lime" <note>original: calx; a powder produced by heating a metal</note> by an extreme and long-lasting fire. He writes that this lime is later resolved into a liquid by a certain dispersing power of hot water boiling over fires, and finally freezes into a salt. <margin>The opinion of Arnald of Villanova.</margin> And Arnald of Villanova <note>a famous 13th-century physician and alchemist</note> teaches that these same things pass into lime by the help of a certain silvery liquid, after many moistening decoctions. <margin>The opinion of Lully.</margin> Lully, however, who is more scrupulous in this matter than Arnald and Geber, instructs that white or red wine should be poured over it, and warmed by innumerable vapors, so that it turns into lime or vanishes entirely; however, a certain thin and imperceptible substance settles, which he hints is that innate force of all things contained beneath the hollow of the moon's heaven, or the "soul of the world" <note>original: mundi animam</note>. By this, he contends that the aforementioned spirit is purified from its body. 

<margin>The opinion of Aurelius Augurellus. The opinion of Albertus Magnus. The opinion of Pantheus.</margin> Aurelius Augurellus <note>an Italian humanist who wrote the poem *Chrysopoeia*</note> is of nearly the same mind in his books on *Gold-making* <note>original: Chrysopoeia</note>, except that he remains silent on distillation. Albert, surnamed the Great <note>Albertus Magnus, a prolific medieval scholar</note>, the most sharp-witted debater among those who have treated this art, while he differs with Arnald in words, he agrees in substance. But Pantheus <note>Giovanni Agostino Panteo, a Venetian priest and alchemist</note>, a recent writer among them, teaches by certain fiery signs that gold can become so soft that it emerges into that corrupting water—or *hydor* <note>original: οδεν; likely a corruption of the Greek 'hydor' (water)</note>, as the Greeks say—and sometimes emerges by its own nature. 

<margin>Various ways to the Philosophers' Stone.</margin> There are indeed very many books, the titles of which bear no author's name, which discuss what they call "sublimation," and to use their vocabulary, "fixation" <note>the process of making a volatile substance stable under heat</note>, which is a certain binding together of both parts, a maturation and an intake into powder. I pass over here what the same authors hold regarding dissolution, distillation, coagulation, ceration <note>original: cereficationem; the process of softening a substance to a wax-like consistency</note>, and many such things. Indeed, they should be passed over, because they bring nothing else to this business but darkness and gloom...
