<margin>*All instructions concerning this art are written in riddles.*</margin>
...[so that they] cast a fog <note>original: "ginem offundant," likely completing the word "caliginem" from the previous page</note> over the matter. And there is almost no one, so far as I know, who has explained the precepts of that Alchemical discipline clearly until now; they have all hidden everything behind riddles and a certain monstrous way of speaking by design. And certainly not without reason: for it did not seem right to not wrap such great mysteries in some kind of riddling coverings and verbal portents, so that the profane crowd, as if from the Eleusinian Mysteries <note>ancient Greek secret religious rites; here used to mean secrets only for the initiated</note>, would be forever driven away from daring to examine them. For what is more absurd and intolerable than the crowd of the unrefined and insane common people, relying on such impenetrable defenses—already raising their horns enough as it is—should go about more insolently? Thus Pythagoras and Plato obscured their philosophy with their numbers; and Aristotle testifies in a certain letter to Alexander that he published some books as if they had not been published at all. Thus also Lullius <note>Ramon Llull (c. 1232–1316), a philosopher and writer to whom many alchemical works were later attributed</note> writes that his "wine" must be treated so harshly and strangely that it fails into ash or something lighter, or vanishes completely. He asserts that, treated thus, it vomits out that "fifth nature" of his <note>the Quintessence, the pure or spiritual essence of a substance</note>. Moreover, he uses that for his stone; and the stone for reforming and ennobling metals. Tell me, I ask, what on earth does wine have, or has it ever had, or do you think it will ever have in common with metals? He seems to differ from nature no less than one who thinks a man is born from a donkey, a lion from a man, or anything else more alien. Furthermore, how many horrors does he everywhere fashion for himself and his students out of the letters of the alphabet? As if he orders ridiculous things: that often 'b' must be taken, 't' left behind, and 'a' changed to 'r', or if you prefer, 'r' into 'a', and a thousand others (for I am inclined for a moment to play the part of Momus <note>the Greek god of mockery and criticism</note> and pursue Lullius with sharper accusation). And so, shamelessly eluding the reader's mind, he thrusts upon them mutual exchanges of letters as a description of the philosopher's stone. "But," you will say, "those letters designate the individual things needed to perfect that stone." Indeed, things are designated that touch neither heaven nor earth. For what are the "menstruum" <note>a solvent, typically used to extract essences</note> or "menstrual solvent"? What are "rectified moonworts" <note>original: "lunaria rectificata"</note>, saltpeter, the quintessence, and innumerable things of that kind, even though very different from each other, [all aiming] for a single and unique stone? For even if that thing—whether it is a stone or something else not entirely unlike a stone—turns itself into many and various forms and produces things that seem most remote from its nature, when in fact they are not distant at all, the substance is nonetheless one thing from the very beginning; nor does it admit anything foreign to itself, otherwise everything would come to nothing. 

<margin>*Description of the Philosophical Work.*</margin>
And therefore, Lullius is rightly accused by many of manifest lying: unless perhaps by pressing that liquid of wine down into the fifth substance, the material for the stone is most conveniently drawn out, or rather...

...this is the work which a certain Execedistes <note>possibly a specific alchemist or a pseudonym used in the author's circle</note> once placed before my eyes, showing indeed great furnaces and the same wreathed with various glass vessels. 

<margin>*Vessels.*</margin>
The vessels each had sediments in their seats...

...foundations, and an inner sacred gift dedicated to a different purpose. For why should I hide such a divine thing any longer? <margin>Various forms.</margin> Within it was a rotating mass, displaying an image of the very world itself. Indeed, there the earth appeared standing in the middle of everything, surrounded by the clearest waters; it rose into various hills and rugged cliffs, bearing manifold fruit, as if watered in due season by the rains of the moist air. It seemed to be exceptionally fertile with wine, oil, and milk, as well as every kind of precious stone and metal. Then the waters themselves, like the sea, surged toward the shore and onto the very surface with a certain transparent salt—sometimes white, sometimes red or tawny, or ruddy, and variegated with many other colors besides. <margin>Fire.</margin> Moreover, all these things were moved by their own fire, though it was an imperceptible and ethereal one. One thing especially seized me with unbelievable admiration: that this machine confidently asserted it could produce so many things—unique, diverse, and each complete in its own kind—from a support that was still small and weak, but which, having gradually become more robust, would finally return and coalesce into one.

<margin>Philosophical salt.</margin> Here I observed that species of fusible salt, in no way inferior to aphrolith <note>original: "aphrolitho"; literally "foam-stone," a term used for various salts or porous minerals like meerschaum</note>, and <margin>Philosophical quicksilver.</margin> that quicksilver <note>original: "argentum vivum," literally "living silver" or mercury</note>, to which the name of Mercury was given by the ancient authors of this discipline. It resembled that very "Lunaria" <note>A symbolic alchemical plant or substance, literally "of the moon"</note> of Llull, climbing against the flow of water, shining by night and day, and endowed with the power of gluing things together. <margin>What the "menstruum" is to Llull.</margin> Here also was the menstruum <note>In alchemy, a "menstruum" is a powerful solvent used to dissolve solids; the term is derived from the lunar cycle</note>, by which Llull understands the Moon <note>Silver</note>, for if she is neglected, there is no place for the "paralysis" <note>likely meaning a cessation or stagnation of the alchemical process</note>. Why should I again defend him from objections? He chose to provoke them only so that the matter itself might shine more clearly through dispute. For just as poets sometimes use "the Moon" to mean a month, and "the Sun" for a day (because the Sun completes its course according to the motion of the heavens every single day, but the Moon only every month), so, conversely, Llull takes "the month" to mean the Moon, and for that reason calls her the "menstruum."

Furthermore, he spoke of the "fifth substance of wine" <note>the Quintessence</note> in place of the gem-bearing river, which is the very material of stones. In it are seen aspilates <note>a fire-colored or glowing gemstone mentioned in antiquity</note>, golden shimmers, sardonyxes, lychnites <note>a "lamp-stone" said to glow in the dark</note>, sards, specular stone <note>translucent stones like mica or selenite</note>, all kinds of large pearls, and gems. Moreover, if he used letters as signs, Aristotle did the same. One should no more wonder at Llull for writing in such an obsolete and foreign way than at Aristotle. <margin>The Philosophers' Egg.</margin> Indeed, Aristotle himself, in the book *The Secret of Secrets* <note>original: "secretis secretorum"; a popular medieval book of advice and occult lore attributed to Aristotle</note> (if indeed that book is by Aristotle), calls the animal, vegetable, and metallic stone an "egg." <margin>The egg of the Pythagorean bean.</margin> And Pythagoras, if we believe Marcellus, called this the "bean." And Caelius <note>Ludovico Ricchieri, known as Caelius Rhodiginus, a Renaissance scholar</note>, in the fourteenth book of his *Ancient Readings*, expressed the idea through a certain similarity that the entire machine of the world consists in an egg. <margin>Wonders concerning the egg.</margin> He called its shell or bark the "earth"; the cold and moist liquid nearest to this, "water"; the spirituous, hot, and moist part within, "air"; and the yolk, "fire." To which I might add a pebble... <note>To "add a pebble" is a classical idiom meaning to cast a vote in favor of or to agree with an opinion</note>

...with sweet-smelling, green, living things, found everywhere, yet known to very few; rising in the middle of the sea, translucent, fleeting, and volatile until, joined with its own sulfur, it passes into a complete stone. Moreover, that Gold and Silver are initially "Libyan stones" <note>original: "Lybicontes"</note>, and shortly after "Carthaginian stones" <note>original: "carchedunij"</note>, when they are driven toward "coal-stone" <note>original: "anthracitem," a stone that glows like a burning coal</note>. Both, however—lest I seem to take back what I have said <note>original: "palinodiam ceciniſſe," to sing a recantation</note>—are the spirit and life of that common gold, even if they originate elsewhere. For they originate from the purest gold having no waste, and from its own silver. But both, as has been said, are for a brief moment in the hands of the unrefined masses; it is neither the gold of a blacksmith nor silver. For it cannot be such when it is freshly dug from the mine, surrounded by earth and stone. I add this: that gold and silver do not seem to be clearly in that matter, nor are they present in actuality—as Arnaldus <note>Arnald of Villanova (c. 1240–1311), a famous physician and alchemical writer</note> also writes—but only in potential and power. And lest I delay anyone longer with these matters, I will say in one word what that matter is. Indeed, I will speak and bring into view what no one until now has noticed in unrolling the volumes of this discipline, nor has anyone committed to writing. For it is nothing other than **fusible salt**; even the name of the work itself proclaims this: **Alchemy** <term>Alchemy: the author suggests a false but symbolic etymology here, linking the word to the Greek 'als' (salt) and 'cheo' (to melt), thus 'the melting of salt'</term>, that is, the fusion of salt. And so that everyone may easily persuade themselves of this, it happens that every nature,

<margin>The qualities, names, and nature of the stones.</margin>

every name, and all qualities which they attribute to the "Stone," we can apply to salt itself. For first let us look at what they say: that the stone is animal, vegetable, and metallic. Furthermore, it is cheap, sold at a lowly price, found always and everywhere, born in the Mediterranean Sea, existing in any human being, and receding into and giving birth to anyone, easily melting and hardening, most friendly to the divine and human body. <margin>

The magnet is a living stone.
The effects of salt.

these things not apply to salt? Salt itself is both animal and living and metallic. Is not salt drawn from animals, and is there not in it a certain swift and wonderful power of penetrating, purging, and preserving from rot? But if it pleased Thales of Miletus <note>an ancient Greek philosopher, one of the Seven Sages</note> to say that the "Herculean stone"—that is, the magnet—was a living thing because it seemed to draw and compel iron: why then should we not also call salt "living," since it marvelously penetrates, purges, binds, dissipates, represses, and thins? And who would deny that it has a vegetable soul, since it alters, increases, and generates? Salt is altered; it grows into a "coal-stone" <note>original: "Anthracitem"</note>, putting forth certain little branches in the manner of a plant, and generates the philosophical mercury <note>original: "hydrargyron philoſophicam"</note>.

<margin>The wonderful power of salt.</margin>

What of the fact that it is believed to have a certain genuine power of procreation, by this very argument: that it awakens and sharpens seminal vigor? Indeed, there are those who believe that by its taste alone women become pregnant...

# METALLIC METAMORPHOSIS
### PAGE 45

<margin>The origin of Venus.</margin>
...and from there, they say that Venus, the principle of generation, was born from the salt-sea; Athenaeus also records this, and they therefore call her "salt-born" <note>original: ἁλογενῆ (halogene)</note>. 
<margin>Metallic salt.</margin>
Geber <note>An Arabic alchemist, likely referring here to the "Pseudo-Geber" whose Latin works were foundational to European alchemy</note> also shows that metals themselves can be converted into salt without difficulty, so that no one should think there is no such thing as a metallic salt. 
<margin>Salt from every natural compound.</margin>
Indeed, it is found in the mines themselves, in the Mediterranean Sea, and everywhere in every natural compound thing, and at all times: because it can be made from every natural compound at any time. Moreover, it is present in man himself by his very nature. Does it not pass into his very substance and sell at a most trivial price? Furthermore, what melts or hardens more quickly? 
<margin>Salt is divine to Homer.</margin>
Homer indeed calls salt "divine." And Plato wrote that salt was most dear and familiar to divine things. We also find it recorded as a proverb that "nothing is more useful to the human body than Salt and the Sun."

<margin>What imperfect metals lack.</margin>
But let us look a little deeper: what do those metals that are not perfect <note>In alchemy, "imperfect" metals like lead or iron were thought to be "diseased" versions of "perfect" metals like gold</note> lack most? You might say they lack purification and, especially, a "tincture" <note>A substance or "dye" capable of changing the color and nature of a metal</note>. I ask you, what penetrates more deeply or more swiftly to stain a thing with color, whether it be white or red? What purifies better, or what protects more against corruption and rot? 
<margin>What is Alchemy?</margin>
Add to this that those very authors, from heroic times until now, named this work "Alchemy" <term>Alchemy: The author here uses a folk etymology, suggesting the word comes from the Greek "als" (salt) and "cheo" (to pour/fuse), meaning "salt-fusion."</term> not without some great cause. Why then shall we not also say that all efforts of the students of this art should be directed toward obtaining a fusible salt from somewhere? For unless it were fusible, it would never rest in union with fused metals. 
<margin>The Stone from foul things.</margin>
Nor should the stench attributed to the "Stone" turn you away from this opinion. For salt carries with it the odor of the thing from which it grew; thus you may gather that it should be drawn from foul-smelling things, such as menstrual blood, urine, or human excrement.

<margin>The tempered nature of flesh.</margin>
To this we add that several authors have written that this Stone is found among vile excrement. There are even those who stubbornly assert that it is the dung of certain animals or the putrefied flesh of animals, and therefore call it "animal-like," as if it comes from animals. With these voices, Themistius <note>A 4th-century Greek philosopher and commentator</note> agrees, stating that the flesh of animals possesses a nature tempered in its qualities. From these things, the matter of the philosophers' stone and its origin becomes clear. It remains for us to teach how those things which are its origin are turned into salt, and how that salt is turned into the Stone—what kind of thing it is, and why it is so called. For it is not truly a stone, but only has a certain likeness to a stone. Once these things are untangled, that which we promised at the beginning regarding both the theory and practice of this art will be complete. 
<margin>The remote matter of the stone into salt by fire alone. The power of the art. Virgil's Aetna. The Power of Fire.</margin>
However, those things are turned into their own salt by fire alone; it is so effective that whether things are very soft or very hard, they can all be changed and transformed into another nature by this art. If anyone should marvel at this:

> *Let him ponder the truest sayings of the obscure book*
> *Of Heraclitus: that nothing is produced there that is insurmountable;*
> *Even the densest bodies, as he says, often [yield to the power of fire]* <note>original: This is a quote from the "Aetna," a poem once attributed to Virgil, discussing Heraclitus's belief that fire is the fundamental element.</note>

<margin>Manifold fire.</margin>
But since fire is manifold <note>original: "multiplex"</note> in this art, we must see which we should chiefly use. Indeed, a great controversy has arisen and remains among the experts of the art regarding this matter. For some use dung—and not even the three species described by Columella <note>Lucius Junius Moderatus Columella, a Roman writer on agriculture</note>, but specifically horse dung. Others use grape skins and seeds; others the heat of ashes; others of bran; others a lit wick; others charcoal, and especially that of juniper, because they say it burns for an entire year without failing. Others claim that the warm vapor of water, which they call a bath <note>original: "balneum"; likely referring to the *balneum Mariae* or water bath used for gentle heating</note>, is the fire peculiar to this work.

<margin>Fire for the Stone.</margin>
Count Bernard of Trevisan <note>A 15th-century alchemist famous for his search for the Philosophers' Stone</note> argues for a certain "ethereal" fire, enclosed and similar to human heat, a view supported by many. To me, however, it seems that from all these, the one to be chosen is that which the necessity of the work itself demands. For at times we shall use horse dung, and at other times a lit wick, warm threads, or glowing coals.

<margin>Three degrees of heat for the Stone.</margin>
Not without reason do they establish a threefold degree of heat: one mild, to be used at the beginning of the work; another a little stronger, used for calcination <note>original: "calcem"; the process of reducing a metal to a powder by heat</note> once the elements have coalesced into one; and the last, intolerable, by whose power we reach the desired end. For the entire power lies in the fire. By this, we discern and tear apart that raw and undigested mass into those four elements; further, we compose those same elements and force them into one. By this, we turn it into lime and perfect that which was begun.

<margin>The quality of fire at the start and the end of the work.</margin>
And unless the fire is gentle and mild at the beginning, it will bind and constrict the matter rather than dissolve it. Conversely, unless it grows strong when the matter requires being turned into lime, the labor of the craftsman will be frustrated. As the method of beginning was, so should be the manner of finishing. However, just as in all things one must see to what extent—and although each has its own measure—nevertheless, as Cicero says, "too much offends more than too little." So too in this business a certain governance must be applied, and the heat should be reduced rather than intensified.

<margin>A distant description of the Stone's matter.</margin>
For these things, which we said were made into one, are of the number of those things which Aristotle wrote move with contrary motion in some places. If anyone turns their mind to his words, they will undoubtedly distinguish those things from which that fusible and philosophical salt <note>A secret substance in alchemy that is neither purely metal nor purely salt, but the "key" to transmutation</note> ought to be chosen. For these things are of such a kind that, although they gush from the same source, one is poured out by fire while the other is compressed. For when the body liquefies and flows, the spirit congeals: and this is done at the same time. Who would not desire such a great thing...

# METALLIC METAMORPHOSIS
### PAGE 47

...has he achieved? Truly, I carry these things out not as almost everyone else does, for the learned and those skilled in these matters alone, but for my own "crowd"—that is, for the cruder and unskilled—since a teacher is indeed unnecessary for the learned.

<margin>The unyielding locks of this work.</margin>
But since there is no place in this art that does not require deeper investigation—as it is introduced by many in no other way than <term>enigmatically</term> <note>original Greek: "ainigmatikos," meaning in riddles or obscurely</note>—and it is one of those three unyielding "locks" of this work (which are: knowledge of the matter, the discovery of the vessel, and the method of fire), nothing is more manifest at this time. 

<margin>The vessel of the Stone. The various operations of the Stone.</margin>
I spoke of the Vessel. For an abundance of vessels is of no use for this matter: a single glass receptacle suffices and satisfies, shaped like a small flask or an oblong egg, so that the separated and distinct elements can be rotated in a circle, and by mutual collision, produce the Stone—conspicuous and incomparable in its powers of altering, increasing, and generating. For since this one vessel is abundantly capable of all the operations performed on the Stone—that is, sublimations, solutions, distillations, coagulations, wax-softening <note>original: "cereficationum"; the process of softening a substance to a wax-like consistency</note>, and as they say, calcinations and fixations—why would we need many?

<margin>The colors of the Stone’s matter.</margin>
In this beginning, when it is dissolved, a black matter is seen; later, a multicolored one; then white and bright; and finally red. But indeed, the vessel must be most tightly sealed, lest the enclosed and internal air or spirit fly away, lured out by the external and free air—a misfortune that could scarcely be repaired. 

<margin>The method of sealing the vessel.</margin>
The method of sealing is familiar to the glassmakers themselves. Next follows what it contributes to, once the Stone has grown from the proper matter, in a suitable vessel, and with a fitting fire, and has been led to its perfection. 

<margin>The fruits of the Stone.</margin>
And it contributes greatly to mercury <note>original: "hydrargyro"</note> for the preparation of wealth, and to potions and pills <note>original: "catapotijs"</note> for health. According to the school of Lully <note>Ramon Llull, a 13th-century philosopher and purported alchemist</note> and others, this is the most difficult and laborious thing to accomplish. One use belongs to Medicine, the other to this art, and to what they call our "medley" <note>original: "farraginis"</note>. It is mixed with purified mercury first in such a portion that the quantity of mercury is ten times greater, then a hundredfold, then a thousandfold, then ten-thousandfold, and finally infinitely. This indeed is the immense multiplication of the Stone for fermenting, namely gold and silver: ending in the latter case in a white and bright lime, and in the former in a red one. 

<margin>What the Stone is and why it is so called.</margin>
Whence it happens that it is also called a "Stone." For a lime <note>original: "calx"; referring to the powdered residue left after intense heating</note> is nothing other than a cooked stone. It is a powder so subtle that it cannot bear even the slightest breeze. It is marvelous how penetrable it is. But experience itself will teach you these things better. 

<margin>The time for completing the Stone.</margin>
I shall conclude, then, if I add one word: the time in which the Stone is brought to completion, whether in whiteness and brightness or in redness, is not fixed. This is the work of both the craftsman and of nature. No one fails to see how slow and how little-ripened nature's progress is. Sometimes it is completed in nine, twelve, or eighteen months, but very rarely; sometimes, as is customary, it lingers for more or less three years.

<header>ON THE LAW</header>

## Concerning the
# LEGALITY OF THE ART OF ALCHEMY,

->That is,<-
->The judgments and responses of various authors, and especially of<-
->legal experts, regarding the everyday question:<-

->***Whether Alchemy is a legitimate art.***<-

->From the Sibyl.<-

> I have nine letters, I am four syllables, consider me well.
> The first three: each has two letters, 
> The rest have the remaining letters. And five of them are voiceless,
> And of the total number, there are twice eight hundreds,
> And three times three tens with seven; do you know who I am?
> You shall not be uninitiated in the wisdom I possess.
<note>This is a Greek Sibylline riddle often cited by Renaissance alchemists. The solution is the word "Arsenic" (Arsenikon), which they believed proved the ancient, prophetic origins of their work.</note>

->*Interpretation from Cardano’s book On the Variety of Things.*<-
->BOOK X. CHAPTER 52.<-

<image-desc>An ornamental initial letter 'C' decorated with foliate scrolls and floral patterns within a square frame.</image-desc>

**W**hen I had fallen into these discussions, the illustrious Aimery de Ranconnet <note>Aimery de Ranconnet (d. 1559) was a famous French jurist and scholar</note>, the presiding official of Paris, demonstrated that this art was approved by a Sibylline poem. He did so with such precision that, although the responses of such oracles are usually ambiguous, the words of the riddle in this case seemed clearer than the light of the sun. Therefore, I shall subjoin those things which that learned man expressed with wondrous skill, just as I received them from him while I was in Paris. The words are: "I have nine letters," etc., as above. 

He says, therefore, that it is a name consisting of nine letters, containing four syllables. The first three syllables contain only two letters each, while the rest (the fourth syllable) contains the remaining letters, namely three. In this name, <term>Arsenic</term> <note>original Greek: "arsenikon" (ἀρσενικόν)</note>, all things seem to agree beautifully: for it consists of four syllables *Ar-se-ni-kon* (ἀρ-σε-νι-κόν). The first three syllables each contain two letters; the fourth and last contains three. Thus, there are nine elements <note>meaning letters</note> in total. These points are entirely clear through experience, as they are manifest in the Greek. 

He then adds that five of these are "voiceless" <note>consonants</note>, so that we may understand there are only four vowels: α, ε, ι, ο. The remaining five he called voiceless, that is, non-vowels, which are ρ, σ, ν, κ, ν. Then he adds that the number signified by these voiceless letters is "twice eight hundreds and three times three tens," that is, it is contained in two hundred and eight and three times three decades. This is nine and eight times ten, which is one hundred and seventy, so that the total number is 370. This number is signified by the five voiceless letters... 
<note>This passage refers to gematria, where letters have numerical values. The math in this specific edition's Latin commentary for the sum of "Arsenikon" is notoriously complex and often differs between manuscripts.</note>

<page-num>49</page-num>
<header>ON ALCHEMY.</header>

...if you only take the repeated letter—that is, *nu* [ν]—once. For when ε, ο, ν, and κ are taken, they make up the same amount; among the Greeks, ρ signifies 100, σ signifies 200, χ signifies 50 <note>In standard Greek numerals, χ represents 600. Cardano is likely following a specific variant or corrupted manuscript tradition to make the riddle's math work</note>, and κ signifies 20. Collected together, they make 370. Then he adds "with seven," which is τ, signifying 300, and "seven," namely decades, for it refers back to what came before. The proper reasoning of the phrasing seems to resist this in three ways: "twice hundreds," "seven decades," and "with" used for "plus." However, he discards the second *nu*, although the Sibyl does not say to do so, and reads τ instead of χ or ψ. For the manuscript has *syn chepte*, which means "with seven added." He said this might easily be true, as there is little difference in form between χ and τ. Finally, he concludes that whoever knows this will not be lacking in his own wisdom. In this, it might seem strange that the prophet wanders so far from the point. But these and far greater things are the privileges of prophets, and especially of those who are divinely inspired or frenzied. Added to this is the fact that the matter itself agrees with the words and the explanation of the name, as we have taught elsewhere; for through arsenic, copper passes into the likeness of silver, and gold is contained within orpiment <note>original: auripimento. Orpiment is a yellow arsenic sulfide mineral once used as a pigment and in alchemical attempts to create gold</note>. Even if it is not this, the Sibyl might indicate something else very useful. Whatever the case, the interpretation or discovery is entirely admirable—at least so much so that it would not be unworthy of the books *On Subtlety* <note>A reference to Cardano’s famous work *De subtilitate rerum*, which explored the secrets of the natural world</note> if they were not already finished. Thus, in arsenic, there is a foundation of some present utility and a beginning of the work, just as in vitriol <note>original: calchantho. Vitriol was a term for various sulfate minerals used to change the surface color of metals</note> there is the beginning of the transformation of iron into copper, for the color is changed immediately.

->*From Thomas Aquinas in Aristotle’s Meteorology, Book 3, at the end.*<-

The immediate material of metals is sulfur and <term>quicksilver</term> <note>original: argentum vivum; the liquid metal mercury</note>, as the Alchemists say: so that in the rocky places of the earth, sulfur and quicksilver are generated through a mineral power; then, from these, different metals are generated according to their different mixtures. Hence, even the Alchemists themselves—through the true art of Alchemy, which is nevertheless difficult because of the hidden operations of the celestial power (which is called "mineral power")—sometimes achieve the true generation of metals, since those hidden operations, because they are hidden, can be imitated by us through the aforementioned principles, or through things begun by them.

->*From the same author in the Summa Theologica, Part 2-2, Question 77, Article 2.*<-

If, however, gold were to be made through Alchemy, it would not be unlawful to sell it as gold, because nothing prohibits art from using certain natural causes to produce true and natural effects; as Augustine says in Book 3 of *On the Trinity*, Chapter 8, concerning those things which are done by the art of demons.

->*From the same author in the Summa Theologica, Part 2-2, Question 96, Article 2.*<-

If natural things are simply applied to produce certain effects for which they are thought to possess a natural power, it is not superstitious or unlawful to use those things or effects.

->*From Suidas, on the word Alchemy.*<-

Alchemy <note>original: χημεία (khēmeia)</note> is the preparation of gold and silver. Diocletian burned the books...

<meta>catchword: LAW-</meta>

...the gathered books he burned, because the Egyptians had plotted a revolution against him, and he treated them harshly and as enemies. At the same time, he sought out and burned the books written by the ancients about the <term>alchemy</term> <note>original: "Chemia"</note> of gold and silver, lest the Egyptians should thereafter acquire riches by that art, or, relying on an abundance of money, rebel against the Romans again. <note>This refers to the Roman Emperor Diocletian, who allegedly ordered the destruction of alchemical texts in 297 AD to suppress Egyptian uprisings.</note>

### From the same author, under the entry for *Digas*.

The Golden Fleece, which Jason took from Colchis while crossing the Pontic Sea with the Argonauts, along with Medea, daughter of King Aeëtes. This, however, was not a fleece as the poets say, but was a book written on skins <note>original: "pellibus". The word for "skin" or "hide" (pellis) is here used to suggest a parchment manuscript.</note>, containing instructions on how gold might be made through alchemy. It is probable, therefore, that people at that time called it the "Golden Fleece" because of the profit and benefit that could be obtained from that book.

### From Pliny, Book 34, Chapter 4.

There is also one method of making gold from <term>orpiment</term> <note>original: "auripigmento," a yellow arsenic sulfide mineral</note>. The hope of this had attracted the Emperor Gaius <note>Caligula</note>, who was most greedy for gold. Therefore, he ordered a great weight of it to be smelted, and he clearly produced excellent gold; but it was of such a small weight that he felt a loss, having experienced this because of his greed. Even though fourteen pounds of orpiment were traded for it, no one has attempted it since.

### From Cardano, *On Subtlety*, Book 6.

However, it has seemed to many that metals can be transformed, based on the experiment with bronze already mentioned above. They even seem to change color and weight due to fire, and therefore it is likely that their substance can also be changed. It was even believed that some had done this, as happened before the most illustrious Prince of the Venetians <note>The Doge of Venice</note> a few years ago, with the wise men of the city assisting a certain pharmacist from Treviso <note>original: "pharmacopola Tarvisino"</note>; traces of this event still remain. Since certain species of plants are transformed into one another in turn, it should not seem strange that metals can be transformed. 

But the matter is not quite so, for either none or not all can be transformed into one another. For iron and bronze—since both exist with similar weight and thinness, and neither of them resists fire—if they change color and hardness, they can be converted from one into the other, either truly or at least without any obvious difference. None of the remaining metals can be changed into gold and silver; the only doubt is whether silver can be changed into gold. I think this can happen: for in order for silver to become gold, it lacks density (by which it must become heavier) and color. But these can be added to the metal; if the silver is rendered denser, its "oiliness" <note>original: "pinguedo," an alchemical term for the combustible or volatile principle within a metal</note> will be removed, it will resist fire better, and, as I said, it will gain weight.

### And a little later.

This is what that pharmacist from Treviso seems to have achieved, who in the presence of the Prince and the wise men of the Venetian Republic, changed <term>quicksilver</term> <note>original: "argentum vivum," or mercury</note> into gold.

# ALCHEMY.

## LEGAL OPINIONS OF JURISTS AND THE HIGHEST
### Doctors of Both Laws <note>original: "V. I. D." (Vtriusque Iuris Doctor), referring to one who has mastered both Civil and Canon law.</note> regarding the question:

->Is Alchemy a lawful art?<-

#### From Oldradus, legal opinion 74, on sorcery, number 1.

The question is whether an **Alchemist** commits a sin, or if the art is prohibited. And it would seem that it is so, and that the art of Alchemy is prohibited, because the text <note>Gratian’s Decretum, 26. q. 1. c. episc.</note> says that anyone who believes any creature can be made, or changed for the better, or transformed into another species or another likeness except by the Creator Himself, is an infidel and worse than a pagan. Furthermore, these Alchemists are "forever learning, yet never arriving at the truth of knowledge" <note>A reference to 2 Timothy 3:7</note>; and no wonder. Thus they provide the occasion for many deceptions. Nor is it a science that leads to piety, as is usually said of astrology. Indeed, it could not be done without the smelting of gold, which seems to be prohibited by law <note>Codex Justinianus, De auri publici persecutoribus, Book 10.</note>.

**On the contrary**, it seems that those who produce gold or silver from tin, lead, or another base metal—provided they do not do this through the magic arts or anything else hateful to the laws—are not to be blamed, but rather praised, as the law says <note>Codex Justinianus, De thesauris, Book 10.</note>.

These men are **miners** <note>original: "metallarij"</note>, who by their own labor provide benefits for themselves and the State <note>Codex Justinianus, De metallariis, Book 11.</note>, and the laws favor them because of the public utility that seems to result from their office. For they may enter another person's land against the owner's will to search for metal. Note there that this would not otherwise be permitted. Nor do they say that one <term>species</term> <note>In medieval philosophy, a "species" was the essential nature of a thing; many argued one metal could not become another because their "essence" was fixed.</note> is changed into another (as is charged against them), because that is not possible. Rather, they say that from one species of metal (namely, tin), another species of metal (namely, gold) can be produced. Nor is this inconsistent with reason; for we see that sometimes a living thing is produced from a dead thing, as we see in the worms from which **silk** is produced, and in many other cases. And **glass** is produced from a plant <note>referring to the use of plant ash in glassmaking</note>; how much more so from metals, in which there is a greater agreement and likeness. For (as they themselves teach, and as is held in the book *On the Properties of Things* in the chapter on Alchemy) all metals proceed from the same principle: namely, from **sulfur** and **quicksilver** <note>original: "sulphure & argento vivo" (mercury)</note>. But by the power of the elements, some have a greater influence in one place than in another: in one mine tin is made, in another silver, in another gold, and so with the others.

Since, therefore, "art imitates nature" <note>A fundamental Aristotelian maxim: "Ars imitatur Naturam"</note>, these Alchemists do not seem to sin if, through this power which exists in herbs, stones, or the elements, they wish to make silver from tin. For since they are as if from the same principle and are similar, the transition is easier for those things that share a common essence <note>original: "habentibus symbolum," a term from logic/physics regarding shared qualities.</note>. For there are many powers implanted in

### From Panormitanus <note>Niccolò de' Tudeschi (1386–1445), a hugely influential jurist in Canon Law</note> on the chapter *Ex tuarum* regarding sorcery, in the Decretals.

But following the aforementioned, a question can be asked, which Oldradus <note>Oldradus de Ponte, a 14th-century lawyer famous for his legal "consilia" or opinions</note> poses and treats in his 69th legal opinion: whether **Alchemy** is prohibited and whether those practicing it sin. And it would seem so. Because one species is changed or transmuted into another, as when lead is made into silver, or brass into gold, etc. But besides God, no one can transmute one species into another <note>26. q. 5. in the section beginning "quisquis ergo"</note>.

Oldradus, however, concludes the opposite: that indeed one species is not changed into another diverse one, since all metals proceed from the same source, namely from **sulfur** and **quicksilver** <note>original: "sulphure & argento vivo"; "living silver" or mercury, considered the "parents" of all metals in medieval alchemy</note>. But where there is a better influence of the stars, there a more precious metal is produced. Therefore, through the influence of the stars, and with herbs and stones (in which many virtues reside), one species of metal can naturally be converted into another more precious species: which is worth noting.

### From Joannes Andreae <note>A 14th-century professor known as the "fountain and trumpet of the law"</note> in the additions to the *Speculator* <note>Refers to the 'Speculum Iudiciale', a standard legal encyclopedia by William Duranti</note> under the title "Regarding the crime of forgery."

On the contrary, he who out of the mastery of the art—without magic or other things prohibited by law—makes a precious thing out of base metal, is to be commended: because in this he increases the **public wealth** <note>original: "rempub." Nor do they change one species into another different one, but they make one species of metal better, such as silver or gold from tin or brass.

And it is no wonder, since we see silk produced from worms, or glass from an herb, as is held in the *Book on the Properties of Things* <note>original: "lib. de prop. rerum"; the encyclopedia by Bartholomeus Anglicus</note> in the section on the Alchemist: because all metals proceed from **sulfur** and **quicksilver**. ### *From Andreas de Isernia, on the Title of Fiefs: Which things are royal rights.*

What of Alchemy and Alchemists? Say that if they make "sophisticated" <note>original: "sophisticatum"; meaning imitation, adulterated, or chemically "tricked" rather than naturally grown</note> gold, they ought not sell it as pure, because that is a falsehood. Nor is one freed from the charge by paying for the imitation <note>Citing the Digest</note>; for what is "chosen" is not gold. However, if he were to make **true gold**, even though he may not mint the prince's money from it without the prince's command, this gold would belong to the maker. Nothing prohibits an art from using certain natural causes to produce true and natural effects, just as Blessed Augustine says in *On the Trinity* regarding those things which are done by the art of demons. Thus says Thomas Aquinas <note>1225–1274; the "Angelic Doctor" of the Church</note> in the *Secunda Secundæ*, question 79, regarding those things involving voluntary exchange. Likewise, "coinage": that is, the authority to make public money. But here it is asked incidentally, whether an Alchemist, or one practicing Alchemy, should be punished for forgery. You should say no, because it is an art discovered by a perspicacious wit, where as much is spent for as much, and such for such an end.

# ON ALCHEMY

...producing silk, and just as glass is produced from plants, it is even more possible in metals, in which there is a greater natural affinity. For they <note>Referring to the alchemists or natural philosophers</note> say and note in the book *On the Property of Things* <note>Likely referring to the medieval encyclopedia by Bartholomaeus Anglicus</note> regarding Alchemy, that all metals proceed from the same source—namely, from **sulfur and quicksilver** <term>mercury</term>—but by the power of the elements, they have a greater influence in one place than in another. Thus, in one mine tin is formed, in another silver, and in another gold, and so on for the others. Therefore, since art imitates nature <note>A fundamental legal and philosophical principle: *ars imitatur naturam*</note> (as noted in the Digest concerning adoptions, law *Adoptio*), alchemists do not seem to sin if, through the power of herbs, stones, or the elements, they make silver from tin. For since these metals share essentially the same origin and are similar, the transition is easier between things that have a "symbol" <note>original: "symbolum," here meaning shared qualities or a common essence</note> (as in the Institutes, concerning the ways obligations are removed, paragraph 7). Indeed, many virtues are implanted in herbs and stones (16. q. ult. c. fin.). For, as Augustine says, there are certain "hidden seminal reasons" <term>seeds of potentiality</term> within corporeal things throughout all the elements. When the right timing and causes are provided, these burst forth into the species appropriate to their own modes and limits (and in Question 26, q. 3, near the end). Therefore, if they attribute this power to God, they do not seem to sin. Nor is it a great penalty if you have pawned brass for gold, even knowingly (as in the Digest on pawn actions, law 1, and on the crime of fraud, law 2).

->*The same is said by Alberico <note>Alberico de Rosate (c. 1290–1360), a celebrated Italian jurist</note> in his Dictionary, under the entry "Sale."*<-

Whether a sale is rendered illicit and invalid due to a defect in the item sold or because of its hidden quality. Thomas <note>St. Thomas Aquinas</note> says in the *Secunda Secundae*, question 77, article 2, that a triple defect can be considered regarding a thing being sold. One is according to the **species** of the thing: for example, if brass <term>aurichalcum</term> is sold as silver, or wine mixed with water is sold as pure. Another defect is according to **quantity**, weight, or measure: as when someone knowingly uses a deficient weight or an unjust measure. The third defect is on the part of **quality**: for example, if a sick animal is sold as if it were healthy. In these three cases, if the seller offends knowingly, he commits a fraud, the sale is illicit, and he is bound to make restitution. If, however, he does so out of ignorance, he does not sin; yet, when the matter comes to his attention, he is bound to compensate the buyer for the loss. 

From this, it is clear that it is illicit to sell alchemical gold or silver as "true" metal, because it is not pure in the way true gold is, nor does it possess all the same properties—such as the power of gladdening the heart <note>It was a common medieval belief that true gold had medicinal and spiritual properties, including the ability to lift the spirits</note>—nor is it effective against certain infirmities like true gold. If, however, true gold were to be made through Alchemy, it would not be illicit to sell it as true gold, because nothing prohibits art from using certain natural causes to produce true and natural effects, as Augustine says in his book *On the Trinity* concerning those things which are done by the art of demons.

## ON LAW

...three things are principally considered: namely, the matter, the form, and the estimation or value <note>Original: "materia, forma, & æstimatio seu valor." These are the three legal components of valid currency.</note>, according to Law 1 combined with the final Law, with the notes recorded there in the Code, Title on the Value of Money, Book 11 <note>referencing the *Corpus Iuris Civilis*</note>. And note the commentary by **Baldus** <note>Baldus de Ubaldis (1327–1400), a famous professor of law</note> in the chapter *Quanto*, on Oaths. For first, the material must be sound <note>original: "proba," meaning tested or pure</note> according to said Law 1 and Law 1, paragraph 1 of the Digest, on the Contract of Sale, and the said chapter *Quanto*. 

Hence, it would not be permitted to strike coins from Alchemy, which is to be understood as **sophistical** <term>imitation or fake</term> alchemy, not concerning that which is found to be true gold or silver. That such true metal can exist is noted by **Johannes Andreae** <note>A leading 14th-century canon lawyer</note> in his additions to the *Speculum* in the Section on the crime of forgery. He reports—without naming the author—the words of **Oldradus** <note>Oldradus de Ponte, a high-ranking legal consultant at the Papal court in Avignon</note>, whose legal opinion is number 74, beginning "Whether an Alchemist..." And more extensively by Johannes Andreae in chapter 2, on Sorcery. Also by Baldus and Andreas de Isernia in chapter 1, in the title "What are the Regalian Rights," regarding Feudal Customs. And by **Saint Thomas** <note>Thomas Aquinas</note> in the *Second Part of the Second Part*, Question 92. From these sources, they conclude that **Alchemy is a true science and is permitted**. 

Something regarding this is also mentioned by Alberico de Rosate in his Dictionary under the word "Alchemy." And Johannes Andreae says, as above, that in his time there was a master **Arnaldus of Villanova** <note>A famous physician, alchemist, and religious reformer (c. 1240–1311)</note>, a supreme Physician and Theologian, and a great Alchemist. Through that art, he made golden rods, which he allowed to be submitted to every test. And he wrote one book on that science which impoverished a thousand men—either because it was not true, or because it is not understood. 

And while I had a certain colleague in law who was sweating much over that art <note>i.e., working very hard at alchemy</note>, I wished to see one marvelous experiment for the purpose of knowing more. For we had with us an old alchemist, though he was very poor. And in my presence, that colleague of mine caused one ounce of most precious silver to be reduced into the likeness of gold—in weight, in melting, and in its ability to be hammered—except for the color. For it was not saffron-yellow, but changed to the likeness of a leaden color. And that colleague of mine had a way of giving it a saffron color. That material suffered and withstood some tests, but not the **ultimate experiment** <note>Likely the test of "cupellation" or strong acids that would reveal base metals</note>. When mixed with an equal amount of precious gold, it seemed to be gold of twenty **carats** <term>characterum</term>, more or less, depending on how well that material was prepared. 

A certain great Prelate and many old alchemists were amazed by that experiment. And one old alchemist, thinking himself rich, thought he could reduce that material to the true species of gold; but he could not. He then thought the art itself was illusory, especially since so many men in forty or fifty years had not seen such a notable experiment—which nevertheless was **sophistical** <note>Original: "sophisticum," meaning a clever imitation that lacks the true essence</note>. Consequently, I did not wish to see any other experiment. Nor would it be permitted, without consulting the Prince, to mix copper material into gold or silver for minting, according to the law "Whosoever coins," in the Digest, on Forgery; and it is noted in Law 2 of the Code, "Those who forge money."

# ON ALCHEMY

...because it is an art discovered by human ingenuity, just as by a Philosopher. Thus say **Andreas de Isernia** <note>Andreas de Isernia (c. 1270–1353) was a famous jurist from Naples known for his work on feudal law.</note> and **Baldus** in the first chapter of "What are the Regalian Rights," and Baldus reports that **Oldradus** <note>Oldradus de Ponte (d. 1335), a highly influential legal consultant at the Papal court.</note> gave this counsel in his legal opinions.

<margin>**Johannes de Platea** on Law 1, in the Code of the Emperor <note>original: "ca ad R.C." refers to the *Codex Justinianus*, Title "To the Count of the Sacred Largesses."</note>, on the price of silver, regarding treasures, Book 10.</margin>

I ask incidentally: as discussed above regarding the seekers and smelters of natural gold, what of the seekers of **artificial gold**? May alchemists lawfully pursue such gold and be paid, or do they commit **forgery**? **Johannes Andreae** <note>A leading 14th-century expert in Canon Law.</note> in his additions to the *Speculum* under the title "On Forgery" praises those alchemists who, through the mastery of their craft—without magic or other prohibited laws (as per the single Law in the Code on Treasures)—turn base metal into precious metal. They do not change one species into another entirely different one, but rather improve a single species of metal, such as making silver or gold out of tin or bronze. For all metals originate from **sulfur and quicksilver** <term>mercury</term>, but by the power of the Elements, tin is formed in one place, gold in another, and silver in yet another, and so on for each. Therefore, since art imitates nature (as in the Law on Adoption in the Digest), alchemists do not sin if, through the power of herbs, stones, or other elements, they refine a base metal into a more precious one, since both share the same species and origin. Indeed, hidden **"seminal reasons"** <note>original: "seminariæ rationes." This is a philosophical concept suggesting that matter contains latent "seeds" or blueprints that can be brought to fruition under the right conditions.</note> exist within physical things throughout all the elements; when the opportunity of time and cause is given, these burst forth into their proper species in their own ways and limits. This is stated in Law 26, question 5, "nor is it a wonder." Regarding such an alchemist, see Andreas de Isernia and Baldus in the title "What are the Regalian Rights," column 10. Yet, because such work is subject to many deceptions (as noted in "nor is it a wonder") and is not a "science of piety" <note>Original: "scientia pietatis," meaning it does not contribute to religious or moral growth.</note>, I advise abstaining from its practice. Nevertheless, **Master Arnaldus de Villanova** <note>A famous 13th-century physician, diplomat, and alchemist.</note>, a supreme physician and theologian as well as a great alchemist, used to make gold rods in the Roman court which he allowed to be submitted to every test. Indeed, if this work is performed to be turned toward a **pious cause**, it is accomplished by the permission of Almighty God, as per the aforementioned Law and the Decree.

->*There follows a contrary argument by Angelus in his Summa, under the entry "Alchemy."*<-

Is it lawful to practice alchemy? I answer: **Oldradus** holds in his legal opinions that it is, provided they do not act through magic or other means hateful to the law (as stated in the single Law in the Code on Treasures). This is because they are like **metalworkers** who, by their own labor, provide for both themselves and the advantage of the State. The laws favor them because of the public utility that seems to result from their office. For they may even enter a field to search for metal against the owner’s will (as noted in the Code on Metals), which is otherwise not permitted.

# ON THE LAW

...in the single Law of the same [title] and in the Digest, "On acquiring the ownership of things," Law 3. The reason is that (as stated in the book *On the Properties of Things* <note>original: "de proprietate rerum," an influential 13th-century encyclopedia by Bartholomeus Anglicus</note> under the entry "On Alchemy"), all metals proceed from the same principle: namely, from sulfur and quicksilver <term>mercury</term>. However, due to the power of the elements which have a greater influence in one place than in another, tin is formed in one mine and silver in another. Therefore, since art imitates nature (Digest, "On Adoptions," Law: *adoptio*), it is not a sin if, through the power inherent in elements or herbs, alchemists wish to make silver out of tin. For since they share the same principle, the transition is easier among those things having a shared symbol <note>original: "symbolum," referring to the shared elemental qualities—hot, cold, moist, dry—that allowed for Aristotelian transmutation</note> (Institutes, "In what ways obligations are removed," section 1). Since many virtues are implanted in herbs and stones (Decree, Part 2, Cause 26, Question 5, "not a wonder," near the middle).

But notwithstanding these arguments, I believe that the practice is illicit for many reasons. First, because no one is found who truly possesses such an art, even though it is claimed by many. But this is proven false by experience, for we see that those practicing it commonly consume much [wealth], and one must rely on what commonly occurs. Hence it is said of them in 2 Timothy 3: *always learning, and never reaching the knowledge of the truth.* They perform many experiments and never reach perfection; they consume both time and life. Nor does that which they produce have the true essence of gold or silver, but only the appearance. 

Therefore, alchemists are simply to be condemned. This is evidently proven because no one wishes to practice it in public, making it clear that they act wrongly, because *they hate the light.* And if they ever do produce something true, it is either done at a loss when expenses are calculated, or it stems from some deception by inserting real gold, or by some diabolical fallacy. To keep them attentive to such things, the devil sometimes produces real gold for them by secretly placing true gold there. Since, therefore, such an exercise is against the public utility—as is evident from the waste of resources—and because they (commonly) make counterfeit money from these things, those practicing it are simply to be condemned.

# OF ALCHEMY

...by which silk <note>original: "fericum," likely a variant of "sericum" (silk). In alchemical texts, "silk" sometimes refers to the refined texture of a substance or a specific byproduct.</note> is produced. For all metals proceed from the same principle, namely from sulfur and quicksilver <term>mercury</term>. However, by the power of the elements, they have a greater influence in one place than in another: thus, in one mine tin is formed, in another silver, and in another gold. Therefore, the art is licit, provided it is not performed through magic or any other means hateful to the law (Code of Justinian, "On Treasures," Book 10, Law 1). Indeed, those who practice it are to be praised.

Add, however, the *Summa Angelica* <note>A famous 15th-century handbook for confessors by Angelus Carletus de Clavasio.</note> under the entry "Alchemy," which holds that this art is illicit for many reasons. First, because no one is found who truly possesses the authentic art, despite what is said of many; experience proves this false. Second, because we see that those practicing it commonly consume much [wealth], and one must judge based on what commonly happens. Hence, it is said of them in 2 Timothy, chapter 3 (and in the Decree, Cause 26, Question 5, "not a wonder"): *always learning and never arriving at the knowledge of the truth.* They perform many experiments and never reach perfection; they consume both their time and their lives. Nor does that which they produce possess the true nature of gold or silver, but only the appearance. 

Therefore, Alchemists are simply to be condemned. This is evidently proven because no one wishes to practice it in public, which suggests they are acting wrongly; for they "hate the light." And if they occasionally produce something "true," it is either done at a loss once expenses are calculated, or through some deception—such as secretly introducing real gold—or by some diabolical fallacy. To keep them occupied with such things, [the devil] sometimes produces real gold for them by secretly adding it. Since, therefore, this exercise is contrary to the public good (as is clear from the waste of resources) and because they commonly use these materials to make counterfeit money, those practicing it are simply to be condemned.

However, I hold the common opinion: that this art is licit. The arguments in the *Summa Angelica* do not prove the art itself is illicit just because no one [currently] possesses the true art; this is not due to a defect in the art itself, nor do the other reasons hold up, as is self-evident. Both Thomas <note>Thomas Aquinas</note> and Albert <note>Albertus Magnus</note> hold the same view. As to whether profit from alchemy is licit, or if the sale is rendered unjust, Thomas says (as cited above) that if true gold is made through alchemy, it is not illicit to sell it as true. This is because nothing prohibits using art and certain natural ingredients to produce natural effects. However, if it does not have the true "species" <note>the essential nature or internal structure</note> of gold, it is an unjust sale, as it is then sophisticated <term>adulterated or fake</term> gold.

# ON LAW
## Page 60

...have approved it. Only one man contradicts them, Angelus, in his *Summa Angelica* <note>A widely used 15th-century encyclopedia of moral theology and canon law by Angelus de Clavasio</note>. But besides the fact that the authority of a single Doctor against the common opinion is null, as everyone knows, there was certainly one great canonist, Hieronymus de Zavetis, who in chapter 1 of the section *on accusations* <note>original: "de accusat."</note> responded most precisely to each and every one of Angelus's arguments. This is a strong foundation <note>original: "fundamentum adamantinum," literally an "adamantine foundation"</note> built on the authority of great and famous Doctors and Jurists—to say nothing of the authority of Thomas Aquinas, who in two or three places most clearly approved of Alchemy. Pliny also writes in book 34, chapter 4, that in the times of the Emperor Gaius <note>Caligula</note> there were alchemists. Nor is it relevant what he says—that their craft was not profitable. Firstly, because in the question of whether Alchemy is a lawful art, we do not ask whether it is lucrative or fruitful, but only whether it is prohibited by divine or human Law. Secondly, because it is possible that those craftsmen of whom he speaks were not sufficiently skilled, while others might be more expert; as we commonly say, there is a wide difference among craftsmen (referencing the law *inter artif. ff. de solut.* <note>A reference to the Digest of Roman Law regarding the varying quality of services</note>). Furthermore, the things that Suidas <note>A 10th-century Greek encyclopedia-lexicon</note> relates concerning Alchemy and the artificial making of gold are marvelous: that the Egyptians were able to sustain a long war against the tyrant Diocletian by relying on their art—that is, their craftsmanship.

But let us look at some other arguments. For Aristotle writes in the *Metaphysics* <note>original: "Metaphyl."</note> books 2 and 4, that art imitates nature in certain things, and that many natural things can be produced and perfected by art. He names <term>colcothar</term> <note>iron oxide or vitriol residue</note> and <term>chalcanthum</term> <note>green vitriol or copper sulfate</note> as examples, saying that those two "inks" <note>original: "atramenta," used here for mineral salts used in pigments/dyes</note> are not only born in minerals but can also be produced by art. Let a third example be set forth concerning salt. For (as Pliny says in book 31) salt is either made or it grows. In Poland there is mineral salt, while in France there is manufactured salt, and the latter has the same properties, nature, and efficacy as the former. A fourth example is <term>electrum</term> <note>an alloy of gold and silver</note>, which Pliny in book 33, chapter 4, and many others write is not only natural but also manufactured. Regarding this manufactured and artificial kind, legal texts speak in the Digest <note>original: "ff. de legat."</note> and the Institutes <note>original: "Instit. de rer. divis."</note>. A fifth example is quicksilver <note>mercury</note>, which the aforementioned Pliny in book 33, chapter 1, says is in one case native and in the other manufactured; and he calls the latter <term>hydrargyrum</term> <note>original: "Hydrargyrum," from the Greek for liquid silver</note> to distinguish it from the other. Guillaume Philandrier, in his commentaries on Vitruvius <note>A famous Roman architect</note>, counts four kinds of it: two native and two artificial. In the same place, he shows that steel, <term>sandarac</term> <note>red arsenic sulfide</note>, verdigris, <term>chalcanthum</term>, and cinnabar are in some cases produced naturally and in others manufactured by the art of men. Since these things are so, we can conclude without absurdity: just as art can imitate nature in so many other things, it is not unreasonable to say that it can imitate nature in the operation of gold and silver. Certainly Cardano <note>Girolamo Cardano, a 16th-century Italian polymath</note> writes in book 16 of *On Subtlety*, and many say this is known to them, that copper can be made from iron by applying <term>chalcanthum</term>; and Cardano in the same...

# OF ALCHEMY.
## Page 61

...the same book <note>Referring to a previously mentioned source, likely a history or legal treatise</note> testifies that a certain apothecary from Treviso, in the presence of the most illustrious Prince of the Venetians and the wise senators, converted quicksilver <note>original: "argentum vivum," literally "living silver"; mercury</note> into gold. It is true that Julius Scaliger <note>A famous 16th-century Italian scholar and physician</note> denies that he believes this, but he relies on a weak argument: namely, that if the Venetians had seen this, because they are possessed of such greed (as he himself writes) that they would even make a treaty with the Turk, the enemy of the Christian name, they would never have let that apothecary go. Instead, they would have compelled him by tortures to reveal his art, and perhaps would have hung him on the gallows <note>original: "gabalo"</note>. But it is likely that the apothecary protected and provided for himself through a public pledge of safe conduct, or perhaps by a hostage or some other security. Certainly, it is not honorable to suspect the worst of everyone in all matters.

What is certain is that there were in previous centuries, and are now, countless grave men who practiced that art and declared it to have been profitable for them. Among these were Albertus Magnus <note>A 13th-century German Dominican friar and polymath</note>, the Count of Treviso <note>Bernard Trevisan, a famous 15th-century alchemist</note>, Augurellus <note>Giovanni Aurelio Augurello, author of the alchemical poem *Chrysopoeia*</note>, Avicenna <note>A Persian polymath and one of the most significant physicians of the Islamic Golden Age</note>, Geber <note>Jabir ibn Hayyan, the "Father of Chemistry"</note>, Lullius <note>Ramon Llull, a Majorcan philosopher and mystic</note>, Bonus of Ferrara, Morienus, and Tolad, and especially Arnaldus de Villanova, a most eminent physician. We see also in our own times that Jean Fernel <note>Physician to King Henry II of France</note>, who is considered a prince in the medical art, in his book *On the Hidden Causes of Things* <note>original: "de abdit. rer. caus."</note>, held this same art in the highest regard <note>original: "ad unguem tenuisse," literally "held to the fingernail," meaning he mastered it perfectly</note> and was practiced in it—although toward the end, he jokingly eludes the unwary reader using three verses from Augurellus. However, the authority of that one man, Fernel, outweighs the authority of many other contradicting physicians (as some say).

But principally and before all else in the question: **Whether any art be lawful**, it must be considered whether it is prohibited by any divine or human law. For lawful and unlawful things are distinguished in Law 1 of the Digest *on concubines*, the law *when the senate* in the Digest *on doubtful matters*, and Law 1 and throughout the entire title of the Digest *on guilds and corporations* <note>The author is citing the *Corpus Juris Civilis*, the foundation of Roman Law; "ff." is a standard abbreviation for the *Digest*</note>. As for Divine Law, I certainly find no text where Alchemy and the making of gold are prohibited, even though the divine legislator Moses prosecutes countless vices and crimes in Leviticus and Deuteronomy. Nor do I think he prohibited distillations and the use of alembics <note>A chemical still consisting of two vessels connected by a tube</note>, or the making of gold or silver, any more than the casting of jewels, rings, and other such ornaments with which Solomon and other Kings were adorned. It is unknown to no one how great the use of plates and foils of gold was among the people of God, especially in the temple of Jerusalem.

Furthermore, as for Civil Law, certainly not a single letter could be shown in the *Digests*, the *Code*, the *Institutes*, or the *Novellae* <note>The four parts of the Roman Law collection</note> that pertains to the prohibition of Alchemy. On the contrary, the art of the Melters <note>original: "Fusorum ars"</note> is approved, praised, and decorated with rewards in Law 1 of the Code *on the excuse of craftsmen*. Here, Vessel-melters <note>original: "Vascularii fusores"</note> are frequently named, as if practicing an art that is (without controversy) legitimate, in the law *according to Labeo*, the final section of the Digest *on prescribed words*; the final law of the Digest *on obligations and actions*; the penultimate law of the Digest *on legacies of gold and silver*. And concerning Mine-workers, they practice a legitimate art...

<summary>The author defends alchemy by listing famous historical and medical authorities who practiced it and argues that the craft is not prohibited by the Bible or Roman civil law.</summary>

-># ON THE LAW<-
## Page 62

<header>ON THE LAW</header>

it cannot be doubted from the title in the *Code on Metal-miners*, book 11 <note>original: "Cod. de Metallariis lib. xj." This refers to the *Codex Justinianus*, part of the body of Roman law, which contains regulations for mining.</note>. Regarding Canon Law <note>The body of laws and regulations made by Church authority</note>, two texts are usually brought forward as opposition, but it is easy to respond to both. The first is in the chapter *Spondent* <note>original: "c. spondent," referring to the papal decree *Spondent pariter* issued in 1317</note> under the "Extravagants" <note>original: "Extravag." These were papal decretals not originally included in the main collections of Canon Law</note> regarding the crime of forgery. There, Pope John XXII condemns alchemists; however, he does not condemn them to death, but only to perpetual infamy. But that text was not written infinitely and generally about all alchemists. Rather, it specifically and properly concerns only those who—to use the words of the text—"forge gold or silver through a sophisticated <note>In this context, "sophistical" means deceptive or counterfeit</note> transmutation." Therefore, that text does not apply to those who do not make a rejected or adulterated gold, but rather produce genuine and true gold. As John Andreae <note>A famous 14th-century expert on Canon Law</note> testifies in his additions to the *Speculum* <note>The *Speculum Iudiciale*, a standard legal manual</note>, Arnaldus de Villanova <note>A celebrated 13th-century physician and alchemist</note> was accustomed in his time to make rods of gold which he submitted to every possible test. Therefore, all the Doctors of Law—the civil lawyers as much as the canonists—did not concern themselves with that "Extravagant" decree of the Pope, as we said above. Indeed, Giovanni Augurello <note>Giovanni Aurelio Augurello, an Italian humanist poet</note>, a great poet, freely dedicated and presented his little work on alchemy to Pope Leo X, and it is well known that this gift was most pleasing to him. Let this response to that text suffice; and I shall set aside the fact that many today do not accept the authority of that legislator because he was a Pope. They say that if his authority is approved in one chapter, it would also have to be approved in the very next chapter—where he established certain things according to his own whim regarding the Franciscans and other monks—and thus the law *he who is not compelled* <note>original: "l. qui non cogitur," a reference to the Digest of Justinian (50.17.156), used here to argue for legal consistency or limitations of authority</note> would have to be applied.

The second text that is opposed is in the chapter *Episcopi* <note>The *Canon Episcopi*, a famous medieval legal text regarding witchcraft and superstition</note>, case 26, question 5, which is said to be taken from the Council of Ancyra <note>original: "Auquirensi." The author believes this is a misspelling</note>, and it is written as follows: "Whoever believes that any creature can be made, or transformed for better or worse into another species or another likeness, except by the Creator himself who made all things, is an infidel." First of all, the citation of the Council of "Auquirensi" is ridiculous, as such a council never existed or could have existed. It should be corrected to the **COUNCIL OF AQUILEIA**. But even more ridiculous is the citation of that text where those are condemned who believe a transformation into another species can occur. Certainly, this has no more to do with our question than what the Emperor writes: that it is possible for all things to be converted into money <note>original: "l. 2. C. de constit. pecun." A reference to the Code of Justinian regarding the valuation of goods</note>. For that text does not speak of the species of metals or similar things, but of the "species" <note>The Latin word *species* can mean both a biological "type" and an "appearance" or "phantom"</note> of persons: that is, of sorcerous women <note>witches</note> who said that they were transformed at night into various species of animals, and wandered through the woods and groves with Diana <note>The Roman goddess of the hunt, often associated in the Middle Ages with the "Wild Hunt" of witches</note>. Therefore, in the section *Satan himself* <note>original: "§. siquidem satanas"</note> (says the text), he transforms himself into different species of persons. Thus, it is ridiculous to twist a text that speaks of the diabolical transformation of persons to apply to the transformations of metals, which can be done through the industry and skill of certain craftsmen without any diabolical or magical artifice, as Thomas Aquinas showed in the previously mentioned places. Indeed, there is a text under the same question in...

<summary>The author argues that legal bans on alchemy, specifically by Pope John XXII, only target counterfeiters and frauds, not those practicing "true" alchemy. He further dismisses religious bans on "transformation" by clarifying that those laws refer to witchcraft and demonic illusions rather than the physical transmutation of metals.</summary>

--- Page 69 ---
<meta>This page concludes the legal and philosophical defense of alchemy. Following the discussion of historical practitioners, the author now addresses the theoretical possibility of transmutation through "seminal reasons" and defends the art against the common charge that its practitioners are often counterfeiters or sorcerers by distinguishing the skill itself from those who abuse it.</meta>

-># OF ALCHEMY<-

C. And it is no wonder, as it is written: There are within physical things, throughout all the elements, certain <term>hidden seminal reasons</term> <note>original: "occultae seminariae rationes." This is a philosophical concept, rooted in Stoicism and St. Augustine, suggesting that God placed "seeds" of all potential things into the fabric of creation, which await the right conditions to manifest.</note>, which, when a temporal or causal opportunity is granted, burst forth into their destined species. I will also add this, which is proven by our laws: medicine can be made from poisons or poisonous substances. This suggests that things which are poisonous by nature can be corrected and transformed into health-giving remedies through art and ingenuity, as the legal text regarding the <term>Mithridatic antidote</term> <note>original: "Mithridatico." A famous "universal" remedy named after King Mithridates VI, who reportedly made himself immune to poisons.</note> implies in the law "that often," in the section on "poisons" <note>original: "l. quod saepe, §. venena. ff. de contr. empt." This refers to the Digest of Justinian, 18.1.35.2, a foundational text of Roman law.</note>.

There remains that argument that many alchemists create counterfeit money; many have also been sorcerers, impious men, atheists, or necromancers. It is also said that Raymond Lull and Paracelsus were tainted by the magical arts. The piety and integrity of those who raise these points are to be praised; nevertheless, they must be asked to consider that the vices of the craftsmen are by no means to be blamed on the art itself. For the art is one thing, and the craftsman another; the use of the art is one thing, and its abuse another. This is found in the law "whosoever" and the following section <note>original: "l. quicunque & l. seq. ff. ad leg. Corn. de fals." Referring to the Cornelian Law on Forgers in the Digest.</note> where the art of minting money is approved, but those who tint or forge gold or silver coins are condemned.

Likewise, in the first law of the Digest on "extraordinary trials," professors of medicine are praised, yet among them are said to be imposters who use incantations, curses, and exorcisms. Likewise, <term>Mathematics</term> <note>In Roman law, "mathematicians" often referred to astrologers or diviners, whose practices were frequently restricted or banned.</note> is simply condemned in the second law of the Code on sorcerers, yet not all mathematicians are to be condemned, but only the imposters. Likewise, poisoners are punished by death according to the law on capital crimes, yet poisons themselves are not condemned, as was just stated from the law "that often." If arts were to be condemned because of the abuse of their craftsmen, which one today would be approved? Would it be Jurisprudence (Law), in which there are so many <term>shysters</term> <note>original: "rabulae." A derogatory term for unlearned or unscrupulous legal pleaders.</note>? Would it be Medicine, in which there are so many poisoners? Or Theology, in which there are so many <term>sophists</term> <note>Those who use clever but deceptive arguments.</note>?

Therefore, judgment and discernment should be applied: let the chaff be separated from the grain on the threshing floor; the bad fish from the good in the net; and counterfeit coins from the honest ones in the State. Let those who <term>counterfeit</term> <note>original: "Sophisticantes." Those who use "sophistry" or deception to fake the appearance of precious metals.</note> gold or silver be separated from the skilled craftsmen. Let the sharpest punishments, investigations, and legal inquiries be established against forgers and corrupters of currency. But (as the Legal Consultant says): "Let the penalty for a crime committed by others be removed from those who are touched by no fault" <note>original: "alieni admissi poena ab iis quos nulla culpa contingit, removeatur." A quote from Digest 48.20.11.</note>.

### THE END
