->TO THE MOST EXCELLENT MAN<-

# PETER SEVERINUS THE DANE
## CHIEF PHYSICIAN TO THE MOST SERENE KING OF DENMARK.

->*Thomas Muffet the Englishman*<-
->wishes health and prosperity.<- <note>original: "εὖ πράττειν." A standard Greek greeting meaning to "do well" or "fare well."</note>

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial Q featuring floral patterns and a small animal figure in the corner of the frame.</image-desc>

Ever since I first applied my mind to the love of chemistry, most distinguished Severinus, I have greatly desired that its excellence might become known to every student of medicine. Indeed, I have drawn such health and sweetness from it that I would hardly consider it the mark of a man—let alone a philosopher—not to wish that these benefits be shared with others. 

However, I saw that your most ingenious "Idea" <note>This refers to Severinus's seminal work, *Idea Medicinae Philosophicae* (1571), which sought to provide a theoretical framework for the chemical medicine of Paracelsus.</note>, which is worthy of being preserved in cedar oil <note>original: "cedro dignissimam." An ancient expression meaning a work is worthy of immortality, as cedar oil was used to protect papyrus from insects and decay.</note>, was not received with sufficient honor by the common herd of physicians. I saw that you had lost both your "oil" <note>The author is playing on the Latin idiom "oleam et operam perdere" (to lose oil and labor), meaning to work in vain. The "oil" refers to both the lamp oil used by students and the chemical oils Severinus worked with.</note> (with which you intended to soften even stones) and almost all your effort. I truly feared that they would act much more unfairly toward this little book of mine, since they were in no way swayed by the bait <note>original: "δελεήτρῳ"</note> of such elegant and divine speech as yours. 

Perhaps this happened because you believed the "Anti-chemists" to be dry and sober men; you thought they should be bathed not with salt, but with oil, and led toward a sense of the truth with soft speech, as if by some Theban plectrum <note>original: "plectro quodam Thebaico." A reference to the musical pick (plectrum) of Amphion of Thebes, whose music was so persuasive it moved stones to build the city walls. Muffet suggests Severinus was too gentle in his persuasion.</note>. I, however, am of a different mind, and I give myself over entirely to this opinion: they should no longer be bathed in oil, but rubbed with salt, and roused either by the branding iron of the satirists or the stings of the logicians. 

For many of them have begun to hate Chemistry with such intensity that they shudder at the mere mention of its name; indeed (such is the foolish intemperance of their minds), they are forced to vomit at the sound of it. Others, it is true, strongly praise chemical remedies—but whenever, through their own negligence, Vulcan <note>The Roman god of fire, here used to represent the alchemical furnace or the process of heat-based transformation.</note> has committed a fault...

sent out, they attack the art anew so many times, or they traduce the demonstrator. Nor does a small number of those come forward who grant the Chemist every honor only so long as he exercises his skill outside the metallic or mineral province. For they believe they must abstain from those minerals with a greater religious dread than from a horned serpent or a viper; but by what shadow of reason they do this, I cannot quite grasp. For if they detest the poison of those minerals, why do they employ the viper? No more leprous animal exists, nor is any mineral found so harmful. <note>Viper flesh was a common ingredient in Renaissance medicine, particularly in "Theriac," used as an antitoxin. Muffet is pointing out the hypocrisy of using toxic animals while fearing purified minerals.</note> Add moreover, that God has instilled such a great <term>antipathy</term> <note>original: "ἀντιπάθειαν." A natural, constitutional aversion or repulsion between two things.</note> between humans and serpents—a greater one than you will ever see between man and minerals—so much so, that at the mere sight of them, as if seeing a public enemy of the human race, we tremble all over. 

Furthermore, since mineral salt is found not only in every vegetable by which we are nourished or altered, but even in every animal: surely it is necessary either to provide nothing at all to the sick, or to approach the use of minerals, however reluctantly. Moreover, since we know this order of the "sublunary liturgy" <note>The "liturgy" of the world below the moon; the divine order and service of nature.</note> was prescribed by God: that minerals should supply nourishment to vegetables, these to beasts, and beasts to humans; how great (good God!) is the stupidity, or what ignorance bewitches us, that we do not confess the greatest similarity between humans and minerals? 

More rightly, in my opinion, did he speak who called man a <term>Microcosm</term> <note>Literally "little world." The philosophical theory that the human being contains within themselves all the elements and powers of the greater universe (the Macrocosm).</note>: seeing as in his nature something of God, of Angels, of beasts, of plants, of the devil, and finally of the whole universe has been placed; and certainly not without merit. For in truth, as much virtue as dwells in us, so much of God is within; as much wickedness, so much of the devil; as much reason, so much of the Angels; as much movement and voluntary sense, so much of the beast; as much growth, so much of the plant; as much of **salt, sulfur, and mercury**, <note>The *Tria Prima* or three primary principles of Paracelsian chemistry. Man is, like all other mixed things, made from the mineral of the earth; and into their own dust all things will return, sooner or later, after the dissolution of the body is complete. Revived by the mere shadow of your reputation, I easily persuade myself that I shall truly and solidly triumph over all those who revile chemical remedies. You would have received this *Apology* last year, had I not been daily expecting that "golden response" of yours against the Anti-Paracelsist. ...to lay low with a small wave. # EPISTOLA
### DEDICATION

Man is, like all other mixed things, [made] from the mineral of the earth: and all things will return to their own dust after the body’s **analysis** <note>original: "analysin" — in this context, the chemical dissolution or breakdown of the body into its component parts.</note> is complete, sooner or later. But why do I bring these **owls to you** <note>original: "noctuas ad te" — a reference to the proverb "bringing owls to Athens," similar to the English "carrying coals to Newcastle," meaning to give something to someone who already has it in abundance.</note>, who spend your life in Athens? Or why to those **haters of wisdom** <note>original: "Misosophos"</note>, who like parrots neglect the one teaching them and disregard the hay, and will never emerge from their labyrinths full of monsters, even with the help of Ariadne’s thread? 

Yet it pleased me to attempt something to call them back, if not with the hope of success, then at least with the will to try; for **"by trying, the Achaeans came to Troy,"** <note>original: "ἐς Τροίην πειρώμενοι ἦλθον Ἀχαιοί" — a Greek proverb emphasizing that persistence leads to victory.</note> and **"for mortals, all things are achieved by effort."** <note>original: "Καλλίσᾳ παίδων, πειραθλὼ πάντα τελεῖται"</note> There are many reasons why I would dedicate these first skirmishes of our army to you. First, your extraordinary kindness toward our countrymen, which two years ago in your homeland you revealed to our most illustrious legate, **Peregrine Bertie** <note>Lord Willoughby de Eresby (1555–1601), a prominent English diplomat and soldier.</note> (son of the most noble Duchess of Suffolk), and especially to me—not by a small measure, but from a full granary. 

Then, because to dedicate a medical treatise <term>healing art <note>original: "ἰατρείην"</note></term> to men unskilled in medicine (as most nobles and senators are) seems the same as offering a farmer a praise of Monarchy, or a soldier the science of agriculture. But above all, I was moved (excellent Severinus) by the contemplation of your singular doctrine and proven learning in this cause: refreshed by the mere shadow of which, I easily persuade myself that I shall truly and solidly triumph over all those who revile chemical remedies. 

You would have received this *Apology* last year, had I not been daily expecting that golden response of yours against the **Anti-Paracelsian** <note>Likely referring to Thomas Erastus, a major critic of Paracelsus's chemical theories.</note>. But since I knew that you—distracted either by the ingratitude of the age, the sweetness of silence, or royal business—had not yet sent the auxiliary forces of chemistry: I considered it my duty in the meantime to seize upon the arrogant **haters of chemistry** <note>original: "Misochemicos"</note> and [strike down] their own <term>haughtiness <note>original: "ὑψηλοκαρδίαν" — literally "high-heartedness" or pride.</note></term> with this first skirmish, as if by a single little shepherd... <note>Muffet is likely leading into a comparison of himself to David using a sling against the Goliath of traditional medicine.</note>

# TO THE STUDENTS OF PURE OR CHEMICAL MEDICINE

## Thomas Moffet, Physician, Sends Greetings.

<image-desc>A decorative woodcut initial letter 'V' featuring foliate designs and scrolls.</image-desc>

*I find that the clever saying of the comic playwright* <note>A reference to the Roman playwright Terence</note> *is indeed true, dearest brothers: that a wise man is driven to act by these three things: Necessity, Law, and Custom. Were it not for these, I would have refrained not only from this type of writing but from publishing any of my books at all. For I see such ease available to everyone for the printing of their works that even the most shameless Venus* <note>A metaphor for immoral or trivial literature</note> *and any foolish opinion has found its way to the press. Nevertheless, since it is necessary to encourage you through writing—since I cannot reach you through the living word—pardon will be granted (unless I am mistaken) to necessity; and to us will be attributed not a passion for writing, but a spirit for teaching the truth. Furthermore, we are warned by the shortness of nature and life that trees should be planted, sooner or later, which may benefit a future age; and that man was created for civic life, as well as for the distribution to others of those things he has received from God, the Best and Greatest. Moreover, I might seem to regard Zwinger of Basel* <note>Theodor Zwinger (1533–1588), a Swiss physician and scholar</note>*, Severinus* <note>Petrus Severinus (1542–1602), a Danish physician and leading proponent of Paracelsian medicine</note>*, and my other excellent teachers—whom Hippocrates commands us* **to regard as equal to our own parents** <note>Original Greek: ἶσα γενέτῃσιν ἡγήσασθαι</note>*—with too little honor if I did not dare to freely defend their chemical remedies (in which they especially delight) against any enemy, when they are sprinkled with various accusations by shameless men, and to keep their innocence, immunity, and right intact and protected* <note>The Latin "sartum tectum" literally means "patched and roofed," a legal idiom for keeping something in good repair</note> *by every nerve and means. Nor would I do these things for their sake alone (for to rely on the authority of men in a physical* <note>Meaning a debate regarding natural science or physics</note> *debate seems clearly* **absurd** <note>Original Greek: ἄτοπον</note>*), unless I also saw in practice that physicians deprived of chemical remedies are like blacksmiths who use a blunt axe for cutting, or perhaps one broken in the middle. Finally, since I see it is customary for the most excellent men to take every account by which they might remove from themselves not only the crime but even the accu-*

...[lest they] set themselves apart from the group; and let them defend their own innocence before the people both in words and in writing. I trust that I will be doing nothing new or wrong if, by repelling the weapons thrown at me, I ward off future ones; and if I might recall these raving petty followers <note>Latin: *nepotulos*, literally "little grandsons," used here disparagingly for the imitators of his opponents</note> to a better harvest (according to my strength). 

For now, driven by I know not what sting of pride, they cannot keep measure in their insults, and they triumph at every table over the books of that *Antiparacelsist* <note>A reference to Thomas Erastus (1524–1583), a fierce critic of Paracelsus</note>, as if over the spoils of Metellus <note>A reference to the Roman General Metellus, famed for his military triumphs</note>. Yet if those poor wretches could see how little strength his battle-line holds, and if they examined his own arguments on the scale of truth, justice, and equality: surely they would flee from his banner with no less speed than Mars, that swiftest of the Gods, fled from the embrace and adulterous bed of Venus, after he had exposed himself to the mockery of gods and men <note>A classical reference to the myth where Vulcan caught Mars and Venus in a golden net</note>. 

For in the first part, what else does he show us but the great impiety of Theophrastus <note>Paracelsus’s given name was Philippus Aureolus Theophrastus Bombastus von Hohenheim</note>? Which surely theologians would have handled more accurately, and even more justly. For let physicians care for what belongs to physicians; let craftsmen handle their own tools <note>A Latin proverb meaning "everyone should stick to their own trade"</note>. Since he himself is a man, he ought to have been more fairly disposed toward another man: or at least not so far laid aside his humanity as to take delight in cutting the throats of the dead and raging against the deceased. 

What if Paracelsus felt something contrary to Holy Scripture regarding the creation of the world and divine administration? How did he differ in that from pagan writers? Or why do we not bear his fictions with the same mercy that we grant to those who hate ecclesiastical discipline (of whom the Antiparacelsist reveals himself to be not the least) or to Galenic impiety? 

But since it is abundantly clear that he has leapt over the rules of "universality, essentiality, and primary truth" <note>original: "κατὰ παντὸς, καθ' αὑτὸ, καθόλου πρῶτον" — technical terms from Aristotelian logic regarding the requirements for a scientific demonstration</note> and the very law of humanity: I do not wish to stir this mud <note>original: *linum*, literally "flax" or "thread," but likely a typo or metaphor for a tangled mess or "limum" (mud)</note> any further, lest I stir up a most unpleasant odor for you (whom I have always intended to please), and hinder myself as I hasten toward greater things. 

I know that the Anti-chemists <note>Those who opposed the use of chemical medicines in favor of traditional herbal/Galenic ones</note>, even if attacked by no one, will collapse under their own weight along with that God of idolaters <note>Likely referring to Galen, whose authority was treated as divine by traditionalists</note>, and have already wasted away from a long-standing heat of spontaneous madness. However, since they will know that I [prepared] this [little book] not so much with a mind to torture them or in expectation of triumph, but for the sake of their own health...

# ON THE RIGHT AND SUPERIORITY OF CHEMICAL MEDICINES.

->Apologetic Dialogue.<-

->PHILERASTUS THE CHEMIST.<-

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial letter 'A' containing floral motifs and vine-like scrollwork.</image-desc>
I HAVE opened my plan to my teacher regarding the deceiving of the Chemist; he praises, commends, and proclaims it; he even promotes this work with his prayers, and has equipped me with various types of weapons and a multitude of tricks. However, to tell the truth, I would rather fight with the Aetolian boar <note>The Calydonian Boar from Greek mythology, a monstrous beast sent by the goddess Artemis</note>, with a bear, a lion, or a Hydra <note>original: *excetra*, a multi-headed serpent or water-snake</note>, than with these Chemists: who overwhelm anyone speaking to them with the foulest smell of sulfur or with mercurial fumes <note>A common complaint from traditional physicians was the "sooty" and toxic nature of early laboratory chemistry</note>. I also hear that a certain Chemist dwells not far from here, who is prepared to pickle us Galenists <note>Followers of the ancient physician Galen, who relied on herbal mixtures rather than chemical minerals</note> like herrings <note>original: *haleces*</note> in salt, and afterwards hang us up in the smoke. By Pollux <note>A common Roman oath</note>, unless my signs fail me, he lives here in the neighborhood; but look, there is the man coming out. Listen, heaven and earth, while I devise Daedalian deceits <note>Cunning or labyrinthine tricks, named after Daedalus, the mythical craftsman of the Labyrinth</note>, and learn all of this man's skill through a new pretense. **CH.** Phew! I think either a wild cat or a weasel has passed through here; it smells so bad. **PH.** Shall I approach? Shall I stop, or stay? Indeed, my mind is certain; I will seek him, no matter how far from home he may be. **CH.** Greetings, stranger. **PH.** And greetings to you, inhabitant. **CH.** Whom do you seek so anxiously, guest? If I can be of any help in finding him, give the command.

## APOLOGETIC DIALOGUE

**PHILERASTUS:** Indeed, I accept your kindness, and when I return to my homeland, I will gladly proclaim it. I am seeking a Chemist; for the great effort you have given in finding him for me, I shall always love you dearly. At the first opportunity, I will return the favor.

**CHEMIST:** Although hardly anyone is worthy of such a grand name, nevertheless, I will not deny that I am called such by the people.

**PHILERASTUS:** Oh, happy Philerastus that I am! I see the desired goods in the harbor itself. What God, or what such opportunity has brought this? My master, my patron, my most sweet father, greetings!

**CHEMIST:** You are talking nonsense, Philerastus; for I do not remember ever being your master, or you being my servant. But from where have you sailed, I pray? From what homeland do you originate?

**PHILERASTUS:** I set sail from Galenic Athens <note>original: *Athenis Galenicis*; a metaphorical reference to traditional medical universities that relied exclusively on the ancient teachings of Galen</note>, and I consider Germany my homeland.

**CHEMIST:** Why then was this journey here, traveler? Why do you greet me with such mockery? What was lacking in Galenic Athens that you have put in at this shore?

**PHILERASTUS:** Because where I see nothing except the corruption of morals, a poverty of knowledge, and the emptying of wallets <note>original: *loculorum exenterationem*; literally, the disemboweling of purses</note>, even if a scepter were offered to me there, it would not be a desired place to stay.

**CHEMIST:** Soft words, I beg you. I realize the men of such works are Athenians, and if they are truly like that, you are right to flee, and you do well, stranger, to carefully avoid their company.

**PHILERASTUS:** Indeed, the whole race of Athenians and Galenists are among men, in my opinion, like vipers <note>original: *vi-pelli*; likely a typo or variant for *viperis*</note>, aconite <note>a type of poisonous plant, also known as monkshood</note>, and chameleons. They feed the eyes and minds with the elegance of their color or brilliance, yet they are of no good use.

**CHEMIST:** Stay, I pray. If the Galenists should transgress the precepts of ethics, I would wish the theologians to detect it and the politicians to punish it. But it is your duty, since you are a physician, to prove their errors in medicine. For that law of knowledge, "in itself" <note>original: *καθ' αὑτὸ* (kath' auto); an Aristotelian logical term meaning a property that belongs to the essence of a thing</note>, sufficiently convinces us how little it belongs to the Logician to run over into another's province. But tell me on your honor, stranger: Have you deserted the Galenists forever? Or have you come to taste my conversations and steal my secrets?

**PHILERASTUS:** I, come to steal your secrets? I could not possibly do it; or even if I were very much able, piety would forbid it.

**CHEMIST:** Yet many of your kind come here, and they greet me flatteringly; they call upon me courteously, asking that I support them. They heap divine praises upon both my labor and my art. Yet, when they have returned to their school, they reveal their resentment and freely—or rather, rudely—rave against the supporters of chemistry. Some are like this: they love Chemistry as much as they think it benefits their own business; but when it requires expense, then they reject it as a useless science.

**PHILERASTUS:** And yet I embrace and love it so greatly, as is right to love: and nothing remains of such value to me that I would not give it for the sake of learning Chemistry. For Chemistry is the source of solid philosophy, the key of wisdom, the soul and marrow of physics, the root and goal of medicine, toward which wise men have aimed. Do you wish me to proclaim more?

**CHEMIST:** Nay, enough and more than enough, stranger; for I would prefer Chemistry to be praised by one who...

### ON CHEMICAL MEDICINE

<meta>catchword: ipso-</meta>

[The Chemist continues:] ...she <note>referring to Chemistry</note> had always lived in praise. I rejoice, however, that she has prevailed to such an extent that she has even obtained her own eulogy from the mouths of her enemies. But answer me in a few words: why do you come to give your name to Chemistry, when so many distinguished princes of physicians have rejected it? For from the Greeks, **Hippocrates, Polybus, Aristotle, Nicomachus, Theophrastus of Lesbos, Herophilus, Serapion, Dioscorides, Galen, Thessalus, Trallianus, Archigenes, Rufus of Ephesus, Aetius, Oribasius, Alexander of Tralles, Paul of Aegina,** and **Actuarius** are on your side <note>The Chemist is listing the "Galenists," the traditional authorities taught in universities</note>. On your side also are **Avenzoar, Albubeter, Isaac Beimiram, Albaterius, Albucasis, Jacobus Alkindus, Avicenna, Averrhoes, Joannitius,** etc., among the Arabs. To you also belong all those—whether Italians, Spaniards, French, Germans, or English—who practiced medicine three hundred years ago. Since, therefore, so many illustrious "Atlases" of the medical art, covered in the white hair of old age, have attacked or at least remained ignorant of our science; you, a mere youth, are wasting your efforts, having undergone every danger of sea and land for the sake of learning this thoroughly.

**PHILERASTUS:** But I have learned that knowledge is acquired not by age, but by talent, and I see that in most matters, the worst opinion is the one in which the majority agrees. For, good God, how great and serious a council of men took that Christ—the First-Philosopher <note>original: *Protophilosophum*; here meaning the original source of all wisdom and truth</note>—and after inflicting Him with false accusations and reproaches, delivered Him to the whip, and did not stop until He was killed by the most vile death on the cross. Now, if those "clear-sighted" Fathers and our own foremost Patrons did not recognize Him when He was revealed in the flesh—shown even to the blind and bleary-eyed by the testimony of years, prophecies, and miracles—how much more easily could they have erred in the very principles of medicine, and left some part of it to us either in a raw state or entirely unknown? Is it really likely that all medicine was enclosed within the hearts of idolaters, or in the single fountain of **Galen**, such that we must impose a necessity upon Christians to drink it either from the mouths of heathens or from no spring at all? 

Rather, let us hold most firmly to this **axiom** <note>original Greek: *αξιωμα*</note>: that the profession of Christ is useful for all things, and that we perceive the power of all His promises so fully that he who sincerely worships Him will, for that very reason, receive a greater increase in his vocation, whether it be medical or physical <note>meaning "natural philosophy" or the study of nature</note>. Moreover, just as Christ Himself (whom we acknowledge as the head of the church) was undoubtedly the most skilled in every discipline among men, so too does the law of physical equity command that Christians should surpass all heathens—not only by way of resemblance and **Kabbalistic interpretation** <note>original: *Cabalistica anagoge*; a method of finding mystical or spiritual meaning in texts</note>, but by the very fact of their faith. I call to witness **Solomon**, the Apostles, and all their disciples, as well as several physicians of this current age who, inspired by the divine spirit, have surpassed the Jews, Greeks, Arabs, and Latins in both the science and the practice of medicine. For in Anatomy, the very vestibule of all medicine, how ruinous were the slips of the ancients! How false...

### ON CHEMICAL MEDICINE

...had always lived with praise. I rejoice, however, that it <note>Chemistry</note> has prevailed to such an extent that it has obtained its own praise even from the mouths of its enemies. For among the Greeks: Hippocrates, Polybus, Aristotle, Nicomachus, Theophrastus of Lesbos, Herophilus, Serapion, Dioscorides, Galen, Thessalus, Alexander of Tralles, Archigenes, Rufus of Ephesus, Aëtius, Oribasius, Alexander of Tralles, Paul of Aegina, and Actuarius are yours. **PHILERASTUS:** But I have learned that knowledge is acquired not by age, but by talent, and I see that in most things, the opinion in which the greater number agrees is the worst. For, good God, what a council of how many and how grave men brought forth Christ, that **First Philosopher** <note>original: *Protophilosophum*; here Philerastus frames Christ as the ultimate source of all wisdom and natural philosophy</note>, afflicted with false accusations and insults, to the whip, and sent him to be killed by nothing less than the most vile death of the cross. For in Anatomy, the vestibule of all medicine, how destructive were the errors of the ancients! how false...

### APOLOGETIC DIALOGUE

...of theirs physically <note>original: *physicè*</note>, and abhorrent not only to divine letters <note>Holy Scripture</note> but also to the senses themselves? Indeed, almost everyone has been so ignorant of Method that few, indeed hardly any, grasped what specific method a physician might have need of. Finally, in the preparation of medicines, all have gradually slipped from truth to opinion, from the senses to imagination, and from demonstration to error; nor have they ever returned to a sound mind until these last few years.

**CHEMIST:** Truly, although it is the custom among Galenists <note>Followers of the traditional medical system of Galen</note> for their tongues to differ from their hearts, yet you speak so sincerely, and in my opinion so divinely, that I will permit nothing to remain closed within me that it interests you to know.

**PHILERASTUS:** If you should perceive one thing in my mouth and another in my heart, I plead no cause, O Chemist, why my reputation, my safety, and my very life should not be forfeit in your eyes.

**CHEMIST:** Come, I shall test your faith, relying on your talent; see to it, then, that you do not become more unfaithful to me than I am to you.

**PHILERASTUS:** Indeed, unless I wish ill upon my own heart, I wish the very best for you; and I will sooner be unfaithful to myself than faith should be lacking toward you.

**CHEMIST:** I accept the condition; follow me to my house.

**PHILERASTUS:** Hail, temple of nature! How long I have waited for you—but good heavens! How small these little buildings of yours are?

**CHEMIST:** Ants are not large either; yet they commend and record the cleverness and craftsmanship of nature more than the tall machines of giants.

**PHILERASTUS:** But what, I pray, are those letters that remain carved before the door?

**CHEMIST:**
->THE CATHEDRAL OF THE CHEMISTS: AGAINST WHICH<-
->ALL THE COLONIES OF THE GALENISTS SHALL NOT PREVAIL.<-

**PHILERASTUS:** A crude lodging indeed, and far unequal to bearing such a name; for the walls are not clothed in Corinthian work, nor are they adorned with emblems on the outside. Atlantes <note>Statues of male figures used as columns</note> are missing from the vestibule, and decorative tiles are lacking on the roof; nor are the folding doors carved by a Daedalean hand <note>referring to Daedalus, the mythical master craftsman</note>, after the model of a Cathedral.

**CHEMIST:** You seek the exterior ornament of houses, guest; I have deliberately not added it. For I consider it shameful to pursue external splendor—it is a sign of ambition, not philosophy; of folly, not knowledge. Since even your **Hippocrates** condemns excessive stupidity <note>original Greek: *ἀξυνεσίην* (asynesian)</note> in physicians, you tell me in vain of decorative tiles, Corinthian work, or a Daedalean hand—I who am an Englishman; and in buildings I would rather imitate sobriety than this new madness for building <note>original Greek: *οἰκομανίαν* (oicomanian)</note>. Furthermore, houses adorned with such great expense are very much like the jars of many pharmacists <note>original: *Pharmacopœorum*</note>: which gleam outside with gold and are polished with Phrygian embroidery, but inside contain nothing, or only skeletons, and—if the truth be forgiven—the corpses of medicines.

**PHILERASTUS:** You speak the truth. Do not take what I said harshly; for we are accustomed to estimate the excellence of an art from the artist's wealth, furniture, ornament, elegance, and pride—little mindful of nature, whom we observe hiding a vast treasure of gold in the commonest earth of all houses. But now, having seen enough of the bark...

<header>APOLOGETIC DIALOGUE</header>

...their physics, which is abhorrent not only to divine scripture, but also to the senses themselves? Finally, in the preparation of medicines, all have gradually fallen away from truth to opinion, from the senses to imagination, and from proof to error; and they never returned to a sound mind until a few years ago.

**CHEMIST:** Truly, although it is common for the Galenists <note>Followers of the ancient Greek physician Galen, who dominated medical thought for over a millennium</note> to have tongues that differ from their hearts, you speak so sincerely and, in my opinion, divinely, that I will allow nothing to remain hidden in me that you are interested in knowing.

**PHILERASTUS:** If you perceive one thing in my mouth and another in my heart, I plead no cause, Chemist, against my reputation, safety, and life failing in your sight.

**CHEMIST:** Come, let me test your loyalty. Relying on your talent, see to it that you do not become more unfaithful to me than I am to you.

**PHILERASTUS:** On the contrary, unless I wish ill upon my own heart, I wish you the best; I would sooner be unfaithful to myself than loyalty fail toward you.

**CHEMIST:** I accept the condition; follow me to the house.

**PHILERASTUS:** Hail, temple of nature! How long I have waited for you! But, goodness! How small these little dwellings of yours are?

**CHEMIST:** -> THE PALACE OF THE CHEMISTS: AGAINST WHICH <-
-> ALL THE COLONIES OF THE GALENISTS SHALL NOT PREVAIL. <-
<note>original: "BASILICA CHEMICORUM: CONTRA QUAM OMNES GALENISTARUM COLONIAE NON PRAEVALEBUNT." This is a parody of the biblical phrase "the gates of hell shall not prevail," asserting that chemical medicine is the true, "apostolic" medical faith.</note>

**PHILERASTUS:** It is a crude lodging indeed, and far unequal to bearing such a name; for the walls are not dressed in Corinthian work, nor are they adorned with emblems outside; Atlantes <note>Architectural supports carved in the shape of powerful men</note> are missing from the vestibule, and decorative tiles are lacking on the roof; nor are the doors carved by a Daedalian hand <note>Meaning a master craftsman, after the mythical inventor Daedalus</note>, according to the model of a Palace.

**CHEMIST:** You seek the exterior ornament of the house, guest; I purposely did not add it. For I consider it shameful to pursue external splendor—it is a sign of ambition, not philosophy; of folly, not knowledge. Since even your Hippocrates <note>The "Father of Medicine," whom both sides claimed to respect</note> condemns excessive senselessness <note>original Greek: ἀξυνεσίην (asynesian) — a lack of understanding or stupidity</note> in physicians, you speak to me in vain of decorative tiles, Corinthian work, or a master’s hand—I who am an Englishman; and in buildings, I would rather imitate sobriety than this new house-madness <note>original Greek: οἰκομανίαν (oicomania) — an obsession with building grand estates</note>. But now that the shell has been sufficiently viewed, to [the kernel...]

# ON CHEMICAL MEDICINE

...famine is required to reach the kernel. **CHEMIST:** Enter, then. But before you proceed, step into this dressing room <note>original: *apodyterium*, the room in a Roman bath where one undressed</note>, and there strip off credulity, and afterwards laziness. **PHILERASTUS:** I agree with what you command regarding laziness, and I feel it is necessary. But whoever strips off all credulity entirely will find that this discipline leaves no deeper a footprint upon them than wheat sown in the sea. For according to that Aristotelian saying, *the learner must believe* <note>original: δεῖ μὲν τὸν μανθάνοντα πιστεύειν</note>, so that you may have a student who is free-thinking, modest, benevolent, attentive, teachable, and like clay to be molded into any shape. **CHEMIST:** On the contrary, intelligence suits a student, while credulity does not. For if you subject yourself to this Athenian <note>Referring to the Greek philosophical tradition, particularly Galen</note>, you will mock the immortality of the soul, the omnipotence of God, the creation of the world, and the entire doctrine of Christians, following the example of Galen; and nothing was so wickedly defended by him that it would not, in turn, be confirmed by your own vote. Therefore, do not place faith in me, nor in anyone else, further than what we say that is either manifest to the senses, or congruent with reason, or in agreement with the divine scriptures. **PHILERASTUS:** You advise rightly. **CHEMIST:** Now descend into the bath, and wash away opinion, deceit, pride, and the remaining hindrances to the sciences. **PHILERASTUS:** Consider it done; see, I return to you now with my ears washed and a purified <note>original: *defecato*, meaning filtered or cleansed of dregs</note> soul. Do you wish for anything else? **CHEMIST:** Only that, having laid aside your academic cap and silken gown, you put on the chemical cloak—of a rougher texture, perhaps, but far more suitable for our operations. Now, in place of a book, take up the toothed forceps; let them be your teacher. You are now perfectly equipped; this is how it suits a physician <term>physicum: a natural philosopher or doctor of medicine</term> to be adorned. Now follow me. **PHILERASTUS:** By my faith, what do I see here? What kind of furnaces, and how many? I pray, what is the name of this place? **CHEMIST:** The Place of Toil <note>original: Πονητήριον (Ponētērion)</note>. **PHILERASTUS:** A hard and harsh word. **CHEMIST:** Perhaps to you, whom Galen has rendered idle until now, sitting in a heated room <note>original: *hypocausto*</note>. But those who prefer labor and sweat (for which the Gods are said to sell all things) to any most desirable leisure are of a different mind. **PHILERASTUS:** But truly, such a selection of glassware, vessels, and all these furnaces is not acquired at a low price; Vulcan <note>The god of fire, here meaning the fuel for the furnaces</note>, leaven, clay, and the tools to be produced also consume much money. **CHEMIST:** As if you had forgotten that saying from the Comic Poet <note>The Roman playwright Plautus</note>: *It is necessary to spend if you seek profit.* Yet the expenses will not be so great that they will not be surpassed a thousand times by the profit. For in exchange for money, you will buy incomparable science, the demonstrator of all Physics; no merchant has ever enjoyed such a happy exchange, and no moneylender such fruitful interest. Do not, therefore, get stuck in that mud of avarice; but rather imitate Montanus, Fernelius, Villanova, Fracastoro, Cardano, Gesner, Zwinger, Aragosius, Brückmann, Platter, and the "golden chick of Denmark," Severinus <note>Petrus Severinus (1542–1602), an influential Danish physician and follower of Paracelsus</note>; who, having made such long detours into Greece, Arabia, and the entire province of ancient medicine, were not ashamed to be late-learners <note>original: ὀψιμαθεῖς (opsimatheis)</note> of this art, their own...

### DIALOGUE APOLOGY

...and to build for old age a laboratory of this kind, or some most honorable monument.

**PHILERASTUS:** You name memorable men, who are the sole ornaments of this century. Relying on their authority, I thirst most greedily for Chemistry <note>original: *Chemia*</note>. For whenever I am about to attempt something, I am accustomed first to argue with myself: is it right to do this? Then: have other good men done it before me? Indeed, our choice is confirmed when we sense that the most prudent and famous men, who lived their lives in honor, want the same as we do and act as we do. 

But here I am stuck <note>original: *aqua mihi haeret*, a Latin idiom meaning "the water stops," used when one is at a loss or in a bind</note>: is it more right to follow in the footsteps of so few men, or to follow the opinions of the ancients, who in this gymnasium of preparations <note>original: *praeparationum palaestra*, referring to the practical workspace of the lab</note> seem to be either nothing at all, or clearly strangers? Forgive me, I pray, if I now run back to the positions of the Galenists <note>Followers of Galen, the 2nd-century physician whose theories dominated medicine for over a millennium</note>. I do it not so much out of love for them or hope for victory, but for the sake of knowing the truth, and so that I may seem to have laid aside all blind belief.

**CHEMIST:** I praise your plan, and in turn I answer you: to imitate the ancient physicians in all or most things is just as if you were seeking a model from a crude, unfinished work. For medicine around the time of Hippocrates <note>The "Father of Medicine" (c. 460 – c. 370 BCE)</note> was like a fetus recently conceived: in it, only confused outlines and rough sketches of limbs could be seen. Later, Galen distinguished this with a formal method, and posterity—both the Arabs and the Greeks—made it richer with a various supply of medicines scraped together from quacks and barbers. 

Yet none of them progressed so far as to understand or teach the method for distilling rose water—and these are the "illustrious architects of medicine"! Indeed, there is no part of Medicine where they did not leave some most foul error, which a later, wiser generation wiped away like a fertile sponge.

**PHILERASTUS:** You speak the truth, and in my judgment it can even be felt by the senses themselves. For just as old men perceive things differently than boys—the latter seeing rightly, the former according to the constraints of their age—so too it deserves no wonder that we, in this "graying" of the world <note>The idea that the world is in its final, most mature stage</note>, find certain things unknown to the fathers, or bring "the hand of Apelles" <note>original: *Apellis manum*, a classical reference to the Greek painter Apelles, meaning to put the finishing touches on a work</note> to their inventions. After all, they themselves saw Medicine only through a cloud, and to use your word, in a state not yet embryonated <note>original: *embryonatam*, meaning undeveloped or fetal</note>. 

Therefore, just as Avicenna <note>A Persian polymath (c. 980–1037) who was a central figure in the Islamic Golden Age</note> looked for truth in Galen, and Galen for diligence in Hippocrates, and Hippocrates for method in the ancients, so too it is the mark of a slave bound to a grumpy master—not an educated explorer of science—to seek nothing beyond what is in the writings of one or all authors. 

Now, however (omitting the faults of the ancients), I ask that you explain the names and the use of the furnaces.

**CHEMIST:** That one is called Neptune, the Sea, or Mary <note>original: *Maria*, likely referring to the *Balneum Mariae* or "Mary's Bath," known today as a double boiler</note>, or the Temperate Zone. This one is the Horse’s Belly <note>original: *Venter equi*, a term for a warm digestion process, often using the heat of decomposing dung</note>. That one is called the Hens’ Nest; and there, indeed, Egypt is placed. To the right are Persia, Mauritania, Etna, the Serpent, the Furnace of Sloth, and the Ostrich’s Belly.

**PHILERASTUS:** Alas! What you say seems to seek ash <note>A pun on looking for hidden meanings in the fire</note>. Away with that ambiguity! By using it, you seem to not want to educate me...

### ON CHEMICAL MEDICINE

...the beginner, but the Chemists seem to even put the advanced students to flight. 

**CHEMIST:** Indeed, they do this on purpose, and with great right. For beyond the fact that no law forbids the *coining of new names* <note>original Greek: *onomatopoein*</note> in new arts, it is also sanctioned by the voice of Hippocrates and by fairness: that sacred things should be handed down obscurely to profane men, *before they are initiated into the mysteries of knowledge* <note>original Greek: *prin ē telesthōsin orgioisin epistēmēs*</note>. Add to this that nature catches its own majesty in a secret silence, and offers us the nut of the chestnut hidden only within a husk and a rough covering; although in truth I affirm that no name has been imposed on things by Chemists which a person imbued with a perfect knowledge of **Polygraphy** <note>The study of various ways of writing or secret scripts</note>, **Etymology**, **Notation**, **Analogy**, and **Physical interpretation** would not understand at the first reading. They are so far from deserving a clarification of terms, or being rightly blamed for obscurity. 

**PHILERASTUS:** I do not object, yet in my mind, to use only that speech in teaching the sciences which only some **Cabalista** <note>A practitioner of Cabala; here used to mean someone who searches for secret or mystical meanings</note> can reach—like a **Delian swimmer** <note>original: *natator Delius*; an ancient proverb referring to someone who can navigate a text so deep and difficult they might "drown" without expertise</note>—seems to be nothing other than inviting men to a most sumptuously prepared dinner and then driving them away with masks and faked ghosts just as they are about to sit down. But my eyes hasten to see the preparations of those medicines which your books claim are superior to all others. 

**CHEMIST:** Come here then, and enter into this **Zodiac**. 

**PHILERASTUS:** I remember seeing a cleaner place; but for what reason do you call it a **Zodiac**? 

**CHEMIST:** Because here the *signatures* <term>signatures: the theory that the physical appearance or qualities of a substance indicate its medicinal use—for example, a heart-shaped leaf treating heart disease</term> of animals are kept—not those imaginary ones of the Astrologers, but true and vital ones. For I maintain that a double life exists in animals: one which works in themselves, and another which works in us; when the first vanishes, the second takes command: and it provides either a medicine for the alteration of the body, or food for its nutrition. 

**PHILERASTUS:** Truly, since you do not want me to be gullible, I deny that life exists in dead animals; for by the same reasoning, one could prove with no trouble that life exists in stones, metals, and stars, just as in beasts exhaling their souls. I, however, recognize only a threefold life: rational, sensitive, and vegetative: a thing which not only **Aristotle**, but every nation of physicians before **Paracelsus** was born has defended. 

**CHEMIST:** And yet in that you wander through a hallway of errors, you Athenian <note>The Chemist addresses Philerastus as "Athenian" to emphasize his reliance on classical Greek philosophy</note>. For your **Galen** asserts in clear words that life is either nothing other than powers, or the action of powers. If, therefore, power exists in dead animals, metals, stars, and stones: why should we not say that life exists in them? Is this opinion to be tolerated in Galen, and condemned in Paracelsus? Has not **Hippocrates** also noted throughout his books *On Diet* that the preservation of life is done through food, and its manifestation through operations? Thus, just as a human is said to live as long as they can perform the actions predestined for a human; so also as long as a **Magnet** <note>lodestone</note> attracts iron, amber attracts chaff, and **Rhubarb** attracts bile <note>a reference to rhubarb's traditional use as a purgative to expel "yellow bile"</note>, so long ought life to be attributed to them by a sober and dry judgment, not by a drunken...

### APOLOGETIC DIALOGUE

...human imagination.

**PHILERASTUS:** You define life, then, **Chemist**, as nothing other than an energy implanted *from within* <note>original Greek: *endothen*</note> all things; that is, a disposition of a human toward human actions, of stars toward astral ones, of Angels toward angelic ones, of brutes toward brutal ones, of plants toward those of plants, of minerals toward mineral ones, of metals toward metallic ones, of foods toward alimentary ones, and of medicines toward medical operations.

**CHEMIST:** You conclude correctly. And indeed, since death is nothing else but a perpetual cessation from preordained actions: why shall we admit that animals die completely before they are stripped of every action for whose sake they were predestined?

**PHILERASTUS:** Do animals, then, while participating in a soul, live for themselves? And once destitute of this soul, do they live afterward in us, and bring forth "magnetic" <note>In this context, "magnetic" refers to a sympathetic or attractive force through which a substance acts upon a specific part of the human body</note> actions? Is this what you mean?

**CHEMIST:** Precisely. For that reason, I speak of the "life" of a bull’s spleen not only as that which attracts, digests, and expels within the body of the bull, but also that which, in us, clears obstructions of the spleen and provokes the menses. In the same way, the "life" of a beaver's testicles <note>Castoreum, a substance from beaver glands, was a common historical remedy</note>—insofar as it pertains to us—is said to be that which cures "suffocations of the womb" <note>A historical term for hysteria or uterine distress</note> and aids a lingering fetus. So also the salts and oils of the human skull, of the elk, of vipers, of toads, and of crayfish have obtained a vital faculty against **Epilepsy**, **nightmares** <note>original: *incubum*</note>, **leprosy**, **plague**, **quartan fever**, etc. The logic of other things is no different; only he who does not feel the heat of a fire or does not see the roundness of the heavens fails to see that "life" exists within them.

**PHILERASTUS:** I understand, but where are you leading me now?

**CHEMIST:** Into the physics of plants, filled with the **Sulphur, Salt, and Mercury** <term>These are the 'Tria Prima' or three prime principles of Paracelsian chemistry: soul (Sulphur), body (Salt), and spirit (Mercury)</term> of all vegetables.

**PHILERASTUS:** But since you have granted me the favor that I may *speak freely* <note>original Greek: *parrhesiazein*</note> with you, I pray it is not troublesome to hear those things which our side is accustomed to object against these chemical extractions of vegetables.

**CHEMIST:** On the contrary; unless it is troublesome for you to speak, it is a pleasure for me to listen.

**PHILERASTUS:** They assert that they have practiced medicine for many years with the greatest success using the "crude" preparation of vegetables. They claim these have exercised their powers in purging, altering, and dispersing the humors <note>The four bodily fluids (blood, phlegm, yellow bile, black bile) that Galenic medicine sought to balance</note>—which are the primary works of the art—no less than these new preparations. Furthermore, they cry out that it is to be feared lest bodies be suddenly changed by those more "subtle" extractions, and that in the process, a great loss of **native heat** and **original moisture** <note>In traditional medicine, these were the vital internal "fuels" of life; their depletion was thought to cause aging and death</note> might occur. Nevertheless, they do not condemn Chemistry in any way; but they affirm they do not see why it should be extolled above all other preparations of the apothecary shops.

**CHEMIST:** Truly, I greatly praise that they do not condemn Chemistry, and I likewise disapprove of those who use only chemical medicines for every disease. For when one must wage war against mice or ants, the strength of a Pygmy would suffice; however, he who struggles with a lion or an Etolian boar has need of the hand of **Hector** or the strength of **Giants**. That is, in my opinion, he needs chemical medicines. Or, so that you may look upon their excellence as if placed before your eyes, tell me what kind of [excellence] the Galenists [see] in...

### ON CHEMICAL MEDICINE

...for wasting diseases <note>original: *atrophia*</note>, do they not command a specific diet? **PHILERASTUS:** Certainly; they prescribe that foods which produce healthy juices <note>original Greek: *euchymos*</note> should be boiled; they order their juice to be squeezed out, the fat separated, the waste rejected, and the nourishing part divided from the non-nourishing. For if the extraction of the best juices of foods is necessary to restore the body, how much more is it appropriate to cleanse and purify all medicines intended to alter the body? Consider also that the parts of some remedies are poisonous, some are destructive, many are useless, and none are health-giving except perhaps by accident. **PHILERASTUS:** What is this I hear? Are not the powers of medicines so entirely mixed together by nature that they cannot be drawn out separately by any human invention?

# APOLOGETIC DIALOGUE

This history can be applied to the most familiar aspects of human nature; for if things are presented while infected by the monthly waste <note>original: *menstruo*</note> in which they were born, they will leave behind various dregs. If these remains stay in the body for too long without being excreted, they will produce measles, smallpox, leprosy, and the most poisonous diseases. How much more, then, is it necessary to separate the pure from the impure, the dead from the living, and the destructive from the familiar and useful in <term>Hellebore</term> <note>a plant used as a powerful, often dangerous purgative</note>, <term>Colocynth</term> <note>bitter apple, a drastic laxative</note>, <term>Spurge Laurel</term> <note>original: *Coccognidio*</note>, <term>Turpeth</term> <note>a medicinal root</note>, <term>Spurge</term> <note>original: *Esula*</note>, <term>Rhubarb</term>, <term>Senna</term>, <term>Agaric</term> <note>a medicinal fungus from larch trees</note>, and finally in all purgatives? In these, there are not "many" good things as in the medicines of Egypt, but "a few good things mixed with many baneful ones." <note>original Greek: "πολλά... παῦρα μὲν ἐσθλὰ μεμιγμένα, πολλά δὲ λυγρά." A reference to Homer’s Odyssey regarding Egyptian drugs.</note> Indeed, not even the spices most familiar to the human heart are so perfectly purified by the hand of nature that they do not offer us the opportunity and impose the necessity of working to purify them further. 

For a pound of <term>cinnamon</term> yields only half an ounce of oil; a pound and a half of <term>cloves</term> yields only four ounces <note>original: *quartarium*</note>; an ounce of <term>nutmeg</term> yields half a drachm; and four ounces of <term>aloes wood</term> yields one drachm. Yet in that oil, or <term>sulphur</term> <note>the flammable, "soul" principle in alchemy</note>, all that aromatic power lies hidden as if in a certain fundamental and spiritual moisture. The same logic holds in the extraction of <term>anise</term>, <term>cumin</term>, <term>carrot seed</term> <note>original: *dauci*</note>, <term>fennel</term>, <term>roses</term>, <term>saffron</term>, and so on: the parts that remain as the smallest essence are the ones into which the entire power is channeled. Thus, it can be said of them just as it is said of ants: **Nature is greatest in the smallest things.** 

If, therefore, the secret power <note>original: *arcanum*</note>—whether it be a purgative, a sweat-inducer, or something to provoke urine or vomiting—resides in the <term>sulphur</term> alone, what business do we have with the <term>mercury</term> <note>the "spirit" or fluid principle</note> or the <term>salt</term> <note>the "body" or solid principle</note>? If it is in the <term>salt</term> or the <term>mercury</term>, why is the <term>sulphur</term> given? Since eighty useless, non-purging grains are found in one hundred and twenty grains of <term>rhubarb</term>, why do the <term>Galenists</term> <note>followers of traditional Greco-Roman medicine</note> not remove them when they are about to purge the sick? Why do they mix them in? Does it seem right to serve the shells when the nut is what ought to be eaten? Since even in a pound of <term>saffron</term> ten ounces of poison are detected (which the <term>Chemists</term> were the first to discover), then unless your <term>Athenians</term> <note>the Chemist's nickname for the traditional academic doctors</note> could play with human skin with impunity, they would have long ago removed those poisons by separating the foreign matter through a tincture. 

Therefore, Guest, acknowledge now the excellence of <term>Chemistry</term>: by its benefit you will learn **Living Anatomy**, which illuminates the <term>salts</term>, <term>mercuries</term>, and <term>sulphurs</term> of simple substances—indeed, it reveals their <term>influences</term>, <term>signatures</term> <note>the physical signs on a plant indicating its healing use</note>, <term>powers</term>, <term>stars</term>, <term>lives</term>, and <term>resurrections</term>.

**PHILERASTUS:** Truly, the brilliance, elegance, and richness of your Chemists have so drawn me over to your side that there is great doubt whether I shall ever be enticed back to the school of <term>Galen</term>. However, you have not answered this: the common remedies have had the best success, and their use has been healthy for many men.

**CHEMIST:** Why should they not be? Nevertheless, just as a knife cuts wood in one way and an axe in another, so too we quickly and with almost no effort immediately remove those infirmities which...

### ON CHEMICAL MEDICINE

...to eradicate these, the Galenists would not suffice in the space of even one month. I am not lying, stranger, I am feigning nothing; and I will prove that the matter is so through the voice of practice and the weight of reasons. Must one not, in any medical operation, act calmly, quickly, and safely <note>original Greek: ἡσύχως, ταχέως, ἀσφαλῶς</note>—that is, pleasantly, quickly, and safely?

PH. One must indeed, for our senses suggest this very thing, and Hippocrates commands it. But why is it not possible to achieve these three goals with common medicines?

CH. Because fate does not will it. For if someone's body must be purged, with what instrument would you say it should be done, O Athenian?

PH. Perhaps with Rhubarb, Aloe, Senna, <term>Mechoacan</term> <note>a Mexican root used as a purgative</note>, <term>Agaric</term> <note>a medicinal fungus</note>, <term>Polypody</term> <note>a type of fern</note>, Oak Mistletoe, <term>Epithyme</term> <note>dodder of thyme, a parasitic plant</note>, Cassia pulp, or Manna.

CH. These medicines are safe, I admit, but they are not pleasant enough because of their excessive bitterness, sweetness, or at least their excessive quantity.

PH. Then I shall resort to stronger ones: <term>Scammony</term> <note>a harsh resinous juice from a vine root</note>, <term>Turpeth</term> <note>a medicinal root</note>, Spurge Laurel, Spurge, or <term>Elaterium</term> <note>a potent purgative derived from the juice of the squirting cucumber</note>, which neither present an unpleasant taste nor require a large dose.

CH. But if they are administered alone, you will not purge safely; if they are seasoned with many spices as the moderns usually do, the purging will be no more pleasant than if you had administered three drams of Rhubarb or three ounces of Manna. Thus, if you use mild purgatives administered in the common quantity, you lose speed; if you use stronger ones, you lose safety; and if you use either one with Galenic safety, you lose the pleasure because of the excessive dose or the foul taste and smell.

PH. But in the apothecary's shop, we have various purgative compositions mixed with such skill that they are thought second to none for evacuating the body quickly, safely, and pleasantly.

CH. Ah, mention your shop no more! If I were to examine it without prejudice and—as the Greeks say—"without passions" <note>original Greek: ἄνευ παθῶν</note>, I would easily prove that no purgative composition of the ancients possesses those virtues that Hippocrates desired. For if you offer the *Hiera* of Galen <note>original: *Hieram Galeni*, also known as "Holy Bitters," a famously foul-tasting ancient medicine</note>—an invention of the gods, if the gods please!—what could be imagined more offensive to the stomach, the nose, and the palate? What could be more unpleasant to all the limbs? I candidly and truly admit that those <term>electuaries</term> <note>medicinal pastes mixed with honey or syrup</note> like *Hamech*, *Diaphenica*, *Catholica*, and the rest, were so hated by many patients (while I, unskilled in Chemistry, was forced to use them) that even I myself began to be hated by them; by chance, simply seeing me would move them to vomit. Although these things were unpleasant enough on their own, they are administered in such great quantities by the men of your school that they seem not to be treating humans, but choking horses. O, the unhappy condition of princes, who offer their bodies as lodging houses—or rather tombs—for such impurities! What shall I say of your pills, as large as musket balls? <note>original: *globulo ferentariorum*, referring to the bullets used by light-armed skirmishers</note>. You are accustomed to prescribing them in the number of seven in honor of seven-hilled Rome, or nine in the name of the Muses; you never use an even number, because "God delights in an odd number." You have pills of lead, gold, "useless" pills, "very useful" pills, pills of darkness, pills of light, and the pills "without which I wish to be"... <note>The Chemist is making a pun on the famous *Pilulae sine quibus esse nolo* ("Pills without which I do not wish to be"), suggesting he'd rather be without them entirely.</note>

<summary>The Chemist critiques traditional Galenic purgatives for being bulky, foul-tasting, and dangerously inconsistent, arguing they fail the Hippocratic standard of acting quickly, safely, and pleasantly. He mocks the large doses and superstitious numbering of apothecary pills, contrasting them with the efficiency of chemical medicine.</summary>

### APOLOGETIC DIALOGUE

...which I do not wish them to be, once they are summoned: and thus with beautiful names you cover up the most unpleasant medicines, as if hiding an asp behind a leaf. I will say nothing of syrups—long and short, magistral <note>custom-made for a specific patient</note>, common, and various others; I know not whether they are the ravings of learned men or the games of women. I pass over aromatic confections likewise, for nothing is more childish: for if you infuse into boiled sugar a little distilled oil of cinnamon, anise, cumin, pearls, amber, musk, or roses, I will be your slave if you do not prescribe a more pleasant and effective medicine than those compound confections like "diacinnamon," "dianise," "diacumin," "diamargarite," "diamber," "diamusk," or "diarosate aromatic" <note>Traditional compound medicines often used the prefix "dia-", from the Greek for "made of," to denote their primary ingredient</note>. 

PH. Truly, you do not just examine our pharmacy; you exhaust it! Yet indeed, my own mind has also shrunk from those confections, seeing them as either ineffective or full of danger. For whenever I wish to purge bile, I am accustomed to write in this manner: 

*Take: 2 drams of choice rhubarb, 1 scruple each of Indian spikenard and cinnamon; let them be infused in endive water overnight; to the strained liquid add 1 ounce of solutive syrup of roses and 1.5 ounces <note>original: "sequunciam," likely a contraction of "sesquiunciam"</note> of syrup of chicory with rhubarb.*

Or thus: *Take: 2 ounces of choice manna, 2 scruples of rhubarb infused in endive juice, 5 drams of <term>diacatholicon</term> <note>a universal laxative electuary</note>, 2 drams of <term>Tryphera persica</term> <note>a traditional complex electuary used for purging</note>, with chicory water in which 1 dram of <term>agaric</term> <note>a medicinal fungus</note> was previously infused; let a potion be made.* 

If, however, the form of a pill is more convenient, I write thus from the *Medical Syntax of Colmar*: 

*Take: 4 scruples of <term>species Hiera</term> <note>literally "holy powder," a very bitter purgative</note>, half a dram of choice rhubarb, half a scruple each of hartshorn, ivory shavings, and cinnamon, with enough syrup of agrimony to make 9 pills.*

*Take: 1 scruple and 12 grains of tincture of rhubarb; 3 drops each of distilled oil of spikenard and lign-aloes <note>aromatic wood of the aloe tree</note>.* 

If indeed phlegm is to be evacuated, prescribe: 

*Half a dram of tincture of <term>turpeth</term> <note>a medicinal root</note>; 6 drops of oil of anise; 2 drops of oil of cloves. Mix.* 

Or thus: *Take 16 grains of tincture of spurge; 2 drops each of oil of anise and cinnamon.* 

Whenever you purge black bile <note>the humor associated with melancholy</note>: 

*Take half a dram of tincture of Oriental senna, 5 grains of tincture of black hellebore, 2 drops each of oil of anise and fennel, and 1 drop each of parsley and cinnamon. Mix.* 

And thus with a tiny amount of medicine you will accomplish more than if you had instituted those most tedious recipes. Such is also the condition of our aromatics, diuretics, <term>diaphoretics</term> <note>medicines that induce sweating</note>, <term>anodynes</term> <note>painkillers</note>, and emetics; which you will find explained more fully in our chemical <term>Antidote-book</term> <note>a pharmacopoeia or collection of remedies</note> soon to be printed (unless I am deterred by the ingratitude of men), and carefully applied to every suffering. 

PH. Truly, these remedies of yours are superior to those of Sennert, Cordus, Wecker <note>Famous medical authorities: Daniel Sennert, Valerius Cordus, and Johann Jacob Wecker</note>, and even the Augsburg pharmacists and all the formulas of the spice-sellers, in the allure of their taste and flavor, the smallness of the dose, and the speed of their operation—as even we most stubborn Athe[nians]...

O, the unhappy condition of princes, who offer up their bodies as inns, or rather as tombs, for such impurities!

Lead pills, golden pills <note>Pills were often coated in lead or gold foil to preserve them or for prestige</note>, useless pills, useful pills, pills of darkness, pills of light, without which I wish to be...

*Take four scruples of the species Hiera <note>Hiera Picra, or the "Holy Bitter," a traditional purgative powder of aloe and canella</note>, half a dram of selected rhubarb, half a scruple each of deer horn, ivory shavings, and cinnamon, with a sufficient quantity of syrup of eupatorium <note>A syrup made from the herb Agrimony or Hemp-agrimony</note>: let nine pills be made.*

If, however, phlegm must be evacuated, prescribe: 

*Half a dram of Tincture of Turpeth <note>A root used for purging</note>, six drops of oil of anise, and two drops of oil of clove. Mix.* 

Or like this: 

*Take 16 grains of Tincture of Solar Spurge, and two drops each of oil of anise and cinnamon.* 

Whenever you would purge black bile <note>In the theory of the Four Humors, "black bile" was associated with melancholy and chronic illness</note>:

And thus, with a tiny amount of medicine, you will accomplish more than if you had prepared those most tedious recipes. Such is the condition of our aromatic, diuretic, sweat-inducing, pain-relieving, and vomit-inducing remedies: which you will find explained more fully in our *Chemical Antidote-book*, soon to be printed (unless I am deterred by the ingratitude of men), and diligently applied to every suffering.

### ON CHEMICAL MEDICINE

I shall easily prove my case by citing the testimonies of princes, counts, and other heroes, as well as citizens and even theologians. For not only have these remedies begun to be used and valued in the courts of the Emperor and the King of Denmark, but they are also so uniquely sought after by our courtiers and the more sensible part of mankind that they constantly grieve when they cannot always use them. But just as the sharpest and best razor, when used by a foolish surgeon, inflicts a lethal rather than a healing wound, so too do all the safest and best chemical remedies have a bad reputation because of the ignorance of those who use them; and "the craftsman's error" <note>original Greek: *kai to tou technitou sphalma*</note>—against all sense of justice—"is considered to be the fault of the art" <note>original Greek: *nomizetai einai tēs technēs*</note>. **PH.** I will not, I say; for what does this have to do with a physician? 

**CH.** Skillfully applied, they make one blessed, and—to use the common saying—almost "equal to a god" <note>original Greek: *isotheon*</note>.

**CH.** Beware of saying that, lest perhaps you inflict such a wound upon both the ancient and modern schools as will not later admit a scar <note>An idiom meaning a wound so deep it can never be healed or covered up</note>.

**CH.** Fine! As if you do not likewise give plants and animals to men as medicine only when they have first lost that vegetative soul.

**CH.** On the contrary, your friends err more truly with you than the Athenians cry out. And to speak of stones, who will deny that those invisible spirits of the **magnet** <note>original: "magnes"</note> are more subtle than ours, by which it attracts iron from far off...

**PH.** <note>The Physician; however, the context of the argument suggests the Chemist (CH.) takes over here to defend mineral use, despite the OCR's "PH." label, as he begins listing the benefits of metals.</note> On the contrary, Athenian <note>In this period, "Athenians" often referred to the traditionalist medical faculty of Paris, who styled their city the "New Athens" while strictly adhering to Galenic medicine.</note>, both of their opinions regarding harmful and harmless metallic substances are too dreadful to even slightly resemble the truth. For long experience has proven that **gold** <note>original: "aurum"</note> does much to strengthen the heart, **silver** <note>original: "argentum"</note> the brain, **iron** <note>original: "ferrum"</note> the spleen, and **copper** <note>original: "cuprum"</note> the liver—whether they are quenched while red-hot in an appropriate liquid, or administered after being reduced into their **saffron** <note>original: "crocum" — a term for a fine metal oxide powder</note> and essence.

Furthermore, **glassified Lead** <note>original: "Saturnus vitrificatus" — Lead was associated with the planet Saturn</note> (not otherwise than if it were a kind of bile) moves the bowels; **sulfur** nourishes the lungs, and the **liquid of crystals** flushes the kidneys like some excellent whey. **CH.** <note>The Chemist</note> Beautifully put! As if you do not give plants and animals to men only after they have already lost their vegetative soul.

**PH.** But when I said that Mineral or metallic medicines have no kinship with the human body, I wanted this to be understood: they do not contribute to the **restoration of the spirits** <note>In early medicine, "spirits" were subtle fluids that carried life and sensation through the body</note>. Nor do I see how their cries can finally be proven false. For the parts of all metals, stones, and minerals are so **thick** <note>coarse or dense</note> that they cannot enter into our body, which is very **rare** <note>porous or thin-textured</note> and endowed with the subtlest spirits.

**CH.** Indeed, your friends err more truly than the Athenians cry out. For certain minerals pass through not only the human body, but through gold, tin, and lead like a kind of lightning. **Quicksilver** <note>Mercury</note> proves that I say nothing far from the truth by its own example; for its cold spirits strike a man from far off with paralysis, while its hot spirits affect the distiller with a remarkable burning of the head. And to speak of stones, who will deny that those invisible spirits of the **magnet** are subtler than ours, by which it [attracts] iron...

Surely wine pressed from grapes is raw; but cooked by the heat of the sun it becomes sweet and **<term>pleasant to drink<note>original: *ἡδύποτον* (hēdypoton)</note>**. ...once burned, they lay aside the poison implanted in them and are rendered healthy by the fire. Furthermore, experience teaches that many medicines are most sharp and hostile to our bodies as long as they retain their old nature; but once tamed by the violence of fire, they become suitable for healing. I see you gather from those words: that arsenic, mercury, antimony, and any other eroding and highly poisonous metallic and mineral substances obtain a healthy power by the benefit of fire, and if they are reduced to their salt (just like vipers <note>It was a common belief in early modern medicine that the flesh of a venomous viper, when processed or burned into "salts," became an antidote to its own poison and a powerful cure-all.</note>), they lay aside all malignancy, putrefaction, poison, corrosion, and sharpness. **CH.** You gather correctly: and so that you may believe the same, you may choose no poison from the whole storehouse of Nature which I would refuse to drink after it has undergone **fixation** <term>fixation<note>In alchemy, the process of making a volatile substance "fixed" or stable so that it no longer evaporates or changes when exposed to fire.</note></term> in the fire. **PH.** Do you then condemn antimony, vitriol, arsenic, mercury, and other medicines of that kind that are not yet fixed? **CH.** Most clearly, unless they happen to be mixed with those things which either soften their sharpness or restrain their malignancy like a bridle; for in this way their readiness to harm is removed, and their medicinal faculty, having found a suitable vehicle, as it were, will be exalted. **PH.** I easily agree. But two doubts still trouble me, which I wish to be quickly uprooted. First, I do not understand: by what reasoning do medicines burned even unto fixation retain their medicinal power? Second, I fear that from long burning much **empyreuma** <term>empyreuma<note>A term for the "burnt" smell or taste of organic matter; in Galenic medicine, this was often considered a toxic byproduct of improper preparation.</note></term> is acquired—something that no right-thinking philosopher would deny is most unpleasant and very harmful to us. **CH.** I will uproot both doubts by the living voice of both your Galen <note>Galen of Pergamon (c. 129–216 AD), the ancient Greek physician whose theories dominated medicine until the chemical revolution.</note> and our own experience. For who has ever smelled empyreuma or noticed a failure to act in Theriacal salts <note>Salts derived from Theriac, a famous ancient "universal" medicine made of dozens of ingredients.</note> that receive so many species of flowers and spices? Only this is lacking: that they do not act with such great danger; and in my opinion, it is more desirable to lack that danger than to enjoy it. Understand, therefore, that this is the nature of fire—not just any fire, but the chemist's fire: so that it always retains the **arcanum** <term>arcanum<note>The "secret" or essential healing principle of a substance, which the chemist seeks to liberate from raw matter.</note></term> lurking now in the salt, now in the sulfur, now in the Mercury, and never allows it to fly away. As for empyreuma, **Pyrotechnia** <note>original: *Pyrotechnia*. Literally "the art of fire," used here as a synonym for chemistry or alchemy.</note> shows us this: the longer medicines remain in the fire, the less "burnt matter" they have in them, because the foreign sulfur has vanished through long combustion. **PH.** You have conquered me, Chemist; and you have conquered me so thoroughly that I, who sought to fish out your skill with certain sneaky little questions, had intended to return to Galenic principles; now, I will not refuse to serve a perpetual servitude there, and I will take the place of a cinder-cleaner, a clay-worker, or a watchman—in short, I will accept any condition that helps in learning this most excellent science. **CH.** You do well, Athenian <note>A scholarly epithet meaning a "learned man" or "wise seeker."</note>; for as the comic poet said: *There is a God who sees us and governs all things; to the well-deserving, good will happen; to the ill-deserving, the equal shall be given.* <note>original: *Eſt qui nos videt atque omnia moderatur Deus; Bene merenti, bene eveniet; male merenti par erit.* A quote from the Roman playwright Plautus.</note> Therefore, keep those secrets you have seen to yourself, mindful of that...

<header>APOLOGETIC DIALOGUE</header>

The truly golden law of Hippocrates states: <note>original: "τὰ ἱερὰ πράγματα ἱεροῖσιν ἀνθρώποισι δείκνυται, τοῖς δὲ βεβήλοισιν, οὐ θέμις"</note> "Sacred things are revealed to sacred men, but for the profane, it is not permitted." **PH.** You warn one who is mindful; does anything further remain? **CH.** Only this: that you never hereafter be called Philerastus <note>Philerastus likely means "Lover of Pleasure" or "Lover of Erastus."</note>, but Philalethes <note>Philalethes means "Lover of Truth." Come now, I wish you to be the prefect of the distillation province, and to preside over my remaining servants. I must hasten to a certain sick man living far from here. If in the meantime any small difficulty troubles you, signify it by letter; and I shall take diligent care that it is removed by the very first messenger. Farewell. **PHILAL.** And farewell to you; return to us even swifter than Pegasus; for until I embrace you again, even if I embrace you tomorrow, it feels like an age. Farewell.

# FIVE MEDICINAL LETTERS
## WRITTEN BY THE SAME AUTHOR.

->TO PHILALETHES HIS BROTHER.<-
->*The Chemist sends greetings.*<-

You write that a certain Galenist <note>A follower of Galen, the 2nd-century physician whose theories dominated medicine for over a millennium. Galenists usually opposed the "new" chemical medicines.</note> has come to you, equipped with a great number of insults and lies, as if with thonged spears. Although he does not demand that a shield be brought out, but rather a lash, it has nevertheless pleased me to find time to answer him, so long as this sick man with whom I now stay grants me some leisure. *He objects, you say, that the Chemists entirely depart from the authority of the fathers:* a thing which, if they do in some matters, I judge to be an honorable shame; but if in all (as he maliciously invents), I deem it most unfair. For I strongly approve that saying of Hippocrates, and I praise the opinion of all physicians: <note>original: "ἥνπερ ἐκ περιπτώσεως φοιτήσῃ τὴν ἀρχὴν, καὶ τὴν καταφορὴν ἐκ τῶν φαινομένων μεθοδεύῃ"</note> "Indeed, if one proceeds from a chance occurrence at the start, and directs the course of treatment based on the things observed." For truly, an argument flowing from demonstration and practical work is elegant, while one proceeding from imagination alone is inelegant and fruitless. It is no different with the Chemists, Philalethes, who leave Galen in various places with the same freedom with which he himself once defected from the opinion of his ancestors regarding the "single element." But let us hear the rest of the insults with which he has set out to burn down my "Chemical Palace" <note>likely referring to the author's body of work or a specific laboratory structure.</note> as if with a fire of evils. *He says that Chemists are ignorant of all more polished learning: that they have not read the Greek authors, have scarcely greeted the Arabs from the threshold, and have been taught only by Paracelsus—whom he calls a drunkard, a mage, an impostor, a quack, a wandering charlatan, an architect of obscurities, and one taught by dross, earth, and hatred.* Finally, he has vomited out a great flood of such words—I know not whether from his heart or from a more foul mouth. But, lest he think us only spirited in the chemical wrestling-ground,
