Regarding the vices of Paracelsus, I offer this as a response: It is rare to see a man without vice; I love him most who errs the least. But surely he must be a rather meddling Galenist, and no less wicked, who carries a "serpent's eye" in the breast of Theophrastus <note>Theophrastus was the birth name of Paracelsus. To carry a "serpent's eye" means to look with malice or extreme scrutiny at another's faults while ignoring one's own.</note> while meanwhile failing to see his own crimes. However, even if he were shameful and most contaminated by every name of vice: I have often said it is the duty and sign of a Chemist not to imitate anyone or anything blindly, but to seize what is good and transfer it to the use of life. For just as Venus, offering and attaching herself, excites a lustful youth, but does not burn a chaste and modest young man: so too the vices of Paracelsus or any other author perhaps delight a wicked mind, but they do not move a Chemical or purified mind. Natural Kabbalah, Pyrotechny <note>The art of using fire in chemical extractions and transformations.</note>, the exaltation of medicines <note>A chemical process intended to increase the potency or purity of a substance.</note>, the contemplation of physics, festivity, wonderful invention, the singular genius of Paracelsus; these delight, capture, allure, and attract Chemists. Unnatural magic, drunkenness, slander, contempt for method—all these things are rebuked by Chemists, not only in those Greeks and pagans, but even in Paracelsus himself. But so that I may reveal his own gods to that slanderer, whoever he may be, I assert that there is no vice in Paracelsus that could not also be ascribed to his own Hippocrates and especially to Galen, or some equivalent of it.

*Paracelsus was obscure:* I admit it, and the cause demands it. But Hippocrates was also most obscure, and neither his words nor his meanings were understood by Galen. *He ignored method:* Hippocrates also did not know it, or at least despised it, while he thrust upon us a raw, undigested, unrefined medicine, full of confusion and tautologies. Perhaps he did so with the intention that the opportunity for all labor should not be taken away from his posterity, whose laziness he foresaw. He adds further: *that Paracelsus sometimes sets down contrary principles; and that Proteus <note>A Greek sea-god capable of changing his shape at will.</note> does not differ from himself as much as Paracelsus differs from Paracelsus.* But unless pardon is given for this <term>mnemonic</term> <note>original: μνημονικῷ (mnēmonikō). But *Paracelsus was also a magus, an impostor, and had commerce with demons. He indulged in drunkenness so much that for whole days and nights...*

# Thomas Muffet.

Britain, though divided from the rest of the world, flourishes as the mistress and protector of all the arts. Here the sciences reside, here Medicine dwells, here is the temple of Hygeia and Panacea <note>The Greek goddesses of health and universal remedy.</note>. Here Hippocrates, an exile from his own people, is welcomed, and the works of Galen are polished by the writings of those whom he himself once called "bears, lions, boars, and utter barbarians" <note>Galen, writing from the perspective of the Roman Empire, often looked down upon northern European "barbarians."</note>. Therefore, while I do not personally fault that multilingual skill found lacking in Paracelsus, I would not want it to be so highly praised by that Galenist slanderer as if it were essential to the nature of a good physician. For it is not so much <term>multilingualism</term> <note>original: *polyglottia*</note> as <term>effective action</term> <note>original: *polypraxia*</note> that makes a doctor; and a doctor’s work is hired by the sick for his skill, not his oratory. Furthermore, since many of the Greeks knew no language except their own native tongue, a difficult but necessary choice is given to the Galenist: either he must condemn the "Atlases" <note>The foundational pillars or supporters.</note> of his own school, or he must frankly admit that a man trained only in his native tongue can be a leader of medicine.

Moreover, his own Hippocrates, whom he pretends to love, contends that these seven things suffice for perfect medicine: *Nature, instruction, a place fit for study, education from childhood, devotion, industry, and time.* He is correct; for things proceed under Nature’s guidance, but if she resists, all efforts become void. Nature is like the field; instructions take the place of seeds; education from a tender age corresponds to the farmer who sows at the right time; a place fit for study corresponds to the air that supplies nourishment to things growing from the earth; devotion is the cultivation; industry is the servant of cultivation; and finally, time strengthens all these in the physician so that he may be perfectly nourished. 

When these seven qualities coincide in a student of medicine, Hippocrates says he can become a physician, traveling through cities <term>not in word only</term> <note>original: *mē logō monon*</note>, <term>but also in deed</term> <note>original: *alla kai ergō*</note>. However, he does not require that <term>excessive talk in many tongues</term> <note>original: *polyglottologian*</note>, which perhaps adorns a doctor but does not make one. Such a skill is more useful for establishing the elegance of his person than the essence of being a doctor. And indeed, what other benefit does that skill bring, except that we may seem learned in words when the facts are lacking—which is a mark of foolish ambition—or so that we may understand Arabic or Greek authors, which is quite fruitless? For when all these authors have been read through, what else do we carry away, I ask, than several bundles of errors, obscurities, sophisms, lies, contradictions, and the hindrances of deceptive experiments, in exchange for a single ear of truth? This will be the praise of the multilingual, this their ornament—and thus it was necessary to describe them. If they have any use in medicine, it is certainly this: that they know how to translate books from one language to another. This will not only fail to increase their skill in medicine but will even greatly diminish it, while they are forced to devote their labor to words, neglecting facts and practice.

*But let us proceed further: "Paracelsus was ignorant of Logic, Physics, Astrology, and Geometry."* And what shall I say of those followers of Galen, none of whom has defined his own art in a way that satisfies others or himself? For one contends it is an art; another, a science; a third...

# THOMAS MOFFET #

...Britain, though divided from the rest of the world, flourishes as the mistress and protector of all the arts. Here the sciences sit; here Medicine makes her home; here is the temple of **Hygieia** <note>The Greek goddess of health.</note> and **Panacea** <note>The Greek goddess of universal remedy.</note>; here Hippocrates is welcomed while in exile, and the works of Galen are polished by the writings of those very people whom he himself called bears, lions, wild boars, and utter barbarians. Therefore, regarding that multilingual skill found lacking in Paracelsus: just as I do not find fault with it, I would not wish it to be so highly praised by that Galenist slanderer, as if it were essential to the being of a good physician. For a physician is made not so much by **much-speaking** <note>original: "πολυγλωττίᾳ" (polyglottia)</note> as by **much-doing** <note>original: "πολυπραγίᾳ" (polypragia) - referring to clinical practice and experience.</note>; a doctor is hired by the sick for his labor, not his oratory. Furthermore, since many of the Greeks knew no language other than their own native tongue, a difficult but necessary choice is given to the Galenist: either he must condemn the "Atlases" <note>The foundational pillars or supporters.</note> of his own school, or he must frankly confess that a man instructed only in his father's language can indeed be a leader of medicine.

Moreover, his beloved Hippocrates—whom he only pretends to love—contends that these seven things suffice for perfect medicine: *Nature, instruction, a place suitable for study, education from childhood, zeal, industry, and time.* And rightly so; for they proceed with Nature as their leader, and if she resists, all efforts become void. For Nature is like the field; instructions take the place of seeds; education from a tender age corresponds to the farmer who sows at the right time; a place suitable for study corresponds to the air which provides nourishment to things springing from the earth; zeal is the cultivation; industry is the servant of that cultivation; and finally, time strengthens all these things in the physician so that he may be perfectly nourished.

Hippocrates says that when these seven things come together in a student of medicine, he can become a physician who travels through cities **not in word only, but in deed** <note>original: "μὴ λόγῳ μόνον... ἀλλὰ κ' ἔργῳ"</note>. He does not require that **many-tongued skill** <note>original: "πολυγλωττίαν" (polyglottian)</note>, which perhaps adorns a doctor but does not make him one; it is more useful for the elegance of his person than for establishing the essence of a physician. Truly, what other benefit does such skill bring, except that we might appear learned in words when the actual substance is lacking (which is a mark of foolish ambition), or so that we may understand Arabic or Greek authors (which is indeed quite fruitful)? 

For I ask you, after reading them all, what else do we carry away but several bundles of errors, obscurities, sophistries, lies, contradictions, and various hindrances of deceptive experiments, all for a single ear of truth? This shall be the praise of the multilingual, this their ornament; this is how they ought to be described. If they have any use in medicine, it will surely be this: that they know how to turn books from one language into another. This will not only fail to increase their skill in medicine but will greatly diminish it, while they are forced to devote their labor to words, having neglected actual things and practice.

But let us proceed further: *Paracelsus was ignorant of Logic, Physics, Astrology, and Geometry.* And what shall I say of those followers of Galen, none of whom has defined his own art in a way that satisfies either others or himself? For this man contends it is an art; that man, a science; a third...

# CHEMICAL LETTERS

...both and neither, but in a certain way; the fourth defines it by its end; the fifth by its work; the sixth by its outcome; the seventh says *Medicine is the art of preserving health*: but he adds this as well, *in the human body*. As if indeed the nature and name of medicine belonged more to this than to the curing of plants, or even to <term>veterinary medicine</term> <note>original Greek: κτηνἰατρικῇ</note>. Truly, as for the Physics of the Pagans, since it is of no use even to Christians, I strongly desire it to be unknown not only to Paracelsus but also to me. Add also that no <term>axiom</term> <note>original: ἀξἰωμα - a self-evident truth or established principle.</note> is placed so firmly within it that it cannot be instantly shattered by a single argument, like a potter’s little jars at the strike of a pebble. Our astrologers too, about to predict (if it pleases the gods) on what day, what hour, and what moment a patient will die or recover, stumble upon a stone themselves as they go out, and, unaware, return home ridiculous with broken legs. Such ignorance is also found among the Geometers, that they claim to hold the exact circumference of the earth and sea; yet they know as much as the most ignorant about how far London is from the little town of Iselin. 

Because that Galenist does not blush to call Paracelsus the "hatred of heaven and earth," he seems to have jumped over the barriers of shame with great effort. For he was most dear to heaven on account of his supreme skill in astronomy; and dear to the earth on account of his living anatomy of mixtures, from which he led forth not that common little soul, but another **operative** power, gifted with various tinctures, stars, influences, and powers. These things I had to write in favor of Chemistry against that Galenic slanderer: whom I do not doubt would now buy for much gold the fact that a Chemist knows nothing, even if nothing is worth so much that he should repent of his insults, since he is abusive by the decrees of fate and his own will. This alone I add and command as a <term>finishing touch</term> <note>original: *colophonis loco* - literally "in the place of a colophon," meaning the final stroke or peak of an argument.</note>: if he does not stop snarling at the doors any longer, let him be driven from the house as quickly as possible: or at least let him be sent to that place where iron is accustomed to be worn away by iron. Farewell, and honor this "Sparta" which you have obtained with your virtue, just as you have done before. Given at London, the 4th day before the Calends of February, 1583 <note>January 29, 1583.</note>.

### TO PHILALETHES THE GERMAN
->Greetings from a Chemist.<-

You have written again and again that you do not wish that Galenist to be driven from the house: yet he finds nothing to blame in you except this: that you seem to rely on the senses alone for the thorough learning of medicine. Truly, if he knew how much weight the testimony of the senses carries regarding physical things, he would become more silent than a fish and would not blush to feel and act just as you do. For had it been without the senses, reason would never have conceived of any movement of nature; but by their ministry, reason was led as if by the hand from singular things to a knowledge of a more universal nature, and established various laws both of things and of sciences. Hence reasoning is not undeservedly called by Hippocrates, **"a certain synthetic memory of things perceived through the senses."** <note>original Greek: μνήμη τὶς ξυνθετικὴ τῶν μετ’ αἰσθήσεως ληφθέντων</note>. For the <term>intellect</term> <note>original: διάνοια - the faculty of discursive reason.</note>, seeking its beginning from singular things, finally reaches the truth...

## THOMAS MUFFET

...leads to the same end; however, as often as it proceeds not from evident observation but from a probable fiction of reason, it leads a man onto a path (if I may use the word of Hippocrates) that is clearly impassable. Indeed, in the management of physical things, Christ himself, the source of all reason, 
<margin>John 20:27</margin>
<margin>Luke 24:39</margin>
openly teaches that the greatest faith must be placed in the senses. For when that "Twin" Thomas doubted somewhat concerning the resurrection of Christ, He said: <note>original Greek: φέρε, τὸν δάκτυλόν σου ὧδε, καὶ ἰδὲ τὰς χεῖράς μου, καὶ φέρε τὴν χεῖρά σου, καὶ βάλε εἰς τὴν πλευράν μου καὶ μὴ ἄπιστος γίνου, ἀλλὰ πισός</note> "Bring your finger here, and see my hands; and bring your hand, and put it into my side; and do not be unbelieving, but believing." And again: <note>original Greek: ψηλαφήσατέ με καὶ ἴδετε. ὅτι πνεῦμα σάρκα καὶ ὀστέα οὐκ ἔχει, καθὼς ἐμὲ θεωρεῖτε ἔχοντα.</note> "Handle me and see, for a spirit does not have flesh and bones, as you see me having." Would that by the example of so true a Teacher, philosophers had established their physics according to the rule of the senses, rather than the dream of their own imagination! 

If you were to ask these men now by what means sensible bodies are made from non-sensible elements, or how acidic things are made from tasteless ones, they do not answer, "Come, touch, see; apply your eye and finger"; instead, they say "Believe, contemplate, imagine," and learn that Aristotelian rule: <note>original Greek: δεῖ μὲν τὸν μανθάνοντα πιστεύειν</note> "The learner must believe." Truly, this is an illiberal saying, and quite unworthy of so great a patron of philosophy. For nothing more disastrous can happen to a novice physician than to build the foundation of his art upon credulity, mere thought, opinion, uncertainty, sand, a marsh, or <term>the Syrtes</term> <note>A reference to the Syrtes, dangerous quicksands off the coast of North Africa, used here as a metaphor for an unstable foundation.</note>. 

How much better it would be to imitate those men who, when they are about to build, look at various houses—those that are soundly, elegantly, conveniently, and precisely made—so that by seeking an example from the best of each, they may build a similar dwelling for themselves at their own expense. For this reason, they make a selection of the foundation from one, the walls from another, and elsewhere the <term>private chambers</term> <note>original: zetarum — specifically heated rooms or suites in a classical house.</note>, the frontage of the courtyards, or the roofing. If they are even able to discover and add something of their own, that is counted as a gain and will be a great honor to them. For why should it not be that, just as masters of architecture have added many excellent things unknown to our fathers, it should also be so in medicine? For medicine is so much a rival to architecture that they use the same method of construction. 

Therefore, do not believe even the most ancient physician, nor even Apollo himself, any further than he gives a true <term>demonstration</term> <note>original: ἀπόδειξιν (apodeixin) — a formal proof or logical demonstration.</note>, sanctioned by the reckoning of the senses and the voice of long observation. Indeed, that great Galen, the "God of the Galenists," affirms in distinct words against the Sophists that all physical axioms take their origin from the senses and through the senses, and if we depart from them, no demonstration will remain. 

But he objects that *it is hardly safe to follow the judgment of the senses, because they are so frequently and easily deceived. For if the organ is impaired, the medium corrupted, the object placed too near or too far, or the manner of receiving it is unfit, then not only the ears, but the tongue, nostrils, skin, and even the very sentinels of the eyes are mistaken. Indeed, among a thousand men enjoying health (as far as can be judged), few perceive perfectly, and in the same way as others; for what is acidic to one is harsh to another; what seems sharp to one, seems bitter to two others, etc.*

<meta>catchword: [fallun]tur, &c. — they are deceived, etc.</meta>

### CHEMICAL LETTERS

...is sought, etc. Come now: let us grant the principle that the Galenist <note>A follower of Galen, the 2nd-century Greek physician whose theories dominated medicine for over a millennium.</note> seeks for the sake of argument: yet he will never persuade anyone that the senses were so completely dulled that, while the mind remained sound, one would deny the whiteness of snow or the heat of fire. Or if he were to do so, would you not think him unworthy, a man to be worn down on all sides by the torments used for the insane? 

But he objects again: *it is shameful to commit judgment to the senses while excluding reason.* Such a thing has never even entered our minds, not even in a dream. But just as a magistrate in the forum does not rush his sentence, but leans toward one side or the other based solely on the report of eyewitnesses: so too in medical controversies, we wish for reason to judge—but only according to the prescription of the senses, which serve reason in the place of messengers and as go-betweens. 

And for this reason, we establish that the material cause of the human body is "earth," enriched by that threefold substance of Salt, Mercury, and Sulphur <note>Known as the *Tria Prima*, these were the three fundamental principles of matter according to Paracelsian chemistry.</note>; not because Paracelsus, Isaac, or Geber <note>Geber (Jabir ibn Hayyan) and "Isaac" (likely Isaac Hollandus) were famous alchemical authorities.</note> affirms it, but because we see, touch, and taste those three principles, and through the teaching of the senses, we recognize them to be true. 

Since Galen did not admit this doctrine, listen to the shameful errors into which he imprudently fell. For while there had long been a controversy among the ancients as to whether the differences in tastes <note>Original: *sapors*</note> arose from the elements or from some peculiar matter: Galen said that this was entirely to be attributed to the mixing of the elements. 

<margin>2. On the faculties of simples</margin>
From where, then, did Galen get acidity? Surely from a very weak heat that changes the medicine or food but does not overcome it. This can be seen in unripe apples and in the belches of half-digested food. But what could be perceived as more acidic than "rooted" vinegar <note>Concentrated acetic acid.</note>, or the oil of vitriol and sulphur <note>Sulfuric acid.</note>? Both of these consist of such extreme heat that they have begun to be called "fiery medicines" for that reason. 

<margin>7. On the faculty of simples</margin>
Now let us come to sweetness, which according to Galen’s pleasure is procreated from a most temperate heat: whether it be innate (as in honey) or acquired, as all things that are made sweet by fire. However, the liquor of ceruse <note>Lead acetate, also known as "sugar of lead" because of its dangerously sweet taste.</note> and the "butter of vitriol" (both being very sweet substances) sufficiently prove that sweetness can be prepared by the most violent fire. 

Finally, that remarkable bitterness of opium clearly demonstrates that this taste is not born from immoderate heat alone; something which Galen, I know not whether he proved more or merely invented. 

Also, having despised the judgment of the senses, Galen turned pulses into poets, playing at *Spondaic, Pyrrhic, Tribrach, Doric, Ionic, and Sybaritic* rhythms <note>Galen famously categorized the rhythms of the human pulse using the names of Greek poetic meters and musical modes.</note>. Sometimes he even ascribes *Lydian* music to them, mixing *Spondaic with Pyrrhic, Trochaic with Iambic, and Dactylic with Anapestic*; finally, he divides their various reciprocations by other names, perhaps, but much more obscure ones. 

From this, you may see that we should approve not whatever Hippocrates, Galen, Avicenna, or Paracelsus writes, but that to which the senses, the eyes, and experience bear witness: from which all physical knowledge (if any now exists) is drawn as if from the very spring itself. Therefore, apply...

# THOMAS MUFFET

...much rue, celandine, fennel, eyebright, and many remedies for sharpening the sight <note>original: "oxydertica remedia." These herbs were traditionally used to treat eye ailments and, metaphorically here, to clear intellectual vision.</note>, so that the eyes of men—as if infected by the filth of bleary-eyed scales—do not look upon medicine with a distorted view, seeing nothing, or too little, or the wrong things entirely through the lens of mere authority. I say, do not allow anyone’s authority to bind you; rather, having tasted the opinions of individuals, you should correct those that are false and confirm those that are true. In this way, at last, you will attain medical Theory and Practice—not the kind they dreamed of, but that which you yourself, as an <term>eyewitness</term> <note>original: "αὐτοθεασάμενος" (autotheasamenos). A Greek term meaning one who has seen something for themselves.</note>, know to be good. Finally, show yourself to be a Chemist; see each thing for yourself, and hold fast to what is yours: accurately separate the homogeneous (the pure) from the heterogeneous (the impure). 

For what does a physician have to do with the causes of the soul? Let the Theologians dispute that. Let the cooks examine the causes of flavors; let the painters examine colors; the perfumers, scents; the musicians, sounds. For you, it should be enough to know what benefits and what harms your subject. You will never truly see these "secondary qualities" <note>In ancient philosophy, primary qualities were hot, cold, moist, and dry; secondary qualities were things like smell, taste, and color. Muffet argues these are best understood through chemistry, not abstract physics.</note> that affect the external senses by looking at the mixture of primary qualities or any other fiction of the philosophers. Instead—if you long to see this—perform a living anatomy upon vegetables, animals, and metals; and where the tincture, flavor, or scent dwells, where the poison hides, and where the <term>Antidote</term> <note>original: "Theriaca." Originally a specific herbal jam used against venom, it came to mean any potent medical remedy.</note> of the medicines lies hidden, see it not with another’s eyes, but with your own. This is indeed a province worthy of all physicians growing old in, and it is full of practical exercise. And so, I have made it clear that the judgment of a physician must be in harmony with the judgment of the senses, and I do not doubt that even a Galenist would say the same as I. Farewell. Given at London, February 8, 1583.

### TO PHILALETHES THE CHEMIST. GREETINGS.

You ask of me, Philalethes <note>A pseudonym meaning "Lover of Truth."</note>, what a novice physician should do in this great variety of authors and sects: whom should he follow most? Hippocrates, Galen, Avicenna, Paracelsus? This one, that one, all of them, or none? Believe me, this is a burning question and full of difficulty. Nevertheless, if the matter stood by my vote, I would agree with all physicians only as far as they agree with the truth; and I would leave them only as far as they leave the truth behind. Otherwise, it would seem like the tyranny of Phalaris <note>A cruel tyrant of ancient Sicily, known for his "bronze bull" torture device; here used to represent intellectual tyranny.</note> rather than the decree of justice, if those whom Nature brought forth as free men were to be enslaved to the judgment of a single philosopher, as if they had been recently bought at a slave auction. 

For since, according to that famous saying of Hippocrates, "Medicine is long" <note>A reference to the first Aphorism of Hippocrates: "Life is short, Art is long."</note>—whether compared to the age of the Physician, the course of time, the difficulty of judgment, or the uncertainty of experiment—how could I allow myself to be persuaded that the "finishing touch" was so applied to medicine by one man, or even by all of them, that nothing could or should be added or taken away? Yet I see most people are excessive evaluators of ancestral doctrine, fleeing to the authority of the Fathers as if to some <term>Maenian column</term> <note>A landmark in the Roman Forum where debtors and criminals were judged; Muffet uses it as a metaphor for a place where people cling to old, shameful systems.</note>, and adopting that weapon of the Pythagoreans: <term>"He himself said it."</term> <note>original: "αὐτὸς ἔφα" (autos epha). This refers to the followers of Pythagoras, who accepted the master's word as absolute proof without needing further reason.</note> Indeed, as this system collapses, they seek help from the papists, and immediately summon those "ass-sized reinforcements": *One must believe the fathers, the councils, and the successions...*

*To the families of the Asclepiads <note>Followers of Asclepius, the Greek god of healing; here referring to traditional physicians.</note>, to the customs of the Arabs, and the rites of the Academies, etc.* Yet the example of Paracelsus <note>original: "Helvetium." Paracelsus (1493–1541) was a Swiss physician who famously burned traditional medical books to signal a new era of chemistry-based medicine.</note> proves that he alone knew better and discovered more medicines than all of them combined. Indeed, I see that the very entrance to medicine—local anatomy—is of such great magnitude that five hundred Olympiads <note>A period of four years; he means that even two thousand years of study is not enough.</note> of physicians have not been enough to fully grasp it. For who does not see that fiction of Aristotle’s, that certain nerves take their origin from the heart? Who does not laugh at the error of Plato, who established a double passage in the lungs: one for drink and food into the stomach, and the other as a carrier for air? Hippocrates also and Galen (of whom the former stripped medicine bare, while the latter expanded it) were caught in various and most false paradoxes by Vesalius, the sun of anatomists. Yet Columbus <note>Matteo Realdo Colombo (c. 1516–1559), an Italian anatomist.</note> corrected Vesalius, Falloppio corrected Columbus, and my most dear teacher Felix Plater <note>Felix Plater (1536–1614), a renowned Swiss physician and professor at Basel.</note> corrected both; after so many centuries, he noted new and most beautiful things regarding the position, use, and formation of the body's parts. And so Alpha corrects Beta, and Beta corrects Gamma; nor indeed will even the "Omega" <note>The final or ultimate anatomist.</note> be so diligent an anatomist that he will not be corrected either by another’s pen, or at least by himself. Is it now at all likely, Philalethes <note>A pseudonym meaning "lover of truth," frequently used in early modern scientific correspondence.</note>, that nothing should be added to or taken away from medicine, in whose harbor are found so many rocks of error, upon which blind youth strikes at every first voyage? But let us set sail further out and look for a moment at physiology, the sum of which is this: *the human body arose from humors, the humors from elements, and the elements from principles.* But if you ask from which humor man is made, they answer: from bile, from both types of phlegm <note>Referring to the "four humors" theory: blood, yellow bile, black bile, and phlegm.</note>, and from blood, all coming together into a certain common humor called "seed." But if you inquire further, whether the human body or that seed is older by nature? Good God, what gaping ignorance you may see here, what fear! For if they assert the first, then the effect must exist before the cause, which is absurd; but if they deny it, then man was made from something other than human seed, and they destroy the "eternity of the world" which they had made the foundation of their entire religion. Nor is it any different in the doctrine of the elements: for some want the element to be one, others multiple, others infinite, countless, or immobile; these say there are two, those say three, some four, and others affirm there are eight. Yet all agree in this with mutual voices: that no element that is truly an "element" can be perceived by our senses, being destitute of all taste and color. If you then ask how a mixture of tasteless elements produces so many kinds of tastes and colors, they run to that shield of Galen: <margin>Galen, *On Simple Faculties*, book 2, chapters 2 and 3.</margin> *Where the sense grows dull, there one must go toward reason as the more divine part of man.* For sense is common to the beasts along with man: *but that more lucid eye of reason perceives those things which escape the too-dull edge of the senses.*

# THOMAS MUFFET <note>Thomas Muffet (1553–1604) was an influential English physician and member of Parliament who championed the use of chemical medicines.</note>

<margin>Galen, *On the Differences of Pulses*, Book 2</margin>
And so, by the response of a versatile philosopher (through which it is easy for an impudent man to prove whatever he wishes, or even to dilute whatever he wishes), they claim that a necessary and noble question has been satisfied. But if Galen mocks the school of Moses and Christ because in it certain theses are held that are established by no physical demonstration—as he himself asserts—how much more rightfully ought we to receive Galenic physiology with laughter and hisses, which, even in physical matters, testifies not to the demonstration of the senses but to the dreams of the imagination?

<margin>Galen, *That the Soul’s Behaviors Follow the Body’s Temperament*</margin>
Indeed, to make the analogy <note>original Greek: ἀναλογία (*analogia*)</note> more equal: if Galen thinks that Hippocrates should not be believed as a witness, but only as a demonstrator, why should we not listen to Galen himself with equal liberty when he demonstrates, and in turn reject him when he raves? But you ask: *Is more trust to be placed in those ancient writers, or rather in the moderns?* Certainly in these more recent ones. Because in this aging era of the world, we have acquired not only the gifts of languages but also an extraordinary method. By its benefit, we read the writings of the ancients not as a confused heap of hurried work, stuffed together as they were born, but as something elegantly arranged, distinguished by their proper places, chapters, and limbs, and illustrated in various ways. In this way, we seem like a crow sitting on the peak of a tower; although compared to the crows on the ground it resembles a tiny sparrow, nevertheless, because of its elevated position, it sees further than they do and judges objects more accurately. For let it be granted that nothing is said by the moderns that was not said before; nonetheless, you will find many things that are said more correctly, plainly, elegantly, clearly, extensively, or subtly. For example: the great Hermes Trismegistus <note>original: "Mercurius ter maximus." A legendary Hellenistic figure associated with the origin of alchemy and hermetic philosophy.</note>—born around the time of Moses—treated Chemistry, but so obscurely that neither his contemporaries nor even the later Latins could understand him. Afterwards followed Zoroaster, Solomon, and after him the family of the Arabs; yet among them, before Geber <note>Jabir ibn Hayyan (c. 721–c. 815), a Persian or Arab polymath often considered the father of chemistry.</note>, no one to our knowledge defined Chemistry, divided it, or enriched it with its own instruments, actions, matter, and effects. To this, however, Paracelsus and other distinguished Chemists added both clarity of speech and an order of things, and they can truly affirm that saying of themselves: *That man dictated us, and we him.*

<margin>Galen, *On the Usefulness of the Parts*, Book 1</margin>
Indeed, although Galen pays the highest honor to Hippocrates as the founder and father of medicine, he nevertheless frequently argues that his speech is not exact, but improper, obscure, disordered, and indistinct—at times deficient, and at other times superfluous. And when he finds a lack of diligence in him, he rebukes his confused and disordered tradition.

<margin>Galen, *On the Method of Diet in Acute Diseases*, Book 2</margin>
Sometimes he silently accuses him of ineptitude, forgetfulness, error, and falsehood; and regarding the drugs to be given to those with pleurisy, he disagrees with him entirely. I will tell you a most delightful story, my dear William <note>Likely referring to William Paddy, a contemporary physician and friend of Muffet.</note>, about a certain Galenic idolater and admirer of antiquity. Since this man condemned anything that was not ancient and written by Galen himself or Hippocrates, I offered him a little book by Hippocrates on elegance to a certain German...

# Chemical Letters

...falsely attributed to a certain person: when he had read it through, he accused it of folly, curiosity, <term>disorder <note>original Greek: ἀταξία (*ataxia*), meaning lack of order or discipline</note></term>, and obscurity, even adding the insult of "cynical moroseness." But when I showed, by producing the original tablets, that it was not the writing of the genuine Hippocrates, the wretch blushed and, fed up with his own life and infamy, he fled. I advise you, therefore, not to be bound to swear by the words of any master <note>A reference to the Roman poet Horace’s phrase *nullius addictus iurare in verba magistri*, a famous motto for intellectual independence</note>, and to surrender yourself to no writer at all. Instead, after diligently examining both the ancients and especially the moderns, grant them only as much credit as they grant to demonstration—without which, it is ridiculous to affirm anything, as the examples of Geometry show. Fare well: and as much as you love me, take care that you are well. Given at London, May 5th, 1582 <note>Original Roman numerals: CIↃ. IↃ. LXXXII. The OCR transcription "XXII" is likely a misreading of "LXXXII" (82), fitting Muffet’s active period in the late 16th century.</note>.

### TO PHILALETHES THE CHEMIST, MUCH HEALTH <note>original Latin: S.D.D. (*Salutem Dicit Datque*), a standard letter-writing greeting</note>

You have often asked me, Philalethes, since I suffer myself to be bound to no author, whether I follow myself, and whether I grant more to my own judgment than to the decrees of all the "classic" writers? I do not wish this. Rather, let me be led by the **light of nature**, not by that blind impulse of nature by which we strive for the forbidden and, having abandoned the truth, join ourselves to error. 

What, then, do you understand by the "light of nature"? Do we soak up art by nature, or do we obtain knowledge through our lineage? I do not maintain this either. For when we are newly born, we seem like "erased tablets" <note>An early reference to the *tabula rasa* or "blank slate" theory of the mind</note>, on which the actual practice of knowledge is not inscribed; rather, a certain meager potential grows through the kindness of fate, the "midwifery" of teachers, and the passage of time. 

What, then, is the **light of nature**? It is a kind of "lightning bolt" of our original nature or integrity, not innate to us but instilled by God: by which we discern the false from the true with a more divine eye of the mind. In fact, I believe there are two kinds of physicians: some are <term>taught by God <note>original Greek: *Theodidactos*</note></term>, such as the Apostles were; while others are illuminated indirectly by that lightning bolt, such as the ancient Chemists were. 

And just as lightning flashes now from this region of the sky, and now from that: so also the light of nature draws its origin from various places. Sometimes it comes immediately from God, as in Adam—the <term>First-Formed <note>original Latin: *Protoplastus*</note></term>—who, while he was upright in life and pure of crime, not only knew all things but also gave names to them all. But after the First-Formed migrated into his own ego and turned away from that state of piety, that first light of nature was finished. In its place, fantasy, error, and opinion infected him and all his posterity through a certain secret contagion of the seed. 

From this it has happened that the greatest part of what we know is the smallest part of what we do not know; indeed, it has brought it about that truly *nothing* is known, if you define science as the perfect knowledge of a thing. Yet those people come closest to this perfection who, lacking that whiter and brighter lightning-flash of nature, enjoy its "vicar" <note>A "vicar" acts as a substitute or proxy for a higher power</note>—one that is indeed denser and thicker, but which nevertheless points out the way to the truth for us and, in a manner of speaking, points its finger. For example: Innocence...

-># THE WORKS OF THOMAS MUFFET<-

...that famous Adam, by divine inspiration, perfectly knew the essence, nature, and **hypostasis** <note>original: *hypostasin*, referring to the underlying substance or fundamental reality of a thing</note> of his own body and indeed of every body, including the efficient, formal, instrumental, and finally, the final causes. We, however, seem to know the same things, but as if through a cloud and "in part," as the **Apostle** <note>St. Paul, referencing 1 Corinthians 13:12: "For now we see through a glass, darkly... but then shall I know even as also I am known"</note> says; that is, through analogies, similarities, inferences, and the comparison of the **macrocosm** <note>the universe as a whole</note> with the **microcosm** <note>the human being as a "little world" reflecting the universe</note>. Hence we say that the body of man consists of only **sulfur, Mercury, and salt**: not because we know this as perfectly as Adam did, but because both the natural and the artificial resolution <note>chemical decomposition or analysis</note> of all kinds of bodies shows that this is the case. But how are we persuaded that this <term>axiom <note>original Greek: ἀξίωμα (*axioma*), a self-evident principle</note></term> is true—that bodies are composed first of those things into which they are ultimately dissolved? Truly, numbers and syllables make this plain; just as they were composed, so you may see them, when resolved, contain as many individual units as they represented when they were joined. And so, by an analogy made from bodies to accidents, from nature to art, and from one art to another, those **three principles** are truly drawn out, which shall never fall, even by the effort of any **Galenist** <note>A follower of the traditional medical system of Galen, which relied on the four humors rather than chemical principles</note>. For there is one and the same law for nature and for art. For all things are similar, however dissimilar they may seem, and all things are in harmony, though they may seem in discord. Wherefore **Hippocrates**, not without merit, showed the management and operation of all nature within us by making a comparison with the effects of the arts and sciences. For in truth, the spirit of the iron-working parts is the substance; the generative faculty is the weaver of the web; the temperament is the potter; <margin>See Hippocrates, Book 1, *On Diet*, chapter 8.</margin> digestion is the goldsmith; hearing is the Musician; taste is the cook; and the diet is so much a rival to architecture that whether you look at the action or the end goal, you see scarcely any difference. Indeed, Hippocrates proves that nature has implanted a "fickle mind" in men from the fact that they feel one thing, say another, and do another, and the very same people occasionally hand down contrary teachings about the same things. He notes that certain deceptive arts are found, such as wrestling, trading, drinking, and gaming, which we all admire when someone performs them skillfully and we think them to be a virtue; yet we do not understand the cause, which proceeds from the very likeness of nature. If the **Galenists** could sufficiently grasp this harmony of nature and art, they would never deny that millers, bakers, cooks, <term>archaei <note>original: *archaeos*, referring to the "Archeus," a Paracelsian term for the internal "alchemist" or vital force that governs bodily functions</note></term>, chemists, distillers, porters, carriers, caterers, musicians, **Parmenones, Getas, Claraetas** <note>Stock characters of clever servants and messengers from ancient Roman comedy, used here to represent various functional "roles" or "agents" within the body</note>, Daedaluses, sculptors, goldsmiths, fullers, weavers, messengers, smiths, and architects can be found in the human body; and much less would the authors of such words be mocked more than "cynically." Did not that most wise **Ecclesiastes** <note>King Solomon, traditionally the author of the Book of Ecclesiastes</note>, speaking as if from the oracle of God, <margin>Ecclesiastes chapter 12.</margin> call the hands the "keepers of the house," the bones "strong men," the teeth "grinders," the eyes "watchmen," the lips "doors," the ears "guards," the windpipe a "singer," the hair an "almond tree," the spinal marrow a "silver cord," the veins a "pitcher," the liver a "fountain," the heart a "wheel," and the pericardium a "cistern"? But why this? Surely it is from the light of nature, which...

-># CHEMICAL EPISTLES<-

->G 3<-

...which he noticed clearly enough that nothing could be more aptly compared with these parts, if you consider their function and use. Do you wish for me to reveal to you some errors of the **Galenists** <note>Followers of the ancient Greek physician Galen, whose medicine was based on the four humors (blood, phlegm, black bile, and yellow bile)</note>, into which they have fallen to the perpetual infamy of their name because they despised the light of nature? Hear one, and it is a notable and remarkable one. When God said that man was made from the soil, what else did He intend, **Philalethes** <note>original Greek: "Lover of Truth," a common pseudonym or form of address in alchemical texts</note>, than that one eager to understand human matter should weigh the substance of the soil, distinguish it, dissect it, and examine it; implying, of course, that the principles of the human body are to be found there, and are not to be found elsewhere. Lacking this light, the Galenists ascended to the regions of fire and air, and descended into the waters, and thus—with the earth mixed among these—they fashioned a man not according to God’s prescription, but by a pleasing invention of their own fantasy. Furthermore, though they see neither blood, nor phlegm, nor yellow or black bile in the earth: nevertheless, they affirm that by both law and nature, man is nothing other than these.

**Paracelsus** <note>Philippus Aureolus Theophrastus Bombastus von Hohenheim (1493–1541), the Swiss physician who pioneered the use of chemicals and minerals in medicine</note>, on the contrary, and other distinguished Chemists, having drawn so much light from God, realized that the material principles of man were hidden in the earth from whence he came. With continuous and unremitting labor, they dissected its veins, opened its entrails, broke its bones, and liquefied its marrow; they left no stone unturned so that they might diligently examine the bodies contained therein. But finally, by the benefit of <term>Pyrotechny <note>original: *Pyrotechnia*, the "art of fire," a term for chemical science</note></term> and Alchemy, and through their long and more than Herculean labors, they discovered nothing simple in the earth except the *vaporous, the inflammable, and the fixed*: and nothing mixed that was not composed of these same simple things.

Wherefore they established that the principle of man is also twofold: one part volatile, the other truly fixed. The volatile is in turn twofold: first the vaporous, which is called **Mercury**, and second the inflammable, which has obtained the name of **sulfur**. **Mercury** is the vaporous principle of the body: in itself boundless, moist, liquid, and the vehicle of the natural balsam: incorporating **sulfur** with **salt**, just as water incorporates lime with sand. **Sulfur** is the inflammable principle of the body, fatty, light, uniform, and the nourishment of the vital balsam. **Salt**, however, is the fixed principle of the body, providing weight, solidity, and the greatest strength, yielding by itself neither to iron nor to fire.

Of these principles there are two kinds of differences: some are domestic, when compared to themselves; others are exoteric, when compared with others. That principle in man is called "domestic" which is born to keep the body in its integrity; but that which corrupts it is called "foreign." This foreign principle is either born from the parents and causes perpetual ill health, or it is contracted from a nurse or external diet, and induces a long-lasting <term>dyscrasia <note>a medical term for an imbalance or "bad mixture" of the bodily principles, leading to disease</note></term> of the body. In order that we may more correctly examine each particular nature of the foreign and domestic principle, it is worth the effort to investigate all sulfurs, salts, and all Mercuries...

# OF THOMAS MUFFET

...it will be necessary: so that in this way, sulfur compared to sulfur (like purple fabric compared to purple) may allow the natural to be more easily distinguished from the non-natural. Now, all sulfur in the macrocosm <note>The universe or "greater world"</note> (which is the light of the microcosm <note>Man, the "lesser world," who mirrors the universe</note>) belongs either to perfectly or imperfectly animated things. The perfectly animated include animals and vegetables; the imperfectly animated include Minerals. 

Finally, the sulfur of animals and vegetables is found as either native or artificial. Native is that which nature itself ejects and releases to be handled by the senses: such as the exuded fats of all animals, the beeswax of bees, tree resins, the "tears" <note>Exuded sap or resin droplets</note> of larch, turpentine, fir, storax, pitch, and mastic, etc.; and the gums of cherry, lac, laserwort, all-heal, cedar, frankincense, myrrh, and so on. Artificial sulfurs, however, are oils, ardent spirits <note>original: "spiritus ardentes," flammable distilled liquids like alcohol</note>, resins, tears, and combustible gums extracted from both—that is, from animals as well as vegetables. 

Mineral sulfurs are likewise drawn out by the benefit of both art and nature. By nature: such as amber, bitumen, oils, fats, sulfurs, and the spontaneous "efflorescence" <note>The formation of powdery crusts on surfaces</note> of all oily bodies beneath the earth. Various artificial sulfurs are also extracted from pyrite, jet, coal, bitumen, "earth of the sun" <note>original: "terra solis," likely referring to a solar or gold-related mineral extract</note>, and finally from every metallic substance in which that combustible sulfur is found. 

And so much for the types of sulfur; yet no more varieties are found in the macrocosm, whether made by art or nature, than are found in the bodies of the whole human race. For just as animal differs from animal, tree from tree, and mineral from mineral: so it is clearly evident that men do not have the same face, nor color, nor symmetry, nor the same texture, nor the same sulfur in all respects. 

For those whom the **Galenists** <note>Followers of Galen's theory of the four humors</note> call "melancholics" abound in a pitchy, naphtha-like, black, dense, and impure sulfur. The "bilious," however, abound in a sulfur that is waxy, saffron-colored, amber-like, fir-like, yellow, transparent, and subtle. The "sanguine" have a sulfur that is amaranthine, clove-scented, red, clear, scarlet, and of a moderate temperament. Finally, the "phlegmatic" are also endowed with sulfur, but it is cherry-like, Arabic <note>referring to Gum Arabic</note>, mastic-like, gummy, white, compact, lumpy, gluey, thick, and catches fire with difficulty. 

Furthermore, just as in the macrocosm certain sulfurs are benign and suitable for nutrition, while others are solely medicinal; so it is in the human body, where a sweet sulfur nourishes the sulfurous parts, but a foreign sulfur is sent to the gall bladder and is used as a stimulating medicine to purge the bowels. 

In addition, just as in the macrocosm some sulfurs are found to be very hot, like petroleum, while others on the contrary are Narcotics, such as those of henbane, opium, and vitriol; so also petroleum is found in the body as the author of fevers, both universal and particular, internal and external. Conversely, the sulfur of vitriol and opium is seen [as effective] in "suffocation of the womb" <note>A historical diagnosis for various symptoms in women, then attributed to a displaced uterus</note>, fainting, the "dead evil" <note>original: "malo mortuo," a chronic skin disease or form of leprosy</note>, leprosy, and other diseases. And just as some sulfurs are very thick, others are subtle,

# CHEMICAL LETTERS
### G 4

...subtle, some intermediate (as fossil coal <note>original: "carbo fossilis," referring to mineral coal mined from the earth</note>, liquefied sulfur, and "exalted" amber among minerals; naval pitch, resin, and turpentine among vegetables; tallow, grease, and lard among animals; and those manifold graduations of vinous spirits among artificial products show clearly enough). In the same way, diverse sulfurs are found in humans, whose coarseness produces long-lasting fevers, while their subtlety produces shorter ones.

And just as fossil coal sustains not only a longer-lasting but also a more vehement flame than a lamp—because the lamp enjoys a more subtle fuel while the coal a denser one—by the same logic, the same argument can be applied to fevers. Sometimes the sulfur of these fevers is spiritual <note>Light or airy</note>, as in an Ephemera <note>A fever lasting only one day</note>; sometimes a bit thicker, as in synochal fevers <note>A continuous, non-remitting fever</note>; often even very thick, as in tertian fevers <note>A fever recurring every third day</note>; and sometimes extremely thick, pitch-like, and very similar to fossil coal, as in quartan fevers <note>A fever recurring every fourth day, often the most difficult to cure</note>. 

From this arise those varieties of paroxysms, fevers, and crises, as well as their lengths, brevities, transplantations, mixtures, and true rules of behavior. If Hippocrates had seen this, he would have asserted not only that many fevers arise from some sulfuric matter, but all of them universally; he would have attributed no burning either to the spirits of the air or to phlegmatic spirits. For who has ever caught air, or water, or even earth, being ignited when it was devoid of all sulfur? But if you have never seen this in the macrocosm <note>The "greater world" or universe</note>, how then could you find it in the microcosm <note>The "lesser world," meaning the human body</note>?

Truly, you might be persuaded by "burning darts," lightning, candles, comets, "leaping goats" <note>original: "capra saltante," a historical term for flickering atmospheric lights or meteors</note>, sparks, falling stars, *ignis fatuus* <note>Will-o'-the-wisps</note>, Helena, Gemini <note>Terms for types of St. Elmo's Fire seen by sailors</note>, or other meteors burning like fire, that the air can sometimes catch flame. You show yourself too credulous, however, by not noticing that their flame did not take its origin from the air itself, but from a certain fatty exhalation. Depending on its thickness, subtlety, abundance, or scarcity, all those ignited "fire-gnats" <note>original: "tipulæ," used here to describe flickering or darting points of light in the sky</note> in the air turn out clearer, more transparent, darker, more opaque, shorter, or longer-lasting. 

Furthermore, since it is not the nature of heat to be ignited, but rather to ignite whatever can be burned: why do we define a fever as "ignited heat," and often claim it comes from phlegmatic or earthy matter? Neither of those could be ignited even a tiny bit if deprived of every kind of sulfur. Indeed, all watery things (such as we define phlegm to be) as well as truly earthy particles are born to extinguish fire; they are far from nourishing it when poured over it. Therefore, sulfur alone is the fuel and seat of every sublunary fire <note>Fire found on Earth, beneath the sphere of the Moon</note>; all other things grow hot only from the mixture or, so to speak, the proximity of this sulfur. 

And so much for sulfur. But just as other parts of the body are called sulfuric "by excellence" <note>original: "κατ’ ἐξοχὴν," meaning preeminently or by way of distinction</note>—namely tallow, the omentum <note>The fatty lining of the abdomen</note>, lard, grease, glands, marrow, bile, and whatever oily thing is seen here and there—so also some parts are called "Mercurial" in the same way, such as water and what is commonly called phlegm, and their receptacles...

<summary>Muffet argues that all human fevers are caused by the ignition of internal "sulfur," with the duration and intensity of the fever determined by the sulfur's density, similar to how different fuels burn in nature. He challenges traditional humoral medicine, asserting that air and phlegm cannot burn on their own without this sulfuric fuel.</summary>

# THOMAS MUFFET
### G 4

...common; likewise some are salty, such as bones, the heavier viscera, ligaments, cartilages, tougher membranes, serum, kidneys, nails, hair, etc., in which, when resolved by art <note>The "art" refers to alchemy or iatrochemistry—the process of breaking a substance down into its primary chemical components.</note>, more salt is found than mercury or sulfur. 

If, however, you desire to learn the action and truly wonderful revolution of Mercury in the human body, you must first look upon it in the "greater world" <note>The Macrocosm or the universe at large, which Paracelsian physicians believed was mirrored within the human body (the Microcosm).</note>, the mirror of particular nature: where as many waters and incombustible liquors as are found, so many mercuries are also discovered. Nor is it otherwise in us (O Philalethes) <note>original: "Philalethes," meaning "Lover of Truth," a common way to address a scholarly reader in alchemical texts.</note>; for some of us abound in mineral mercury, others in vegetable, and others in animal mercury. 

And among the minerals, this man's Mercury is marked by the Sun <note>Gold</note>, another's by the Moon <note>Silver</note>, a third by Venus <note>Copper</note>, a fourth by Jupiter <note>Tin</note>, a fifth by Saturn <note>Lead</note>, a sixth by Mars <note>Iron</note>, and a seventh by Mercury <note>Quicksilver</note>. From the vegetables, truly, this man has obtained most of the Mercury of balm, thistle, sage, or betony; that man, of satyrion, celandine, valerian, or birthwort <note>original: "brassatella," likely referring to *Aristolochia* or a similar herbal remedy</note>. From the animals, however, the Mercury of the lion, tiger, puppy, cow, horse, bear, or elephant is communicated now here, now there; if not in its very essence, then marked by the same powers. 

Finally, the Mercury of men is either natural or foreign. Natural Mercury is sweet, mild, and neither hot nor cold beyond the second degree, nor exceeding its due quantity. But foreign Mercury, like quicksilver, possesses a dyscrasia <note>An unhealthy imbalance or "bad mixture" of elements.</note> of both extreme heat and cold; it is prepared to putrefy, corrode, weaken, enervate, and undermine the very bones—the foundations of the whole human fabric. From this, therefore, are born apoplexies, paralyses, follies <note>original: "fatuitates," referring to mental impairment or loss of wits.</note>, rheums, dropsies, leucophlegmasia <note>A pale, dropsical swelling of the body.</note>, edemas, ptyalisms <note>Excessive salivation.</note>, and inundations of the stomach, brain, heart, bladder, spinal cord, and other parts—not from "pituita" or "phlegm," which are nothing but fictitious names <note>Muffet is explicitly rejecting the traditional Galenic theory of the Four Humors in favor of chemical causes.</note>. 

And having explained these things regarding the volatile principle of the body <note>Mercury was considered the "volatile" or spiritual principle in alchemy.</note>, I now come to the anatomy of Salt, or that fixed principle. Now, Salt is also either domestic or foreign: the former is pleasing, mild, preserving from putrefaction, the bond of unity, and the proper seasoning, as it were, of health. But the latter (namely the foreign) has contracted acrimony, acidity, burning, bitterness, erosion, stinging, stimulation, and perforation from a vice in the seeds of fate <note>A reference to hereditary conditions or predestined physical flaws.</note> or from its own intemperance, being the author of all ulcers (both internal and external), boils, abscesses, and openings of the skin. 

Furthermore, the species of Salt in man are said to be varied. Some arise from minerals: arsenical, ferruginous <note>Iron-like</note>, venereal <note>Copper-like</note>, vitriolated, aluminous, gem-like, ammoniac, or crystalline. Others are taken from plants: nettle-like, water-pepper, peppery, opiated, tartaric, arum-like, ginger-like, and so on. Others truly from animals: viperine, wild-beast-like, wolf-like, dog-like, lizard-like <note>original: "stellionares," from the *stellio* or spotted lizard.</note>, cantharidean <note>Derived from the Spanish Fly beetle.</note>, scorpionic, tarantular, etc. And not without merit; for just as a man is affected differently by the bite of a tarantula than by a lizard or a viper: so...

# CHEMICAL LETTER
### G 5
<meta>catchword: tiles</meta>

Indeed, a certain salt excites laughter, tickling, and a most pleasing itch; another, however, causes immense bodily pain, restlessness, insanity, and rabies <note>original: "hydrophobiam"</note>; so that you would think the man was not pricked by an internal stimulus, but wounded from the outside by a rabid dog. And just as the desert vipers <note>original: "dypsades"</note> by their bite induce great thirst, the Hemorrhois snake a flow of blood, the Amphisbaena inflammation, the Basilisk death <note>original: "mortificationem"</note>, the Asp sleepiness, the *Drynius* <term>heart-distress</term> <note>original: Greek "καρδιωγμὸν" (kardiogmon), referring to a gnawing pain at the mouth of the stomach or heart</note>, the spotted lizard a livid bruising, the salamander freezing, the venomous spider the plague, the jumping spider blistered sores, and the centipede rot: so also the salt of dropsy, of menstruation, of pleurisy, of corrosive ulcers <note>original: "phagedænicus"</note>, of mercury, of carbuncles, of boils, of narcotics, of pestilence, of herpes, and of gangrene produces these same symptoms, wherever it has established a center or a home for itself after its separation has occurred. 

For as long as this salt is submerged in the mercurial fluids flowing here and there through the veins and wider vessels, it cannot ulcerate the body, both because of its constant motion and the uncertainty of its location, and because it is mixed with a fluid contrary to itself. Wine shows this to us: when it is fresh must, it resembles a divine nectar in its sweetness and excellence, and wonderfully charms the tongue and palate of those who drink; however, once the separation of its parts and spirits has occurred, it throws off a very salty and sharp <term>tartar</term> <note>In Paracelsian medicine, "tartar" refers to the stony deposits found in wine casks, which were used as an analogy for stones, gout, and other "crusting" diseases in the human body</note>, as well as a very acidic and plainly corrosive vinegar. 

Since, therefore, the number of fluids flowing in the body is infinite, it is no wonder if such diverse appearances and operations of salts appear, giving birth to various types, forms, and figures of ulcers, and various symptoms. And thus you clearly see that the <term>Light of Nature</term> <note>The alchemical belief that nature reveals its secrets through visible analogies and signatures</note> is nothing other than the analogy of that Great World <note>the Macrocosm or universe</note> with the Microcosmic body; you see also that the art of nature and nature itself agree in art, and that the same power is the operator of both, although to the Galenic mind (for Hippocrates felt otherwise) these things seem not only different but even opposite. 

Farewell: and love me as you usually do, dearest Philalethes <note>A pseudonym meaning "Lover of Truth"</note> of my soul. Given at London, June 17, 1583 <note>original: "15. Kal. Quintilis," using the Roman calendar</note>.

### TO ENDYMION OF LUDDIPOLIS
### From the Chemist, Greetings.

<margin>See the Life of Galen and Galen himself, Book 9 on the properties of simple medicines, and the book on the composition of medicines according to their types.</margin>

You strive to prove with many arguments, Endymion, that travel is not necessary for a future physician in your country; and yet you do not notice meanwhile how great and heavy an axe-blow you have dealt to your own Galen, whom you always praise. For although you believe with him that medicine was born and perfected, he nevertheless undertook various journeys to Egypt, Alexandria, Palestine, Cyprus, Lemnos, and Rome; sometimes to confer with physicians, sometimes to obtain balsam, Lemnian earth, and other medicines not growing at home for the race...

# THOMAS MUFFET
<meta>catchword: as often as</meta>

<margin>Pliny, Book 29, Chapter 1.</margin>
...he might deliver his **votive tablets** <note>original: "tiles," likely referring to the *tabulae* or plaques left by cured patients in temples</note>. Hippocrates himself, that man of Cos, shortly before the Peloponnesian War, when he understood that Medicine stood in need of fixed principles, traveled to various places. He transcribed the histories and cures of diseases not only from the temple of Aesculapius <note>The Greek god of healing; his temples (Asclepeia) served as early hospitals where patients left records of their cures</note>, but also from the spoken words of all philosophers and physicians; and thus, from manifold experience and diligent observation, he was the first to bring Medicine into being. The most abundant witnesses of his travels are those *Epidemics*—or rather, his *Apodemic* observations <note>A play on words: Muffet calls the *Epidemics* "Apodemics" from the Greek *apodemikos*, meaning "belonging to a journey"</note>—in which he made such progress that no **Galenist** <note>A follower of the traditional medical system of Galen (2nd century AD)</note> has yet been found who could reach the skill of Hippocrates, let alone surpass it. 

Indeed, only he who is himself a stranger to their lives and writings could be ignorant of the fact that the Arabs visited various regions and crossed over to islands for the sake of knowledge. Truly, to show that you have written plainly nothing of value, I declare that there is no physician, whether here or elsewhere, flourishing with true praise and erudition, who has not also left his homeland for a time and brought back various things from other nations to enrich the art of Medicine. But you say: *"Those for whom everything grows at home have no need to import food from elsewhere, and they can live content with their own agriculture."* Nevertheless, those whose region is merely sterile, where agriculture makes little progress, must engage in trade and keep away internal hunger by fetching nourishment from elsewhere. 

As for your writing that your academies and cities are so rich in the number and excellence of physicians that foreigners seek from them a model of knowledge: though I might wish for this most of all—being myself a **Londoner** <term>Ludipolensis</term> <note>Muffet uses a Latinized term for a resident of London</note>—the reality of the matter proves it false. For in which of our academies is a local **Anatomy** <note>A public dissection</note> performed even once in a decade? (If, however, I were to speak of "living" Anatomy <note>likely referring to clinical observation of living patients</note>, which nevertheless seems the greatest part of Medicine, you would hardly understand me, you **Endymion** <note>A figure from myth who slept forever; here used to mean a dreamer or someone oblivious to reality</note>). Who demonstrates **Physiology** <note>The study of the natural functions of the body</note> not by the testimony of opinion, but of the senses? Who leads the novice to the sick, and there shows him the affected part, the type of ailment, the cause of the ailment, the sequence of causes, the limit of the disease, its transplantation, its connection, and its degree, with a true and sincere mind, after the example of Hippocrates and the **Paduans** <note>The University of Padua was the world leader in clinical medical education and anatomy during the Renaissance</note>? 

Furthermore, what hope is there for a good future physician when those primary and **Royal professors** <note>original: "Regii antecessores"</note> read in no order, but snatch up now this little book, now another, and spend an entire year in explaining—or rather entangling—ten **aphorisms** <note>Short medical maxims, specifically those of Hippocrates</note>? Is this how one teaches the art, reads methodically, instructs the novice, and completes the study of Medicine? These rather seem to be the duties of a Medical Lecturer: to hand down the entire art to the disciples beginning with both types of Anatomy, and to apply every effort toward their quickest and truest education. But this title does not fit your **vanguard leaders** <note>original: "Antesignanos"</note>. Their speeches, works, and virtues cannot bear such a heavy burden. It pities me, as I live, and I grieve with tears that occasionally fall for the misfortunes of our Academies.

# CHEMICAL LETTERS
<page-num>107</page-num>

as often as I see some students of medicine brought forth into the field like certain most noble horses; who, however, if you see them running in the **double course** <note>original: *diaulo*, a Greek term for a race where the runner turns at a post and returns to the start</note>, are found to be either fearful, or prone to throw their riders, or gasping for breath, or weak-jointed, or falling headlong. And this is not so much by their own fault as by the vice of their Predecessors, from whom they received infinite defects of doctrine and impediments to knowledge in place of the one true interpretation. How much better it would be for a medical novice, cultivated in those languages and the humanities, to betake himself in the very bloom of his youth to the **Paduan Athens** <note>The University of Padua was the preeminent center for medical and anatomical study in the 16th century</note>, where in a single summer he might learn the forms and synonyms of nearly all herbs, and in the course of one winter learn the anatomy of corpses. In the following year, let him carefully weigh Galenic physiology—read accurately from the very elements to the perfection of the body and the full explanation of all actions—and let him learn all those signs which are called either pathological, etiological, or even prognostic. 

And so, having successfully spent two years, let him then join himself as a perpetual companion to the lecturers and diligently observe their **Practice** (which he will very easily obtain); and thus, warned by the errors of others or educated by their prudence, he will gather a most rich harvest for himself. From a good Physicist he will emerge as the best Physician, and like that man in Homer, **superior to all others** <note>original Greek: πάντων ὑπείροχος ἄλλων, a famous exhortation from the Iliad</note>. But as for Chemistry, the marrow or rather the soul of all Pharmacy: although it is cultivated by some most skilled men in your region so that they might be a source of wonder to the sluggish **Galenists** <note>Traditional physicians who relied solely on herbal medicine and often rejected chemical remedies</note> wasting away in leisure; yet the science of all those, when joined with the skill of foreigners in this part, will seem as much smaller as the Sun is larger than the Moon, or as the springs and basins of water are more abundant than the streamlets flowing from them.

> *you value Padua, Basel, Paris, Bologna, Montpellier,*
> *and other distinguished overseas Academies; this*
> *one thing we nevertheless often observe: those*
> *traveling there for a long time have returned home*

> *while others have learned among the Italians such lust,*
> *among the Germans drunkenness, among the*
> *Swiss boorishness, among the French hypocrisy,*
> *which they never afterward set aside upon returning to*
> *their homeland. And these are the principal ornaments*
> *of travelers, which you cannot enjoy without the mark of*
> *a bad man, and which you cannot lack without a loss of reputation.*

<margin>Odyssey, Book 4.</margin>
To which I respond: there is a great variety of travelers, and not all set out with the same mind, nor return with the same benefit. Therefore, I require judgment in travel, and indeed that of **Odysseus**; lest when physicians must philosophize with the Muses alone, they be turned by some **Cup of Circe** <note>A reference to the sorceress in the Odyssey who turned men into animals</note> into swine and **unmanly men** <note>original Greek: ἄνδρας ἀνήνορας, spiritless or weak men</note>, to use the poet’s word. But if the novice abstains from her house and the songs of the Sirens, and does not easily surrender himself to leisure...

# THE CHEMICAL LETTERS OF THOMAS MUFFET
<page-num>108</page-num>

[...he shall have learned not] to be deceived, and will perform only those things which belong to the art—not the art as you describe it—but he will return more learned than Hippocrates, and will keep his homeland safe and sound <note>original: *fartam tectam*, a legal metaphor meaning "in good repair"</note> from infinite diseases, those most pernicious traitors of the body. Arise therefore, Endymion, and recover yourself with haste. No longer imitate those fireside philosophers <note>original: *focarios... philosophos*, literally "kitchen" or "hearth" philosophers who never leave the house</note> who spend their whole lives in a bedroom, where no one is rained upon nor burned by the sun, and who prefer the authors of their own library to the theater of Nature herself and her living voice. 

Arise, I say, collect yourself; God helps the industrious. With this flint <note>original: *igniario*, a tool for striking fire; here used metaphorically as a "spark" of inspiration</note> I have given you, may you burn more and more each day with a zeal for travel. Even if you are not moved by my prodding, at least let the authority of Hippocrates, Galen, and Avicenna move you; for though they were the princes of all Medicine, they nevertheless drew their knowledge from various regions and foreign springs. Indeed, they were ashamed to be more desirous of leisure than of knowledge, and believed that erudition must be purchased not only with labor, but also with one's very breath <note>or "spirit," likely referring to the physical effort of travel</note>. 

Therefore, Endymion, you are now safe nowhere. A precipice lies before you, and an enemy looms behind; if you condemn travel, you damn Galen, wound Hippocrates, and slay Avicenna. If you approve of it, you condemn yourself and run back to my side—the very side you deserted all too rashly. Yet, since it is better to turn back than to run the wrong way—and the path to good habits is never too late—even in this old age of yours, sell your estates, take to the sea, visit foreign lands, build furnaces, learn **Chemistry** <note>original: *Chemiam*, referring to iatrochemistry or alchemy</note>, and cultivate a **new Medicine** that does not waver with opinion, but is confirmed by the senses. Unless you do this, it will be rightly said of you and those like you what **Martial** <note>The Roman poet Martialis</note> once wrote concerning lazy sailors:

> *You idle, boys, and you know nothing,*
> *More sluggish than lethargy and resin;*
> *And even now, wandering through the calm waves,*
> *You play at leisure in a safe hull.*
> *I do not think you are sailors, but **Argonauts**.* <note>original: *argonautas*, here a pun on the Greek *argos* (lazy/idle) and *nauta* (sailor), contrasting them with the heroic Argonauts of myth</note>

Listen: and at long last, wake up, Endymion.

->Given at London, March 29, 1584.<-

# THEOBALD VAN HOGHELANDE
# OF MIDDELBURG’S BOOK ON THE 
# DIFFICULTIES OF 
# ALCHEMY.

->*In which it is taught what a student of True Chemistry, aspiring to perfection, ought to know and what they ought to avoid.*<-

### Preface.

<margin>Alchemy is a part of natural philosophy.</margin>
That the most noble part of natural philosophy is that which treats the principles, causes, properties, passions <note>original: *passiones*, referring to the ways substances are acted upon or undergo change</note>, and transformations of metals, no one will call into doubt without doing an injustice to the subject. I have added "transformations" so that I might not seem to speak only of that common part of Physics <note>original: *Physices*, here meaning the general study of the natural world</note> which determines the matter and form of metals, their place of generation, their flexibility, color, taste, smell, and similar things; but rather about that part which, most of all, teaches how to convert one metal into another. <margin>It is taught that the transformation of metals is possible.</margin> Moreover, that this is possible requires no demonstration, since experience provides proof, eyewitnesses in almost every part of the world confirm it, and the most weighty authors assert it. <margin>Experience: Georgius Agricola, Book 9, *On the Nature of Fossils*.</margin> <note>Georgius Agricola (1494–1555) was a German mineralogist known as the "father of mineralogy."</note> For iron, by means of waters springing spontaneously from the earth—and even by an easy artifice—is changed into copper <note>original: *aes*</note>, and quicksilver <note>mercury</note> cooked with sulfur is changed into silver, though without profit unless a greater skill of the craftsman is applied. <margin>By witnesses.</margin> There remain in France, England, Germany, Bohemia, and the Low Countries <note>original: *Belgio*</note> those who, with their own hands, having cast a very small quantity of a certain powder (which they had received prepared by others) into mercury heated by fire, brought back from it silver or gold that could withstand every test. <margin>By authority: Book 6 of *On Subtlety*; Book 1 of *Occult Philosophy*, chapter 14; In the additions to the *Mirror*, under the heading "Concerning the crime of forgery."</margin> Cardano <note>Girolamo Cardano (1501–1576), an Italian polymath.</note> relates that in the presence of the prince and the most illustrious senate of the city of Venice, mercury was converted into gold by a pharmacist of Treviso. <margin>All metals are of the same essence, but differ accidentally.</margin> <note>In Aristotelian terms, "accidental" differences are outward traits that do not change the core "essence" of a substance.</note> Cornelius Agrippa <note>Heinrich Cornelius Agrippa (1486–1535), a famous German scholar and occultist.</note> says that by the "spirit of gold," or rather by its form or a purer part of it, imperfect metals and mercury can be turned into gold, and that he himself had seen and known this.

<margin>
That the transformation of metals is possible is proved by analogy.

Transition into similar things is easier than into dissimilar things.
