<margin>
Book 1 of *On Minerals*, chapter 7. A wonderful metamorphosis. Georgius Agricola seems to suggest this spring is in Iceland, near Mount Hecla. Book 2 of *On the nature of those things which flow spontaneously from the earth*, where there are more examples of these. And Book seven of *On the nature of fossils*.
</margin>
Andreas the Jurisconsult <note>original: *I. C.* for *Iuris Consultus*, a legal expert</note> testifies that in his time, Arnaldus de Villa Nova <note>A famous 13th-century physician and alchemist</note> was in the Roman court and made certain golden rods, which he allowed to be submitted to every test. But why is it surprising if anyone believes metals can be exchanged among themselves—which are the same in matter and essence, and are distinguished only by "accidents" <note>In medieval philosophy, "accidents" are non-essential qualities like color or hardness</note>, namely by the place of their generation and by a greater or lesser degree of "decoction" <note>original: *decoctio*, the natural process of "ripening" or cooking within the earth</note>—when we see the same thing happen in trees, crops, and plants? It is certain that earth, wood, twigs, shells, and the skins and bones of animals are converted into rocks and stones by the power of natural waters flowing spontaneously, and by the power of "lapidification" <term>lapidificandi virtute: the natural force or "virtue" believed to turn organic matter into stone</term>. Yet what is more diverse than stone and wood, or animal hides and bones? For they differ in their whole genus and substance. Concerning earth, it is too well known to need proof. I will bring forward only certain things most worthy of report from Albertus Magnus <note>Albert the Great (c. 1200–1280), a Dominican friar and influential philosopher</note>, who relates that in his time, in the Danish sea near the city of Lübeck, a large branch of a tree was found, and in it a nest with chicks, which together with the branch and the nest had been turned into stone. And that the Emperor Frederick <note>Frederick II (1194–1250), Holy Roman Emperor</note>, when he had heard there was a spring in which everything immersed was turned to stone, sent a sealed glove there for the sake of exploring the truth. When half of it had been submerged in the spring for some days along with part of the seal, while the remaining part was not changed at all, the half immersed in the waters was turned to stone. 

But perhaps they will admit the transformation of metals, being convinced by the testimony and consensus of most famous men; yet they will deny that it can be done with profit and with infinite "augmentation" <note>The alchemical process of increasing the quantity or potency of the philosopher's stone or the resulting gold</note>. I think they should be countered in this way: if in legal judgments where one's property, life, or reputation is at stake, two

<margin>
Unblemished witnesses must be believed.
</margin>
or three witnesses must be believed according to both divine law and civil law, it is even more equitable for this to be applied in the Chemical art <note>Alchemy</note>, which is proven true by reasons, analogies, examples, and witnesses—not just three or four, but almost innumerable. For we have the writings of most learned and upright men, such as Saint Thomas Aquinas...

### PREFACE.

<margin>In the place cited above.</margin>
The testimonies of Hermes Trismegistus <note>A legendary Hellenistic figure associated with the origins of alchemy</note>, Ramon Lull, John of Rupescissa, Marsilio Ficino, and Arnaldus de Villanova—whom the legal expert <term>John Andreas</term> <note>A famous 14th-century canon lawyer</note> calls a Theologian, a supreme Physician, and an Alchemist—as well as Rhasis <note>The Persian polymath Al-Razi</note>, Avicenna <note>The famous Persian philosopher and physician Ibn Sina</note>, and many others who are beyond all reproach, attest that this is a most true art and an imitator of nature, its own mother. Why should we judge that faith should be withdrawn from such illustrious men, and believe instead certain "smatterers" <note>original: *sciolis*, meaning those with superficial or pretentious knowledge</note> who, with perverse judgment, scoff that the art is vain and fraudulent? They claim it was handed down enigmatically and obscurely for no other reason than to exercise the wits of idle men. 

<margin>A Philosopher does not knowingly lie.</margin>
Far be it from us to think that those ancient philosophers of venerable authority would have deliberately wished to commit any falsehood to memory; they always devoted the greatest effort to inquiring after the truth, and sought fame for posterity not from trifles and empty things, but from arduous and sublime matters resting on a true and stable foundation. 

<margin>That Alchemy is true is proved by the consensus of nations.</margin>
To this is also added the consensus of diverse nations: for the records of the metamorphosis <note>The transformation or change of form</note> of metals belonging not only to the Latins, but also to the Greeks, Egyptians, Arabs, Chaldeans, French, Germans, Spanish, and English, are thumbed daily by the hands of curious men. All these cry out as if with one mouth (though in different languages), 

<margin>Nothing is more sublime than Alchemy, except the Sacred Scriptures.</margin>
that the art is most true, and that nothing—after the Divine Law, in which is the salvation of the soul—has been granted to man in this world by the most high God that is more magnificent or sublime. Therefore, they preach that it must be investigated with the greatest zeal and sought with wakeful labor. 

<margin>Why the art is contradicted. Abuse, or the error of the operators, or ignorance do not invalidate the art. *Book on the Soul*.</margin>
Perhaps those who deny the art are deceived by this: that while infinite numbers of people devote themselves to chemistry, they see no one who boasts of having attained the knowledge. But to the wise and those who scrutinize the causes of events, nothing happens that is worthy of wonder. 

<margin>Why one very rarely achieves the art.</margin>
For how few people work with the proper <term>matter</term>? <note>In alchemy, the "First Matter" was the essential starting material, the identity of which was a closely guarded secret</note> Scarcely one in thousands. What wonder is it, then, if they are frustrated in their intended end? 

<margin>Greed and poverty are great obstacles.</margin>
Therefore, Avicenna said not foolishly: *He who takes what he should, and mixes and works as he should, from that proceeds what should proceed.* And many unlearned...

He explains that the frequent failure of practitioners is due to human error and greed rather than a flaw in the science itself.</summary>

### PREFACE.

<margin>
Secrets are not to be made public.
Proverbs 10.
</margin>
...tinuity. Indeed, they are plainly unlearned and uncultured <note>original: *ἄμουσοι* (amousoi), a Greek term for those "without the Muses," meaning those lacking education or refinement</note>, who do not understand even common Latin speech, let alone the metaphors and analogies of the wise. Others, although they may be learned and of sharp wit, do not possess the necessary books—either because they refuse to pay the price for them out of greed, or because they cannot afford them due to poverty, or perhaps because they cannot find copies in the places where they live and they dread traveling. Those, however, who have obtained both the books and the art by the grace of God, remember the saying of Solomon: *A wise man hides knowledge, but the mouth of a fool is near to ruin* <note>Proverbs 10:14</note>. For there are certainly reasons why those who know the truth do not reveal themselves. But if we must deny things simply because we have rarely or never happened to see them, the credibility of all history, both sacred and secular, will be diminished.

<margin>Book 13, at the end.</margin>
For who would believe in the sulfurous and fiery rain from heaven that brought the destruction of Sodom and Gomorrah, or the strength of Samson, and so many other things whose like are never told except in fables? 

<margin>
Things whose causes are unknown or which happen rarely should not be accused of being false.
</margin>
Who, while running through the *Annals* of P. Cornelius Tacitus <note>A famous Roman historian (c. 56–120 AD)</note>, would not burst into laughter upon reading that a fire in the Colony of the Juhones <note>Referring to a passage in Tacitus's *Annals* regarding the Ubii people; the "fire from the earth" was a well-known historical curiosity</note> was extinguished not with water, but with clubs and clothes stripped from the body? Does he not seem to be telling a fable? And yet, we believe it could have happened then, and we know for certain it happens quite often today in the territory of Liège <note>A region in modern-day Belgium famous for its coal mining</note>, where miners cut out bituminous coals <note>early reference to fossil coal</note> from beneath the earth—black like stones—for use in the hearths and forges of blacksmiths.

<margin>
*On the Origin and Causes of Subterraneans*, book 2, and book 4 of *On the Nature of those things which flow spontaneously from the Earth*.
</margin>
Who would not believe that mere lies are being told by Georgius Agricola <note>Known as the "father of mineralogy," his 16th-century works laid the foundation for modern mining and geology</note> when he says that on Mount Hekla in Iceland, there is a fire that consumes water but does not burn tow <note>coarse flax or hemp fiber</note>? But investigators of natural causes know that the bitumen <term>bitumen</term> <note>A naturally occurring petroleum product, like asphalt or tar</note> from which that fire is stirred is actually extinguished by dry things and nourished by water. But they are greatly mistaken in their opinion, since many from among the common people everywhere know that those who have been witnesses to nature and art are the ones who truly know, while those who value this knowledge cheaply, as if it were unworthy, are the ones who rave.

<margin>No wise man has ever denied the art.</margin>

### PREFACE.

<margin>Those who dispute about things unknown cannot reach a correct conclusion.</margin>
...for nearly all arguments brought against this art proceed from nowhere else than ignorance of those things done within the art. Thus many speak of substantial forms, the proportion of things to be mixed, and the vessels of Nature and art; yet, by disputing about things they do not know, they reach unknown conclusions. Therefore, leaving those matters aside, I proceed to the goal of my proposition.

<margin>What the Philosopher's Stone is.</margin>
The intention of the philosophers of this art is to artificially produce a certain mineral virtue from the purest seed of gold and silver—yet with the benefit and assistance of Nature—in the form of a most subtle white or red powder. This powder can be multiplied infinitely and has the power to penetrate <term>quicksilver</term> <note>original: *argentum vivum*. Literally "living silver," known today as mercury; alchemists viewed it as the "mother" of all metals.</note>,

<margin>The virtues of the Stone.</margin>
and other base and impure metals in an instant, cleansing them of all impurities and bringing them to the more perfect state of gold or silver. It also has the power to restore a sick human body, returning it to its true balance, or to preserve a healthy person in health until the limit fixed by God.

<margin>The Philosopher's Stone, the Elixir, and the Medicine are the same thing.</margin>
The Arabic philosophers call this powder, endowed with such great virtue, the <term>Elixir</term> <note>original: *Elixir*. Derived from the Arabic *al-iksir*, referring to a dry powder or transformative substance.</note>, while the Latin philosophers call it "the Medicine" and their "Stone." However, I would wish younger students to be warned that the name "Stone" is used broadly and in various ways.

<margin>The widely used name of the Stone. Chapter 10 of the first part of the *Rosarium* <note>The *Rosarium Philosophorum* (Rosary of the Philosophers), one of the most famous illustrated alchemical treatises.</note>.</margin>

Furthermore, the principles that constitute the Elixir are called stones, and these are three in number:

<margin>The three principles of the Stone.</margin>
namely, <term>quicksilver</term>, <term>Sulfur</term>, and <term>Tincture</term>; or <term>Body</term>, <term>Spirit</term>, and <term>Soul</term>; or <term>Earth</term>, <term>Water</term>, and <term>Fire</term>—and a fourth resulting from the first two, which is <term>Air</term>. The Sages of this art have bestowed these names upon them.

<margin>In the printed treatise.</margin>
Regarding quicksilver, one must understand that saying of Avicenna <note>A Latinized version of Ibn Sina, the Persian polymath whose medical and philosophical works dominated European universities.</note>: "The third stage of the work is the reduction of the stone into natural earth." Or perhaps it is because almost all metals are generated within stones, and the Elixir must necessarily be made from metals if those metals are to be converted.

<margin>7.
Chapter 17, practice of the *Testament*.</margin>
Or it may be because of **mineral Salt**: wherefore some say, "The Salt of the metals is the stone of the philosophers." Lullius <note>Ramon Llull (c. 1232–1315), a Majorcan philosopher and polymath to whom many alchemical works were later attributed.</note> calls Salt a stone because it certainly resembles a stone when it remains in its place. But there may be another, more hidden reason why this medicine is called a stone, which the philosophers have concealed; although the first reason, by the consensus of many, is the truth... <note>The catchword "veri-" indicates the text continues "verissima," or "most true," on the following page.</note>

...might be more likely. <margin>Many falsely persuade themselves that the Elixir is easy to prepare.</margin> Indeed, a mad opinion has invaded the minds of many: that the stone of the philosophers is entirely easy to make, prepared with light work, and happens by some fortune or chance, provided the will to inquire is not lacking. ### ->PREFACE.<-

...is discussed by everyone today. There is one who might seem to have written his little book on the metamorphosis of metals <note>likely referring to a contemporary alchemical treatise, possibly by an author like Giovanni Battista Nazari or similar</note> out of a certain zeal of charity, were it not clear to the more skilled that he handed down this science far too sparingly. He claims the art is so easy that if it were shown in action or by practice itself, it would hardly be believed. 

<margin>A Story.</margin>
When I was still a young man living in Paris, I remember hearing that a certain gardener had gathered useless and wild-growing herbs into a pile and set fire to them so that, once they were reduced to ashes, he might prepare lye <term>lixivium: a solution of alkaline salts leached from wood ashes, used for cleaning</term>. But as it happened, a lead pipe for channeling water had been forgotten or gone unnoticed in that place due to its age; by the force of the fire, the lead melted and was converted into gold. This was attributed to the undeniable power of a certain herb mixed in among the others. The story goes that he later found the gold after the ashes were removed, sold it, and received a great price. 

Truly, those who tell such idle tales—if they had tasted the secrets of nature even slightly or used their judgment—would not so easily believe the lies and impositions of such deceitful men. 

<margin>Like is generated by its like.</margin>
They surely should have considered that a human is generated from a human, a lion from a lion, and a plant from a plant; one should not seek in a nature that which is not already within it. For how can a plant provide a tincture <note>the alchemical "dye" or power to transform the color of a metal</note> or "fix" a substance <note>making it stable and resistant to fire</note> and defend it from being burned away, when the plant itself contains neither tincture nor the power of fixation, and is consumed by fire? 

<margin>The error of practitioners.</margin>
Nevertheless, there were—and are still today—those who seek the highest secret of the Philosophers in both animal and vegetable substances. They experiment with whatever comes their way, things they find in notes, in misunderstood books, or in works composed through the fraud and greed of impostors. They hope that they will find by chance what the Philosophers believe must be sought with the greatest labor and continuous study, and obtained from God through prayers. 

<margin>A dangerous experiment. The two reasons why the Stone is sometimes called a "Salamander."</margin>
Thus, not without immense danger, some assert that live salamanders <note>The fire-dwelling lizard of legend</note> should be thrown into a carefully sealed pot and burned. They hope they will bring forth gold from this, when instead they should rather fear death <note>likely a warning against the toxic vapors produced by such experiments</note>. They do this because they believe it turned out well for others based solely on hearsay, or perhaps because the Philosophers sometimes called their Stone—which is perfected by fire—by the name "Salamander," likewise...

### ->PREFACE.<-

...taken from the similarity to the Salamander, which the ancients believed lived in fire and was nourished by it; or, because its body is marked with various spots of color, much like the Stone which changes from color to color, and sometimes even displays many colors at once.

<margin>Response to the cited sayings of the philosophers.</margin>
But to respond in part to the sayings cited above, I say that in the *Assembly of the Philosophers* <note>original: "Turba philosophorum," one of the oldest and most famous Latin alchemical texts, presented as a debate among pre-Socratic philosophers</note> it is not simply said that the art is "women’s work and children's play," but rather this applies after the stone has been fully cleansed and whitened <term>dealbatio: the alchemical process of whitening the "black" matter to reach the second major stage of the work</term>, because from that point on, it is brought to completion by cooking alone. For so says Socrates in that same work:

> I have already demonstrated to you the arrangement of the white lead; once this is known, nothing else follows but the work of women and the play of children. 

But the books of the philosophers and the frustrated labors of those who have tried bear witness to how much difficulty there is in separating, purifying, and joining the elements of the stone. Therefore, the author of the *Lily* <note>Referring to the *Lilium Medicinae* or more likely the alchemical *Lilium*, often attributed to Arnald of Villanova</note>, who most faithfully interprets many sayings of the *Assembly*, writes in this manner:

> Once the stone and its operation are known, it is nothing other than the mockery of women and the play of children. 

And certainly, for those who are knowledgeable and experienced, we concede that the stone is easy to prepare, but it is not so for the inexperienced.

<margin>Why Bernard calls the art easy.</margin>
As for why Count Bernard <note>Bernard of Trevisan, a legendary 15th-century alchemist who supposedly spent 80 years and his entire fortune seeking the Stone</note> asserts the art is so easy, we can assume he is thinking of the latter part of the work, just as Socrates did in the *Assembly*. This is especially likely since, in his entire treatise, he makes no mention at all—or only very sparingly—of the first part, which is the most difficult of all; instead, his parable encompasses only the end of the decoction <term>decoctio: the process of long-term heating or "ripening" the chemical mixture</term>. Or we might say it seemed easy to him because, after so many ill-spent expenses and forty years of labor, he attained the knowledge in the space of two years through the reading of books and by the help of divine grace—knowledge he had previously attempted in vain for the course of so many years. However, we can gather that the practical experience was not so easy for him from the fact that he writes that he knew the art two years before he seriously set his hand to the work.

<margin>Why it is called "light" by others.</margin>
It could be called "light" <note>meaning easy or simple</note> by others in comparison to other manual arts, which require many and various instruments, as well as much physical exertion and labor; whereas this requires only one single material, one vessel, and one furnace with a suitable fire:

He cites authorities like Socrates and Bernard of Trevisan to show that "ease" is only found after decades of study and divine grace.</summary>

<margin>The Philosophers said many things to deceive the unwary.</margin>
...furthermore, while other arts are practiced almost throughout one's entire life, this one, once perfectly discovered and practiced, requires no repetition, since the practitioner has been enriched and has achieved his wish. Who would even dare to deny that the philosophers brought forth such sayings—as they did many others—in order to deceive the unwary? <margin>The preparation of the Stone is difficult.</margin> But I would hope that those who consider this art so easy would call to mind that well-worn adage: *beautiful things are difficult.* <note>original: "difficilia esse quæ pulcra," a Latin translation of the Greek proverb *chalepa ta kala*, emphasizing that anything of great value requires proportional effort</note> Likewise, that saying of Roger Bacon: <note>Roger Bacon (c. 1214–1292) was an English Franciscan friar and polymath; he was frequently cited in alchemical literature as an authority on the "secrets of nature."</note> *In those things where God has placed great virtue, He has also situated great difficulty.* If only they would remember that it is called the "Stone of the Philosophers," not of peasants or the unlearned; by its name alone, anyone who is not completely <margin>In the *New Pearl*</margin> <note>original: "In Marg. Novell.," referring to the *Margarita Pretiosa Novella* (The New Precious Pearl), an influential 14th-century alchemical text by Pietro Bono (Petrus Bonus).</note> foolish might rightly be deterred. Indeed, let them consult Pietro Bono of Ferrara, and he will respond that the search for this art, its truth and its experience, appears stronger, more difficult, more hidden, and of longer duration than the search for all other things. <margin>It is fitting for everyone to know themselves.</margin> Since this is most true, let each person examine himself and show himself to be a sharp judge of both his vices and his virtues before he attempts to enter the inner sanctum <term>adyta: a Latin term for the innermost, most sacred part of a temple, accessible only to priests; used here to describe the deep secrets of alchemical science</term> of this science. Let him carefully weigh whether he finds within himself those qualities which the Philosophers require in their disciples, which are surely many and greater than the common opinion holds. I shall endeavor to the best of my ability to set these out before everyone's eyes, as if on a painted panel. <margin>The order of things to be said.</margin> To propose a certain order for what is to be discussed, I shall distinguish this little book into four parts. 

In the first, I will recount the impediments occurring regarding the person of the craftsman, and certain outcomes. In the second, I will show how difficult it is for the truth to be extracted from the writings of the Philosophers. In the third, I will reveal what difficulties arise regarding the practice, interspersed everywhere (as far as memory allows) with the authorities of the Sages in this art, lest anyone think I am saying anything out of a desire to exaggerate the difficulty more than is fair, or merely to serve my own purpose rather than the utility of the readers. In the fourth, I will demonstrate—by certain reasons and examples—that this art should be avoided by everyone; or, if I am less successful in that, I will show how it may at least be practiced with the smallest possible expense.

<meta>catchword: PART</meta>

<summary>Hoghelande argues that alchemy is intentionally described in deceptive, easy-sounding terms by philosophers to trick the unworthy, whereas in reality, it is a life-altering and arduous task requiring high moral character. He concludes the preface by outlining the four upcoming sections of his book, which aim to discourage the unprepared or at least mitigate their financial ruin.</summary>

*Plato* instructs that in all things, whether the greatest or the smallest, divine help must be implored. Since, therefore, this science—according to the testimony of *Geber*, *Senior*, <note>Senior Zadith, the Latin name for the 10th-century Arabic alchemist Ibn Umayl.</note> and other philosophers—is nothing but a perfect divine inspiration and a secret of the glorious God, who bestows it upon or withdraws it from whom He wills, it befits him especially who desires to be initiated into this art to ask the Triune and One God with a humble mind, that He might deign to illuminate his intellect and confer wisdom upon him. For there is no wisdom except from God, who does not deny it to those seeking and asking with a sincere heart and good intention. But because the Lord does not hear sinners, it is necessary, if the seeker wishes to be heard, that he love, revere, and fear God, from whom he expects every good thing. For the fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom, as the Royal Prophet <note>King David, the traditional author of the Psalms.</note> says. Wherefore *Alphidius* <note>An authority frequently cited in medieval alchemical texts, likely of Arabic origin.</note> says most rightly: *My son, I preach to you the fear of the Lord, as well as love with unfeigned obedience.* And *Senior* says: *You who shall be diligent in the fear of God shall see the secret and the manifest power of this stone, and you shall find it, being instructed by the spirit of the Most High, so that you may know that all wisdom is from God.* And *Hermes* <note>Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary "Thrice-Great" founder of the Hermetic tradition.</note> says: *Son, I advise you before all things to fear God, in whom the endeavor of your procedure lies.* <note>original: "dispositionis," referring to the specific alchemical arrangement or chemical process.</note> Furthermore, let him have a contrite spirit and one shunning sins; because, as the *Wise Man* <note>Solomon, in the biblical Book of Wisdom.</note> says, *Wisdom will not enter into a malevolent soul, nor will she dwell in a body subject to sins.* Whence *Alphidius* says: *You cannot possess this science until you purify your mind for God, and God knows you have a contrite mind.* And *St. Thomas* says: *While having peace with your God, always set before yourself an ordained end in your work.* And *Geber* says: *Sons of iniquity and malevolent depravity, flee from this science, for it is hostile and adverse to you, and it will place you in the misery of poverty.* Let him be humble, nor let him seek this science so that he might surpass others, or boast of possessions and riches. For so *Hermes* says: *It behooves the recruit of this science to repel the vice of arrogance from himself, and to be pious and upright.* And *Alphidius* says: *If you are humble, the Sophia and Wisdom of this art will be perfected; but if not, its procedure will be completely hidden from you.* And the Author of the *Dialogue of Nature and the Son of Philosophy* says: *The arrogant and ambitious are found to be rejected and unworthy, not only by God, but by science itself and every gift of God.*

<header>THEOBALD DE HOGHELANDE</header>

<margin>*An Objection.*</margin>
But someone might cast doubt upon the things stated above, and argue in this manner: You require that a student of this art be a Christian and pious, for otherwise he will not know or adore the three persons in the Godhead and the one God in the Trinity, nor will he be able to love and fear Him. Furthermore, you desire a contrite soul, a conscience pure from sins, and humility—virtues which are specifically required of Christians. Yet, it is well known that Geber, Rhasis, Avicenna, and other Arabs who wrote about this art were Saracens and followers of Mohammad <note>The author uses the terms "Sarracenos" and "Mahometistas" to refer to the medieval Islamic scholars who were the primary sources for European alchemy.</note>, and they did not possess knowledge of the true God. Nevertheless, their books testify that they were most skilled in this science, which we even admit flowed down to the Latins <note>Medieval European scholars who read and wrote in Latin.</note> chiefly from them. Therefore, it seems that neither piety nor the fear of God has anything to do with the matter, provided that talent, books, and wealth are not lacking.

<margin>*The Solution.*</margin>
I respond that they were not lacking in piety, however misguided it may have been, and that they flourished with the greatest virtues and shrunk from crimes, as is clear enough from Geber’s books and the passage cited above. We also know that even the Turks today possess more devotion, and approach their temples and sacred places with greater reverence, and exhibit more brotherly charity toward the needy and the wretched, than by far the greatest part of Christians. Therefore, it is no wonder if God—who examines the intentions of men just as much as their works—has rewarded them with most splendid victories, and with this most precious science of all, and finally with other benefits and temporal gifts, even though they were ignorant of the true worship of God. All these things, however, are small in respect to the eternal happiness which the professors of the Christian faith expect, while those others are rejected. Furthermore, it is better to have a false god whom one fears and worships, and by the fear of whom the wicked wills and misdeeds of men are restrained, than to have no god at all, as many Sophists <note>Here, "Sophists" refers to those who use clever but fallacious arguments, often implying a lack of genuine moral or religious grounding.</note> do. For those are not worthy of the name of Alchemists who seek this science solely with the intent to satisfy their own greeds, and not for the glory of God, or for the comfort of their neighbor, or to relieve poverty.

<margin>*The Prudent Man. The tricks of the Philosophers in hiding the science.*</margin>
But I return to the purpose. Besides what has already been said, let the artificer be prudent and possess a naturally subtle and deep intellect, and let him be strong in excellent judgment, so that he knows how to distinguish true things from false, and the power of nature from works that go against nature. For more often than not, in order to deceive the unwary, the philosophers bring forward certain reasons for their sayings which seem true in appearance and outward show, and yet are false.

<margin>*Chapter 13. On the Investigation of Perfection, ch. 12. The Sum of Perfection. The Book of Secrets, ch. 2.*</margin> <note>These are standard citations for the works of "Geber," the Latinized name of Jabir ibn Hayyan.</note>
Hence Geber says: "We attract only the prudent to the art." The same author says: "We shall hand down the art in such a discourse that it will not happen to be hidden from the prudent; yet for the mediocre it will be most profound, and it will exclude the foolish without recourse." And Haly <note>Likely referring to Haly Abenragel or another Arabic authority whose works were translated into Latin.</note> says: "I have not made this book for the ignorant and the unknowing, but I have composed it for the prudent and those possessing Wisdom." Morienes <note>A legendary hermit-alchemist said to have taught the Ummayad prince Khalid ibn Yazid.</note> says: "Let providence, reason, and firm expectation be employed by the artificer."

<summary>Hoghelande argues that while the great Arabic alchemists were not Christian, God rewarded their natural virtue and piety with alchemical knowledge. He concludes that the "art" is intentionally hidden in riddles to ensure only the intelligent and morally upright can succeed.</summary>

# OF THE DIFFICULTIES OF ALCHEMY, BOOK 125

<margin>*Learned.*</margin>
Let him be learned, so that where natural talent does not reach, this defect may be aided by doctrine. Hence the universal path: "We have hidden this matter with a strong concealment <note>original: "absconditione forti"</note>, so that it cannot be grasped by the unlearned."

<margin>*Skilled in the Latin tongue.*</margin>
First and foremost, let him be skilled in the Latin language; for how else might he understand those things which are for the most part written and published in the Latin tongue? Nor should anyone think that chemical books are translated into another language with the same ease or truth as the books of other sciences.

<margin>*A philosopher.*</margin>
Let him be well-versed in natural philosophy and other sciences. Whence Arnaldus <note>Arnaldus de Villanova (c. 1240–1311), a famous physician and alchemist.</note> says:
> Whoever wishes to reach this science and is not a philosopher is a fool, because this science is concerned only with the secrets of the philosophers.

And Morienes <note>Morienus, a legendary hermit-alchemist said to have taught the Umayyad prince Khalid ibn Yazid.</note>:
> Whoever pursues this science, it is fitting for him to know the other arts and especially Dialectic <note>The art of logical argument and reasoning.</note>, since the Philosophers of this art have spoken only under a veil and figure.

And Alphidius <note>An Arabic alchemical author frequently cited in medieval Latin collections.</note>:
> I have composed this book for no one but a philosopher.

<margin>*In the Key of Philosophy.*</margin>
<margin>*One who knows the principles of Nature.*</margin>
<margin>*The Sum of Perfection, at the beginning.*</margin>
Furthermore, let the craftsman not be ignorant of the principles of Nature and art, because he who ignores the beginning will not find the end. Whence Geber <note>Jabir ibn Hayyan, the influential 8th-century scholar known in the West as Geber, considered the father of alchemy.</note> says:
> He who is ignorant of natural principles within himself is far removed from our art, since he has no true root upon which to found his intention.

<margin>*In the Secrets of Alchemy.*</margin>
And Saint Thomas <note>Thomas Aquinas; although a theologian, several alchemical treatises were attributed to him in the Middle Ages.</note>: I urge that no one presume to begin the work unless he is very skilled and experienced in natural principles. Avicenna <note>Ibn Sina (c. 980–1037), the Persian polymath whose works on medicine and minerals were foundational to European science.</note> says:
> Know the roots of minerals, so that from them you may perform your work.

<margin>*Industrious and hardworking.*</margin>
Moreover, let him be industrious and hardworking, so that what he has attained through natural talent and learning, he may know how to assist with his own industry and labor, and to correct himself if he happens to err. Haly <note>Likely referring to Khalid ibn Yazid, an early patron of alchemy, or the astrologer Haly Abenragel.</note> says:
> This mastery is not given to you for your boldness, strength, and cunning alone, without any labor; for men labor, and God grants fortune to men.

<margin>*The Sum of Perfection, chapter 26.*</margin>
Geber:
> And you indeed should exercise yourself with the greatest persistence of labor, and with the duration of immense meditation; for with those things you shall find it, and without them, you shall not.

<margin>*Constant.*</margin>
The Philosophers also require a craftsman of constant will, who does not presume to try now this, now that—because art does not consist in a multitude of things—but rather that he should persist in the work once begun until its completion, nor leave the work unfinished. Whence Rosinus <note>A Latinized name for Zosimos of Panopolis, a 3rd-century Greco-Egyptian alchemist.</note> quoting Rhasis <note>Al-Razi (c. 865–925), a Persian physician and chemist.</note>:
> In this business, if the difficulty of acting and tedious fatigue make the worker negligent, it deprives him of the expected joy, suffocates hope, and destroys effectiveness.

And the Author of the *Ladder of Philosophers*:
> When you are in the work, let there be assiduousness with patience and fitting expectation; the end of which [negligence] is loss and sadness.

<margin>*Not prone to anger.*</margin>
<margin>*Patient.*</margin>
Let him not be headlong into anger, lest if he does not understand the books at first glance, he should cast them aside; or if the undertakings should succeed less happily, he should break and disturb the vessels, furnaces, and other things necessary for the work in a fit of fury. But on the contrary, let him be patient and long-suffering, waiting with a calm mind for the action of nature, which is very slow. Whence Arnaldus:
<margin>*The Rosary, chapter 3, part 2.*</margin>
> Be long-suffering, and do not seek to finish hastily or quickly...

### ON THE DIFFICULTIES OF ALCHEMY, BOOK I

<margin>The material of the Stone is cheap.</margin>
And another says: The expenses of our art do not exceed the price of two gold coins in its first purchase; however, since it necessarily happens that the operator fails quite often (for the right path is not discerned except through error, as **Baccen** <note>original: "Baccen. in Turba." Referring to a speaker in the *Turba Philosophorum* (Assembly of the Philosophers), one of the oldest Latin alchemical texts.</note> says in the *Turba*. And **Alphil** <note>Al-Phidius, an Arabic alchemical authority.</note> says: *He who does not err does not arrive, and he who does not corrupt does not amend, and he who does not grieve does not rejoice*) a poor man cannot afford to begin again and repeat the work as often as is necessary. <margin>Arriving at the art through many errors.</margin> For so says the author of the *Book on the Perfect Mastery*: Since no one can be certain regarding the experience of this matter, I advise you that, once the action has begun, you do not cease from it. If you have not operated correctly the first time, reiterate a second, a third, and even more if there is need of the work, until you grasp most perfectly what you seek. Neither let the labor of your hands nor the expense of things move you away from this matter, because with persistence you will conquer, and you will receive a reward for the labor of your hands, and a profit from the expenses of the materials. And the author of the *Universal Way* says: it is necessary for the craftsman to arrive at perfection through many labors and errors, for this most excellent work is scarcely led to its end without impediment.

<margin>Let the craftsman have a wealth of books.</margin>
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Let him have a great abundance of books: for no one should persuade himself that any single book can be found which truly describes the whole art in a continuous series of discourse, as many foolishly believe. <margin>A foolish opinion.</margin> For that would be to detract from the majesty of nature, and deservedly, as a traitor of the celestial seal <note>The "celestial seal" refers to the divine secret of the Philosopher's Stone, which was believed to be protected by God.</note>, anyone who dared such things would be condemned by all; he should be forbidden from water and fire <note>A traditional Roman formula for exile/excommunication.</note>, and his writings should be abolished by fire as a pestilence to the world and adverse to public peace. Therefore, it is not in vain that many books were composed on one and the same subject by a single author, so that, evidently, what he delivered in a diminished state in one, he might complete in another. <margin>Philosophers deliver knowledge scattered and in parts.</margin> For so says **Geber**: *We have not proposed to show everything in one volume, since book opens and explains book.* The same says in another place: *Let the wise craftsman study in our volumes, collecting our dispersed opinion, which we have proposed in diverse places, lest it be made public to the wicked or the ignorant.* Moved by that reasoning, **Lull** <note>Raymundus Lullius (Ramon Llull, c. 1232–1315), a philosopher and mystic to whom many alchemical works were attributed.</note> wrote over sixty volumes on this art; others wrote six, eight, or fewer. Or if any author composed only one single book, he also embraced only one part of the work, which some philosophers distinguished into three, more into four, some even into five or six <term>regimens</term> <note>Regimens are the specific stages or "reigns" of the chemical process, such as calcination, dissolution, or fermentation.</note>; many even into two, <margin>Authors divided the work as they pleased.</margin> and they confused these among themselves, so that what is first, middle, or last remains unknown. Or if he included several parts of the work at once, he carried it out briefly, and by interposing many falsehoods among a very few truths. <margin>Final chapter.</margin> Just as **Arnaldus de Villanova**, when he had composed a sufficiently large volume on this art under the name of the *Rosary* <note>The *Rosarium Philosophorum*, a foundational text in Western alchemy.</note>, concludes at the end in this way: *Having completed the discourse, I have given you the methods of the <term>elixir</term> above, not in riddles, but in a plain series of speech, speaking clearly to your discernment; since, God as my witness...*

...nothing in this art is contained better or more perfectly than those things aforementioned, though shortened by brevity; yet for those who understand, they are sufficiently <margin>In the book which is [called] the *Flower of Flowers*. And **Arnald** <note>Arnald of Villanova (c. 1240–1311), a famous physician and alchemist.</note> says: *A book opens a book, and a speech opens a speech.* And truly, by this single hindrance alone, many learned men are greatly delayed from becoming masters of their <margin>Alchemical books are difficult to find and rare.</margin> wishes. For books written about this art are difficult to find, but are obtained from their owners with somewhat greater difficulty; for those who possess them guard them like Sibylline oracles <note>A reference to the legendary, highly guarded prophetic books of ancient Rome.</note>, than which nothing can be more absurd or ill-timed; nor do they easily share them with others by prayer or price, unless the price is quite large.

Indeed, the printed books—which we largely owe to the Doctor of Medicine **Guglielmo Gratarolo** <note>A mid-16th century Italian physician who edited major collections of alchemical texts.</note> and **Pietro Perna**, the printer of Basel (to whose heirs, in my opinion, it would be fair to return thanks if anyone were to attain the art)—are very few in respect to <margin>Caution in buying alchemical books.</margin> those which still lie hidden. Moreover, it often happens that novices of this art buy false and adulterated books, devoid of all reason and doctrine, in place of true and good ones, <margin>Example.</margin> since those books which profess a "practice" <note>Practical instructions or recipes, as opposed to theoretical philosophy.</note> usually please beginners more. I myself knew two otherwise distinguished men, prudent in other matters, one of whom had bought at a great price a manuscript "practice" of **Philip de Rovillasto** of Piedmont—which, unknown to him, had already been printed—while the other bought a certain little French book by a certain **Jean Salinarius** (or de Saumur) on the preparation of salts. Each believed that the true doctrine and practice of the art was contained in his little book; nor did they hope for anything else than that some artist <note>A practicing alchemist or laboratory assistant.</note> be given to them, whose work they might use to extract such a treasure from the books, since they themselves, occupied with other business, could not or did not know how to apply their hands to the work. <margin>The craftsman ought to be studious.</margin> Although they were warned by me in a friendly manner that no truth was contained in those books, and that they should therefore spare their money and make no expenditures, I heard nonetheless that afterwards, ensnared by a false hope of gain, they did not obey my advice, but exposed themselves to be deluded and deceived by others.

However, it is not enough to have many books and those obtained at great cost, unless a diligent, assiduous, and long-term reader happens upon them; for it is not the space of a few months but of years that is needed for understanding the authors' parables, enigmas, equivocations, tropes, figures, and transpositions. Therefore **Agadimon** <note>Agathodaimon, a figure in the *Turba Philosophorum*.</note> says most rightly in the *Turba*: *He who thinks he can quickly take fruit from our books is mistaken; for it would have been better not even to look into them than to have touched them rashly.* For our books

<margin>Terms are used in various ways.</margin>
...of medicine <note>The word "medicinae" (of medicine) completes the sentence from the previous page.</note>, examples occur everywhere of **Lull** <note>Raymond Lull (c. 1232–1315), a major figure in medieval alchemy and logic.</note> and other authors using names interchangeably for a work that is perfected in every way. For thus
<margin>In the *Practice of the Testament*, chapter 2.</margin>
Lull says of the stone and the elixir: "This stone converts every diminished and imperfect body into an infinite Gold-maker and Silver-maker <note>original: "Solificum & Lunificum." These terms refer to the stone's power to transmute base metals into gold (associated with the Sun) and silver (associated with the Moon).</note>,
<margin>In the *Mirror of Alchemy*, chapter 2.</margin>
according to how the elixir shall be refined and prepared." Of the elixir 
<margin>In the *Rosary*, part 1, chapter 23.</margin>
alone, **Roger Bacon** <note>Roger Bacon (c. 1214–1292), an English philosopher and friar often credited with early alchemical and scientific texts.</note> says: "The red elixir turns things yellow <note>original: "citrinat," referring to *citrinitas*, the yellowing stage of the alchemical process.</note> to infinity." Of medicine, **Arnald** <note>Arnald of Villanova (c. 1240–1311), a famous physician and alchemist.</note> says: "If the metal which you must convert by means of the medicine does not have sufficient color, let more of the medicine be added." I could cite infinite authorities of the philosophers on this matter, if there were a need. Despite these points, I will demonstrate with cited examples that the names of the Stone, Elixir, and Medicine sometimes signify an *imperfect* work.
<margin>In the Preface.</margin>
But since I have already spoken abundantly above regarding the naming of the "stone"—when I showed that the mastery is called a "stone" in every grade of the work—I shall make mention only of the "elixir" and "medicine," and first indeed of the elixir. Arnald in the *Rosary*: "Be careful in the 
<margin>Chapter 24, part 2. Chapter 21. *Rosary*, chapter 23.</margin>
preparation of the elixir, and work there wisely." The same author: "The lime <note>original: "calx," the powdery residue left after a substance has been heated or "calcined."</note> which is put into the elixir must be sublimated, so that it is entirely simple and one." Regarding medicine, the same Arnald says: "We calcine the medicine so that it may be dissolved more quickly, and we dissolve it so that it may be better cleansed and melted." But in the place cited before, when Lull says that the stone is of one year and the elixir of another, by the name "stone" he understands the earlier part of the work, in which the matter of the stone is dissolved, divided, cleansed, and joined together once more into one, and finally raised upward from the bodily dregs into the fifth essence <note>The "quintessence," or the purest, most essential part of a substance.</note>. By the word "elixir," however, he understands the later part, which encompasses the fixing and the tinting of that which has been cleansed—not only in this
<margin>In the *Practice*, chapter 22.</margin>
place, but everywhere in others. For thus in the *Codicil*, to "infirm" the work <note>original: "opus infirmare," likely meaning to treat the "sick" or base matter.</note> is nothing other than to attribute the due and natural form to the sulfur or the stone, and afterward to the elixir and the medicine. The same author in the *Testament*: "Our mastery is divided into two parts: namely, in creating the stone, and in composing the medicine." By several other authors, 
<margin>Chapter 5.</margin>
on the contrary, the "elixir" is called the earlier part of the work and the "stone" the later part, as it is for the *Author of the Universal Path*: "The elixir is the first and principal foundation, and the root of the precious stone, which afterward through the second operation is converted into the stone itself, or the medicine." **Bernard** <note>Bernard Trevisan (1406–1490), an Italian alchemist.</note> also, and **Richard the Englishman**, and certain others distinguish the work into three parts: Namely, into the Rebis, the Elixir, and the Tincture (or Medicine). They say the **Rebis** <note>A term for the "double thing," representing the union of opposites, often depicted as a two-headed figure.</note> is the first part, named for the "dual matter" <note>original: "re bina."</note>—namely, the dissolving and the being dissolved; while the Elixir is the second part, in which the soul is extracted from the dissolved body by long boiling (for they thought "elixir" took its name from "boiling" <note>original: "elixando." This is a popular but incorrect medieval etymology, linking the Arabic word *al-iksir* to the Latin *elixare* (to boil).</note>, or because of the affinity of the words, they wished it to seem so.
<margin>In the commentary on the *Emerald Tablet* <unclear>of Hermes</unclear>.</margin>
Hence **St. Thomas** <note>Thomas Aquinas (1225–1274). While many alchemical works were attributed to him, most are considered pseudo-epigraphical.</note> says: "It is necessary at the beginning of our operation that the things to be converted into the elixir be first boiled before one proceeds to the composition of the stone"); while the Tincture is the third part, which Lull also calls the medicine,

<meta>This page continues Hoghelande’s analysis of the confusing terminology used by alchemical authorities. <header>ON THE DIFFICULTIES OF ALCHEMY, BOOK...</header>

...indicates <note>The word "indicat" (indicates) completes the sentence from the previous page: "I could cite infinite authorities of the philosophers..."</note>; but the latter preferred to name the first two stages, contracted into one, as the "stone." For some, the work is also divided into four parts by those who distinguish between the tincture <note>The coloring agent or essence.</note> and the medicine, so that the tincture precedes the medicine; just as the author of the *Counsel on the Marriage of the Sun and the Moon* <note>original: "consilij conjugij massæ Solis & Lunæ"</note> divides the process into *Ir*, *Xir*, *Ixir*, and *elixir* <note>These are likely pseudo-Arabic linguistic variations used to illustrate the refinement of the substance toward the final Elixir.</note>. Therefore, the chemical authors must be read very attentively and with great consideration, since they frequently confuse these terms and many others.

### Chapter 5

<margin>Chapter 5.</margin>
The author of the *Universal Way* <note>An anonymous alchemical text often cited in the medieval period.</note> was not ignorant of this, saying: "The Philosophers in their books have called the elixir 'the stone,' and the stone 'the elixir,' making no distinction of names between the two, so that they might blind the foolish." But to return to the discourse from which I digressed.

<margin>The practitioner devoted to the experiment must be healthy.</margin>
The practitioner <term>artifex</term> <note>Literally "the artist" or "craftsman," the standard term for a practicing alchemist.</note> attempting the experiments must be healthy and of firm strength, so that he may be equal to the labor, which is not small. This is witnessed by **St. Thomas** <note>Thomas Aquinas (1225–1274); though a theologian, many alchemical works were attributed to him in this era.</note>, who affirms that he suffered so much labor, stench, and bodily harm that he would by no means wish to attempt the work again except under compelling necessity. He should not be blind, nor mutilated in his hands. For if he has been deprived of his sight, he will not be able to arrange and mix the matter as is required, nor observe the colors appearing in the work; consequently, he will not be able to govern the fire, for the management of the fire depends on the appearance of the colors, as the *Rosary* <note>The *Rosarium Philosophorum*, a famous 16th-century alchemical text.</note> says: "The colors will teach you how you ought to administer the fire."

<margin>What things the practitioner requires.</margin>
If he lacks hands, he will no longer be helped by those limbs through which this art is perfected, as they serve as the ministers of nature. I have said above that the practitioner ought to be sufficiently wealthy—namely, so that he can buy the necessary books for this art and, leaving aside other business, pore over them; and then, so that he can put his learning to the test. However, he will be able to test nothing unless he has a suitable house, or at least three or four rooms. It is also necessary that he spend money on vessels, furnaces, and a fire to be continued night and day, which must be fed now with charcoal, now with oil, or other material as necessity demands. Furthermore, a servant or a companion must be sought who—while the practitioner is sleeping, busy, or sick—may supply the continuous and perpetually enduring fire, and not allow the seed, which has been nurtured for a long time already, to die out or grow cold.

<margin>Alchemy is the enemy of the poor.</margin>
<margin>**Geber**, *The Sum of Perfection*, ch. 7, and **Albertus Magnus**.</margin>
If all these things are brought together, the practitioner will see that he has need of no small sum of money. For this reason, not without cause, this art is called "the enemy of the poor" by the philosophers, because it requires the expenses of many years. Furthermore, the practitioner must take total precaution lest he be reduced to poverty and become a laughingstock to others, if it should happen that he errs in the work or if the time is prolonged, as happens in most cases. Since, therefore, it is now clear from what has been said what sort of person the practitioner ought to be, and since it is very difficult to find someone upon whom God has bestowed such great blessings of mind, body, and fortune, the whole art is rightly judged difficult and dangerous, and anyone who is not imprudent will avoid it as something most harmful.

<header>THEOBALD DE HOGHELANDE</header>
<meta>catchword: of those [lorum]</meta>

<margin>Magnificent book titles deceive many.</margin>
But perhaps someone will arise and say: "Since you require in others the fear of the Lord, integrity, a subtle and profound wit, erudition, industry, patience, constancy, leisure, books, riches, and not a few other things—and since you confess in this very treatise to being a student of Alchemy—do you claim for yourself those qualities which you so greatly require in others?" I respond that I lack many things, and I confess candidly that if I, as a youth, could have conceived and turned over in my mind all the impediments and difficulties which now appear before my eyes, or if I had been fortunate enough to have a faithful counselor who, by laying out all the obstacles of this art, had recalled me from my undertaking—just as I hope to do with this little book—I would never have entered this arena <note>original: "palaestram", literally a wrestling school or gymnasium.</note>. Indeed, I have often grieved when the memory of lost time comes to mind, that I ever looked at Chemical books even through a lattice <note>original: "per transennam"; a metaphor for a passing or superficial glance.</note>. But the same thing happened to me as to many others: when I was a young man, naturally inclined toward investigating the secrets of nature and moderately endowed with the goods of fortune, a little French book by Count Bernard <note>Bernard of Treviso (1406–1490), a famous Italian alchemist whose writings were highly influential.</note> was by chance offered to me in Paris. First, I admired the magnificent title of the work; then, moved by curiosity, I inspected it, read it, and re-read it. In it, I noticed few ambiguities and little obscurity; indeed, the author spontaneously exhorted the reader to the study of that science to which no other could be compared. He described its virtues, since besides immense riches he promised even memory and health to those seeking it seriously, and added that it was so easy that it could hardly be believed. I was overcome, I confess; I yielded <note>original: "manus dedi", literally "I gave my hands," a Latin idiom for surrendering.</note>. Therefore, with the greatest zeal, I immediately collected as many printed or manuscript books of this art as I could find, and for several months I diligently turned them over. But since among the other authors he most cited the *Assembly of the Philosophers* <note>original: "Turba philosoph:"; a famous alchemical text where ancient philosophers engage in a debate.</note>, which he often calls "blessed," and I had two little books inscribed with the name *Assembly of the Philosophers*, one in the French language and the other in Latin (which was later printed in Basel by the efforts of Petrus Perna <note>A 16th-century printer famous for publishing alchemical and medical texts.</note>), I finally set aside the others and devoted myself especially to the French *Assembly*, which I did not know had been collected by that same Bernard. First, I began to admire the agreement of both books; then, when he introduced Pythagoras speaking about the matter of the stone in this way:

> Our work needs in the beginning nothing but two natures of one essence, of which one is base, the other precious; one hard, the other watery; one red, the other white; one fixed, the other volatile; one corporeal, the other spiritual; one cold and moist, the other hot and dry.

When I read further, I found Bernard concluding his little book on the transmutation of metals with this sentiment:

> our work is made from two mineral substances of one root, or essence, all taken raw and drawn from the mine, clean and purified, joined by a suitable fire, as the matter requires, cooked continuously until the two become one:

And in this one after those...

<margin>Testament, chapter 62.</margin>

and added the reason: that gold is not resolvable except with its own nature. <margin>The author’s error in choosing the matter of the stone.</margin>
However, although I read in the works of these same authors, or similar ones, that the "Mercury of the Philosophers" is not common Mercury, yet under the guidance of that same Bernard, I interpreted it thus: it is true that quicksilver by itself cannot provide the matter for the Philosophers’ Stone, nor can gold alone, as long as they remain separate. But if gold is dissolved by quicksilver and reduced into "first matter"—that is, into Mercury—then it could and should rightly be called the "Mercury of the Philosophers," which would contain within itself the power of its own intrinsic sulfur, by which it would be converted into silver and gold, and afterward into the elixir. I drew this example from the seeds of the male and female; as long as they are kept separately in their own places, they cannot be said to be the matter of a living creature, but only then, if they have been joined in the <term>matrix</term><note>The womb or an environment designed to mimic it.</note>, having been led from potentiality into actuality.

Furthermore, when I read in the *Turba*: "Mix, cook, grind with fire, not with hands." And the philosophers affirmed that the entire work is perfected with one vessel, one furnace, and a single arrangement or "decoction," and that the matter ought to be placed in the vessel only once,

in the likeness of a fetus which is nourished in the womb until its perfection, and after it is brought forth into the light, it is nourished first with milk and a little food, and then, as its strength increases, with greater and more solid food. Thus, certain of the Stone, I sought nothing but the time and convenience to devote myself to the work; and already I was seeking secrecy and solitude, fleeing the company of friends and companions. # THEOBALD DE HOGHELANDE

...[desirous of seeing] and hearing foreign things, I undertook a journey and set out for Italy. as <term>Geber</term><note>original: "Gebro." The Latinized name for Jabir ibn Hayyan, the most famous authority in medieval alchemy. <margin>*In the letter to Thomas of Bologna.*</margin>
Added to this was the testimony of <term>Bernard</term><note>Bernard of Treviso (1406–1490), an Italian alchemist whose works were highly influential on Hoghelande.</note> himself, to whom I deferred greatly. <margin>*In the Testament and Codicil.*</margin>
I interpreted these "proper bodies" to be gold and silver, because among metals they abound most in living silver. I also thought that <term>Lull</term><note>Raymond Lull (c. 1232–1315). When, therefore, I had several times sublimated living silver from the gold powder obtained by filing, and yet found it neither brighter nor more beautiful—but indeed more impure—I then first began to lose confidence and to turn my security into anxiety. Finally, taking heart again since the <term>Assembly of the Philosophers</term><note>original: "Turba philosoph." referring to the *Turba Philosophorum*, one of the oldest Latin alchemical texts.</note> commanded that no material should be taken except that which is raw, pleasant, and sincere; and likewise since Bernard said: "the work is made from two raw mercurial substances drawn from the mine," I began to meditate: If raw material is to be taken, there is no need to waste time and weary the mind in sublimations that will be of no benefit at all.

I thought it was most effective if everything were mixed cold rather than heated, for I considered nothing more foolish than to scorch the matter with a violent fire at the start of the work. I believed that the artists of our age stumbled most in this, for, to save costs or because they do not trust others, they amalgamate gold in the common manner of goldsmiths. Having joined everything in a long glass vessel, hermetically sealed and placed in the <term>athanor</term><note>A slow-burning furnace designed to maintain a steady, uniform temperature over a long period.</note>, I began to supply a slow fire, a method I had tried many times before.

> *As I saw, how I perished, how a wicked error swept me away.*
<note>A quote from Virgil's Eclogues (8.41). In this context, the author uses it to express how he was seduced by the beautiful colors in his flask, which he later realized were a deceptive failure.</note>

And not without cause, for that error—or rather, that illusion presented to my eyes—was later the cause of much labor and expense for me. However, my friend—deceived by a similar demonic art, as is reasonable to believe, as will be clear to any curious person from the letters sent to me and preserved for a perpetual memory of the matter—saw his composition change over many days and turn from color to color. Having hoped that the gold was already largely dissolved, after the twenty-first day, when no further variety of colors was observed and the cold weather became pressing, he abandoned the work. It is a wonder that afterward, when he wished to repeat the work a second time, nothing similar happened, nor was any alteration seen. 

Yet, since we still did not know better despite having faced danger so many times, and since he repeatedly spoke highly of Hungary and Transylvania, I decided to travel there—both to finally release my mind from such heavy care and to decide something certain: whether I wished to pursue the art further or abandon it entirely. Thus, I began to weigh more carefully the things that had happened to me, and to fear the deceptions of the devil, who desires that men of otherwise good will be held back by frivolous things and lies, so that, having left the straighter path, they waste time fruitlessly, nor do they care to investigate the truth in any other way, and finally, having been cast into the abyss of despair, they focus on sophistical work <note>Original: "opus Sophisticum." In alchemy, "sophistication" refers to the production of "false" gold or chemical shams, often involving the use of alloys that look like precious metals but lack their true properties.</note>. And so, when I had returned to my books, which I had not seen for many years past, with my judgment somewhat increased by the results of so many experiments, and when I joined my reading to whatever practice I could, at last, by the favor of divine grace, I began to recognize the sulfur of the philosophers <term>Sulfur of the Philosophers: Not common sulfur, but an essential alchemical principle representing the active, masculine, and "fiery" power required for transformation.</term>, and to understand their writings better from day to day. I saw that I had searched in vain through such long and difficult journeys for that which I had already had at home for a long time, since by the name of "gold," the Philosophers do not mean raw and common gold, but their own. For common gold is a dead body, and it accomplishes nothing unless it is managed by human industry; nor does anything enter the work which has not been digested and sought the "heaven of the air" <note>This refers to the process of sublimation or distillation, where a solid material is turned into vapor—the "spiritual" state—before being condensed again.</note>. Wherefore Lullius says:

<margin>Lullius, *On the Intention of Alchemists*, chapter 1.</margin>
"Some wish to dissolve gold and silver with Mercury, which is a useless thing, unless their bodies are made spiritual through refinement, just as Mercury is, and afterward to join them and keep them over a graduated fire." Likewise, Arnald says:

<margin>*The Rosary*, part 1, chapter 6.</margin>
"No body remaining in its own nature coagulates Mercury, nor does Mercury itself heal bodies <note>In alchemical theory, the "Medicine" or "Elixir" was said to "heal" base metals by transforming them into perfect gold.</note>, since it departs from them during the testing; for coarse things agree less with simple things, and simple things with coarse." Even if these things might seem to have been discussed more extensively than the labor of brevity in this planned work might require, nevertheless, I judged it not done absurdly, nor without benefit to many, who, having been taught by someone else's example, will be more cautious hereafter, since I have discovered that not only I and my friend, but also others have been deceived by such demonic tricks. Although they spent their effort on useless things and handled experiments even contrary to nature, they sometimes had successful beginnings, which, having been interrupted by chance, could never be restored or brought back to the same state. Therefore, I advise that everyone avoid an art so subject to the deceptions of the demon, or at least that one does not trust too much in the first bits of progress he has proposed for himself, unless clear reason appears and the work, when repeated, succeeds happily; indeed, let one count this occurrence among the primary difficulties of the art.

if anything should delay a person, perhaps it is not permanent, or can be compensated for in some way and measure. Unless it stands open, one promises himself access or progress to the inner chambers in vain. Thus, all the work of chemists is mocked, who—unless they hope to perceive some fruit from this art through the writings of the philosophers, well-examined and understood—must be born under such a happy star that they acquire its knowledge through the voice of a living person or through divine revelation. He who

attempts the stone otherwise, and trusts that he will find it by chance, I judge to be insane and fit to be deported to Anticyra <note>Anticyra was an ancient Greek city famous for its hellebore, a plant used in antiquity to treat madness. Having experienced its difficulty, they passed the same on to posterity according to the accepted custom of the ancients. Let us hear what they say. and for no others, though it is most true and entirely certain. *The Lily* <note>Referring to the "Lilium intelligentiae," a common title for alchemical treatises.</note>: We have not composed our books except for ourselves and our sons; he who comes to understand them is one of us; but he who does not understand is an opponent to us. Morienes speaks to the same effect: There are books composed about this art under a "figure" <note>Original: "sub figura." This refers to alchemical allegory, where chemical processes are described as human dramas, myths, or symbolic pictures.</note>, the greater part of which seems very obscure and can be understood only by their own authors. Hortulanus says that only he who knows the operation of the stone understands the words of the philosophers. For he says: O

dearest reader, if you know the operation of the stone, I have told you the truth; but if you do not know it, I have told you nothing. But if one asks why they wrote at all, let him hear the author of *The Universal Way* and Geber: By these things which we shall say, we will entice you, son of doctrine, to investigate the Art itself and to find it truly. But let us look into the methods of hiding, and investigate the cause of the difficult understanding of chemical books. This will become more evident if we weigh the reason why other sciences are easier; for opposites placed next to each other shine more clearly. Every other art and science proceeds in its writings rhetorically and in a
<margin>Various ways of hiding the art.</margin>
certain order through chapters, principles, and terms, with definitions and expositions of names and instruments, by which one arrives at the knowledge and notice of its conclusions and its work; it teaches and explains in whatever ways it can. The Philosophers themselves admit this very thing. Geber <note>Geber refers to the author of the "Summa Perfectionis" (The Sum of Perfection), one of the most influential alchemical texts of the Middle Ages.</note>: We do not hand down our science through a transformation of speech, but we have scattered it in diverse chapters and likewise hidden it where we spoke more openly—not however in riddles, but in a plain sequence of discourse <note>Geber suggests that even when the text looks simple and literal, the truth is "hidden in plain sight" by being broken up and rearranged across different sections.</note>. And the Author of the *Conjunction of the Sun and Moon*: The Philosophers have very often placed the end before the beginning in their treatises, inserting the beginning at the end. Thus they have sometimes suppressed the first work and spoken of the second; sometimes they have thoroughly discussed the first work while leaving out the second; sometimes with the roots <note>original: "radicibus" – the fundamental materials or principles</note> of the science, and sometimes without numbers. Because of this, Hermes <note>Hermes Trismegistus, the mythical founder of alchemy.</note> says in the *Book of Roots* (which is the second of seven), that the wisdom of the author is greater than his book; for he can take away the beginning or the end, with the root or without the root, just like the first inventor. It is therefore no wonder if those studying and working in this science err greatly, because no one dares to assert that this or that was the certain and determined intention of the philosophers, unless he already actually possesses it, or is very close to it.

As for what moved the philosophers to describe this art through obscure similarities and allegories, one universal reason is commonly given: lest it be revealed to the foolish, the unlearned, and the wicked, and lest the unworthy should take possession of such a great treasure to the contempt of nature. But in particular, I find twelve causes. The first is brought forward by the Author of the Universal Way: Lest it be known and recognized that this science is true and entirely certain. And indeed, unless the minds of men were restrained by that uncertainty and doubt, many more would entangle themselves in the unbreakable knots of this art—especially the greedy, the arrogant, and those who burn with the lust for power. The second reason is alleged by Hamuel in the *Senior* <note>The "Senior Zadith," a Latin translation of an Arabic alchemical work by Ibn Umail.</note>: So that they might attribute the art to the glorious God, that He might reveal it to whom He willed and withhold it from whom He willed. Hence Geber says: Our art is kept in Divine power, and is granted to whom He wills and withdrawn from others. And Morienes <note>Morienes was a legendary hermit said to have taught alchemy to King Khalid ibn Yazid.</note>: You should know that the mastery is nothing other than the secret and mystery of the Glorious God. The third reason is described by Hermes: Lest the wicked become powerful enough to perpetrate sins. And by Rosinus: Lest any evildoer, having obtained this Stone, should perform illicit acts to his own detriment. The fourth is found in the same Hermes: Namely, lest the philosophers be forced to give an account for those things which the wicked might do unjustly through their confidence in this art. Pythagoras <note>Pythagoras appears here as a character in the "Turba Philosophorum."</note> gives the fifth in the *Assembly*: God hid this from the people, lest the world...

And Alphidius <note>Alphidius was a frequently cited authority in medieval alchemy, likely of Arabic origin.</note> says: Some of the philosophers, fearing God, did not consider this secret so sublime and precious that they wished to keep it to themselves; indeed, they wanted to write their work clearly. Therefore, they prayed to God that He might allow them to leave this world without being punished for their knowledge. God then taught them to compose a "veiled book" and to write the treatises of the wise within it. Rhasis <note>Rhasis refers to the Persian polymath Muhammad ibn Zakariya al-Razi (c. 865–925).</note> provides the sixth reason.

<margin>6. *In the Light of Lights.*</margin>
If I wished, he says, to explain all things exactly as they are, there would no longer be any place for prudence, since the foolish would be made equal to the wise, and the poor to the rich; nor would any mortal beneath the lunar circle <note>In ancient cosmology, the "lunar circle" or sublunary sphere designated the Earthly realm where all things are subject to change and decay.</note> weep over the hardships of hunger. A seventh reason can be given: so that every wise man, 

<margin>7.</margin>
having found the science with the greatest diligence and most intense study, might love it more, hold it dear, keep it hidden, and give immortal thanks to God the Creator. For thus says the Author of the *Dialogue of Nature and the Son of Philosophy*: We are greatly indebted to the philosophers who handed down this science to us in such a way that, in the process of acquiring it, they rendered us cautious, subtle, and indeed more devoted to God. The eighth reason is that they feared the curses and excommunications of the ancients. For thus says Mireris: The philosophers concealed this and in no way presumed to speak of it, for they forbade it with commands, curses, and anathemas; therefore, I fear to explain this in a most open demonstration as a mere creature.

And Lullius <note>Refers to Ramon Llull, though many alchemical works attributed to him are considered "pseudo-Lullian."</note> says: 

<margin>*In the Apertory.*</margin>

For He Himself will reveal it to whom He wills, and to those whom it concerns.
