<header>THEOBALD VAN HOGHELANDE</header>

<margin>*It is the philosopher's duty to teach.*</margin>
...the property of a wise man is to be able and willing to teach, as is clear from Alphidius <note>Alphidius was a frequently cited authority in medieval alchemy, likely of Arabic origin.</note> cited above, and also witnessed by Hebnebes Haméch <note>likely a Latinization of an Arabic name such as Ibn al-Haytham or a similar author</note> at the end of the fourth book of Plato. He says: "Nothing among the pleasures of this world is sweeter to me than to help a seeker in any branch of this science in what they search for." And Hamuel says in the *Senior* <note>Referring to the "Senior Zadith" or Ibn Umail, a 10th-century alchemist whose "Tabula Chemica" was a foundational text.</note>: "If I am of great reason in science and their hidden tropes are opened to me, and what they have concealed is made manifest to me, and I have grasped this through knowledge, I ought to bring this rightly to the intellect of my successors by using words that are veiled in the open, signifying a hidden understanding," etc. and in another place: "Let God be witness over us: do not bar those of our brothers who are worthy, but do not spread these things to the unworthy."

<margin>*It is not the way of Philosophers to deceive others.*</margin>
It is therefore not to be wondered at if they wrote their books on this art obscurely, or veiled in many ambiguities, since it is certain that this was done by them for a great reason, and not by chance—nor, as many believe, so that they, having been too credulous and deceived themselves, might in turn deceive others. Such behavior does not befit an honest man and a philosopher, who strives to transmit the memory of himself to posterity uncontaminated by any stain.

<margin>*The ancient Philosophers took care that science should not spread to the common people.*</margin>
Nor indeed should this manner of writing seem new or be disapproved of, unless by the same logic we condemn the custom of all the ancients in their philosophizing. For Aristotle, in a certain letter to Alexander, says that he published some of his works in such a way that they would appear as if they had not been published at all. And Plato, in a letter to Dionysius, says: "Take care lest these things ever fall into the ears of men unskilled in discipline and learning." There also exists a letter from Lysis to Hipparchus <note>Lysis of Tarentum and Hipparchus were followers of Pythagoras; this letter was a famous defense of Pythagorean secrecy.</note>, from which I will transfer a few points to this place: "To remember those divine precepts of his (meaning Pythagoras)," he says, "is a pious thing; nor should one share the goods of philosophy with those who have not even been able to dream of the purification of the soul. Nor is it right to extend to everyone those things which we have attained with so much labor, just as it is not permitted to reveal the secrets of the Eleusinian goddesses <note>The "Eleusinian goddesses" refers to Demeter and Persephone, whose "Mysteries" were the most famous secret religious rites of ancient Greece.</note> to profane men; for those who do either of these things will equally be held as unjust and impious."

<margin>*At the beginning of the book on the responses of the philosophers.*</margin>
And further on: "Many have reported to us that they philosophize publicly, which Pythagoras forbade." Porphyry <note>A Neoplatonist philosopher (c. 234–305 AD) who was known for his mystical and difficult writings.</note> also forbids his writings to be communicated to everyone. "You," he says, "take care lest, for the sake of profit or empty glory, you hand these things over to wicked and unworthy men; for no small danger hangs over both you who publish and me who trusted you. These things are to be communicated only to those who have led their lives toward the salvation of the soul; for even the Gods themselves delivered these things to men not openly, but enigmatically."

<margin>*Matthew 7.*</margin>
It is also right to remember the words of our Savior, that pearls are not to be thrown before swine, and that which is holy is not to be given to dogs. But I shall return to the point from which I digressed. Since the philosophers consulted to hide their meaning, now by changing the order, now by mixing false things with the true, now by adding, now by taking away, they obscured—

<summary>Hoghelande argues that alchemical secrecy is not an attempt to deceive, but a traditional philosophical practice intended to protect sacred knowledge from the unworthy. He cites a lineage of authorities from Arabic alchemists like Ibn Umail to Greek philosophers like Aristotle and Pythagoras, as well as the Christian Gospels.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Hoghelande’s discussion on why alchemical authors intentionally wrote in obscure ways. On the previous page, he noted that the wise hide their work to prevent the unworthy from misusing it; here, he details the specific literary devices—enigmas, tropes, and allegories—used to veil the "Great Work."</meta>

<page-num>143</page-num>
# ON THE DIFFICULTIES OF ALCHEMY

<margin>Enigmas increasing the obscurity of the art.</margin>
The authors purposely sought obscurity, increasing it through enigmas, tropes <note>figures of speech where words are used in a non-literal way</note> or figures, allegories, and similitudes to such an extent that whoever desires to be led out of the inextricable twists of this labyrinth has need of the thread of Theseus <note>In Greek mythology, Theseus used a ball of thread to navigate the Labyrinth of the Minotaur; Hoghelande suggests the reader needs a similar guide to understand alchemical texts</note>. Regarding enigmas, let this example from *Aristotle* <note>Referring to "Pseudo-Aristotle," an unknown medieval author whose works were attributed to the famous Greek philosopher to grant them authority</note> the chemist suffice: *“Make from the male and female a round circle, and from it extract a quadrangle, and from the quadrangle a triangle, and from the triangle make a round circle, and you will have the mastery.”* <term>Magisterium: The "mastery" or the finished Philosopher’s Stone, the goal of the alchemical process.</term>

<margin>The Testament, chapter 5.</margin>
<margin>Tropes.</margin>
Likewise that of *Lull* <note>Raymond Lull (c. 1232–1316), a prolific writer to whom many alchemical works were later attributed</note>: *“A thing whose head is red, eyes black, and feet white, is the mastery”*; and a thousand other such examples occurring everywhere. One may observe a trope in this saying of *Senior* <note>Senior Zadith, the Latinized name for the 10th-century Arab alchemist Ibn Umail</note>: *“Take things from their mines, and exalt them to the peaks of their mountains, and lead them back to their roots.”*

<margin>Allegories.</margin>
Allegories are met with everywhere among authors, such as the vision of *Aristaeus*, *Count Bernard’s* <note>Bernard of Trevisan, a 15th-century alchemist</note> story of the king and the fountain, *Senior’s* regarding the hunting of the lion, *Merlin’s* regarding the King preparing himself for war against his enemies, and *Anthony of Viva Petra’s* regarding the virgin desiring to rule, and the fictions of many others, which it would be tedious rather than useful to the readers to collect here.

<margin>Similitudes.</margin>
Reason suggests that I linger a little longer on similitudes and comparisons, since from a poor understanding of them so many errors and so many deceptions take their origin, and so much expense—and what is greatest—so much loss of precious time occurs.

<margin>Philosophers compare the stone to all elemental things.</margin>
The Philosophers, therefore, so that they might exclude the unworthy from the art and hand it over clearly only to the learned and prudent, compared their stone to all things composed of the elements, whether they be corporeal or incorporeal, visible or invisible, celestial or terrestrial. Wherefore you may marvel: *“If you hunt for spiritual things, you do something plausible; if you speak of the corporeal, you speak the truth; if the celestial, you do not lie; if the terrestrial, you report the truth.”* In the stone also are the figures of the heavens, the earth, summer, autumn, winter, and spring, as well as masculinity and femininity. Likewise *Alphidius* says: “Know, my son, that in the books of the wise there are the four elements, and the figure of every vegetable, and of every animal, and of every stone; in which also there is the likeness of the sea, mountains, rivers, heavens, and earths, and of all crops, bodies and spirits, substances and colors.” If, however, anyone expects from me the explanations of everything the philosophers have said, he is mistaken; for this is neither the purpose nor the task here, since it would require its own volume, and it is extremely difficult to always grasp the mind of every wise man, since they often understand not only the manifest forms and external properties of things which are subject to the senses, but also those that are intrinsic and hidden until they are made manifest by art.

<margin>Everything manifest is contrary to its hidden nature.</margin>
For they say that everything outward is contrary to its inward nature; wherefore what is cold and moist in its manifest state is hot and dry in its hidden state. In the same way, one must judge the colors of things, as can be seen in lead, which is livid and black on the outside, [but] on the inside

It emphasizes that the Philosopher's Stone is compared to every element of nature and that its true, internal properties are often the opposite of its outward appearance.</summary>

is red, which is evident from its calcination <term>calcination: the process of heating a substance to high temperatures in the presence of air to change its physical or chemical state</term>, as it transforms into red lead <note>original: *minium*</note>. The same is also seen in vitriol <term>vitriol: a historic term for various sulfate minerals, often green or blue in their raw state</term>, which is clearly blue or green, or leaning toward green, but through roasting is transformed into a red colcothar <note>original: *colchotar*; a term for the reddish residue left after the distillation of sulfuric acid from vitriol</note>. In this way, its deep and intrinsic nature, previously hidden, is revealed to the sight; and conversely, what was previously manifest is hidden. Therefore, since the philosophers have borrowed names from the forms and properties of things—both manifest and hidden—and similarly from colors, and often from the state and condition of the work or from the place where the stone is generated, and indeed from all elemental things, it is no wonder if they vary greatly and call the same thing by different names.

<margin>
The wise always speak the truth, no matter what they name the stone.
</margin>

For they do not care about words, as the *Rosary* <note>The *Rosarium Philosophorum*, a famous 16th-century alchemical treatise</note> says, but about the nature and properties of the things described; and by the name of one thing they often mean another. For things are not subject to words, but on the contrary, words are subject to things. Thus, they have always spoken the truth regarding the force of their intention, even if not regarding the literal force of the speech. Hence *Senior* <note>Senior Zadith, the Latinized name for the 10th-century Arab alchemist Ibn Umail</note> says: "The wise have used various tropes <note>figures of speech</note> in their comparisons, and they differ in names, but the understanding to which they point is the same." And *Alphidius*: "The hearts of irrational animals, gall, the juices of herbs, and everything that is in and on the earth—the wise have multiplied parables, names, and actions concerning this work, so that they might take it away from the foolish and demonstrate it to the intelligent. Know that you do not need those names, but only one name, which is water <note>original: *aqua*</note>, and one action, which is cooking <note>original: *coquere*</note>." And *Mireris* says: "Every wise man has called it by his own name, yet every name is true and direct." For they say this art is like the heavens and the stars, and they have spoken the truth; for in it are the seven planets. Of this thing, they assert that what is raised upward is like the heavens; what descends downward, they call earth; what is hot, they refer to as fire; what is airy, as wind; what is moist, they call by the names of the sea and waters, and the animals of the sea. What pertains to the color of its greenness, they refer to as vegetables and trees; what is joined and dry, they refer to as stones; what is separated, they refer to as sand and say it is ash; what is mobile, they call birds; what is flowing and meltable, they compare to oil; thus its names have been multiplied. And *Anastratus* in the *Assembly* <note>The *Turba Philosophorum* or "Assembly of the Philosophers," one of the oldest Latin alchemical texts</note> says: "The jealous have likened this secret to trees, metals, birds, and reptiles, and varied the names as much as they could." Although these sayings of the wise ought to suffice, nevertheless, for the greater benefit of the readers, it will not be a burden to bring forward certain examples, starting indeed with man, and progressing to animals, vegetables, metals, intermediate minerals, colors, the distinction of the moist and dry, and any similar things.

<summary>Hoghelande explains that the numerous names for the Philosopher's Stone (such as water, oil, or animals) are based on its shifting physical properties during the alchemical process. He argues that while the terminology is diverse and intentionally obscure to keep secrets from the "unworthy," the underlying chemical truth remains consistent among all true masters.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Hoghelande’s argument that alchemical language is metaphorical. # ON THE DIFFICULTIES OF ALCHEMY, BOOK 145

They have compared the stone to the human soul. Whence the Author of *The Marriage of the Sun and Moon* from the *Greater Assembly* <note>original: *Turba majori*; the *Turba Philosophorum* is one of the oldest and most influential Latin alchemical texts</note>, if I am not mistaken, says: 
> Take a man and place him upon the stone, drawing from him until he dies, and the body becomes spiritual; afterward, restore his soul to him.

It is truly a wonder that the unlearned and foolish, who attend only to the sound of the words and not the hidden meaning, do not apply the same logic to similar things when they read such passages. For who would be so insane as to think, according to the literal letter, that a man must be seized, beaten, and killed so that the philosopher's stone may be produced from him, and that finally his soul, once removed, should be poured back into him again?

So too, those who insist on the literal words of the philosophers possess no greater judgment when they believe that the Elixir can be composed from animals, vegetables, intermediate minerals, and stones. Havel, in the works of *Senior* <note>Refers to Senior Zadith, an influential 10th-century Arabic alchemist known in Latin as Senior</note>, rightly mocks these people. These men, he says, claimed that the father of gold and silver is an animal of the land and sea, or a man, or a part of a man, such as hair, blood, menstrual blood, or the afterbirth <note>original: *fecundina*</note>; and some said it is in trees, plants, and herbs; and others in stones, arsenics, and other minerals; and they have been alienated from the truth of the science.

<margin>The stone is sometimes called a helmeted man, a King, or a Queen.</margin>
But let us proceed further. Sometimes the stone is called a "high and helmeted man," specifically when its humidity is caught by distillation through a cucurbit and alembic <term>cucurbit and alembic: the glass base and the "helmet" or still-head used in distillation; the shape of the alembic head resembles a helmet</term>. So also, the compound of the stone is called the King and the Queen. Whence we read in the *Assembly* <note>the *Turba Philosophorum*</note>:
> Venerate the king and his wife, for you do not know when you will have need of those things which improve the king and his wife.

<margin>Man and woman, male and female.</margin>
In this way, they are called man and woman, or male and female, because of their coupling—that is, because of their action and passion <note>In alchemy, the "active" principle (often sulfur) and the "passive" principle (often mercury) must unite</note>.

<margin>Father and mother, son.</margin>
Rosinus <note>A Latinized name for the Arabic alchemist Zosimos</note> says the secret of the art of gold consists of the male and female. Likewise, they are called father, mother, and son, in respect to the parents and the offspring. Hermes says: Its father is the Sun, its mother the Moon. And the *Rosary* <note>The *Rosarium Philosophorum*</note> says: She fosters her son like a pious mother.

Sometimes they speak only of the woman, with the name of the male removed, as Theophilus says in the *Assembly*:
> The woman fleeing her kinsmen becomes domestic to them through herself, though forced;

where "the woman" stands for the humidity of the stone, because it is unstable and inconstant, fleeing from the fire.

Sometimes they speak only of the man. There is no need to bring forward examples of every single instance, as they occur everywhere among the authors. Let it suffice to have advised that all these things are said in different respects; sometimes they speak of the principles of the stone—namely earth, water, and fire, or body, spirit, and soul—as individual and separate things, and sometimes they speak of them all joined together.

<margin>Old man. Youth.</margin>
They have also called the stone an old man and a youth. Whence Rhasis <note>The Latin name for the Persian physician and alchemist Al-Razi</note> says: Our stone is an old man at first, and a youth at the end, because the whiteness <note>original: *albedo*</note> is at the beginning, and the redness <note>original: *rubedo*</note> is at the end. And in the *Assembly*:
> Take a tree, and place within it a man of great age, etc.

But when the earth gradually drinks up its water, it is called a suckling child.

<margin>Suckling child.</margin>
Whence Eminganus in the *Assembly*:
> Behold the suckling child, and do not hinder him, for the secret remains in him.

They are also called brother and sister, paternal uncle, maternal uncle, father-in-law, son-in-law, brothers of the same womb, companions, the red servant, the virgin, the girl, the man in-

<sig>K</sig>
<meta>catchword: -dressed (original: dutus)</meta>

<summary>This page explains that alchemical terms like "man," "woman," "king," and "suckling child" are metaphors for the chemical stages of the Philosopher’s Stone, warning readers not to take these biological descriptions literally. Hoghelande clarifies that these names refer to the interaction of elements (like the "female" moisture fleeing "male" fire) or the transition from the white stage (old man) to the red stage (youth).</summary>

Those who, insisting on the literal words of the philosophers, believe that the <term>Elixir</term> can be composed from animals, vegetables, intermediate minerals, and stones, possess no greater judgment. Havel, in the works of Senior <note>original: *Senior*; referring to Senior Zadith, the Latinized name of the 10th-century Arabian alchemist Ibn Umail</note>, rightly mocks these people. These men, he says, have claimed that the father of gold and silver is an animal of the land or sea, or a man, or a part of a man, such as hair, blood, menstrual fluid, or the placenta; and some have sought it in trees, plants, and herbs; and others in stones, arsenics, and other minerals, and they have been alienated from the truth of the science. But let us proceed further.

<margin>The Stone is sometimes called a helmeted Man, a King, or a Queen.</margin>
Sometimes the Stone is called a "helmeted man" and "tall," specifically when its moisture is received through distillation via the <term>cucurbit</term> <note>the lower vessel of a still</note> and <term>alembic</term> <note>the cap or head of a still, which looks somewhat like a helmet</note>. Likewise, the compound of the Stone is called the King and the Queen. Hence we read in the *Turba*:
> Venerate the king and his wife, for you do not know when you will have need of those things which improve the king and his wife. <note>original: "Veneramini regem & ejus uxorem, quoniam nescitis quando indigetis his, quæ regem & suam uxorem emendant."</note>

<margin>Husband and wife, male and female.</margin>
Thus they are called husband and wife, or male and female, because of their coupling, and their action and passion <note>in medieval philosophy, "action" and "passion" refer to the active agent and the passive receiver of an effect</note>. Rosinus <note>a Latinized name for the 4th-century alchemist Zosimos of Panopolis</note> says: The secret of the art of gold consists of the male and the female.

<margin>Father and mother, son.</margin>
They are also called Father, Mother, and Son, in respect to the generators and the generated. Hermes <note>referring to Hermes Trismegistus, the mythical founder of alchemy</note> says: Its father is the Sun, its mother the Moon. And the *Rosary* <note>referring to the *Rosarium Philosophorum*</note> says: She, like a pious mother, fosters her son. Sometimes they speak only of the woman, leaving out the name of the male, as Theophilus does in the *Turba*:
> The woman, fleeing her own kin, becomes a member of the household for them, though by her own force; <note>original: "Mulier suos fugiens generos illis per se quamvis coacta domestica fit"</note>
where "woman" stands for the moisture of the stone, because it is unstable and inconsistent, fleeing from the fire. Sometimes they speak only of the man. There is no need to bring forward examples of every single case, since they occur everywhere among the authors. Let it suffice to have warned that all these things are said in different respects; sometimes they speak of the principles of the stone—namely earth, water, and fire, or body, spirit, and soul—as individual and separate, and at other times as all together and joined.

<margin>Old man. Young man.</margin>
They have also called the stone an "old man" and a "young man." Hence Rhasis <note>Al-Razi, a famous 9th-century Persian physician and alchemist</note> says: Our stone is an old man at first, and a young man at the end, because the whiteness is at the beginning and the redness is at the end. And in the *Turba*:
> Take a tree, and place within it a man of great age, etc. <note>original: "Accipe arborem, & impone ei magnæ ætatis hominem, &c."</note>
But when the earth gradually drinks up its water, it is called

<margin>A nursing child.</margin>
a nursing child. Hence Eminganus in the *Turba* says:
> Look upon the nursing child, and do not hinder him, for in him remains the secret. <note>original: "Inspicite lactantem puerum, & non impediatis eum, in eo enim manet arcanum."</note>
These same things are called brother and sister, paternal uncle, maternal uncle, father-in-law, son-in-law, brothers of the same womb, companions, the red servant, the virgin, the girl, the man cl-

...clothed in the most beautiful garments, a King crowned with a red crown, and so forth. <note>This continues the description of the "King," a common alchemical metaphor for the perfected Gold or the Red Elixir.</note>

<margin>The Stone is compared to animals.</margin>
In the same way, they likened the Stone to animals because of the blood by which they live, for the soul of every animal is in its blood. For they compared their <term>tincture</term> <note>the color-changing power of the alchemical medicine</note> to blood because of its redness, and because it gives heat and life to the body just as blood does for an animal—which, when deprived of it, is also deprived of life. As the *Lilium* <note>original: *Lilium Medicinae* or a similar alchemical "Lily" text</note> says: "If animals are guided by a slow fire, the compound becomes sweet." And *Acsubufon* in the *Turba*: 
> Take the animal which is called *kenkel* <note>an obscure, likely corrupted term for a mythical or symbolic animal in alchemical literature</note>, and the moisture which it ejects. 

But they did not only use the general name of "animal"; they even descended to specific species. Thus, they called it the Lion, the gryphon, the camel, the horse, the dog, or the calf, either for the reasons mentioned above or because of some property these animals share with the Stone. 

<margin>Albertus, *The Secrets of Alchemy*.</margin>
Hence in the *Allegories of the Wise*, Hermes says: 
> If you consume a third part of your camels, and two-thirds remain, you have already reached your goal. <note>original: "Si camelorum tuorum tertiam partem consumas, duabus tertiis residuis jam ad propositum pervenisti."</note>

This likeness seems to be drawn from the length of a camel's neck, which is like a <term>cucurbit</term> <note>a gourd-shaped glass vessel used in distillation</note> through which the spirit ascends, of which Haly speaks in his secrets: 
> Take a male Corascene <note>referring to Khorasan, a region in Persia</note> dog and an Armenian bitch, and join them together, and they will give birth to a dog the color of the sky. 

<margin>The Stone is likened to birds and all flying things.</margin>
They also gave the names of birds, insects, and all flying things to the Stone because it is raised upward and, as it were, "flies," though also for other reasons. Thus they spoke of the rooster, the hen, the crow, and the eagle. *Alphidius* says: 
> No water becomes a source <note>original: *quelles*; likely a corruption of the German *Quelle* or Latin *qualis*</note> unless it be that which is made from the beetles of our water. 

<margin>To fish.</margin>
They likewise compared it to fish, as *Mundus* says in the *Turba*: 
> Take a part of the gall of a fish, and a part of the urine of a calf, etc. 

And in the riddles of the Sages: 
> There is in our sea a small round fish, lacking bones and legs, etc. <note>This is a famous alchemical riddle referring to the "mercury of the philosophers."</note>

<margin>To parts of animals and their humors.</margin>
They also compared it to parts of animals: the heart, liver, stomach, head, brain, eyes, belly, breasts, nerves, and veins. Also to their <term>humors</term> <note>the four bodily fluids: blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile</note>: bile, blood, phlegm, and melancholy. Hence *Morienes* <note>a legendary 7th-century hermit and alchemist</note> says: 
> Take the phlegmatic and the choleric, and grind the blood with them. <note>original: "Accipite phlegmaticum, & cholericum, & terite sanguinem cum eis."</note>

They also used everything originating from animals, such as hair, placentas, nails, as well as menstrual blood, seed, and milk. They did this because, just as animals are generated from the seeds of the male and female, grow by the addition of menstrual flow, and are nourished by milk (which is nothing other than menstrual flow or blood "twice-cooked"), so too is the Stone. 

<margin>In the book titled *The Flower of Flowers*. To excrement.</margin>
Hence, Arnald [of Villanova]: 
> It is nourished by its own milk, that is, by the sperm from which it originated in the beginning. 

They also compared it to the excrement of animals—dung, urine, and sweat—because of the "dregs" of the Stone and the separation of the pure from the impure, or because of its foul odor and the evaporation of its superfluous moisture, which is called "infant's urine" by Lullius <note>Ramon Llull, a 13th-century philosopher to whom many alchemical works were later attributed</note>. I could here assign many other reasons for these names from the "star-like" writings of Plato and his commentator *Hebnabes Hamech*, but I do not wish to be tedious. 

<margin>To an egg.</margin>
They even compared the Stone to an egg, because just as in an egg there is white and red—namely the white and the yolk—and the shell which takes the place of the earth, so...

[nature], so it is also in the stone. They also called the stone "poison," and compared it to the basilisk, the dragon, the viper, the salamander, the serpent, lizards, and other reptiles, and the toad. Whence we read in the *Riddles of the Wise*:

<margin>Treatise 2.</margin>

And the *Rosary* <note>The *Rosarium Philosophorum*, a famous 16th-century alchemical florilegium.</note>:

<margin>On venomous animals and reptiles.</margin>
The reason for this can be given: just as the basilisk, the viper, and similar venomous creatures kill living things with their breath, touch, or bite, and as poisons pervert human nature, so too does the <term>sulfur</term> of the philosophers <term>mortify</term> <note>to "kill" or solidify a liquid substance</note> <term>quicksilver</term> <note>original: *Mercurium vivum*</note> by its vapor and touch, and changes its nature. Conversely, the stone is also called a <term>theriac</term> <note>a universal antidote or wonder-drug</note>, an antidote, a medicine, and a medicament; because just as poison is driven from the heart by theriac and medicines, or its power is blunted and sick bodies are restored to health, so through the Elixir, the "poison" of the Mercury is taken away. As it passes into gold, a healthy temperament is granted to it, and the other "leprous" and impure bodies of the metals are cleansed and transmuted into gold or silver.

<margin>Theriac and medicine.</margin>
Therefore, the Author of the *Perfect Mastery*—whether that was Rhasis <note>Muhammad ibn Zakariya al-Razi (c. 865–925), a Persian polymath and alchemist.</note> or another:

> "The Elixir is an antidote, medicine, and cleanser composed of clear species for all bodies that must be purged, cured, and converted into true <term>silver-making</term> and <term>gold-making</term> <note>original: *Lunificum & Solificum*</note> substances."

<margin>On vegetables.</margin>
They also likened the stone to trees, shrubs, plants, herbs, roots, flowers, and all vegetables. Whence Balgus says in the *Turba*: "Certain fruits come forth from the most perfect tree in early spring and flower at the beginning of their emergence."

<margin>Treatise 1.</margin>
And Hermes to the *Assembly of the Wise*:

> "The juice is extracted in 150 days."

Also in the *Riddles of the Wise*:

> "It is the root which should be ground with its stalk and juice, etc."

Thus we read everywhere of white and red roses, of <term>Lunaria</term> <note>Moonwort, associated with silver</note>, <term>mercurialis</term> <note>Mercury herb</note>, sea purslane, <term>chelidonia</term> <note>Celandine</note>, and <term>geldo</term> <note>Weld or dyer's weed</note>, and many others. And this is certainly because of the **green color** which is characteristic of vegetables. Wherefore Mireris says: "No vegetable nor any fruit appears by germinating without a green color being there; similarly, the germination of this thing is green," although in some cases the philosophers seem to have followed either the naming or the "dry heat" of the thing.

<margin>On the images and figures appearing in the work.</margin>
But since I have dealt with reptiles and vegetables, certain names could also have been given to the stone—beyond the reasons already stated—because of the wonderful variety of shapes that appear in the work itself. Several colors emerge simultaneously, just as we sometimes imagine wonderful forms of animals, reptiles, or trees in the clouds or in fire; as I found in a certain fragment of a book ascribed to Moses, in this manner: "When the body has been dissolved, there appear—"

<margin>Quicksilver.</margin>

This page explains how the "spirit" and "body" of the work are named after minerals, acids, and a spectrum of colors.</meta>

-># ON THE DIFFICULTIES OF ALCHEMY, BOOK 149<-

...they calcine metals and make them flow. And since some of these are volatile, they compared them to **spirit**, but the fixed ones they compared to the **body**.

<margin>Of Alums.</margin> Alums and <term>vitriols</term> <note>original: *atramenta*; literally "blackings," a term for metal sulfates like iron sulfate used in making ink and corrosive acids</note> are astringent and abound in raw moisture; 
<margin>Of Vitriols.</margin> but when <term>calcined</term> <note>burned to a powder or reduced by high heat</note>, they are drier and fiery, and assume a red color, much like a stone which at first suffers from excessive humidity when dissolved, but that moisture perishes through long <term>coction</term> <note>a prolonged heating or "cooking" process</note>, and it is finally turned into redness.

<margin>Strong waters.</margin> The philosophers also compare their **spirit** to <term>strong waters</term> <note>original: *aquis fortibus*; corrosive mineral acids like nitric acid</note>, because just as waters composed of salts, vitriols, and alum corrode and dissolve metals, dividing and separating them from one another, so also the spirit or "water of the philosophers" dissolves its own **body** and separates the <term>tincture</term> <note>the essential coloring principle or "soul" of the metal</note> from it. Whence the author of the *Lesser Rosary* <note>original: *Rosarium minus*; a famous medieval alchemical text</note> describes the praises and works of strong water. "It dissolves," he says, "the solid and renders it liquid; it cleanses the unclean, corrodes the superfluous, penetrates all things, softens the hard, and is the key to the entire art," etc. Lullius <note>Ramon Llull, a major medieval philosopher and mystic to whom many alchemical works were attributed</note> also frequently uses strong waters.

But since something must also be said about intermediate minerals, likewise salts, vitriols, and alums in the third part of this book, I shall pass on to **colors**, from which the philosophers have borrowed infinite names.

<margin>Colors.</margin> I have shown above that the Stone was called by the name of all green vegetables; but since, besides that and other intermediate colors, the philosophers enumerate three principal ones—namely **black**, **white**, and **red**—they have most especially named the Stone after them.

For because of its **blackness**, they took names from the designations of all black things. Thus it is called antimony, pitch, coal, the raven, the **raven’s head**, lead, burnt copper, and burnt ivory. Hermes says: "The raven’s head is the origin of the art," <note>original: *Caput corvi artis est origo*</note> that is, the blackness. And Socrates in the *Assembly* <note>original: *Turba Philosophorum*, one of the oldest Latin alchemical texts</note>: "Without lead, no true tincture is made that has power," that is, without blackness.

Because of its **whiteness**, they took the names of all white things, wherefore the whitened stone is called talc, marble, silver, ivory, flower of salt, bones, crystal, crystalline lights, pearls, lime, eggshells, calcined moon <note>silver</note>, snow, hail, <term>potash</term> <note>original: *cineres clavellati*; literally "clubbed ashes," a source of potassium carbonate</note>, white earth, white stone, and a white, starry, splendid powder.

Likewise, from all things red, reddening, or made red by art. Therefore the **red stone** is called saffron, cinnabar, minium, red hematite stone, burnt human blood, egg yolks, calcined alum, corals, and gold. I have not provided examples because they occur everywhere in infinite numbers.

Similarly, because we need two natures or qualities in the work—namely the **moist** and the **dry**—they called their **Water** by the name of every moist thing: 
<margin>Every moist thing.</margin> vinegar, urine, sweat, milk, syrup, broth, and innumerable others. Bacon <note>Roger Bacon, the 13th-century English friar and scientist</note> in the *Assembly*: "Give it back its own sweat." And Borates in the same place: "Rule the stone with syrup of pomegranates."

<margin>The Sea.</margin> Also by the name of the sea, and of seas and rivers; hence Mireris named "three seas," meaning the three quicksilvers or three waters which the philosophers need in their work...

### PAGE 150

...the philosophers <note>original: *sophi*; a Greek-derived term for the wise or the adepts of the art</note>, namely the sea of Egypt, the sea of the south, and the sea of the Indians. And Aristhenes says in the *Assembly of the Philosophers* <note>original: *Turba Philosophorum*; one of the oldest and most influential Latin alchemical texts, written as a debate between Greek philosophers</note>: "Take the body, and place it in the waters of our sea."

<margin>In the book on figures and images.</margin>
Senior <note>original: *Senior*; the Latin name for the 10th-century Arabic alchemist Ibn Umail</note> says: "The wise have named their stone a 'sea' because from it their clouds and rains ascend." Hence Lucas says in the *Assembly*: "Take the cloud and cook it with its own body until it becomes tin." They also used the name of "gall" <note>original: *felle*; bile produced by the liver</note> and "galls." Hence Rosin <note>original: *Rosin*; likely a Latin corruption of Zosimos of Panopolis, a 3rd-century alchemist</note> says: "The galls of which the philosophers have spoken are nothing other than the water of sulfur." This is perhaps because of the yellow color of bile, or because they are bitter, hot, sharp, and stinging.

<margin>Of Oil.</margin>
They also wish their <term>tincture</term> <note>the concentrated essence or "soul" of the stone capable of transforming metals</note> to be understood by the names of oil, butter, fat, and ointment. This is because just as all fatty substances stick more tenaciously and are not easily washed out of cloth, clothes, or other things they have fallen upon, so too the tincture of the philosophers remains fixed once it has entered its own body.

<margin>Rosary, part 2, chapter 11.</margin>
Hence that saying of Arnaldus <note>Arnald of Villanova, a famous 13th-century physician and alchemist</note>: "Water washes and purifies, but oil tints and colors." Hermes says: "The ointment of our earth is sulfur." Senior says: "Fatness and fats are names for the divine water."

<margin>Of everything dry.</margin>
In the same way, they understand their "earth" by the name of "everything dry," as well as stone, sand, lime, ash, and so forth. Hence Attamanus in the *Assembly*: "Take the old sea stones." And Dardaris says in the same place: "Take the white moist thing, cook it, and soak the sand."

They also use the names of all things that dry, constrict, coagulate, aggregate, and attract. For this reason, the stone is also compared to a magnet and iron, or to sperm and the womb <note>original: *matrice*; literally 'matrix'</note>. Hence Pythagoras in the *Assembly*: "Know that the thing which the philosophers have described in so many ways follows its partner without fire, just as the magnet follows iron; nor is it compared to sperm and the womb without cause." Conversely, the "water" is called by the names of all things that dissolve, moisten, soften, loosen, rarefy, purge, wash, and cleanse. Hence the saying: "Our water is the soap of the wise, washing away all uncleanness." So too it is called a knife, a carver, a blade, or a sword, because it divides the pure from the impure and separates the soul from the body.

<margin>To Heaven. To Earth. To the Planets.</margin>
The philosophers ascended from earthly things to heavenly things, and they compare their materials to heaven. Hence Hermes: "Heaven is the male to the female, but earth is the female to the male." And they compare it to the Planets, as in the *Allegory of the Wise*: "Our work is made from the seven Planets. First from Saturn, second from Jupiter, third from Mars, fourth from the Sun, fifth from Venus, sixth from Mercury, and seventh from the Moon." They also speak of the conjunctions of their Planets, and of oppositions, and eclipses of the luminaries, and of the tail and head of the dragon <note>the points where the moon's orbit crosses the ecliptic; in alchemy, these often represent the beginning and end of a process</note>,

<margin>Chapter 24.</margin>
just as Lullius <note>Ramon Llull, a Majorcan polymath to whom many alchemical works were attributed</note> does in his *Testament*. And Anastratus says in the *Assembly*: "The Moon is joined to the light of the Sun." And another says: "Mercury meets the rays of the Sun."

<margin>To Wind. To Vapor.</margin>
Similarly, they compared their resolved substances to smoke, wind, air, and vapor. Hermes says: "The wind carried it in its belly." And Morienes says: "If the white smoke were not there, the gold of the *ethees* <note>original: *ethees*; likely a corruption of the Greek 'ethereal' or a specific volatile spirit</note> would not be completed." And Pythagoras says in the *Assembly*: "The knowledge of this art is nothing but vapor and water."

<meta>This page continues the exploration of alchemical nomenclature, moving from liquid metaphors like "sea" and "oil" to metaphors of transformation based on nature, domesticity, and the cosmic order. <page-num>151</page-num>
<header>ON THE DIFFICULTIES OF ALCHEMY</header>

<margin>Names vary according to the diversity of the work.</margin>
Indeed, the adepts have even moved on to things that do not exist, mentioning **virgin’s milk** and **milk of birds**. *Hermes* <note>Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary founder of alchemy</note> says: "Hidden things will appear, and the virgin’s milk shall be whitened." We read of this "milk of birds" <note>original: *lacte volatilium*; a metaphor for a volatile white distillate</note> in his works and also in the *Assembly of Philosophers*. So much for the names of the stone itself or its components; yet no less a variety of names arises from the diversity of the work and the "governance" <note>the controlled application of heat and timing</note> of that same stone.

<margin>From the Book of Divine Interpretations.</margin>
*Rosinus* <note>likely Zosimos of Panopolis</note> shall be my witness, of whom I will cite a single example:

> You should know, he says, that crushing and whitening are necessary; thus, in whatever ways things are whitened and crushed, or refined, or divided, or separated—or by whatever operations these things are done, or through what substances—they have received their names and likenesses from those methods, operations, and substances. And because certain things are purified through <term>distillation</term> <note>the process of vaporizing and condensing a liquid</note>, as water is through an **alembic**; some through <term>sublimation</term> <note>heating a substance until it turns to vapor and then solidifies again in the upper part of the vessel</note>, as spirits are; some through solution, as salts; some through washing, as clothes; some through burning, as lime; some through division, as metals are separated from one another through <term>cupellation</term> <note>original: *cineritium*; a method of refining precious metals using a bed of ash</note>; and some through straining, as through a cloth or filter: when it is said "sublime" or any of these other things, understand that you must then "whiten," and so forth.

<margin>The work of the stone is likened to the four seasons of the year.</margin>
They also compare the work to the four seasons of the year. For they compare the **solution** of the stone to winter, because winter is cold, moist, and rainy. They compare **coagulation** to spring, which is warm and moist, producing flowers and causing all vegetation to sprout. They compare the **reddening** <note>original: *rubefactionem*; the stage where the matter turns deep red</note> to summer, which is hot and dry; and the **fixation** <note>rendering a substance resistant to heat</note> to autumn, in which the fruits are gathered. But to put an end to these comparisons, I conclude briefly: everything that can be said or discussed concerning the elements and their qualities—concerning their confusion in the <term>first matter</term> <note>original: *materia prima*; the primordial, chaotic substance from which the world was formed</note>, their distinction, their properties and sufferings; concerning the creation of the world and its beginning and end; concerning corruption and generation; concerning matter and form, potential and act; concerning virtues and vices, peace and war, the victor and the vanquished, the pursuer and the fugitive, love and hate; concerning the strong and the weak, the healthy and the sick; concerning things that burn and things that hinder burning; concerning unity and multitude, conception and birth; concerning life, death, and resurrection; concerning paradise, its height and glory, and concerning hell and the abyss, and much more besides—all this can be said of this venerable stone.

<margin>Nothing in the world can be compared to the stone.</margin>
Hence *Senior* <note>Ibn Umail</note> says:

> This stone is different from all other stones in its natures and its perfection, and in its intake of nourishment and its growth during its preparations. Nothing of our ordinary operations can be compared to it, because it is of the "seed of the world" <note>original: *semine mundi*; implying it contains the creative spark of the universe</note> and possesses much blessing. And if it were as some people think—made of ordinary stones, or earths, or plants—it would not be called "Wisdom," since neither death nor life exists in those things, nor marriage, nor conception, nor the generation of offspring, nor nourishment. For our preparations, which we know from our "animals" and our "stones" which we have seen and worked upon, do not come from the vanities and preparations of those common things.

This, therefore, is that stone...

<meta>This page continues Hoghelande’s explanation of why alchemical texts are so difficult to read. # THEOBALD DE HOGHELANDE

...wonderful, to which no other thing in the whole world can be compared, and into which the unwise stumble. These are the bonds, more than those of **Vulcan** <note>In Roman mythology, Vulcan forged inescapable chains; in alchemy, this refers to the confusing terminology of the "art of fire" that traps the uninitiated</note>, in which they are held entangled who follow the sound of words and not the hidden meaning veiled beneath them. Whence the same **Senior** <note>original: *Senior*; referring to Zadith ben Hamuel, a 10th-century Arabic alchemist</note> says: "The hearts and eyes are blinded, and the ears made deaf to these likenesses and judgments in all men: they read and do not understand; they study and do not perceive; they are ignorant of the truth and <margin>Where the error of practitioners comes from.</margin> they cast it away. But he who wanders from the truth will be plunged into vanity." And in another place: "Men do not understand the words of the wise, nor do they perceive what is intended; hence they declare the truthful to be false, and they justify the false according to their own opinions; they should lay the blame upon themselves, not upon the wise." For their error comes from ignorance of the sages' intent when they hear diverse words unknown to their understanding, since they contain a hidden meaning; yet they understand only according to the literal letter and outward designation, and thus they are deceived, while the truth remains buried in secret.

<margin>Equivocations.</margin> Having explained the metaphors of the **Stone**, and the obscurity arising from them, let us move on to <term>equivocations</term> <note>the use of a single term to mean multiple distinct things</note>, which alone—even if no other cause of obscurity were present—could turn away a mind that is not sufficiently steadfast from its purpose. This method of concealment is the opposite of the previous one; for there, one thing is called by many and infinite names, but here, many and diverse things are gathered under a single name. Truly, this method of teaching is much more obscure than the other and holds more difficulty, since such a great and unusual variety of names might easily cause even a prudent man some doubt or suspicion of a trap; yet in discerning equivocations, no one can bring enough wit or prudence unless they are very well-versed in the writings of the philosophers. I will bring forward two examples, and I will go no further than the matter of the **Stone**, which all assert without distinction consists of **mercury** <note>original: *argento vivo*; literally 'living silver' or quicksilver</note> and **sulfur**; and I will choose these especially so that beginners may become accustomed to understanding the books of the philosophers,

<margin>Equivocations of sulfur.</margin> since they are the principles of the art, and of the entire work, and the foundations. Let us weigh, then, the various ways they are spoken of by the philosophers. But first, <margin>1.</margin> concerning **Sulfur**, which is more famous for being used for "buttery" and common combustible sulfur than to need an example. <margin>2. In the Codicil. In the Practice of the Testament, ch. 22.</margin> For it is also taken for the "philosophical earth": Whence **Lullius** <note>Ramon Llull, a 13th-century scholar to whom many alchemical works were attributed</note> says: *It is the property of our quicksilver that it be congealed from the vapor of its sulfur.* The same author: <margin>3.</margin> *Our sulfur is a subtle earth or a dry water, in the belly of which the fire of nature is strongly multiplied.* **Morienes** <note>Morienus, a legendary hermit-alchemist</note> also uses it for quicksilver, the other part of the stone: *When **Laton** <note>a term for the 'unrefined' metal or base of the Stone</note> is burned with sulfur, and softness is frequently poured over it, then all its obscurity and blackness is taken away from it.* That is, when the philosophical earth is moistened by its own water or quicksilver. And **Rosinus** <note>likely Zosimos of Panopolis</note>: *Nothing acts upon the **Sun** <note>a metaphor for Gold</note> except our sulfur, which turns the Sun black and consumes it.*

<summary>Theobald explains the alchemical concept of 'equivocation,' where one term like 'sulfur' can mean common sulfur, philosophical earth, or even mercury, depending on the context. He warns that failing to look past the literal word to the hidden intent is the primary cause of failure for practitioners.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Theobald van Hoghelande’s explanation of the "equivocation" and "diversity" of terms used by alchemical authors. He is currently discussing how alchemists use "contradiction" as a tool to hide their secrets and test the intelligence of their readers.</meta>

<header>THEOBALD VAN HOGHELANDE</header>

...are joined of that kind. I could bring forward many more examples of this sort in this place, were it not that I judge they should be omitted for the sake of brevity. Let us therefore proceed further and list other methods of concealment as well, among which is **Diversity**; but since that will be treated more extensively in the third part of this treatise, where the discussion will be on the diversity of matter and the regimes of the art, 

<margin>*On Contradiction.*</margin>
it seemed fit to say something here only regarding **contradiction**, which is cognate and close to it. In other sciences, this would be shameful and worthy of blame, and could call their truth into doubt; in this art, however, the philosophers do not consider it a vice. Instead, they deliberately contradict not only others but themselves, clearly to exercise the reader and test their judgment, to see whether they err in their choice of natural things and accept those things which are against nature rather than friends of nature, or vice versa: 

<margin>*In the Light of Lights.*</margin>
**Rhazes** <note>original: "Rhasi"; referring to the 9th-century Persian physician and alchemist Abu Bakr al-Razi</note> himself affirms this. "In the book of the alchemists," he says, "I introduced a perfect **ferment** <note>In alchemy, a substance added to a base metal to "leaven" it into gold, like yeast in dough</note> described plainly in the notes and easy to search for, which I then asserted in the same work was *not* a ferment. But he who is strong in discernment and flourishes in wisdom, if he wishes to scrutinize the interior of our speech, will rejoice to have found both its location and its beginning." 

<margin>*Sulfur is called male. Chapter 22.*</margin>
Let us cite other authors and review what they say about **sulfur**: some call it the male of the female (that is, of **quicksilver** <note>original: "argenti vivi"; literally "living silver," the common name for mercury</note>), while others conversely call it the female of the male. 

<margin>*In the commentary on the Tablet of Hermes.*</margin>
And indeed **Lully** <note>Raymond Lully, a famous philosopher to whom many alchemical works were attributed</note> calls it male in his *Practical Testament* in this manner: "Our sulfur has the power of sealing and forming something like itself, and therefore we say that it is the father and the masculine seed." 

Likewise, the Blessed **Thomas Aquinas** <note>The famous theologian was also credited with several alchemical treatises in the medieval period</note>: "The purest and most subtle substance of the sulfur contained within the bodies themselves is like a paternal seed, active and formative." 

And the *Rosary* <note>original: "Rosarius"; referring to the *Rosarium Philosophorum*, a fundamental alchemical text</note> says: "As long as the blackness lasts, the dark female dominates, which is the primary power of the stone, and which is also called the sharpest **vinegar**." 

Now, it was shown above that by "vinegar" is meant the **water of the stone** and **quicksilver**; since that is called the female, then the earth or the sulfur of the stone must necessarily be the male. 

<margin>*Sulfur as female.*</margin>
And while these writers agree in placing sulfur in the role of the male, others conversely place it in the role of the female; among these is **Arnald** <note>Arnald of Villanova, a 13th-century physician and alchemist</note>. 

<margin>*In the book "Flower of Flowers."*</margin>
For he says: "When the earth begins to retain the Mercury with it for a little while, then the male acts upon the female—that is, the Mercury upon the earth." 

And the *Lily* <note>original: "Lilium"; likely referring to the *Lilium Intelligentiae*</note> says: "Through gentle **decoction** <note>The process of heating or boiling a substance to extract its essence</note>, the male—that is, the quicksilver—receives the staining spirit from the female—that is, from the sulfur." 

**Cerus** also says in the *Assembly* <note>original: "Turba"; the *Turba Philosophorum*, one of the oldest Latin alchemical texts</note>: "Take the quicksilver in which there is masculine power." 

How much the knowledge of the aforementioned matters matters is known to the diligent reader of books, who everywhere encounters the names of male and female, husband and wife, agent and patient; if he does not know how to distinguish these, he labors in vain. But someone might say that sulfur and quicksilver alternately act and are acted upon, and therefore it is no wonder if they receive the name now of the male and now of the female, according to that saying of the *Lily*: "That which acted first, namely the female, then begins to be acted upon by the male, and that which..."

### ON THE DIFFICULTIES OF ALCHEMY, BOOK I

At first, the female—that is, **sulfur**—was drawing, but now she is drawn by the male—that is, **quicksilver** <note>original: "argento vivo"; also known as mercury. In alchemical theory, sulfur and mercury are the "parents" of all metals.</note>. <margin>Another example concerning the matter of the stone.</margin> I shall bring forward other examples into the open, in which no such suspicion <note>referring to the ambiguity mentioned on the previous page</note> falls—namely, regarding the matter of the **philosophers' stone**, which many affirm to be a single thing. As **Arnaldus de Villanova** says to the King of Naples: "All things that are in the stone are necessary to it, and it needs nothing else, for the stone is of one nature and one thing." And the *Lilium* <note>The *Lilium Alchimiae*, a famous medieval text often attributed to Arnaldus</note> says: "You do not need many things but only one thing, which in every stage of our works is turned into another nature." <margin>To Eutychia.</margin> And **Rosinus** <note>An Arabic alchemist, often identified as Zosimos of Panopolis in Latin translations</note> says: "Be certain that there is one thing from which everything you seek is made." And while these authors recommend unity, others, on the contrary, recommend plurality. <margin>On the Investigation [of Perfection], Chapter 3.</margin> <margin>Ibid, Chapter 12.</margin> And especially **Geber** <note>The Latinized name of Jabir ibn Hayyan, the most influential figure in medieval alchemy</note>. He says: "We seek to make one substance, yet one aggregated from many." The same author says: "It is called the 'one stone' of the philosophers, even though it is extracted from many bodies or things." And in the *Allegories of the Wise*: "Take away the blemish from the bodies, but that does not happen except in two or three species, and in many things; for in one simple thing it is not done at all." And **Philotis** in the *Turba* <note>The *Turba Philosophorum* or "Assembly of the Philosophers," an ancient alchemical dialogue</note>: "The first composition is made from many things." I have shown the contradiction between different authors; now it remains to be shown how the same author contradicts himself in the same book, and sometimes in the same chapter. <margin>Another.</margin> And the first that occurs is that saying of **Pythagoras** in the *Turba*: "Pure water is from sulfur alone"; and immediately in the following discourse of the same book, **Belus** asserts the contrary, saying: "Pure water is not from sulfur alone, but composed of many things, which are made into one sulfur <margin>Another.</margin> from many sulfurs." Similarly, **Bacsem** in the *Turba* says: "The philosophers have divided the work into various names; for they said 'to mix, to cook, to sublime, to whiten, to grind, to roast, to congeal, to make rust, and to dye.' These are many names, yet the **regimen** <note>The "regimen" refers to the specific method of governing the alchemical fire and process</note> is one." And immediately, when he seems to present one continuous action—namely, **decoction** <note>The process of boiling or heating a substance in a liquid</note>—he adds the opposite in this sentiment: "And if the philosophers knew that one decoction and grinding were sufficient, they would not repeat their sayings so much; they did this so that the compound might be ground and cooked continually, and that you might not grow weary of the labor." **Arnaldus** also, when he says in his *Rosarium*: "What you do for the **white**, you do for the **red**, because this medicine is one in essence, and similarly one in its way of acting." Likewise in another place: "There is one stone for making the white and the red at the same time and all at once." Likewise: "The work for the white and red is one," and he repeats in the beginning of the tenth chapter that the work of gold and silver agree in all things. Yet, in the same chapter, as if forgetful of all he said before, he says: "The work of the white is for whitening, and the work of the red is for reddening; therefore, do not mix the work of one stone with the work of another, because you would err greatly if you did otherwise." <margin>Another.</margin> Another example from the same author: "You need to labor in the refinement and solution of the bodies, for they are strong, and they need a long preparation and continuous operation, so that..."

<meta>This page continues Van Hoghelande’s argument regarding the intentional obfuscation used by alchemical authors. It follows a discussion of Geber’s contradictory instructions on whether to begin with calcination or dissolution.</meta>

<header>THEOBALD VAN HOGHELANDE</header>

...first they should be calcined, and afterwards dissolved; since when they have been calcined <note>Calcination is the process of heating a substance to high temperatures in air to change its physical state, often reducing it to a powder or ash.</note> they are more easily dissolved, because the heat of the fire, penetrating the parts of the body, makes the water enter after it, and thus it is more receptive to dissolution. In the same chapter, as if yawning and waking from sleep, he says it is expedient for bodies to be dissolved by water alone without calcination.

Is it to be thought that such a great teacher, so brilliantly versed in other sciences, suffered a lapse of memory? Far from it; rather, he did this intentionally and with great effort, not only in this place but in many others besides. Likewise, **Lull** <note>Raymond Lull (c. 1232–1315), a major philosopher to whom many alchemical works were later attributed.</note> and others do the same, whose similar examples occur everywhere; it is not necessary to bring them all together here, as I must pass on to another art of veiling the doctrine. This is the use of unusual and unknown names, or if the names are known, they are twisted to an entirely different meaning, so that the authors seem to speak in a peculiar idiom by which they understand one another. <margin>Unusual names.</margin> Thus, besides the metals which they have distinguished by the names of the planets—namely, calling gold the **Sun**, silver the **Moon**, copper **Venus**, iron **Mars**, tin **Jupiter**, lead **Saturn**, and quicksilver <term>Mercury</term> <note>The "seven metals of antiquity" were traditionally linked to the seven celestial bodies known at the time.</note>—they have introduced infinite others. Such terms include **Laton**, **Azoth**, **soul**, **Lion**, **Dragon**, **foliated earth**, **Cambar**, **marteck**, **kahul**, **adkibrick**, **boritis**, **zandarich**, **muchal**, **Corsuphle**, **ferment**, **menstruum**, **coagulum**, **poison**, and countless similar words. Indeed, they have especially entangled everything with the names of gold and silver, so that the meaning of such vocabulary can hardly be extracted even by many years of study. Thus **Morienes** says: "The ferment of gold is gold." **Hermes** says: "Sow your gold in foliated earth." **Rosinus**: "Unless you put gold into gold, you have nothing, because the great is not in the small." Likewise in the ***Turba*** <note>The *Turba Philosophorum* (Assembly of the Philosophers), one of the oldest Latin alchemical texts, translated from Arabic.</note>: "The Sun does not tint unless it is tinted." And **Lull**: "This science chooses gold for the father and silver for the mother, because our medicine is elicited from those two bodies prepared in the same sulfur and arsenic." <margin>Characters.</margin> The difficulty arising from unknown or non-vulgar words is increased in no small measure by unknown characters <note>Alchemical symbols used as a shorthand for substances and processes.</note>. For besides those of the planets known to almost everyone, they have assigned peculiar characters to sulfur, salts, inks, aluminous minerals, and intermediate minerals—even to the elements themselves, and to calcination, sublimation, and other operations of the art. Many have also used the transposition of letters, or hidden numbers and signs, in writing their books. <margin>Transcription.</margin> But nothing hinders students quite as much as the ignorance of those who transcribe books. These scribes omit words they do not understand or think are absurd, or what is worse, in wanting to "correct" the text, they pervert the entire sense and the author’s meaning; they even frequently transfer the <gloss>glosses</gloss> <note>Explanatory notes written in the margins of a manuscript.</note> of ignorant men into the main text. <margin>Translation.</margin> Nor are those who translate books published in a foreign language into another free from a similar vice, as can be seen in several places in the later Latin edition of **Count Bernard** <note>Bernard of Trevisan, a legendary 15th-century alchemist.</note>, and in **Morienes**, which was translated from Arabic into the Latin language by Ro—

<meta>catchword: berto (referring to Robert of Chester, the translator of Morienes)</meta>

<header>ON THE DIFFICULTIES OF ALCHEMY</header>

<margin>Variety of styles</margin> ...[Al]bert of Castra <note>original: "Alberto Castrensi." Likely refers to a medieval translator or scholar. The OCR begins mid-word, suggesting a continuation from the previous page's last sentence.</note> differs so much from another translation that in many places he seems to be an entirely different author. The style of the authors of this science is likewise manifold and varied, which brings no small hindrance to readers. For some organize their discourses physically—that is, naturally and according to the progression of nature—while others follow the manner of teaching used by physicians; some explain matters arithmetically, and some even follow the rules of Astronomy and Geometry.

<margin>Physical style.</margin> They speak naturally and philosophically <note>In this period, "natural philosophy" was the study of the physical world, encompassing what we now call biology, chemistry, and physics.</note> regarding corruption and generation, action and passion, the elements and their qualities, matter and form, the faculties and powers of the soul, the four seasons of the year, vapors and rains, the Rainbow and its cause, man and woman, conception and birth, the fetus, and many other things.

<margin>Medical style.</margin> Those who follow the style of physicians discuss the healthy and the sick, the change of temperaments <note>original: "complexionum." In medieval medicine, "complexions" or temperaments were the balance of the four humors (blood, phlegm, yellow bile, black bile).</note>—namely, from cold and moist to hot and dry, and vice versa—about rawness and digestion, the inspection of urine, and the "Crisis" <note>In medicine, a "crisis" was the turning point of a disease; alchemists used this to describe the critical moment a metal transformed.</note> of the birth and origin of the Stone, which they compare to the crises of acute diseases and putrid fevers, so that once the first movement is seen, one can testify to the end.

<margin>Arithmetical style.</margin> Arithmeticians have also obscured this science with their distinctions of numbers in part and in whole; for they have hidden the boundaries and the goal of the entire work in divisions of numbers, just as they do with weights, since they add to and diminish the sum of the "root" at will, sometimes integrating the whole through its parts so that the unlearned cannot grasp it. An example of this is that of **Senior**: <margin>Chapter 4.</margin> 

> Understand the principle of number: the first and the second, and you say two; and those are three in number. Then you say three, which are six in number. Then you say four, and they become ten manifest numbers, but four hidden ones. <note>**Senior** refers to Senior Zadith (Ibn Umail), a 10th-century Arabic alchemist whose work was highly influential in the Latin West.</note>

And that of **Eximenus** in the *Assembly*: 

> I command you to coagulate the quicksilver <note>original: "argentum vivum."</note> so that two become three, and four become one, and two become one. <note>The *Turba Philosophorum* (Assembly of the Philosophers) is one of the oldest Latin alchemical texts, written as a debate between Greek philosophers.</note>

The author of the *Book of Three Words* also says that it is necessary to extract two from three, though they do not extract three from two; rather, by "three," two and seven are understood. And **Hermes** says in the *Seven Treatises*: 

> It is the water that divides itself into four others: namely, one to two, and three to one, of which the third part belongs to the color, and two-thirds to the moisture; these are the weights of water according to the wise. <note>**Hermes** refers to Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary founder of alchemy.</note>

<margin>Astronomical style.</margin> Philosophers speak astronomically of the zodiac and the signs of the zodiac, of the poles, of their exaltation and fall, of conjunctions and oppositions, and of the eclipses of the luminaries; of the infusion of Solar light into the Moon and stars; of the shifting nature of **Mercury**, <note>original: "Mercurij natura versipelli." The term "versipellis" suggests a shape-shifter or something that changes its skin/appearance.</note> who is good and fortunate with good planets, but evil and unfortunate with bad ones; and of the operations of the planets upon these lower things, and similar matters.

<margin>Geometrical style.</margin> Geometrically, they speak of boundaries and angles, of the square, the triangle, and the circle, and how the square and triangle ought to be made round, and vice versa. Hence that saying from the *Rosary*: 

> Convert the quadrangle into a round, and you shall have the mastery. <note>The *Rosarium Philosophorum* (The Rosary of the Philosophers) is a famous 16th-century alchemical treatise known for its series of symbolic illustrations.</note>

Likewise, regarding the [construction] of the furnace...

### THEOBALD VAN HOGHELANDE

<margin>The Book of Alchemical Secrets, in the preface.</margin>
Haly <note>Likely referring to Khalid ibn Yazid, an early Umayyad prince to whom many alchemical works were attributed.</note> says that the rules of Geometry are necessary for the construction [of the work]. He who possesses this book, he says, should read something of Geometry and learn its measurements, and correctly assemble the construction of the furnaces <note>original: "clibanorum." Alchemical furnaces were complex structures designed to maintain specific temperatures over long periods.</note>, and not exceed the proper limit.

<margin>Impossibility</margin>
To these things, finally, add that the philosophers seem to prescribe impossible tasks. Because of this, every treatise on the art could appear not only difficult but entirely deceptive and fraudulent; for they command the elements to be distilled, washed, and cleansed, and finally—which seems ridiculous—to be joined together with a specific weight.

<margin>Book of Secrets, chapter 9.</margin>
Haly: You must take the stone and separate its natures—that is, the four elements: earth, water, air, and fire.

<margin>The Rosary of the Philosophers, part 2, chapter 8.</margin>
Arnald <note>Arnaldus de Villa Nova (c. 1240–1311), a famous physician and alchemist.</note>: When you have the elements divided, wash them—namely, the water and the air by distilling, but the fire and the earth by strongly calcining <note>original: "calcinando." Calcination is the process of heating a solid to high temperatures to drive off volatile substances or oxidize it, often reducing it to a powder.</note>. If anyone thinks the elements are named metaphorically here—for example, as in the distillation of wax or honey, where what comes out first is called "water" <note>original: "phlegma." In early chemistry, this referred to the watery, tasteless distillate.</note>, the second is "yellow oil" and takes the name of "air," the third is "red oil" and takes the name of "fire," while the dregs remaining at the bottom take the name of "earth"—that person is undoubtedly mistaken. For Arnald says in the previously cited passage that the "fire" must be calcined, which cannot take place in red oil, as it is easily flammable. Furthermore, the philosophers do not care for elements that can be felt by the touch, as it is said in the *Turba* <note>The *Turba Philosophorum* (Assembly of the Philosophers), one of the oldest Latin alchemical texts.</note>.

<margin>The Rosary, part 2, chapter 24.</margin>
Concerning the weight of the elements, the same Arnald says:
> Take care in the compounding of the Elixir, and work wisely there, so that you know how much you should add of water, of air, of earth, and of fire; otherwise, if you do differently, the work will not be valid.

But what mathematician has ever been found so subtle that he has encompassed the invisible elements—I mean air and fire—and the impalpable ones by measure or weight? Especially since Eximenus <note>A speaker in the *Turba Philosophorum*.</note> says in the *Turba*:
> "Two of the elements are seen, and their virtue and work are known; the other two are neither touched nor seen."

It seems no less absurd that they say the elements must be converted, since that seems to be the work of God and nature alone. Hence the Alchemist Aristotle <note>A pseudo-Aristotelian alchemical persona popular in the Middle Ages.</note> says:
> "Convert the elements, and you will find what you seek."

<margin>The doctrine of the elements is most obscure.</margin>
And truly, by this tradition of the elements, the philosophers have so obscured the art that many people, hindered by this difficulty and failing to grasp their meaning, shrink back from the study of these books, or believe all these things to be mere fictions invented to hide the art—especially since philosophers say the whole work is finished by one thing and a single process. I will not deny that I was once among their number, though undeservedly, since now I confess with Raymond Lull <note>Ramon Llull (c. 1232–1316), a Majorcan polymath to whom a vast body of "Pseudo-Lullian" alchemy was attributed.</note> that the whole art depends on the division and cleansing of the elements. For thus he says:
> "The whole mastery is to divide the elements from the metals, and to purify them, and to divide the sulfur of nature from the metals."

<margin>The whole mastery depends on the elements...</margin>
For the whole labor is in this, and the entire exhaustion of the mastery lies in the division of the elements and the sulfur. And Arnald says: "If you do not divide the elements of the stone, [you] cannot..." <meta>The sentence continues onto the next page with the catchword: conjun- (likely "conjungere," meaning "to join").</meta>

<summary>This page discusses the "mathematical" style of alchemical writing, focusing on the literal and metaphorical complexities of separating and weighing the four elements (fire, air, water, earth). Van Hoghelande cites authorities like Haly, Arnald of Villanova, and Raymond Lull to explain that while these tasks seem impossible or fraudulent, they constitute the core labor of the alchemical "mastery."</summary>

### PART THREE

# IN WHICH THE DIFFICULTY
# OF PRACTICE IS DISCUSSED.

<margin>
Through experiments I have discovered many things which are thought to be false or impossible.
</margin>
So far, I have spoken of the obstacles arising from the craftsman himself or from the difficulty of understanding the books; it follows that I should begin the discourse on the third part of this treatise, which will deal with practice <term>Praxis: From the Greek, referring to the actual physical work or laboratory application of alchemical theory as opposed to "Theoria" (contemplation).</term>. Although this part might seem to depend entirely on understanding the books—since once the books are understood, the "matter," the management of the work, and the rest that follows seem capable of being known—nonetheless, because investigating the theory of the art is one thing, and attempting it and applying one’s hand to the work is another, many things are discovered by experience itself which could not be grasped through theory alone. Many things that appear easy at first glance are found to be extremely difficult when one attempts the practice; and conversely, it seemed better to treat it in detail. I can certainly affirm to anyone that I would never have understood the philosophers reasoning about the "division of the elements" had I not discovered the sulfur of nature and art <term>Sulfur of nature: In alchemy, "sulfur" usually represents the active, combustible, and masculine principle of a substance, not merely the chemical element sulfur.</term> through working and experimenting. Yet, let no one think I profess a complete mastery of this science because of that, since experience has often mocked me as I tried, and I still desire the knowledge of many things which I do not even dare to hope for, both due to the lack of books (though I have over a hundred copies), and because of the many obstacles by which I do not deny I am held back.

<margin>
The material of the stone is called by the names of all things. Book to Eurychia.
</margin>
But as I begin this third treatise, the "Matter" <note>original: "materia." The raw starting material intended to be transformed into the Philosopher's Stone.</note> first comes to mind, which is the base and foundation of the whole philosophical work; if this is laid recklessly, nothing solid can be built upon it. Although the Philosophers say this matter is one, they have called it by more than a thousand legions of names, as Rosinus <note>Rosinus is the Latinized name for Zosimos of Panopolis, a foundational Greco-Egyptian alchemist.</note> says—namely, by the name of every thing found in the earth, the sea, or the air. They have compared it to all things; they have called it a hermaphroditic monster, male and female, heaven and earth, both corporeal and spiritual, chaos, a microcosm <note>original: "microcosmum." Meaning "little world," a concept suggesting that the alchemical work mirrors the creation and structure of the entire universe.</note>, a confused mass containing within itself all colors and all metals in potential, and than which nothing in the world is more wonder-
