of the work. Let those seekers know that the philosophers do not speak of common salt, but of that mineral salt which they require in their work; they are led by a similarity to calcined things <term>calcination: the process of heating a substance to high temperatures to reduce it to a powder or "ash".</term>. Since salt can be extracted from all such things, they rightly say that salt is also extracted from the lime of their metal—yet by this, they mean nothing other than their "earth." According to that statement of an anonymous author: "That which remains below in the cucurbit <term>cucurbit: a gourd-shaped glass vessel used in distillation.</term> is our salt, that is, our earth." And in the *Allegory of the Sages*: "Note that these bodies are the alums and salts which flow from our bodies." And the author of the *Philosopher’s Ladder* says: "The work of the second water is to exalt the earth into a wonderful salt by its own attractive power alone."

<margin>The error of those placing the art in "middle minerals" and marcasites.</margin>
Some have sought the matter of the Stone in "middle minerals"—in tutty <note>original: "tutia," a term for zinc oxide crusts found in furnace chimneys.</note>, magnesia, and marcasites <note>original: "marchasitis," a general term for various metallic ores, often iron pyrite.</note>—and especially in antimony. For since the philosophers say that metals and their Stone consist of sulfur and quicksilver <term>quicksilver: mercury.</term>, and these can be drawn out of antimony by a simple craft, they believe nothing stands in the way of the matter of the Stone being sought there. But while it is not enough for the philosophers to simply have sulfur and quicksilver—rather, they want them to be pure, clean, lacking all contamination, homogeneous, and non-combustible, but rather persevering over the fire and melting—the quicksilver and sulfur of antimony are, in their roots, impure and unclean. They can be purified by no craft; furthermore, they are heterogeneous, easily retreating from the fire, or else they do not flow. Thus, the nature of antimony and the remaining marcasites will be held suspect by all sane men.

<margin>In stones and gems.</margin>
Certain people seek the principles of the art in stones, gems, and crystal. But if those things which approach more closely to the nature of metals cannot provide the matter of the Elixir, then surely neither can gems, crystal, or other stones. For if that which seems more likely to be the thing is not that thing, then surely neither is that which is less likely. Therefore, since these cannot produce alterations in the bodies of metals (because they do not "enter" them—for nothing alters what it does not penetrate), and since they do not provide a metallic fusion but only a glass-making fusion, or none at all, they are to be rejected as entirely foreign to the art. This is the very thing Alphidius commands:
> "Beware, my son," he says, "and separate yourself from dead bodies and stones, because in them there is no path. For their life is not increased, but rather tends toward nothingness; such are salts, orpiment <note>original: "auripigmenta," a yellow arsenic mineral.</note>, arsenic, magnesia, marcasite, tutty,"

As Geber says: "Sulfur has a homogeneous and most strong composition, and is of a uniform substance." In the same place: "It gives the complete weight to each of the metals, and it purifies and brightens them from their foulness." And a little later: "By God Most High, it illuminates every body, since it is light and tincture." Likewise Pythago-

...as in the *Assembly of the Sages* <note>original: "Turba," referring to the *Turba Philosophorum*, one of the oldest Latin alchemical texts.</note>: "Clean sulfur water is from sulfur alone." And Acubofon says in the same place: "Sulfurs are contained by sulfurs." I respond that Geber <note>Geber refers to the Latinized name of Jabir ibn Hayyan, though the works cited here are likely by a 13th-century European author writing under his name.</note> describes the truth most learnedly and sharply, as is his custom, yet he hides it within wondrous veils of words, not unlike a man who would hide a grain of wheat beneath a great heap of chaff. Therefore, he speaks not of the common and combustible kind, but of the sulfur of the philosophers. For this reason, he adds in that same passage that it must not be used without the mastery <term>mastery: also called the "magistery," the specific alchemical process or secret knowledge required to transform a substance.</term>, because without it, sulfur provides none of these things, but rather corrupts and blackens the work.

<margin>The Height of Perfection, chapter 85. <note>original: "Sum. perf. cap. 85," referring to the *Summa Perfectionis Magisterii*.</note></margin>
And elsewhere, where he speaks of the nature of sulfur and arsenic, he says that sulfur has within itself two causes of corruption: an inflammable substance and an earthy dross. Through the first part of its nature, it cannot withstand the fire, since it always burns and is burned, and it creates blackness in every work. Through the other part, it possesses neither fusion <term>fusion: the ability of a substance to melt and blend with metals.</term> nor ingress, because if it were fixed, it would prevent fusion; yet it is never fixed unless it is first calcined. When it is calcined, however, it can by no means be melted in the craft, because it is reduced to an earthy substance.

<margin>The Rosary of the Philosophers, part 1, chapter 3.</margin>
<margin>The difference between common sulfur and that of the philosophers.</margin>
Geber wrote these things concerning common sulfur, as did Arnaldus <note>Arnaldus de Villa Nova, a 13th-century physician and alchemist.</note> and all others. Anyone even moderately well-versed in chemical books can easily see how much this differs from the sulfur of the philosophers. Common sulfur is entirely foreign to quicksilver <note>original: "argento vivo," literally "living silver."</note>, whereas the philosophers' sulfur is sought from the innermost bowels of the quicksilver of perfected bodies <note>"Perfected bodies" usually refers to gold and silver.</note>. It is nothing other than a simple fire—one that does not scorch, but is living, giving life to other dead bodies, maturing them, and supplying the defects of nature. For it is itself of a superlative maturity, being perfect in its own nature and further purified by the craft. Senior <note>Senior Zadith, the Latin name for the 10th-century Arab alchemist Muhammad ibn Umail.</note> says: "The Sages satisfied men when they said: our sulfur is not the sulfur of the common people; for common sulfur is consumed by fire, but the white sulfur of the wise burns with a combustion of whitening and improvement."

<margin>Regarding common quicksilver.</margin>
Since, therefore, the matter of the Stone cannot be drawn from any of the things mentioned above, it seems to follow that quicksilver must provide it to us, as the Mercurial nature alone corresponds to all the known traits of the matter of the philosophical Stone. For quicksilver alone is incombustible and homogeneous; it either remains in the fire with its whole substance or retreats from the fire with its whole substance. It preserves against burning, effects fusion, and perfects bodies. Indeed, those bodies are less burned and possess greater perfection which participate more in its nature; those with less, have less perfection. Avicenna <note>A famous Persian polymath whose name was frequently attached to alchemical treatises in the West.</note> also affirms this: "It alone receives into itself what is of its own nature and rejects what is foreign; and since it is metallic, it contains within itself everything we need for our mastery." But lest these things be understood as referring to common quicksilver, one must note its flight <note>referring to mercury's high volatility and tendency to evaporate when heated.</note>, which cannot be stopped except by the power of sulfur joined to it or by a metallic vapor. For the Philosophers also say that their Mercury is not the Mercury of the common people. Still, since in the first place...

<meta>This page continues Hoghelande's investigation into the materials of the Great Work. Having previously discussed the limitations of common sulfur, he now examines the role of gold and silver—often called the Sun and the Moon—and the necessity of "corrupting" or breaking them down to reach a higher state of purity.</meta>

# THEOBALD DE HOGHELANDE

...to be more cleansed, since it is necessary for the elixir to be cleaner and purer, as well as more subtle <note>In alchemy, "subtle" refers to a substance that has been refined or vaporized into its most potent, non-bulky form.</note>, than gold or silver itself. But their necessary cleansing cannot be achieved because of their very strong natural composition, which cannot be weakened except through corruption <note>In the alchemical worldview, "corruption" is a positive stage where a substance is broken down or "killed" so that its spirit can be released and reborn in a more perfect form.</note>. But what corruption can happen to gold, which is changed by neither earth nor water, nor burned by flaming things, since it is even improved in the fire? As Pliny says: <margin>*Natural History, book 33, chapter 3.*</margin> "Of gold, the noblest of all bodies, nothing is lost by fire; its substance endures through conflagrations and funeral pyres." 

But someone will say: Since nothing beneath the lunar sphere is exempt from corruption, it must be that a way can be found to corrupt even gold itself. I admit this; for how else could sulfur, quicksilver <term>quicksilver: mercury</term>, and oils be made from it, and finally its very color or tincture? This was pointed out as if with a finger by that incomparable and supreme searcher of nature’s secrets, the most illustrious Giambattista della Porta of Naples, the glory of our age, in his book titled *On Natural Magic*. <margin>*The form of gold must not be destroyed in the work.*</margin> But to corrupt gold for the purpose of generation [new growth] while preserving its inner form—*this* is the work, this is the labor. 

Therefore, some teach that it should be mixed with quicksilver <note>original: "argento vivo"</note> that has been prepared with great artistic skill; for in that way, and no other, can it be exalted beyond its natural perfection, but this is achieved only by a craftsman of the most skillful intellect. Yet if this is done, there will then be multiple things, whereas the philosophers recommend unity in their work. Furthermore, they affirm that their starting material is vile and of small price, while gold has the highest price after gemstones. 

<margin>*In gold, silver, and Mercury.*</margin> Those who were a little more scrupulous in this art teach that one should mix gold with silver and Mercury, so that gold takes the place of the father, silver the place of the mother, and Mercury is the seed of both. <margin>*In the Emerald Tablet.*</margin> Whence Hermes <note>Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary founder of alchemy.</note> says: "Its father is the Sun, its mother the Moon, the wind carried it in its belly." The same author says: "The Dragon does not die unless it is killed along with its brother and sister—not by one alone, but by both together, namely by the Sun and the Moon." 

And Avicenna <note>Ibn Sina, a Persian polymath whose medical and alchemical works were highly influential in the West.</note> says: "I advise that you work only with Mercury, the Sun, and the Moon, for the conjunction of these two bodies is necessary in this art for both the white and the red work <term>white and red: refers to the "Albedo" and "Rubedo" stages of the alchemical process, leading to silver and gold respectively.</term>." And Morienes <note>A legendary 7th-century hermit and alchemist.</note> says: "Let the fools search, and in searching err concerning any old thing, for they will not reach the goal until the Sun and the Moon are reduced into a single body." 

They also add a reason: because if only one of them were in the Stone, the medicine would never flow easily, nor would it give its tincture; and if it did give it, it would fly off into smoke, because there would be no vessel for the tincture within it. But whoever wishes to set his hand to the work should first diligently examine what those species and things are that the philosophers call "Sun" and "Moon," lest he lose both his labor and his oil <note>original: "operam & oleum... perdat," a Latin idiom meaning to waste time and resources.</note>, as the proverb goes.

This point reminds me that since the philosophers proclaim certain wonderful and unbelievable things about their Stone— <margin>*Why the Stone is called the "thing of all things."*</margin> which, if misunderstood, could lead one devoted to experiment into various and wandering errors.

<summary>Hoghelande discusses the paradox of using gold in alchemy: it is the most perfect and indestructible metal, yet it must be "corrupted" or broken down to create the Elixir. He explores the traditional triad of Gold (Sun), Silver (Moon), and Mercury as the necessary components for the Great Work.</summary>

### ON THE DIFFICULTIES OF ALCHEMY, BOOK I

...could [be achieved], before I proceed further, I will interject a few things 
<margin>In the book *On Figures and Images*.</margin>
that will be not only pleasant to know but also extremely useful to all seekers of the truth. First, however, it occurs to me that the philosophers have said their stone is "every thing" <note>original: *omnem rem*</note>. They did this, as the *Rosary* <note>The *Rosarium Philosophorum* (The Rosary of the Philosophers), a 16th-century alchemical treatise.</note> says, because it contains within itself everything it requires and everything necessary for its own perfection. The philosophers testify to this truth everywhere, especially Senior <note>Senior Zadith, the Latinized name of the 10th-century Arab alchemist Ibn Umayl.</note>. He says: "The Stone of the Wise is perfected in itself and from itself; it is the root, the branches, the leaves, the flowers, and the fruit. For it is like a tree whose branches, leaves, and fruit come from it, through it, and to it; it is the whole, and from it comes the whole." He also says: "The Stone of the Wise, which they have called 'every thing,' has within itself everything it needs from the body, from the sun, from the waters, from the spirits, from the souls, and from the tinctures" <term>tincture: a potent liquid or spirit believed to be capable of transmuting base metals into gold</term>. It is also called by every possible name, as the
<margin>Five reasons why it is called by every name.</margin>
*Rosary* says, for the sake of its concealment, and because of the dignity of its nature, its various chemical procedures <note>original: *regimina*</note>, the wonderful variety of colors appearing during the work, and the participation of all the elements existing within it. Pythagoras says in the *Turba* <note>The *Turba Philosophorum* (Assembly of the Philosophers), one of the oldest Latin alchemical texts, which presents a fictional debate between ancient Greek philosophers.</note>: "They have called it by many names because of the excellence of its nature." And the *Lily* <note>The *Lilium Intelligentiae*, another medieval alchemical text.</note> says: "Sometimes in the operation of the stone, all the colors that exist in the world today or can be imagined appear; thus, its names are diversified by various philosophers according to the different colors appearing in the work." There is also another reason: because this stone is perfected from all four elements, it is called by the name of any elemental thing. There is even a third reason: so that the foolish might not recognize it. Furthermore, the philosophers call their stone animal, vegetable, and mineral—not because it can be made indiscriminately from animals, vegetables, or minerals, as many people mistakenly think, spending their money and labor on them in vain. Rather, they call it "animal" because of the soul <note>original: *anima*</note>, which properly belongs to man, the most noble of animals (if it is even right to count man among the animals); though the philosophers also attribute a soul to these minerals and vegetables, though not in the same sense. Bonellus says in the *Turba*: "Our brass <note>original: *aes noſtrum*</note>, just like a man, has both a body and a soul." It is also named so because of the blood, which is proper to animals and without which they die. Thus the *Lily* says: "The spirit turns the body into a tinted spirit, just like blood; for that which has spirit also has blood." And Dardaris says in the *Turba*: "Nothing should be used in the entire procedure except the permanent water, for its power is spiritual blood." Morienes says: "That which best joins the bodies together is blood, for it gives them life and unites them, and makes one body out of them all." Aristotle says: "Blood is the soul, and the soul is life, and life is our stone." This is not because there is
<margin>Comparison of the nature of the stone with the nature of man.</margin>
actually a spirit, soul, or blood within it of the kind found in man, but rather by a certain elegant comparison. For just as a man is said to be dead when the soul is separated from the body, and his corpse remains like a statue...

### THEOBALD DE HOGHELANDE

...rather similar to [something else] than to a human: so also in the stone, once its better and radical essence—which gives the stone its form and tincture <term>tincture: the transformative essence or "soul" of the stone capable of changing metals</term>, and which is the "soul" of the philosophers—has been separated, there will remain a certain formless matter. Regarding its metallic form, since it is no longer within the care of nature, it has no proper name. As Morienus <note>Morienus was a legendary 7th-century hermit said to have taught alchemy to the Umayyad prince Khalid ibn Yazid.</note> says: "every body, when it lacks a soul, will be dark and obscure" <note>original: *omne corpus cum anima caruerit, tenebrosum & obscurum erit*</note>.

And just as we believe that in the resurrection the soul will be restored to the body, and the bodies will thereafter be eternal and incorruptible; so in this art, once the body has been deprived of life <note>original: *exanimato*, literally "de-souled"</note> and purified by fire and water through the proper regimen <term>regimen: the controlled sequence of heating and chemical operations</term>, its soul—that is, the tincture extracted not from elsewhere but from its own body—is returned to it. Then, for the first time, it takes on its metallic color and form, but more illustriously than it had before. 

What I have said is true by the common consensus of the wise, and I shall prove it by producing their own opinions. Hermes <note>Hermes Trismegistus, the mythical founder of alchemy.</note> says in the *Allegories of the Wise*: "The spirit extracted from the stone is white, but the soul is red; when these are returned to it, it lives and rejoices, because it is adorned with its former beauty and light. It is most joyful then, especially when it has risen again, because it dies no more." 

Zion <note>A speaker in the *Turba Philosophorum*, one of the oldest Latin alchemical texts.</note> says in the *Turba*: "The tincture of the stone is the life of those things into which it enters, and the loss and death of those from which it is extracted." 

Bonellus says in the same work: "That nature from which moisture has been taken, when it is left through the nights, appears like a dead man. Then that nature requires fire until the body and its spirit are turned into earth, and then it becomes dust like a dead man in his tomb. When these things are finished, God will return its spirit and soul to it, and with all infirmity removed, that thing is strengthened; after its corruption, it is improved, just as a man after the resurrection becomes stronger and younger than he had been in this world."

### ON THE DIFFICULTIES OF ALCHEMY

...animals, because of the respiration of air. Hence Bonellus says in the *Assembly of the Philosophers* <note>original: *Turba Philosophorum*, one of the oldest and most influential Latin alchemical texts, written as a record of a meeting of pre-Socratic sages.</note>: "The breathing in of men is from the air, which after God is life to them; similarly, copper <note>original: *æs*, a term often used in alchemy to refer to the "base" metallic body of the work.</note> is inspired by moisture, by which, receiving life, it is multiplied and increased like all other things." And so much for the animal stone.

<margin>Why the stone is called vegetable.</margin>
They have called it "vegetable" indeed from its resemblance to the vegetative soul, which is nevertheless common to animals. It is defined as a certain power in living things that converts nourishment into the substance of the entity being nourished, so that it might preserve it in its being, lead it to its proper size, and grant it the power to generate its like in its own species. Since therefore these three powers—namely the Nutritive, the Augmentative, and the Generative—are found in the stone (although not in quite the same way as in plants), they have named it "vegetable" for no absurd reason.

<margin>The four nourishing faculties in the stone.</margin>
Furthermore, just as the power of nourishing requires four other subservient faculties to perform its duty—namely, the Attractive, Retentive, Digestive, and Expulsive—these same faculties are observed in the Work. By the **Attractive**, the substance of the stone draws from Mercury <note>The alchemical "Mercury" or "Quicksilver" is not the common metal, but a "living" principle of fluidity and transformation.</note> that which it needs in the craft and which is familiar to itself; it does this through an elemental virtue seeking to fill a vacuum. By the **Retentive**, it retains the heat of the "cooking" <note>original: *coctionem*, the long process of heating the matter in a sealed vessel.</note> by reason of the vacuum's appetite. By the **Digestive**, it transforms what is retained into the likeness of its own substance, just as quicksilver is changed into the substance of coagulating sulfur <note>In alchemical theory, all metals were thought to be composed of varying proportions of Sulfur (the active/fiery principle) and Mercury (the passive/watery principle).</note>. By the **Expulsive**, nature expels what is not suitable for it; for water does not, as someone says in the *Assembly*, add more weight to the body than it already has of metallic moisture within itself, because the moisture of the water passes away, while the metallic moisture remains. Lest anyone think these are my own fictions, let him look at the *Codicil* of Raymond Lully <note>Ramon Llull, a 13th-century polymath to whom many alchemical works were later attributed.</note>, and his *Testament*, chapter 32.

<margin>Chapter 16.</margin>
As for the fact that the stone grows and can generate its like—although it is not necessary to prove it, since this is the very end and goal of the entire chemical study—I will nevertheless propose several sayings of the philosophers on that matter. I begin with Marsilio Ficino <note>A famous Italian priest and scholar of the Renaissance, known for translating Plato and writing on "natural magic."</note>, who in his book *On the Chemical Art* speaks thus: "It is decreed among those most learned in philosophy that the stone can tinge <note>tinge: to transform or "dye" a base metal into gold or silver.</note> innumerable parts. For every spirit can be multiplied, but no body can; and since our stone has been made most volatile, and so to speak spiritual, and entirely fiery—having been repeated often through many-layered solutions and coagulations—why would you not believe the stone can tinge innumerable parts? This is clear if, with a sharp wit <note>original: *emunctis naribus*, literally "with wiped nostrils," an idiom for being discerning or sharp-scented.</note>, you have smelled the reason of nature and its wonderful gifts from within. For the more you dissolve the Sun <note>The "Sun" (*Sol*) is the alchemical code for Gold.</note> and coagulate it repeatedly, the more you will be able to tinge. Likewise, the more wives a man takes, the more offspring he will have." The author of the *Philosophical Treasury* also says: "The water of the wise is like a grain of wheat; for it is nourished and putrefies, and is corrupted, then it germinates, rises again, and multiplies itself."

<margin>The Rising Dawn.</margin>
And another says <note>Referring to the *Aurora Consurgens*, a famous 15th-century alchemical manuscript often attributed to Thomas Aquinas.</note>: "The philosophers wish to nourish their metallic grain until it is vegetated, and brings forth fruit, such as it is itself." Also the author of the *Dialogue of Nature and the Son of Philosophy* says: "The stone or medicine which...

...[that which] you seek sprouts and is multiplied, just as a grain of wheat falling into good soil, when it has died, brings forth much fruit: therefore when it is decomposed <note>In alchemy, the "death" or corruption of a substance—often called putrefaction—was seen as the necessary first step for its rebirth and multiplication.</note>, you will be able to produce many other grains from it.

<margin>Why it is called the mineral stone.</margin>
The stone is called **mineral** for this reason: that its matter, or the things from which it is composed and constituted, are mineral and metallic; they cannot be from elsewhere if metals are to be transmuted. If anyone 
<margin>Objection.</margin>
alleges, by the same reasoning, that it could be called a vegetable or animal stone because its origin is from vegetables or animals, I respond 
<margin>Solution.</margin>
that there is no underlying reason—rather, it is plainly repugnant to nature—that metals should be found in animals or vegetables, since their principles <note>The "principles" are the fundamental building blocks of a substance, such as Mercury and Sulfur in the Aristotelian-Alchemical view.</note> are plainly diverse and can in no way be mixed together so as to persist in the fire. For philosophers, some similarity suffices (even if not fitting in all respects) to attribute any quality to their Stone. Nor should anyone flatter himself because the fluidity of quicksilver <note>mercury</note> is halted by the juices of certain herbs, or because a color other than the natural one is sometimes induced in it (once coagulated) or in imperfect metals by things which have their origin from animals or vegetables. These things act only extrinsically <note>on the surface level</note> and do not penetrate deeply, nor do they induce a metallic form unless it be a corrupted one; but they can never give the true form of gold and silver. 

But that the reasons I have brought forward for why the stone is called animal, vegetable, and mineral are true, the Sages themselves will be my witnesses. For thus says Rosinus <note>original: *Rosinus*; the Latinized name for Zosimos of Panopolis, a famous early alchemist</note>: "Take this animal stone—that is, having a soul in itself, namely a mercurial one—sensing the presence and influence of its magnesia <note>a term for the 'raw material' of the stone</note>, its magnet, and its calamine, and its summit through local motion, by following and fleeing." Also the Author of the *New Light* <note>original: *novi luminis*; likely referring to a common alchemical treatise title before the more famous work by Sendivogius</note>: "It shows certain powers of the soul; it moves and is moved, it acts and it suffers." 

Rosinus continues: "Vegetable, that is, communicating its power implanted in nature to its own kind, multiplying the power of its influence just as a root [communicates] to the trunk or to herbs." 
<margin>Chapter II.</margin>
"Mineral, because it is extracted from a mine." The Author of the *Universal Way*: "The philosophers have named the stone vegetable because it vegetates and grows." 
<margin>Book on the Nature of the Sun & Moon.</margin>
"Animal, because it has a body, soul, and spirit, like animals. Mineral, because the things from which it is composed are mineral in their nature." Michael Scotus <note>a 13th-century scholar and advisor to Frederick II, known for his works on alchemy and the occult</note>: "The stone is called mineral because it is made from minerals alone; vegetable because it is nourished and increased, which are vegetative powers; animal because it is refreshed by scent and corrupted by stench," 
<margin>Chapter I.</margin>
though this last point should not be understood according to the literal sound of the words <note>Alchemists often used sensory terms like "scent" or "stench" to describe chemical reactions and the purity of vapors</note>. The Author of the *New Light*: "This is the stone which is found on the summit of mountains and is deservedly called mineral. It is also said to be animal because it has a soul; it is also called vegetable because it vegetates." 

<margin>The Philosophers must be believed.</margin>
Therefore, there is no reason why learned men and followers of alchemy should seek other explanations; let them believe the Sages and their Masters, if only they [desire] to be their disciples...

He argues against using actual plant or animal matter in alchemy, asserting that only mineral substances can produce true gold and silver.</summary>

...they desire. Nor should they fear that an Elixir composed of minerals is less conducive to health than that which they seek in vegetables and minerals, since all philosophers and physicians alike have always commended the exceptional qualities and virtues of gold.

<margin>The Elixir is nothing but spiritual gold.</margin>
The Elixir, however, or the **Philosopher’s Stone** <note>original: "lapis philosophorum"</note> of which we speak, is nothing but gold, but a thousand times more perfect than common gold. Indeed, if it were not gold, the study of alchemy would be in vain, since the principle of making gold must necessarily proceed from gold, just as the principle of making fire proceeds from fire. For it could not transmute imperfect metals into gold unless it were gold itself; for like is generated by its like. I do not deny that certain Elixirs can be made from honey, wine, and similar substances taken from animals as well as vegetables to preserve and sometimes even heal human bodies; but these have nothing to do with our Elixir of which we treat, to which they are in no way comparable. In fact, in the context of metallic transformation <note>metamorphosis</note>, they are to be set aside and rejected as useless.

<margin>The sophistry of the wise.</margin>
If the Philosophers say at times that their Stone receives assistance from other things, and they name foreign substances alien to the nature of metal, they usually do so with a certain qualification—namely, that some things are more "closely related" than others. 
<margin>Treatise.</margin>
And this is one of the most common deceptions <term>sophisms<gloss>logical fallacies or tricks of language used by alchemists to hide their secrets</gloss></term> of the wise in this art. For this reason, Hermes <note>Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary father of alchemy.</note> wished the student of philosophy to be possessed of profound reason. Furthermore, some think the Stone is called mineral, animal, and vegetable by philosophers because it does not only bring human and metallic bodies to health and a true balance <note>temperamentum</note>, and exercises its power over them, but also over vegetables; 
<margin>Practice of the Testament, second to last chapter.</margin>
because, as Lull says <note>Raymond Lull, a major figure in medieval alchemy to whom many "Testaments" were attributed.</note>, it rectifies all plants in the springtime through its great heat. For if a quantity of it the size of a millet seed were dissolved in water and placed around the trunk of a vine, or in the heart of a tree, flowers and leaves would be produced by art, and they would bear fruit in the month of May. Although this reasoning is not improper, the authority of the philosophers will always carry greater weight with me, especially since there is discovered in it something more of energy and hidden doctrine than can be perceived by just anyone.

<margin>Why the Stone is said to be in everything and everywhere.</margin>
Now let us examine why they have said their Stone is found in every thing and in every place. I have shown above, from various sayings of the wise, that the **Philosopher’s Stone** consists of **Mercury** and **Sulfur**, or water and earth—elements which are most conspicuous in the Stone—and I have demonstrated that both are called "the Stone." Since, therefore, there is no corporeal thing which does not consist of water and earth, and no place void of the moist or the dry, they rightly affirm that their Stone is findable everywhere. Hermes says: "Our art requires two natures: namely, the Moist and the Dry." And in the *Allegories of the Wise* <note>original: "Allegorijs Sapientum"</note>: "Two stones of the Wise are found on the banks, and on the peaks of mountains, and in the bellies of rivers, and in the walls of royal houses; they are even found cast out in dung;"

# THEOBALD DE HOGHELANDE

By these words, it is certain that nothing else is understood than water and earth, or the moist and the dry. But because the spirit or "water" predominates in the work—since the entire mastery <note>original: "magisterium," the process of the Great Work</note> is done with it, from it, and through it—the teachers of this science have said that this is to be found everywhere. Thus Hermes says: "The secret of any thing and life is in one water, and this water is capable of receiving nourishment, in humans and in others, and in water is the greatest secret: for it is water which becomes the grain in the wheat, and the oil in the olive, and the gum and various fruits in certain trees, and the beginning of the generation of men is water." Hamuel in Senior <note>A reference to the *Tabula Chimica* by Senior Zadith, an influential Arabic alchemical text translated into Latin.</note> says: "There is no thing in the world more known than the stone; every person and every man needs it, and it is with him, nor can he even be without it." By "all things," the philosopher intends to mean water; for water is found in every place—in valleys, in mountains, and with the rich and the poor, the strong and the weak.

<margin>In the Keys of Philosophy.</margin>
And Alphidius says: "When he says our Stone is from a vile thing, lacking price in the eyes of men, loathed, which men trample underfoot in the streets and from which they distance themselves, what else does he mean but water?" The author of the *Conjunction of the Mass of the Sun and Moon* <note>original: "Conf. conjugij massa Solis & Lunæ"</note> says: "The Stone is called vile because it is of no price in the eyes of the ignorant, yet it is most dear, because without it nature does not work—namely, without the moist; for the stone of the philosophers is aqueous and moist, and moisture is considered most vile."

<margin>The Book of Light.</margin>
And Rupescissa <note>Johannes de Rupescissa, a 14th-century alchemist known for his work on quintessence.</note> says: "The nature or matter of the stone is a thing of cheap price found everywhere, because it is a viscous water." Others did not look to water alone, but to all the elements which are in all things.

<margin>To Thomas of Bologna.</margin>
Hence Count Bernard <note>Bernard of Treviso, a legendary alchemist.</note> says: "When the Philosophers say that the stone is made from every thing, they mean it is made from the four elements, from which every generable and corruptible thing is made." And the *Rosarius* <note>The *Rosarium Philosophorum* or "Rose Garden of the Philosophers."</note> says: "It is found everywhere on account of the participation of the elements." Rosinus says: "Just as man is composed of the four elements, so too is the stone; therefore the stone is in man." Some wish for "radical moisture" <note>original: "humorem radicalem," the essential life-fluid believed to sustain living beings</note> to be understood by such sayings, or the heat innate to all things: for every thing in the world—that is, every elemented body—has within itself a radical or formal heat by cause of which it persists; and there is no thing so cold that it is not cherished under the heat included within it as if in a root.

<margin>Book on the Chemical Art, ch. 27.</margin>
Some prefer to interpret these things figuratively, among whom is Marsilio Ficino; but I believe they do so more to show off their intellect or out of a desire to veil the truth than because they truly feel that way. For example, when it is said the stone is "everywhere," it is understood to be in the whole glass, or in all things—that is, in all metals, which are their "things," 
<margin>In the Emerald Tablet.</margin>
according to that saying of Hermes: "All things are born from one thing." There, Lord Thomas <note>Likely referring to pseudo-Thomas Aquinas.</note> and Hortulanus interpret "things" as "metals." At "all times" refers to the time of its own work; and in "every man" refers to his own constitution <note>original: "complexionis," the balance of humors</note>. Lullius <note>Ramon Llull, the Majorcan polymath to whom many alchemical works were attributed.</note> in a certain place wished nature to be considered, namely that the stone may be found in every thing in which it is made by nature; for it is foolish

...to seek something which is not in the thing itself. And another says: "The Stone of the philosophers is in all things in which it is nourished." Although these things are true, the intention of the philosophers is directed toward nothing other than the elements, and especially toward **water**, just as I have said.

<margin>Knowledge of the regimen is necessary, but most difficult. From the Book on Figures and Images. In the Key of Great Wisdom. The Testament, chapter 29.</margin>
Having enumerated the difficulties arising regarding the knowledge of the true <term>matter</term> <note>The "materia prima" or starting material of the Great Work.</note>, which is the key to the entire art, let us proceed to its preparation, and consider whether the Wise are any clearer on this subject. For it is of no use to know what the stone consists of unless its preparation is likewise made known; a task which **Senior** called the most difficult of all things. And **Baccen** says in the *Turba* <note>The *Turba Philosophorum*, or Assembly of the Philosophers, one of the oldest Latin alchemical texts translated from Arabic.</note> that its <term>regimen</term> <note>The "regimen" refers to the specific sequence of heat levels and chemical operations required to perfect the Stone.</note> is greater than what can be comprehended by reason. **Mandinus** says in the same place: "Ignorance of the regimen has caused very many to go astray." **Senior** remarks: "Many know our stone, but do not know its power; but even if they knew its power, what would it be worth unless they knew the operation?" They cannot know the operation, however, except through the gift of God, or through the teaching of a Master who may teach it. And **Lull** says: "Nothing in this science is secret, except the mode of work and operating." We shall find that Lull spoke the truth if we examine the individual modes of preparation and the variety of authors more diligently. For some have described the regimen of the stone so succinctly that they seem to have handed down mere riddles. Thus **Geber** <note>Jabir ibn Hayyan, the foundational figure of Arabic alchemy.</note>

and the Author of *The Perfect Mastery* say: "The perfect preparation of bodies and spirits is through the removal of the superfluous and the addition of what is missing." **Morienes** <note>Morienus, a legendary hermit who supposedly taught alchemy to the Ummayad prince Khalid ibn Yazid.</note> says: "The work is nothing other than the drawing out of water from the earth, and the returning of the same upon it." **Lull** describes various modes of operation here and there,

for in one place he says: "Two operations are necessary for you: corruption, which is done under the preservation of its form, and generation." The **Rosary** <note>The *Rosarium Philosophorum*, a famous 16th-century alchemical compendium.</note> says: "Kill the living, and revive the dead." Another says: "Dissolve, coagulate, and tinge." For **Arnaldus** <note>Arnaldus de Villa Nova, a prominent 13th-century physician and alchemist.</note> and **Lull** and certain others assign four modes of operation: Dissolving, washing, congealing, and fixing.

The author of the *Stairway of Philosophers* and **Ripley the Englishman** <note>George Ripley, a renowned 15th-century English alchemist.</note> hand down twelve modes of operation: calcination, dissolution, separation, conjunction, putrefaction, congelation, <term>cibation</term> <note>cibation: "feeding" the material with fresh moisture to compensate for what was lost during heating.</note>, sublimation, fermentation, exaltation, multiplication, and projection. **Geber** and **Arnold** in the *Flower of Flowers* list eight: sublimation, descension, distillation, calcination, dissolution, coagulation, fixation, and creation. **Haly**: "All operations of this art are contained under six things, which are: to flee, to melt, to wax, to whiten, to dissolve, and to coagulate." **Senior** teaches seven dispositions: namely, sublimation, calcination, dissolution, washing, waxing, coagulation, and fixation. **Avicenna** lists as many, but not in the same order: sublimation, dissolution, putrefaction, washing, coagulation, calcination, and fixation. Others list still others, all of which there is no need to collect in this place.

<margin>The diversity [of opinions] confuses the minds of readers.</margin>
Since, therefore, the authors vary so greatly, and it is inevitable that the minds of readers are distracted by such a multitude of operations, who could trust that they will ever see light in such thick darkness? Does not such diversity necessarily breed difficulty? For one calls dissolution the first step of the work, another says calcination, a third says sublimation, and so on for the rest. For if the first order varies, it is necessary that the subsequent ones vary as well. But if they were at least in agreement regarding the definitions of these <term>regimens</term> <note>The specific stages or methods of heat and processing in the alchemical work.</note>—but they are not even that, since each defines them according to his own whim. For calcination is said to be the pulverization of a thing by fire through the loss of its humidity which holds its parts together; yet some teach to calcine their bodies not with fire, but with water—among whom is **Lull**.

<margin>In the *Apertorio* <note>The "Opener" or "Opening," a work attributed to Ramon Lull.</note>.</margin>
For he says: "The calcination of the earth is not done by fire, as the <term>Sophists</term> <note>In this context, "Sophists" refers to "false alchemists" or those who follow only the literal, superficial meaning of the texts.</note> believe, but by its own proper spirit." However, it was said above that in this art, the term "spirit" indicates nothing other than **water**. But how can there be such a difference, when one commands the body to be deprived of moisture, and another commands water to be added? The same must be judged regarding dissolution: while it is defined as the reduction of a dry thing into water—which cannot happen except through the union of the solvent and the thing to be dissolved, so that the body becomes spirit and the spirit becomes body—**Arnold**, asserting the contrary, says: "To dissolve is to divide bodies," which is nothing other than to separate the parts of a compound and make two or more out of one.

...and that the whole work of the philosophers is completed by a single sublimation. For so says **Arnold** <note>Arnold of Villanova, a famous 13th-century physician and alchemist.</note>: Our "Water" sublimates bodies not by the common sublimation understood by the "fantastical"—who believe that to sublimate is to ascend higher or to be raised by fire—but for the philosophers, to sublimate is to make subtle, to cleanse, and to purify <note>original: "defæcare," meaning to remove the dregs or "feces" of the matter.</note>. Thus, they differ greatly in the remaining modes of operation, and if I wished to examine them more diligently, I would become too long-winded. I will add only this: since it is clear from the above that many "regimens" <note>Regimens are stages or sets of instructions for the alchemical process.</note> of the work are described, some nonetheless reject all variety and desire only a single <term>decoction</term> <note>The process of heating or "cooking" a substance in a liquid.</note>, following the example of nature in the places where minerals grow, or the example of a fetus in the womb. As the *Rosary* <note>The *Rosarium Philosophorum*, a key 15th-century alchemical text.</note> says: "Although the philosophers often say, 'put it in its vessel and close it firmly,' it nonetheless suffices to put it in and close it once, until the whole mastery is fulfilled; anything more than this comes from evil."

<margin>The Testament, chapter 14.</margin>
**Lully** <note>Raymond Lully, a Majorcan philosopher to whom many alchemical works were attributed.</note>, however, requires three gradual transmutations, or rather "digestions," in the likeness of those that occur in the human body, of which the first is in the stomach, the second in the liver, and the third in the veins and the limbs. Such great diversity among the authors cannot help but pour the greatest darkness <note>original: "caliginem"</note> over the eyes of those who work and study.

<margin>The knowledge of weights is most difficult and especially necessary.</margin>
But let us pass on to "weights" <note>In alchemy, "weights" refers to the specific proportions of ingredients used in a recipe.</note>, and first let us hear from the masters themselves how much it matters to know them. For no matter how well the matter has been prepared and mixed, unless the quantities of the things are just and according to reason, the craftsman labors in vain. The author of *Perfect Mastery*: "Beware that you do not approach the composition before you find the complete weights of the things to be composed." The author of the *Dialogue of Nature and the Son of Philosophy*: "Due proportion is the key to all secrets."

<margin>*Rosary*, part 2, chapter 24.</margin>
**Arnold**: "All things exist under a defined limit and a certain disposition. Therefore, there is a need for a weight for every weight, and a measure for every measure." **Haly**: "If the quantity of the weights is unsuitable in the compound, with the parts of its nature exceeding through increase or decrease, the property of the compound is destroyed along with it, and its effect becomes useless and void." **Chambar** in the *Assembly of Philosophers* <note>The *Turba Philosophorum*, one of the oldest Latin alchemical texts.</note>: "If you prepare it without weight, a delay occurs, and it will be considered an evil." **Rhazes** <note>An influential Persian physician and chemist.</note>: "He who is ignorant of weights should not labor in our books, for the philosophers have placed nothing in their works, nor hidden anything else, except this." Those who have spent time in the books of the philosophers will find that Rhazes spoke the truth; for the authors diverge so much that it is shameful to report it, and even if it were not shameful, I would not be able to do so. Yet if they would only name a single weight for the solvent and the solute, we could certainly achieve it by some guess—if not on the first try, then at least through many turns—by placing such various parts in glass vessels until, by the favor of divine grace, we achieved it. This is especially true since it seems to matter little whether a little more "water" <note>In this context, "water" usually refers to the chemical solvent or mercury used in the process.</note> is added or not; for one must think that if a few more parts of water are added, the body is dissolved more quickly but hardens <note>original: "coagulari"</note> more slowly; whereas if fewer are added, it is dissolved more slowly, but hardens more quickly, so...

<margin>The variety of the Wise regarding weights. *Book of Furnaces*, chapter 19.</margin>
...so that all things fall back into one; yet the philosophers do not seem to go beyond a twelfth part in this regard. For **Geber** <note>The Latin name for Jabir ibn Hayyan, the most influential figure in early alchemy.</note> and **Marsilio Ficino** <note>The famous Renaissance philosopher and physician.</note> take twelve parts of water; **Count Bernard** <note>Bernard of Trevisan, a legendary 15th-century alchemist.</note> takes ten; **Senior** <note>Senior Zadith, an 11th-century Arabic alchemist.</note> takes nine, according to the number of the "nine eagles." Hence some say: "Between nine and twelve, you cannot err." But the *Turba* <note>The *Turba Philosophorum* (Assembly of the Philosophers), one of the oldest and most cited Latin alchemical texts.</note> asserts that three parts of water and one of the "body" should be used. Others take more or less: some command water to be poured over so that it stands three fingers above.
<margin>On the art of chemistry: chapter 19.</margin>
But granted that someone has attained that first weight required for the dissolution of the body, I do not see what is to be expected regarding the rest—those weights required in the composition of the purified elements and the addition of the <term>tincture</term> <note>The concentrated essence or "medicine" used to transform base metals into gold or silver.</note>. For in those, a much greater variety is seen; the authors do not stop at twelve parts of water or earth, but go up to fifty and more. 
<margin>*The Rosary*, part 2, chapter 13.</margin>
For **Arnold** <note>Arnold of Villanova, a 13th-century physician.</note> says: "infuse the water by turns while grinding, until the earth itself has drunk a fiftieth part of its own water." Others take less water and more earth; others affirm more water and less earth should be taken, so that one cannot extricate oneself from so many and such great labyrindths—especially if one considers the operation of nature, whose secrets in the combination of <term>sulfur</term> <note>The active, "masculine" principle of fire and stability.</note> and <term>quicksilver</term> <note>original: "argenti vivi," meaning mercury, the passive, "feminine" principle of fluidity.</note> can be sought or known by us through no investigation. 
<margin>Philosophers confuse the weights of the first, second, and third regimen.</margin>
Added to this is another difficulty: that the philosophers do not distinguish, when they prescribe weights, whether they wish them to be used in the first, second, third, or fourth work <note>Alchemical "works" or "regimens" are the sequential stages of the process.</note>; but mixing everything together—speaking now of the solution of the body, now of the conjunction of the elements, and sometimes of both at once—they confuse the proper proportions of the parts. But if they only spoke of weighing water and earth, which can be felt and seen! Now, since they even want air and fire to be balanced <note>In alchemy, the four elements (Earth, Water, Air, Fire) must be brought into a specific mathematical harmony.</note>, I cannot but judge the proportion of weights to be most difficult, and I must weep for the fruitless labors and errors of many craftsmen. 
<margin>How necessary the knowledge of the vessel is.</margin>
Next, let us discuss the **vessel** in which the <term>mastery</term> <note>The *Magisterium*, or the successful completion of the alchemical work.</note> is made. Knowledge of it is most necessary, as it is like the womb <note>original: "matrix."</note> in animals, in which they are generated and receive growth and nourishment alike. For the material, its preparation, or the knowledge of weights will not help the craftsman at all unless he has a suitable vessel in which to complete the operations of art and nature. For "place" is the principle of generation, and the place generates the thing placed within it; nor does it matter, as **Albertus** <note>Albertus Magnus, a 13th-century scholar and saint.</note> says, whether something is done in artificial vessels or natural ones; for in both, elemental and celestial virtues operate, provided the artificial ones are shaped after the fashion of the natural ones. 
<margin>In the preface of the *Secrets of Alchemy*.</margin>
Hence **Haly** <note>An Arabic authority, possibly Khalid ibn Yazid.</note> says: "Unless the matter of the mastery finds a vessel suitable for it, the whole work is destroyed, and its workers do not find what they seek; nor does the thing itself come forth into the effect of generation, because when it does not find the cause of its generation or its root, a collapse of destruction happens to the heat itself in the operations." And **Morienes** <note>A legendary 7th-century hermit and alchemist.</note> says: "If the ancient sages and those who followed them, had not given their expositions about qua-..." <note>The text cuts off here, continuing on the next page; the original Latin catchword "litate" suggests the word is "qualitate," meaning "about the quality."</note>

<summary>Hoghelande details the frustratingly contradictory ratios (weights) given by different alchemical authorities and argues that the choice of vessel is as vital as the ingredients themselves, comparing the vessel to a biological womb.</summary>

->**M**<-

<page-num>177</page-num>

<header>BOOK ON THE DIFFICULTIES OF ALCHEMY</header>

...if they had not found the [proportionality] of the vessel in which the <term>mastery</term> <note>The *magisterium*, or the successful completion of the alchemical process.</note> is finished, no one would have ever reached its perfection. However, since they say this vessel is unique, its discovery brings no small hindrance to seekers, nor does it seem likely that such diverse regimes of the art can be carried out in a single vessel—namely **sublimation**, **calcination**, **distillation**, **solution**, **inceration**, and the like. Therefore, either it cannot be unique, or so many preparations of the matter will rightly be judged as nothing but mere fictions and verbal riddles, unless perhaps someone understands the "water of the philosophers," which is sometimes taken to mean the vessel itself. 

<margin>The water of the philosophers is their vessel. From the *Book of the Flower of Flowers*.</margin> 

Hence **Hermes** <note>Hermes Trismegistus, the mythical founder of alchemy.</note> says: "The vessel of the philosophers is their water." And **Arnaldus** <note>Arnaldus de Villa Nova (c. 1240–1311), a physician and alchemist.</note> states: "The Stone, as the philosophers say, is made in one vessel; and they speak the truth, for our whole mastery is made with our water and from it. For it dissolves the bodies, and calcinates them, and reduces them to earth, whitens them, and purifies them." Likewise, another author says: "In our water all modes of operations occur, namely sublimation, distillation, solution, calcination, and fixation; they occur in said water as if in an artificial vessel." **Sulphur** is also named the "vessel of nature" by **Lull** <note>Raymond Lull (c. 1232–1316), a Majorcan philosopher to whom many alchemical works were later attributed.</note> in a certain place.

However, although all operations are said to be possible with water, it is nevertheless necessary that the water itself be contained in some physical vessel, regarding which the wise disagree the most. 

<margin>Diversity of the Wise in describing the vessel of the work.</margin> 

For different things are prescribed by different masters: one prescribes glass with a long and narrow neck and a round belly; another a <term>cucurbit</term> <note>The lower part of a still, shaped like a gourd.</note> with an <term>alembic</term> <note>The "cap" or lid of a still used to collect vapors.</note>; a third a vessel with two pipes; some a vessel upon a vessel; others an <term>aludel</term> <note>A series of pear-shaped pots used for sublimation.</note> or a sublimatory, and infinite other designs. Many do not require one single vessel for the whole work, but different ones for each of its regimes, so that such great diversity is an indicator of the greatest difficulty. 

To this must be added the various shapes of vessels taken from some similarity to either the substance or the operation itself. For thus **Haly** <note>Likely Haly Abenragel, an Arabic astrologer and alchemist.</note> calls the vessel an "egg": "Take," he says, "the egg, and strike it with a fiery sword, for it is its closure." Some also call it a "sifter" or a "sieve," because in it the parts are divided and purified, and in it the mastery is perfected. **Senior** <note>Senior Zadith, an 11th-century Arabic alchemist.</note> says: "Sift it with a sieve and thread," that is, with a cucurbit and alembic. And **Mireris** says: "It must be sifted seven times with its own sieve." Some have named their vessel "marble," because in it the material of the philosophers is ground. 

It is also called a "sepulcher." Hence in the *Turba*: "Let a sepulcher be dug for that dragon, and let the woman be buried there with him." And all of this is for the sake of its concealment; nor is it likely that the philosophers described it anywhere in open words, as **Maria** <note>Maria Prophetissa, an early alchemical authority often identified as Miriam, sister of Moses.</note> testifies, who speaks in this manner: "The philosophers teach everything except the vessel of Hermes, because it is divine, and hidden from the nations by the wisdom of the Lord; and those who are ignorant of it do not know the regime of truth, because of their ignorance of the vessel of Hermes." The author of the *Lily*, Senior, says that the vision of it is to be sought more than written descriptions. 

<margin>Difficulty regarding the size of the vessel.</margin> 

But the difficulty arises not only from the shape of the vessel, but also from its size, namely lest it be larger or smal[ler]...

# THEOBALD DE HOGHELANDE

<margin>Regarding the sealing.</margin>
...[unless the vessel] be smaller than is proper. For if it is larger, the vapors of the stone or the subtle spirits will be too widely dispersed and will not return to their body. But if it is smaller, the revolution of the stone’s elements cannot be fulfilled, and its germ will be suffocated. For just as the revolution of the elements occurs through the movement of the firmament—by which subtle bodies strive to ascend higher, while that which is heavy remains below—so too do the philosophers claim it happens in the work of skilled chemists. Likewise, no small difficulty lies in the sealing of the vessels: for within them are the most subtle spirits, which, if they are not contained, will cause the <term>mastery</term> <note>original: "magisterium"; refers to the successful completion of the alchemical process.</note> to perish. Hence the *<term>Rosary</term>* <note>original: "Rosarius"; likely referring to the *Rosarium Philosophorum*, a foundational 16th-century alchemical text.</note> says: "Keep the vessel and its fastening secure, so that it may be powerful in the preservation of the spirits." Certainly, if there were only a single, linear, and continuous boiling in the work, a long vessel would seem sufficient, the neck of which could be constricted and sealed with a glowing iron; but since they command that the matter be sublimated, distilled, and calcinated, I find no reason how the airy vapors can be contained in the vessel—no matter how the clay or glues are prepared—unless the vessel must be broken after each operation. Yet the wise sufficiently imply that this is not necessary when they say that the entire <term>mastery</term> is perfected in a single vessel.

<margin>
Knowledge of fire is necessary.
*Secrets of Alchemy*, chapter 8.
</margin>
Let us proceed further to fire, without the knowledge of which every operation of the craftsmen is invalid, since the benefit and the harm of this thing proceed from the appropriate use of fire, as **Haly** <note>Likely referring to the Arabic alchemist Khalid ibn Yazid or Haly Abenragel.</note> says. And **Plato** <note>The author refers to "Pseudo-Plato," an alchemical persona attributed to the Greek philosopher.</note> says: "Fire adds benefit to the perfect and harm, or corruption, to the corrupt." Thus, when its quantity is good and suitable, it brings perfection; but when it increases in things beyond measure, it corrupts both—namely, the perfect and the corrupt. And **Alphidius** <note>An Arabic alchemist often cited in medieval Latin texts.</note> says: "The agent in this whole world is one thing, namely heat; for without heat, there is no motion or action, as heat is the root of the very arrangement." **Morienes** <note>A legendary 7th-century hermit and alchemist.</note> states: "The greatest efficacy of this work is weighed in its fire, for with it the minerals are prepared, and the souls are retained in their bodies; fire is also its entire nature and its perfect test." And: "If you know how to give fire, water and fire are enough for you." **Maria** <note>Maria Prophetissa, an early alchemist often credited with inventing the water-bath (*bain-marie*).</note> says: "The whole governance lies in the tempering of the fire."

How difficult it is.
Treatise 2.
</margin>

For many know the substance, but they are ignorant of the regulation of the fire, in which lies the whole perfection." **Hermes** <note>Hermes Trismegistus, the mythical father of alchemy.</note> says: "The science of fires is a wonderful gift." But someone will perhaps ask why the regulation of fire is unknown, since art imitates nature as much as it can. In minerals, we see a path that is, as it were, linear—namely, a slow and equal heat—because it cooks the metals in the deep recesses of the earth and leads them to perfection. ### On the Difficulties of Alchemy

...then it would be necessary for the Stone of the Wise to be produced from that source. One could certainly reason correctly in this way if nature had provided the seed of the Stone in a pure state and perfect in every respect, just like a grain of wheat or the seed of another vegetable, which, when committed to the earth, nurtured by the heat of the sun, and moistened by the dew of heaven, rises up into a form similar to that from which it took its origin without human assistance. But it is not <margin>*Testament*, ch. 88</margin> granted to nature by God—as *Lullius* <note>Ramon Lull (c. 1232–1316), a Majorcan philosopher and polymath to whom many alchemical works were later attributed.</note> says—that she can generate the philosophers' stone without ingenuity and the operation of human hands. Therefore, the philosophers command that the Stone be freed from its bodily mass, and then cleansed of its superfluities. To achieve this, they describe various "regimens" <note>technical stages or methods of heat management</note>, all of which cannot be accomplished with a single slow fire. For this reason, some hand down four principal grades of fire, ignoring the intermediate stages between them. And although the Elixir could be perfected by a single fire that is equal throughout, it would be extremely difficult to judge how that fire should be composed and how such heat might be stirred up, since authors vary greatly on this point. For some assert that their matter should be contained in the heat of a bath <note>a *bain-marie* or water bath</note>, or of ashes, or of sand. The author of the *Lily* <note>The *Lilium Intelligentiae*, an alchemical treatise.</note> says that the fire of a flame should be used, which reverberates above the vessel: "With the Dragon," <note>original: *Dracone*; here referring to the raw chemical matter, often symbolized as a dragon or serpent</note> he says, "placed and buried in the vessel, let a fire of five dried logs be lit in the pit of the furnace, which should be continuous and neither decreased nor increased." *Alphidius* <note>An early Arabic alchemical authority often cited in Latin texts.</note> requires the heat of dung. <margin>A variety of fires.</margin> For he says: "To cook by fire is to hide the matter in moist horse manure, which is the fire of the wise." Others seek that heat in grape skins, sawdust, straw, and juniper coals. *Morienes* <note>Morienus Romanus, a legendary hermit and alchemist who supposedly taught King Khalid ibn Yazid.</note> praises pigeon dung and olive leaves. Many think the philosophical fire should be nourished with oil, tallow, butter, or "burning water" <note>original: *aqua ardente*; an early term for distilled alcohol or ethanol</note>. They compare this to the heat of a healthy man, or of a hen sitting on eggs, or the heat of the Sun while it is in Aries <note>the spring season, suggesting a moderate, life-giving warmth</note>. Furthermore, *Count Bernard* <note>Bernard of Trevisan, a 15th-century alchemist famous for his long search for the Stone.</note> describes a certain "ethereal" heat—vaporous, digesting, continuous, not violent, subtle, surrounding, airy, enclosed, non-burning, altering, penetrating, and living. *John Pontanus*, whose letter is prefixed to the practical work of *Philippe de Rouillac*, describes a truly miraculous fire, and one which can scarcely be understood by anyone, in this sense: it is mineral, it is equal, it is continuous, it does not vaporize unless it is stirred up too much; it partakes of sulfur, it is taken from somewhere other than the matter, it destroys all things, it dissolves and congeals, and likewise it calcines; it is artificial to find, and it is a shortcut without any expense, or at least very little; and that fire involves a moderate ignition, which performs all the required sublimations, and which is not grasped except through solitary and profound meditation. I would think that he means the "Water of the Philosophers," which is oftentimes called "fire" by the wise. For so say *Menardus* and *Dardaris* in the *Assembly* <note>The *Turba Philosophorum*, one of the oldest Latin alchemical texts, written as a transcript of a meeting of ancient philosophers.</note>: "Quick-silver <margin>Philosophical water is called fire.</margin> is a fire that burns bodies and mortifies bodies more than [any other]..."

### THEOBALD DE HOGHELANDE

...than fire. And another says: <note>original: "Ignis quem tibi ostendam est aqua"</note> "The fire which I shall show you is water." But it seems an obstacle that he says it is taken from somewhere other than the matter itself. Thus, the "earth of the Philosophers" is also sometimes called fire. For this reason, the author of *The Ladder of the Philosophers* <note>original: *Scala philosophorum*, a 14th-century alchemical treatise</note> says: "Know that our water is oil, and our earth is dry fire." Therefore, since we do not know which of so many kinds of fire we ought specifically to choose, the entire inquiry into it will rightly be full of difficulties. The philosophers increase these difficulties significantly <margin>Four types of fire among the philosophers.</margin> when they often speak of four kinds of fire: namely, the Elemental, the Natural, the Unnatural, and the "Against Nature." A craftsman should have a complete knowledge of all of these before he undertakes the work. Concerning fire, I find this riddle: "The shore of the sea, the blood of a man not fully consumed, and the red juice of the grape is our fire."

<margin>Difficulty in knowing the furnace. *Book of Furnaces*.</margin> It is clear that the secret of the furnace is also contained under the heading of "fire," since fire cannot be produced except in a suitable furnace. That many kinds of furnaces are reviewed here and there by the philosophers can easily be gathered from Geber <note>Geber is the Latinized name of Jabir ibn Hayyan (c. 721–815), the most famous figure in early Islamic alchemy. The "Book of Furnaces" mentioned here is likely the *Liber Fornacum*.</note>, who alone (to pass over other authors) enumerates seven: namely, those for calcination, sublimation, distillation, descension <note>a process where material is melted and forced downward through a filter</note>, solution, and fixation. Yet, they seek only a single furnace, which, when they wish to point it out—its proper name being concealed—they call the "Secret Furnace." The craftsman can similarly err through the increase or decrease of this furnace. <margin>On the proportion of furnaces.</margin> For a large furnace gives a great fire, and a small one a small fire; just as from its thickness or thinness, a thick furnace gives a condensed and strong fire, while a thin one gives a weak one. Likewise, spacious vents give a clear and large fire, while narrow ones give a weak one. Therefore, a craftsman must labor above all else to find an equal proportion for the fire he seeks.

<margin>The time of the birth of the stone.</margin> It remains for me to say something about the rise and birth of the Stone, and about its limits. For every natural action, having its own motion and a determined time in which it is perfected and finished in a greater or lesser space of time (as the Philosopher <note>Aristotle</note> says), must necessarily mean that the Stone of the Philosophers will have its own certain and determined time within which it arises and is completed. The philosophers maintain <margin>When it is said to be born.</margin> that it is born after the most accurate cleansing of its elements and its purification from all defilements. This occurs in a certain "whiteness" <note>term: <term>albedo</term>; the second of the four major stages of the alchemical *Great Work*, symbolizing purification.</note> which shines with an admirable brightness, surpassing all the whiteness of the world. It flees and vanishes from the fire unless the craftsman knows how to put an end to the "decoction" <note>the process of heating or boiling</note> and, at that very hour, join the "soul" to it. This is like a fetus in the womb, which is continually perfected from the beginning of conception until the time of birth; at the time of birth, it is perfect in itself, yet if it does not exit then, it is suffocated and dies, because it then requires the help of the "expulsive virtue." And when it is born, it then needs its final perfection, because it lacks the movement of walking, knowledge, and speech. In the same way, this Stone is born perfect in itself,

sed <note>catchword: "but"</note>

### ON THE DIFFICULTIES OF ALCHEMY, BOOK [I]

...but it lacks the tincture <note>The transforming "dye" or essence that changes base metals into gold.</note>, the stable fixation <note>The process of making a substance resistant to fire.</note>, and the matrimonial union <note>A common metaphor for the chemical bonding of mercury and sulfur.</note>; therefore it requires the help of an artist who can extract it immediately and complete it before it flies away from the fire, or before it grows old and becomes sickly.

<margin>In the *Key of the Philosophers*.</margin>
> From this, Morienes <note>Morienus, a legendary 7th-century hermit-alchemist said to have taught the art to the King of Egypt.</note> says: "The root of this science is in the hour of its composition."

And Alphidius <note>An Arabic alchemical author often cited in medieval Latin texts.</note>:
> "Every creature can be increased until it is perfected, but when it reaches the peak of perfection, it tends toward the damage of diminution, or it declines: all things in the world direct their journey along such a path. We see something similar happen in those things subject to our will, namely in the baking of bread and the making of honey and sugar; when they have reached the completion of their boiling, they are perfect and must be removed from the fire, for if they are cooked further, they are burned and destroyed."

It is necessary, therefore, for the craftsman to be attentive and watchful, so that they do not exceed the limit in the work, and to follow the advice of the author of the *Lily* <note>original: *Lilius*, referring to the treatise *Lilium inter spinas* (The Lily Among Thorns).</note>, who says:
> "Hold to this work with Hermes so that it is continually repeated until the change is made visible to the sight, so that the vision of the work itself may teach you."

<margin>The variety of time-limits in the work.</margin>
The philosophers have never indicated this time-limit except mystically and quite obscurely, and they have varied it on purpose so that it could not be truly grasped or known by anyone except through the grace and kindness of God. For without knowing that, a knowledge of all the aforementioned things is of no help. Some define this limit as one year, according to that saying of Plato:

<margin>In the fourth book, or the *Stellics*.</margin>
> "The fewer days of preparation is the circuit of the greater light <note>The "greater light" refers to the Sun; its circuit is one year.</note>."

Others say nine months, some one hundred and fifty days, or one hundred and twenty, or even one hundred; some say eighty or seventy, or even forty. There are also those who define this limit as nine or seven days, or even three, and in infinite other ways. Yet there is but one limit and one day—indeed, an hour and a moment, as some believe—in which the perfection or the total destruction of the work occurs.

<margin>To Eutychia.</margin>
> Moses <note>In alchemical literature, "Moses" often refers to a pseudonymous author or is linked to the sister of Moses, Miriam/Maria the Jewess.</note>: "This work happens as suddenly as clouds coming from heaven, as Hermes says, and even in the blink of an eye."

And Rosinus <note>A Latinized name for the 4th-century alchemist Zosimos of Panopolis.</note> similarly:
> "This work is completed in a single moment, and its efficacy lies in the purification of the stone from its oily substances and other things that hinder its power."

Hinting at the difficulty and danger of knowing this limit, Mireris Mimensidum <note>A character or author mentioned in the *Turba Philosophorum*.</note> addresses the seeker thus:
> "If you work philosophically and do not exceed the limit in the work itself, you will be twice blessed; if you see this happen suddenly, wonder, terror, and trembling will come upon you—therefore, work cautiously."

And Plato:
> "Beware lest in the putrefaction <note>The stage of decomposition or blackening (*nigredo*).</note> you reach a harmful limit; for if the work suffers a delay during the solution, perhaps it will increase into corruption; therefore, beware of this."

And someone in the *Assembly* <note>original: *Turba*, referring to the *Turba Philosophorum* (The Assembly of the Philosophers), one of the oldest Latin alchemical texts.</note>:
> "Though you have performed all things by reason, if you are nevertheless ignorant of the whitening <note>original: *dealbatio*, the *albedo* stage of the work.</note>, you lose the joy you hoped for."

And another in the same place:
<margin>Book of Alchemical Secrets, Ch. 7.</margin>
> "If the compound...
