...if it is managed more than is proper, its light, taken from the sea <note>In alchemical symbolism, "the sea" often represents the primordial mercurial fluid or the source of the "mercury of the philosophers."</note>, is extinguished. Likewise, Haly <note>original: *Haly*; likely referring to Khalid ibn Yazid or an Arabic author known as Haly Abenragel, frequently cited in alchemical compendia.</note> says: Our Stone is life to him who knows it and its making; but for him who does not know it, does not make it, and is not certain of when it shall be born—or who thinks it to be some other stone—he has already prepared himself for death and his money for destruction. For unless he finds this honored Stone when it has germinated, no other shall rise in its place.

<margin>The Key of Philosophy.</margin>
<margin>Treatise 2.</margin>
And Alphidius <note>An Arabic alchemical authority frequently quoted in the Middle Ages.</note> says: When this Stone is guided and its form is perfected, then it is fit for the operation, before melancholy <note>original: *melancholia*; here referring to the "blackness" or the state of stagnation and decay if the process is mismanaged.</note> abounds upon it, and before air is generated within it and it grows old. Hermes <note>Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary founding father of alchemy.</note> says: If you extract it from its distress and guide it by reason during the days known to you, it will be a companion and suited to you, and you, as its leader, will be adorned by it. But Arnaldus <note>Arnaldus de Villa Nova (c. 1240–1311), a famous physician and alchemist.</note> adds: The addition of the disposition and the preparation must be within the mastery of the philosophers and the practitioners, because Nature cannot surpass her own motion. For there is a certain time that she has for impregnating, for giving birth, for nourishing, and for working. Thus, when you have the earth impregnated, wait for the birth; but when it has given birth, you must nourish it until it can endure every fire. 

The philosophers emphasize this difficulty of the Stone’s "rising" in no small measure, since they knowingly confuse this limit with the end of the first and last decoction <note>The process of "cooking" or heating the substance in the vessel.</note>. They speak now of the limit of one, now of the end of the other, so that they might distract the minds of the readers, 
<margin>The nature of the stone must be known before the craftsman begins the work.</margin>
preventing them from grasping their true intention. For this reason, Parmenides <note>A Greek philosopher who appears as a character in the *Turba Philosophorum*, one of the oldest Latin alchemical texts.</note> in the *Turba* advises us well that we should not approach the work unless all the conditions and natures of the Stone are known, in this manner: "Intend to know first of all what it is that putrefies <note>The process of breaking down matter so it can be transformed.</note> and renews nature, and what its taste is, and what things it has naturally near and far, and how they love each other, and how after love, corruption and enmity happen to them, and how those natures embrace each other, and how they become concordant in a slow fire." When these things are known and perceived, then apply your hands to the work. But if you are ignorant of these stated qualities, do not approach this work, because it is entirely harmful, a source of misfortune and sadness. Therefore, since those things we have said above regarding the matter of the Stone—its governance, weights, vessel, and fire—are quite difficult to find and know, then to know the precise time of the birth and rising of the Stone is the most difficult of all; indeed, as some would have it, it is supernatural and divine. Justly, then, its entire practice shall be judged most difficult.

<margin>The secret of the art.</margin>
The philosophers also have another secret, which is hidden by them in marvelous ways. I pass over it here, since I have found nothing certain about it yet, because Lull <note>Raymond Lull (c. 1232–1316), a prolific writer whose name was attached to many alchemical works.</note> speaks of it most sparingly, and all others whom I have read remain silent, except for one, Senior <note>Senior Zadith (Ibn Umail), a 10th-century Arabic alchemist.</note>, or his interpreter Hamuel, who touches upon the same mystery in a single word. Let them see, therefore, and finally open their eyes and come to their senses—those who attempt so grave and difficult a work without an understanding of the books. May they prosper.

<page-num>183</page-num>
<header>BOOK ON THE DIFFICULTIES OF ALCHEMY</header>

<margin>Why the art is so rarely attained.</margin>
There are those who imagine the work of the Stone to be so light and easy that any peasant or uneducated person—provided they are lucky—could possess knowledge of it or hope for some fruit from it. However, it is sufficiently clear to those endowed with intellect that the Stone is prepared neither by chance nor by accident, but must be produced by day and night study and labor, aided by the grace of God. For this reason, Lully <note>Raymond Lully (c. 1232–1315), a major figure in medieval logic and alchemy.</note>, giving the reason why it is so rarely found, says:

> Men are ignorant of nature and its natural combination and operation, nor can they assist nature by reason of their ignorance, until they have passed through universal philosophy <note>original: *philosophiam universalem*; referring to a comprehensive understanding of the laws governing the natural world.</note>, which reveals things that were hidden and unknown to them. Therefore, our Stone belongs to us and not to peasants, and is entirely a product of our philosophy, just as a son belongs to the father who begot him.

Thus far Lully.

### THE FOURTH AND FINAL PART OF THIS BOOK,
->which teaches that the Chemical art should be avoided by everyone<-
->and provides a conclusion.<-

<margin>Many learned men have not attained knowledge of the art.</margin>
I believe I have said more than enough above regarding the three kinds of impediments that make this science so difficult. Even if someone is not moved by these great obstacles or called away from their purpose, but continues to press on, trusting in their own wit and judgment, and <unclear>hopes</unclear> that all obstacles can be removed or overcome by their industry to reach their goal, let such a person become more cautious by the example of others. Let them look, as if from a watchtower, at the failed studies of the most learned men who have published books on this art. Let them examine the short works of Giovanni Laceschi <note>An Italian alchemist whose works were often debated.</note> and the observations on them by Tauladanus <note>Robert Tauladan, a 16th-century commentator on alchemical texts.</note>; let them see the book on the Chemical art by Lorenzo Ventura <note>Lorenzo Ventura (16th century), author of *De Arte Chemica* (1571).</note>, who boasted that he had brought three hundred and fifty volumes of this science into the library of the illustrious Count Palatine, and had fifty more besides those. Yet, you will see the shameful and prodigious errors of these men—to say nothing of those in our own age who have undertaken to explain and clarify the *Rosary* <note>original: *Rosarium*; likely the *Rosarium philosophorum*, one of the most famous series of alchemical woodcuts and texts.</note> of Arnald of Villanova and the chemical booklets of Paracelsus. These men are not ashamed to confess themselves to be the paraphrasers and interpreters of authors they do not understand. But just as the madness of the former deserves laughter, the frustrated labors of the latter deserve pity; for though they were distinguished in doctrine and erudition, and spared neither labor nor expense in searching out the secrets of metals, the truth was nonetheless hidden from them by the will of almighty God, who searches the hearts and minds of men. This serves as a great example to those who rashly pursue this art.

<margin>An example to be taken from others.</margin>
For if the practice of this art—indeed, the very material itself—was hidden from such learned and famous men who did not lack the books of various authors, what hope is there for me and those like me? We are less powerful in wit and erudition, and we do not even have the books (which is the greatest thing in this pursuit), possessing very few compared to those which Ventura says he had at

<margin>The unlearned are to be entirely excluded from the art.</margin>
...what can finally be expected of those who have not even greeted the **Muses** <note>Meaning they have no basic classical education.</note> from the threshold, who understand neither the roots of minerals nor the manner of their generation? They have never cared to investigate the secrets of nature, but are led only by greed, ambition, or similar wicked desires; they hurry to these banquets with unwashed hands like cattle to their fodder. Truly, I judge this art to be as easy for them as if they were trying to pull the stars down from heaven with their bare hands. Thus, it is no wonder if, relying on bad beginnings, they meet a worse end, since they are forced to spend their old age in sorrow and poverty after their wealth has been boiled away. They experience in themselves the "metamorphosis" they expected to find in the metals, of whom it could be wittily said: *What they had—namely riches—they lost; what they did not lose they have—namely poverty and misery.* <note>original: "Quod habuerunt, scilicet divitias, amiserunt, quod non amiserunt habent, paupertatem scilicet & miseriam." This is a play on a classic logical riddle.</note>

<margin>The art should be avoided due to its uncertain end and outcome.</margin>
Furthermore, since knowledge of this art falls to very few, and that only by the benefit and mercy of God—whose will is unexplored by us, and whose judgments we should rather fear than presume anything for ourselves—and since the time we spend in this age is so brief and precious that it cannot be restored by any wealth, one provides very poorly for oneself by preferring uncertain and doubtful outcomes over certain and secure ones. Rather, let him pursue **Theology**, **Law**, **Medicine**, **Architecture**, or similar fields, in which even moderate talents can progress so far as to help others with advice, labor, or resources, and gain for themselves a name, fame, riches, and honors, or at least provide for their family. For no one is barred from the State or from performing any duties even if they have not reached the very highest peak of their faculty or science, which happens very rarely. Not all theologians are equal in doctrine or science to **St. Augustine** or **Thomas Aquinas**, nor are all jurists equal to **Papinian** <note>Aemilius Papinianus (142–212 AD), a celebrated Roman jurist.</note> or **Bartolus** <note>Bartolus de Saxoferrato (1313–1357), an influential medieval legal scholar.</note>, nor physicians to **Hippocrates** or **Galen**, nor architects to **Proclus** or **Archimedes**. Nevertheless, even today many are held in high esteem who are distinguished by different degrees of learning within these same faculties, and they have no reason to repent for lost or poorly spent time.

<margin>A comparison.</margin>
But in the **Chemical art** <note>alchemy</note>, the plain opposite occurs. I am accustomed to compare it to a certain very high mountain, which is steep and rugged on the northern side, but gently sloping on the southern side. This mountain divides two regions: one is the northern region, very rarely lit by the sun, but mostly covered by dark clouds and thick gloom, blasted by the strongest winds, bristling with forests, rough with thorns and briars. It has no path, but the ground is entirely hindered by mud, or snow and ice, and it produces nothing for the comfort or necessity of man. The other region, to the south, is illuminated all day by the sun, fanned by the sweetest breeze, distinguished by vine-bearing hills and trees fertile with every kind of fruit, watered by sweetly flowing springs and streams, and by meadows green and a thousand...

...filled with various kinds of flowers, most beautiful houses, and shaded groves; in short, whatever could be desired for living well and blessedly in this world may be found there in the greatest abundance. Yet, there is no entry to it except through a mountain. <margin>Obstacles of the Alchemists.</margin> He who sets out to pursue the Alchemical Art <note>original: "Chemica"</note> imprudently and without counsel enters a region exposed to the north wind, and plunges himself into the greatest difficulties. He longs to enjoy the delights of that other, southern region, but he finds no well-trodden path. The mud swallows his footsteps, the snow and ice deceive him with their slipperiness, thorns and brambles prick him, and finally, a steep and rocky mountain prevents him from ascending to the summit. <margin>The path to knowledge is prepared by labor and study.</margin> What should he do? In vain would he weary heaven with prayers and sighs, unless he takes up an axe and, with strength and the greatest labor, cuts away the trees and thickets, breaks the rocks with iron and fire, and opens a path for himself among them. Or, if God and the stars favor him, someone might lower a ladder or a rope from the highest peak of the mountain, by which he might be pulled upward to look down upon the garden of pleasure, and finally gather its fruits with full hands, satisfy his hunger, and quench his thirst. Thus, after enduring the harshest labors, he may enjoy the long-desired rest. <margin>It is very rare for anyone to attain the art through the teaching of another.</margin> But how few are those who have the stars so kind to them, or who ascend the mountain by another's help? For who would dare to reach out a hand to another, unless that person is distinguished by faith, constancy, generosity toward the poor, and holiness of life—one whom he has long experienced through many trials to be not arrogant, not ambitious, but humble and mild, seeking not his own glory but the glory of God? <margin>The practitioner must either retreat quickly or persist constantly in the work.</margin> <margin>All obstacles must first be removed.</margin> Therefore, it is necessary that whoever has entered that region unwisely should either turn back, or, if he wishes to proceed further, let him not fear solitude. Let him steady his steps against the wind; let him ward off the cold with double clothing and furs and other warmth; let him fit boots to his legs because of the mud; let him support his gait on the ice with a staff tipped with iron; and finally, let him prepare steps for himself on the mountain and ascend to its very peak by his own prowess <note>original: "suoque Marte," literally "by his own Mars," a Roman idiom for one's own strength or effort.</note>. If he does not do this, he will be deprived of all the fruit of his labors. It is to be feared that he may eventually fall from the mountain's cliffs and be mangled with weakened or mutilated limbs, or be swallowed by a muddy abyss, or be trapped by deep snow and ice, or be torn by thorns, or end his life miserably through hunger, cold, and thirst. In other professions and sciences, no one labors or exercises their talent in vain; even if they do not reach the very top, they at least earn some rank among their peers. <margin>All study of the Alchemists is in vain unless they attain the full art.</margin> But he who handles Alchemy <note>original: "Chemica"</note>, unless he truly masters the <term>metamorphosis</term> <note>The "transformation" or transmutation of base metals.</note> of imperfect metals into gold and silver—which is the goal of the art and the conclusion of all study—he has ground down his life in vain and will suffer the repentance of time unwisely lost. Who then, unless he is imprudent—I speak not of princes and nobles, for whom it matters little if they spend a few hundred gold pieces annually on a most honorable, beautiful, and pleasant thing, provided all is done with reason and counsel—but for men of my station, who, I say, would pursue such uncertainties, from which nothing but...

### THEOBALD DE HOGHELANDE
<meta>catchword: quis-</meta>

<margin>*The miserable life of those for whom success yields loss.*</margin>
...expenditure of time and labor, and expect poverty and lack, rather than those things from which certain rewards, honor, riches, favor among one's own people, and admiration are expected? What is more foolish than to seek those things which, after you have obtained them with the greatest labor and no common expense, you do not even dare to make public? How miserable do you think your life will be when, in the height of fortune, you lack fortune <note>meaning: even if you find gold, you cannot spend it without drawing dangerous attention</note>, and because you cannot do what you wish, you feel the shackles cast upon you, so that you might rightly say with Horace <note>original: "Horatio"</note>:

> To what end is fortune given to me, if I am not granted to use it?

<margin>*Let each be a friend to himself rather than to anyone else.*</margin>
<margin>*Nothing is enough for the ungrateful.*</margin>
<margin>*Hope is deceptive as it very rarely happens.*</margin>
<margin>*Why the study of alchemy should be avoided.*</margin>
<margin>*Alchemy makes a person restless.*</margin>
<margin>*Proverbs 13. It creates diseases and other troubles of mind and body.*</margin>
<margin>*It costs a great deal.*</margin>
<margin>*It makes one hated and infamous.*</margin>
But you will be able to do good for others; that is indeed splendid and magnificent, but not even this can be done except in secret. Then, so that you may be a friend to others, you will be an enemy to yourself; to promote others, you will depress yourself and commit yourself to a double-edged fortune, your mind always suspended between hope and fear. To give to others, you will first consume your own goods, lose your flowering youth, and cast yourself into the deepest abyss of despair? For not even any gratitude is to be expected from ungrateful relatives, kinsmen, and friends, who will think you give with a stingy hand not out of love, but out of abundance, even when you might give most generously—if, that is, you have attained your wish. But if you have not, no one will even return a farthing <note>original: "teruntium"; a coin of tiny value</note> to you, even if you have spent your all; rather, you will be laughed at and, exposed to the mockery of all, you will waste away. 

And since not even one in ten thousand who practice Chemistry <note>original: "Chemica"; here meaning alchemy</note> attains the goal set for himself, is it not rather to be feared that you will lose your labor along with those ten thousand, than that you will obtain the sought-after thing with that single one? Wherefore I would wish all and each to be amiably asked and warned to avoid Alchemy like a plague and a certain carcinoma <note>cancerous growth</note>; for it creeps in once you have admitted it, and feeds upon the inner parts of a man; it gnaws at the soul and allows no rest because of the hope of great goods. This hope, no differently than the fear of evil, makes human life not only difficult and laborious but hastens old age and death. "Hope deferred," says the wise man, "afflicts the soul" <note>A reference to Proverbs 13:12</note>; if this is true in other things, it is certainly most true in this art. Who now could enumerate the diseases which the fumes, stenches, the exhalations of raw and sublimated quicksilver <note>original: "argenti vivi"; mercury</note>, and the inhalations of other poisonous things, the long nights without sleep, and the daily labors bring to the bodies of Alchemists? Who could report the burns from strong waters <note>term: "aqua fortis"; nitric acid used for dissolving metals</note> or glowing metals? Who could recount the weariness of soul while they see their hopes fall into vanity, contrary to what they presumed? Who could briefly touch upon the innumerable expenses, while on one hand glass vessels, on the other iron pots, then crucibles or clay resisting a strong fire, quicksilver, marcasites <note>term: "marchasitæ"; iron pyrites or other metallic minerals</note> of gold and silver and other metals, and similar things are sought from the very veins of the earth at a great distance? Scoundrels, good-for-nothings, and cheats <note>original: "nebulones, frugiperdæ & sycophantæ"</note> are even summoned from other provinces and from across the Alps to deceive. I omit the infamy which for the most part accompanies these gold-seekers <note>original: "auripetas"</note>, and the doubtful judgments of men about them, while any—

<header>ON THE DIFFICULTIES OF ALCHEMY, BOOK I</header>

...and as he perceives them, he speaks of them; one person suspects an impostor, another a forger or a counterfeiter of coins. Those who judge less harshly claim he is a spendthrift of his own property, ill-advised and rushing headlong into poverty of his own accord; many even pity him, as though his very salvation had been despaired of.

<margin>The difference between true Alchemy and false.</margin>
But although these previous descriptions are as far from the followers of true Alchemy as heaven is from earth, and could never apply to the true <term>philosopher</term> <note>In this context, a "philosopher" is not just a thinker, but a master of the "hermetic philosophy" or alchemy</note> who cleverly searches out nature’s secrets—since he requires neither many nor expensive materials, nor needs to seek elsewhere for what is found for sale everywhere—and though he is in no danger from vapors or fumes, yet before he reaches that point where he understands the writings of the sages, knows the "matter" of the art and its governance, and other necessities, he will likely spend a great deal while testing many things. Nor can he be entirely safe from toxic exhalations, nor escape the harsh judgments of the common people. I will remain silent for now regarding those otherwise honest and learned men who, at the mere mention of the name "Alchemy," shudder just as if they had seen some savage wild beast, trembling in a way and judging it a fraud before they even understand it.

<margin>The art is not despised without God's judgment.</margin>
Thus, this art—the most worthy of all—is judged cheap and wicked, not without the providence of Almighty God. While this may seem difficult and unfair to beginners at first, as time passes and they begin to grasp and "taste" the obscure sayings of the philosophers, and some of them (though very few) reach their goal, they then rejoice in their hearts. This joy is not so much due to the hope or abundance of gold and silver, but because the art is judged impossible and empty by others. They secretly laugh at the stupidity and malice of those who mocked them long ago; for they can safely ignore the gossip of men—even if some suspicion of the divine grace granted to them arises—by appealing to their own higher mastery.

<margin>The vain judgments of men.</margin>
What would people say? "Do you think," they might ask, "that if this man were overflowing with such great riches, he wouldn’t do this or that? He would support a large household, buy property, build structures, and walk about in pompous clothing followed by a troop of servants, attempting some great feat." This would be true enough if everyone were of the same mind—were it not for the fact that both in ancient times and in our own age, there are those who have learned to carry wealth moderately. They do not exalt themselves because of it, but instead loathe arrogance, vanity, and the world's empty shows, choosing instead to embrace a secure and steady humility, untroubled by any waves or floods. Let those who think such different things know that this art is given by God only to the <term>poor in spirit</term> <note>original: "pauperibus spiritu," a biblical reference to the humble and those detached from worldly greed</note>.

<margin>To whom the Art properly belongs.</margin>
For on this point, <term>Alphidius</term> <note>An Arabic alchemical authority, likely a corruption of a name like Al-Kindi or similar, frequently cited in medieval Latin texts</note> says: "God has granted this art to the rational sons of Adam, and thereafter as a possession for the poor." Let them hear <term>Blessed Thomas</term> <note>Referring to Thomas Aquinas; during the Renaissance, several alchemical works were attributed to him, though modern scholars doubt his authorship of them</note> saying: "This art either finds a man holy or makes him holy"—not because the art does this by itself, but because it is impossible for the practitioner not to prostrate himself humbly before the face of God and give immortal thanks to Him, who has given such great treasure and wisdom to so very few...

<header>THEOBALD DE HOGHELANDE</header>

...attained only by the mercy of God <note>original: "sola Dei misericordia"</note>. Therefore, it is no wonder if he keeps himself within the limits of reason, and meditates only on himself, neglecting those things which belong to the glory of God and charity toward his neighbors. And why, after all, should he make public to the common people things that may soon become obscure even to himself?

<margin>
Things that can harm their author should not be made public.
</margin>

<margin>
The story of Bragadin.
</margin>

The things that happened just a few years ago to Bragadino <note>Marco Bragadino (c. 1545–1591) was an infamous Venetian alchemist and charlatan who claimed he could multiply gold; he was eventually executed in Bavaria.</note> are common knowledge. While he was professing the art of transmuted base metals into gold in Venice, and was being hailed by the people as the "Great Alchemist" par excellence, he was approached by the governor Piccolomini. This Piccolomini, who had been outlawed by certain princes of Italy, sought a loan of thirty thousand gold coins; furthermore, he imprudently desired to be taught the art so that he might thereafter provide for himself as much as he wished. Bragadino was paralyzed with fear, as he neither possessed the sum requested nor, much less, knew the art. Yet, because of the man's cruelty and recklessness, he dared not refuse anything and promised both. but as he delayed and shifted his ground, making now this excuse and now that, the other man pressed him more sharply and threatened him with death unless he fulfilled his promise; for he did not wish to be laughed at or undervalued by anyone. Thus, Bragadino was forced to protect himself with a crowd of guards against the ferocity of the man lying in wait for him. This would have been of little use to him, however, had not Piccolomini, unmindful of himself while laying a snare for another, fallen into the nets himself and been captured. Bragadino then escaped, though he was reserved for a worse fate later. 

It could perhaps happen, however, that the same art might one day fall into the hands of the unworthy, whom God—not as a fierce avenger but as one who uses both the good and the evil for the glory of His name—might punish atrociously as an example to others. I heard from a certain nobleman of our age about an Italian monk who, trusting in this art, renounced his religion and his order and came to Germany so that he might live more freely, having come to loathe the cowl and the hardships of the monasteries. But while he conducted himself incautiously, two men insinuated themselves into his closest intimacy; they later murdered him in a forest during a journey—a most terrible crime. One of them showed a powder found on the monk to various princes and great men as his own, and deceived many people with a thousand impostures under the false name of science <note>In alchemy, a "powder" or "projection powder" was the finished Philosopher's Stone in powdered form, used to catalyze the transformation of lead into gold.</note>.

<margin>
It is better to learn from the danger of others than from one's own.
</margin>

<margin>
The debate of the ancients concerning the highest good.
</margin>

Who, therefore, would not take warning by the example of these two and hide his secret? For if revealed, it brings either death or, at the very least, perpetual fear and voluntary exile far from one's homeland and kin. For a long time, there was much controversy among the ancient philosophers as to what constituted the <term>highest good</term> <note>original: "summum bonum"; the ultimate goal of human life</note>: while one praised virtue to the skies, another praised glory, pleasure, the absence of pain, health, strength, security of mind, and similar things. Truly, it is not to be doubted that the greatest part of them, if they had possessed any knowledge of the <term>Philosopher’s Stone</term>, would have preferred it to all the aforementioned things and all other things in the world, since through it, immense riches and everything that can be obtained with gold and money may be had,

<summary>Hoghelande illustrates the dangers of revealing alchemical secrets through the historical examples of the fraud Bragadino and a murdered monk. He argues that the Philosopher's Stone is the true "highest good" sought by ancient philosophers due to its infinite power.</summary>

->### THEOBALD DE HOGHELANDE<-

<margin>Senior in the *Key of Wisdom*.</margin>
Even if their meaning seems impossible to grasp, do not cast aside a book after reading it once, twice, or thrice simply because you do not understand it. Instead, reread it ten, twenty, or even fifty times and more. Then, observe where the authors agree most closely, for there the truth lies hidden; but above all, keep in view what is possible within nature. Thus the Philosopher says: let your intention be according to nature.

<margin>3.</margin>
Furthermore, the seeker must know the roots of minerals so that they may perform their work from them; otherwise, they will labor in vain.

<margin>4.</margin>
One should not use the labor of others, for no one devotes themselves to a task for another with the same spirit as they do for themselves.

<margin>The Art is impatient of partnership.</margin>
Moreover, this Art, much like a kingdom, is impatient of partnership—unless souls are joined by faith, innocence, and especially by the love of God. Accordingly, <term>Geber<note>The Latinized name of Jabir ibn Hayyan, a legendary 8th-century figure considered the father of Islamic and European alchemy.</note></term> does not without reason list the "amputation of limbs" among the obstacles to the Art. But who appears more "limb-truncated" <note>original: "membrorum truncationem"; Hoghelande uses this metaphorically to describe those who rely on others' hands and eyes rather than their own.</note> than those who seek the Art through the work of others, and thereby confess themselves unworthy of investigating natural things? Therefore, anyone distracted by other business who lacks the leisure to devote themselves to the reading of books or the practice of the Art should rather abstain from it, for they can expect nothing fruitful from their desires. 

However, if one abounds in wealth and does not fear the expense, they should seek out an honest and learned man, skilled in the most common languages and moderately practiced in ordinary <term>distillations<note>The process of purifying a liquid by heating it into vapor and then condensing it back into liquid.</note></term>, <term>sublimations<note>The process where a solid substance is heated and turns directly into vapor, then cools back into a solid; often used to purify materials like sulfur or mercury.</note></term>, and <term>calcinations<note>Heating a substance to high temperatures in the presence of air to reduce it to a powder or "ash."</note></term>. This is not because these common methods are strictly necessary in this specific Art, but so that the man may know how to distinguish philosophical works from common ones. Let the patron establish an annual salary for him and supply the books and instruments necessary for the Art—but with the mindset that he will not be bitter about the loss of his money, even if for several years the craftsman does not even know where best to begin. For no one should think they can put their hand to the work after reading just any book (which might be false or composed by some impostor), but only after a span of several years, when they believe they truly understand the authors. Thus we read in the *Allegories of the Wise*: "Do not begin the work before you know it, because if you do not know the work, you will err, and your labor will perish in vain."

<margin>5.</margin>
Once an assistant is accepted, do not change them without a great cause, even if they seem a bit slow to one who is in a hurry. Keep "street-peddlers" and the unlearned who profess themselves to be Alchemists far from the light; they cannot teach anyone what they themselves do not know. If anything can be learned from them at all, it consists entirely of the various types of furnaces and fires and their degrees, which can be learned from them for a small gift. Or, if they must be kept for that reason, let the vessel always be kept sealed and covered on the outside. If the matter must be inspected, or taken out, or if something must be mixed, send them out of the house.

<margin>6.</margin>
Let everyone beware of books and papers containing various "recipes" (as they call them) which promise "whitenings" or "reddenings," the multiplication of gold and silver, or the extraction of gold from copper and silver.

<margin>7.</margin>
Nor should one easily believe those who promise shortcuts to the work, or the Elixir...

He warns against "get-rich-quick" recipe books and stresses that the Art requires years of preparation before physical work begins.</summary>

### ON THE DIFFICULTIES OF ALCHEMY, BOOK

...of the perfect elixir's increase; for nature must have its complete time in which to perfect its action. If anyone disturbs its motion, they will accumulate not profit but loss and inconvenience for themselves. No one can give increase to the Elixir, or intensify its power, who does not thoroughly understand the art and has not previously brought the work to completion through the path of experience. 

<margin>8.</margin>
Let them flee all vulgar <term>sublimations<note>The process of heating a substance to a vapor and then condensing it back into a solid, used for purification.</note></term>, <term>calcinations<note>The process of heating a substance to a high temperature to cause chemical dissociation or change.</note></term>, and <term>solutions<note>Dissolving a solid into a liquid.</note></term>; for no utility is to be expected from them, since the rule of the philosophers is far different from that of commoners. 

<margin>9.</margin>
Avoid everything that costs a great deal. If one believes the Art is situated in gold and silver, let them take a small quantity of them—such as one <term>drachma<note>A small unit of weight, roughly 3.9 grams.</note></term> or at most two. If the beginnings are successful, they can later repeat the work with a greater weight. 

<margin>10.</margin>
Despise all <term>cementations<note>A process involving heating a metal in contact with a powder (the "cement") to change its properties.</note></term>, and oils, and "gradual waters" <note>original: "aquasque graduales"; these were corrosive acids or liquids intended to refine metals step-by-step.</note> with which some boast they can achieve marvelous things, since there is little profit in them, and more loss and danger. For let us grant that some gold or silver might be extracted from imperfect metals by that method; certainly it will be meager, and will hardly compensate for the expenses and labors, nor will it admit any further increase. 

<margin>11.</margin>
Reject all vegetables and animals, or things derived from them, as well as intermediary minerals; take nothing except metallic nature. Let the seeker stick to that and spend their effort there; otherwise, they will lament their labor, expenses, and time. 

<margin>The Sum of Perfection, Chapter 7.</margin>
Nor, however, should they promise themselves a prosperous outcome simply because they worked with the proper material; for as <term>Geber<note>The Latinized name of Jabir ibn Hayyan, a legendary authority in alchemy.</note></term> and other philosophers testify, this whole Art depends upon God, who grants or withdraws it from whom He wills. He is sublime and glorious, filled with all justice and goodness: for if God saw a faithful mind in a person, as the <term>Lily<note>Likely referring to the *Lilium inter spinas* (The Lily Among Thorns), a common title for alchemical texts.</note></term> says, He would surely reveal the truth to them. 

<margin>Conclusion.</margin>
Accordingly, if anyone is frustrated in their desires, let them not curse God, nor blame the philosophers for their own ignorance, nor reproach them; rather, let them blame themselves, who presumed more of themselves than was right, and who did not obey the one advising them to abstain from the Art.

->THE END.<-

# SUMMARY OF THIS WORK.

**Part One** *contains three treatises.*

*The first of these teaches the three principles of Physics <note>In this context, "Physics" refers to Natural Philosophy, the study of the physical world</note>, which indicate the Theory of Chemistry.*
*The second [teaches] the three principles of chemical practice.*
*The third contains manual practice and its application to the work.*

**Part Two** *teaches seven philosophical steps, through which the minds of students may reach the peak and goal of truth and its virtues in this art.*

->EXHORTATORY EPISTLE<-

[...either because they see him] to have easily surpassed any Physicians of our century, as well as those of old, as much in experience as in art; or because he not undeservedly rebuked ignorant Physicians, Natural Philosophers <note>original: "Physicos", referring here to those who study the laws of nature</note>, and surgeons in general for their enormous errors. Nor do those men see how shamefully, being conscious of their own failings, they confess their ignorance, since he endeavors not so much to mock the ignorant as to teach them, and strives to highly praise and exhort all those who are learned in their art. Learned men do not take that rebuke to themselves, as if it did not concern them, but they have tried to imitate his admirable experience rather than to disparage it. 

On the other hand, those who are wise only in their own conceit are usually unwilling to approve of anything of which they are ignorant; such men, moved by an all too boorish envy, sharpen their teeth against those who strive to benefit everyone with their labor. Therefore I exhort you, brothers (lest such a great outrage remain unavenged), take up the pen against those who are not only ashamed to so greatly corrupt the medical art, but even to persecute those whose entire study is continually occupied with recovering the truth buried within this art. 

This our teacher certainly accomplished; while having traveled through infinite regions, he alone in our century restored chemical medicine <term>Medicina chemistica: the school of medicine, pioneered by Paracelsus, that used mineral and chemical preparations rather than just herbal ones</term> (not without the greatest expense). Behold the reward for his merits which he receives from ungrateful men: namely, slanders after his death. While he himself was living, no one dared to bark against him; now that he is dead, the defenseless prepare for war. 

Well then, good men, let us resist, lest that vile heap—increased by this example—should presume to overthrow the good arts along with their pious and true professors, if not by right, then at least by injury. It is not because they can achieve anything by themselves, but because they see themselves entirely destitute of strength, that they give themselves up as prey to giants; for they know that these monsters of men cannot bear any arduous or noble work which they themselves have not performed. And lest they be diminished in honor by something more excellent later in that great work they have undertaken (namely, to cast Jupiter himself from his throne <note>A classical metaphor for attempting to overthrow the highest established authority or God</note>), since they draw the highest honors and riches from it, they do not fear to increase their crowd with dejected men: so that what for ages [could] not...

# EXHORTATORY EPISTLE

*...[those who] could not [surpass him]* by art or talent, now strive to match him by sheer numbers and money. Nevertheless, some of these "giants" <note>A disparaging reference to powerful or wealthy individuals who lack true intellectual depth.</note>, who have tasted the sweetness of nectar for a short while, being enticed by its pleasantness, are accustomed to summon men—especially those whom they have discovered to be imbued with the doctrine of Theophrastus <note>Theophrastus von Hohenheim, the birth name of Paracelsus.</note>. They do this not because they delight in their company, but so that they may hunt with smooth words and promises, in order to learn from them the writings of Paracelsus, which surpass their own wits. 

Still not content with this, they demand to have a double portion of everything those men have ever practiced. Once they have obtained this, they will soon seek out some frivolous excuse to pretend they have received a great injury from them; they will try to terrify them with quarrelsome words, so that (as they think) the men hardly dare to open their mouths <note>original: "hiscere," meaning to gape or mutter in protest.</note> to speak. They say: "This work of yours is childish, and unworthy of our authority; if it dealt with Theology or the laws, the work would be pleasing to us. Go away, we do not need your services." Thus they are accustomed to impudently dismiss good men, empty-handed and defrauded of their labors and art. 

O Almighty Father, what kind of Theology do these men seek, who "pile mountain upon mountain" <note>A classical allusion to the Giants of mythology who piled Mount Ossa on Mount Pelion to storm heaven and overthrow the gods.</note> to cast you down from the heavens? What kind of laws do those demand who cannot tolerate justice? If you are not practiced in such deceitful arts, brothers, do not go even if you are called—unless you wish to experience the truth of this story at your own peril. 

Having experienced it myself, I exhort and warn you to hold to the doctrine of our teacher, who wrote: *Let no man belong to another, who can be his own master.* <note>original: "Alterius non sit, qui suus esse potest." This was the famous personal motto of Paracelsus, emphasizing intellectual and spiritual independence.</note> In the meantime, first in Christ, and finally in Theophrastus, dearest brothers, farewell; be not unmindful of how much we owe to our teacher,

->though he be dead, again and again,<-

->PREFACE TO THE READER.<-

*You have here, best of readers, the Theory and Practice of the whole chemical art, of which (unless you so choose) you cannot remain ignorant after reading this little compendium. Read and reread it many times, with the attention of a tranquil mind, passing over nothing hastily or without consideration. For if you gather the scattered thoughts of our mind, none of those things which are beautiful in this art will ever be able to remain hidden from you. You will find here, beneath a hard bark, the liquid <note>original: "laticem," a poetic term for sap or fluid; here referring to the essence or "juice" of the medicine.</note> of true medicine, with which you may (by the help of God) relieve yourself, as well as your friends and the poor, from the ailments of the body. Do not regret your labor in performing the practice which we have described for you: for by building, we ourselves are made builders in this art, not by reading alone. If it should happen that you do not achieve your wish at the first or second attempt, do not lose heart, but repeat the matter a third and fourth time. It happened often to me, though I erred, that I became master of that which my soul desired. Nothing prevents a man from reaching this art more than faint-heartedness and impatience. I would wish to warn you of this one thing now: that in the beginning you do not exceed the limits of medicine for the human body; for if you seek the metamorphosis <note>Transmutation of base metals into gold.</note> of common metals, you will deplore your error. Farewell; regard our labors with a fair and good mind.*

## What Chemical Philosophy is.
### CHAPTER I.

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial C featuring stylized floral motifs and scrollwork.</image-desc>
Chemical Philosophy <term>Chemistica Philosophia: The study of the hidden natures of substances through both laboratory work and contemplation.</term> teaches how to investigate the hidden forms of things according to the truth of the matter, and not its outward appearance. The true disciples of this art enter upon two paths: Opinion <note>In this context, intellectual reasoning or theoretical framework.</note> and Experiment. For those who happen to rely on only one of these, it is inevitable that they—and others—will be deceived by their doctrine or their work. However, whoever examines both and judges one by the other, they shall not be frustrated in their labor, nor shall those others to whom they bring help or counsel. Opinion indeed presupposes doubtful things, yet through philosophical reasoning they appear true, which finally experience <note>The text breaks here to the next page.</note>

## *What Nature is.*
### CHAPTER II.

Among Chemists <note>Here referring to practitioners of "Spagyric" or Paracelsian alchemy.</note>, nature is defined as the activity of the Heavens with the Elements in the generation of all things that exist. This artifice <note>original: "artificium," referring to the skillful design of the natural world.</note> is perfected by a twofold instrument: namely, disposition and influence. Nature, by breaking down matter <note>original: "corrumpendo"; in alchemy, the "death" or decay of a substance is required for its rebirth into a higher form.</note>, prepares it for the receptivity of form and the influences of the heavens; which finally, at its determined time, breaks forth into action and a specific form. This is what that saying of the philosophers means: *The form acts according to the disposition of the matter.*

## *What Form is.*
### CHAPTER III.

Form is the action and potential of the ethereal region within the elementary region. Through the mutual transmutation of the elements, nature prepares matter, enclosing the form within it like a seed in a womb <note>original: "matrici," literally a matrix or womb; the receptive vessel of nature.</note>: being pregnant by this virtue, nature brings forth the specific act just as a mother produces an offspring. This is what the philosophers mean when they say: *Form is drawn out from the potential of matter.* For matter itself is capable of giving birth to that which is generated within it by form. It must be concluded, therefore, that form is the agent acting upon the matter which suffers its action, between which magnetic nature offers itself as the intermediary, like a master craftsman. This nature, indeed, from the universal form of the whole, never ceases to excite specific forms daily, nor is it any more idle than the motion of the heavens.

## *What Matter is.*
### CHAPTER IV.

For us, Matter is the entire elementary region, which although divided into four parts (which we call elements)—fire, air, water, and earth—there are nevertheless two principal ones, namely fire and water. For air seems to be nothing else than water resolved <note>original: "resoluta," meaning evaporated or broken down into vapor.</note> by heat during the creation of the world, while earth is water thickened or rather dried out by heat and dryness. Fire, by its own nature, strives to convert water into itself as much as it can; to accomplish this more easily, it seeks two mediums, according to both qualities of each:

...properties: first, so that by its own heat it might consume the coldness, and by its dryness it might consume the watery moisture. We see clouds suspended by the heat of fire, holding a middle position between water and fire; for if the heat of the fire—which is weaker around the surface than in the center <note>original: "metullio," likely a variant of "medullio," meaning the marrow or core.</note> of its sphere—is overcome by the coldness of water, this middle thing is converted into one of the extremes (as the victor). Thus fire, by nature's design, is frustrated in its effort; while it strives to consume one thing, it generates another from it, which in turn returns to that from which it was generated. This circulation of transmutation is the most powerful cause of generation.

We see fire perform a similar task in bodies composed by nature. Let wood be an example: when it is brought to the fire, its sulfur <term>Sulphur: In alchemical theory, one of the "Three Principles" (with Salt and Mercury); it represents the combustible, oily, and soul-like quality of a substance.</term> does not catch fire before all the watery moisture has been converted into air. However, once this moisture is consumed, the fire passes likewise into air and finally into itself, while the more solid parts of the wood fall away into ash or earth. Therefore, it should not be said that the elements of such wood have been destroyed, but rather that they have been separated from their composite state, each returning to its own proper sphere.

On this matter, a doubtful question was raised among the philosophers: whether fire consumes more than it generates? It seems sound to say that the operations of ethereal <note>referring to the celestial fire of the stars and sun</note> and elemental fire <note>referring to terrestrial, physical fire</note> are equal. For if more were consumed by elementary fire than was generated by ethereal fire, a vacuum <term>Vacuum: A void or empty space; traditional physics held that "nature abhors a vacuum" and would shift matter instantly to fill any void.</term> could be designated in the nature of things, which would be utterly absurd. If, however, the ethereal fire generated more than the elementary fire consumed, the surplus could not be contained in its already determined place; thus, the order of nature would necessarily be dissolved. But it may be answered more briefly: nothing is consumed by fire, but through the mode of transmutation, what recedes from one element approaches another.

Thus, wise Nature carefully provides for the awakening of new forms every day from the elements (transmuted among themselves in this way) and from form itself. In this way, what was deformed through corruption <note>original: "corruptionem," the process of breaking down or decaying.</note> is reformed through generation; thus the operation of nature is circular, just like the movement of the heavens. Many overly curious natural philosophers <note>original: "physiologi," referring to those who study the physical laws of nature.</note> who lack experience in these matters are accustomed to thrust this argument upon us to attack the "essence" of the chemists. But they will not conquer us unless they bring something stronger. They say: "Natural bodies consist of four elements; where then will the fifth element be?" 

We answer that all natural bodies consist of the four elements together with "Form," which is also a "something," and the purest part of any composite. Nor do they consist of these alone, because a true union cannot occur except through some bond <note>original: "vinculo"</note>; otherwise, there would only be contact or collision. For the primary qualities <note>The four basic qualities: Hot, Cold, Moist, and Dry.</note>, because of their mutual opposition, cannot come together into one. Therefore, it was necessary for them to be composed into elements possessing two qualities, so they might be joined more easily. By this bond, Nature composes all bodies. The philosophers are accustomed to...

To conclude concerning the elements, therefore, we say that they are threefold, namely: Simple, Compound, and Decompounded. Simple elements are those which are neither corrupted nor undergo composition; it is not *from* these, but *through* these, that all other inferior elements exercise their powers, which they also receive from them. Compound elements are those which are put together and suffer corruption. Decompounded elements are those which already meet in a state of composition through the process of corruption. Whoever knows how to convert the latter into the former—the impure into the pure, and the compound into the simple—will be the greatest chemist and a fine maker of wonders.

### *On Corruption.*
### CHAPTER V.

Alchemical corruption <term>Corruption: In alchemy, this does not mean moral decay, but the "breaking down" or "rotting" of a substance so it can be transformed into something new.</term> is nothing other than the resolution of a whole composite of nature into its constituent parts. Indeed, every composite, if it is resolved, must necessarily be dissolved into that from which it was first composed. Therefore, natural bodies are resolved into the elements and into the quintessence <note>The "fifth essence" or purest spiritual core of a substance.</note> of which they consist. We should not think this contradicts the opinion of Paracelsus <note>Philippus Aureolus Theophrastus Bombastus von Hohenheim (1493–1541), the famous Swiss physician and alchemist who founded the "Three Principles" theory.</note>, who says that every natural body can be resolved by art into only three things: namely into Salt, Sulfur, and Liquor <note>original: "Liquorem," often used interchangeably with Mercury in Paracelsian thought to represent the spirit or volatile part.</note>. This is because air is always found mixed with the liquor or the sulfur. Thus, it is not a feat of art to enclose pure air, entirely separated from the other elements, in any vessel. Although nature leaves no vacuum but fills it with composite air from the beginning of creation, that air is not separated from the elements by art, but remains mixed. It is daily before the eyes of chemists that nothing can be drawn out of bodies by the art of separation except water, oil, and earth. And although the oil may be clearer at the beginning of distillation than at the end, it cannot be called different in its nature, but only in its "accidents" <note>An "accident" is a philosophical term for a non-essential quality, like color or smell, that doesn't change what the thing actually is.</note>: that is, it is more "burnt" at the end than at the very beginning.

It remains for us to say that our alchemical corruption differs from natural corruption in this: that it pulls individuals away from their species and back toward their genus. No artisan, once the specific form of things has been destroyed, can again introduce that same form into that matter. Nature, however, can daily arouse forms similar to the previous ones from the elements—separated by whatever means from any bodies—and with the greatest effort, she strives to expand the genera into species for the preservation of individual things. But because the corruption of one thing is the generation of another (as the Academics say), we shall rightly speak next of generation.

## *On Generation*
### CHAPTER VI.

<warning>Text at the left margin is partially obscured due to tight binding/gutter.</warning>

Generation <term>Generation: In alchemy, this refers to the "birthing" or creation of a new substance or state of matter following the "death" (corruption) of the previous form.</term> is said to be the hiding of what is manifest, and then the manifestation of what was hidden. For all bodies are contained within three dimensions: namely, manifest Height, hidden Depth, and the Breadth that lies between them. The Philosophers <note>Referring to ancient authorities and alchemists.</note> hand this down to us secretly in these words: *There is no passage from one extreme to the other, except through a middle point* <note>original: "Non fit transitus de extremo ad extremum, nisi per medium"</note>. This means that from the manifest form of any body, the hidden form cannot become known to us except through the "corruption" (or breakdown) of the manifest state. It is through this breakdown that the property of the hidden state is revealed. This will be demonstrated geometrically so that it may be better understood physically.

Suppose one face—or rather, one surface—of a solid geometric body (designated by the letter A) is turned toward us. It is positioned so that the remaining planes are not entirely visible. We can measure the length of this surface which is manifest or facing us; let us suppose it is 5 feet. There is also the height of the remaining surfaces opposite one another (labeled b, c, f), whose planes do not become known to us except through the breadth of 4 or the depth of 6. When these are multiplied <note>original: "ducta in se," a mathematical term for multiplication.</note>, they make 24. These, in turn, when multiplied by the manifest height of 5, reveal 120 cubic feet, which were previously hidden from us.

Chemists are accustomed to investigating the latent forms of natural bodies in a very similar way: through a "middle" process—namely, the turning of manifest forms into hidden ones. This turning occurs through the corruption of the specific form and the generation of a more general form. Specifically, this involves the conversion of "decompounded" <note>Complex substances already made of multiple parts.</note> elements into compounds, and the conversion of impure things into pure.

->*On the Excellence of the Ternary.*<-
### CHAPTER VII.

By the sacred Ternary <term>Ternary: The number three, which alchemists viewed as a divine number of completion, often representing the union of Soul, Spirit, and Body.</term> the whole world was constructed in order, number, and measure through Unity. For Unity <term>Unity: The number one, representing the source of all things, God, or the Primal Matter.</term> is not a number, but a covenant of harmony. The Binary <term>Binary: The number two, representing duality, division, and the separation of matter.</term>, however, being the first number and the source and origin of discord, was severed from Unity through the assumption of matter; it cannot be joined back into one again except by a most indissoluble bond, which is only one. He certainly labors in vain who strives to couple equals with equals, for equals come together into one only by means of the unequal <note>The author argues that two identical things cannot truly merge; a third, different element is needed to bind them.</note>. God delights in an odd number <note>original: "Numero Deus impare gaudet." This is a famous quote from the Roman poet Virgil's Eclogues (VIII, 75), often cited by alchemists to prove that nature and the divine favor the stability of the number three over the instability of the number two.</note>. Therefore, the Unary <note>The principle of the number one.</note> binds and animates the binary (that is, one and one) through the simplicity of Unity into a ternary, by an indeed insoluble knot; for one cannot be divided into any parts. Indeed, one and one cannot be joined by two, since the "two" which ought to bind them are themselves dissolvable into one and another. Therefore, let the binary be rejected, and the ternary will be reducible to the simplicity of unity: as Johannes Trithemius <note>Johannes Trithemius (1462–1516) was a German Benedictine abbot and a polymath. He was a key figure in the history of cryptography and the occult, influencing later figures like Paracelsus and Agrippa.</note> says in his letter to Germanus Gnaeus, and elsewhere: "This ascent, my Germanus, is not human, but [is familiar] only to those..."

## On the Elemental World.
### CHAPTER VIII.

The elemental world is seen to consist primarily of three parts: Minerals, Plants, and Animals. Beyond these, nothing can be found in this world (at least that which falls under the senses). Therefore, making a beginning from minerals, as if from the foundation of the other parts, I shall come to the remaining material bodies. Earth is indeed the foundation and the vessel of all things, of celestial influences as well as solid bodies. All celestial motions occur around its center. All heavy things are carried toward its center, unless they were held back by the benefit of the earth's solidity. And all light things flee from its center. As Hermes Trismegistus <note>A legendary Hellenistic figure to whom many foundational alchemical and philosophical texts, known as the Hermetica, were attributed.</note> says in that most secret of secrets (which they call the Emerald Tablet): 
> "*The Earth is its nurse*," <note>original: "Terra nutrix"</note>

and a little further down, 
> "*It ascends from the earth into heaven, and again descends into the earth: thus it receives the power of superior and inferior things.*" <note>original: "Ascendit à terra in cœlum, & iterum descendit in terram: sic recipit vim superiorum & inferiorum."</note>

In the same place we see that he has ascribed the powers of inferior things primarily to the earth. For she is the producer of wonders from the seed of heaven and the menses of her sister <note>Referring to the Moon, whose "menstruum" or fluid was thought to influence earthly generation.</note>. As the same Hermes says: 
> "*The Sun is the father of the one thing, the Moon is indeed the mother, the wind carried this thing in its belly (and again as before) its nurse is the earth.*" <note>original: "Rei unius pater est Sol, Luna vero mater, portavit ventus hanc rem in ventre suo... nutrix ejus terra est."</note>

## On Minerals.
### CHAPTER IX.

Minerals are those things which are found hardened in the bowels of the earth by a mixture of earth and water, in various forms and species according to their different proportions. Of these there are three kinds: namely stones, metals, and intermediate minerals <term>intermediate minerals: substances like salts, vitriols, or alums that possess qualities of both stones and metals.</term>. And although all these things are generated from a proportional mixture of earth and water, they nonetheless consist of all four elements, just as plants and animals do: for it was said above in the fifth chapter that every liquid and sulfur contain hidden air within them. 

Stones are forged by nature from much earth and little water, to a greater or lesser degree; therefore they are not meltable, but rather crumble in fire. That some turn out brighter than others and transparent is due to a greater purification and clarification of the earth performed by nature: since we see that even by art, the driest ashes turn into transparent glass, yet art—even by its most inquisitive imitation—cannot replicate even the smallest work that was easiest for nature. 

Metals, on the other hand, are forged from much water transmuted into quicksilver <term>quicksilver: also known as mercury; alchemists believed it was the "mother" or liquid principle of all metals.</term> and a little earth converted into sulfur <term>sulfur: the "father" or fiery principle that gives metals their form and color.</term> by nature: thus it happens that they are meltable rather than crumbly. By long-lasting cooking, the water is thickened (provided it does not evaporate); conversely, the earth becomes bright: for [what is] hidden [becomes] manifest... <note>The text continues on the next page, completing the word "manifestis".</note>

-># OF THE CHEMICAL ART<-

[ma]nifest things, and these to those, are always and in all things contrary. Metallic principles differ in a threefold state: they are either **most remote**, such as a mixture of earth with water; or **remote**, like vitriol <note>A term for various sulfate minerals, often used in alchemy as a starting material for creating acids.</note>; or they are **immediate**, such as quicksilver <note>original: "argentum vivum"</note> and sulfur. From these latter two, according to the purity of both, or the impurity of one or the other, or both, nature is said to generate metal—noble or less noble, or altogether ignoble—by subterranean heat over the course of barely thousands of years. 

Thus it happens that the longer minerals have been under the obedience of celestial influences, the more they are rightly thought to have acquired most effective celestial virtues with a firmer and stronger power among those things that have corporeal forces to restore and preserve. And the metal is more noble the less its metallic form has been oppressed by its matter. The general form of metals is equal in all, but because of the varied disposition of matter (as was said above in chapter two), it breaks forth into various specific forms. 

But if the universal form is joined to matter disposed with an equalized proportion of parts, it must break forth into the most noble species of all: into gold. For the location already contains equalized parts; nature also knows how to apply proportionate heat as an instrument. 

Gold, therefore, is no colder than its heat, nor hotter than its cold; likewise, it is no drier than its moisture, nor more moist than its dryness. It is tempered on all sides, united, and compacted by nature with such perfection that it is thought to yield to no artificial fire whatsoever. However, the philosophers say that by natural fire, it can be resolved into its "first matter"; unless it is resolved into this, it would be impossible for it to be digested in the human stomach. Because it is not said to be burned by the most vehement fire (which conquers other metals and consumes stones), but is rendered purer and more perfect, until it reaches the highest degree of its perfection. Then, the philosophers say, it "rejoices" in fire like a **Salamander** <note>A mythical creature believed to be able to live in and endure fire without being consumed.</note>. 

I think they [the philosophers] mean not monetary gold <note>original: "monetario"</note>, but gold so purified by **antimony** <term>antimony: A semi-metal used in alchemy to "purify" gold, as it alloys with and carries away base metals.</term> that nothing of any other mixed metal remains in it. Therefore, all those who attempt to make **potable gold** <term>potable gold: "aurum potabile," a legendary medicinal elixir made of liquid gold believed to grant longevity and cure all ills.</term> (as Marsilio Ficino <note>An influential Italian priest and scholar (1433–1499) who sought to reconcile Platonic philosophy with Christianity and medicine.</note> says) seem to labor in vain unless they first resolve the gold into its first matter—that is, into quicksilver and sulfur—which matter is the first, proximate, and immediate source of all metals. 

This, then, is the conclusion regarding gold: because of its perfection and its likeness to the celestial Sun, it has been allotted the name "Terrestrial Sun" <note>original: "terrestris Solis"</note> by the philosophers. They also named pure silver (which goldsmiths call **cupelled** <term>cupelled: refined in a cupel, a shallow porous cup used to separate precious metals from base metals like lead.</term>) the "Terrestrial Moon" <note>original: "terrestrem Lunam"</note>. Lacking in color, constancy, and weight, there is a lack in silver of that compaction and restriction of pores by which metals acquire weight, as does quicksilver. 

Everything that is naturally **cooked** <term>decoctum: refers to the alchemical process of maturation or "digestion" through steady heat.</term> is made first black, second indeed white, and thirdly red; which last color is excessive, and from perfec[tion]...

It argues that gold must be returned to its primary state before it can be used in medicinal elixirs like potable gold.</summary>

...superabounding in its composition. For every natural body to be perfect, it is required that it should not fail in anything, nor exceed the limits of perfection; this perfection holds the middle path in all things. Now, the middle between black and white is pale, just as between white and a greater perfect red, there is citrine <note>A yellowish-orange color highly significant in alchemy as a stage of the Great Work.</note>. Hence it is that gold, holding the middle between white and red, has a citrine color, neither exceeding nor diminished. Citrine is nothing other than a determined proportion, a middle between red and white color. From this, it also happens that all those who think that silver and the remaining diminished common metals can be transmuted into gold by means of gold are deceived, as are those who listen to them willingly. For gold has no more color than it needs to color its own quicksilver <note>original: "argentum vivum"</note>.

Experience has taught learned men that a medicine can be made from gold which can dye pure silver, or another rightly purified metal, into the perfect color of gold; however, no more gold is produced by this art than the weight of gold from which such a medicine was drawn. Therefore, the counsel of those who urge that one should seek in a place what is not naturally contained within it seems foolish: such as seeking a superabundant color and superfluous weight in gold to bestow upon others. Even if gold possessed these, it would not be gold, but something more colored than gold, and not a perfect metal. 

If this perfection of transmutation is not found in gold for the reasons already alleged, it certainly will not be found in any other mineral (for what is not found as a quality of perfection in the perfect should not be sought in the imperfect), nor will it be in plants, and even less in animals. These are further removed from gold by nature and agree less in the generation of gold than gold itself; for nature rejoices in a nature similar to itself and is transmuted into it more easily than into a foreign nature. 

But since the transmutation of an imperfect body requires the highest perfection or a **perfect medicine** <term>medicina perfecta: A substance, often identified with the Philosopher's Stone, capable of "curing" the base nature of metals to make them perfect gold.</term>, which cannot be drawn more closely from anything than from a most perfect thing of its own nature—for the more powerful and closer things are always to be chosen in all matters for an easier transition—and since every perfection of bodies depends on the **temperament** <term>temperamentum: The balanced proportion of the four primary qualities (hot, cold, moist, dry) and the elements.</term> of their parts in composition, nothing will be more balanced than gold, nor closer to this work. 

Therefore, this perfection of transmutation must be sought from gold, or from nothing at all. Without a doubt, those philosophical men, greedy or thirsty for no mined or common gold, describe transmutations not of common or mined metals, but of their own "philosophical" ones. These men, looking to their own age and to posterity, have tried with the greatest labors to find—by considering the temperament of mined gold—the temperament of "fictitious" gold <note>original: "auri fictitij," referring to gold produced through the art of alchemy rather than extracted from the earth.</note>, which they extracted not only from one body, but from various things, whether vegetable, mineral, or animal. Therefore, the gold of the philosophers is...

...a certain tempered medicine <term>tempered medicine (medicina temperata): A substance where the four primary qualities—heat, cold, moisture, and dryness—are perfectly balanced, allowing it to heal or transform other bodies.</term> compiled by art, which, like a form separated from its own body, has been reduced to such subtlety that it acts upon any object presented to it—just like a celestial form—upon matter prepared by nature. Indeed, the universal form, once it has taken on a specific character, when it is separated from the individual, retains its active power, which it can then impress upon a foreign body by the virtue of unity, whose powers it has now assumed; it then makes all things one with itself—even if this medicine was drawn from an untempered individual. For by art, the elements of any thing or things can be reduced into a single tempered harmony.

Now we must speak of the remaining lower metals: namely Tin, which the philosophers dedicated to Jupiter (hot and moist); Copper or brass, which they dedicated to Venus (cold, though slightly hot and moist); Lead, to Saturn (cold and dry); and Iron, to Mars (hot and dry), because of the similarity of these stated qualities. These likewise seem to correspond to the four complexions <note>These are the four temperaments: Sanguine (Jupiter/Tin), Phlegmatic (Venus/Copper), Melancholic (Saturn/Lead), and Choleric (Mars/Iron).</note>—not as humors in the physical body of the physicians, but as elemental qualities in a composed body—due to the aforementioned qualities. Therefore, whenever a Choleric, Melancholic, Phlegmatic, or Sanguine person could be brought to a balanced state <note>original: "ad temperiem"</note> by a most tempered medicine, the philosophers considered that Copper, Iron, Tin, or Lead had been transmuted into gold. 

Thus, beneath the common metals, the wise hid physical and philosophical medicines, which they also prepared from common metals for the transmutation of their own—that is, the "philosophical" metals. They did this through double-meaning <note>original: "sub æquivocatione"</note> so that such a great treasure of medicine might remain hidden from the ignorant masses. Meanwhile, even learned physicians who made no small profession of philosophy could scarcely understand this until ***Aureolus Theophrastus Paracelsus***, Doctor of both medicines <note>Likely referring to his mastery of both traditional medicine and alchemical/chemical medicine.</note>, a ***Swiss*** and noble man of more divine than human genius, uncovered the whole matter. Through his long travels and his fellowship with learned men in every place, he published it in countless books for the favor of learned men and for the common utility—writing mostly in ***German***, so that he might provide abundance to those who lacked knowledge of the ***Latin*** tongue. 

Following the freedom of this teacher, I have wished to treat this matter perhaps more openly. For I would desire others to profit as much through me as I have through him. Now it remains for me to speak of the mineral intermediates, which correspond to their extremes, such as all the <term>marcasites (marchasitæ): In early chemistry, this term referred generally to metallic ores or "half-metals" rather than the specific iron sulfide mineral known today.</term>. There are found golden marcasite, silver, tin, and leaden (this last of which I believe to be antimony or ***Stibium***), which I have seen; the rest are so far unknown to me, such as the copper and iron varieties. There are also <term>magnesia: Usually refers to manganese ore or a type of white earth in this context.</term>, <term>tutty (tutia): Zinc oxide gathered from the flues of smelting furnaces.</term>, <term>orpiment (auripigmentum): An arsenic sulfide mineral used as a yellow pigment and in alchemy.</term>, arsenic, many salts, alums, sulfurs, and others of that kind, which contribute more to physical transmutation than to that common metamorphosis which, if not unknown to philosophers, at least

...otherwise neglected. Therefore, they are called **middle minerals** <term>middle minerals (mineralia media): Substances like antimony, bismuth, or ores that possess qualities of both metals and stones but do not fit perfectly into either category.</term> because they do not entirely resemble metal, nor stone in every part, but have the greatest affinity with both. Concerning one of the extremes—namely, **stone**—it would be superfluous to treat it specifically, since this has been discussed more than enough by Pliny, Albertus Magnus, and other most approved authors. It is only fitting for my purpose to state the difference between a metal and a stone: specifically, a stone neither melts nor is it malleable under a hammer, whereas a metal is workable under the hammer and can be melted by fire. Middle minerals, however, melt but are not extended <note>That is, they are not ductile or malleable; they cannot be beaten into sheets.</note>; instead, they shatter into fragments, in which they resemble stone, but in their melting, they resemble metal.
