## *On Vegetables.*
### CHAPTER X.

**Vegetables** are things that take nourishment from the earth through a fixed root. These are of three kinds: namely, **herbal** plants, which are vegetables that do not remain in the earth beyond a year or a little more, but after the leaves and stems have dried out, they are propagated by nature through the decay of seed dropped into the earth. **Arboral** vegetables (trees) are the largest, which rise up through solid roots into solid trunks and branches, and are preserved for many years. **Plant-like** vegetables are intermediate between these, larger than herbs but much smaller than trees, yet reflecting the form of both; they remain green and are preserved longer than herbs, but they perish sooner than trees. 

But because these things are known to all philosophers, however mediocre, I thought they should be passed over briefly; noting only this: just as they provide nourishment to living things, they likewise provide a medicine once they have been purified by art from their own corrupting matter. For the power of the "form" <note>In Aristotelian and Alchemical philosophy, the "form" is the active, identifying principle of a substance that gives it its specific healing properties.</note> is hindered by the matter that restrains its action. It will be better to separate this "form" outside the stomach than in the stomach of the sick person, which is already too weak to perform this separation. Truly, if they are to be food, they must be presented with the body; for the more general parts of the body—such as the natural **liquor**, **sulphur**, and **balsam** <note>balsam: In early modern medicine, this refers to a preservative vital fluid within the body that prevents decay.</note>—each ought to be nourished by its like. For excesses and defects causing imbalance <note>original: "intemperiem"</note> must be reduced to equality by their contrary—namely, a tempered substance; this must be most diligently considered by the physician, both in preparing vegetable medicines and those drawn from the parts of animals.

---

## *On Animals.*
### CHAPTER XI.

**Animals** are bodies that, moved by themselves naturally, take in nourishment through a mouth. Chemists <note>original: "Chemici" — referring here to alchemists or early chemical physicians who studied the transformation of matter.</note> do not without reason consider a threefold motion in natural things: **Corrupting**, **Generating**, and **Animating**. Philosophers say that motion happens either by itself <note>original: "per se"</note> or by accident. That which happens by itself is natural, acting as a cause, such as the motion of the **First Mover** <note>The "Primum Mobile," the outermost sphere in the geocentric model of the universe which provides motion to all other spheres.</note> and of the **Zodiac**...

<meta>This page concludes the author's preliminary discussion of natural philosophy—specifically the types of motion and the categories of the soul—and begins the second book of the treatise, which focuses on the practical application of alchemy.</meta>

<page-num>206</page-num>

...of the Zodiac, or caused, as in the motion of things toward generation and corruption. That motion which occurs accidentally or locally is either rectilinear or curvilinear. Rectilinear motion is perpendicular, oblique, or transverse. Perpendicular motion is that which is carried upward or downward. Curvilinear motion is either circular or winding. Circular motion is either rolling or rotating. A knowledge of these motions is not useless in this art, but because these matters pertain to the Philosopher and the Geometer—both of which a Chemist <note>original: "Chemistam"; in this context, the author refers to the alchemist or practitioner of the "Chemic" art.</note> ought to be—let what has been said so far suffice. Animals have this in common with vegetables: both take in nourishment for their growth, though animals do so by the mouth and plants by the root, the latter being inferior in their senses to living creatures. There are three kinds of living creatures: those that crawl upon the earth, those that fly in the air, and those that swim under the waters. In brute animals <note>“Brute” here refers to non-human animals, which were believed to lack a rational soul.</note>, there is a double motion of the soul: the vegetative and the sensitive. In the human soul, a triple motion is found, for to the preceding two is added the motion of the rational soul, which is perpetual.

### BOOK TWO.

#### *On Chemic Practice.*

##### CHAPTER I.

<image-desc>Decorative initial 'P' within a square woodcut border featuring foliage and vine motifs.</image-desc>

After we have treated the theory of the Chemic art as far as is lawful, it remains now to prove by experiment or by the senses that which the Chemist can grasp through imagination or the intellect. The **practice of Chemists** is a sensory demonstration made manifest from hidden things; it reveals what the philosopher has attained through the certain and known reasons of philosophy and the intellect regarding the latent forms of natural things. For I do not believe one should stand so firmly by the writings of authors alone that, if a better experiment teaches something, it should not be preferred over the opinions of those who often happen to assert and judge things they have not thoroughly looked into—things which are inconsistent even with themselves. The Chemic skill revolves chiefly around three things: namely, the **place**, the **instrument**, and the **operation**. The place is twofold: specifically, the furnaces and the vessels containing the matter itself. The instrument is also twofold: the corrupting fire <term>corrupting fire (ignis corrumpens): Fire used to break down or decompose a substance into its components.</term> and the generating fire. Likewise, the operation is twofold: **dissolution** and **coagulation**.

#### *On the Chemic Place.*

##### CHAPTER II.

The furnace itself, or the vessel containing the matter, is considered by Chemists to be the proper **place**. Furnaces vary among different craftsmen, and vessels are formed in various ways according to anyone's judgment. But according to the three perpendicular motions—namely upward, downward, and sideways—we shall here first set forth a threefold and unique furnace, never before seen until this time, by which three different operations can be performed...

## BOOK TWO.

...to a double height—that is, two stones high—leaving a small door through which the coals can be stirred with an iron tool; this is marked with the letter **B**. The four corners of the lower chamber are to be closed, but those of the upper vaulting are to be left open, so that the heat can enter into the side furnaces through these openings. Four iron sliders <term>spatulae<note>original: "spatulae"; flat iron plates used as dampers to regulate airflow and heat.</note></term>, marked with the letters **AA**, will close these small openings; these can be raised and lowered. Above this furnace, we shall erect a small tower <term>turricula<note>original: "turriculam"; the central fuel reservoir of an athanor, designed to feed charcoal into the grate via gravity.</note></term> made of earth, or preferably copper, wider at the bottom than at the top, marked with the letter **C**. This can be closed with an earthen lid marked with the letter **D** once the tower has been filled to the top with coals. In the upper vaulting, we will place some burning coals to ignite the fresh fuel. Thus, the entire tower will empty itself gradually throughout the whole day while providing us with a continuous fire in the meantime. When we see the coals running low, we shall refill the tower as before. By this device, a continuous fire can be maintained for several hours. 

On the four sides of the said furnace, four other furnaces are to be fitted, designated as **E**, **H**, **G**, and **F**. Each of these is constructed from two inverted earthenware shells <term>conchae<note>original: "conchis"; bowl-shaped ceramic vessels used here to form the combustion or heating chambers.</note></term> joined at their rims, such that three of the upper shells have bottoms perforated with round holes six or seven fingers wide in diameter. The upper shell of the fourth furnace, marked **F**, should have its bottom completely cut out, so that a water bath <term>balneum maris<note>original: "balneum maris"; literally "bath of the sea," a method of gentle heating using a vessel of water.</note></term> with a flask <term>cucurbita<note>original: "cucurbita"; a gourd-shaped glass or ceramic vessel used for distillation.</note></term> (marked with the letters **K** and **L**) may enter. 

All the upper shells should be pierced with holes through which a chickpea <note>A common historical reference for the size of small ventilation or "breather" holes.</note> could pass, as marked with the letters **A** and **B**. Each of the lower shells should have a small door cut into the side near the bottom, four fingers wide and six or seven high. These four small doors should correspond directly to the four openings of the lower central furnace, so that the aforementioned iron sliders can be inserted between them. They must move freely so they can be raised or lowered to regulate the fire when it is necessary to open or close them. 

Now we have the complete furnace, which we are accustomed to calling <term>acedia<note>original: "acediae"; from the Greek word for sloth or lack of care. This "lazy" furnace, or athanor, was designed to run for long periods without constant attention.</note></term>, both because it is slow in operation due to its gentle fire, and perhaps because it pleases the lazy <note>original: "pigris".</note> for the reason that once the tower **C** has been filled with coals, the fire does not need to be tended for several hours—a duration you can measure by the height of the tower.

### *Concerning Vessels.*
### C A P. V.

I consider vessels not to be mere chemical instruments, but rather the secondary place of matter and substance, second only to furnaces. This is no different than how the nature of the earth makes use of the globe and its caverns in place of vessels in the cooking <note>original: "decoctione"; the process of heating a substance to ripen it or extract its essence, a concept borrowed from the way heat "cooks" minerals in the earth.</note> or generation of minerals; it is the same in animals, where the womb <term>matrice<note>original: "matrice"; literally "matrix," a common term for the womb or any place where something is generated.</note></term> serves as the vessel, and the uterus takes the place of a furnace. For the vessels of Chemists are made partly of glass, or the most compact potters' clay, and partly of copper or other purer metals, the forms of which can be seen above where we have illustrated the furnaces.

### *Concerning the instrument of the Chemists.*
### C A P. VI.

The proper instrument of Chemists, as it is also of nature, is fire, which is under the control of the craftsmen. For fire is either external or internal. External fire is either violent, or tempered through three degrees, or very mild and similar to natural heat, such as [nature] <note>The text cuts off here, but the catchword indicates the sentence continues with "nature."</note> for itself

### *Concerning Vessels.*
### CHAPTER V.

I consider vessels <term>vasa<note>original: "vasa"; refers to the containers like retorts, flasks, and crucibles used to hold chemical substances.</note></term> to be not merely chemical tools, but to hold the second most important place for the processing of matter and substance, following the furnaces. In this, art mimics nature: just as nature uses the globe of the earth and its caverns as vessels for the cooking <term>decoctione<note>original: "decoctione"; the process of heating a substance in liquid, here used metaphorically for the natural "ripening" or purification of minerals deep underground.</note></term> or the generation of minerals, so too in animals the womb <term>matrice<note>original: "matrice"; literally "matrix" or womb, the place where development occurs.</note></term> serves as a vessel, while the uterus functions as a furnace. 

For the vessels of the Chemists <note>In this period, "chemist" and "alchemist" were often used interchangeably to describe those who studied the transformations of matter.</note> are made partly of glass, or of very dense potter's clay, and partly of copper or other purer metals. One can see their shapes in the illustration above, where we have depicted the furnaces.

The specific instrument of the Chemists, as it is also for nature, is fire, which is under the control of the craftsmen. Fire is categorized as either external or internal. External fire is either violent, or tempered through three degrees, or very gentle and similar to natural heat, of the kind which nature—

# BOOK TWO

...which nature employs in the generation of things. **Internal fire** is specific to every substance and is naturally inherent, which the Chemist must also take into account. Chemists use **violent fire** either during **calcination** <term>calcination<note>A process of heating a solid to high temperatures in the presence of air to reduce it to a powder or "calx."</note></term>, or for sublimating drier substances, or for melting metals. They use **tempered fire** in stages during **distillation**, whether it be ascending or descending. They use **natural-like fire** when they rot <note>original: "putrefaciunt"; putrefaction is the process of allowing a substance to decay or ferment in a warm, moist environment to break it down.</note>, digest, congeal, or fix substances through circulation. These operations are defined in the following chapter.

### *Concerning Operation.*
## CHAPTER VII.

**Operation** is defined as the application of hands and instruments to execute the chemical work. The chemical work is twofold: **Solution** and **Congelation**. The **solution** of a "body" <note>In alchemy, a "body" usually refers to the solid, physical matter or metal being worked upon.</note> is calcination. **Congelation** is the thickening <note>original: "condensatio"</note> of a "spirit" that has been turned into vapor. 

**Solution** is usually performed in various ways at the discretion of the artist, either by itself or together with its partner—namely, **congelation**. 

It is done **by itself** when a body is hidden away in an earthenware vessel and, because the exhalation of its spirit is not held back, it is crumbled into a very dry "lime" <note>original: "calcem"; the powdery residue left after calcination.</note>. This is also commonly done by placing the material in a clay pot and stirring it constantly until it is dried into a powder. 

Indeed, **solution** and **congelation** happen **together** when a body is placed in an earthenware or glass **cucurbit** <term>cucurbit<note>A gourd-shaped vessel used for boiling or distilling liquids.</note></term> and dried, while the vapor is held back by a glass **beaked helmet** <term>alembic head<note>original: "galea rostrata"; a cap with a long spout used to capture and direct distilled vapors.</note></term>. In this way, the spirit that was dissolved into the air is thickened again into a watery body and collected in a glass receiver vessel placed below. By this method, the earthy body is dissolved into "lime," and the watery part into an airy spirit, which is then thickened back into a watery body in a single operation. The common people call this "distillation," but the Philosopher <note>likely referring to Aristotle or a master alchemist</note> properly calls it "separation."

**Solution** can also be performed simultaneously with **congelation** using a closed **reverberatory vessel**—two earthenware vessels glued together with a strong "lute" <note>original: "luto"; a paste or cement used to seal alchemical vessels airtight.</note> so that the material cannot breathe. Through a reverberatory furnace, they usually call this **sublimation**. 

There is another type of **solution** performed by itself which they call **putrefaction**, occurring when a dry body is again sprinkled with plenty of water, sealed in a double cucurbit, and placed in a **lazy furnace** <term>athanor<note>original: "acediae furno"; a furnace designed to maintain a steady, gentle heat for long periods without constant attention.</note></term>. If the body is soaked in only a little water, it will be thickened by the same artifice; since the dry overcomes the wet, it is then called **congelation performed by itself**. 

In a **Bain-marie** <term>Mary’s Bath<note>original: "balneo Mariae"; a water bath used to provide gentle, even heat by surrounding the vessel with hot water or steam.</note></term>, a solution occurs which can be called putrefaction, using a double vessel suspended over vapor, or immersed halfway in water but enclosed all around in steam.

The last and most beautiful type of **solution performed by itself** occurs when a liquid—having been frequently refined <note>original: "rectificatum"</note> and thinned by distillation—is hidden away in a double glass vessel or a **pelican** <term>pelican<note>A circulation vessel with two side-arms that loop back into the main body, allowing vapors to condense and flow back down repeatedly, mimicking a pelican feeding its young from its own breast.</note></term>. With the top part of the vessel rising out of the furnace, it is provoked by a slow fire until no more vapor rises, but instead stays in the

## Concerning Operation.
### CH. VII.

Operation is defined as the application of hands and instruments for carrying out the chemical work. The chemical work is twofold: namely, **Solution** and **Congelation**. Solution of a body is calcination. Congelation is the condensation of a spirit that has been driven into a vapor. Solution is usually performed in various ways, at the discretion of the artist, either by itself or together with its companion process, namely, congelation. It is done "by itself" when a body, stored in an earthenware vessel, is crumbled into a very dry <term>ash<note>original: "calcem"; the crumbly residue left after heating, often called a "calx."</note></term> through the unhindered exhalation of its spirit. This is also usually done with the material lying in a pottery pot, with the matter constantly stirred until it is dried into a powder.

Solution and congelation happen together when a body, placed in an earthen or glass <term>cucurbit<note>original: "cucurbita"; a gourd-shaped vessel used in distillation.</note></term>, is dried while the vapor is so retained by a glass <term>beaked helmet<note>original: "galeam rostratam"; the top part of a still, also called an alembic head, which directs vapors into a receiving vessel.</note></term> that the spirit is dissolved into air and congealed again into a watery body, then received in a glass vessel placed below. By this method, the earthy body is dissolved into ash, and the watery part into an airy spirit, which is again congealed into a watery body; this is done in a single operation, which the common people call **distillation**, but the Philosopher more properly calls **separation**.

Solution and congelation can also occur together through a closed <term>reverberatory vessel<note>A setup where heat is "echoed" or reflected back onto the material from the walls of the furnace or vessel.</note></term>, using two earthenware vessels glued together with a thick <term>lute<note>original: "luto"; a paste or cement used to seal alchemical vessels airtight.</note></term> so that the material cannot breathe: in a reverberatory furnace, they usually call this **sublimation**.

There is another kind of solution "by itself" which they call **putrefaction**, when a dry body is sprinkled again with much of its own water, enclosed in a double cucurbit, and placed in the **"Lazy" furnace** <note>original: "acediæ furno"; also known as an athanor, a furnace designed to maintain a steady heat for long periods without constant attention.</note>. But if the body was soaked in only a little water, or at least a smaller amount, it will be congealed by the same craft; when the dry overcomes the moist, it is then called congelation "by itself."

In **Mary’s Bath** <note>original: "balneo Mariæ"; a water bath (bain-marie) used for gentle, even heating.</note> or the "Bath of the Sea," a solution occurs that can be called putrefaction; this happens in a double vessel suspended over vapor, or immersed up to its middle in water, yet enclosed all around in vapor.

The final species of solution "by itself," and the most beautiful, occurs when the liquid, often rectified and rarefied by distillation, is stored in a double glass vessel or a **pelican** <note>A specialized alchemical vessel with two side-arms that return condensed vapors back into the main body, allowing for "circular" distillation.</note>, with the top part of the vessel projecting out of the furnace. It is urged by a slow fire until no more vapor rises, but in the

# BOOK THREE.

->*On the Chemist's Practice.*<-

->CHAPTER I.<-

In the preceding treatise, we defined the operations of the Chemists; in this one, however, we shall bring them into action, insofar as they serve the needs of medicine. For it is not our purpose to treat individually those things which have been written by others in the past; rather, we shall endeavor to propose certain general methods of operating to students, by which they may most easily grasp all the preparations of natural medicines <term>natural medicines<note>original: "physicarum medicinarum"; medicines derived from nature through chemical processes based on natural philosophy rather than folk tradition.</note></term>. Therefore, by demonstrating the use of a **triple furnace**, we will teach how to distill and prepare into natural medicine the three parts of the world—namely, the vegetable, mineral, and animal. For the mineral part, we will take **Roman vitriol** <term>Roman vitriol<note>A type of iron or copper sulfate, used here as a raw material for creating powerful acidic oils.</note></term>, which we will prepare into an oil in the middle **reverberatory furnace**, and by that same fire, wine will be distilled into a **quintessence** <term>quintessence<note>The "fifth essence," a highly purified and potent extract, often an alcohol-based spirit believed to hold the life-force of the substance.</note></term> in the upper furnace; in the lowest, the **descensory furnace** <note>A furnace designed for "distillation by descent," where heat is applied from above and the product flows downward.</note>, the more solid parts of animals will be turned into oil and water. 

Whoever knows how to rightly imitate these three operations from the demonstration we provide, there is nothing that will come to his mind which he should despair of being unable to prepare by natural reason <note>That is, through a scientific understanding of the substance's nature</note>—not by mere trial and error <note>original: "empirica"; refers to "empirics" who practiced medicine through experience alone without a theoretical or "physical" framework.</note>. I say this so that it may be seen by all what the difference is between natural and empirical preparations. For it befits a true natural philosopher <note>original: "physicum hominem"</note> to prepare his own substances <note>original: "individua"; individual entities or raw materials</note> (called **Simples** <term>Simples<note>Herbs or substances used on their own for medicinal purposes, rather than in complex mixtures.</note></term> by the apothecaries) without the mixture or addition of any other thing that might change the nature of the substance being prepared. Finally, he will be able to mix or temper such juices or powders—already purified by themselves—into a medicine if he wishes; but the simpler a medicine is, the more powerful it will be. Nor is there cause for us to fear that some physicians once wrote that simple medicines are harmful, since they use that term ("simple") differently than Chemists do. Physicians say that **Rhubarb** <note>original: "Reubarbarum"; a common medicinal root used as a laxative.</note> is a simple, but Chemists assert it is a composite, which they demonstrate both by art and by experiment, not with words alone. But when empirics try to imitate natural philosophers without knowledge of physics—

## *On the preparation of Vitriol into an oil.*
### CHAPTER II.

Take three or four weights of Roman or Hungarian vitriol <term>Roman or Hungarian vitriol<note>These refer to naturally occurring iron or copper sulfates. "Roman" vitriol was often a term for blue vitriol (copper sulfate), while "Hungarian" could refer to various mineral salts from that region.</note></term>, which, placed in an earthen pot capable of sustaining a strong fire, should be burned over glowing coals until whatever moisture it contains evaporates. Or rather, you shall distill all the moisture to preserve the spirit, as will be described below. When you see a hard mass at the bottom of the vessel, throw glowing coals into and around the pot; in this way, you will calcine <term>calcine<note>The process of heating a substance to high temperatures in the presence of air to remove volatile components or to oxidize it.</note></term> it into a very red mass. Finally, let it be removed from the fire, the pot broken, and the mass pounded into a powder. Place this in an earthen long-necked **cucurbit** <term>cucurbit<note>A gourd-shaped vessel used in distillation, forming the lower part of an alembic.</note></term> made of the same clay from which goldsmiths' melting pots are usually fashioned, leaving two-thirds of the vessel empty.

Place the pot, previously fortified with lute <note>original: "luto"; a protective paste or cement used to seal joints and protect glass from direct heat</note>, in a transverse position, as is shown in the drawing of the middle reverberatory furnace <term>reverberatory furnace<note>A furnace that reflects or "reverberates" heat from the roof onto the material being processed.</note></term> and marked with the letter G. To the protruding neck, fit a glass vessel designated by the letter O (which they call a **retort**), placed in cold water and submerged with a lead ring so that the vacuum does not cause it to be lifted by the water. The joints must be secured with strong lute so they do not breathe <note>i.e., so no vapors escape</note>. Then the fire is to be kindled under the cucurbit, and gradually increased through four stages, each of which should last two hours, until it is entirely buried in glowing coals. That violent fire must be continued until the retort, which was previously dark and filled with spirits, now gradually clears so that what it contains can be seen inside. 

When this is perceived, the work must stop, and once the fire has consumed itself, let the receiving vessel be separated. Whatever oil it contains should be removed, stored in solid glass, and kept for use, sealed with the best artificial wax. You will find the method for making this kind of wax in the book that **Philipp Ulstad** <note>A 16th-century Nuremberg physician and alchemist famous for his work on distillation.</note> titled *The Heaven of the Philosophers* <note>original: "Coelum Philosophorum"; a widely influential 1525 manual on chemical medicine.</note>. It should be noted that the earthen cucurbits must not be damaged by the fire or contract even the smallest crack, otherwise the oil and the labor will be lost; therefore, care must be taken that they are made from the best earth. The **chalcanthum** <term>chalcanthum<note>Another term for vitriol or copperas; essentially a metallic salt.</note></term> or vitriol must also be very well dried before it is distilled, otherwise the oil will be drenched with much **phlegm** <term>phlegm<note>In early chemistry, "phlegm" refers to the watery, tasteless, and medically inert part of a distillate.</note></term>; this, however, can be removed by distillation in **Mary's bath** <term>Mary’s bath<note>Commonly known as a "bain-marie," this is a water bath used to provide gentle, even heat.</note></term>, so that the pure oil remains at the bottom of the vessel.

BOOK THREE.

### *On the preparation of the quintessence of wine.*
## CHAPTER III.

You should place a copper cucurbit <term>cucurbit<note>A gourd-shaped chemical vessel used in distillation; the lower part of an alembic that holds the liquid to be heated.</note></term> marked **L.L.**, filled to a third or halfway with very strong red or white wine, and covered with its own beaked copper cap <note>original: "galea rostrata"; the "helmet" or head of the still where vapors collect.</note> and sealed with lute <term>lute<note>A clay-like paste used to seal the joints of chemical apparatus to prevent the escape of vapors.</note></term>, upon a tripod in the ascending furnace. You will join a serpentine coil with a cooling vessel marked **K.K.** to the beak of the cap, so that the tube of the cap enters the tube of the serpentine. Take care with the joint, lest the spirit of the wine escape. At the end of the serpentine, you shall apply a glass vessel to receive the water. It will be distilled in the uppermost furnace by the same fire with which the oil of vitriol is distilled: only note this, that if the heat should be more vehement than is proper, the hole beneath the tripod should be blocked with a piece of brick. If the heat is still too intense, the brick blocking the opening should be fortified with lute at the joints. If by chance the fire is more violent than is right, let the copper cucurbit containing the wine be placed in an earthenware bowl <note>original: "cupellam terream"</note> marked **K.** filled with ashes. If you desire a lighter heat, place two bowls, one inside the other; you will have a very gentle fire when you have placed ashes two fingers wide in the bottom of the ascending furnace. In this way, you will be able to manage the heat tempered according to your judgment. 

When a good portion of the wine has passed through the serpentine into the vessel placed below, remove it, substituting a new empty receiver. When you now receive very little water, taste it to see if the spirit is still flammable <note>original: "ardens spiritus"; literally "burning spirit," referring to alcohol content.</note>; if it is no longer so, you shall separate the serpentine from the cap and remove the cucurbit from the furnace, setting aside the cap from the body of the cucurbit. Empty out the dregs remaining in the cucurbit and put in fresh wine. Finally, attach the serpentine to the cucurbit as before, and fill the cooling vessel with fresh cold water; do everything in all respects just as before until you have gathered a great quantity of ardent water <note>original: "aquæ ardentis"; a common term for distilled alcohol.</note>. You shall do no differently with this than you did with the wine, distilling it twice through the serpentine, and finally through glass instruments in this manner: After all the ardent water has passed through the copper vessel, place it in a glass cucurbit **L.** with its cap **M.** and in its receiver **N.**, in an earthenware bowl filled with ashes **K.**, and distill it three or four times, and as many times until, when ignited, it burns away entirely, leaving no phlegm <term>phlegm<note>The watery, non-flammable residue left after alcohol has been distilled or burned.</note></term> behind. You will be able to convert the ardent water rectified in that manner into a quintessence <note>original: "quintam essentiam"</note> by circulating <term>circulating<note>A process where a liquid is continuously distilled and condensed back into its own vessel, often to "ripen" or purify it.</note></term> it in a pelican <term>pelican<note>A specific circulatory distillation vessel with two side-arms that return the condensed liquid to the main body, resembling a pelican pecking its breast.</note></term> or a double vessel, just as will be shown when we demonstrate the use of the athanor furnace <note>original: "a-ediosi furni"; likely a corruption of "athanasii," referring to the Athanor or "undying" furnace designed for constant heat.</note>.

You should place fragments of the bones of any animals, or of woods such as guaiacum <note>A dense wood from the Americas, famously used in this period to treat syphilis.</note>, juniper and its berries, ivy, ash, and other solid materials, into an inverted earthenware cucurbit **E.** with its—

### On the quintessence <gloss>& the three in general</gloss>.
### CHAPTER VI.

It is a wonder and unbelievable to the common folk that the spirit of wine <term>spirit of wine<note>The "spirit of wine" refers to concentrated alcohol (ethanol) obtained through repeated distillation.</note></term>, when drawn from its body and entirely separated through the continuous motion of circulation, has the power to extract any other spirits from their own bodies—whether they be vegetable, mineral, or animal—by simple infusion alone. Truly, the chemical philosophers <note>The author uses "Philosophi chemistæ" to refer to alchemists who combine theory with laboratory practice.</note> hold nothing to be more true or more proven by experiment than the fact that active principles, when separated from their passive parts, act upon any compound. Through the sharpness of the acting spirit, they dissolve that compound and segregate its spirit through "symbolization" <note>This refers to the alchemical principle of "like attracts like."</note>: for like things are attracted by their likes when not hindered, and a spirit naturally desires to be freed from the bonds of the body to return to its origin, or to be joined to something similar to itself. Therefore, it is not to be wondered at if the fifth virtue and first essence <term>quintessence<note>The "quinta essentia" was considered the purest, most medicinal part of a substance, representing a fifth element beyond earth, air, fire, and water.</note></term> of wine attracts the powers of all things infused within it and separates them from the elements by dissolving the natural bond, as the spirits overcome the passive parts through desire and action. What was said previously regarding the spirit of chalcantus <note>original: "chalcanti"; blue vitriol or copper sulfate.</note> seems to apply perfectly here as well. What else, then, remains for the physician except to consider the nature of "simples" (as they call them), as well as the strengths and powers of minerals and animals, and to separate these from their bodies so they may be administered to the suffering according to the nature of any disease? I am not here to teach medicine, but the chemical art, for those who take delight in better arts than the preparations of medicines handed down by some.

### On the simple distillation of metals.
### CHAPTER VII.

Almost all chemists teach the distillation of metals, some using vinegar distilled many times, or a sharp lye; many others use waters or juices drawn from sharp substances. But I shall now show a way of distilling any metals without any mixture, but by themselves—which I believe has been handed down by no one until now, or at least if it has, I do not remember having read it anywhere. Every metal that is consumed by fire will be distilled by evaporation if it is placed by itself in a <term>bocia<note>A type of wide-bodied glass or ceramic flask used in distillation.</note></term> or an earthen cucurbit <term>cucurbit<note>The lower part of a distilling apparatus, named for its gourd-like shape.</note></term> with a beaked helmet <term>galea rostrata<note>An "alembic" or cap placed on top of the cucurbit with a projecting "beak" to direct vapors into a receiver.</note></term>, and closed tight with strong lute <note>A clay-like cement used to seal joints.</note>. This is done through the fire of liquefaction <note>The intense heat required to melt metal.</note>, provided it is held in that same state of melting for a very long time. All the vapor, being caught by the helmet, will be congealed within it; from there it will be sent down into a vessel placed below to receive the liquid, leaving the body of the metal friable <note>Crumbly or easily powdered.</note>. That metal evaporates is testified to us by what often happens to those who cast bells and engines of war <note>original: "tormentorum bellicorum"; cannons or artillery.</note>...

### On the distillation of those things which abound most in juice.

->### CHAPTER VIII.<-

Previously we spoke of those things that are dry and less juicy, which ought to be distilled by descent <note>Distillation "by descent" involved heating a substance so that its oils or essences melted and flowed downward into a receiver, rather than evaporating upward.</note>; now we shall discuss those which are full of juice. These, on the contrary (because they are raised more easily than others), are to be distilled by ascent, using glass vessels, or at least earthenware ones glazed on the inside, and not copper or lead, unless they are later rectified <term>rectified<note>To "rectify" a substance is to purify it through repeated distillation, removing impurities left behind by metal vessels.</note></term> more frequently in glass, as was said above regarding distilled wine. Whatever liquids are distilled in metallic vessels contract harm from the metal, the more so as the metal is less perfect. We are speaking of those liquids which must be administered internally to the sick. There is no reason for a critic to object that we now praise and then condemn metals. For we reject the poison existing in the imperfection of the metal, but we approve of the balsam <note>In this context, "balsam" refers to the preservative, life-giving essence found within a substance.</note> by which the metal is preserved unhurt for a very long time from internal and external poison. What if I bring something else harder to chew for the spiteful? Namely, that poison is driven out by the balsam of poison, not by poison <note>This reflects a core alchemical principle: the purified essence (balsam) of a substance can cure the toxicity of the raw substance.</note>, because such beets <note>original: "betae" — the author likely uses "beets" as a metaphor for simple or rustic truths that are unpalatable to sophisticated "spiteful" critics.</note> are unfamiliar to their lips? Will they turn their nose and tongue against me? Therefore, they shall not deter my mind from my purpose, but I shall share with honest and studious men those things which the highest dispenser of light <note>A common alchemical reference to God as the source of all hidden knowledge and illumination.</note> has given. But because enough has been said about metals for those who have a mind and wit, I shall return to those things I proposed to treat in the present chapter. Therefore, roots, foliage, flowers, fruits, and similar things of that kind which are softer—likewise the blood and flesh of animals, cut into small pieces or bruised (and if you wish, their juice expressed)—placed in a glass cucurbit <term>cucurbit<note>A glass or earthenware vessel shaped like a gourd, used as the boiling flask in a distillation apparatus.</note></term> with a beaked cap <term>alembic<note>The "galea rostrata" or beaked helmet is the top part of the still that collects vapor and directs it into a cooling tube.</note></term> and a receiver, should be distilled in a Mary’s bath <term>balneum Mariae<note>A water bath (bain-marie) used to provide gentle, consistent heat.</note></term>, or in ashes, first with a slow fire of the first degree, so that between one drop and the next you can count twenty-four beats <note>original: "calculos" — literally "pebbles," used here as a method of counting time.</note>. You will continue this fire until, in your judgment, a tenth part of the whole liquid seems to have ascended; then you will remove the receiver, and having emptied it, attach it again: for that which is phlegmatic <term>phlegm<note>In alchemy, "phlegm" is the watery, tasteless, and medically useless portion of a distillate that often comes over first.</note></term> and of no value in all things (except in wine) usually ascends first. Soon thereafter you will urge the fire until it reaches the second degree, so that the interval between two drops is a count of twelve. With this fire, you will receive five times as much liquid as the phlegm you took away before, that is...

# BOOK THREE

<meta>catchword: water</meta>

...downward as something more suitable for medicinal use, and keep it: for that which remains in the **cucurbit** <note>A "cucurbit" is a gourd-shaped glass vessel used as the base of a still; original: "cucurbita"</note> usually brings with it something of fiery powers and no small amount of scorching. However, so that the curiosity of researchers into these matters may be satisfied, I shall proceed to the extraction of the **simple oil** from any material. Remove the cucurbit from the **Mary's bath** <note>A "Mary's bath" (balneum Mariae) is a water bath used to heat substances gently and evenly</note> after it has first been cooled, so the glass does not break, and after drying it with a cloth, let it be placed back into the ashes <note>A "sand" or "ash bath" allowed for higher temperatures than a water bath</note>. Finally, with a **fire of the third degree** <note>Alchemists categorized heat into four degrees; the third degree is a strong, hot fire, often compared to a boiling heat</note>, so that the interval is the number three, draw off all the water until you see the number increased by that same fire; then, with the fire increased to the highest level, you will see a black liquid, in the manner of a thick oil, rise up in great quantity, which will take on a scorched smell. 

Indeed, this stench, which it contracted from the fire, can be corrected through **digestion** <term>digestion<note>In alchemy, digestion is the process of exposing a substance to gentle, continuous heat to mature or purify it.</note></term> in this way: pour the first and last waters back onto that oil—or if you prefer, use spring water that has first been distilled—and in the **vessel of putrefaction** (marked as "I" in furnace "G"), so that the vessel is placed in a Mary's bath or a sea-water bath and sealed, let it digest for several days. Finally, let all the water be distilled in a **helmeted cucurbit** <note>A cucurbit fitted with an alembic head (galea or "helmet") for collecting vapors</note> by means of the Mary's bath. Again, let other distilled spring water be poured on, digested, and re-distilled: this can be repeated until the oil loses its stench. The oil always resides at the bottom of the cucurbit unless you make the bath boil very violently; then the purer substance of the oil will rise. You shall then expose this to the sun in a glass flask closed with perforated paper, or in winter, by the minimal heat of a sluggish furnace. By this path, the simplest oil can be drawn out from any material. If, however, anything remains in the cucurbit which cannot rise by the water bath, let it be forced out by the ash bath and through a tube in a **cooling vessel** <note>A condenser; original: "refrigeratorio"</note> full of cold water.

### On the distillation of seeds and all dry things.

#### CHAPTER IX.

Water and oil can be drawn from fresh seeds at the same time in the manner we described in the previous chapter. Truly, from dry things, oil is extracted by a **vehicle** <term>vehicle<note>A "vehicle" is a secondary liquid added to a dry substance to help carry its essential properties during the distillation process.</note></term>, that is, by the sprinkling of some external moisture. Some are accustomed to use wine, others **burning water** <note>Ardent water or "aqua ardens," an early term for distilled alcohol/ethanol</note> as a vehicle; but since these seem to change the substance of the thing, I praise spring water that has been distilled at least twice. 

After the dry seeds have been crushed into a powder, let the powder be sprinkled a little so that it is moderately moistened in a glass cucurbit, covered with its **beaked helmet** <note>An alembic head with a pouring spout; original: "galea sua rostrata"</note> but not luted <note>"Luting" was the process of sealing joints with airtight paste; here, the author suggests leaving it unsealed so more liquid can be added easily</note>, so that it can always be sprinkled with a fresh vehicle when needed. Let these be placed in furnace G or H upon earthen plates, so that only the helmet stands out from the cover of the furnace, and let the water mixed with oil be distilled with a slow fire until the powder becomes dry; then let it be moistened again. If, however, the oil does not flow with the water, let the fire be increased; let this be repeated often until...

# THE ART OF CHEMISTRY

...no oil should flow with the water. You shall separate the water from the oil by means of a **Mary's bath** <note>original: "balneum Mariæ"; a water bath used for gentle, even heating</note>; all the water will rise, while only the oil remains below in the bottom of the **cucurbit** <note>original: "cucurbita"; a gourd-shaped glass vessel used as the base of a still</note>. This oil can be **rectified** <term>rectify<note>To purify a liquid by repeated distillation.</note></term> through exposure to the sun or through **digestion** <note>gentle, continuous heating</note>, as was stated above. It is advisable to receive the oil through a water-cooled **condenser** <note>original: "refrigeratorium aqueum"; a device to cool vapors back into liquid</note> to avoid scorching. Some are also accustomed to using glass **retorts** <note>original: "retortis"; a flask with a long, downward-pointing neck</note> so that the spirit may flow out more easily, since it does not have to be lifted to such a great height as it does in upright cucurbits.

### *The distillation of solid substances.*

### CHAPTER X.

Solid substances which melt by fire can be distilled by themselves. They are found in two general types: either vegetable, such as gums of all kinds, or mineral, such as **jet** <note>original: "gagates"; a minor gemstone and organic mineral derived from decaying wood under high pressure</note> and underground coal. Vegetable types include frankincense, myrrh, labdanum, styrax, calamite, mastic, juniper gum, and camphor. Once crushed, these are placed into simple distilled water for an **infusion** <note>soaking to extract properties</note> underground in a very damp place for several days. When they have been dissolved, let them be distilled just as was described above regarding dry seeds. Some add wine or **spirits of wine** <note>original: "ardentem aquam"; literally "burning water" or high-proof alcohol</note>, but in my judgment, these change the nature of the substances. Minerals, such as jet, bitumen, and underground coal, can be distilled by themselves in a glass retort protected by a strong **luting** <note>original: "luto"; a clay or paste used to seal joints or protect glass from direct flame</note>. This should be done over a slow fire at first; finally, when the fire is increased, the liquid may be collected. These oils can also be extracted by **descent** <note>original: "per descensum"; a method where the heat is applied from above and the liquid flows downward into a receiver</note>.

### *The distillation of bubbling substances.*

### CHAPTER XI.

Certain things are very difficult to distill because of their bubbling; therefore, one must find a way by which their "bodies" can be held back, so that they do not retreat into the **alembic head** <note>original: "galeam"; the "helmet" or cap of the still</note> along with their spirits. Of this kind are honey, wax, turpentine, and resins. When these are placed in a tall cucurbit, small river pebbles should be placed on top of them to hold down the foam. One must proceed with a moderate fire until the liquids flow out. The first liquid is usually white, because it is mixed in a certain way with **phlegm** <note>original: "phlegmate"; the watery, tasteless, and inactive part of a distillate</note>. The second is yellowish. The third, however, is red, because it has more fiery powers than the second. Some add fragments of bricks or tiles, but while they think they have made a simple oil, they actually have a compound one—more an "oil of brick" than an oil of the substance for which it is named. Others throw in tree leaves and fragments of wood, but all these things seem to contribute something of their own, which the aforementioned pebbles do not do. Thus far, we have set down all the preparations necessary for medical practice so exactly that the art of preparation cannot remain hidden from anyone endowed with talent.

# BOOK THREE

...physical medicines from any mixed bodies—that is, those composed of elements—which are usually called **simples** <note>original: "simplicia"; a term for single medicinal ingredients, often herbs, as opposed to complex compounds</note>. Now, however, so that each person may emerge more ready from the reading of this little work, it will not be tedious to add the three most powerful stones of the philosophers: namely the mineral, vegetable, and animal stones. The fact that I have placed their titles under a riddle <note>original: "ænigmate"</note> was done not so they should remain hidden, but rather so that clever readers may become accustomed to the obscure writings of the philosophers through exercise, and thus the final parts of this work may correspond to the first. Therefore, best of readers, receive this with a joyful heart; read and reread it, and you shall find that you are not frustrated in your labor.

### *The easiest enigma, through which that medicinal and mineral stone is revealed.*

### CHAPTER XII.

> **V**isit the **I**nterior of the **T**erra <note>earth</note>; by **R**ectifying, you shall **I**nvenit <note>discover</note> the **O**ccult **L**apis <note>stone</note>, the true medicine.
<note>This sentence is a famous alchemical acrostic: **V.I.T.R.I.O.L.** The original Latin text is: "Visitabis interiora terræ, rectificando, invenies occultum lapidem veram medicinam."</note>

### *Method of preparation.*

We shall **calcine** <term>calcination<note>A process of heating a substance to high temperatures in the presence of air to oxidize it or remove volatile components.</note></term> six pounds of this stone, now manifest to us, in an earthen pot in this manner. We shall build a furnace of fired bricks around the pot, placing them one above the other so they do not touch. In the middle, upon a brick fragment, let the pot be placed, open at the top. With charcoal lit around the pot and increased over time up to the very top of the furnace, let the stone be dried until it no longer smokes; this can be done in half an hour. Once this is done, let us throw burning coals into the pot, so that whatever material is inside may be excellently calcined in the middle just as it is from the sides. After a quarter of an hour, the coals are to be removed if the matter requires speed; if not, let them be consumed of their own accord until the pot cools, and finally, having been removed, let it be broken. If the stone has not turned sufficiently red, or if any white remains in it, let it be ground in a mortar, and the powder placed in another pot similar to the first; lying over glowing coals in the furnace, slightly changed (as it shall seem best), let it be constantly stirred with a spoon or an iron rod until it is red enough according to your judgment. The placement of the pots and the shapes of the furnaces follow below.

This calcination, however, is only done when the matter requires haste to obtain this oil; otherwise, **crude vitriol** <note>original: "vitriolum crudum"; naturally occurring sulfate minerals, likely iron or copper sulfate</note> is distilled with far greater benefit in nine **cucurbits** <note>gourd-shaped glass vessels</note> and as many glass **helmets** <note>original: "galeis"; the 'alembic' or cap of a still</note>, by reserving its **spirit** <note>the acidic, volatile essence</note> hiding within the **phlegm** <note>original: "phlegmate"; the watery part of the distillate</note>. This is done by **cohobations** <term>cohobation<note>The process of repeatedly distilling a liquid from its own solid residue to increase its potency.</note></term>, as is found everywhere in almost all the books of **Paracelsus** <note>A famous 16th-century Swiss-German physician and alchemist who pioneered the use of minerals in medicine.</note>. Nevertheless, the oil can be drawn out from the **dead head** <term>caput mortuum<note>The useless or "dead" solid residue remaining after distillation or sublimation.</note></term>, either together or separately, for many illnesses.

<header>OF THE ALCHEMICAL ART</header>

<image-desc>A rectangular furnace constructed of brick or stone. Inside the open top, a large ceramic vessel (cucurbit) is seated, surrounded by active flames.</image-desc>

<image-desc>A cylindrical furnace made of masonry. At the base is an arched opening for fuel, with flames emerging. On the top of the structure, a large round-bottomed vessel is nestled, with flames licking around its sides.</image-desc>

Next, we must have a **cucurbit** <term>cucurbit<note>A gourd-shaped chemical vessel (from the Latin 'cucurbita' for gourd) used in distillation as the lower part of the apparatus containing the substance to be heated.</note></term> made of earthenware. It should be composed of such a material that it can withstand a very fierce fire—similar to that used for the melting of metals—for several hours without damage. Such vessels can be made at **Cologne** <note>original: "Coloniam Agrippinam"; Cologne was a major center for the production of high-quality stoneware and refractory ceramics in the Renaissance.</note> and **Haguenau** in Germany, by reason of the excellent clay found in those places. 

But if such vessels cannot be obtained, let us at least ensure that the potters mix one third part of their own clay with two third parts of a powder made from crushed fragments of **goldsmiths' crucibles** <note>Recycling broken crucibles, which were already designed to withstand extreme temperatures, was a common way to create "refractory" or heat-resistant ceramic bodies.</note>. We present a cheap yet precious price to the **caduceus-bearing dragon** <note>original: "draconi caducifero"; the dragon is a common alchemical symbol for volatile matter, and the "caduceus" (the winged staff of Hermes) identifies this as a form of Mercury.</note> to be devoured, for a sixth part of itself. ### CHAPTER XV.

It is common for everyone who is ignorant of this art—even if they are highly learned men from the Universities—to disapprove of it. And what wonder is that? For they have never heard of such a thing, nor have they experienced it. It does not follow that the art should be condemned simply because learned men have remained ignorant of it. Indeed, many things have come to light in our century which were unknown to the ancients, just as many things are now hidden from us which were once most familiar to the ancient fathers. What does not pass into oblivion through the injury of time or the laziness of men? Nevertheless, the thing itself does not perish along with the memory of it; rather, after it has lain buried for a time, it will emerge—either in this century or in others—by the will of God. For within God's breast, all praiseworthy and good arts rest from eternity alongside His wisdom. Almighty God distributes His gifts to whom He wills, and He takes them away from the ungrateful who abuse them.

There is no doubt that God revealed a certain medicine to the ancient fathers through His **Holy Spirit** <note>original: "Spiritum Sanctum"</note>, by which they might protect against the **corruption of the flesh** <note>that is, physical decay and disease</note>, especially to those with whom He spoke and entered into a covenant. But after man’s vain desire to be wise by his own power led them to seek health from themselves and in things other than Him in whom salvation and redemption lie, their minds became blind. Led into a **labyrinth** <note>The author uses the "labyrinth" as a metaphor for the confusing, non-systematic nature of traditional herbal medicine of his time.</note>, they tried now this herb, now that, tomorrow this root and then another, and the next day some mixture. Thus, by experimenting day after day, they never reached the goal, nor do they possess true certainty in their doctrine. Always sticking in that doubtful labyrinth, they never happen to **reach Corinth** <note>original: "adire Corinthum"; a reference to the classical proverb "Non cuivis homini contingit adire Corinthum," meaning "It is not every man's luck to reach Corinth"—implying that mastery or success is difficult and not for everyone.</note>.

And what seems even more absurd is that men are perhaps never content with what they have. God gave to every nation what He willed it to possess, both for food and for medicine. What happens then? Our enemy teaches us to despise our own things and always to crave what is foreign. Yet we have within us—and more powerfully within our very selves, though not derived from us—whatever we seek outside of us or from others. Let us see how the **Pagan Gentiles** <note>referring to the ancient Greek and Roman philosophers</note> might argue against us Christians in this matter. For they say that nature seeks a nature similar to itself and rejoices in its own nature; but if it is joined to a foreign nature, the work of nature is destroyed. This is a wonderful saying to those who do not properly consider what nature is, but to those who know nature, nothing can be more true.

**Nature is threefold** <term>triple nature<note>The author divides the natural world into three categories: Universal (laws applying to all), Particular (specific properties of a species), and Mixed (a complex, often hindered state of matter).</note></term>, namely: **Universal**, **Particular**, and **Mixed**.
*   **Universal nature** applies to all things and operates through all things.
*   **Particular nature** applies to its own like, and is threefold by reason of its parts.
*   **Mixed nature** belongs more to matter and less to the spirit; for this reason, it can be said to act with impediment.

Upon this [Mixed nature] the entire medicine of our century depends. Therefore, according to this principle, we approve less of those things which have been **taken** <note>the text breaks here, continuing with the word "taken" on the next page.</note> from outside the nature of a climate for medicine—

### *The third enigma, through which the stone most powerful for medicine—called the "animal stone" by the philosophers—is revealed.*

### CHAPTER XIV.

We offer a cheap price <note>original: "Precium vile," referring to the alchemical idea that the Great Work begins with common or "vile" matter</note> that is yet dear to the **dragon** <note>a symbol for mercury or raw, volatile matter</note> who bears the **wand** <note>original: "caducifero," the caduceus or staff of Mercury</note>, for its sixth part to devour. Once tasted, that restless serpent immediately stops in its tracks; driven into a deep sleep, it is given to be swallowed by waters flowing from two fonts, one white and one green. This continues until the next summer returns, which with its fierce heat dries the waters, and the dead corpse appears in the depths of the sea. 

When this corpse is thrown into the fire, it comes back to life; having reassumed its wings, it flies into the air, yet it leaves behind in the fire the offspring which it brought forth from the conception of the "price." Because this offspring is born in fire, it must be nourished by fire like a **Salamandra** <note>a mythical lizard believed to live in and eat fire</note>, until it has grown to maturity and becomes exceedingly red and bloody. Then it must be washed and submerged in waters more blessed than those of its mother, so that through its death the languishing might live more happily. 

From the body, which has now been made pale, the soul is separated along with the blood; this is the "price" for us, so that all bodies may have power over the common ones. The philosophers have found that this soul, being healthy in every part, when poured into a sick body, restores it to a state clean of every stain through the simplicity of its virtue. This is the most perfect and simplest medicine of all medicines, leaving nothing corrupt in the human body; rather, it refreshes all languid parts and transforms into a balanced state whatever was imbalanced or imperfect. By the simplicity of its union, it makes peace between mortal enemies <note>referring to the conflicting "humors" or elements within the body</note> and, through concord, grants life (God willing) to the half-dead in this world, and bestows health upon sick bodies.

## *Conclusion of the previous work.*

### CHAPTER XV.

It is the custom of all those who are ignorant of this art, even if they are most learned in the Universities, to disapprove of it. And why is this surprising? Since they have never heard of such a thing, nor experienced it. It does not follow from this that the art should be condemned simply because learned men have been ignorant of it. Many things have indeed come to light in our century which were unknown to the ancients, just as many things are now hidden from us that were very familiar to the ancient fathers. What does not pass into oblivion through the injury of time, or the laziness of men? Therefore, the thing itself does not perish along with the memory of it; rather, after it has lain buried for a time to those of that era, it will emerge in this century, or in others, by the will of God. In His breast all praiseworthy and good arts rest from eternity alongside His wisdom. Almighty God distributes His gifts to whom He wills, and takes them away from the ungrateful who abuse them.

There is no doubt that God revealed a certain medicine to the ancient fathers through His Holy Spirit, by which they might protect against the corruption of the flesh—and especially to those with whom He spoke and entered into a covenant. But after the vain desire of men to be wise by their own power led them to seek health <note>original: "salutem," which carries the dual meaning of "health" and "salvation"</note> from themselves and in other things than in Him in whom there is health and redemption, their minds became blinded. Led into a labyrinth, trying now this herb, now that, tomorrow this root and then another, the day after some mixture—and thus experimenting day by day—they never reached the goal, nor do they possess the true certainty of their doctrine. Always sticking in that doubtful labyrinth, **it never happens that they reach Corinth.** <note>original: "nunquam contingit adire Corinthum," a Latin proverb implying that not everyone has the means or luck to reach a difficult or expensive destination.</note> And what seems even more absurd is that men are never content with their lot. God gave to each nation what He willed it to possess, both for food and for medicine. What then? The enemy <note>referring to the Devil</note> teaches us to despise what is ours and always to crave what belongs to others.

We have within us—and even more strongly within ourselves, though not *from* ourselves—whatever we seek outside of us or from others. Let us see how the Gentile Pagans might rebuke us Christians on this point. For they say: **"Nature seeks nature similar to itself, and rejoices in its own nature; if it is joined to a foreign nature, the work of nature is destroyed."** <note>This is a fundamental alchemical axiom: "Nature rejoices in nature."</note> This is a marvelous saying to those who do not well consider what nature is, but to those who know nature, nothing can be truer. Nature is threefold, namely: **Universal**, **Particular**, and **Mixed**. 

**Universal nature** applies to all things and through all things. **Particular nature** applies to what is similar to itself, and is threefold by reason of its parts. **Mixed nature** applies more to matter and less to the spirit; therefore, it can be said to act with difficulty. Upon this [mixed nature] the whole medicine of our age depends. Therefore, according to this, we less approve of those things which were taken for medicine from outside the nature of the climate <note>The author suggests that medicines should be sourced from the patient's own environment or "climate" rather than exotic, imported ingredients.</note>...

...taken, than those things which are of the same climate. In the same way, the particular nature of a different climate is less suitable than that of the same climate. The **universal nature** of a different climate operates sometimes more, sometimes less, according to the various influences of the heavens: yet it is more beneficial than a particular or mixed nature of one's own climate. 

And according to this reasoning, there will be a **threefold medicine**: 
1. The **metaphysical** of the unity <note>original: "unarij," referring to the Monad or the single source of all things</note>, 
2. The **physical** of the ternary <note>original: "ternarij," likely referring to the three alchemical principles of Salt, Sulfur, and Mercury</note>, 
3. And the **vulgar** of the binary <note>original: "binarij," referring to the duality of common medicine, often associated with the two-fold nature of humors</note>. 

This last one has obtained the name of "simple" in this age, though that name was once given to the first two, and more fittingly so. Hence it happens that those who have devoted their labor only to the medicine of "mixtures" <note>this refers to standard Galenic herbal preparations</note>—although they may be sharp of wit—cannot achieve knowledge of that **universal medicine** which is able to heal all diseases indifferently. 

They are led by this reasoning: "No medicine," they say, "can be assigned which is not hot and dry, or hot and moist. How then can a hot and dry medicine drive out a disease that is excessively hot and dry? Since this ought to be done with a cold and moist remedy, for **opposites are cured by opposites**? <note>original: "contraria contrarijs curantur," the fundamental rule of traditional Galenic medicine</note>" 

But their major premise must be denied, because in every mixture or individual thing, something else is found besides the hot, cold, dry, or moist element. This substance, which is separated from all these by our art, is neither moist, nor dry, nor cold, and even less hot, but is something **ethereal**, like the heavens <note>original: "cælum," referring here to the "Quintessence" or Fifth Essence, which exists beyond the four physical elements</note> set apart from the lower elements. For this reason, this medicine is called "Heaven" by the philosophers, because it acts upon our bodies in no other way than the heavens act upon the things below; and also because it is of an incorruptible nature compared to the body from which it was taken, just as the heavens are compared to the elements.

For the elements are dead in themselves, and unless they are brought to life by the soul or the **Spirit of the World** <note>original: "spiritu mundi," the invisible animating force believed to permeate the universe</note>, they produce nothing. It is like the earth that has not been under the open sky: no matter how rich it may be, it produces nothing. But placed under the bare breeze, it brings forth its herbs and little animals. Yet there is nothing so solid in the globe of the earth that it can prevent this soul from penetrating even to its center. The **generation of metals** teaches us this, occurring in the bowels of the earth where there are no openings or vents. 

We see, therefore, a difference between the generation of vegetables and animals, which does not happen except by the medium of free air, and the **generation of metals**, which cannot occur except in vessels closed on all sides. For if an exit were open to the metallic vapors, they would never congeal into metal, but would vanish into the air. From this we judge that the soul in metals is more penetrating than in animals and vegetables, since it has penetrated the extremely solid stony "vessels" <note>referring to the rock surrounding the ore</note>, which the sharpest spirits of others cannot penetrate. He who would think that elements generate by themselves would be considered a philosopher no more than a fool who would want to assert that a woman is naturally impregnated without a man. Although the element or subterranean fire may burn the earth into sulfur...

...even if [heat] excites water into an airy vapor, things nevertheless cannot be animated except through the penetrating soul <note>original: "animam penetrantem," likely referring to the *Anima Mundi* or World Soul which alchemists believed gave life to matter</note>, of which we have spoken above. **Elementary fire** <term>ignis elementaris: the physical fire found on earth, as opposed to the "celestial fire" of the stars or the "central fire" of the earth's core</term> possesses an active power for **corruption** <note>In this context, "corruption" refers to the breaking down or decomposition of substances so that new life can emerge</note>, not for **generation**, as stated above. Furthermore, he who denies that elementary fire has its first origin in the center of the earth—from whence it naturally rises toward the hollow of its own sphere—is not worthy of the name of philosopher; for such a man confesses he does not know that the fire of corruption exercises its mastery over the remaining elements.

The benefit of **generation** <note>The act of creation or bringing forth life</note>, however, is owed to the heavens, not to the elements: by this we may conclude that all generation occurs between the heavens and the elements. Now we must see what the offspring of such a birth might be; certainly, the end of generation is the product, just as the end of corruption is generation. But to speak more plainly, the offspring is a **mixture** produced from the substance of both parents <note>The "parents" are the Heavens (active/masculine) and the Elements/Earth (passive/feminine)</note> for the sake of its own perfection. Every individual is a perfect mixture; for although a thing may sometimes be deformed in some part, this is not to be ascribed to nature nor to the form (which cannot err), but to **unprepared matter** <note>original: "materiæ indispositæ"</note>, as was said above. 

They seem, therefore, to err greatly who call individuals "simples" <term>simplicia: in pharmacy, "simples" are individual medicinal herbs, used on their own rather than in a complex compound</term>, and especially vegetables: unless perhaps they do this in respect to medicines composed of many mixtures and individuals, and thus they dream that any single mixture is a "simple." From this comes the name of **Simplists** <note>original: "Simplicistarum," referring to herbalists or apothecaries who focused solely on plant-based "simples"</note> applied to those who devote their labor to the identifying of vegetables. 

Now let us return to that **simple medicine**. Whoever denies that such a medicine can be given—one which, by its own incorruptibility, is able to correct any corruption indifferently—denies that the heavens sustain or govern the lower world. But lest we seem to wish to prostitute the secrets of nature with allurements, let a few words suffice for the **sons of wisdom** <note>original: "sapientiæ filijs," a common term for initiated alchemists</note>: they easily understand what we mean by these things. But those who are ignorant of our art and laugh at it, let them flee far from here, since it is placed there for their ruin: so that seeking they may not find, and hearing they may not understand. One must not cast roses and pearls before swine, lest they trample them under their feet like beets <note>original: "betas," a reference to a proverb suggesting that swine find no flavor in refined things</note> unsuited to their lips. The sons of wisdom draw their nourishment from the spirit, not the mouth, so that they may live by the mind more than the body. In the meantime, however, they desire that there be a **healthy mind in a healthy body**, until, released from the bond of nature, these three <note>likely referring to the alchemical trinity of Salt, Sulfur, and Mercury, or Body, Soul, and Spirit</note> might live again as one,
->united for eternity.<-

# THE CHEMICAL ART
<page-num>226</page-num>

...taken, than those which are of the same climate <note>In historical geography, a "climate" refers to one of the seven latitudinal zones of the earth, each believed to be governed by a specific planet or celestial influence.</note>. In the same way, the particular nature of a different climate is less suitable than that of the same. The universal nature of a different climate operates sometimes more, and sometimes less, according to the various influences of the heavens; nonetheless, it contributes more than the particular or mixed nature of one's own climate. 

And according to this reasoning, there will be a triple medicine: namely, the **metaphysical** of the unity [unary], the **physical** of the trinity [ternary], and the **vulgar** of the duality [binary]. This last one has been granted the name of "simple" in this age, though that title was formerly bestowed upon the first two, and more appropriately so. 

Hence it happens that those who have devoted their efforts only to the medicine of mixtures <note>Medicines made by mixing physical herbs or minerals, rather than through alchemical distillation or "exaltation."</note>, though they may be sharp of wit, cannot attain knowledge of that universal medicine which can heal all diseases indifferently. They are led by this reasoning: "No medicine," they say, "can be assigned that is not either hot and dry, or hot and moist. How then could a hot and dry medicine expel a hot and dry disease? For this must be done by a cold and moist medicament, since **opposites are cured by opposites**" <note>original: *contraria contrarijs curantur* — a fundamental principle of Galenic medicine.</note>. 

But their major premise must be denied, because in every mixture or individual thing, there is found something other than the hot, cold, dry, or moist element. That which is separated from all these by our art <note>The "art" of Alchemy.</note> is not moist, nor dry, nor cold, and even less is it hot, but it is an **ethereal thing** <note>original: *æthereum quid*</note>, like the heavens segregated from the lower elements. For this reason, this medicine is named "Heaven" by the philosophers, because it acts upon our bodies no differently than the heavens act upon the lower world, and also because it is of an incorruptible nature compared to the body from which it was taken, just as the heavens are in respect to the elements. 

For the elements are dead by themselves; unless they are vivified by the **soul** or the **spirit of the world** <term>spiritus mundi: a subtle substance believed by alchemists to permeate the universe, acting as the bridge between spirit and matter</term>, they produce nothing. This is like earth that has not been under the open sky: no matter how "fat" <note>fertile or rich in minerals</note> it may be, it produces nothing. But placed under the naked breeze, it brings forth its herbs and little animals. Yet nothing in the globe of the earth is so solid that it can prevent this soul from penetrating even to its center; the generation of metals teaches us this, occurring as it does in the bowels of the earth which have no opening or vent. 

We see, therefore, the difference between the generation of plants and animals—which does not occur except through the medium of free air—and the generation of metals, which cannot occur except in **vessels closed on all sides** <note>original: *vasis undique clausis*. This refers to both the natural rock cavities where ores form and the "Philosopher's Egg" or sealed flask used by alchemists to mimic nature.</note>. For if an exit were open to the metallic vapors, they would never congeal into metal, but would vanish into the breezes. From this, we judge that the soul in metals is more penetrating than in animals and plants, since it has penetrated very solid stone vessels, which the sharpest spirits of other things cannot penetrate. 

He who would think that elements generate by themselves would be considered no more a philosopher than a fool who would claim that a woman could be naturally impregnated without a man. Although the element or subterranean fire may burn the earth into sulfur, and...
