# BOOK THREE

<page-num>227</page-num>

...it stirs water into an airy vapor, nonetheless they cannot be animated except by a penetrating soul, about which we have spoken above. Elemental fire possesses an active power for corruption, not for generation, as stated above. Again, whoever denies that elemental fire has its primary origin in the center of the earth, from where it naturally rises to the hollow of its sphere, is not worthy of the name of philosopher; for he confesses he is ignorant that the fire of corruption exercises its mastery over the remaining elements. But the benefit of generation is owed to heaven, not to the elements; by this we can conclude that all generation occurs between heaven and the elements. 

Now we must see what kind of offspring <note>original: "fœtus"</note> comes from such a birth; certainly it is the end of generation, just as the end of corruption is generation. But to speak more clearly, the offspring is a mixture <term>mixtum: a compound or "mixture" of elements forming a new substance</term> produced from the substance of both parents toward its own perfection. Every individual is a perfect mixture, because although it may sometimes be deformed in some part, this is not to be ascribed to nature nor to form (which do not happen to err) but to predisposed matter (as was said above). 

They seem, therefore, to err greatly who call individuals "simples," and especially plants; unless perhaps they do this in respect to medicines composed from many mixtures and individuals, and thus they dream that any single mixture is a "simple." From this comes the name of **Simplists** <note>Historically, "Simplers" or "Simplists" were herbalists who dealt with "simples"—medicinal plants used on their own rather than in complex chemical distillations.</note> applied to those who devote their work to the recognition of plants. Now let us return to that simple medicine. 

Whoever denies that such a medicine can be given—one which by its incorruptibility is able to correct any corruption indifferently—denies that heaven sustains or governs lower things. But lest we seem to want to prostitute the secrets of nature with flattery, let these few words suffice for the **sons of wisdom**; they easily understand what we mean by this. But those who are ignorant of our art and laugh at it, let them flee far from here, since it is placed there for their ruin: so that "seeking they may not find, and hearing they may not understand" <note>A paraphrase of biblical warnings regarding parables and secret knowledge.</note>. One must not cast roses and pearls before swine, lest they trample them under their feet as if they were beets <note>original: "betas." The author uses "beets" as a metaphor for common, lowly food contrasted with pearls.</note>, unaccustomed to their lips. The sons of wisdom draw their nourishment through the spirit, not the mouth, so that they may live more by the mind than by the body. Meanwhile, however, they desire that there be "a healthy mind in a healthy body" <note>original: "mens sana in corpore sano"</note>, until, released from the bond of nature, these three <note>Likely referring to the Tria Prima: Salt, Sulfur, and Mercury, or the human trinity of Body, Soul, and Spirit.</note>—united once again into one—may live for eternity.

...they examine the mysteries of nature. Truly, I do not wonder at this, when I notice that such men take it very badly that after their studies—acquired through long labor and no small expense, through which they have already grown gray hairs—certain new things should come into the light. These things, if not unheard of, are at least little or not at all understood, yet they are far superior to their own: they are so proven by the most ancient authorities and by recent experience to anyone of sounder judgment that they cannot be undermined by any arguments. Those worn out by old age <note>original: "senio confectos"</note> are ashamed to learn, especially those who are accustomed to teaching others, moved by a rustic rather than a philosophical shame.

Have we not also suffered the loss of time, labor, and expense in the Academies <term>Academis: the traditional universities of the Renaissance era</term>? Yet we are not afraid to pull back our foot <note>original: "pedem... retrahere," a Latin idiom for retreating from a path or changing one's mind</note> from the lesser things so that we may fix it upon more stable ones. We do not, for that reason (as those men do), despise those things taught in the universities and reject them entirely as if they were nothing; we say only this: that we have learned far better things through experience than by the frequenting of lectures. Nor do I doubt that there will be many who, while they cannot criticize the thing itself, will seek the slightest opportunity—either of unpolished speech or of the order in the treatment—by which they may gnaw at what they cannot tear apart.

But so that there may be a response to both types of critics: it is certain that those who are most intent on the things themselves care very little for the useless circumstances <note>i.e., the outward flourishes or trivial details</note> of things, both because they see that the longest human life is insufficient to know the matter purely, and because there is no place for a cloak <note>original: "pallio," here meaning a disguise, cover, or deceptive rhetoric</note> in the profession of truth. True things are less accustomed to be colored by elegance of speech or loquacity.

## On Speculative Philosophy.

### CHAPTER I.

<term>Speculative Philosophy: from the Latin *speculari* (to watch or observe); here it refers to the theoretical branch of philosophy focused on the contemplation of truth through the mind, rather than through physical experimentation</term> is said to be the voluntary withdrawal of a well-composed mind from the body, by which the soul may more easily occupy itself with the knowledge of truth. For observing well and truly, a good disposition of the body is required, so that it does not hinder the mind. This can be acquired in two ways: namely, by nature or by art. That which is natural can be assisted by art, and one may also obtain that which nature has denied in this regard; this is achieved primarily through the use of reason, then by sobriety of diet, and by <term>Philosophical medicines: specialized chemical or alchemical remedies intended to purify the body's humors to facilitate higher mental functions</term>—by applying one of these remedies, or all of them together. But so that it may be better understood what these things mean, we must come to the last terms of the definition.

The mind is called "well-composed" whenever the <term>spirit: (*animus*) the higher, rational, and immortal seat of human consciousness</term> is joined to the <term>soul: (*anima*) the animating or vital principle that acts as a bridge between the physical body and the spirit</term> by such a bond that it is able to restrain the appetites of the body. Let a "good disposition of the body" be understood as when it is less subject to its own corrupt appetites; and it acquires its best state when it has attained a more excellent <term>temperament: the balance of the four primary qualities (hot, cold, moist, dry) or the three principles (Salt, Sulfur, Mercury)</term> of its component parts; then it seeks its own desires less and becomes more obedient to the mind. Whatever the body hungers for is corrupt. Indeed, it can desire nothing except through the faculty of the soul, which is the mover of the body. The soul moves simply, without a conception of good or evil. The body receives this kind of motion and, through its own corrupt nature, seeks to carry it out in evil, unless the spirit resists, which advises nothing but good.

The soul, therefore, is situated between good and evil; it has its opinion of good through the good, and of evil through the evil. The good permits (and not otherwise) such evil to occur because of the continuous resistance of the moved good; this can properly be called the "stubbornness of evil" against the spirit that advises all good. So that these things may be better understood, it must be known that man consists of three most powerful parts: namely, the Spirit, the Soul, and the Body. The Spirit is called the "breath of life" <note>original: *spiraculum vitæ*</note>. Indeed, the Soul is the organ of the spirit—that is, the spirit’s instrument—just as the Body is the organ of the soul. The soul is the life of the body and the "middle substance" between the spirit and the body. If the soul clings more to the spirit, the Mind <note>original: *Mens*</note> and the "internal man" arise. If, on the contrary, it clings more to the body than to the spirit, it does not become a mind, but is called the "external man" and an "abyss of darkness."

The spirit also delights in three things: Reason, Intellect, and Memory. Reason represents the image of speculation to the intellect; the intellect presents it to the memory to be preserved in secret. First Reason is the perpetual and inviolable order of the Eternal Mind, of which man was made a participant by the gift of God, along with the intellect, which [the reason]...

[Of rea]son is the apprehension: not unlike Memory, which can indeed be called the preservation of [things]. The Soul consists of two things: namely, Motion and Sense. Motion is either natural or accidental; but because I have treated this in our <term>Key: (*Clave*) a reference to the author's other writings or perhaps a specific "key" to his philosophical system</term>, I will pass over it briefly here.

Sense is the perception of a thing seen, heard, tasted, smelled, or touched. For the limbs of the body, through which the senses are perceived by the soul, we properly call the "organs of the senses." The perception of the senses recalls to memory the knowledge of past things by the representation of present ones. Brute animals have this in common with humans: for they recollect things only through sense when present objects are offered to them. 

There is also another root of memory, which is most excellent, which requires no mediating representation, but rather cultivates said memory only by the diligent agitation of a never-idle spirit, and makes it perpetually flourish. This continuation of memory follows the cultivation of reason and is unique to man alone. 

Therefore, sense belongs commonly to the animal [nature], while reason is specifically intellectual: for brute animals do not understand except through the present sense. Rational animals understand through the intellect, moved by reason and sense, whether as a later result or as a medium.

Furthermore, the spirit <note>original: *animus*</note> and the body are opposites in their principles, which can never be joined except through the mediating soul <note>original: *anima*</note> which participates in both of these enemies. But because one of the extremes is perfect and the other imperfect, if the motion occurs from the perfect through the medium, it passes into the perfection of the imperfect, and vice versa. 

By this principle God created all things, so that they might come together from three into one; for He is the author of peace and union. Two and One are enemies. Let the duality <note>original: *binarius*; refers to the number two as a symbol of division or conflict</note> be rejected, so that the trinity <note>original: *ternarius*; the number three, representing completion or the Holy Trinity</note> may come together into unity, as has been discussed more broadly in the *Key*; I will not repeat it more copiously here. 

The spirit is equal in all, but the mind <note>original: *mens*</note> is not equal in all. There are very few who have the soul joined with the spirit; many participate in the mind to a greater or lesser degree; most, cherishing the body in the soul and the soul in the body, do not recognize the spirit; these have no mind, but only madness. 

Thus, the mind is well-received whenever the spirit and soul, coming together, are so received by the body that from these three one harmonious and inseparable thing is made. But this friendship can in no way occur except through separation, without which there is no <term>metaphysical conjunction: a philosophical union of different substances (like spirit and matter) that goes beyond physical laws</term>. 

One is alone, and if it remains alone, it is impossible for it to be joined with another. If, however, it is to be joined with another, it is necessary for this "other" to be separated from that One, since there is nothing besides that One. And because the parts of the One symbolize or have sympathy with the One, they easily come together into one; and they do so more easily the less they are separated from the One by intervals. Therefore, the distraction <note>here meaning "pulling away" or separation</note> of the mind from the body is necessary, so that the union of the one and the other may occur. But since union requires perfection, from the perfect extreme (as I said above) through the medium it makes...

# *On Speculative Philosophy.*

## *CHAPTER I.*

<image-desc>A square woodcut decorative initial 'S' featuring a landscape with trees and a building in the distance.</image-desc>Speculative Philosophy is defined as the voluntary withdrawal of a well-ordered mind from the body, by which the spirit may more easily engage in the pursuit of the knowledge of truth. For proper and true speculation, a good disposition of the body is required so that it does not hinder the mind. This can be acquired in two ways: namely, by nature or by art. That which is natural can be assisted by art; furthermore, one may attain that which nature has denied in this regard, chiefly through the use of reason, then by sobriety of diet, and by <term>philosophical medicines: likely a reference to alchemical or spagyric preparations intended to purify the physical body for spiritual work</term>—employing one or all of these remedies together. But so that what these things mean may be better understood, we must examine every term of the definition, right to the very last.

A "well-ordered mind" is so called whenever the spirit <note>original: *animus*</note> is joined to the soul <note>original: *anima*</note> by such a bond that it is able to restrain the appetites of the body. A "good disposition of the body" should be understood as when it is less subject to its own corrupt appetites; and the best disposition is reached when its component parts have acquired an excellent temperament <note>meaning a balanced mixture of the four bodily humors</note>; then it desires its own things less and becomes more obedient to the mind. Whatever the body desires is corrupt. Indeed, it can desire nothing except through the faculty of the soul, which is the mover of the body. This soul moves simply, without any conception of good or evil. The body receives this kind of motion and, through its own corrupt nature, seeks to carry it out in an evil way, unless the spirit resists it, which advises nothing but good. Therefore, the soul is situated between good and evil; it has its opinion of the good through the good, and of evil through the evil. The good permits such evil to occur (and not otherwise) because of the continuous resistance of the "moved good," which can properly be called the stubbornness of evil against the spirit that advises all good. 

To better understand these things, it must be known that man consists of three primary parts: namely, the Spirit <note>original: *animus*</note>, the Soul <note>original: *anima*</note>, and the Body. The Spirit is called the "breath of life." The Soul is indeed the organ of the spirit (that is, of the breath), just as the Body is the organ of the soul. The soul is the life of the body and the intermediate substance between the spirit and the body. If the soul clings more to the spirit than to the body, the Mind <note>original: *mens*</note> arises, as does the "internal man." If, on the contrary, it clings more to the body than to the spirit, there is no mind, and it is called the "external man" and the "abyss of darkness." 

The spirit also delights in three things: Reason, Intellect, and Memory. Reason represents the image of speculation to the Intellect, and the Intellect presents it to the Memory to be preserved in secret. Reason is the first perpetual and inviolable order of the eternal Mind, of which man was made a participant by the gift of God, along with the intellect, which [belongs to] reason...

...the transition to the imperfect, so that it may perfect it. Through this kind of distraction <note>separation or withdrawal</note> of the mind from the body (which some call a **voluntary death**), the Spirit <note>original: *animus*; the higher rational mind</note> and the Soul <note>original: *anima*; the vital life force</note>, joined together, acquire power and dominion over their body. This is a power which the Spirit alone did not possess before, because of the resisting medium through which the natural transition must occur. For enemies do not come together except through a neutral mediator on the side of discord, who is nonetheless a participant on the side of reconciliation for both.

By this principle, finally, <term>judicial astronomy</term> <note>the practice of predicting human fate or character based on the stars; astrology</note> is undermined. It teaches that the arrangement of the stars inclines the will, but does not necessitate it. For the stars are far inferior to the minds of men; likewise, a base thing can do little or nothing to influence what is fundamentally more noble than itself. 

Truly, if human bodies should conquer the soul and reduce it to the slavery of a corruptible body, I will not deny that the bodies of the stars—being then more noble than those of men—can imprint their passions <note>influences or effects</note> upon human bodies. Briefly: **the wise man will rule the stars**; the fool is not only subjected to them, but even to the lower things and to every kind of misery. The wise man is he who, having attained a Mind, cultivates it; the fool, however, is he who loves the body within the soul, or the soul within the body, while the Spirit is neglected. This is also proven by the divine word:

> *He who loves his soul (understand: in the body) shall lose it, and he who hates it (as stated above) keeps it for eternity.* <note>original: *Qui diligit animam suam...*; a reference to the Gospel of John 12:25</note>

He is said to love his soul in the body who follows his own depraved appetites; on the other hand, he who does not follow them, but delights in the thoughts of vanities, is seen to love the body within the soul. He "hates" his soul in the body who curbs the appetites of the flesh, and he hates the body in the soul who resists vain speculations. 

It seemed right to add this: among the most esteemed authors, and especially theologians, "soul" is sometimes used for "spirit," and "spirit" for "soul," interchangeably. From this, one should not infer that the Spirit and Soul are one and the same before the composition of the mind, but rather after it. In this, the philosophers agree with the theologians; for whether we call the mind "spirit" or "soul," by the naming of one we do not exclude the other, because of the union already formed. A union is not called "true" unless it is inseparable. Nevertheless, the beginnings of a union cannot be cast down if they do not achieve their effect; because of this, it remains possible for a mind that is still imperfect to be called more or less by either name. Those who attain a perfect mind are very few; those who have a beginning of one are many; but those who have none at all are the most numerous.

Now coming to the anatomy of the body (as mentioned above), I say that a good physical disposition of the body is necessary for true **speculation** <note>deep philosophical or spiritual contemplation</note>. This is surely because the body, out of its corrupt nature, greatly weighs down the soul and hinders it, so that it cannot perceive the actions of the spirit. It is given by nature to some to be more fit than others for making this separation, specifically those to whom, by accident during their formation, a natural corruption...

...being, absolutely no or at least very least corruption has been added. Less fit are those who, beyond the corruption they were born with or that which they have added to themselves, further hinder their reason through their own insolence and a disordered way of life. Such are those who, agitated by worldly cares, neglect those things which are eternal outside this world, and who use those things which nature provided for necessity more generously than is proper. Therefore, just as a thing is hindered by the addition of something harmful, so it can be helped by the removal of that same thing.

There are, therefore, **philosophical medicines** <note>Spagyric or alchemical preparations intended to be "purified" versions of natural substances</note> created through the <term>Alchemical art</term> (the most excellent art of all). These are separated from their own original bodies; through the natural power of acting which they possess over their own body—and which they retain even after the removal of their "patient" <note>In this context, the "patient" or passive material part of a substance that normally weighs down its active "agent" or spirit</note> part—they are able to perform that same action upon an external body. Indeed, they can do so more excellently than nature had granted them to perform within their own original bodies. 

Now, whatever exists in the nature of things, having both form and matter, desires to be perfected in its own kind; this natural desire is the most powerful cause of the perfection of all things. And since nature rejoices to be joined to a nature similar to itself and is delighted by it, when the Mind <note>original: *mens*</note> conquers—helped by a medicine similar to itself—the body is forced to comply with that same nature. This is just as the Soul <note>original: *anima*</note> was previously forced to comply when the body, strengthened by similar corrupting things, was the conqueror. 

Lest this seem absurd to anyone, I will add this: any nourishment is changed into the blood of the person nourished, taking on the same nature as the nourishment itself. Nature teaches us an example of this in those who feed on the flesh of fierce animals, for they steadily become most fierce themselves. <note>A common early modern belief that the "spirit" of food influences the character of the consumer.</note> Nothing is taken in as nourishment by nature except that which is "subtle" <note>refined or pure</note>; the coarse and dreg-like parts are rejected as waste. Furthermore, nature ejects any waste from superfluous nourishment through the pores as sweat, or through the bladder, or as tears. 

This moved our teacher **Theophrastus Paracelsus** to say that every limb of the body has its own "stomach" in which nourishment is digested, and in which the separation of the superfluous from the necessary occurs. <note>Paracelsus (1493–1541) proposed that an "internal alchemist" or *Archeus* resided in every organ to separate nutrients from toxins.</note> If, through the weakness of the "stomach" of any limb, this kind of superfluity is not separated due to poor digestion, this superfluous nourishment forces the flesh in that limb to grow into a corrupt tumor, which they have called an <term>abscess</term> <note>original: *apostema*</note>, or it causes the bones to be extended beyond their natural shape. 

I have seen examples of this in many people: namely, that all the ribs on one side were extended beyond their natural order for this reason, raising a hump beneath the shoulder blades in addition to the pain. Because this superfluity could not be purged into an abscess due to the hardness of the bones, it dilated into a growth without any purging, and with great pain, for it was no longer suppressed. 

In a **philosophical medicine**, nothing coarse or superfluous is left behind. Therefore, uncorrupted nature takes in this entire medicine and, without the need for separation, transmutes it into a nature like itself, being entirely free from waste. # SPECULATIVE PHILOSOPHY
<page-num>236</page-num>

...nature <note>original: "rupta natura"</note> being broken, it is called the **natural balsam**, which is naturally implanted in all bodies. Through this, their color and moisture—even those that are natural—are preserved from corruption as much as possible. When this balsam is lacking, the human body becomes leprous; but when it recovers through an increase [of the balsam], that which was already corrupted due to the scarcity of that same balsam is expelled as waste. **Philosophical medicine** differs from physical medicine in this: the latter [physical], when passed into the stomach united with its body, is separated no differently than food into a threefold nourishment and a twofold waste product. The former [philosophical] is instead transmitted into **balsam**, **Mercury**, or **Vulcan** <note>original: "Vulcanum"; in alchemical terms, this refers to the transformative power of internal heat or the "inner alchemist" of the body</note>. For it is necessary that the three most powerful parts of the physical body—blood, salt, and sulfur—be nourished by things similar to themselves.

Hence it happens that daily food and drink are consumed along with their bodies: for every element is sustained by an element, but all things come together simultaneously and are preserved in a balanced temperature by the **ethereal** <note>The "aether" or fifth element, thought to be the substance of the heavens and the source of life</note>. We make our balsam and its companions as conformable to this ethereal substance as possible, because there is in the human body a certain substance conformable to the ethereal which preserves the remaining elemental parts within it and makes them continue according to their strengths. 

Thus, the **spirit** of the philosophical medicine, joined with its **soul** and separated from its body, transmutes the mental parts into a substance like itself; it also preserves the physical body from corruption and corrects what is corrupted. We do not deny that our body can possess a **metaphysical medicine**—specifically when its body has been made spiritual, and the spirit has put on this body. This is what the philosophers mean when they say the **fixed is made volatile**, and finally the **volatile is made fixed** <note>A core alchemical maxim: "solve et coagula," meaning to dissolve the solid and solidify the spirit</note>. Certainly, a physical body cannot be cured by a more excellent body than a metaphysical one, nor can the human mind be better composed than by a metaphysical disposition—after the gift of divine grace, however. 

From all this, we conclude that **speculative philosophy** consists in the separation of the body once the mental union has been made. But this first union does not yet make a **Sophus** <note>A Wise Man or Master; from the Greek "Sophos"</note>, but only a mental disciple of **Sophia** <note>Wisdom</note>. The second union—that of the mind with the body—produces the **Sophus**, who hopes for and expects that third, complete, and blessed union with the First Unity. May Almighty God grant that we all be made such, and may He be the One in all. By His help, we now proceed to the first degree of truth of this most happy philosophy—a study found to be true by the more sincere philosophers—though not before those things which preceded are explained more clearly by a certain recapitulation.

# PHILOSOPHY. 237

...God does not listen; instead, He rejects their prayers as blasphemies. It would certainly be a great madness for men to ask God for bread but be unwilling to plow and sow; it is no less madness to desire a sound mind and expect it while applying no diligence at all to acquiring it. But the greatest madness is if anyone were so lazy as to think that this mind could be acquired by labor alone, without first imploring the grace of God. He fills the diligent with His blessing when they seek what is beneficial; God does not listen to the negligent, even if they ask. One is truly said to "ask" not only with the mouth, but with the heart, or when one demands something with deep affection. Therefore, before we proceed to the first step of Philosophy, I thought that students should be warned to implore divine help, and thereafter to apply the most accurate diligence in preparing themselves to receive grace of this kind. This treatise discusses this preparation only; grace, however, must be sought from above from the Giver of Lights, **God, the Best and Greatest** <note>original: "D. O. M." for *Deo Optimo Maximo*</note>. Let no one think that I have defined the mind above any more than Paul <note>The author refers to the Apostle Paul’s teachings that spiritual gifts come from God rather than human effort alone</note> teaches in the same words that faith must be sought from God alone, not from one's own strengths, nor from anywhere else but God Himself.

And because there are three principal parts of this **artificial preparation** <term>artificialis dispositio: the technical, intentional process of preparing the body or mind for philosophical work</term>—namely, the physical, the moral, and the metaphysical—it was necessary to proceed by each path in this treatment, which will become clearer to readers later. It is impossible for a man of an evil life to possess the treasure stored away for the "sons of wisdom," and an unhealthy person is ill-suited to seek it, and much less to find it. This is the reason why we speak of correcting corrupt moral and physical states through **metaphysical medicines**.

Within the human body lies a certain **metaphysical substance**, known to very few, which requires no medicine at all but is itself an incorruptible medicine. But because it is overwhelmed by the corruptions of physical bodies and hindered from exercising the power to complete its actions, philosophers have recognized through a certain divine inspiration that this virtue and celestial vigor can be liberated from its chains: not by its contrary (as **physical medicine** <note>Traditional medicine of this era followed Galen, who taught that diseases should be treated with their opposites—e.g., treating "hot" fevers with "cold" herbs</note> teaches), but by its like. Therefore, when something is found—whether inside a person or outside—that is conformable to this substance, the wise have concluded that **like must be strengthened by like** <note>original: "similia similibus esse corroboranda"</note> through peace rather than war, and that contraries should be driven out by contraries.

From these things, it is clear that there is a threefold medicine for fragile things: namely, the metaphysical, the physical, and the moral. For the **artificial preparation** of the physical body, we use a metaphysical remedy, by which we ward off its corruption toward natural digestion and expulsion; this is achieved through nature operating by means of an internally strengthened **form** <term>form: in the Aristotelian sense, the essential nature or life-force that gives a body its specific characteristics</term>. This is the preparation of our physical body performed in a metaphysical manner, through which we arrive more easily at **separation** <note>In alchemy, "separation" refers to the process of isolating the pure essence or "spirit" from the impure material body</note> without the hindrance of corrupting influences. ### *On the Philosophical Study, and the First Step.*

### CHAPTER II.

The study of philosophers is the diligent inquiry of the true and the necessary. The "True" is that from which nothing is absent, to which nothing can be absent, and much less can anything hinder it. The "Necessary" is everything that we cannot be without. Truth, therefore, is the highest virtue and an impregnable fortress, held by very few friends but besieged by innumerable enemies, now hated by almost the entire world, but an invincible pledge to those who possess it. In this citadel is contained the true and indubitable **philosopher's stone** <term>lapis philosophorum: here used metaphorically for the ultimate Truth or Divine Wisdom, rather than just a physical substance</term> and treasure, which, neither eaten by moths nor dug through by thieves, remains forever while all other things are dissolved—placed as a ruin for many, but for others unto salvation. This is the thing commonly regarded as most cheap, greatly despised, and hated, yet not actually hateful, but lovable and precious to philosophers above gems and refined gold <note>original: *aurum obrizon*</note>: the lover of all, an enemy to almost all, reachable everywhere, and found by very few or almost none, crying out through the streets to all: "Come to me all who seek, and I will lead you into the true path." This is that thing preached only by true philosophers, which conquers all things and is conquered by nothing, penetrating every hard and solid body and heart, and solidifying everything soft, and strengthening everything hard to be resisted. It makes itself met by all of us, and we do not see it, shouting and saying with a loud voice: "I am the way of truth, pass through me: because there is no other transition to life," and we do not want to hear it. It emits a scent of sweetness, but we do not perceive it. Daily it offers itself to us liberally in sweetness as a feast, and we do not taste it. ...abundance <note>original: *[abundan]tia* - completing the word from the previous page</note> it is able to grant to those who are failing, and to always abound equally. 
For what can be such a thing, except that alone which gives being to everything that is, and receives being from no other? Rather, it is being itself in its totality—all that can be—which nothing can hinder, because outside of it there is nothing. That which is nothing, truly is not; and conversely, that which truly is not, is nothing. Whatever is outside of truth truly is not: because truth is that one thing which is everything that truly exists. Therefore, falsehood—which is nothing except that which is contrary to true being, and which ought not to be, existing only through the privation of true essence—is nothing: because it truly is not. Whence true philosophers conclude that **sin** and **death** are nothing <note>original: *peccatum & mortem nihil esse* - this refers to the Scholastic doctrine of *privatio boni*, where evil has no independent existence but is merely the absence of good</note>, because they do not proceed from true being, but from the privation of true essence. But let us see what the doctrine of the pagan <note>original: *gentilium* — referring here to the pre-Christian Greek and Roman philosophers</note> philosophers is. They define the highest good <term>Summum bonum: the ultimate goal or supreme value in a philosophical system</term> as "living well," which they divide into the honorable and the useful. ## *On the second degree of philosophers, which is called Knowledge.* ##

### CHAPTER III. ###

<unclear>Co</unclear>gnition <term>Cognitio: the process of gaining certain understanding or "Knowledge"</term> is the certain and indubitable resolution of opinions conceived about the truth of anything, achieved through experience. Opinion is a doubtful presumption of truth clinging in the mind. Experience is the manifest demonstration of truth. Resolution, indeed, is the definition of a doubt. We cannot become certain about any doubt otherwise than by experiencing it, and nowhere better than within ourselves. Therefore, let us verify what we said above regarding truth, making our beginning from ourselves. We said above that piety consists in the knowledge of oneself; hence it is that I begin philosophical knowledge from that very point. Truly, no one can know himself unless he knows *what* he is, rather than *who* he is, upon whom he depends, or to whom he belongs (for no one is his own master according to the law of truth), and for what end he was made. Once these things are known, piety begins, which is concerned with two things: namely, the Creator, and the creature similar to Himself. It is impossible for a creature to know itself by itself, unless its Creator is known first. How can an effect be known before its cause, since the cause precedes every beginning, its middle, and its end? Or shall someone instead approach the matter from the end?

God is without beginning and end, existing through Himself, filled with all glory, which He did not wish to possess alone out of His own liberality, but rather to make us—whom He fashioned in His own image—sharers of it, as the first exemplar and mystery of His generosity. How is it then that we remain ignorant of that wondrous secret <term>Arcanum: a hidden or profound mystery, often used in alchemy and spiritual philosophy</term> concerning the truth? # CONTEMPLATION #

...from which <note>referring to the "massa" or material of the human body mentioned on the previous page</note> we were made more prone to any vile thing than to that which, despite our lowliness, made us most precious: indeed, we would have been superior to the angels if we had remained in such a rank of dignity. Marvel, all you wretched mortals who are with me, that the supreme craftsman of things <note>original: "summus rerum artifex" — a common metaphor for God as the Divine Architect</note> wished to handle with his hands the most vile material from the mud of the earth, and from it raise up the most precious creature. Let us not think this was done without reason, but rather so that we may recognize what we are, and restrain ourselves from the pride of arrogance. By doing otherwise, every one of us hates the poor man whom God chose, even though he consists of the same mass from which we were all made. From this it follows that God is not a respecter of persons <note>original: "personarum non sit acceptor" — a theological concept meaning God does not judge by outward status or wealth</note>, but is a lover of poverty and humility, and an enemy of lofty pride. No one can know the Creator better than a craftsman is known from his work. 

We see, therefore, who He is: one who from the most vile can raise up the most precious; certainly none can do this except Him who created both. In no way can a butler transform wine into water, yet He can do it who created both wine and water. He did something even greater when He transformed earth into a living soul, and what is greatest of all, He endowed it with the supreme gift of blessedness: namely, His own **image** and **likeness**. Through these, it is granted to all to be saved who receive this gift; but what will be given to those unwilling to receive it freely? Certainly nothing. Let them, therefore, have what is theirs, so that the place of justice may be preserved. What each has chosen from the beginning is his own—namely, damnation. The gift of eternal salvation is free for those who receive it with thanksgiving. Since, therefore, we are at once a vile and a precious thing, let each of us see what he prefers: the matter is clearer in itself to those who understand than it would be through further explanation. 

We know the vile thing that we are, and the most excellent One from whom we proceeded. It remains in this business that we weigh carefully why, or for what end, we were made. Almighty God created the first man, **Adam**, in His **image** and **likeness**, so that he might exist for God Himself unto eternity for His glory, and might be immortal, not anxious, lacking nothing, always rejoicing in God, and not subject to earthly passions. But because he did not acknowledge such a great gift, he made it vile. He knew, however, that he had been made perfect and wise, but he did not remain in that knowledge. Let us consider, therefore, how much good the knowledge of this gift brings, and how much evil the contempt for this gift and the Word of God has brought; for it rendered him mortal from being perpetually immortal. For he who dies eternally lives forever in the agony of death and never ceases to die. Hence it is that this is called "perpetual death," just as that is called "eternal life" in which we shall live for God forever and never cease to live. Since, therefore, our first parent had made us all rebels and enemies along with himself, Almighty God, moved by mercy, wished to enter into peace with us who had become hardened—He who is the author of peace. Who will be so stone-hearted that, when he [hears of divine peace...] <note>The text ends mid-sentence; the catchword "vinae" suggests the next word is "divinae" (divine)</note>

# PHILOSOPHY #

Q 3

<meta>catchword: who</meta>

...of divine goodness, who, having turned this mystery over in his mind, would not be reconciled with his enemy, even though he has received an injury from him? How does it finally happen that among mortals, neither the one who gave offense nor the one who suffered it wishes to approach the other for the sake of reconciliation? Certainly for no other reason than that no one knows himself, and consequently, neither knows God his creator, nor his neighbor as an equivalent creature. Thus it happens that he who is ignorant of peace does not embrace it. For peace is the root of mercy. For he who does not have peace will not exercise mercy, nor will he attain it until he has peace. There is no reason to confuse peace and mercy here; because peace is the cause of mercy, just as <term>piety</term> <note>original: "pietas" — here referring to a sense of duty, devotion, and right relationship with God</note> is the cause of peace. Therefore, if we have peace with God through the knowledge of piety, we are necessarily going to have it likewise with our neighbor, whether enemy or friend. This is especially true when we consider that the **Supreme Craftsman of things** <note>original: "summus rerum artifex"</note>, through the embrace of peace, showed his mercy to a little worm <note>original: "vermiculo" — a common metaphor in this period to emphasize the vast distance between the majesty of God and the lowliness of humanity</note> who was a slave to the devil. 

O wretched mortals, how many of us expect mercy from God, yet do not acknowledge our misery before him? From where, I ask, does Mercy <note>original: "Misericordia"</note> come, if not from the confession of misery <note>original: "miseriæ"</note>, through a contrition of the heart made for the sake of amendment? If we are finally no longer ignorant of our own misery and that of our brothers, but weigh it with an equal balance, we—who have become wealthier in the goods of this age—will not consider ourselves more abundant in eternal riches than those who are completely destitute of the world's wealth. Who among mortals truly considers this, and will not comfort a needy brother with the sharing of the goods entrusted to him alone in this world? Show me one who considers this, and I will soon show you someone who acknowledges such a divine secret. 

In all these things, God has not yet wished to fully explain His love toward us. Truly, even as His justice accuses us—which can no more be diminished than His mercy—did He not wish to spare us rather than His own son, in whom **Peace and Justice** have kissed each other? <note>A reference to Psalm 85:10, often interpreted as the moment where God's demand for justice and His desire for mercy were reconciled in the person of Christ.</note> Why then do we not kiss one another, having been made equal brothers in Christ, when the Supreme Craftsman of things kisses us, wretched little worms, and in His only-begotten Son makes the most excellent creatures out of the most vile ones, made so by their own evil? All who acknowledge God in the Son, and likewise the Son in the Father through the Holy Spirit [whom they do not resist], also acknowledge their brother, and none others. 

These are the true and indubitable foundations of true philosophy. But because they are not yet known by all, though heard by many, a doubt might still cling to the minds of some who are not yet well-resolved, as to whether the imagination of these aforementioned things can excite the love of truth in us. It would be worthwhile for them to set aside this ambiguity by an experiment conducted by themselves and within themselves, in the following manner. Let each one carefully consider within himself those things spoken of above, having tasted—

->SPECULATIVE MATTERS<-

...from every side, let him meditate more often with a sincere heart: thus, little by little, he will perceive a few sparks shining more and more daily before his mental eyes, and they will grow into such a great light that in time everything necessary to him will become known. He will no longer hesitate in the truth in any way. Instead, by gradually becoming accustomed to the exercise of piety and justice through the ritual and path previously described, he will feel a tranquility of soul. Drawn by this at last, he will understand that there is greater delight in the spirit than in the body. True knowledge does not begin until the Soul—presented with a comparison between eternal and fleeting things, and between life and death—chooses to be joined to the spirit <note>original: "animus" — often used to distinguish the rational or higher spirit from the "anima" or life-force soul</note> with a greater delight for this attraction than for the Body. From this knowledge the Mind <note>original: "Mens"</note> arises, and the voluntary separation from the body begins. The soul, looking on one side at the filth and death of the body, and on the other at the excellence and perpetual happiness of the spirit, desires to be connected with the latter (by the arrangement of the divine breath) while utterly neglecting the former. Thus it hungers for this alone, which it sees has been determined by GOD for salvation and glory. The Body is then compelled to stoop into a union with both of these who are now united.

This is that wondrous transformation <note>original: "transmutatio"</note> of the body into spirit, and the spirit into body, about which the Sages have left us this saying: **make the fixed volatile, and the volatile fixed** <note>This is a central axiom of alchemy. It refers to the process of "spiritualizing" matter (making the solid "fixed" body into "volatile" spirit) and "materializing" spirit (fixing the spirit into a stable, perfected body).</note>, so that you may have our mastery. Understand this to mean: make the stubborn body manageable, so that through the excellence of the spirit agreeing with the soul, it becomes a most constant body, capable of enduring all trials. For gold is tested by fire, by which everything that is not gold is rejected. O most excellent gold of the philosophers, by which the children of wisdom are enriched—not by that common gold which is so greedily desired!

Draw near, you who seek the treasure of the philosophers with such varied effort! First, recognize what that stone is which you have rejected before you seek it. It is a miracle above all miracles that anyone should hunger for something unknown to them; it certainly seems foolish for men to seek a thing whose truth they do not know while investigating it, for no hope is left in such a search. I advise all those searching, therefore, to first know the true existence of what they seek before they begin the search; in this way, it will not happen that they are frustrated by their labors. The wise man seeks what he loves, and he cannot love what he does not know; otherwise, he would be a fool. From knowledge, therefore, is born the love of all truth, which alone flourishes in all true philosophers.

### Recapitulation of the second degree.
#### CHAPTER III.

There is no reason for anyone to think that I wish to treat only of theological matters; rather, I speak of things which should not be hidden even from a commoner <note>original: "rusticum" — a peasant or unlearned person</note> or from children. Yet, from these things—when they are sought more deeply than the literal word sounds—men draw all science and art in all things, both celestial and secular.

->PHILOSOPHY<-

...the sons of wisdom bring forth. In vain do you all labor, seekers of the hidden secrets of nature, when, having entered upon another way, you attempt to discover the virtues of earthly things through earthly means. Learn, therefore, to know heaven through heaven, not through the earth; rather, learn to know the virtues of this [earth] through those of that [heaven]. For no one ascends into the heaven which you seek, unless he who descended from heaven (which you do not seek) enlightens him <note>original: "Nemo enim ascēdit in cælũ... nisi qui de cælo... descendit" — a paraphrase of John 3:13, applied here to alchemical enlightenment</note>. You seek an incorruptible medicine, which might not only transmute bodies from corruption into a true temperament <note>a perfectly balanced state of the elements or humors</note>, but also preserve those tempered bodies for a very long time: such a thing you will never be able to find anywhere else than in heaven. Heaven, by its own power, through invisible rays converging from every side into the center of the earth, penetrates all elements, and generates and nourishes all things composed of those elements. No one can generate within himself, but only in something similar to himself, which also comes from himself. Even the mixed offspring retains the nature of both parents within itself, such that in it both parents are found in potential and in act. Who will hesitate any longer—unless he be as dull as a stone—in this philosophical generation?

If this knowledge is still not sufficient for you, friend reader, along with that which was given in our *Key* <term>Clavis: a common title for an introductory or explanatory text that "unlocks" alchemical secrets</term>, there is no reason for me to discuss this with you at greater length. But lest there remain any handle <note>opportunity or cause</note> for you to complain about me, I shall say more. Learn to know from yourself whatever exists both in heaven and on earth, so that you may become wise in all things. Are you unaware that heaven and the elements were once one, separated from each other by divine craftsmanship so that they might be able to generate both you and all things? If you know this, the rest cannot escape you, or else you lack all intellect. Again, in every generation, such a separation is necessary as I said above must be done concerning yourself, before you set your sail <note>original: "velum applices" — a nautical metaphor for beginning a voyage or endeavor</note> toward the studies of true philosophy. You will never make the one thing you seek from other things, unless that which you have heard (and will hear more of in the following) first becomes one within yourself: for such is the will of God, that the pious may obtain the pious work they seek, and the perfect may complete the other thing upon which they were intent. To men of ill-will, nothing is given to reap except what they have sown: indeed, what is more, very often their good seed is turned into tares <note>original: "lolium" — a weed that mimics wheat, often used as a metaphor for spiritual failure</note> because of their malice. Act, therefore, so that you become such as you wish the work you seek to be.

### *Concerning the third philosophical degree.*
#### CHAPTER IV.

Philosophical love is called the union of secrets from one back into one through peace. Peace is truly the concord of parts within the whole through union. God especially loves union, because He is one, and whatever He ever created, He enclosed under union. From one determined thing, made through one indefinite thing, proceed all things which are finite, and again each thing tends toward its own "one" by natural instinct: from which, if any should deviate, they are judged by philosophers to be contained under the secret binary <note>the number two, representing duality, division, or the fall from unity</note>, and must be reduced to union through the ternary <note>the number three, representing the reconciliation of opposites and the return to divine order</note>. # SPECULATIVA
### [The Speculative Philosophy]

God [created] heaven and earth: and all things that are in them, united together in a hidden way, yet separate in their manifestation. Under the name of "earth," the Elements are included, which are contained by heaven, and they embrace one another with such a bond of love that its like is scarcely seen among other creatures. We see brute animals joining in pairs by a divine order with a more sincere bond when they consist of purer elements, such as birds; the rest agree less due to the lower purity of the matter from which they are forged, yet they are joined, though more indiscriminately. Let us come to the most excellent creature created from the vilest matter, namely man, whom God created from the slime of the earth—an animal movable by itself, which He then made one with a rational spirit. Who does not perceive that, by the occasion of his being moved by this spirit alone, he is more irregular than other living beings? Yet insofar as he is truly made rational, no work among the works of God can be more excellent.

From this man, while he was still in that most excellent state before the Fall, God separated woman, bone of his bone and flesh of his flesh, so that they might be united more firmly than other living beings. Things are not said to be "united" unless they were first separated from a single whole; otherwise, they are merely "joined" <note>The author distinguishes between *uniri* (uniting things that were once one) and *conjungi* (joining two foreign things together). In alchemy, true "union" requires substances of the same root.</note>. Since he could not procreate within himself, it was necessary to procreate in another. For this reason, human generation is to be revered above all others, <margin><image-desc>A hand with a pointing finger (manicule) emphasizing the following passage</image-desc></margin> because it happens between two who were previously one, and are made one again by divine marriage, as Scripture testifies:
> And the two shall be in one flesh, for whose sake each shall leave father and mother and cling to his other part. <note>original: "Et erunt duo in carne una..." — a reference to Genesis 2:24 and Matthew 19:5</note>

One should not think otherwise than that the husband is the wife's inseparable other part of her body, and she is his; when we see them behaving otherwise, we shall judge them not to be united, but only joined—not by true love, but for the sake of base gain or the extinguishing of illicit appetite; when that fire cools, everything grows cold at once. Such is not <term>philosophical love</term> <note>original: "amor philosophicus" — in alchemy, this refers to the chemical affinity and permanent bonding of substances during the "Alchemical Wedding."</note>: for kindled by an utterly inextinguishable fire, it is not put out; those who are united through the spirit remain spirits in union, while those joined through the body, the bodies are easily dissolved. There is also the specific love of parents for children and children for parents, which can in no way be compared to the philosophical: for a father would not wish to suffer the loss of even his smallest joint for his child, nor a son for his parent, much less a sister or brother for their sibling, or any friend. Who would willingly undergo death for himself, let alone for someone else?

Where, then, is this love to be sought? Certainly nowhere else than from where love itself proceeded. "God so loved the world" (understand this as "man") <note>original: "Sic Deus dilexit mundum" — John 3:16</note> that He willed His own Son to be born a man, who could die for men, and by His death pay the debt of justice—the death by which we were to be punished. For the Son of God could not die, but having been made man, He died as a perfect man, the Son of Man, and as a just one [fulfilling] justice...

<summary>This page argues that true "philosophical" union—the goal of alchemy—is modeled on the biblical creation of Eve from Adam, representing a reunion of separated parts into a single, inseparable whole. The author contrasts this permanent, spiritual bond with the fleeting physical attractions of the animal and common human world, eventually pointing to Christ's sacrifice as the ultimate expression of this love.</summary>

# PHILOSOPHY

...completed. O, how wondrous is the love of God toward men! It is not from the empty philosophy of Aristotle, nor from the rest of the wise men of this world, that such happy waves flow—waves which we (while that philosophy keeps us occupied with vain studies) pass by, O wretched companions! This divine love calls our minds to another kind of philosophy.

->*A colloquy in which the Spirit attempts to draw the Soul and the Body to himself.*<-
->*The speakers are Spirit, Soul, Body, and the Philosophy of Love, designated by these letters:*<-
->*S., A., B., & Ph.*<-

**S.** Come now, my soul and my body, flee now and follow your spirit; let us ascend this high mountain standing before us. From its summit, I shall show you this two-way path <note>original: *iter hoc bivium*. This refers to the "Pythagorean Y," a traditional symbol where a single path splits into two: a difficult path of virtue and an easy path of vice.</note> about which Pythagoras spoke through a cloud and without light. Our eyes have been opened, and the Sun of piety and justice shines before us; with it as our guide, we cannot turn aside from the way of truth. Turn your eyes first to the right, so they do not see vanity before they have perceived wisdom. Do you see that shining and impregnable castle?

**A. & B.** We see it.

**S.** Within it dwells Philosophical Love, from whose fountain flow the living waters; whoever tastes them once shall thirst for vanity no longer. From that place, so pleasant and sweet, one must progress straight to a more pleasant place still, where Sophia <note>The Greek word for "Wisdom," often personified in alchemical texts as a divine bride or the goal of the Great Work.</note> dwells. From her fountain also gush forth waters far more blessed than the first; if enemies should taste them, they are compelled to enter into peace. Of those who arrive there, most tend to strive higher, but not all achieve what they desire. There is a place beyond those mentioned which mortals can scarcely approach, unless they have been taken up to the rank of immortality by the divine power. But before they may be introduced, they are forced to strip off the world, leaving behind the spoils of this fleeting life. Once they have arrived there, they no longer fear death; rather, they daily embrace it more sweetly than anything in the world was ever judged sweet enough for their embrace. Whoever progresses beyond these three places vanishes from the eyes of men.

But if you wish to see the second and third places, let us ascend higher. Look: above the first crystalline citadel, you see another of silver; beyond that is a third of adamant <note>A legendary stone of indestructible hardness, often identified with diamond.</note>; the fourth, however, does not fall under the senses until one has gone beyond the third. This is the golden place of perpetual happiness, free from anxiety, and filled with every everlasting joy. Now let us turn our eyes to the left. Look, you see the world full of pleasures and riches, in which nothing can displease the fading eye; but let us see the end of this pilgrimage. You clearly perceive a dark valley filled with smoky gloom at the edge of the horizon.

**A. & B.** We see it indeed.

**S.** When those who enter this wide way reach that place, their comforts are turned

# SPECULATIVE PHILOSOPHY

...into torments, of which there is no end: for if you would lend a more attentive ear, you could perceive from here a howling, unless the rumor of their joy—those who so anxiously strive for their own ruin—prevents you.

**A. & C.** We hear it indeed, but how is it that they do not return here?

**S.** Because they do not see this valley of misery <note>original: *miseriæ vallem*</note> until they have passed the final path of repentance <note>original: *pœnitentiæ*</note>, after which there is no return.

**A. & C.** Are there other paths by which they might turn aside from that grave danger?

**S.** Indeed, there are only two side-paths, pressing toward us here to the right, as you see. For from this place where we now stand, it is necessary for all who repent to make their passage through the first citadel, so that they themselves may see what you see now.

**A. & C.** We wonder that they do not see the valley of misery sooner.

**S.** It is no wonder, for the path is flat, easy, and pleasant, seducing men by its allure; moreover, the horizon is narrow on any plain. But if they had ascended here as we have, they would have perceived the exit of both paths.

**A. & C.** By what names are they called?

**S.** They are called the **Broad Way of Error**; the first of the side-paths is the **Way of Infirmity**, the second the **Way of Poverty**, and this one in which we stand is called the **Way of Truth**. At the entrance of each is placed an angel of the Lord, who is called the **Drawing of the Divine Spirit** <term>tractus: the theological and alchemical concept of a magnetic pull or spiritual attraction that God exerts upon the soul to lead it toward salvation.</term>. Here, in this first pass, he draws everyone; if wretched mortals resist this drawing, the reins are loosened for the stubborn. The Lord still waits for those who have entered the way of error, until, having for a while abused worldly delights, they fall into bodily infirmities <note>original: *infirmitates*</note> through their own petulance—and not undeservedly, for that was the very thing by which they were drawn into error. Very few who happen to recognize their error return to this place through the first way of repentance. The remaining greatest part, with those who did not repent in the first place, proceed further in their stubbornness. Some who refused to be corrected through infirmity, and others who have not yet been corrected, are permitted to fall into poverty for their own sake; of these, very few enter the second way of repentance. But most proceed, blinded in their error, until they fall into the pit from which one may not rise.

**A. & C.** We see few returning through the ways of repentance.

**S.** The body prevents this.

**C.** But I would rather die a hundred times than complete the broad way to its end.

**S.** You speak thus because you have seen; but see that you are mindful of this hereafter.

**C.** Wherever you go, I will follow most readily; but before we depart from here, tell me, I pray, how it happened that we did not enter the broad way?

**S.** Those to whom it was given from heaven to receive the first drawing of the Lord should credit God, not themselves.

**C.** Yet all are drawn.

**S.** True, but not all receive the drawing.

**C.** What is the cause of this?

**S.** Because, standing at the crossroads <note>original: *bivio*; likely referring again to the Pythagorean Y mentioned on the previous page.</note>, they turn their eyes more toward the vanities on the left than toward this river of living water <note>original: *viventis aquæ*</note>, which flows with such admirable craftsmanship from the summit of the mountain where we now stand.

**C.** What is the name of the mountain and the river?

**S.** The name of both is the **First Drawing of the Lord**.

**C.** Are there other drawings...

# PHILOSOPHY

...drawings <note>original: *tractus*; here referring to the spiritual "pulls" or "attractions" mentioned on the previous page</note> besides these three which you have already explained? **S.** There are many intermediate ones between these, which are felt by everyone in their own conscience, but they are held in low regard by those who are unwilling, as was said before, to receive them. **C.** What is it in this river that you lead us to that is so admirable? **S.** Have you, or has anyone, ever seen such a vast quantity of water falling from so high a place without a terrifying roar? Are you unaware that hanging water <note>likely referring to a waterfall or a suspended aqueduct-like stream</note>, which exceeds all the powers of the world, can terrify even the most intrepid man—or even the intrepid Mars himself (if such a one exists)—by the stirring of the sound and the wind, as can be seen in many places? **C.** Certainly, I have been on certain hills where the water flowing down from a bridge far off was enough to terrify and agitate the passers-by with its wind, able to throw down even the strongest; unless, by some industry and by regaining their strength, the minds of the men conquered their fear and made a passage for themselves.

**S.** The first drawing <note>original: *tractus*</note> in this place is the admiration of the river; it is followed by the desire to taste the water, and a great love for seeing its origin. This love draws the one who tastes it—just as a magnet <note>original: *adamas*; traditionally referring to a diamond or a loadstone/magnet</note> draws iron—to this place, so that he may see what the distinctions of things are. **C.** I would never have considered this by myself, even if I had seen the opposite happen in lower places. **S.** Your eyes are made of flesh, which do not perceive those things that transcend the world. Those who see things superficially, or only from what is manifest, do not think there is anything else in the nature of things besides that which falls under the senses. It does not happen that such people—as many as there are—reach this place, unless their spirit feels and receives the "drawing" of the Lord, arising from the wonderful consideration of the river and the mountain, and by a special gift.

**C.** This one thing I still desire to know from you before we depart from here: What is the meaning of such a difficult approach to such pleasant places, both because of the roughness and narrowness of the path, and because of the perfectly straight course of this river, such that nothing could be drawn more straightly even with a stretched string? **S.** I see that you, my Body, willingly <note>original: *libenter*; this matches the catchword "liben-" from the previous page</note> prolong your delay here, so that you may feast your eyes longer on worldly masks <note>original: *larvis*; can mean ghosts, masks, or delusions</note>. The fact that these masks so often twist you toward the left (even if you seek the right) gives me cause to suspect that you inquire about these things not so much out of a curious desire for knowledge, but because you see that once you have withdrawn from here, you will be deprived of the sight of the world. **C.** Let us set these matters aside; answer me at least. **S.** Regarding the difficulty, so that you may be satisfied, understand first that there is no path to glory other than by the cross <note>original: *per crucem*</note>. Just as there is no access to any arduous thing except by the greatest labor, it would be easy to hold a light thing in low esteem, and difficult to value a heavy one. The lightness of the roughness is the end, just as life is the end of death, and as the breadth is the end of narrowness. Furthermore, everything that leads into the path of truth ought to be straight and lacking in ambushes or windings. Now you have what you wish for, and there is no reason for us to linger further; follow us. **C.** Let this be the last thing. **S.** You have now heard everything that is necessary; I will not delay. **C.** At least, you, Soul, stay with me for a little while. **A.** Neither you, nor the Spirit...

### SPECULATIVE PHILOSOPHY

I would have gladly deferred, but I remained silent until I heard the reasons of both. The things that the Spirit speaks please me, as do yours; they bring nothing but delay to my ears. 

**Body:** I see that I, miserable man, am now about to be conquered. 

**Spirit:** Truly miserable; follow us, so that you may become happy with us. 

**Body:** If only! But what can I alone do against two? 

**Spirit:** Be silent; after a few days, you will deal alone with the alone. 

**Body:** What do I hear? Perhaps you, who are our guide, will lead us into trackless wastes? 

**Spirit:** Far be it; I will be with you as long as you exist. 

**Body:** Reveal, then, what this riddle means. 

**Spirit:** Just as the eyes are, so is the intellect; and all things you possess are carnal <note>meaning "of the flesh" or purely physical</note>. 

**Body:** At least let me understand. 

**Spirit:** What if you do not perceive the things before your eyes? When I speak of things you do not see, how will you perceive them? 

**Body:** Beyond the fact that this stony, narrow, and thorny path twists me in miserable ways, you aggravate this mass—which is heavy enough on its own—with your words. 

**Spirit:** I am only trying to lighten it. 

**Body:** You have not done so. 

**Spirit:** How would you like it done? 

**Body:** By speaking plainly. 

**Spirit:** I have not learned your ways. 

**Body:** I will achieve nothing with you alone. Hey, my soul, whom I have always held dear, won't you speak? Won't you provide help to your most faithful friend? 

**Soul:** I am in doubt between you two; I play the part of each equally. 

**Body:** Yet you follow the spirit more willingly than me. 

**Soul:** You are completely delirious. 

**Body:** If only I had stayed at the crossroads. 

**Soul:** You would have done that. 

**Body:** I could not without you, without whom I can execute nothing. 

**Soul:** Nor can I stand my ground without the Spirit; without whom, it is necessary that I be without you. 

**Body:** And you have learned to speak in <term>parables</term> <note>original: *parabolice*; speaking in allegories or spiritual metaphors rather than literal facts</note> in such a short time? 

**Spirit:** Is it anything but simple? But because the speech is naked, yet you are enveloped in darkness, it seems <term>amphibological</term> <note>ambiguous or capable of two meanings</note> or allegorical to you. 

**Body:** I will achieve nothing with you; I will be silent, just as you yourself were a while ago, so that you might reserve these things for me for the future. 

**Soul:** Nothing but good. 

**Body:** The Spirit seduced you. 

**Spirit:** Not at all; rather, I lead her and you here to salvation. 

**Body:** So you say. 

**Spirit:** You will not believe before you see. 

**Body:** Do you lead me as a blind man? 

**Spirit:** Exactly; and you have never spoken more truly. 

**Body:** Woe! Intolerable crime! Will you persuade me that I lack my own eyes? 

**Spirit:** Indeed, I will teach you. 

**Body:** I will listen, please. 

**Spirit:** Did you see us at the root of the Mountain of the Lord drink from the river of the fountain of love? 

**Body:** You didn't drink? 

**Spirit:** Behold, now you have openly confessed your blindness. 

**Body:** Why did you not bid me drink with you? 

**Spirit:** Because you cannot until you see with us. 

**Body:** When will that finally happen? 

**Spirit:** When you have become one of those to be united with us. 

**Body:** Again, when? 

**Spirit:** When we have arrived together at the <term>adamantine</term> <note>original: *adamantinam*; referring to something unbreakable, like diamond or hard steel</note> citadel of truth. 

**Body:** Let us hurry then, lest I, though seeing, be called blind any longer. Look, we have reached the first citadel; I will knock. 

**Body:** What need is there? The gate lacks doors. 

**Spirit:** It is not fitting for a traveling stranger to enter another's home without first asking leave. Bid us be introduced, whoever you are that rules here. 

**Philosophy:** What guest, rare indeed, calls out? 

**Spirit:** Three disciples of philosophy. 

**Philosophy:** What do you seek here? 

**Spirit:** To learn Philosophy. 

**Philosophy:** What need is there to learn again those things you have already learned? 

**Spirit:** Until now we have fed on thistles; we are <term>longing</term> <note>original catchword: *anhela-* from *anhelantes*; literally "panting" or "gasping" with desire</note> for happier beets—

# PHILOSOPHY.

...we long for. **Philosophy:** Do you desire to fill your belly with beets? <note>original: "Betis"; likely a pun on "beta" (the vegetable) and a low-quality or basic form of sustenance.</note> **Companions:** With any food better than what we had before; for the grasses we grazed on—now stinging from the left, soon from the right—left behind the sharpest thorns between our teeth, which makes such food sickening to us. **Philosophy:** I hear that you have been steeped in ways more unrefined than our school allows. But because we are not accustomed to refusing any who come to us, you shall be let in—but not before you lay down your horns <note>In an academic context, "horns" often referred to the arrogance or "bestial" nature of uninitiated students (beania), or perhaps the stubbornness of logical disputation.</note> before the gate. **Companions:** We are ready to obey your commands. **Philosophy:** It is our custom that new disciples be examined. **Companions:** So be it. **Philosophy:** What is philosophy? **Companions:** It is the love of Wisdom. **Philosophy:** What is Wisdom? **Companions:** It is the highest wisdom of the truth of all things. **Philosophy:** What is love? **Companions:** It is an insatiable desire for known truth. **Philosophy:** From where do you have these things? **Companions:** From the drawing of the Lord. **Philosophy:** Through whom? **Companions:** Through those whom He taught first, so that they might teach others. **Philosophy:** What did you hear in the Universities? **Companions:** The philosophy of Aristotle. **Philosophy:** What does this teach? **Companions:** To bicker contentiously, and to argue stubbornly "for and against," as they say. **Philosophy:** "For and against"? What kind of Chimera <note>A mythical beast made of mismatched parts; here used to describe a logical monster or absurdity.</note> beast is this? **Companions:** I know not what kind of sophistry it is; it allows one to twist a matter now to the right, then to the left, like a man with a nose of wax <note>A "wax nose" (nasus cereus) was a common 17th-century metaphor for a text or argument that could be molded to mean anything the speaker wanted.</note>. It was perhaps devised by some "big-nosed" <note>original: "nasutulo"; meaning a sneering or overly-critical person.</note> fellow who, after unjustly rebuking others with that ridicule, invented this to escape the hands of others. **Philosophy:** For what use? **Companions:** For the sake of showing off one’s learning. **Philosophy:** Is it therefore a deceptive teaching? **Companions:** At least that which we heard is, for those who are most steeped in it have the least wisdom. **Philosophy:** In that you are truly wise—that those are most wise who understand less concerning things that can be perceived. Before you enter here, your names must be written in the register of our School. **Companions:** My name is Spirit (or Mind), hers is Soul, and the third is Body. **Philosophy:** Close enough companions. **Companions:** Indeed, three brothers born of a single birth. **Philosophy:** Having first called upon the true light, speak thus with me:

> O Almighty Father, eternal God, Creator of all things in heaven and on earth, who created us in your image and likeness, not so that you might reduce us to nothing, but that we might exist for your glory: give us the grace of your Holy Spirit, by which we may be able to understand and know what your will is, so that by your help we may do it, and in your light we may see light, and following the truth with true love, we may attain it. Amen.

Enter now, for the glory of God and your own salvation, the gates and gymnasium of philosophical Love, in which perpetual love is taught. Sit down at the feast, so that each may be refreshed by his own food and drink. First, let us pray to God:

> The eyes of all look to you in hope, Lord, and you give them food in due season; you open your hand and fill every living thing with blessing. Man does not live by bread alone, but by every word that proceeds from the mouth of the Lord.

Body, eat and drink the physical things set before you; your companions drink in their food not with the mouth, but with the ears. I shall now take care of them. Spirit and Soul, lend your kind ears—
