...-ize. <note>The word "Philosophabitis" (You shall philosophize) or a similar term begun on the previous page concludes here.</note> Although I do not doubt that you first heard of the effectiveness of philosophical study and knowledge through the Lord's drawing and His angel, nevertheless, being heavier then with the weight of the body than you will be now, you were scarcely able to bear everything. It would be worth the effort, before you come to the fountain of love, to briefly review those things which will seem necessary here. 

Before the Fall of Adam, neither the broad left-hand path nor the "valley of misery" existed; instead, the way to these most happy places lay open to everyone from every side. After man’s first disobedience, the Lord narrowed this once vast road into a very tight and difficult path (as you see), at the entrance of which He placed a Cherub angel, holding a double-edged sword in his hand, to keep everyone away from entering the happy fatherland. Turning away from here because of the sin of their first parent, the sons of Adam constructed for themselves a broad path to the left—the one you have avoided. 

Much later, God, the Best and Greatest <note>original: "D.O.M." for *Deo Optimo Maximo*</note>, entered into the "secrets of His secrets." In these mysteries—while love took pity and justice brought accusation—He decided to snatch the sword of His wrath from the angel's hands, substituting a golden triple-barbed hook in its place, while the sword was hung upon a tree. And so God's wrath was changed into love, while justice was preserved. 

Before this happened, that river did not exist as it does now, gathered into a single stream; rather, before the Fall, it was spread equally over the entire world like a dew. But afterward, it returned to where it had come from. Finally, when "peace and justice kissed each other" <note>A reference to Psalm 85:10</note>, the water of grace descended more abundantly, flowing from on high and now washing over the whole world. Those who turn toward the left side—some of them see the sword hanging in the tree and know its history, but because they are too rooted in the world, they pass by. Some see its power but neglect to investigate it; others neither see it nor wish to have seen it. All of these direct their pilgrimage straight to the valley, unless some are pulled back toward Mount Zion by the hooks of recovery <note>original: "resipiscentiae," meaning a return to one's right mind or "coming to"</note> or repentance. In our own age (which is the age of grace), the sword has been changed into Christ our Savior, who ascended the tree of the cross for our sins. All these things signify the times of the laws of nature, of the divine law, and then of grace. Now hear what the state of the "path of errors" is.

### The Fabric of the World.

**Philosophy:** God said to Adam after the Fall: "In the sweat of your face you shall eat your bread, and in pain your wife shall give birth." He cursed the earth because of man, and it was made barren—though previously it produced the most abundant fruit without any cultivation, but only by heavenly plenty. But even though it is now worked by human labors, it seems to bear little but thistles and thorns. From that time when man stripped himself of truth, necessity itself made him anxious about seeking food and clothing. This necessity is the "other mother" of studies and the inventor of the first arts, such as agriculture and the practice of herding. And so there began the first...

<meta>This page continues Philosophy’s speech regarding the history of the human condition. ### PHILOSOPHY. 255

...the first and sincere humans sought only what they could not do without; the impure, however, seized not only those things, but everything weaker than themselves, whether by right or by wrong. Nakedness taught the first man to cover his bare flesh with leaves; eventually, as human industry <term>industria: in this context, a mix of hard work and inventive ingenuity</term> gradually increased through necessity (as is its way), they covered themselves with the skins of animals. 

Soon after, hunger taught them to dig, to sow, and to gather the harvest in its season; to care for flocks, herds, livestock, and pastures; to nourish the family; to establish customs and the laws of nature; and to preserve peace by protecting themselves and their herds from the harshness of rain and weather with huts and roofs. All of this was the burden of basic necessity in the beginning. 

Content with these arts, the first fathers of the age lived happily in times of peace. But once the earth was filled, it was no longer possible for everyone to have their own portion of land, or for all to be farmers and shepherds. Instead, those who possessed nothing had to serve others in various ways. Curiosity produced various kinds of clothing and structures; from this, tailors, shoemakers, and smiths—those governed by the "needle and the hammer"—took their origin. The wealth gained from their labor allowed some to seek leisure, acquiring only as much land as was needed for food and clothing. For others, wealth grew; seeing the scarcity in one place and the abundance in another, they engaged in commerce <term>mercimonium: trade or merchant activity</term>. Thus came carriers and drivers of beasts of burden. 

Even the preparation of food developed its own crafts: for the sake of helping travelers, the arts of the baker, the oven-tender, the butcher, the cook, and the wine-merchant were devised. In the beginning, all these things were managed in good faith, until self-interest and brotherly hatred broke in. From that moment, the character of humanity changed. The hunger for possession grew alongside wealth, continuing to this very day, where no man trusts another, nor even himself. 

For his own convenience, each man turned huts into splendid houses, which eventually grew into villages, towns, fortresses, and cities; suburbs expanded into great metropolises. Yet these were not immune to hatred. Later, through the corruption of time, idle men appeared who wished to live not by their own work but by the labor of others; this birthed war, especially among neighbors. This, in turn, gave rise to the construction of ditches, walls, ramparts, and bastions as a defense against such injuries. 

To fuel every kind of vice—for leisure is known to be their nourishment—a cursed and diabolical invention was brought up from the underworld: cannons and engines of war <term>tormentorum: a general term for heavy artillery or siege engines</term>. By these, the very society of the human race would have collapsed, had it not been for divine help. This was the final development of these "new arts," completing the structure of the world. 

And because of the variety of these things, those who love the world call it "beautiful" <note>original: *mundum*. This is a play on words, as the Latin *mundus* means both "the world/universe" and "clean, elegant, or ornamental."</note>. But you, my listeners, must judge what kind of beauty this is; for the more these things abound, the less peace they bring and the more anxiety they cause. As you have heard, everything concerning the world is fleeting; neither the poor man nor the rich man can [keep even] a hair of these things...

Now listen, I beg you, to the pilgrimage of this passing world.

### *The pilgrimage of the world, which we call the way of error.*

**A**t the completion of twenty-one years of age <note>literally "thrice seven years," a traditional age of maturity</note>, the greater part of humanity reaches the crossroads of choice. The course of everyone is checked by a pull from the hook of the Lord’s angel. But many crawl under it, others leap over it; and while a tiny few are caught by the pull, the vast majority break out between the hook and the entrance of the path. They all flee from salvation, as many as strive to escape this pull, and they enter the world without any restraint. Most of these people, having abused their luxuries and worldly pleasures, are permitted by the Lord our God in His mercy to fall into poverty, so that they might be drawn back to the earlier path of repentance <term>resipiscentia: literally a "becoming wise again," referring to the internal act of realizing one's error</term>. Yet the human race is utterly futile; since resisting God has become innate to them, they do not stop seeking ways to escape—by their own efforts—the snares they have set for themselves. They do not seek help from Him, on whom alone every gift of mercy depends. 

Because of this, they have built a massive workshop for themselves on the left side of the road, where every kind of trade is practiced. Over this house presides Industry <term>industria: in this period, it refers to human cleverness, hard work, and the inventive ability to solve physical problems</term>, who receives everyone except the idle and the lazy. On one side are the literary workshops of various studies, where those who had neglected their education through carelessness betake themselves. These people often move to the manual workshops located on the other side, where they test through experience those things once committed to writing by the wise of old; they do this so that they are not led into deceptive opinions by the written word, being inexperienced in practical matters. Others who have practiced commerce to their own ruin, and those who have fallen into poverty while devoted to manual arts, dream day and night of "new forms of things" and unheard-of inventions. These are offered for sale everywhere by merchants and craftsmen at a price, so that they may repair their losses and then reach for even greater wealth. 

Once they have achieved this, they depart from Industry and head toward the second region of the world. They make their passage across the "bridge of infirmity." Before this bridge, a second "pull" from the Lord tries to lead the lost sheep back to the true fold. Of these, only a very few enter the path of repentance. The rest stubbornly cross the bridge and use the wealth they have now gained through Industry even more licentiously than before. But because the good God wishes to draw them back, He allows illnesses to take hold of them. Then, seeking a remedy from themselves once again rather than from Him, they flock to a hospital <term>xenodochium: a Greek-derived term for a place that cares for the sick or strangers</term>, also built on the left and very large, over which Medicine presides. There, a huge number of pharmacists, surgeons, and physicians are found, each performing his own duty. Once health has been recove-

Once they have reached the third region of the world, one can see nothing but the bent backs of the elderly, the wrinkles on their faces, their limping, their lamentations, and their sighs; one can hear a heap of other such miseries, and whatever fate awaits each man, until he arrives at the final inn of death. ->**The Way of Truth.**<-

**Philosophy.** You heard before that the sword of the angel of the first pass was suspended from a tree above the riverbank; in its place (now in this time of grace) there hangs before our eyes God and the Son of God, Christ the restorer of the human race. He draws those passing by more effectively through his manifest love—veiled by no symbols—than a magnet draws iron, unless perhaps the dregs of the world and "garlic" <note>original: *allium*. In ancient and medieval lore, it was commonly believed that garlic could neutralize a magnet's power; here it serves as a metaphor for worldly distractions that block divine attraction.</note> stand in the way. Whoever is drawn by admiration of the river appearing from afar and by the example of inexhaustible love offered close at hand, let them come here to us. We, as many as are ministers of truth, gladly receive you to be instructed, so that you may hear more extensively hereafter. However, before that happens, having now taken food and drink, let us give thanks to God, who has given all things necessary to everyone. 

We give You, God the Father, immortal thanks, because You have deigned to nourish us with your Word and your creatures, and to lead us even to this place in the hope of a better life; Your will be done, so that what was begun through You alone may be perfected in us. Amen. 

Now let us go to the fountain of love, so that you may drink. Look, quench your thirst: you shall no longer be called Mind <term>Animus</term> or Spirit <term>Spiritus</term>, nor Soul <term>Anima</term>, nor two things from now on, but you shall be called one unified Intellect <term>Mens</term>. Having been made stronger, you may be able to resist your enemy, the Body, with which you must struggle manfully until, completing the very course of nature, it is actually separated from you. Afterwards, you may hope that this same body will be joined to you again through a divine mystery—purer and more refined—to the glory of Him who created all things. By what means you must fight, you will hear from the following fourth step: namely, the **Assembly** <term>Frequentia: likely referring to a gathering of the faithful or a specific stage of spiritual discipline</term>. I will now accompany you as you approach it, as far as the first milestone. Meanwhile, I will briefly depict before your eyes the progress of the entire Way of Truth. Leaving the Assembly and having been instructed, you will arrive at the camp of Wisdom <term>Sophia</term>, where you will be received and refreshed by a food far more potent than before. Up until now, you have tasted only milk...

For (until you become stronger, and having been made more robust, you are able to bear it) you are still **children** <note>In a spiritual sense, meaning novices or those newly reborn in faith.</note>. For Virtue will teach you how great the fruit of true love is, and how much delight the submission of the body brings to the mind; indeed, it is no less than the victory of a soldier over his enemies while striving for the palm of honor. ### *A Dialogue, in which the Mind and the Body are the interlocutors.*

**C.** <note>Corpus/Body</note> Oh! Who has now become my companion? Where are you, my soul? **M.** <note>Mens/Mind</note> Look, I am here; what do you want with me? **C.** I do not see you. **M.** Now again you confess that you are blind, just as before. **C.** Where then is the **Spirit**? **M.** And do you seek me even while I am present to you? **C.** Good God, do you both now speak with a single voice? **M.** What is the wonder in that? Are you unmindful of what I said above: that you would have to deal with only a single thing, whereas you had complained that you had to deal with two? **C.** What am I hearing? Have you somehow bewitched <note>original: *fascinasti*</note> my eyes? **M.** Far be such bewitchment from me. Truly, since we have both taken a draught from the fountain of love at the same time, we have been reduced into one, so that you should no longer think you must battle with two, but with a single mind. **C.** **Mind** <note>original: *Mens*</note> gives the beginnings to many things: to tables <note>original: *mensæ*</note>, to measures <note>original: *mensuræ*</note>, and to months <note>original: *mensibus*</note>. **M.** Would that you had also learned to measure the table <note>Likely a metaphor for moderation in eating.</note>, and that you would remember that there will be an end to your months. **C.** You say a marvelous thing: you know it is impossible for me to live without food. **M.** I know this and another thing as well: that man does not live by bread alone—are you ignorant of this? **C.** From what do you live? I have not yet seen you eating. **M.** Again you bring your blindness into the open. **C.** How so? **M.** I live from every word that proceeds from the mouth of the Lord. **C.** Would that it were permitted for me to live thus. **M.** In the future it will be permitted for you too (though not before you die). **C.** You mention something far too harsh. **M.** It is nothing but pleasant. **C.** You make death out to be pleasant? **M.** Indeed, to those who have known her. **C.** Do you know her? **M.** I know her most especially. **C.** I pray you, describe her to me—she who shows herself as something to be feared by all. **M.** I will most willingly comply with you in this matter; no one fears her except you. **C.** Not you? **M.** Not in the least. **C.** You are insane from too much wisdom, to say more. **M.** You are. **C.** Yet I know everyone abhors her. **M.** You think so. <note>original: *Rere*. A play on words with the following phrase *E re*.</note> **C.** Speak so that you may be understood. **M.** I shall speak to the point <note>original: *E re dicam*</note> so that you may understand: the mind of man is immortal; therefore it does not fear death; indeed, it manfully overcomes it. The body is entirely subject to death, which is why it dreads it above all else. **C.** How do you know that the mind is not subject to death?

<meta>This page continues the dialogue between the Mind and the Body. In the previous section, the Mind challenged the Body's spiritual blindness. **M.** <note>Mind</note> It is known from this principle: everything that takes its origin from death is mortal; that which derives its beginning from life does not die, nor does that which exists as a medium between life and death when it clings to life. **C.** <note>Body (Corpus)</note> You speak in riddles that are far too obscure. **M.** I speak only of things that are clear. **C.** What then is life? **M.** It is the soul of the body. **C.** And what is death? **M.** It is the deprivation of life. **C.** I have not come away any more learned from this explanation. **M.** Listen: what you consider to be death is for me the beginning of eternal life. Nothing more pleasant could happen to us, if only it were not so troublesome to you. Truly, you detest death because you know that by it you are deprived of worldly delights; but you are ignorant of the fact that there is less comparison or similarity between those delights and eternal joys than there is between gall <note>A bitter substance, often used in contrast to the sweetness of honey to represent suffering or sin.</note> and honey, which I know you have tasted at some time. Finally, so that you may better understand this difference, you should consider what you already know: that the continuation of all the worldly pleasures that could ever happen to you brings only boredom—or rather, I should say, nausea—and what is far worse, it brings infirmity and sometimes even death. If you now crave food, after you have filled your belly with it several times, you will seek something else; when you are satisfied with that, you seek yet another, and you will never cease seeking in this world for things that you will find have failed to satisfy your desires. And what of drink? While it passes through the channel of the throat, it delights; but when it can no longer enter further, it causes great torment, yet you cannot abstain from that which kills you. You fear the very death that you bring upon yourself! O wretched and insatiable body, which knows not how to beware of what harms it, and fears that which is its very self! You see then that the human Body, when out of harmony with its mind, is unhappier than the beasts, since irrational animals desire nothing beyond what is necessary for them. Rational beings, however, seek out what is necessary least of all, but instead solicitously procure that which kills them. Let us now turn to those things sought outside the body for its use, such as riches of every kind. Because of these, the bodies of men—those who have not followed the mind—are tortured daily in strange and various ways. What do they not attempt? What dangers do human hearts not undergo, by which they drag the soul to destruction and pull the wretched body away from the spirit? They do this for no other reason than to fashion an idol for themselves out of their own body. Adorned with fine purple linen and scarlet, with necklaces and bracelets, they are not afraid to silently worship this body above God. Who will deny that this is a greater idolatry of oneself than of any other, or that death is the end of all these things? O ignorant body, you fear nothing except yourself: for through your own appetite, death took its beginning within you. You desire nothing except what comes from yourself—namely, the corruption that brings on the death you fear. See then how little you are consistent with yourself; how can you resist others when you cannot even resist your own impulses? Recover your senses, I beg you, while you still can. Cling to us, and do not wait until it is too late to desire what is good. We have now reached the **Gardens of Abundance**; there you will be allowed to hear more concerning this matter.

->*Recapitulation of the fourth Chapter, and the third step.*<-

Know, brothers, that all things which have been said above, and will be said in the future, can be understood as referring to alchemical preparations. For the separation of the parts of man, which we said occurs through speculative Philosophy, is to be understood in the same way as the separations of other bodies performed by fire. And unless such a separation occurs, Alchemists labor in vain seeking the universal medicine <note>The "panacea" or "Philosopher's Stone" believed to be a cure-all and a substance of transformation.</note> which can heal all diseases without distinction. Everything said about man in this book must be considered most diligently, for there is not a single word in it that does not refer to the chemical art <note>original: "artem chemicam"</note> and was not placed there for its clarification. Such is the "philosophical love" between the parts of inanimate things, and such is their enmity, as it is in the parts of man. Truly, in those things no more than in man, a true union cannot be achieved unless the corruption <note>Here meaning impurities or the state of being mixed with "lesser" elements.</note> of the said parts is first removed before they are joined. Therefore, your task is to make peace between enemies so that friends may come together as one. In all imperfect bodies—those falling short of their ultimate perfection—friendship and enmity are born together. If this enmity is removed by human wit or industry, the remaining part must necessarily return to its ultimate perfection, which we described in the union of man. Therefore, separate the parts from every body by fire; purify the impure parts, while those that are already pure require no cleansing. Mix pure things with pure, though the heavier things should be <term>sublimated</term> <note>The process of heating a substance until it becomes vapor, then cooling it back into a solid to purify it.</note> before the lighter ones; thus will be created what was called above the "fixed volatile" <note>An alchemical paradox where a substance is made stable (fixed) yet maintains its spiritual or active power (volatile).</note> and the "spiritual body." So far we have touched upon the comparison to physical alchemy; therefore, we must pause here until we have followed through with what remains in metaphysical alchemy.

The reader must be warned here, however, to understand these things through a careful comparison, or else he will necessarily be confused. Therefore, it will not be a burden to explain the difference between things that might cause doubt. Whenever in the future I mention "inanimate things," I wish it to be understood as referring to vegetables and minerals. Although these possess their own <term>vegetative soul</term> <note>In Aristotelian philosophy, the most basic level of soul responsible for growth and nutrition, shared by plants and animals.</note>, they are called inanimate to distinguish them from sentient beings. I spoke of "inanimate bodies" above so that no one would think I wish to contradict the alchemists, who attribute spirit, soul, and body in their own way to all natural bodies—a fact they can demonstrate to the eyes of anyone who denies it, whenever necessary. Likewise, I use the term "sensitive" <note>original: "sensitiva"</note> for irrational animals, and I do not mean rational beings. Although humans have a <term>sensitive soul</term> <note>The level of soul responsible for perception and movement.</note> alongside their rational soul, I shall use the term "rational" to signify their higher nature. Finally, regarding these matters, one must not be ignorant of the fact that rational separation is twofold: namely, voluntary, of which we spoke above, and natural...

which does not pertain to chemists. Of sensible and inanimate things, there is also a twofold separation: the natural and the artificial, the latter of which concerns chemistry. Voluntary separation <note>In this context, the author refers to the mental or spiritual separation of the soul from worldly concerns through contemplation.</note> happens while the parts remain within the whole, whereas natural and artificial separations do not. The instrument of voluntary separation is the spirit and the breath of life; for natural separation, it is death; and for artificial separation, it is fire. 

There is nothing to stop you now from being able to equate the alchemy of rational beings <note>original: "rationalium alchemiam," referring to the spiritual or biological processes occurring within human beings.</note> with that which can be performed through the separations and unions of sensible, inanimate things in the future. Do not think it was in vain that I put forward "Rational Alchemy" first, for if this and natural alchemy are not understood, you will necessarily remain ignorant of the artificial art <note>The physical practice of laboratory alchemy.</note>. But lest I seem to have neglected natural Alchemy, you shall now hear just enough about it to understand the rest. I shall begin with separation.

You know that when man has finished the term appointed to him by nature, he is resolved into his parts (which we stated above to be Spirit, Soul, and Body). This is performed by the corruption of death. Through the extinction of the natural fire, as the radical moisture <term>Radical moisture (original: "humore radicali"): a medieval medical concept of a vital, oily fluid present from birth that acts as the body's fuel. When it is "dried up," the fire of life goes out.</term> fails, the Spirit and Soul recede, leaving the body behind. This body is then separated again into its elemental parts through the process of putrefaction within the earth. Each element returns to its own: the earth devours what is earthy, the water what is watery, and so with the others. The spirit and soul return to where they came from—not to remain forever separated from the body, but so that they may be joined as one in a better composition through divine artifice. After this union, they shall never be separated again. This is the greatest inseparable power of union: the compacting of parts into a single whole.

Furthermore, unless the elements of rational bodies are nourished by elements, they cannot retain the spirit and soul. Food and drink cast into the stomach are "cooked" into digestion (for the separation of the parts of bodies cannot happen except through corruption or putrefaction). Through the artifice of nature, the pure is separated from the impure, so that the earth, water, air, and fire of the human body are nourished by the better substance of the earth, water, air, and fire of the food and drink. The more impure matter of those elements is ejected through the bowels or other emunctories <term>Emunctories: organs or paths, such as the kidneys or pores, that carry off waste or "superfluities" from the body.</term>. Each part of this gross matter again seeks its own element, as we have said. 

Fire within man is a voracious element, consuming the other purer elements. This is why nourishment is necessary; otherwise, the fire consumes itself. Once the fire is spent, no place remains for the soul or the spirit. Such fire is indeed fire, but it is also the union or "soul" of the other elements—without it, no elements are held together, but instead fall apart. In the elements, there is a "philosophical love." Embrace this alone if you wish to be a physicist <note>In the 17th century, a "physicus" was a student of nature or a physician, rather than a modern physicist.</note> or a natural philosopher; otherwise, you will turn out to be not a healer of nature, but a destroyer of it.

### *On Assiduity, the Fourth Philosophical Step. Chapter V.*
### *In which Mind, Body, and Assiduity converse.*

**Mind:** I greet you most warmly, O Assiduity <note>original: *Frequentia*. In this context, it refers to the steady, repeated application of the mind to a task or virtue—constancy.</note>.

**Assiduity:** I bid you also be well, most welcome travelers and guests. From where do you come, I ask?

**Mind:** From the philosophy of love, we make our journey toward the camps of virtue.

**Assiduity:** I ask that you stay with me a while, until the labors you have undertaken on your pilgrimage may be relieved, refreshed by some rest.

**Mind:** We shall most gladly obey you in this matter.

**Assiduity:** Enter then these diligent gardens, and enjoy freely those things which are in them as if they were your own.

**Mind:** We give you great thanks.

**Assiduity:** Not to me, but to Him to whom all things belong: to God, clearly. Sit down; those things with which I can receive you are prepared. Let us pray to God:

> Deign to nourish us, O Almighty Father, with your blessing. Amen.

Care for yourself, O Body, while I feed the Mind. Listen, Mind: Since Assiduity is the perseverance of a concept regarding the love of truth, there is no other approach to the virtues except through constant application. In this place, there is no rest; hence it is that no place here seems built for lethargy, but rather the watchful inhabitants of the garden of virtues wait under the open sky. 

Do you see this land? Unless it were continually cleared, instead of the sweet flowers and herbs it produces, it would yield nothing but thistles and nettles. It will happen no differently with the Body you carry around if you become sluggish. This Body has been given to you as a colony <note>The author uses the term *colonia* to suggest the Body is a territory that the Mind must settle, govern, and cultivate.</note>, just as these gardens are committed to me day and night. Whatever weeds <term>original: *lolium*; literally "darnel" or "tares," a common grain-mimicking weed</term> grow over it must be removed by you. You can overcome this in no better way than when you have removed gluttony <note>original: *crapulam*; refers to the physical distress or "hangover" caused by over-indulgence in food or drink.</note>; for it is surely that which induces sleepiness and laziness. 

You shall also remove idleness <note>original: *otium*; while sometimes meaning "leisure," here it refers to the "idle hands" that lead to vice.</note>, so that the most powerful root of vices may perish. Grant nothing to the body beyond what is necessary; whatever is in excess grows into a vice. You have heard above what is necessary for the body; now hear what is healthful for it and for you. 

If you neglect to correct the Body, it will go badly for you because of it, and badly for the Body as well. Because the faculty of reason has now become yours, not its—which reason it has cast aside—you must consider the knowledge of God committed to you (as indeed it is). Therefore, you shall not be excused on its account, since you are in the position of its teacher <term>original: *pædagogi*; a tutor or guide, often a slave in antiquity who supervised a child's conduct</term>, nor shall it be excused on your account, because it first made itself a slave from a free being. 

See, then, how I deal with the gardens; I care for them in two ways: namely, by weeding and by watering. In the former, I pull out the useless, overgrowing herbs by the roots, lest they suppress the good ones in their growth. You must do the same with your body: first rejecting evil thoughts and enmity from yourself, you shall restrain the body from every evil work. It is not fitting for a teacher to teach one thing and do another; for if you give the Body the opportunity for sinning, why, I ask, would you catch it? The Body contemplates nothing; it is the Mind that exercises the silent operations of the imaginations, which the Body then finally attempts to carry out. Conce—

[Perce]ption belongs to the mind, but execution belongs to the body. What if I were to pull up darnel <note>original: *lolium*; a weed that often grows among wheat</note> and meanwhile sowed tares <note>original: *zizaniam*; another invasive weed</note>? Would I have corrected anything other than the very fault I myself committed? See to it, then, that you do not attribute more to the body than it is capable of. It is true that the body itself is more prone to carrying out wicked concepts, and it delights in them more than in good ones; but if you cast away all evil thoughts and substitute good ones in their place, the body will be able to perform nothing but what is good, or else cease from all evil. This is one method of conquering the body; now hear the other.

If I only protected my gardens from useless weeds, I would certainly have achieved little or nothing, since another far more necessary care must be applied to those things that have been planted: namely, irrigation. This is the other half of the nourishment for plants, without which they cannot grow. In this same way, you shall water your Body with living water, which is the Word of God. Meditate on this night and day, and on nothing besides this, so that the body can neither speak nor do anything other than that very Word. You see now that bodies can be very well compared to fields or gardens, which we read that Christ our Savior also did in the Gospel. "The good seed," He says, "which falls into well-tilled earth, brings forth good fruit." <note>A reference to the Parable of the Sower found in Matthew 13.</note> It is no different with the Word of God: when it falls upon a softened heart, it nourishes the body of him whose heart has been contrite and humbled.

It is certain that from the time of the first Fall, the hearts of men have been hardened like stones; unless they are softened by the Word of God, they remain hard forever. Pharaoh’s heart was hard from his mother’s womb (as all hearts are), but because it was not softened by the Word of God, it remained hardened. We are all born rebels and enemies to God, and we remain so until that enmity is rooted out by the Great Husbandman <note>original: *summum agricolam*; God as the divine gardener</note>, to whom you, O Mind, must show yourself a servant. You have the seed, the field, and the water; nothing more is lacking except assiduous, uninterrupted labor. You must never cease to revolve in your mind those things you have already heard, and will yet hear; otherwise, through neglect, you will give an opening to your enemy. These are the things which Lady Virtue <note>original: *hera virtus*</note> has commissioned to be said to you, by whom you shall be more extensively taught. We give great thanks to God, who deigns to illuminate our hearts with His light and to make them softer by His word. Amen. Go forth happily, brothers, and seek Virtue.

### *Recapitulation of the fifth chapter and the fourth step.*

It is impossible for any craftsman to become prompt and fit in his art except by a frequency and assiduity of work through which he acquires a habit. What would it have profited a baker to have seen another baker working often, and very often, unless he himself, putting his hand into the dough, repeated the act so many times that, having now become a habitual baker, he was able to teach another? This is what usually happens to certain people who desire to learn the Chemical Art <note>original: *Artem Chemicam*; Alchemy</note>: some think they can attain it by reading alone, others by only a very few operations; which nevertheless...

Among all the arts that Nature has ever granted, this is held to be the most difficult and the least understood. It is truly a <term>Herculean labor<note>A task of enormous difficulty, referring to the twelve labors of the Greek hero Hercules.</note></term>, surpassing the Mind, Body, and lifespan of men, unless it is granted to one among hundreds of myriads <note>original: *myriadum*; a myriad is ten thousand, so this refers to one in millions.</note> to prevail—that is, to reach the perfect aim of the art. Some are able to uncover many secrets of nature through the greatest study and labor, which they apply to medical practice, more than any other things previously discovered outside of the said art. But to find that <term>Universal Medicine<note>Also known as the Panacea or the Philosopher's Stone, believed by alchemists to cure all diseases and perfect the soul.</note></term>, of which we spoke above, has until now happened to very few: only to those who, by the grace of a merciful God, were first able to lead themselves back into the very state they desire; that is, those who have cleansed their own bodies from impurity and have also removed the clouds from natural bodies. I urge any seekers of this art to pray to God assiduously, to study, and to work; it cannot be otherwise than that they shall attain what they have asked for from the Giver of Lights <note>A reference to James 1:17.</note> in the name of Jesus. But first, let them consider what it means to "ask the Father in the Son": it is surely nothing other than to demand only that which is for the glory of God the Father and the Son. Many are accustomed to wishing for what seems useful to them, but they obtain from God only what is truly useful. I say this to many in few words: God helps diligent and frequent efforts, but He despises the negligent. Let us love the good, so that we do not crave the evil.

### *A Dialogue, in which Mind and Body act together.*

M. Did you hear what <term>Frequency<note>original: *Frequentia*; here personified as the virtue of Constant Application or Assiduity mentioned on the previous page.</note></term> said? B. ...unless it dies, it remains alone and will not bring forth fruit. <note>A reference to John 12:24: "Unless a grain of wheat falls into the earth and dies, it remains alone; but if it dies, it bears much fruit."</note> Or, in a more Christian manner: unless the grain is joined through union with the dead body, both remain separate without fruit. **C.** And do you make a <term>wax nose<note>original: *nasum cereum*; a common Latin idiom for a text or principle that is easily manipulated or twisted to suit one's own purposes.</note></term> out of Grammar? **M.** You are still a rebellious Body; I see we must hurry toward Virtue. ### Of Virtue, the fifth degree of philosophy.

### CHAPTER VI.

**M.** O Sacred One, command your gates to be opened to us. **V.** Who are you who wishes to approach us? **M.** We are two little recruits <note>original: *tyrunculi*; literally "young recruits" or beginners.</note> of philosophy. **V.** What do you seek? **M.** To learn Virtue. **V.** You ask for a just thing, which should by no means be denied to you. What teachers did you have before? **M.** Philosophical Love and Constancy <note>original: *Frequentia*; in this context, it implies regular attendance or diligent practice.</note>. **V.** I am glad such ones gave you your beginnings. What moved you to take up these studies? **M.** The desire to know the truth. **V.** The knowledge of truth is the root and mother of all things that God has ordained. But to what end do you desire to know it? **M.** So that we may be able to practice it. **V.** Toward whom? **M.** Toward God and neighbor. **V.** A good intention indeed, to which I pray God gives a happy outcome. What are your names? **M.** My name is Mind, and Body is the name of this one. **V.** From whom did you receive them? **M.** I was called Mind by Philosophical Love; he retains the name Body from the common people. **V.** How does the Mind agree with the Body? **M.** Not at all; everything between us is in dispute. **V.** What do I hear? **M.** The Body finds it painful to leave the world. **V.** Everything that has once put on the world flees from salvation, and it can only be pulled back from it with the greatest effort. Enter, brothers; and I pray you, take in good part what I can provide for your sake! Body, lie down upon your own [belongings] and care for your belly. Mind shall be fed by me. O Heavenly Father, who restores all things, deign to nourish us into eternal life by your word of truth. Amen. 

Listen, Mind: the virtue of things is the truth of each individual thing, and truth is efficacy known through experience, and efficacy is a heavenly influence. Whatever is not from heaven cannot be called virtue, but rather a false image of it. The philosophers of old, who were ignorant of God, depicted virtues for us because they did not understand His Son, in whom all the virtues of God were made. More recent men are also accustomed to divide virtues into Theological and Ethical, than which nothing can be more absurd among learned men: because all virtue is from God, and therefore it is theological. That which is called "ethical," unless it comes from God, cannot be virtue. The "courage" of the Romans against their enemies was actually stubbornness; their "magnanimity" was pride; their "prudence" was fraud and deceit; their "abstinence" was an ambition for honor (and so with the rest). These were vices rather than virtues, because they were performed not for the glory of God, but for the glory of men and themselves. Christian philosophers hold truth alone as...

by virtue, which they divide into Faith, Hope, and Charity. In these three, and within them, all truth consists; and whatever is not found in these is false, as much in rational and sensible things as in those that are inanimate. For faith is the certainty of those things which are heard and not seen: for this reason it is said that faith comes from hearing, because what is seen is not faith, but certain knowledge demonstrated through the eyes. Sacred scripture offers testimony of this:
> You have believed because you have seen. Blessed are those who have not seen and yet have believed. <note>original: "Credidisti quia vidisti. Beati qui non viderunt, & crediderunt." A reference to John 20:29.</note>
There is in natural things a certain truth which is not seen by external eyes, but is perceived by the mind alone. The Philosophers have experienced this, and they discovered its power to be such that it performed miracles: wherefore it is a thing to be wondered at, that men have performed miracles through faith, when even inanimate things can perform the same by the power bestowed upon them. In this, the whole art consists: that a spirit of this kind may be freed from its shackles, just as it was said above that the mind must be made free from the body. The body, therefore, is a prison <note>The "body as a prison" (carcer corporis) is a classic Platonic and Hermetic concept, suggesting that the physical shell prevents the inner essence or "spirit" from acting.</note> by which the virtues of the soul are hindered, and the spirits of natural things cannot exercise their powers. The efficacy of the spirit of such inanimate things is of the same kind and quality—relative to its subject—as **undoubting faith** is in man. Therefore, true faith is the virtue of men, and the truth of their efficacy belongs to all other things. For example, a physicist <note>original: "physicus"; at this time, this referred to a student of nature or a physician.</note> inexperienced in the things of nature would not want to believe that the carcass of any venomous animal, even if completely dry and parched, when placed over a wound infected with poison or a pestilential abscess, draws all the venom into itself. This is very well known to chemists, those searchers of nature's virtues, and they have confirmed it through the magnetic force of nature. Since such people do not believe that nature can provide what she is able to do, being unworthy of her virtues, they do not deserve to attain even the smallest secret from the storehouses of nature herself. If they see some experiment of someone else, they do not inquire further as to the reason why such a thing happens; but content with the experiment, they only use it. In this ignorance the greatest part of physicists remains stuck, saying, "it has this property," without curiously investigating from whence it comes. But the chemical physicist is not content with the experiment alone, nor merely that it comes from heaven, but asks from which part of heaven, performing an "anatomy" of the "great creature" <note>The "Great Creature" refers to the Macrocosm, or the Universe itself.</note> and making a comparison with that which can be made of the microcosm <note>The "Microcosm" refers to Man, viewed as a miniature map of the universe.</note>. This he strives to accomplish by four modes and instruments, namely: <term>Geometry</term>, <term>Hydromancy</term>, <term>Pyromancy</term>, and <term>Astronomy</term>. 

<term>Geometry</term> <note>Literally "earth-measurement." Here used to mean the study of the element of Earth.</note> of the lands in natural things; <term>Hydromancy</term> <note>Literally "water-divination," but here used as the study of the element of Water.</note> of the waters; <term>Pyromancy</term> <note>Literally "fire-divination," here used as the study of the element of Fire.</note> of fires; and <term>Astronomy</term> of the celestial virtues. These are the investigations which the craftsman, moved by philosophical love, gladly undertakes, relying on hope (by which he is also nourished) to arrive at that truth of the matter in which he has an innate faith. It is clear, then, that Hope is the stimulus of faith, or the certainty of future truth. Unless one knows for certain...

...[believing] that he will acquire what he pursues, his effort grows cold; but when he has confirmed a confident opinion, aided surely by practice and talent, there is nothing he cannot achieve. Truly, in this place it must not be ignored that faith is proven through charity <note>original: "charitatem." In this context, charity refers to *Caritas*, or divine, selfless love.</note>, just as a good or bad impulse can work for good or for evil. Some, understanding the matter, have said that charity must begin with oneself; which I think should be understood thus: a Christian man must first acquire the habit of virtue for himself through practice before he is able to exercise it toward others in action. Learn then, O Mind, to exercise charity toward your own body by restraining its vain appetites; thus it will be ready with you for all things. I will strive to make this happen, that it may drink with you from the fountain of virtue, and both then having become one, you may have peace in union. O wonderful efficacy of the fountain, which makes one out of two, and creates peace between enemies! The fountain of love can make a mind from spirit and soul, but here it makes one man from mind and body. We give thanks to you, Father, because you have deigned to make your children participants in your inexhaustible fountain of virtues. Amen. Go now, having been made a wise man, to Power, from whom you will learn Constancy; and fare you well.

### *Recapitulation of the sixth chapter and the fifth grade.*

In every thing there is its own virtue and a heavenly influence, which nevertheless can by no means be seen by external eyes, but only by its effects. We see the attraction of iron caused by a Magnet, but the magnetic force lying hidden in the stone itself we cannot see, because it is a spirit and does not fall under the senses; so it is with other things. Wine has diverse powers within itself, which were known by philosophers through the experiment of the <term>chemical art|Alchemy or early laboratory chemistry</term> in its separation: its Spirit heats and dries out, yet its Body produces the complete opposite; for it moistens with cooling, the experience of which can be seen in the water (which they call burning <note>original: "aqua ardens." This is a historical term for distilled alcohol or ethanol, which could be set on fire.</note>) and in vinegar. 

These faculties are entirely contrary because of the separation, whereas before it they were not so diverse, because then they participated more in the mixture through a natural union. Who (unless out of his mind) would deny that such virtues exist in all other natural bodies to a greater or lesser degree? He will be no philosopher who denies that bread or grain has a spirit within itself no less efficacious than the spirit of wine, although it is not as abundant in bread as in wine; yet it is equally effective for an equal quantity of its spirit. If such [a spirit] can [be obtained] from bread and wine...

If spirits can be separated by art <note>The author uses "art" to refer to alchemical or laboratory processes.</note>, how much more should their separation be natural within man? From these things, <term>philosophical transmutations</term> <note>Alchemical changes involving the fundamental nature of a substance.</note> can be understood: do we not know that the purer substance of both bread and wine is transmuted into flesh and blood? And that from an invisible vegetable form, a visible animal form is made? Because of this, it is not the species of things that are changed, but their forms. Who will still doubt that philosophical transmutations can be achieved through art within man, far better than those which nature herself performs through the transmutation of bread and wine? For there are other bodies in the nature of things which possess a greater natural power and celestial influence, from which spirits can be separated—no differently than from wine and bread—and transmuted into the substance of man, into flesh and blood; and this can be done more excellently through art than through nature. But why should I repeat these things so often, which are clearer than light to philosophers? Let him who is unwilling to give credit to this try it through the chemical art <note>original: "artem chemicam." At this time, chemistry and alchemy were not yet distinct disciplines.</note>; and if he be ignorant of it, let him learn before he tries. For if he attempts to do such things through the common art of distillation, he will "lose both his oil and his labor" <note>A Latin idiom, *oleum et operam perdere*, meaning to waste one's time and resources on a fruitless task.</note>. No one should be forced for his own benefit, but only warned; for if he despises the warning, he does so to his own loss, not to the loss of the one who warns him.

# ON POWER, THE SIXTH STAGE.
## CHAPTER VII.

->*A dialogue in which Power and the Man are the interlocutors.*<-

**Man:** Open, I pray, divine Power.
**Power:** Who wishes to be introduced here?
**Man:** A Man.
**Power:** From where do you come?
**Man:** I am sent by Virtue.
**Power:** For what purpose?
**Man:** For confirmation in the virtues which I received from the minister of truth.
**Power:** Rightly so, but by what means do you believe this can happen?
**Man:** Through Power.
**Power:** Whose power, then?
**Man:** The Power of Truth.
**Power:** In what do you think Truth resides?
**Man:** I do not doubt that all truth is situated in the power of the Most High alone.
**Power:** Now you have shown yourself worthy of confirmation; therefore, pay attention to the things I am about to set before you. Power is the <term>Constancy</term> <note>original: "Constantia." Here meaning steadfastness or the stabilizing force of virtue.</note> of the virtue received from the Lord. It is not for anyone to think that he can have even the smallest spark of virtue from anywhere else than from God. But if someone seeks it from himself, or from another source than what has been said, he will obtain vice for his own destruction instead of virtue. Thus the Gentiles <note>The "Gentiles" here refers to the ancient Greeks and Romans or pagans.</note> were once accustomed to hunt for virtues through "heroic works" (as they called them) for no other reason than to leave a reputation of themselves to posterity, wretchedly placing their "highest good" and happiness in that fame. Truly, the outcome of such "memorable" deeds has clearly taught us what happened to them. Their kingdom, because it was founded upon sand and not upon the rock, was bound to fall; of which ruin indeed not much...

### *Recapitulation of the seventh chapter, and of the sixth grade.*

Although virtues are extracted from natural bodies, even inanimate ones (as has been said), they will not be fit for any excellent work unless they are further led to their extreme power through the <term>Chemical</term> <note>At the time of this writing, "chemistry" and "alchemy" were often used interchangeably to describe the art of purifying and perfecting matter.</note> art. The more they are purified and subtilized through diligent chemical observation, the more they approach their primary celestial influence; consequently, they penetrate and act more effectively. Thus, the work they achieve in <term>Medicine</term> for any infirmities whatsoever is truly to be regarded as a miracle.

### *Concerning the seventh miracle, and the final Philosophical grade.*

## CAP. VIII.

A miracle is the effect of the constancy of Truth. In the declaration of this, we shall use only a single example, through which the miracle will be clearly revealed. A certain Philosopher, having been seized by a tyrannical Emperor because of his profession of truth, was subjected to this martyrdom: he was to be crushed alive with a pestle in a carved iron-stone mortar. He said:
> Pound away, tyrant! Pound this little body; you will never pound my mind. <note>original: "Tunde tyranne, tunde corpusculum hoc, mentem nunquam contundes meam." This is a famous story attributed to the philosopher Anaxarchus while being tortured by the tyrant Nicocreon.</note>

Since this troubled the Emperor—as he did not wish the philosopher to speak the truth any longer, which he could not bear to hear—he ordered the executioner to cut out the philosopher’s tongue. But the philosopher bit it off with his own teeth and spat it into the Emperor's face before his body could be crushed into a pulp. O, the admirable constancy of the man, which...

### *Recapitulation of the seventh grade, the eighth chapter, and the conclusion of the entire preceding work.*

Just as there are seven philosophical grades through which the way to sublime things is open to the mind, there are also seven chemical operations through which the practitioner can reach that most excellent secret of medicine. Chemical **putrefaction** <term>putrefaction: the breaking down of matter through decay, seen by alchemists as a necessary stage for rebirth</term> is compared to the study of the philosophers; for just as philosophers are prepared for knowledge through study, so natural things are prepared for **solution** through putrefaction. To this is compared philosophical knowledge, for just as bodies are dissolved through solution, so are the doubts of philosophers resolved through knowledge. No differently than the frequenting of studies follows from philosophical love, the first union among chemists occurs through **congelation** <term>congelation: the process of a liquid thickening or becoming solid</term> by means of diligence and the repetition of operations. Just as the company of philosophers sharpens their wits, so the parts of bodies are refined by chemical **ablution** <note>original: "ablutione chemica"; literally a washing or purification process.</note>. In the same way that philosophers are united through virtue, elements are joined in their smallest parts through **composition**. As philosophical virtues are confirmed through power, so spirits are fixed in their bodies through **fixion**, so that they no longer flee. Not otherwise than as philosophical works show their virtue through a miracle, chemical medicines reveal their perfection through **projection** <term>projection: the final stage of the Great Work, where the "philosopher's stone" or medicine is cast upon a substance to transform it.</term> You now have, best reader, the entire intention of our work; if you do not profit from this in true metaphysical philosophy as well as in natural and chemical philosophy, you have no reason to complain of me, because I have most clearly declared to you whatever was obscured by others. Fare thee well, and look with favor upon this little work, whatever its worth may be.

## PHILOSOPHICAL TINCTURES

I would end here, if my philosophical love for students did not hold me back and advise me to add the philosophical **tinctures** <term>tinctures: in alchemy, these are potent liquid extracts believed to have the power to transform or heal.</term> of our teacher **Theophrastus Paracelsus**, by which cures can be effected both externally and internally through the renovation of the blood. These are the simplest and most powerful medicines drawn forth by the alchemical art. I have described the method of their preparation, together with their administration, from the *Great Surgery* <note>A reference to "Die grosse Wundarzney" (1536), one of Paracelsus's most influential works.</note> of the aforementioned Paracelsus, so that those things said above concerning philosophical medicines might be more easily understood.

### *Concerning the tincture of the Sun—that is, of Gold.*

Once the **tincture of the Sun** <note>original: "tinctura Solis"; the Sun is the traditional alchemical symbol for gold.</note> has been extracted, its body remains white; the tincture, however, is pure and is separated from the impure—that is, from its own body:

<meta>This page continues the practical application of alchemical theory introduced at the end of the previous section. Having established the philosophical grades, the text now provides specific laboratory recipes for creating a "tincture" meant for medical rejuvenation.</meta>

P H I L O S O P H Y. 271

This separation is necessary. The **tincture** <term>tincture: in alchemy, a concentrated extract or "soul" of a substance, often used for healing or transformation</term> must be clarified or "exalted" in its own grade, which is doubled five times—reaching a level of 240 <note>original: "quinquies bis 24"; the author describes a numerical progression of refinement cycles</note>—it does not progress higher than this. Then it can be administered to anyone for the renovation of the blood to its original state, as will be described in the instructions for administration.

->*The extraction is as follows.*<-

The "body" [of the metal] must be broken down from its metallic nature through hammering and by using salt water; then the residue should be washed with fresh water. Afterward, the tincture is extracted by **spirit of wine** <term>spirit of wine: high-proof alcohol, used here as a solvent</term>. Finally, it is raised up from the tincture, and then it remains at the bottom.

->*Extraction with salt water.*<-

Salt water is made from salt that is naturally very pure and white, without the boiling or artificial preparation by which salt is usually made. Let it be liquefied several times, and thereafter, as a powder, let it be mixed with the juice of **radish roots** and stirred within it. Then, let it be distilled after it has dissolved, and let it be mixed with equal parts of **green blood** <note>original: "sanguineo viridi"; likely a reference to green vitriol (iron sulfate) or verdigris, which alchemists called "green lion" or "green blood"</note>. Distill everything five times, and in this liquid, a leaf of **Gold** <note>original: "Solis" (of the Sun); the alchemical symbol for gold</note>—purified by **antimony** <term>antimony: a metalloid used in alchemy to "purify" gold by removing base metals</term>—is dissolved into powder. Let it be washed finely with pure distilled water until the saltiness departs; for salt allows itself to be washed away and does not mix deeply with the substance, but is separated.

->*Spirit of wine is made in this way.*<-

Take one measure of the best pure, unmixed wine, whether red or white. Place it in a **circulatory vessel** <note>a glass vessel where vapors can rise and then flow back down, allowing for continuous distillation</note> that has been very well "luted" <term>luted: sealed airtight with a paste of clay, lime, or wax</term> and blocked shut. Submerge the vessel in a **water bath** <note>original: "balneo maris"; literally "bath of the sea," a double-boiler used for gentle heating</note> to the depth of the wine, and let it boil for ten natural days. Finally, once cooled, let it be distilled in a **cucurbit** <term>cucurbit: the lower, gourd-shaped part of a distilling apparatus</term> or a flask by a cold process for as long as it takes for the spirit to ascend. When it has given its sign <note>likely a change in the appearance of the vapor or "tears" in the flask</note>, you will stop immediately; for what follows is **water of life** <note>original: "aqua vitae"; a lower-proof alcohol</note>, not the spirit. Pour this spirit of wine over the residue itself—which is like a fine powder (Alcool)—so that it floats six fingers deep. Place the vessel, very well sealed, into a warm bath, where it should remain for a month. Then the **tincture of Gold** will rise into the spirit, and a white powder will remain at the bottom of the vessel; these two must be separated from each other. Melt the powder, and it will become a white metal. Allow the spirit to evaporate, as is the custom of the art, and a juice will remain at the bottom like a liquor. You shall refine (graduate) this five times in a **retort** <term>retort: a glass bulb with a long, downward-pointing neck used for distilling liquids</term> of sufficient size for the quantity of the liquor. Such refinement happens only through "elevation" <note>the process of vaporizing and re-condensing to purify a substance</note>, which makes the matter subtle, but it is not permitted to be refined beyond the **quintessence** <term>quintessence: the "fifth essence" or purest, most potent form of a substance</term>; this is designated as 2. 4. 0. Otherwise, it is burned by proceeding further.

->*The method of administration is.*<-

You shall give one **drachm** <term>drachm: a traditional unit of weight, roughly 3.9 grams</term> of this, mixed with one ounce of **Venetian theriac** <term>Venetian theriac: a famous medicinal paste consisting of dozens of ingredients, used as a universal antidote and panacea</term>, to be taken on an empty stomach; one **scruple** <term>scruple: a small unit of weight, about 1.3 grams</term> each time.

Afterward, the patient should be covered in bed and made to sweat; this should be continued for ten or twelve days.

->*There is also a most excellent tincture found in coral for the purification of the blood.*<-

Its "body" should be ground finely into an **alcohol** <term>alcohol: in this context, the word refers to an impalpable, microscopic powder rather than a liquid</term>, and its **tincture** <term>tincture: the concentrated essence or "soul" of the substance</term> should be extracted just as it is from gold, using **spirit of wine** <note>original: "spiritum vini"; high-proof distilled wine</note>. At the same time, let it "ascend" <note>original: "ascendant"; a reference to the vapor rising during distillation</note> sixteen times, and afterward let them be separated through distillation. The ascent should be performed over a completely bare fire; thereafter, in **Mary’s bath** <term>Mary’s bath: a water bath or double-boiler (bain-marie) used to provide gentle, even heat</term>, the liquid must be separated six times and poured back over the dregs once more. This oil should be administered with **theriac water** <note>original: "aqua theriacali"; a medicinal water made from theriac, a famous ancient "universal antidote"</note>, specifically by drinking one **scruple** <note>approx. 1.3 grams</note> of the oil with one **drachma** <note>approx. 3.9 grams</note> of the same water.

Theriac water is made with five ounces of spirit of wine, two and a half ounces of **theriac**, one ounce and two drachmas of **Roman myrrh**, and two drachmas of **oriental saffron**. Let all these be mixed and distilled together at once; let them be administered as was previously described.

->*The dosage for administration is:*<-

One ounce and two drachmas of it should be mixed with ten ounces of **chicory water** or **germander water**, and two drachmas of this mixture should be given in the morning and the evening. Afterward, the patient should fast for five hours after taking the dose, and for the same amount of time after dinner. This should be continued for six or seven days. Distilled waters of **fumitory** <note>original: "fumo terrae"; literally "smoke of the earth"</note> or chicory and similar plants may also be given.

->*Tincture of Balsam.*<-

Take half an ounce of **balsam** and twenty ounces of spirit of wine; place them together in a **pelican** <term>pelican: a specialized alchemical vessel with two "arms" that allow distilled liquid to flow back into the base, creating a continuous cycle of "circulation"</term> or a double vessel, and let them be circulated in the Sun for a month. Once this is done, it allows itself to be distilled together with the spirit through an **alembic** <term>alembic: a distillation apparatus consisting of a gourd-shaped flask and a cooling cap</term>; this distillation is better here than using a **retort**, provided this mixture remains together in one composition. To this, you shall add half an ounce of other balsam, and let the sealed vessel be digested so that the added balsam can be mixed with the others, thus perfecting that which comes out of its body. For whatever is to be **graduated** <note>original: "graduari"; to be raised to a higher level of potency or purity</note> must have its substance terminate in a single body. And when this has been made **volatile** <term>volatile: capable of being evaporated or turned into vapor</term> as described above, add another half-ounce of balsam, which you will "exalt" as before, continuing to add and graduate it up to two ounces. This is the most powerful preparation of Balsam, which renovates and heals what other preparations cannot; for the sake of its own preservation, it has acquired this virtue from the heavens above all other things.

# PHILOSOPHY.

### *The administration is as follows.*

From that balsam prepared by itself <note>original: "per se"; meaning prepared without external additives or through its own inherent process</note>, you should give a weight equal to five barley grains with old white wine twice a day, until it appears that the blood has been restored.

### *Tincture of Antimony.*

It has been discovered in this world that nothing purifies gold better than **antimony** <note>original: "antimonium"; a brittle, silvery-gray metalloid used in alchemy to "devour" impurities in gold</note>; therefore, in man as well, if it is prepared as a drink, it can perform the same service, and even better. There is no reason for the learned to marvel that our teacher makes this comparison. Let them first learn to recognize and compare the **Anatomy** <note>referring to the structural correspondence between the universe and the human body</note> of the great and first creature with the last, before they pass judgment. Just as the sun holds primacy among the stars, and gold among the metals, not otherwise does man hold the primacy among living things: for the sake of whose perfection all these things coincide metaphysically into one.

Therefore, just as Antimony thoroughly cleanses gold and consumes other metals, so may it purge man, for the reason we have stated, without the clearing of the bowels, but by a **radical** <term>radical: from the Latin 'radix' (root); meaning a deep cleansing that affects the very root or essence of the person</term> purgation, by which it spiritually eradicates every superfluity. This is a most excellent **arcanum** <term>arcanum: a profound secret or a powerful "inner" mystery of a substance</term>, the structure of which is as follows:

Take the best antimony made into an **alcohol** <note>original: "in alcool facti"; a fine, impalpable powder</note>, which you shall heat in a **reverberatory furnace** <term>reverberatorio: a furnace that deflects heat onto the substance from the roof, rather than applying flame directly</term> well-sealed for a month. From this it will become volatile—first white, then yellow, and finally a light red or saffron—which you shall extract from the "essence of its lily" <note>original: "esse sui lilii"; the 'Lily' is a Paracelsian term for the purest, most medicinal part of a metal</note> by **spirit of wine** <note>distilled alcohol</note>, so that it floats twenty fingers above. Leave it thus, well-sealed, until it is colored, as you know: this is the highest preparation of the Lily, which purges a man from the roots, both inwardly and outwardly.

### *Its administration is as follows.*

In a cask of fresh wine in September or October, for every twenty measures, let half an ounce of this tincture be placed, and let both be allowed to digest and be purified together. Patients should drink from this wine for three or four weeks, or longer, in preference to all other drinks, or even without others.

### *Tincture of the Salt of the Philosophers.*

Take salt of gold, salt of Antimony, salt of **lemon balm** <note>original: "salis melissæ"</note>, half an ounce of each; eight ounces of pure rock salt. Mix them together, and let it be eaten on a slice of bread on an empty stomach. Do not wonder that we here include salt of gold and salt of antimony, which are not common salts, but **philosophical** ones: after you have learned those things which it is proper for you to know in this art, you will wonder no longer.

### *Another Philosophical Salt.*

Take salt of **germander** <note>original: "gamandreæ"</note>, salt of **chicory**, salt of **valerian**, one ounce of each; half an ounce of salt of **wormwood**; one drachma of salt of **vitriol** <note>original: "salis vitrioli"; a sulfate salt</note>; and one pound of pure common rock salt. Mix them together, and let it be eaten as described above.

THEORETICAL PHILOSOPHY

### *The secret through which the things set forth above are clarified.*

Heaven and earth, through man, bring forth man, who is their son, daughter, and offspring: from heaven he receives intellect, and from the earth his body. Because he is from the earth, he exists within his body, and to the earth he shall return; yet because of the heaven that is within him, he is of the **firmament** <note>original: "firmamento"; the sphere of the stars and the source of celestial influence</note>. Furthermore, he possesses one thing more as a gift from God, through which he can master the stars, provided he has learned it from God. Heaven and earth are joined together, and so too are heaven and man; but just as man is from the earth, he must be understood according to the earth and from it. Yet, insofar as he is from heaven, he must also be judged according to heaven. Therefore, man, heaven, and earth are one, as are air and water. If man knows how to transmute things in the **macrocosm** <term>macrocosm: the "greater world" or the universe at large</term> (such as turning all things into salt), how much more should he know how to do this in the **microcosm** <term>microcosm: the "lesser world," referring to the human being as a reflection of the universe</term>, which is within himself? He can do outside himself only what he first knows within, provided he recognizes that man’s greatest treasure is within man, and not outside him. From within himself proceeds (albeit indirectly) that by which he works externally upon what he sees with his eyes. Therefore, unless he be mentally blind, he will see—that is, understand—who and what he is inwardly, and by the **light of nature** <note>a Paracelsian concept referring to the innate wisdom or divine spark within the natural world that allows for true understanding</note> he will know himself through external things.

It is certain that natural **Salt** <term>Salt: in alchemical theory, one of the three "primes" representing the physical body, stability, and preservation</term>, the balsam of his body, is generated from a man's blood; it contains within itself both corruption and preservation from corruption. For in the nature of things, there is nothing that does not contain as much evil as it does good. Likewise, natural **Sulphur** <term>Sulphur: the alchemical principle of soul, heat, and combustibility</term> is generated from the bones and flesh; it is ignited by the drying out of natural fluids, and sometimes consumes itself and the entire body. The cause of this fire is that man was, from the beginning, sulphur; this was transmuted into flesh and blood, which are the "middle matter" of man. Nature, or the **first matter** <term>first matter: the original, undifferentiated substance from which all things are made</term>, greatly hates this middle matter and tries to reduce it back to itself. When it succeeds, earth and ashes remain—the remnant of man’s first matter and the subject of his final state. Because man is generated in a state of corruption, his own substance pursues that corruption with hatred. 

Hence it happens that the natural sulphur of man recedes from its "middle" creation back toward the "first" creation; as it approaches this state and assumes its nature, it passes into an elemental operation. This elemental fire is the cause of corruption, and it is ignited by the **invisible sun**—unknown to most—which is the **Sun of the Philosophers** <note>original: "sol philosophorum"; a spiritual source of heat and life-force used in alchemical transformation, distinct from the physical sun</note>. Such are the virtues within man that, through the power of corruption, they are able to dry up the moisture; in this way, they reduce the salts of man into the nature of **lime** <note>original: "calcis"; calx or quicklime, the powdery residue left after a substance is burned or oxidized</note>, through which the body passes into a sulfurous state. Thus, the body is reduced to the first matter, for which it has been made ready to receive the fire that corrupts man back to his first essence—just as we see in other creations, such as in the earth or the mountains. And although the bodies are not the same, the operations are the same; it is not

# PHILOSOPHY

The fire is the same in its outward appearance, yet the same in its essence. The Sun is invisible within human beings, but visible within the earth; nevertheless, both arise from one and the same sun. Indeed, man is the fuel in which the sparks of this fire—struck by the whetstone (namely, **Mercury**) and the steel (Heaven)—take hold as kindling and exert their powers. The **Archeus** <term>Archeus: in Paracelsian thought, the internal "master chemist" or vital force that directs the body’s functions</term> naturally practices the chemical art within man, just as an artificial chemist in his forge acts as a transformer of minerals, separating three things—namely, chemical **realgar** <note>original: "realgar"; in this context, it refers to the volatile, sulfurous, or impure parts of a substance that must be separated from its essence</note> and Gold—from the ore. For as long as these remain together, each has no power on its own; but when they are separated, each expresses its own active powers within man. Such a "horizon" exists within him—not in terms of raw strength, but in the perfection of its creation. 

Thus, natural art acts upon the **microcosm** <term>microcosm: the human being seen as a miniature reflection of the entire universe</term> so that man may be separated into "gold" by the action of his own internal lightning. The chemist, in his own place, separates the ore into **dross** <note>original: "loppam"; the waste or slag left over after smelting</note> and the realgar into smoke, vapor, or a sublimated body. The Archeus performs this within man through "Vulcanic arts" <note>the "arts of Vulcan" refer to alchemy and the transformative power of heat/fire</note>, until the substance is brought to its ultimate matter. For it is the ultimate matter of things that rejoices in its own exaltation, just as gold, once separated from the other two substances, triumphs in the fire—as does glass.

... Nor can I remain silent about what **Theophrastus Paracelsus** <note>Philippus Aureolus Theophrastus Bombastus von Hohenheim (1493–1541), the Swiss physician and alchemist who founded the school of "iatrochemistry"</note>, our teacher, further wrote concerning the secrets of the terrestrial Sun, specifically the difference between the **quintessence** <term>quintessence: the "fifth essence" or purest, most concentrated medicinal core of a substance</term> of gold, **potable gold** <term>potable gold: "aurum potabile" or drinkable gold, considered a legendary universal medicine</term>, and the oil of the same. The quintessence of the sun is a tincture extracted by the spirit of wine, the method of which we have set down above. Potable gold, however, is when the gold is dissolved into a drink along with other spirits and liquids. But the oil of gold is when a pure oil is made from the substance of the gold alone.

---

->*Description of Potable Gold.*<-

Take one ounce of gold leaf or gold powder; let this be dissolved into a juice. You shall add as much distilled vinegar as is sufficient, and distill it afterward. Separate the components from one another, and repeat this until no flavor of the additives remains. Next, let all the components be immersed together in five ounces of **water of life** <term>water of life: "aqua vitae," usually referring to high-proof distilled alcohol or brandy</term>, and let them be **digested** <note>alchemical "digestion" involves gentle, continuous heat to mature a substance</note> in a **pelican** <note>original: "pellicano"; a specialized alchemical vessel with two side-arms that allow condensed vapors to circulate back into the body of the liquid</note> for one month.

---

->*A description of its "water of life" is as follows.*<-

Take ten pounds of **burning wine** <note>original: "vini ardentis"; distilled spirits or alcohol</note>; take one handful each of roses, lemon balm, rosemary flowers, **wallflower** <note>original: "cheiri"</note>, leaves of both kinds of hellebore, and marjoram. Take two ounces each of cinnamon, mace, nutmeg, cloves, grains of paradise, all types of pepper, and cubebs. Take six ounces each of the juice of **celandine** <note>original: "chelidoniæ"</note>, **mullein** <note>original: "tapsi"</note>, and lemon balm, and five ounces of bean-stalk ashes. Mix them together and allow them to digest in a "pelican" vessel for twelve days; finally, separate the liquid and reserve it for the use we have described above.
