They call those men "donkeys" <note>In this context, the "donkey" is a symbol of humble, patient endurance, often associated with Christ’s entry into Jerusalem, whereas the author's opponents use it as an insult for stupidity.</note> who reveal their deceptions and errors to the world. These people prefer their own bearers to their parents, since it is arranged by nature that like is always drawn to like by a magnetic virtue. These unfaithful ones are not worthy to ride a donkey with us, in imitation of Him who is the highest wisdom; hence it happens that they have chosen monsters for themselves. Truly, this riding of monsters is not without its own omen. It is no wonder if at some time you wished to rouse your spirited donkeys, O Lord God, who are moved to kick out against such monstrous offspring while they rage, driven so stubbornly into pride and ignorance. 

If this kind of men were worthy of the donkey, they would certainly submit themselves to the yoke of patience, which needs neither bridle nor halter. They would also imitate this quality in the donkey: namely, that they would examine their steps, as it does, step by step with patience and modesty, lest they fall into ignorance. That is, they would more diligently test their own foundations, to see whether they consist of solid stones taken from the rock of truth.

They do not see that it would be more honorable to frankly confess their error and be led by repentance to the center of truth and the path of life, than to persist stubbornly in it, being carried along the wide road to destruction and perdition. 

Indeed, so that they might do this, we ask you, Almighty God, that you deign to open the eyes of these men, and that their mind might become an eye; and that, drawn by the divine spirit of your grace, they might return to the center of your true wisdom. From that fountain, may they draw living waters, having cast away the gushing filth in which they have been submerged until now. Alas, they still persist in these things all the more stubbornly the more they are made known to true men and the more frequently they are warned by them. 

Good God, powerful and merciful, you know to what great dangers the sick are exposed due to the introduction of the false medicine of the unfaithful, especially in this time, which is more corrupt than all others...

## AN EXPLANATION OF THE FIRST TWO
### chapters of Genesis according to
### *Physics.* <note>The author uses "Physics" (Greek: *physis*, nature) in the traditional sense of "Natural Philosophy"—the study of the physical world and how it works.</note>

There is no need for debate that the Spirit of God teaches us true Physics <term>Physics: here meaning the study of the natural world and its laws</term> from the mouth of Moses in the holy book of Genesis. For who would dare to deny that nature itself had its beginning at the creation of the world? Or who would affirm that it exists anywhere else but in the heavens and in the elements? Every Christian will admit that Moses, the prophet of God, speaks nothing at all from himself in this place, but has reported purely and sincerely to the people of Israel only those things which he had heard from the mouth of God. If anyone should perhaps doubt this, they should be rightly judged as someone to be hissed out <note>original: "explodendus"; literally to be driven off the stage, or rejected from the community</note> from the assembly of the faithful; for such a person should neither be listened to further, nor admitted to a pious and truly Christian conversation unless they repent.

Therefore, in teaching the people of Israel (chosen by God), Moses—acting on God's command—begins with Physics through the narration of the creation of the world and the first visible creature of nature. He did this so that, through the wonder of such magnificent works of God, he might better and more easily draw his recent and still unrefined <note>original: "rudes"; meaning those lacking formal education or spiritual maturity</note> disciples toward higher things—namely, to the supernatural—and lead them to the knowledge of their supreme Creator. 

Thus, from the beginning, he teaches them that before the most high God created man (His final creature) in His own image and likeness, He willed to create from nothing a dwelling place for him, and within it everything that would be necessary for his use. Nor did He want this creation to be devoid of the image of His own unity, which He had established as the first visible creature. This creation was also produced in a most beautiful order, arranged by "number, measure, and weight," <note>This is a reference to the Book of Wisdom 11:20: "But thou hast ordered all things in measure, and number, and weight," a foundational concept for medieval and early modern science.</note> and He adorned it with a certain admirable craftsmanship. He decreed to use these three things as instruments, or as the first ideas and forms, in this work of His.

From this we conclude, not without consideration or rashness, that men ought to have drawn the principles of the foundations of their arts and sciences—especially medicine, which first presented itself as a necessity to man after the Fall <note>The "Fall" refers to the expulsion of Adam and Eve from Eden, after which humanity became subject to disease and death, making medicine necessary.</note>—with the highest reverence and thanksgiving. This is especially true because we see that the supreme Creator used these means, even though He did not need them at all. For He who is almighty God could have created all things by a single command. 

However, He decided to act in this way so that He might give examples to us men (who are powerless in ourselves), according to whose standard we might aptly compare whatever we were to do in this world. He intended for us to recognize all our wisdom as originating from the fountain of wisdom—God—and not from anywhere else, and that we might give Him all the thanks for it. Therefore, from such divine patterns, we shall show that our principles, both Physical and Medical, have (as is right) their origin and source:

# PHYSICS

And this we shall strive to demonstrate with the strongest arguments—namely, the holy scriptures—and with undeniable examples, against which the infidels <note>original: "infideles"; here referring to non-Christian or secular philosophers who rely solely on reason without faith</note> may rage as they wish. We have also decided to declare the opposing principles of these people, so that both sides might be clear to the whole world, and it may be free for judicious men to discern, in the meantime, the true foundation from the false.

We are greatly comforted that we depend upon the fountain of truth, and in this we imitate the Christian doctors rather than the infidels; for our enemies can bring nothing against us except the authorities of men—men who are even rejected by God and who are utterly ignorant of the truth existing in God alone. Let one person be shown to us among those wise infidels, those ancient professors of the arts, or rather the teachers of their own inventions, who has known God in truth; or who was not a blasphemer against God and the Son of God (like that prince of his own Medicine, **Galen** <note>Claudius Galenus (129–216 AD), the most influential physician of antiquity, whose works dominated Western medicine for over a millennium. The author criticizes him for his paganism.</note>), or an idolater, and led astray by a spirit of contradiction.

Nonetheless, they want whatever they write and teach to be held as truth; led indeed by that reasoning which they do not even blush to put forward impudently. "In the treatment of the arts and faculties," they say, "it is not a matter of the knowledge of God, but this pertains to **Theology**"—as if they concluded that those arts should be possessed and practiced without God. What blasphemy is this? From this it appears clearer than light that those who utter such things do nothing out of love for their neighbor, but only out of greed. Can there be a true physician and true medicine without their Creator? But let us set aside men of that sort who even think such things, and let us finally recall ourselves to the concept of our own mind.

God, certainly, is a pure and simple essence consisting through Himself, incomprehensible by any other, invisible, indefinable, and indivisible. He is prefigured to us through **Unity** <note>The number one; in this philosophical system, Unity represents perfection and God, while higher numbers represent a fall into complexity and strife.</note>; which indeed, lacking multiplicity, does not admit any contradiction, and therefore no weakness. The world, therefore, since it was created by God in the image and likeness of unity, persists in that union, although it is ordered through numbers (as mention of these is made in **Genesis**). For these numbers still retained the nature of union under man's obedience, and they produced no multiplicity until man, seduced through the duality of the **Binary** <term>Binary: the number two; in Hermetic and Pythagorean thought, the "Binary" represents the first departure from the "One," signifying division, conflict, and the origin of evil</term>, plunged into the confusion of multiplicity, contradiction, and disobedience. 

Having stripped off the garment of perfection and the health of body and mind, wretched man contracted the stain of every vice, weakness, and disease. Previously, he did not need any medicine, until he fell into this disease—the source of all kinds of diseases—deprived of all health. Since, therefore, the first origin of all diseases happens to man through his departure from unity, it is necessary that all health consists in this unity alone, and must be sought in it. Now let us see into what diseases he has fallen: namely, into confusion, and the apprehension of both deaths <note>Likely referring to the death of the body and the "second death" or spiritual damnation.</note>. Therefore, badly affected in spirit and body,

->*In the sweat of your brow you shall eat your bread.*<-

This bread is to be understood not only as that by which the body is sustained for nourishment, but also as whatever is necessary for natural life. For a diseased and unhealthy body, the remedy for its life is bread; if the body is deprived of it, just as if it lacked food, it becomes subject to death. Indeed, at a very great cost, we have exchanged the "bread of blessing" for the "bread of sweat," pain, anxiety, and care. Therefore, the Bread of Medicine (not that which is acquired through this art <note>The "art" of medical practice</note>, but that which is necessary for recovering health) is to be sought nowhere else than in the place where we lost it—namely, in the garden of unhappiness and unity, which we have undertaken to explain briefly, from the perspective of Physics <note>original: "Physicè"; in this period, "Physics" referred to the study of all natural phenomena and the inner workings of the soul and body, not just mechanics.</note> alone. 

We previously touched upon the fact that the world itself was founded by God in the image and likeness of unity. Since its pure and sheer simplicity—without the multiplicity with which it was endowed from the beginning of its creation—is clearly known to us by its wondrously perfect roundness. For we see that a spherical body, no matter how large and no matter which way it is moved on a plane, rests only upon a single tiny point, which it has as its foundation; and this, as its hidden center, it makes manifest everywhere upon the surface. From this, one might not wrongly conclude that every sphere is no greater than its center, since it reflects nothing other than that very point, and being everywhere always like itself, it enjoys a fellowship with unity. In that mystery, certain great secrets lie hidden, both natural and supernatural, as well as much wisdom regarding the foundations of the arts and sciences. If, therefore, the world had remained in its unity, there would have been no need for a physician nor for medicine. Thus, the end of all medicine is that the sick person be led back to unity, upon which we have founded the true principles of Physics and Medicine. It remains for us to carry out what we have begun, with the help of the divine will and according to our strength.

### ON THE BEGINNING OF CREATION.

->*In the beginning God created the heaven and the earth.*<-

There are various opinions among some regarding the principle of the creation of the world. There are some among others who deny that this can be referred to time in any way, because time did not yet exist, and it <note>time</note> took its origin later from the "evening and the morning." Others maintain that it denotes an order, as if it were said: "first of all things." But these words—namely, *in the beginning*—seem to require interpretation beyond every common manner and reason of speaking, both in terms of time and in terms of order:

The author is analyzing the phrase "In the beginning" to determine if it refers to time, place, or a deeper metaphysical principle.</meta>

<page-num>336</page-num>
# PHYSICS #

Since Moses would have rather said **at the beginning** <note>original: "à principio"</note> in that sense of time—as some common interpretations even have it—or **among the first**, **firstly**, etc., these words also do not seem to designate a place. For it is a sin to wish to include the Word of God—God himself—within any place. Even before the creation of the world, no place could exist or be assigned. Since the infinite breadth of divine immensity has no boundaries, it follows that there is no "place" in the infinite, which is defined by the circumscription of limits. What then does Moses seem to mean by "the beginning" <note>original: "principium"</note>? The same thing indeed appears—spoken, however, under correction—as Saint John in chapter 1, using a similar but not different phrase with the same meaning; with this only exception: that his treatment is more **Theological** than this one, which seems most especially to be natural and **Physical** <note>In this context, "Physical" refers to *Physica*, the study of the natural world and its underlying laws.</note>.

Therefore, the Word of God, who is God, can be contained in no place, as said above, but rather encompasses and encloses all things within Himself, so that He is excluded by none. Consequently, if God was "in the beginning" of creation (which is to be piously believed), it necessarily follows that this "beginning" was not a place. Yet this "beginning" was something, in which the eternal Word of God created heaven and earth. Saint John testifies that Moses spoke well and correctly, sounding the same note as he did and with the same words. Otherwise, one could argue in this passage about improper speech or an error of the translators. It would be safest, therefore, to understand it no differently than the words themselves sound, according to pure and sheer simplicity. 

The greater part of interpreters assert that Moses accommodated his speech to the weakness of the still-unrefined intellect of the Israelite people and the fledgling Church. We indeed concede this. Truly, however, we do not see how it came to be that he did not also instruct them plainly and simply regarding this "beginning"—unless, perhaps, because it was not fitting for the unworthy to be participants in so great a mystery equally with others. Thus it is to be believed that Moses simply narrated all that he had heard from the Lord, and did not defraud his people; yet if there were things he attained through the intellect by a peculiar gift of God, it is not at all doubtful that he also revealed those things—which are not openly written—to the teachers. 

For the sacred scriptures testify that distinguished intellects existed among the children of Israel at the time when Moses was teaching **Genesis**, who could have borne far greater things than the unlearned people. What he taught them privately, however, I leave to other men studious of such mysteries to judge concerning this matter. Indeed, it would be very pleasing and delightful for me to hear, along with the rest, what pertains to this matter. This uncreated mystery, therefore, was prepared by the highest **craftsman** <note>original: "opifex"</note>, God, so that there would never be anything like it, nor would it ever return to what it was. And even if all things were to return into their first essence, they would not return into the Great Mystery, nor into their first matter. For what has been corrupted cannot be restored, nor is it restored; but it certainly returns into that very thing which existed before the Great Mystery. From that uncreated Great Mystery, many other special mysteries emerged. One should think no differently of the Great Mystery: in the separation of carnal and insensible things, each was brought into its own form. Yet nothing that was cut away perished, nor was it cast aside, but everything was made into a form and essence. Truly to be admired...

To finally come to the declaration of the principle: Who is ignorant, I ask, that even the smallest building requires its own principle, from which it rises into perfection, and is such a foundation in which or upon which it is built? If, therefore, the principle of every building is its foundation, what shall hinder us from saying that the physical principle of so great a work as we perceive this universal world to be was its foundation? In this principle, there is also a supernatural principle, upon which it was created and founded. Is it not known that two foundations are necessary in all man-made buildings: one from the same matter of which they consist; the other upon which they rest, and without which they cannot persist? It is necessary, therefore, for these two to be joined together, even though they exist of different conditions and natures. Furthermore, one is part of the building, as are the stones first cast upon the ground; the other, however, is outside the building, yet without it the building cannot stand, such as the ground by which the weight of the entire structure is sustained. Therefore, the principle of the creation of the world is its foundation. Someone will perhaps ask: which of these do we establish as the principle? Enough and more has been answered through what has been said: namely, each joined to the other, so that either they must be one, or that which is built upon them must fall. Nor is it yet sufficiently clear, through what has been said thus far, what this so admirable principle of creation is. Nevertheless, all things that do not fill a place due to a lack of physical body—such as all spirits—can be understood through the "center," because both spirits and centers are incomprehensible. Nor do I think we should overlook the truly marvelous nature of the center as it pertains to the formation of a sphere, according to the study of Nature. For as equal lines flow out from it in every direction and touch one another, a solid spherical body arises from that point. There are as many points on the surface as there were lines flowing from the center. From this, it is clear that a sphere, no matter how vast, lacks a base <note>By "base," the author means a flat side; a perfect sphere touches a plane at only one infinitesimal point.</note> and cannot rest on a flat surface unless it is held there. We conclude from these points, then, that it is not absurd to say every sphere is born naturally and physically from its center, through the rays of its unmoving center extended to a just surface—that is, a surface equally bounded and determined. And although these things may seem quite crude to you, having never heard them before, you should nevertheless consider them such that even those endowed with a brilliant sharpness of mind could find enough for contemplation and study throughout their entire lives; yet you must think that they can hardly grasp even a thousandth part of the center’s nature. Truly, whoever held a thorough knowledge of the nature of the center (as a certain most excellent man in the attained Philosophy <note>original: "adepta Philosophia." Just as there is no end to the center, so too is the infinite abyss of its powers and secrets beyond what any pen can describe. Therefore, we must rest for a while from describing and discussing it, until we have contemplated other things from the study of Nature that we think are noteworthy regarding the creation of the world. We will add only this: that a rough and unpolished image of the center is being presented here, as well as of those things which can proceed from it, which we offer to be decorated by those who cultivate a more refined style. It is enough for us now if we have established some sort of path for those studious of the secrets of nature, by which a way to higher things might lie open. We are the doorkeepers; may you, best of readers, be the one who penetrates more deeply into the hidden places, or may you be the one appointed by Him whose role it is to call each person to his life’s gift and duty.

## *The earth was formless and empty.*
<note>original: "Terra erat inanis & vacua." These are the Latin Vulgate terms for the Hebrew "tohu wa-bohu."</note>

By "formlessness" <note>original: "inanitatem," meaning emptiness or lack of purpose.</note>, what else can we see understood in this context except a lack and a need, which was eventually to be supplied by plenty? And by "emptiness" <note>original: "vacuitatem," meaning void or vacancy.</note>, do we not see, beyond a physical space, a state of sterility and unfruitfulness that was also to be restored to a better condition, as is clear from what follows? By a certain conjecture, the reason for this terminology appears to be that this element—compared to the others which are by their nature fluid, mobile, and rare—is stable, firm, and solid, being more closely related to the center. It is also more suitable for bringing forth creatures necessary for human life, better at supporting them, and more familiar to us than the other elements.

### PHYSICS
342

...to be understood as a mass, until the first division—namely, the division of light from darkness.

->*And God said: Let there be light, and there was light.*<-
<note>original: "Fiat lux, & facta est lux."</note>

Once the primordial matter and form of the world were completed, God willed to create light. For light is the spirit in which the life of natural things was placed by the Lord the Creator. This was surely a work intended to fulfill what was said concerning the earth and the abyss—specifically, the illumination of the latter, and the filling of the former's emptiness and void. It was, therefore, the first adornment of the heavens and the elements, and also the third and most powerful member of the "ideal world" <note>term: "ideal world" (mundus idealis). In Renaissance philosophy, this refers to the world as it exists in the mind of God, containing the perfect patterns or "ideas" for all created things.</note>. For this reason, it is commended to us in the first place by the supreme Creator and approved as good in these words:

->*And God saw the light, that it was good.*<-

One might hesitate at this point, wondering if God did not also see that the heaven and the earth were good. Truly, whoever looks upon these words with a pious mind understands that everything created by the only good God is nothing but good. Furthermore, just because one thing might be "more good" than another, the dignity of the "lesser good" is not thereby diminished. For the individual members of one and the same body are assigned their own specific role and duty by the will of their Creator, so that one does not envy the other. We read the same thing regarding charity <note>original: "charitate," often translated as "love" in the context of the theological virtues of Faith, Hope, and Charity (1 Corinthians 13).</note>: that it is greater than hope and faith. Yet it does not follow that the other two are of less value. Indeed, elsewhere we read that man is saved by faith alone. Therefore, for God "to see the good" (as a certain upright man said) is for Him to approve the good for our sake.

->*And he divided the light from the darkness.*<-

A similar doubt might arise: whether the darkness was not approved by God, since the good light is divided from it. Indeed, when something is divided from "the good," it often seems to be evil—as is the case with the separation of the sheep from the goats <note>A reference to the Last Judgment in Matthew 25:32-33.</note>. However, in Genesis, this division should be understood no differently than how we later read of the division of the waters from the waters (the upper from the lower), the heavens from the earth, and man from woman, and similar things. For a bond of union and a connection remains between them through a mutual longing; this arises because the parts were divided from one and the same source, rather than being born from different origins.

->*And he called the light Day, and the darkness Night.*<-

It is known that the day arises from light, and that night is introduced by the obstruction of that light. Light is obstructed by the placement of an opaque or dense body in its way, such as the sphere of the earth creating the shadow of night. Therefore, to cover light with darkness is to close the day; likewise, when night is driven away by light, the day is introduced.

### *And there was evening and morning, one day.*
<note>original: "Et factum est vespere & mane dies unus."</note>

The division of parts that remain in union is here explained. By "middle," we understand the light and the "artificial day" <note>term: "artificial day" (dies artificialis). In medieval and Renaissance timekeeping, this refers specifically to the period of daylight from sunrise to sunset, as opposed to the "natural day" of 24 hours.</note>, and by "evening," the night and the darkness; these two parts together constitute a single "natural day." This darkness must also be understood as the natural kind, which God willed to serve us. It is entirely different from the "outer darkness" that arose outside of or beyond nature, into which we read that the evil angel <note>a reference to the fall of Lucifer</note> was cast. Furthermore, regarding the phrase "one day," it is the opinion of the Doctors and the men of old that this should be considered by us with the greatest reverence. They believe that in the creation of the **intelligible world**, this day was completed as a concept in the divine mind, and is not to be numbered with the other five days. They maintain that this sensible and visible world was materially established according to the pattern of that "ideal world," and therefore its counting began later, from the "second" day. For the first number—namely, duality—is representative of matter, just as unity represents form, or rather, the "first idea." Unity is the offspring of unity, just as the number four is of duality. Therefore, they hold that the world was created divinely as "one" in the ideal sense, and not as "first"; and afterwards, it was created materially under the first number that represents its idea in sequence. For it seems impious to want to confine "Unity" under the laws of number and order; although human reason teaches that number consists of unities, we should not think that the ultimate Unity is to be counted within the series of numbers. Indeed, "unities" differ from "Unity" no less than the confusion of a multitude differs from simplicity. Because multiple unities create a multitude, the singular Unity cannot admit them in any way. For this reason, Moses said that the evening and morning became "one day" <note>original: "diem unum"</note>, and not the "first day," as many versions have it; there is no doubt that this occurred through a certain inadvertence of the translators. Thus far we have spoken of the creation of the **intelligible world**, which it would be a sin to assign to any place other than the infinite Word of God (which itself admits no place). Finally, we must now speak of the **visible world**, established according to the pattern and image of the former, having its foundation and principle in the great uncreated mystery.

# PHYSICS

->Let there be a firmament.<-
<note>original: "Fiat firmamentum."</note>

The creation of the visible world is narrated by Moses as having been made on the second day—which, among the numerical days, can rightly be called the "first." For it is from this day that the history of the material creation of the world begins its sequence. Moses further teaches that heaven was made through the creation of the **firmament** <note>term: "firmament" (firmamentum). From the Latin *firmare* (to strengthen or fix), this refers to the sky or expanse that separates the waters above from the waters below.</note> in the midst of the waters. This corresponds most aptly to what was said above regarding the waters: namely, that the "Spirit of the Lord moved over the waters." From this it is clear enough that all things previously existed as "waters," which the most high Creator had taken up and prepared for Himself as the primary matter of His material creation. Furthermore, the "middle" here is not to be understood as a point equidistant from two ends, but rather as a sequestration—just as we say a mediator or moderator is in the "middle" between two opposing parties so that the laws of friendship are not confused. In no different a way was the firmament created by the Lord as a "middle" here, so that henceforth the lower waters would not be mixed with the higher. Moses teaches this very thing, speaking from the mouth of the Lord: *and let it divide the waters from the waters*; as if He had said, "let it divide heaven from the elements."

->*And he divided the waters which are under the firmament.*<-

This division corresponds quite neatly to the one made between the light and the darkness; however, it is understood in the sense that the pure is divided from the impure. I ask you: what is purer than light, and what is more impure than darkness among all created things? In the second place, heaven is far and wide purer than all the elements. Accordingly, we see that the first division of those things contained under the unity of the "waters" was that of light from darkness (done on the "one" day), and the second was the division of heaven from the elements (following on the next day). From this, through physical contemplations, the first foundation of **Chemistry** <note>term: "Chemistry" (Chemia). In this context, it refers to the alchemical tradition of "Spagyrics"—the art of separating, purifying, and recombining substances.</note> takes its origin. Indeed, the most important practice of that art is concerned with the division of the pure from the impure in anything produced by nature. From what has been said, therefore, it is established that "pure" refers to the light and the heaven, while "impure" refers to the earth and the elements, separated by the divine "middle" of the firmament. # GENESIS

He laid the foundations of Physics primarily upon the upper part of Genesis. This was especially necessary for the successive generation and propagation of those things which God first created in the elements by the power and wisdom of His word. For nothing can generate within itself, but only in another which has been taken from itself. Therefore, the primordial waters were necessarily divided, so that the later division of Adam from Eve would correspond to that first division, and vice versa.

->### GENESIS<-

On this day, which is called the third, the **second member** of the visible world was created, namely the element under the name of "dry land," <note>original: *sub aridæ nomine*; a reference to Genesis 1:9–10, where God calls the dry land "Earth."</note> which was previously called "earth." It is as if Moses had said: in the beginning of the world, God created its superior part, the heaven, and its inferior part, the elemental earth. It might be asked why Moses made mention of the earth from the beginning, rather than the other elements such as water, fire, and air? The reason is indeed readily apparent: it was done because the earth is the lowest of all elements, and no other could better denote the lower part of the world. Furthermore, it is because this element alone among the others is stable and fixed; from its center, as if from a fountain or foundation, the rest seem to sprout and rise upward by the **artifice of fire.** <note>The author uses "artifice" (*artificio*) to describe the natural process or "craft" by which fire acts upon matter.</note> Who is ignorant—unless he is unacquainted with true Physics—that fire, the lower element, has the first root of its origin in the center of the earth? From there, it finally rises tirelessly by its own nature toward the hollow of the firmament; and, penetrating and passing through the bodies of earth and water, it carries the purer and more subtle parts with it, turned into air, up into the middle region. When it reaches there, it cannot penetrate higher, as the firmament prevents it. Consequently, its heat, now weakened by too much extension and overcome by the cold of the subtle earth and water and of the middle region, gives way. Together with the air and earth, the fire is turned into water through condensation; everything having thus become heavy, it falls back down to the earth and water, returning to the place from which it had come. **Physiochemists** <note>A term for scholars who combined natural philosophy (physics) with alchemical practice.</note> call this the **circular motion**, and they imitate it in their own operations just as they imitate other natural processes.

Therefore, the four elements, having been made volatile by the artifice of fire, receive in this manner from the higher stars the **masculine seeds of nature** <note>In the hermetic tradition, the stars were often seen as "masculine" influences that "impregnate" the "feminine" elements of the earth.</note> through an influx and impression occurring in the middle region (as demonstrated by **meteoric generations**). <note>The formation of atmospheric phenomena like rain or stones.</note> These seeds are afterward carried down by the aforementioned descent into their own four **matrices** <note>wombs or centers of origin</note> so that they may conceive and produce their offspring, which have been ordered from the beginning of their fertilization by the Supreme Creator for the propagation of all things generated from them. Of this generation there are four fathers and as many mothers; but of the other kind of generation, which occurs through influx alone, there is only one father and one mother—namely, the **Sun and Moon** in general, though in species there are many intermediaries of generation, as many as there are remaining astral bodies.

Furthermore, I shall not remain silent regarding what the wise **Chemists** <note>The author likely refers to alchemists following the tradition of Paracelsus.</note> understand by their "elemental earth" in their art. It is surely the very same thing that **Paracelsus** <note>Philippus Aureolus Theophrastus Bombastus von Hohenheim (1493–1541), a Swiss physician and alchemist who pioneered the use of chemicals and minerals in medicine.</note> wished to impress upon us through his **salt**. <note>Paracelsus taught that all matter was composed of three principles: Salt (body/stability), Sulfur (soul/inflammability), and Mercury (spirit/volatility).</note> For in that salt, the four elements have their seat and dwelling as if in their own home. This can indeed be demonstrated to the eye by a simple experiment, as will be discussed more broadly below.

### *And let the dry land appear, etc.*

The change of the name from "earth" to "dry land" for this single element—namely, the earth—indicates clearly enough that Moses wishes to explain in what sense he uses the word "earth." When he says, *God created the heaven and the earth; the earth was void and empty,* he refers not only to a single element, but to all the elements having a common center at the heart of the earth and founded upon the uncreated center. Otherwise, he would have said as before, *And let the earth appear.* He makes his meaning clearer by saying, *he called the dry land "earth."* It is as if he were saying: "I want you to understand that by 'dry land' I mean that earth which appeared from the gathering of the waters into one place from the four elements."

### *The gatherings of the waters he called seas.*

Moses made no mention of the bubbling of springs, or of those things which arise from them, such as rivers and others; he designated all the lower waters by the name of "seas" alone. Therefore, it is easy to make a conjecture from this that the former arise from the latter; that they bubble up through the pores and channels of the earth and flow back to their origin. They leave behind their saltiness in the earth and, by passing through it, are transformed into sweetness. The subterranean fire effects this very thing: it causes a sweet vapor to be raised up, while the salt remains behind with the earth to which it belongs. This is clearly visible to the eye of the **Chemist** <term>Chemicis: here referring to alchemists or early chemical practitioners</term> in the distillations of seawater or any brine: the sweet distilled water is carried upward while the salt settles at the bottom. # G E N E S I S.

[ocea]ns, lakes, and so on, proceeding from one and the same place, globe, and their single sphere, united at once under the firmament by the gathering of the waters. Fleshly eyes do not see what the eyes of the mind see, for the body of the earth itself hinders them. On the earth's surface, though seas, bays, lakes, and other such things appear divided or segregated to us, nevertheless they flow together into one and the same center. ->*And God said: Let the earth bring forth, etc.*<-

However, insofar as they lack sex, seed is given to them within themselves; and since they are deprived of free movement, they cannot come together like **locomotive beings** <note>Animals capable of moving from place to place.</note>. Therefore, the **Physicists** <note>The "Physicists" (Physici) refers to early natural philosophers who studied the physical world.</note> seem to be most delusional when they attribute sex to plants through their names of "male" and "female." For the similarity of external forms in natural things (even with some small difference) between two things, such as plants, should not be judged as a matter of sex, but should rather be referred to different species. 

Some, wishing to avoid this error, have fallen into a far greater one, assigning "greater" and "lesser" to these under one and the same name. By this very thing, they inadvertently admit their ignorance of the powers and virtues of natural things, from which names should have been given rather than from outward forms. It seems foolish to assign a male that differs in species from its **matrix** <term>matrix: used here as the "womb" or originating source</term>. Furthermore, the earth is the matrix and mother of all plants, but their seed is the father. See, I pray, in what species the parents of these things can agree! It is not so with animals and locomotive beings, where each parent agrees in species with the other.

# PHYSICS: THE FOURTH DAY.

## And God said: Let there be lights in the firmament of heaven, and let them divide the day and the night.

Moses repeats here what was said earlier under the <term>ideal form</term> <note>The author distinguishes between the "ideal" or conceptual creation in God's mind (Day 1) and the "material" realization of those concepts (Day 4).</note>—namely, *let there be light*—but now shows it as having been made in material form. For it appears that light is one thing, while a "luminary" (a light-bearing body) is quite another. It is just like the spirit and the body: although they are joined into one, the one is not the same as the other. In almost the same way, light and the luminary are related (to use a coarse example) as the flame and the oil in a lamp, except that in a lamp these are consumed, whereas in the heavenly bodies they are more enduring. Indeed, it is clear that light was created before the luminaries. Therefore, after the Most High God had adorned the earth with "vegetating vigor" <note>original: "vegetanti virore," referring to the life-force of plants.</note>, He wished to decorate the heaven with innumerable lights, as had also been stated in the previous order. *The earth was without form and void*; and soon after it is added, *And darkness was upon the face of the deep*. 

It should be noted that a wonderful mystery lies hidden in this order of events. For the supreme Creator of things wished to create plants before the sun and the other lights, lest perhaps wicked men might believe that plants were created by the stars, or that they received their primary powers and virtues from them. He did this so men would not attribute to the creatures what belongs to the Creator alone. Nevertheless, the greater part of mankind fell into this very error, as can be seen among the unfaithful who worship the sun and stars, neglecting the true God—or at least remaining ignorant of Him. We Christians, however, credit all virtues, both natural and supernatural, to the single power of God alone in all things. And although we confess (as is right) that all things were first created by God alone, and likewise animated and endowed with their virtues, we nevertheless see that in the ongoing propagation of those things which were to be generated in the elements after the initial creation, He chooses to use His own "means." These means include the powers of the higher lights, which also proceed from Him, as it is read:

*And let them be for stations and seasons.* <note>original: "Et sint in stationes & tempora." The author uses "stationes" (positions or stations) where standard biblical translations usually say "signs" (signa).</note> Are not the stations of the seasons, days, and years, according to their changes, the **secondary causes** <note>In medieval and Renaissance philosophy, God is the "Primary Cause" of everything, while natural forces like the sun or gravity are "secondary causes" through which He works.</note> for the production of things from the earth? Yet they remain dependent on the First Cause, namely God. This is evident from the text: *That they may shine in the firmament of heaven, and illuminate the earth.* Who, I ask, doubts that natural light is the life of natural things, just as that supernatural light is spiritual life? For Christ asserts to us that He is the light and the life of the world. Likewise, John says: *He was the true light* (he says) *which illuminates every man coming into this world* <note>John 1:9</note>, which is to say, He gives life. By a similar logic, for the earth to be illuminated by natural light is for it to be naturally quickened, just as to be illuminated by the supernatural is to be spiritually quickened. By this opinion, nothing is taken away from the Divine Majesty, since one and the same...

GENESIS.

...from the stars. It is the same power that illuminates the heavenly bodies and which illuminates the earth through them. Light is thus the <term>ideal form</term> <note>The author uses the Platonic concept of an "idea"—the perfect, spiritual blueprint—to explain that light is the spiritual essence of life.</note> of life, while darkness is the image of death. It was indeed said, *And darkness was over the face of the abyss.* What else should we understand by this than that the abyss at that time was still devoid of natural and supernatural life and light, and that God then first created the supernatural life of natural things when He said, *Let there be light*, and those things that follow.

->*And let them divide the day and the night.*<-

This is the same as what was said before: *God divided the light from the darkness, and called the light day, and the darkness night.* But although these things appear to be—and indeed are—opposites, such as light and darkness, day and night, God willed and commanded them to come together into one day with these words: *And there was evening and morning, one day.* For the <term>natural day</term> <note>original: "Physicus ac naturalis dies." The "physical" or "natural" day refers to the full 24-hour cycle, as opposed to the "artificial day," which refers only to the hours of sunlight.</note> is known to consist of the artificial day joined with its night. It is quite wonderful and worthy of the highest consideration that in the creation of the world, God willed for opposites to come together into one, just as the bright heaven and the dark elements form only one world; a world which also proceeded from a single principle through division into opposites. 

From this point forward, the venerable <term>Trinity</term> <note>The author argues that because God is three-in-one, nature also reflects this "threefold" structure where two opposites are joined by a third "bond."</note> shining in unity can clearly become known to us in all natural things. For that which must join two opposites into one must itself be a third thing that participates in both. This very thing is the bond of nature, a mutual love situated in nature, acting like the longing of parts that came from a natural unity to return to it again. For God is the author of peace and reconciliation in all things. Where, I ask, would this come from if there were no opposition? A few words are enough for the wise, especially since this passage requires a most sober and silent treatment. Therefore, this secret must not be profaned, since it belongs in a higher place than in a discussion of Physics.

->*And let them be for signs, for seasons, for days, and years.*<-

We see the manifold utility of the luminaries: from the noting of signs appearing in them, which partly and most importantly warn us of God’s wrath stirred up by our sins and incite us to repentance; partly for observations regarding agriculture; likewise for the notation of days and years for annals and other uses that serve to preserve human society and relationships. There are also those who wish for "signs" to be understood as <term>Astronomy</term>, which is to be sought from such signs for the prediction of future events. But this opinion is refuted by Christ, when He says to the Apostles that it is not for them to know the times, because they are reserved in the secrets of God. <term>Paracelsus</term> <note>Paracelsus (1493–1541) was a Swiss physician and alchemist who believed that all things in nature had "signatures"—physical marks that revealed their hidden medicinal or spiritual properties.</note> also does not wish to derive his art from here—which he calls "signed"—but rather from Physio-

<meta>This page continues the exposition of the Fourth Day of Creation (Genesis 1:14-19). Having previously discussed the division of day and night, the author now turns to the "signatures" or signs imprinted on the physical world by celestial bodies and the specific roles of the Sun and Moon in the natural order.</meta>

PHYSICS

Physiognomy is a certain observation of the marks impressed or engraved by the higher things into the lower through <term>influence</term> <note>original: "influxum." In Renaissance natural philosophy, this refers to the invisible flow of power or spiritual energy from celestial bodies down to the earthly realm.</note>, by which the powers and virtues of such things become known to us. This art is not taught in the schools of the unfaithful, nor is it derived from the vain opinions or dreams of men, but from the <term>light of nature</term> <note>original: "luce naturæ." A central concept in Paracelsian and hermetic philosophy, referring to the innate wisdom and divine intelligence present in the created world, accessible through observation and piety.</note>, which is illuminated by supernatural light; therefore, we must seek from the latter in order to obtain the former. Nevertheless, there are certain means granted by the Lord to people of good will, by which their minds are best disposed to perceive and understand these things, and are liberated from every impediment that might hold them back. Yet truly, such things rarely or never happen to lazy and <term>slothful</term> <note>original: "acediosis." Acedia was a specific spiritual ailment characterized by apathy, boredom, or a refusal to engage with divine work.</note> people; and they are especially denied to those who utterly despise such things out of ignorance. Moreover, the signs of lower things are to be considered in two ways: either from external signs, or through the examination of internal ones, which <term>Volcanic Anatomy</term> <note>original: "Anatomia Vulcanica." This refers to chemical or alchemical analysis—using fire (the tool of Vulcan) to reveal the hidden, internal "signatures" or properties of a substance.</note> teaches.

### *That they may shine in the firmament, and illuminate the earth.*

In the preceding sections, this passage has been declared sufficiently and then some, where we compared light to life, and illumination to the giving of life; therefore, it may be passed over.

### *God made two great lights, etc.*

Concerning all lights in general, it was previously spoken in this manner: *Let there be lights in the firmament of heaven*; but now Moses institutes a discourse concerning two in particular, and those the chief ones: the sun and the moon. After God had placed the light in the firmament, so that through the medium of the greater luminary it might not only shine within itself, but also illuminate the elements by day—which were otherwise dark by their own nature—He did not wish for them to be destitute of light at night. Therefore, by His providence, He also created the lesser luminary, which would receive its light from the greater, so that the darkness of the earth's shadows might be illuminated through the night. Thus, whatever dryness had been introduced to the elements by the sun during the day on account of its heat might be irrigated in turn at night by the moon with the <term>dew of heaven</term> <note>original: "rore cæli." It was a common scientific belief that the moon's influence was cooling and moistening, providing a necessary balance to the sun's drying heat to allow plants and animals to grow.</note>; and by the moon's moistening, as by the sun's nourishment, all things might be propagated, by the power of God alone, but through the means that have been stated.

### *And the stars.*

On account of the positioning between the creation of the two luminaries and the stars—specifically, the phrase *to rule over the day and the night*—a doubt could arise whether one should read "with the stars" rather than *and the stars*. It would be as if the meaning were this: that the great lights might also rule over the remaining smaller ones, and especially the moon in respect to its duty and office. Whichever way it is read, it seems that there is little or nothing deviated from the true goal in Physics, but in Theology, *and the stars* is the preferred reading. For

But what then? This is the state of the human race. ->*And he placed them in the firmament of heaven, that they might shine upon the earth.*<-

Moses explains the reason why God placed the luminaries <note>The sun, moon, and stars.</note> in the <term>firmament</term> <note>From the Latin "firmamentum," meaning a vast, solid dome or expanse of the sky that separates the waters above from the waters below.</note> of heaven: namely, so that the darkness, which had been divided from the light and placed among the elements, might be illuminated. Indeed, the matter itself teaches us that the darkness of the abyss was placed within the elements, since the shadow of the earth causes night in the lower region beneath the firmament. For the point of the pyramid of the shadow of night <note>A geometric description of how the Earth casts a cone-shaped shadow into space, creating night.</note> is not raised higher than the <term>elementary region</term> <note>The sphere of the four elements (earth, water, air, fire) extending from the center of the Earth to the moon.</note> can reach. Consequently, it can in no way block the light throughout the entire sphere of the firmament.

->*He made, and he placed, and those things which follow.*<-

This repetition should be understood in no other way than that which occurs throughout the text, <note>original: "Fiat, & factum est"</note> *Let it be, and it was done*; as if it were said: God did not conceive or decide to act before it was already accomplished. By this very fact, it is demonstrated to us that God does not require time to execute his conceptions, but that these exist as cause and effect simultaneously and in the same moment within the Divine mind. Although we see that God sometimes used an interval of time—such as that between the first and sixth days of the world's creation—we should think this was done rather for our instruction, so that we might better understand the works of the Lord and be able to contemplate their excellence more deeply. Otherwise, things that happen in a single moment would be imperceptible to us, since we are barely able to understand even those things which are ordered in time. Furthermore, we are warned by these things to do and execute our own individual tasks with both order and mature judgment. Moreover, we should consider the perfection of the world through the <term>senary</term> <note>The number six, considered "perfect" by ancient and Renaissance mathematicians because its divisors (1, 2, 3) add up to itself.</note> and admire it with veneration. Let us also revere and observe the sanctification of rest from the <term>septenary</term> <note>The number seven.</note>, which denotes the union of the mind with the body, or of the eternal with that which is to come. And most importantly, as we touched upon before, he did this so that he might hold our attention for some space of time in the contemplation of these things—for we are otherwise by nature fickle and unstable in our character and thoughts, lightly passing over even the best and most wholesome things. For what is more delightful than to be occupied and delighted, day and night, with one's whole heart and mind in such admirable works of God? Truly, meditations of such thoughts will not return without fruit; rather, they will sharpen the mind and character to perceive everything that we ought to know and understand in all things. Thus far concerning the light of the luminaries, in accordance with which Paracelsus <note>Philippus Aureolus Theophrastus Bombastus von Hohenheim (1493–1541), a famous Swiss physician and alchemist who sought to bridge the gap between medicine and the natural world.</note> strove to shape the <term>sulfur</term> <note>In Paracelsian alchemy, "Sulfur" is one of the three "Primes" (with Salt and Mercury), representing the principle of combustibility, soul, and vital heat.</note> of nature in natural things. # THE FIFTH DAY.

> *Let the waters bring forth the creeping thing of a living soul, and the flying thing above the earth, under the firmament of heaven.*

A difference is visible immediately from the beginning of the creation of animals, which exists between their life and the life of growing things. The life of plants is called a "germinating and greening" life: but the life of animals is taught in this place to be a "living soul" <note>original: "anima vivens"</note>, which is whatever moves by its own free effort, as the words sound: "creeping thing" and "flying thing." Therefore, it should not be inferred that plants do not live. For they also move according to the condition of their nature, and even by a free and non-violent motion, though not from place to place, as can be seen from their growth and propagation. Furthermore, it should be noted that the Most High commands the waters to produce the flying thing, and not the earth, nor in the earth, but "above the earth and under the firmament"; this is understood as the middle region of the air and elemental fire. For the air is nothing else than water dissolved by fire and persisting in that solution by the word of God. Therefore, by this word—"above the earth and under the firmament"—a clear enough mention of the creation of air and fire has been made for those who understand, since flying things were also produced in part from fire (without which air cannot persist). For it is naturally impossible for the element of air to exist without the element of fire, just as by no reasoning can the element of water be separated from the element of earth, unless it happens against nature. No fire is visible in steel, nor in a whetstone, yet from the frequent clashing of those two, a visible fire appears to our eyes: a true element ignited in the air, which it uses as fuel. While making mention of the air, he cannot remain silent regarding fire, because fire is the most powerful natural cause of the air. By this reasoning, the lower part of the waters beneath the <term>firmament</term> <note>In ancient cosmology, the "firmament" was the solid dome or expanse of the sky that separated the "waters above" from the "waters below."</note> is beautifully divided into the four elements. Furthermore, to return to living creatures, we are taught in this place that birds came forth from the waters. Who can doubt, from what has been said, that air by its very nature approaches closer to water than it does to the nature of the earth itself? Therefore, just as we see <term>creeping or swimming things</term> <note>The Latin *reptilia vel natatilia* refers generally to fish and aquatic life in this context.</note> fill the lower waters nearest the earth, in the same way, winged creatures fill the aerial waters above the earth and beneath the firmament, which are closest to fire and situated in the middle. Creeping things upon the earth also fill the aforementioned air, but they are not raised up above the earth like the winged creatures. Just as it was said above that Moses made mention of fire and air silently under the cover of the other two elements, water and earth, we can also understand that all things generated from earth and water—both those hidden and those manifest—were created through the gathering of the waters and the appearance of the dry land.

The reason Moses did not speak openly about those things which were created by God in the secret depths of those two elements at the same time as the elements themselves may be seen as follows: since his primary intention was to more easily draw the <term>Israelite people</term> <note>The author views the ancient Israelites as "rude" or "unrefined," meaning they required simple, sensory explanations rather than complex scientific or esoteric theories.</note>—who were still unrefined—toward admiration and knowledge of their Creator through things exposed to the senses, he taught them from the excellence of created things that He who had established out of nothing those things they saw before their eyes and which they enjoyed was far more excellent still. If, however, he had spoken of those things lying hidden in the center of the waters and the earth, the instruction would have been more obscure, owing to the lack of a clearly evident demonstration. Furthermore, it was not Moses’s purpose to bring forward every single detail particularly from the very beginning, since those things become intelligible successively, either through the understanding of other things or through themselves. Who can perfectly describe the earth or the waters unless he likewise understands everything that belongs to their substance?

Moreover, stones and metals are the offspring of both elements, according to whether they participate more in one than the other. For both consist of a mixture of earth and water. However, in the generation of stones, the power of earth prevails, just as in the structure of metals, the watery power prevails. To this, we encounter the opinion of the majority of <term>unfaithful Physicists</term> <note>The "unfaithful" here likely refers to secular Aristotelian philosophers or physicians who relied solely on material logic rather than spiritual or alchemical insights.</note>, who assert that stones and metals are in no way fit or suitable for medicine, no matter how they are prepared, unlike plants and animals. They first bring forward this reason: that these things are too hard and more compact by nature than can be digested by the stomach, much less converted into the substance of a human being or associated in any way with the faculties of one's life. Who does not see that these arguments are more childish than worthy of a response? A similar point we might throw back at them is that their own wood, which they call <term>Holy Wood or Guaiacum</term> <note>Guaiacum is a very dense, hard wood from the Americas used in the 16th and 17th centuries as a primary treatment for syphilis.</note>, and many of their other plants and animals, are equally hard and compact, yet nevertheless by them...

If they <note>The author is likely arguing against the "Galenists"—traditional physicians of the time who preferred plant-based remedies over "harsh" chemical or metallic ones.</note> say they do not administer the body or hard matter itself, but only the substance of them extracted by their decoctions: Where, I ask, have they seen true *Chemists* <note>original: *Chemistis*. In this era, "Chemist" refers to what we now call Alchemists or iatrochemists (chemical physicians).</note> give whole metals to the sick to be swallowed? But they might add a supplement to that, simply to appear to have said something to remove the use of metals from medicine. Yet they say: we know that Nature produced not metals, but well-growing plants and other things to sustain human life. We answer from the mouth of their own aphorism that <term>nutrients</term> <note>original: *alimenta*. The author is distinguishing between food, which nourishes the body, and medicine, which acts upon it.</note> are not medicines. Therefore, metals will be better suited for healing the less they pass into nutrition. This is their framework: A medicine (they say) that passes into nutrient ceases to be a medicine. Since no other kind of argument remains for them, they flee to a certain "sacred anchor" of the unfaithful <note>A Latin idiom, *sacra anchora*, meaning a last resort or final refuge.</note>; they call it a distinction, or some other name. Under such coverings, there lie the destruction of the arts rather than true distinctions.

Nor are there those lacking who consider stones and metals to be dead bodies, yet grant life to their own plants. See, I ask, how in their eagerness to harm the *Chemists*, they bring manifest blasphemy against God. What could ever be said of God more detestable than that the author of life created death or anything subject to death? Was not death first introduced into man—the last of all creatures—by the devil alone? What, therefore, broke into the other preceding creatures before his creation? Could the living God, or even Life itself, create death, or anything dead among those things which He fashioned? Far be this blasphemy from us, that even a tiny bit of it should ever enter our minds. It is the part of a Christian truly to believe: that God created heaven, earth, light, and all things through Himself and living in Himself. 

The emptiness and void, as well as the darkness over the face of the deep, had nothing in common with death; nor could they prevent those things created by the author of life from living supernaturally. Among these are the <term>three first principles</term> <note>In alchemical theory, these are Salt, Sulfur, and Mercury—the building blocks of all matter.</note> we mentioned, and the chief members of the world under the divine and mental <term>monad</term> <note>original: *unario*. The "Monad" represents the number one, signaling unity and God.</note>, first conceived in the intelligible world. In whose image this visible world was created under the material monad and <term>triad</term> <note>original: *ternario*. The "Ternary" or number three, representing the Trinity and the three alchemical principles.</note>. Whoever, therefore, does not understand the powers and faculties of the monad and the triad, it happens that he is blinded for a time in the confused darkness of the <term>dyad</term> <note>original: *binarij*. The "Binary" or number two, often associated in this philosophy with division, separation, and conflict.</note>, until he is illuminated by the light of the monad. For Unity alone is life absolute in itself. Duality [the dyad] truly is death, through its dissection from unity, its withdrawal, and its corruption; it is an accidental accessory. However, that Trinity of nature, generated and received from the unity and life of the world, is naturally brought to life. Therefore, rejecting Duality as an enemy of nature, the natural Trinity easily returns to the nature of its parent, namely Unity. But these things more broadly in the following and...

...in different ways, so that the minds of students might more easily be able to refer the <term>secrets</term> <note>original: *arcana*. In alchemical thought, an "arcanum" is a hidden, powerful essence of a substance that contains its healing power.</note> of all things to that highest secret good in all and through all, as if to the center of all life. To return at last to metals and stones: the closer these are to the center, the more they must be judged as having an affinity for natural life. Conversely, the more that vegetables are distant from said center, the less they are partakers of that same life, even though this is not apparent from outward appearance. Do not all the celestial rays of the greater and lesser lights <note>The Sun, Moon, and stars.</note>, however many there are, look toward and reflect back to the center as if to their own natural principle? Therefore, the more tightly they meet in unity, the more they take on the strengths and virtues of natural unity. For one who understands, these few words are sufficient for now. 

But if the world does not see or understand those things which are right before its eyes, how will it perceive the things that lie hidden in the inner chambers of nature, not manifest to its sight? From this it happens that the world considers all things that do not appear on the surface to be nothing. For that same reason, it does not long for heaven, nor does it dread hell, because it sees neither of them. But the Mind, to which all these things are accessible, clear, and manifest, values them more than the things which are open to everyone. One must leave the world to its own pleasures, for it desires nothing more than to be deceived; let it therefore have what it wishes. 

If it were said to the world that the "center" of minerals is a more perfect medicine than the "center" of vegetables, there is no doubt that it would laugh. But if it hears from anyone that more medicinal virtues exist in its <term>Rhubarb</term> <note>original: *Reubarbaro*. Rhubarb was a staple of the Galenic, plant-based medical tradition, used primarily as a purgative.</note> than in all metals and minerals, it applauds this opinion as if it had fallen from heaven. What wonder is this? Even toward the truth and experience that it sees openly, the world is unbelieving. Will it approve of things that it does not perceive even with all the strength of its intellect? 

If the unfaithful Athenians <note>A derogatory reference to the ancient Greek authorities like Galen and Aristotle, whom the author views as "pagans" compared to the "Christian" chemistry of Paracelsus.</note> had understood or written even a tiny bit concerning the opening of the bodies of metals and minerals, and the hunting out of the secrets for restoring life from them—as **Paracelsus** did—nothing would ever have been more worthy, more praised by their followers, nor more accepted in any age. Into what great clamors they would have erupted, so that nothing else could be heard but: "O venerable antiquity of Greece, to which the assembly of learned men has consented for so many centuries!" 

Farewell to the recent discoveries of the moderns, which we see no one praising except their own authors. Nevertheless, they swell up with this pride, even though they have left the most powerful mysteries of nature untouched and intact until now. Truly, if any authority is acquired through age and applause, what greater authority shall approach than that which the "author of lies" <note>Satan.</note>, born before the foundation of the natural world, has claimed for himself? To him, the greatest part of men even now consents. Yet his ancient deceit was not as well known to the ancients as it is to the moderns today. Furthermore, in these times of ours, there has arisen much more clearly...

### A CLEAR AND QUITE BRIEF EXPOSITION
### **of the Enigmatic and Truthful Speech,**
### *left by Mercury Hermes Trismegistus.*

That famous Hermes Trismegistus, surnamed Mercury, being instructed in no common way in the doctrine of Genesis delivered by Moses, left to posterity this <term>spagyric Physics</term> derived from it. But because it was enigmatic and compressed with the greatest brevity, there have been various interpreters of it, according to each person’s different capacity of mind. It is known to everyone that all those who have attacked this most difficult province have mostly turned toward the transmutation of metals in an allegorical sense. I, however, because I saw what was most necessary and most consistent with the author's mind, have explained it for the <term>medical art</term>, for the benefit of students and the sick, and for the advantage of the entire Republic. It is clear from the conclusion which the author makes near the end, that his opinion should not be understood to concern metals alone under the enigma he poses, but also vegetables and animals, which will be explained more widely below in its proper place. Therefore, since I see that the other interpreters have only silently touched upon the other two most general classes of things, I did not wish to imitate them, nor did I decide to refute them, but rather to leave to each his own opinion intact. Anyone who wishes to remove the **leprosy of metals** <note>original: *lepram metallorum*. In alchemy, "leprosy" refers to the impurities or "base" qualities of metals like lead or iron that prevent them from being "healthy" (i.e., gold).</note> will be able to learn of it more exactly from those who have been more anxious about this business than I. If, however, anyone desires to look upon that **universal medicine**, drawn from any of the three aforementioned classes, which is able to heal all diseases of the human body indifferently, I shall strive with all my strength to reveal, for his sake, whatever has been hidden away with me. For it is certain that in all things produced by nature, there are both superior and inferior virtues. Therefore, for a perfect knowledge of natural philosophy, of these three...

A full knowledge of the various kinds of <term>Volcanic anatomy</term> <note>original: *anatomiæ vulcanicæ*. This refers to "anatomy by fire," or the alchemical process of breaking substances down into their core elements using heat (the domain of Vulcan, the god of fire).</note> is exceedingly necessary. It is no wonder that those from whom the hidden mysteries of nature are concealed find it surprising that a medicine of this kind can be discovered—one so universal that it can heal all diseases without distinction. This is because they are carried upward by only a single wing (as the saying goes), and a very heavy one at that. Their minds can scarcely bear even the most obvious things, for they remain so fixedly imbued with what they were taught in their youth that they will not admit better ideas if they are slightly more obscure. Therefore, they are to be left to their own decay when they prove stubborn. We dismiss such people for the present and speak instead to the students of truth.

Furthermore, every thing has its own power or virtue within it, but it also contains its own poison <note>original: *virus*. Here used in the sense of a natural impurity or harmful element.</note>, from which it can be cleansed by the alchemical art. However, because of the varying degrees of these qualities, all things must be tested, and only those which are best should be retained. In this way, this craftsmanship is sometimes relieved of the intolerable burden that weighs upon the artificial extraction of the <term>Sun and Moon</term> <note>original: *Solis & Lunæ*. In alchemical terms, these usually refer to Gold and Silver, or the masculine and feminine principles of matter.</note> from all things.

If, therefore, you follow the opinion of father Hermes <note>Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary Hellenistic figure to whom many foundational alchemical and philosophical texts were attributed.</note>, and join the Sun to its Moon, and nourish their offspring in its own earth with a gentle fire, you will perfect that medicine of which he speaks when he says, *all darkness shall flee from you, etc.*

But indeed, before you undertake this work, you must first return yourself to the simplicity of unity through the alchemist's art applied morally. By this, you may learn first to drive away all darkness of the mind from yourself; afterwards, illuminated from on high, you will perceive the light and the medicine that can expel darkness and ignorance from your own body and mind. Therefore, you must learn with the greatest attention of mind the moral philosophy that I propose to you in the following pages, and you must first diligently practice it within yourself in a moral sense, if you desire to become skilled in the things which father Hermes teaches in this place.

You could not be taught in any easier or clearer words than those contained in this brief discourse on the exposition of the Hermetic art. It teaches that in this fleeting life, no art should be more sought after than this: the art by which we are taught the separation of natural bodies from their **binary** <note>The state of duality, often associated in this philosophy with division, conflict, or impurity.</note> and their reduction into a union through the **ternary** <note>The number three, representing a stable, divine, or perfected unity in many mystical traditions.</note>.

Truly, no better model could be given for the human resurrection than from this teaching. Indeed, the author suggests that the natural bodies of inanimate things—once divided from their spirits and cleansed—can be joined to them again for a "resurrection," which is to say, a state of perfection. Just as human bodies are separated by death from their spirits or souls so that later, by the will of God alone, they may rise again into eternal life through a union better than the first; in no different a way does this art teach us, through the "artificial corruption" of inanimate bodies (which is called **chemical death**), to separate their spirits and souls. This is done to lead them back from their "three-fold state" to a unity—that is, to a better life; though not an eternal one, it is nonetheless more excellent than the life they previously held from nature. For inanimate things live within themselves...

Once these elements have reached a state of union, they reveal this life most clearly through their effects on other bodies, causing them to live without decay until the ultimate boundary of their incorruptible nature is reached. Nor is this true only for inanimate bodies, but also for rational beings in regards to this fleeting life. Therefore, the aim of this <term>Hermetic doctrine</term> <note>original: *Hermeticæ doctrinæ*. Referring to the teachings attributed to Hermes Trismegistus, which combine philosophy, alchemy, and spirituality.</note> is a certain universal medicine. This medicine not only removes the corruptions and all diseases of the body without distinction but also prepares them so that they may live a long life until the end appointed by God—a life which is almost always shortened by various accidents and human recklessness. 

Men should certainly consider that they have achieved much if they have removed so many and such varied corruptions. Beyond the fact that they are able to gain physical health in this way, they also lift all the shadows and veils of the mind. Once these are removed, they easily perceive the truth of both the created world and of God, the creator of all things. For His glory and the salvation of their neighbors, they diligently search, ask, and knock; they do not knock in vain, for they find, receive, and are let in. <note>This is an allusion to the Gospel of Matthew 7:7: "Ask, and it will be given to you; seek, and you will find; knock, and it will be opened to you."</note> 

By no means do we say that salvation is acquired by this medicine; rather, we say that our bodies are only prepared by it so that they do not hinder the reason and mind given by God, which yearn for His glory and our salvation. Indeed, it is the opinion of the followers of a purer and more sincere Christian philosophy that our bodies can "die" voluntarily while our natural life remains. In this state, our spirits or souls are drawn away from their bodies intellectually and supernaturally, without the <term>Physical bond</term> <note>original: *Physico*. This refers to the natural, biological connection between soul and body; the author suggests a meditative state of "separation" or ecstasy that does not result in actual death.</note> being dissolved. 

They are drawn away beyond and above nature solely by the speculative or meditative faculty, as well as by the discipline of the body—not only by the restraint of its appetites but even by their "castration." <note>In this context, "castration" refers to the complete severing or mortification of worldly desires and bodily urges, rather than a literal surgical act.</note> Finally, through the union and alliance of the Divine Spirit with the soul, achieved by the rejection of earthly things and the embrace of eternal and celestial ones, these three are joined into one. In this way, through the likeness of Him who alone is one God in a trinity of persons, we are made closer and more conformed to Him for eternal life and His glory,
