# ON THE SPAGYRIC MEANS OF PREPARATION,
## toward the true knowledge of attained philosophy and the pure sight of the light of nature.
### OF HERMES TRISMEGISTUS.
->With the expositions of Gerard Dorn.<-

It is true without lie, certain, and most true. That which is below is like that which is above. And that which is above is like that which is below, to accomplish the miracles of the one thing. <note>original: *miracula rei unius*. This is the central tenet of Hermeticism, suggesting a fundamental correspondence between the microcosm (human/earthly) and the macrocosm (divine/heavenly).</note>

And just as all things were from one, by the meditation of the one: so all things were born from this one thing by adaptation.

Its father is the Sun, its mother the Moon. The Wind carried it in its belly. Its nurse is the earth. The father of all <term>Thelesma</term> <note>original: *Thelesmi*. A Greek-derived term often interpreted in alchemical texts as "perfection," "will," or the vital life-force that permeates the universe.</note> of the whole world is here. Its power is complete if it is turned into earth.

You shall separate the earth from the fire, the subtle from the dense, gently and with great ingenuity. It ascends from the earth into the heaven, and again it descends to the earth, and receives the power of the higher and the lower things.

Thus you will have the glory of the whole world. Therefore all darkness shall flee from you.

This is the strong fortitude of all fortitude. Because it will overcome every subtle thing and penetrate every solid thing.

Thus the world was created.

From this shall come marvelous adaptations, the manner of which is this. Therefore I am called <term>Hermes Trismegistus</term>, <note>meaning "Hermes the Thrice-Greatest." He was a legendary Hellenistic figure regarded as the author of the Hermetic Corpus, a series of texts on philosophy, magic, and alchemy.</note> having the three parts of the philosophy of the whole world.

What I have said concerning the operation of the sun is complete.

Thus far, having made a certain comparison to the likeness of the world’s creation, he teaches that his <term>spagyric</term> <note>From the Greek *spao* (to draw out) and *ageiro* (to gather). Thus, it finally happens that a terrestrial spagyric offspring of this kind puts on a heavenly nature through ascent, and thereafter by its descent, it receives the nature of the terrestrial center in the manifest, while nevertheless retaining in secret the nature of the celestial center which it had acquired through its ascent. If there be any temporal glory from the whole world, you shall find it in this art, by which indeed you may be able to immediately drive away all obscurity of both body and mind. 

Furthermore, in this medicine, a force and strong fortitude lies hidden beyond every manner of healing. Accordingly, through it, wondrous cures for diseases shall be performed, the manner and way of which you have here in this place, from me, Hermes Trismegistus, through the tradition of this spagyric art under a brief discourse of words. 

I am therefore called Hermes Trismegistus <note>Original: *Hermes Trismegistus*, meaning "Hermes the Thrice-Greatest."</note> for this reason: because I teach that the triple natural philosophy of the whole world is complete in the operation of the spagyric sun. But because these things may perhaps seem to have been fulfilled too briefly, I shall not be burdened, for the sake of those who study natural virtue and truth, to elucidate more fully according to my strength those things which can be explained by no parchment sufficiently, on account of their so sublime excellence.

# NATURAL PHILOSOPHY

...that which is devoid of truth. Although indeed a better definition of both <note>Likely referring to the "truth" and "falsehood" mentioned in the Emerald Tablet's opening lines.</note> cannot be given, it nevertheless cannot be sufficiently understood by those who are scarcely initiated into the sacred and hidden mysteries of nature because of its universality. Wherefore it requires much elucidation, which we have deduced must be taken from division. Thus, "the true" can be understood in two ways. Taken in a purely physical way, it is not without falsehood. From this, it is clear that the author <note>Hermes Trismegistus.</note> does not mean this, but proposes to us a <term>spagyric</term> <note>The art of separating and recombining substances to purify them.</note> truth—that is, one purified from falsehood. For nature is truthful on one hand and lying on the other; she is both incorruptible and corrupt. She obtained truth in her creation through the Word of God, but she possesses falsehood from an accidental addition, and because she gave place to it, she is now forced to keep it. Nor can nature by herself vindicate or separate her truth from her falsehood unless she is aided by the spagyric mastery.

It is clear, therefore, that Physics is concerned as much with the falsehood of nature as with its truth; but the spagyric art is concerned only with the truth of natural things, purified from their own falsehood. Thus, the "truth" of any thing is properly called its incorrupt nature. One should not think, as many do, that Hermes spoke this only in a common way to his "sons" <note>A traditional term for alchemical students or initiates.</note>, as if he simply wished to indicate to them that he speaks the truth. Rather, even under crude speech common to everyone, and even within every minor distinction, he enclosed the greatest mystery of nature. He did this for this reason: so that those who are not his sons might "seeing, not perceive, and hearing, not understand." <note>A paraphrase of Mark 4:12.</note> For secrets cannot be more safely hidden than when they lie concealed under a manifest husk. 

We see that God willed to do this very same thing everywhere in nature in all things: namely, to cover the precious beneath the vile, so that it might not be found by the unworthy. How much gold do vile sand, mud, and rejected stones veil from eyes looking upon those things which the hand of the ignorant casts aside and the foot of the unknowing tramples? How secretly has He enriched regions that are barren on the surface with unknown wealth, which He denied to fertile lands? Why do anxious mortals still complain? Since God has given all things to all, saying:

> Seek first the kingdom of God, and all things shall be added unto you. <note>Matthew 6:33.</note>

Thus, a person's own negligence is the most powerful cause of their poverty and want. Although God willed that there be more poor than rich, so that the latter might exercise their charity toward the former, and the needy might follow Christ by taking up their cross—for He Himself willed to be the poorest of all on earth. Hence it also happens that gold is not found in every stone or any sand, and to know those things which contain it is not granted to everyone from heaven, lest all should become equally rich. 

But let us return to where we started: to the truth of natural things, which Father Hermes teaches must be sought through the spagyric art, and that the pearl must be separated from the vile and the cast-off. He says it is certain and most true that any <term>elemented thing</term> <note>original: *elementatum*; a composite physical body made of the four elements.</note> contains something other than the elements within itself, which indeed is [least of all...] <note>The sentence continues onto the next page.</note>

<meta>catchword: least</meta>

<summary>Dorn explains that alchemical truth (spagyric truth) is the original, incorrupt nature of a substance, which must be separated from its "falsehood" or impurities. He justifies the cryptic language of alchemy by comparing it to how God hides gold in common sand and mud to keep it from the unworthy.</summary>

->TRISMEGISTI.<-

...is extremely well known, but to very few, and to far fewer is it certain. For example: it is known to most people that some stones and some sands contain gold within them, but it is certain to no one except for the one who has tested the matter and extracted it through the experience of the art. This person alone can say that it is certain. Indeed, the author <note>Hermes Trismegistus</note> intends to prove to us in this place that the <term>spagyric art</term> <note>The alchemical process of separating and recombining substances to achieve a purified state.</note> excels all others by a certain authority, which is experience; it is as if he were saying: "I myself have experienced that this spagyric art is true, certain, and most true." For I have learned the certainty of this art not from the authority or writings of men, but from experiment alone.

It should be noted, therefore, that what he said previously regarding "truth without physical falsehood" <note>Referring to the opening lines of the Emerald Tablet: "Truly, without falsehood, certain and most true."</note> for one part, he now repeats more deeply in a spagyric manner, as if he were saying: within physical bodies there lies a certain hidden truth or incorruptible virtue, about which I have been made certain through the spagyric craft. It shall become a certain and most true medicine, provided it is freed from its fetters and from the foul prison in which it is held.

From these things it appears clearer than light that natural philosophers are led only by the opinion of truth—based on some indication of the external <term>physiognomy</term> <note>The outward appearance or "signature" of a natural thing.</note> of natural things, or the false appearance of some effect, or the authority of writers. <term>Spagyric physicists</term>, however, are disciples of experience alone, from which they also learn the certainty of truth. For there are two ways which philosophers may enter: opinion and experiment. Whoever relies on only one of these must necessarily be deceived, along with others, by their teaching or work. However, those who have scrutinized both and judged one by the other will not be frustrated in their labor, nor will those to whom they bring their work or counsel. Opinion indeed proposes doubtful things, which appear true through "philosophical colors," but which must ultimately be verified by experience.

***That which is above*** (he says) ***is like that which is below, and vice versa.*** <note>original: "Quod est superius (inquit) est sicut id quod est inferius, & è contra." This is the most famous axiom of the Emerald Tablet, establishing the correspondence between the heavens (macrocosm) and the earth (microcosm).</note> Having testified to the truth previously, he proceeds to its proof, deduced from a true <term>Physical Genesis</term> <note>A term referring to the alchemical understanding of the creation and generation of the physical world.</note>. It is true, he says, that these lower elements are of one and the same substance as the heaven itself, and they do not differ except by <term>accidents</term> <note>In the philosophy of the time, "accidents" were non-essential qualities like weight, color, or transparency that could change without changing the underlying essence.</note>, such as corruptible and incorruptible, pure and impure, heavy and light, clear and opaque, active and passive, male and female, etc.—all of which are accidents, not substances.

Furthermore, heaven is incorruptible; hence it happens that of those things which are corruptible (the pure elements), none is raised higher than the hollow of the firmament in which the body of the moon travels. We say the cause of this is that the "patient" <note>The receiver of action; in this case, the earthly elements.</note> does not have absolute power over its "agent" <note>The doer of action; in this case, the heavens.</note>, but rather the opposite; thus it happens that the heavens can be mixed with the elements through influence <note>The "influx" or astrological/energetic power flowing from the stars.</note>, but the elements cannot be mixed with the heavens. But although we call the elements "patient," it must be understood in respect to the heaven, since they can act upon each other through the motion of corruption. Just as fire acts upon the earth and...

...drives the water, and water acts upon the fire. Truly, these actions and passions can produce nothing permanent in the elements by themselves without the assistance of heaven. It appears that through fire, by a certain thinning, air is made and generated from water; yet this air is forced back again into water, and the fire—conquered by this water and air—is forced back into itself, returning to the place from which it arose. We do not see the same thing happening regarding celestial actions upon the elements, because from those actions, natural bodies are generated within the elements. These bodies, by their nature, do not return again into heaven or the elements, except against nature, such as through death or by the <term>magistery</term> <note>The "Magistery" refers to the masterful completion of the alchemical process, the "Great Work."</note>. There are also other generations not unlike <term>meteoric</term> <note>In the 16th century, "meteoric" referred to any phenomenon in the atmosphere or "middle region," including rain, lightning, or vapors.</note> ones (although they have not been considered as such until now) which are produced not in the sky, but within the elements of air and fire beneath the earth; these, no differently than ethereal things, are aided by celestial actions and impressions toward the generation of minerals, stones, and metals. Furthermore, since a perfect generation cannot occur in heaven (any more than it can in a male alone), nor in the elements without heaven (any more than in a female without a male), both are instead the two parts of generation. This difference was therefore necessary by the division of two made from one, as will be narrated more fully later. 

Perhaps someone will say: if heaven and the elements are different from one another, how is it that the author says they are the same? He speaks of the identity of substance, not of <term>accidents</term> <note>In Aristotelian philosophy, "substance" is the essential nature of a thing, while "accidents" are non-essential qualities like color or shape.</note>, as he explains in what follows. For it is the nature of substances to generate, and not of accidents—though the latter nevertheless provide assistance and promote natural generation, they work nothing by themselves, any more than they can exist without substance. He concludes this kind of similarity under the unity of substance, saying: *To penetrate the miracles of the one thing.* <note>original: "Ad penetranda miracula rei unius"</note> 

Now he explains in a <term>spagyric</term> <note>Alchemical; specifically the art of separating and recombining elements to purify them.</note> manner those things which he had previously proposed physically, in nearly this way: It is necessary for the admirable spagyric craftsman to have a most perfect knowledge of heaven and the elements, of their identity and their agreement, before he can reach the unique goal of all Philosophy and the limit of universal medicine. By this goal, he may fashion this most general medicament, performing the miracles of the universe through the "one," which alone can heal all diseases indifferently, both those called "incurable" and any others. It is surely not surprising if there are very few medical men who can believe in this art, since it is worthy of the highest admiration even to those who have experienced it, such as Hermes and others; what then will it be to the ignorant? 

Truly, if anyone considers the wonders of God, which are enclosed in nature by Him, though he may marvel for a while, yet with the greatest veneration he will judge it not impossible, if he is truly a Christian. Nevertheless, it is impossible for any mortal to understand this art unless he is first illuminated by divine light; then also by "building" (as they say), he will see the miracles in it bring themselves forth, which to the most learned—

# OF TRISMEGISTUS

### THE SECRETS OF THE WISE

...the secrets of the world’s wise ones are hidden from the eyes and mind. Truly, one who has been enlightened by divine permission can sometimes, in a certain way, enlighten someone else through Philosophical words. Yet, if that person does not subsequently understand, let them consider themselves either not among the chosen, or that the hour of their selection has not yet arrived. For it is sometimes known to happen that after many years, labors, and studies—even those endured with patience at the greatest expense—some are eventually chosen, provided that many knockings, prayers, and diligent investigations have come first. For the first Leader of the <term>spagyrists</term> <note>Spagyrics refers to the alchemical process of separating and then recombining the components of a substance to purify it. The "Leader" here refers to Christ, whose words are being applied to alchemy.</note> says:

> Knock, and it shall be opened to you; ask, and it shall be given; seek from the kingdom of God, and you shall find. <note>original Latin: "Pulsate & aperietur vobis, petite dabitur, quærite à regno Dei, & invenietis." This is an alchemical adaptation of Matthew 7:7.</note>

Nevertheless, very few are found who do not grow weary of the labors and persevere until the very end. Consequently, it happens that the Art <note>The "Art" refers to Alchemy.</note> sometimes suffers an undeservedly bad reputation among such people; they cast upon the Art the blame that they should have instead ascribed to themselves. Therefore, so that my little work in this matter does not seem to have failed anyone by design, I will bring into the open a few things that have been entrusted to me thus far for the understanding of this science—a science most excellent above all others—which teaches the unique and universal medicine of the ancient fathers.

Hear, therefore, you who have ears to hear. It is necessary that a medicine of this kind be incorruptible, penetrative, and agile, just like <term>heaven</term> <note>In Hermetic physics, "Heaven" or "the Heaven" refers to the fifth element or Quintessence, which is eternal and unchanging, unlike the four earthly elements.</note>, which acts upon the elements and every physical body. Let us see, then, what the operation of heaven is within the elements. It is certain that they do not live except for a "short life," and regarding "long life," they are dead in themselves—a life which they lost along with man because of the curse resulting from his sin. 

God did not curse the heaven because of man’s transgression, which is why it retains its "long life." By this reasoning, the elements are "dead" because, being destitute of a long and healthy life, they tend toward the death of a "short life"—namely, the curse of the earth. This curse remains with them only until the beginnings of that most hostile death (that is, diseases) pressing from every side, reach the end of their course in all their products. They are, therefore, like a corpse separated from the soul, insofar as they lack that portion of "long life." 

Unless the heaven flows from all sides into their center, the elements cannot ascend from that center by means of the intermediary fire; nor can they conceive the spiritual seeds of heaven (even when their <term>matrices</term> <note>A "matrix" in alchemy is the womb-like environment—such as a vessel or a specific mineral bed—where a substance is generated or transformed.</note> are made spiritual in the middle region) so that they might descend into corporeal matrices. Indeed, opposite extremes can in no way meet without a middle part that participates in both. 

And so, the "long and healthy life" of natural things is the heaven. Likewise, life is the driving away of death, and the beginning of death is the failing of life. Therefore, whichever physician knows how to join the incorruptible <term>spagyric heaven</term> <note>The "spagyric heaven" is the purified quintessence extracted by the alchemist, mirroring the purity of the celestial heavens.</note> of long life to the internal and languishing "short life" of sick bodies, he shall (God willing) restore that short life through the **miracle of the one.** <note>original Latin: "miraculum unius." A core phrase from the Emerald Tablet, referring to the unity of the work.</note> For the languishing part and the joined incorruptible part—both heavens—are one and the same in substance, which results in...

# PHYSICS

### OF TRISMEGISTUS

...increased by the likeness of that essence, which was previously overwhelmed by corruption, now gains the victory and easily suppresses its enemies. Furthermore, by what art it is possible for us to handle the "heaven" with our own hands and administer it to diseased bodies shall be heard more clearly and in a spagyric <note>Spagyrics refers to the alchemical process of separating a substance into its components—sulfur, mercury, and salt—and then recombining them in a purified state.</note> manner below.

*That which is the lower heaven, therefore, is just like the heaven which is above; and conversely, to perform the miracles of the one thing—namely, the universal medicine.* <note>original: "Quod cælum igitur est inferius, idem est sicut cælum quod est superius, & è contra, ad perpetranda miracula rei unius, medicinæ videlicet universalis." This is Dorn's phrasing of the most famous line of the Emerald Tablet.</note> It is taught clearly enough that "heaven" exists here among us in its power—not only near us, but truly within us and in all things produced by nature. What could be stated more clearly than that the powers and virtues of the incorruptible upper heaven are hidden everywhere in these lower natural things (as if in storehouses), and can be obtained by us through an unlocking with the <term>spagyric key</term>? Likewise, that these lower virtues, impressed by the influence of the higher ones, are called the "lower heaven."

Do you wish to hear this more fully? The union of body and soul through the spirit is life, and their dissolution is death. Therefore, the more a medicine tends toward union, the more it approaches life while departing far from death. Again, union admits no multiplicity. If the cause of life is one, then its effect is also one, and there can be a single restorative medicine of life; for life is nothing other than that union we mentioned. Otherwise, let us hear Hermes Trismegistus discussing the union of the <term>ideal world</term> <note>The "ideal world" (mundus idealis) refers to the universe as it exists as a concept or "Idea" in the mind of God before physical creation.</note> and his own medicine, bringing them together through a comparison:

*And just as all things were from one by the meditation of the one, so all things were born from this one thing by adaptation.* <note>original: "Et sicut res omnes fuerunt ab uno meditatione unius, sic omnes res natæ fuerunt ab hac una re adaptatione."</note> For just as all things were mentally created by the one God through the meditation or conception of a single world through an "Idea," in the same way, all things were produced from this one premeditated world—in effect and in matter—preserving the likeness of the original pattern, and brought into order through a certain division. Likewise, as there is only one God and not many, he willed first to create a single world from nothing in his mind through the One, and subsequently to bring it into effect, so that all things he created would be contained within it: so that God might be one in all things.

However, it seemed right to explain why I have chosen not to follow the opinion of some other commentators in this place, nor in many others. I have perceived from the sequence of words that it is not Hermes' opinion that we should understand "the one" in this passage ("from one") to mean that confused globe which they call <term>Chaos</term> <note>Chaos here refers to the primordial, disorganized matter of the universe often discussed by alchemists as the 'Materia Prima'.</note>; rather, it refers to the one God, the Creator. For he adds afterward: *they were born from this one thing (namely, the premeditated world brought into effect) by adaptation.* He does not say "from the one," as he said before (*they were from one by the meditation of the one*), referring to the thing or the world. Furthermore, we must note the difference that love made between *being* and *being born*. Since from being—

<meta>This page continues Gerard Dorn’s commentary on the Emerald Tablet of Hermes Trismegistus. The previous page ended with the syllable "na-", which is completed here as "nature." # PHYSICS

### OF TRISMEGISTUS

...nature, no thing has the essence of what it is by its own power, but rather every thing is produced or born from it alone, out of that which has its being from nothing; through the word of God alone and His virtue, and it does not have its substance from the word itself; this very thing is the first visible creature, namely nature. Indeed, the author's sentence <note>original: "Auctoris vero sententia"</note> seems corrupted to me, and mutilated by the omission of one word—namely, *created*—due to the negligence of the translators rather than the typography, and I lead the way in restoring it in this manner: *As all things were created from one, by meditation, etc.* <note>original: "Sicut res omnes creata fuerunt ab uno, meditatione, &c." Dorn is proposing an emendation to the text of the Emerald Tablet to clarify that creation requires a Creator's intent.</note> 

Therefore, by these words Hermes suggests that this universal medicine must be made in imitation of the creation of the world, not merely compounded, as is stated more clearly below: *Thus the world (he says) was created.* This little portion also confirms my opinion that I have not wrongly or rashly restored what seemed mutilated. It must be gathered from this that the **spagyric work** <term>spagyric: the alchemical process of "separating and recombining" to achieve purity</term> toward the universal medicine is both begun and completed in imitation of the creation of the world; and therefore, it is supernatural by way of resemblance, even though it is made from natural things. 

Furthermore, the author concludes from the supernatural creation of the world that physical generation occurs through the likeness of natural unity to the supernatural, and not from the unity of the spagyric artifice: for he has not yet arrived at the operation of the latter. But he first attempts to briefly strengthen his position with the firmest arguments against any detractors and the ignorant before proceeding, lest his followers be delayed by the trifles of the reprobate who reject his work. For he adds: *Thus all things were born from this one thing.* 

He teaches that there was a single, most general kind of created things, from which the remaining genera, species, and individuals were born, and are propagated daily even until the end of the age. There is no reason for anyone to think that "one thing" in this place should be referred to the Creator; rather, it refers to one creature, namely **primitive nature**. This also seems to be denoted by the preposition "this" (*hac*). For if the genitive "of one" in the phrase *by the meditation of one* <note>original: "meditatione unius"</note> were referred to the ablative *from one* (*ab uno*)—which would be contrary to all reason of speech, for he would rather have said "they were from one by the meditation of the same"—it is certain that he likewise ought to have said afterward: *thus all things were born from this one [masculine person].* 

These things are said by me only to warn the reader that one must be extremely wary of the doubtful phrasing of philosophers (which they call **amphibology** <term>amphibology: a sentence or phrase that can be interpreted in two ways due to ambiguous grammar</term>). I do not say this because Hermes wrote in this manner, but perhaps his interpreters, envying the author's plain meaning for all others but themselves, rendered it doubtful through their commentaries and interpretations. This will be easily perceived by as many as read other commentaries and acutely weigh the matter itself: namely, that the interpretation of their "Stone," as they call it, is far more difficult than the text and more obscure to the understanding. 

Moreover, what "one" and "one thing" might have stood for in Hermes’ mind is something we should interpret from a medical matter, and not a metallic <note>original: "metallaria". Dorn is shifting the focus of alchemy from making gold (transmutation) to making medicine (the health of the body).</note> one...

<summary>Dorn argues that the Emerald Tablet should be read as a guide to creating a universal medicine by imitating God's creation of the world. He critiques previous translations for their ambiguity and insists the "one thing" refers to primitive nature rather than the Creator himself.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Gerard Dorn’s commentary on the Emerald Tablet of Hermes Trismegistus. # PHYSICS

### OF TRISMEGISTUS

...peculiar, but human. Therefore, God is this one thing, which before all ages was the only being, or a triune being in unity from eternity; and who willed to create one thing, similar to Himself insofar as it is one—that is, one nature, the first visible creature, and one world. For this world consists of **spirit, soul, and body**. It is the opinion of many philosophers that the spirit of natural things is the medium between the soul and the body; others wish the soul to be the medium between them, led by this reason: that the spirit is subtler than the soul, and a more fitting extreme compared to the very dense body, so that the soul is subtler than the body and denser than the spirit itself.

While my own opinion leaves the judgment of this dispute still before the judge <note>original: "sub judice" — a legal term meaning the matter is still under consideration and undecided</note>, I would meanwhile suggest that the spirit should not be separated from the soul any more than light is from its lamp, or the lamp from its firmament. Truly, under the firmament, because the life of natural things is perceived by the senses through the motion of bodies alone rather than by the cause of motion itself—which is the **ethereal fire** <term>ethereal fire: a celestial heat or "vital spark" believed by alchemists to be the primary cause of life and movement</term>—they say by this argument that the spirit is subtler than the soul; for the soul falls under the senses through motion, while the spirit does not.

For the time being, therefore, I will adopt this latter opinion in this place until a better one occurs. For if, according to Hermes, it is granted that the "dense" and the "subtle" are extremes, as the words sound:

> *You shall separate the earth from the fire,* then because before *the Wind carried it in its belly,* <note>Dorn is quoting the Emerald Tablet here</note> that is, the air—it necessarily follows that fire is the extreme and the spirit for Hermes, because it is far subtler than the air in which it is carried.

For the soul is more suited to air than to fire, since the effect of the life-giving motion occurs in the air through a cause proper to fire. In like manner, every cause of motion is subtler than its motion and effect. For example: If a builder must construct a house, three things are chiefly necessary for him: art or skill as the **spirit**; motion or labor as the **soul**; and finally, material as the **body**. Perhaps someone might say that motion in this context is an "accident" <note>In Aristotelian philosophy, an "accident" is a non-essential quality, like the color of a house</note>; we concede this in artificial things, but in natural things we deny it, because that motion is substantially mixed with both the substance of the spirit and the body. 

But in artificial motion, which no nature supports, once the work has been brought to its effect, all motion in it ceases. Concluding, therefore, we say that no motion can occur in any way without a mover and a thing moved. These three are therefore necessary for natural life: the **spirit** as the mover, the **soul** as the motion itself, and the **body** as the thing moved; these, joined together, form a single natural thing. 

The summary fitting of Hermes's analogy to the approval of his mind's concept is this: In a way not dissimilar to how God first created one world by meditation alone, He likewise created one world from which all things are born by adaptation. By "meditation," he wishes to denote the simplicity of unity in mental creation; and afterward, by "adaptation," he hints at the arrangement or order under the number, measure, and weight of matter...

<summary>Dorn explores the alchemical trinity of spirit, soul, and body, arguing that spirit acts as the mover while the soul is the motion itself. He interprets the Emerald Tablet's creation narrative as a model for both natural life and the alchemical process.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the commentary on the Emerald Tablet of Hermes Trismegistus, moving from the definition of God as the "one thing" to the first act of creation: division. The author, likely Gerard Dorn, is exploring the symbolic relationship between the Book of Genesis and Hermetic philosophy.</meta>

# THE PHYSICS

### OF TRISMEGISTUS

fitting. Since therefore the first member of order is number, and the first number is two, if the universal matter of the world is to be arranged in order, it first had to be divided into two (as is right), as is taught in Genesis: namely, into heaven and earth. This is especially true because the first number, two, is suited to prime matter. Hermes himself teaches this very thing, saying: *That which is below is like that which is above.* From these words, it is established that Hermes Trismegistus was taught the Book of Genesis by the Hebrews, even though he was an Egyptian, as Augustine testifies in his book *The City of God*, as well as Suidas and others.

Furthermore, the founder of nature divided the one mass created in his name into two: into heaven, the upper part, and into earth, the lower part. He did this so that what heaven could not do within itself, it might beget in its consort, earth—just as Adam did in Eva—so that the last things might correspond most beautifully with the first, and the first with the last. Therefore, division was very necessary, so that the generation which was once enclosed within the one newly created thing might be brought forth from potentiality into actuality. Beneath that spiritual and bodily <term>binarium: a duality or pair of opposites</term>, a third thing lay hidden, which is the bond of the sacred marriage.

This is the very medium that persists in all things to this day, participating in both its extremes; without them, the medium cannot exist at all, nor can the extremes exist without this medium of theirs, for they are "one out of three." But someone might object, claiming it is the opinion of all philosophers who understand the art that a transition does not occur except through a medium, and specifically from a prior, perfect extreme to the perfection of an imperfect one. Yet Hermes seems to teach here that the beginning of motion must be taken from the imperfect toward the perfect, in order to acquire the highest perfection. It also follows, conversely, that whoever strives against the opinion of Hermes to proceed from the perfect to the imperfect will achieve an imperfect work; because Hermes placed the lower before the higher.

The response is that it is foolish to think the author is teaching a transition here, since he has not yet reached the actual treatment of the art <note>The "art" refers to the Alchemical Work or the pursuit of the Philosopher's Stone</note>; nonetheless, in the art, such an order must be observed from the beginning. For it is certain that these lower elements are more imperfect than heaven, just as it is clear from their simple elements, when brought into their own heaven, through a unity that is foreign to composition. But because we are now occupied with lower things and cannot yet climb to the higher, our business is to handle these things with our hands; it will be necessary for us to ascend from these lower things (which are right before us) to their superiors, which are naturally mixed with them.

So that these things may always become clearer from what follows, we must take up again some of what we have set forth. Just as among us no art can lack its artisan, material, or instruments, so the natural <term>magisterium: the alchemical "mastery" or the process of creating the Philosopher's Stone</term> necessarily requires things that are suited to itself and its ends. Let us begin first with the ingenuity or skill of the artisan, which is the moving cause. Just as wood and

# PHYSICS

the pickaxe itself achieves nothing unless the craftsman moves it into action: so too the heavens and the elements can generate nothing unless the Craftsman, or the celestial craftsmen using the heavens as an instrument, stir up motion as if it were a soul—a middle instrument between the craftsman and the matter of the elements. But let us see by what reasoning this instrumental medium serves as a bond between the extremes. This motion is both double and single, or to be better understood, it is "doubly one": both elementary and ethereal. Let us say, therefore, with Hermes: *That which moves the lower things is the same as that which moves the upper things, namely the spirit*, <note>original: "Quod inferiora movet, idem est quod movet superiora spiritus videlicet"</note> by which the miracles of the "one thing" are performed in many ways, both in a physical and <term>spagyric: an alchemical term referring to the process of separating and recombining substances</term> manner. Truly, motion itself is stirred up in the instrument—namely, the soul—and it has its effect in matter and the elements. It is necessary, therefore, for the soul to be the medium, like an instrument, by which the two parts and extremities meet as one. 

For example, we might not improperly compare the "natural craftsman" <note>the "faber naturalis" refers to the guiding intelligence of nature</note> to the blacksmiths among us. Those smiths first require iron, as well as various larger and smaller hammers, and likewise an anvil and fire. Now, the hearth-workshop of the natural craftsman is the center of the earth, in which the natural lower fire has the beginning of its action and motion, just as our fire begins from flint and steel, etc. Yet, an ethereal fire is given to him, just as to our smiths a mastery of the craft is acquired through genius and constant diligence. These two fires differ from each other partly by <term>accident: a philosophical term for a non-essential quality, like color or speed, rather than the core essence</term>, and partly they agree in substance; they agree in motion, yet differ in its direction, being circular in the heavens and straight on earth. 

Similarly, it should be noted that just as the anvil is the lower instrument for smiths on earth, and the hammers are the superior active instruments, so for the natural craftsman the more solid substance of the elements (such as stones and earth) takes the place of the anvil and the nourishing matter. The stars, truly, perform the office of the hammers. Likewise, we say that the volatile substance of the lower regions in the middle realm—which conceives the seeds of the upper regions—is the matrix carrying them in its womb. Nor should we forget the bellows in this place, which are the natural winds. Nature, therefore, adapts its matter before it gives it form, or grants it motion and soul. 

Consequently, in concluding, we say that the "bond of the world" is made and perfected by a double body, soul, and spirit—both upper and lower—differing only by accident, yet similar in substance. So that these things may be understood even better, it will be worthwhile to explain the mastery of nature more clearly. Which of the philosophers, unless he be some reckless trifler, would dare to assert that the entire world consists of more than three general parts? For these are **Form**, **Light** (or the life of nature), and **Matter**: the first principles of all things. Therefore, whoever wishes to know the world in its substance, it is necessary that these three be most well-known to him first. We must begin, therefore, with their definitions. <meta>This page continues the investigation into how the basic building blocks of the world interact. Having previously discussed the "natural craftsman" and the spirit as a mediating force, the author now focuses on the relationship between the four elements, arguing that they are constantly circulating and transforming into one another rather than being destroyed.</meta>

->TRISMEGISTUS<-

it may appear that there are fire, air, water, and earth, yet two are held as primary: fire and water. For air seems to be nothing other than water dissolved through the power of the **spirit of the Lord** <note>original: "spiritus domini"</note> moving over the waters during the creation of the world; earth, indeed, is water thickened and dried out by the gathering of the lower waters. They are otherwise divided twofold into two manifest elements—earth and water—and two hidden elements beneath them, air and fire. For air lies hidden beneath the water until it is revealed by the actions of fire; and fire lies beneath the earth until it appears through the craftsmanship of man, or otherwise emerges naturally through certain vents, such as on Mount Etna, at Puteoli, and other places. 

Fire strives by its own nature, as much as it can, to convert water into itself. To accomplish this more easily, it uses two means, according to the two contrary qualities of each: first, so that with its heat it might consume coldness; second, so that with its dryness it might consume humidity. Indeed, we see clouds suspended by the heat of fire, holding a middle position between water and fire. If the heat of the fire—which is weaker at its extremities than in the heart of its <term>sphere: in ancient cosmology, each element was believed to occupy a specific layer or "sphere" around the Earth</term> (where it is most intense)—is overcome by the coldness of the dissolved water, this middle ground is converted into whichever of the extremes prevails. Thus fire, by nature's design, is frustrated in its effort; while it strives to consume one thing, it generates another, which in turn returns to that from which it was generated. This circulation is the most powerful cause of generation.

We see visible fire perform no differently in bodies composed by nature. Let wood be an example brought to the fire: its <term>sulfur: in alchemy, sulfur often represents the combustible, oily, or active principle of a substance</term> does not burn until all its watery moisture has been converted into air. Once that moisture is consumed, the fire likewise returns to the air, and then into itself, while the more solid parts of the wood fall away as ash or earth. Therefore, it should not be said that the elements of such wood were destroyed, but rather that each element, separated from its compound, has returned to its own sphere. 

Regarding this matter, a doubtful question has arisen among philosophers: whether fire consumes more than it generates? It seems sound to say that the operations of ethereal and elemental fire are equal. For if more were consumed by the elemental fire than was generated by the ethereal, a <term>vacuum: a space entirely empty of matter, which most ancient and medieval philosophers believed nature would not allow to exist</term> could be identified in the nature of things, which is absurd. If, however, the ethereal fire generated more than the elemental fire consumed, the excess could no longer be contained in its determined place. In either case, the "womb of nature" would necessarily be ruptured or compressed. 

However, it shall be answered briefly and more safely that nothing is consumed by fire, but through the mode of <term>transmutation: the changing of one substance or element into another</term>, that which leaves one element joins another. Likewise, wise nature daily and solicitously procures the raising of new forms from elements transmuted in this way, so that what is arranged through <term>corruption: in this context, the breaking down or decaying of an existing form</term> may be shaped anew through generation; and so the operation of nature...

### PHYSICA

...according to the celestial motions of actions and impressions. Many overly curious natural philosophers, not yet experienced in natural things, are accustomed to thrust this argument upon us, by which they attack the chemists' <term>quintessence: the "fifth essence," a refined substance beyond the four classical elements</term>; but they will not defeat it unless they bring forth something stronger. Bodies (they say) consist of four elements or essences; where then is the fifth element, or what is this "fifthness"? We admit that bodies consist of four elements materially, yet we do not concede that they are composed of these alone, but also of **form**, which is certainly something real and the most powerful part of any composite, after the **bond of nature** by which the elements are glued to their form. For the dense and the subtle cannot, because of their mutual opposition, come together into one by themselves. Therefore, it was necessary for them to be composed through the medium of life, so that they might be more easily joined. Nature composes all things with this bond, which philosophers are accustomed to hand down to us in a riddle: "Make peace," they say, "between enemies, and you shall have the whole <term>mastery: the 'magisterium,' or the completion of the alchemical Great Work</term>."

Concluding regarding the elements, we say they are threefold: simple, composite, and de-composite. **Simple elements** are those which are neither corrupted nor undergo any composition among themselves; it is not *from* them, but *through* them that all other lower elements exercise their powers, which they also receive from them. **Composite elements** are those which undergo corruption and are composed. **De-composite elements** <note>original: "decomposita"</note> are those which have already come together in composition through corruption and generation. Whoever knows how to convert these into those—the impure into the pure, the composite into the simple—will be a most great craftsman of wondrous works.

Furthermore, coming to **form**, we say this is (not what gives being to a thing or its name, as the unbelievers <note>likely referring to those who hold purely materialist or strictly Aristotelian views</note> say) but that which moves the upper ethereal region and the lower elementary region into action, and into the conceptive power of motion. Through the mutual transmutation of the elements into one another, nature readies the **matter**, enclosing the **form** within it like a seed in a womb; pregnant by the virtue of this form, just like a mother's womb, it brings the offspring from potentiality into a **specific act**. This is what the philosophers mean: "Form," they say, "is drawn out from the potentiality of matter." For matter itself is able to give birth, because form is generated within it. Thus, form acts upon matter; what it has received from the **light of nature**—namely, motion and life—it offers itself as a mediator, like a craftsman.

Moreover, the light and life of nature is the **spirit** of universal action upon the elements through form. For this spirit does not cease to renew, from the universal form of nature, the specific forms—originally created by God—which fail through corruption. Craftsmanship of this kind is perfected by a twofold instrument: **disposition** and **influence**. Nature in motion, by corrupting matter through an action excited in the center, disposes it toward a receptivity for the power of form in the middle region, and for celestial influences, which thereafter, at their determined time, burst forth below into specific forms...

# TRISMEGISTIS.

...identifies, according to the condition of the luminaries in the superior arrangement of concurring forms, following the saying of some: *Form acts according to the disposition of matter.* <note>original: "Secundum materiae dispositionem agit forma."</note> But having forgotten the arrangement of the forms as well, or having not understood it, they pass over it, leaving it in silence. It remains for us now to see what Hermes says concerning the genealogy of the <term>spagyric: the alchemical art of separating, purifying, and recombining the essential components of substances</term> offspring. *The Father (he says) of it is the Sun, etc.* <note>original: "Pater (inquit) ejus est sol &c." This is a famous line from the Emerald Tablet of Hermes Trismegistus.</note> What the Sun and Moon are in the upper sky is not for us to explain, since they are very well known even to commoners; however, there are few who understand their actions and virtues. For this reason, an opportunity is given here to describe them: for through a true knowledge of these things, the mind of the reader can reach higher matters—namely, those of the spagyric art.

The celestial Sun, therefore, is the great luminary of the day placed by God in the middle of the heavens. Why it occupies the central place of the sky is a matter clear in itself: namely, so that it may illuminate all the luminaries above and below it, and fertilize the entire world with its rays all the way to its center—upon which center the eye of the Sun and the eyes of the other luminaries are constantly fixed. Just as the source of life of the human body is the center of its heart—or rather, that <term>arcanum: a secret, vital essence or "mystery" hidden within a substance that gives it power</term> which lies hidden within it, where natural heat flourishes, warming, illuminating, and vivifying the other members—in no different way does the Sun naturally vivify all the upper and lower parts of the world with its heat and light, though it accomplishes this through a medium.

For this reason, it is called the "Heart of the World" because of its heat, and the "Eye" because of its light. Indeed, it surveys all things, penetrating even the most hidden recesses down to the very center of the earth. In it, all natural celestial virtues are stored. In short, it is the most noble of all bodies that exist in the created heavens and on the earth. With good reason, therefore, it was called the first father and parent of all things after God, since within it lies hidden the seminal and formal virtue of every thing. Its masculine and universal seed, the first and most powerful, is the <term>sulphur: in alchemy, the active, "fiery," and masculine principle that drives growth and maturation</term> of its nature, the first part of all generations and the most powerful cause.

Hence it was stated by Paracelsus: *The Sun and man, through man, generate man,* <note>original: "sol & homo per hominem generant hominem"</note> because the natural life of all creatures draws its origin through a medium from the Sun, and from its life comes all fleeting life. If the Sun therefore lives, it is necessary that it lives in something: namely, in its <term>radical moisture: the essential "oil" or fluid that sustains the vital flame of any living being and prevents it from being consumed by its own heat</term>, a most pure and simple air, which tempers its heat with its moisture. It would be foolish for many to believe that the Sun is merely celestial fire. For life consists in the union of the spirit with the body by means of the soul, which is moved by this union to the act of natural life. Otherwise, it would be concluded, contrary to the truth, that the Sun does not live; for a natural union always occurs between two things, from whose harmony a third thing results as a single or united entity. Nay, what is more, we say that the Sun is a unique element in which all simple elements are contained—just as in the heavens and other celestial bodies, but in the Sun they exist more perfectly.

### PHYSICS

...because of the life which it pours into others, both those above and those below. The Sun, therefore, is the father and the virile seed of all things naturally generated, and the Moon is the mother, as will be seen below. Finally, Hermes teaches that the Moon is the mother and wife of the Sun, who carries the <term>spagyric fetus: the alchemical offspring or essential "Stone" resulting from the union of solar and lunar principles</term> conceived by the Sun in her womb and matrix, and carries it in the air via the wind, with the earth as its nurse, etc. <note>original: "ventis gestat in aere, terramque nutricem, &c." This is a direct reference to the Emerald Tablet of Hermes Trismegistus.</note> He teaches that the first generation of things is first conceived in heaven, and afterwards perfected on the earth, which we discuss below. For the Sun does not immediately imprint its vital <term>influences: the invisible flow of celestial power or "rays" from the stars to the earth</term> into the lower things, but does so through the Moon, who thirteen times a year <note>Refers to the thirteen lunar cycles in a solar year.</note> conceives from her husband through conjunctions, and giving birth, sends down the offspring, as will be heard later. Yet just as she gives birth daily, she also daily conceives virtues from her husband; not otherwise than any other stars, although more fruitfully during a meeting, due to greater proximity. Conceptions and births of this kind happen not through physical contact, as on earth, but through influences alone and spiritual <term>aspects: the relative positions and angles between celestial bodies that determine their astrological power</term>. 

So it is that when she is seen by us as a full moon, she conceives fewer virtues from the Sun than when she is entirely hidden and joined to the Sun, because of the greater distance; but she receives more in opposition than between lateral aspects. This is because the influences and rays of the sun are more powerful when they are straight than when they are oblique. It should not be thought, therefore—despite that common proverb—that the moon suffers a "defect" <note>original: "defectum pati lunam." A play on words; "defectus" refers to both an eclipse and a physical lack or failing.</note> during an eclipse or when new, since at that time she is most imbued with solar virtues. Rather, because she is then not visible to us—both because of the solar radiance which overcomes and obscures all natural light, and because only the half part which is opaque to us is turned toward us—she seems deprived of light, even though she contains the most of it then. She receives more from the sun than in opposition when she appears entirely full. 

We have decided not to overlook those things which are worthy of consideration concerning these two great luminaries by reason of their divine marriage through the creation in Genesis, from the diligent and inviolate observation of their union at all times, according to the order prescribed for them by God. These two, although separate bodies, are yet of one and the same substance, just as heaven and earth came from one abyss alone; just as here among us, man and woman were once one human, made into two, and afterwards joined again in one flesh. <note>A reference to the creation of Eve from Adam in Genesis 2.</note> However, the Moon's conception of the Sun's virtues is not yet a perfected generation, but only its beginning, which must be perfected in the lower things. The Moon is therefore the medium through which the superior seeds are implanted into the matrices of the inferior things, whence they afterwards bring forth coarser <term>elemental things: substances composed of the four basic elements—earth, air, fire, and water</term>, whether they be mixed or decomposed. 

To repeat these things a little more deeply in a <term>spagyric: the alchemical art of separating and recombining substances to reveal their hidden virtues</term> manner: If the Sun and Moon, then, pour life into lower things, it follows that both are potentially within those things through that life; which power is indeed drawn out from any natural things through the **spagyric art**. For the life of the Sun and Moon is a union through Jupiter, and can rightly be called a long and healthy life. But if a union of Mercury and Mars should occur through Saturn, a sick and short life will result.

# OF TRISMEGISTUS

...because when you have reduced any compound into its <term>Mercury, Saturn, and Mars: alchemical symbols for the essential principles of volatility, solidity/fixity, and transformative heat</term>, and from these you have also extracted the Sun and Moon, and joined them by the temperate middle-ground of both Jupiters <note>original: "mediaque Jovis utriusque temperié." This refers to using the balancing quality of Jupiter—the mediator between the harshness of Saturn and the heat of Mars—to harmonize the elements.</note>, you will make one thing from those three that is more excellent than it had been previously composed by nature, though under another form. For once a physical form is destroyed, it is not within the power of any art to restore the same one, but rather one far better, appearing altered only to fleshy eyes <note>meaning: the physical eyes of mortals, which see only the outward appearance.</note>. With what industry this may be done, nature teaches us from her daily operations, which our own eyes behold, as the author teaches: *The wind carried it in its belly* <note>original: "Portavit ventus in ventre suo." A famous line from the Emerald Tablet of Hermes Trismegistus, referring to the air as the vehicle for the life-force.</note>. We have touched upon this passage previously, which should be sufficient for sharp wits; however, so that I may be of use to everyone, I wish to treat this matter diligently, since it is most worthy of note and contributes greatly to the benefit of those reading the more obscure <term>spagyric: related to the alchemical art of separating and recombining elements to create medicines or purified substances</term> writings. Indeed, all my study is directed toward this: that I may promote, as much as is in me, the efforts of those students of this more hidden philosophy; for I know that while I strive to instruct others and make them participants in my talent, I educate myself through the exercise of these labors—though truly, grace and light depend upon the powers above.

The lower Sun and Moon are indeed raised upward from the center by the mastery of the lower nature, until they reach the upper parts in the middle region. Existing there, the virtues of the superior Sun, infused into the superior Moon (for likes by nature rejoice in likes), are conceived by the lower <term>matrices: wombs or formative environments</term> as superior seeds; for this is the duty and office of a wife. Now it appears most clearly to you what Hermes taught before with these words from the beginning: *That which is below is like that which is above, and so forth.* For the Sun and Moon in the higher heaven and in the lower world are similar in substance, even if they differ in their "accidents"—namely, by a long or short life.

Therefore, under Mars (who exercises the Vulcanian arts in his hearth-workshop, which is to say, the center of the earth), the universal lower Sun lies hidden. By the force of its parent, it breaks out through the wind from the subterranean caverns. With such bellows, Vulcan, or rather the <term>Archeus: a Paracelsian term for the internal "chemist" or vital force that governs the growth and health of a living thing</term> (to speak in the manner of Paracelsus), drives the purer and more subtle parts of the elements away from itself into the "heaven" <note>In alchemy, "heaven" often refers to the upper part of a flask or the higher, refined state of matter.</note>. It carries in its womb (as the words sound: *the wind carried it in its belly*) the lower Sun, containing the purest substance of fire and earth, and also the lower Moon, the most subtle and pure substance of water, hidden under the form of air. By this, the universal and feminine lower seed, carried through the air, is joined to the superior universal masculine seed and to each of the other specific seeds in the womb of the wind and in the matrix of the air. It is certain that air consists of water and fire; likewise, the "heaven" consists of fire and air. Under the name of "fire," the purest substance of earth is understood, ascending together with the fire; and under the name of "air," the purest substance of water is meant, according to the cycles of transmuta—

# PHYSICS

...one into another, from the aforementioned natural artifice. Therefore, the belly and the womb of nature is the matrix fashioned from the purest substance of all the lower elements, converted into volatile air, in which the universal seed of the sun is conceived by the medium of the moon—specified also by the other celestial luminaries for the various distinction of species. Therefore, after the author <term>Hermes: referring to Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary Egyptian sage and purported author of the Emerald Tablet</term> proposed three elements—two under the names of the Sun and Moon, and the third under the name of the wind—he then adds the earth under the comparison of a nurse and its proper name. He says that the earth is the nurse of the offspring of nature previously conceived in the air; and from its breasts every offspring sucks that mercurial milk for its nourishment and the sustenance of its life, namely the thicker substance of water remaining below upon the earth. Thus the volatile part of the elements (as has been heard), like a woman impregnated, soon returning to its fixed part, gives birth to the offspring and nourishes it from the fixed substance until it reaches perfection. Natural <term>spagyrists: alchemists who practice the art of "spagyria"—separating and recombining substances to purify them</term>, having contemplated these turns of generation neither sleepily, nor in passing, nor in vain, could not have learned their spagyric art better, but rather more solidly. Therefore, so that they may generate a spagyric sun, imitating nature, they dissolve a compound made by nature into its parts. Through their <term>Vulcanic Archeus: the internal fire or creative spirit that directs natural processes, named after Vulcan, the Roman god of fire</term>, they artificially drive the sun and moon from the center into the womb of the wind on high, and afterwards nourish them in their earth, and so forth. For just as everything that is generated takes nourishment from the earth, so too the spagyric offspring has nourishment from the spagyric earth: this is understood in two ways. Sometimes it is taken for the lower part of the vessel, just as the upper part is taken for the heaven. Sometimes <term>Spagyric Jupiter: in this context, a purified solid state of matter, often associated with tin or a stabilized metallic base</term>, which is fixed and cleansed of its "sweats" <note>meaning: the volatile impurities or excess moisture removed during heating</note>, is for us the "foliated earth" in which and from which the volatile part—which, after ascending to heaven, was forced to descend into it—is nourished and perfected. Concluding the theory of the spagyric art, the author says:

> *The father of all <term>Thelesme: likely derived from the Greek "telesmos," meaning completion, perfection, or a consecrated object/talisman</term> of the whole world is here.* <note>original: "Pater omnis Thelesme totius mundi est hic." This is a central maxim of the Emerald Tablet, suggesting this "substance" or "force" is the source of all earthly perfection.</note>

It is as if he were saying: "This secret that I propose to you is the father, the origin, and the source of all the most excellent and greatest secrets and mysteries among the other secrets of the whole world." For this reason, it is not to be disclosed to everyone, and least of all to profane men, and barely even to those initiated into the sacred mysteries; and even to them, only within a very brief discourse. For what is more excellent, or more worthy of a philosophical man, than to become a participant in long life through the knowledge and use of the whole of nature, both superior and inferior? Once all the corruptions of a short life, and the obstacles and impediments of the mind—by which it was once darkened and blinded—have been routed and driven far away. Is this not far superior to any fictions of poems, which were devised for idolatry rather than for the knowledge of the one God? Even though they have been wrongly interpreted by some allegorically, as if they encompassed many distinguished mysteries; nevertheless, they are nothing less than the great works <note>original: "magnalia"</note> of the one God alone...

It concludes by defining the "Thelesme" (perfection) of the world as the ultimate source of all mysteries and the key to a long, enlightened life.</summary>

### OF TRISMEGISTUS

...wonders, which they have sung to men regarding so many dreamt-up little gods and little harlots. Although Ovid seems to have sensed something in his *Metamorphoses*, he nevertheless mixed in many frivolous and rather impious things that contribute nothing at all to this matter. What benefit, I ask, do the writings of infidels offer for salvation? Certainly nothing; indeed, they rather call men away from the study of truth while they are intent on these trifles. Yet they are valued more in this iron age <note>The "iron age" refers to a historical period of moral decline and hardship in classical and Renaissance thought.</note> than the writings of pious men who profess one God in all things. Would it not be better for the youth—from whom a most necessary beginning must be had if the world is to be reformed—to learn those things which are the works of God alone, rather than the dreams of men? Indeed, if Physics is taught rightly and as is fair from the sacred Genesis of the world, it leads to the knowledge of God through the wonders of the Creator; and from there, it prepares the souls and minds of men for attained philosophy and heavenly wisdom.

Therefore, if anyone meditates deeply and loftily upon all that God, the Best and Greatest, has done in the creation of the world for the sake and utility of men, then at last he will understand the father of all secrets, and the most excellent mystery of the sacred <term>Thelesma: a term from the Emerald Tablet (often 'Thelema' in other contexts) meaning the 'will' or 'perfection'—the universal life-force or power of the world</term>, and the most secret spagyric work of divine rather than human art, whose father—that is, the supreme secret—is here in this brief, truthful [text].

Furthermore, concluding his theory, the author teaches us to recognize the end of the spagyric work, so that we may know when the labor must cease. **Its power** (he says) **is complete if it has been turned into earth.** Previously we heard that the more subtle parts of the lower element are impregnated by celestial virtues and thereafter return to earth and water; and that the conceptions of such virtues do not achieve their effect of generation sooner. But now, by a similar reasoning, the completion of the spagyric work is taught. Just as when **that which the wind carried in its belly** <note>A famous line from the Emerald Tablet: "The wind carried it in its belly, the earth is its nurse."</note> has been turned or converted into earth, the work will be complete. For indeed, by long and tireless cooking, liquids (even if they do not evaporate but are retained) are thickened, and in the passage of time they are dried into dust or earth. This would commonly seem absurd, but only those who have made a trial of this matter can believe it. Truly, the time is long and tedious, and must be awaited with the greatest patience. The whole business of this tedious matter consists chiefly in the selection and preparation of the more suitable material. For some things are remote, others more remote, and some most remote. Others are near, some nearer, and some most near to perfection. Each of these is most necessary for the spagyric artist to know before he attempts the work; otherwise, he will lament his error.

<header>PHYSICS</header>

...the transformation of one into another, from the already mentioned natural artistry. Accordingly, the belly and womb of nature is a matrix fused from the purest substance of all the lower elements, converted into volatile air, in which is conceived—by means of the moon—the universal seed of the sun, also specified by other luminaries <note>The "luminaries" refer to the planets and stars, which were believed to give specific qualities to the general solar life-force.</note>, toward the various distinction of species. Therefore, after the author Hermes proposed three elements—two under the names of the sun and moon, and the third indeed under the name of wind—he now adds the earth under the comparison of a nurse and by its own name; and he says that she is the nurse of the fetus of nature previously conceived in the air. From her breasts, every fetus sucks that mercurial milk for its nourishment and the sustenance of its life—namely, the thicker substance of water remaining below near the earth. And so the volatile part of the elements (as has been heard), being impregnated, soon returning to its fixed part, gives birth to the fetus and nourishes it from the fixed substance until it comes to perfection.

Natural spagyrists <note>"Spagyrists" is a term for alchemists, derived from the Greek words for "separating" and "combining."</note>, contemplating such successions of generations not sleepily, nor in passing, nor in vain, could not have learned their spagyric art better, but rather more solidly. Wherefore, so that they might generate the spagyric sun, imitating nature, they dissolve the compound made by nature into its parts through their Vulcanian Archeus <term>Archeus: the vital force or "inner chemist" that directs life and growth; here, specifically the alchemical fire named after Vulcan, the god of the forge</term>. From the center, they artificially drive the sun and moon into the womb of the wind on high, and afterwards nourish them in their earth, and so forth. For just as everything that is generated takes nourishment from the earth, the spagyric fetus also has nourishment from the spagyric earth. This "earth" is understood in two ways: sometimes it is taken for the lower part of the vessel <note>The alchemical flask or "philosopher's egg."</note>, just as the upper part is taken for heaven. Sometimes the spagyric Jupiter <note>Jupiter is often used as a code for tin or a specific purified state of the matter.</note>, which is fixed and cleansed of its "sweats" <note>Impurities or volatile excesses removed during heating.</note>, serves as our foliated earth <note>original: "terra foliata"; a specific stage where the alchemical matter becomes flaky or layered like leaves.</note>, in which and from which the volatile part—which, after ascending to heaven, was forced to descend into it—is nourished and perfected. Concluding the theory of the spagyric art, the author says:

> *The father of all the perfection of the whole world is here.* <note>original: "Pater omnis Telesmi totius mundi est hic." The term "Telesmi" is a transliteration of the Greek *telesmos*, signifying completion or the "finished work" of alchemy.</note>

It is as if he were saying: this secret which I propose to you is the father, origin, and source of all the most excellent and greatest secrets and mysteries among the other secrets of the whole world. Therefore, it is not to be made public to everyone, and least of all to profane men, and barely even to those initiated into the sacred mysteries—and even to them, only in a very brief conversation. For what is more excellent, or more worthy of a philosophical man, than to become a participant in long life through the knowledge and use of the whole of superior and inferior nature? This path drives far away all the corruptions of a short life and the obstacles and hindrances of the mind, by which it was once blinded in darkness. Is this not far superior to any fictions of poems, devised for idolatry rather than for the knowledge of the one God? Although some have wrongly interpreted them allegorically, as if they embraced many famous mysteries, they are nevertheless nothing less than the miracles <note>original: "magnalia," completed from the catchword on the following page.</note> of the one God alone...

...one into another, from the already mentioned natural artifice. # PHYSICA
<page-num>382</page-num>

...imitation of [the sun]. <note>The text begins mid-word, likely completing "filius" (son) or "solis" (of the sun) from the previous page.</note> However, since it would be impossible for us to build any artificial vessel in which we were able, like nature, to contain a fire lit in its center and suspended in the middle, and this for various reasons—especially because our artificial fire, except in free and open air, would be immediately extinguished in a closed vessel—it was therefore necessary for our fire to be placed outside our vessel, and under the center of its round bottom, in the likeness of the natural sun. The entire <term>mastery</term> <note>original: "magisterium"; referring to the completion of the alchemical Great Work</note> of this fire consists chiefly in this: that it be continuous and in the same light and vaporous state, like that which, in the center of the world, daily performs the natural mastery of the ascent from the earth into heaven without intermission; as expressed in the earlier words, *With great ingenuity*, <note>original: "Cum magno ingenio"</note> which is to say, very similar to natural fire (which is said to be the "ingenuity" or "wit" of nature). There occurs here the opinion of certain philosophers who reject the idea that metals are generated by subterranean fire, even in part, but who also affirm that generation occurs by celestial fire alone. Meanwhile, they do not see how they not only contradict Hermes, but indeed all of nature. For the celestial sun does not enter materially into the composition of natural things, but only potentially through the influence and impression of form; but elemental fire is the most powerful part of the substance and matter of generated things. To this fire must be compared the internal fire—that is, the fire naturally implanted in the matter of Hermes. This is the opinion of Father Hermes: with the fire acting from the outside upon the center of the vessel's bottom, it propels the <term>spagyric</term> <note>The art of "spagyria" involves separating and then recombining the components of a substance to purify it.</note> fetus from this center toward the higher parts, as the words say: *He shall ascend from the earth to the heaven*, <note>A quote from the Emerald Tablet describing sublimation or vaporization.</note> that is, from the lower part of the vessel (which is sometimes called "earth") to the upper part, which is also sometimes called "heaven" by the Philosophers. This passage can be understood in another way: the offspring of the Sun and Moon ascends—that is, its thick, earthy substance is converted or resolved into "heaven," which is to say, into a most subtle substance similar to the heavens. Next, after the author has demonstrated the spagyric solution to his sons and taught them by what instrument and artifice it is perfected, he immediately adds the <term>fixation</term> <note>The process of making a volatile substance stable and solid under heat.</note> in these words: *And again he shall descend to the earth*, as if he were to say: After the dissolved spagyric substance has stood for some time in obedience to the internal celestial virtues through the artifice of ascent, it returns to its earth at its determined time of maturity. This means that the spirit itself becomes bodily again, which previously had been made into a spirit from a body. This was once wrapped in a riddle by the philosophers: *Make the fixed volatile*, they say, *and again the volatile fixed, and you shall have the whole mastery.* There are nonetheless many other chemical solutions and coagulations necessary in this mastery, which ought rather to be called preparations. It is truly foolish to believe that this spagyric matter is not to be chemically prepared and refined before it is taken up for the spagyric work. This...
