-># TRISMEGISTI.<-

As many natural philosophers as there are from the <term>spagyric</term> <note>Spagyric refers to the alchemical process of separating and then recombining the components of a substance to create a more potent "medicine."</note> art teach this very thing: that preparations are necessary, which they have called purifications, refinements, dissolutions, and solidifications. It is necessary, therefore, for the body to be dissolved into spirit, and for the spirit to be reduced back into a body, if the craftsman intends to imitate nature. For we see it happen naturally that water is dissolved into a cloud, and the cloud is again solidified into water, so that what follows may occur: *And thus it receives the force of the things above and things below.* <note>A central tenet of the Emerald Tablet, suggesting that the alchemical "stone" or medicine contains the power of both the celestial and earthly realms.</note> The author concludes his practice with these words, which correspond appropriately to the first theoretical propositions: *That which is above is like that which is below, and vice-versa.* For by using the singular number—"force"—and not doubling it, he indicates that the power of the nature above is the same as that below, and vice-versa; it is not indeed different, otherwise he would have said "forces," or doubled the singular number. Rather, he wished to teach (so as to confirm what was said above, namely, *To perform the miracles of the one thing*) that the force and power in the union of the superior with the inferior is greatest, reaching even to the miracle of spagyric philosophy.

Furthermore, having completed the practice of this art, he teaches his sons and disciples the utility of this medicine and its use in two ways. First, in these words: *Thus you shall have the glory of the whole world.* For the glory of this world is seen to consist in wealth. For true philosophers do not entirely despise riches, but rather the abuse of them; indeed, they consider a wealthy person in this world happy and glorious who bestows his wealth upon the needy and the poor. Although the widow's <term>mite</term> <note>original: "obolus"; a reference to the biblical story of the widow who gave her last small coin as an offering.</note> taken from her own living was more acceptable to God than the huge, superfluous money of the wealthy, nevertheless, so that the poor might be abundantly helped—and not by a single coin alone—the <term>Lord God</term> <note>original: "D. O. M."; abbreviation for "Deo Optimo Maximo," a common dedication meaning "To God, the Best and Greatest."</note> has sometimes granted riches to some of his people through this art and His own gift, so that they might not think (as those do to whom wealth comes from parents) that it is to be possessed for themselves alone.

However, because I have until now made very little profession of this particular part <note>The author refers here to the "transmutation" of metals into gold or the direct creation of wealth.</note>, I very gladly leave this topic to be elucidated more extensively and copiously by others. Taking up the second part, which concerns the medicine of the human body and the intellect, and continuing this little book for the benefit of students and the advantage of the whole <term>Commonwealth</term> <note>original: "Reip."; abbreviation for "Respublica," referring to the public good or the state.</note>, I shall explain those things that seem to serve this purpose, according to the weakness of my talent. Since, therefore, God wills that the poor be helped not only with gold or silver through brotherly charity, but also by applying remedies to remove their infirmities—as Christ testifies in the Gospel through his rebuke: "I was sick," he says, "and you did not visit me"—Hermes teaches this second and greatest utility of his spagyric medicine, located in the clarification of the body and mind, saying: *Therefore all obscurity shall flee from you.* Just as a double...

# PHYSICA

<page-num>384</page-num>

Since we know there is infirmity of both body and mind, <term>spagyric</term> <note>Spagyric refers to alchemical medicine, which involves the "separation" of a substance's components and their subsequent "rejoining" in a purified form.</note> medicine must also be twofold in its effect, though not in its essence. For the author says, *all obscurity will flee from you*; he does not say "from metals." By "obscurity" nothing else is understood than the darkness of diseases and ailments of the body and mind. Indeed, every sick body is dark; it reflects obscurity not only in its color, but even in its blood, urine, sweat, and all other things. On the contrary, a healthy body openly displays splendor and serenity on all sides. In short, the author’s intent is to teach those who have obtained the spagyric medicine that a tiny portion—even one resembling a mustard seed—taken in any manner, cures all diseases without distinction, on account of the effective simplicity of the union within the medicine, so that no variety or multitude of diseases can resist it.

Furthermore, there are various obscurities and infirmities of the mind, such as madness, mania, fury, stupidity, and others of that kind, by which the soul is darkened and defiled; these are most perfectly cured by this single spagyric medicine. Nor does it only restore health to the soul, but it even sharpens the wit and mind of men, so that all things are miraculously easy for them to perceive and understand, and nothing of those things which are in the higher and lower realms <note>A reference to the alchemical axiom "as above, so below," suggesting the medicine grants insight into both celestial and terrestrial secrets.</note> remains hidden from them. In summary, all bodies of natural things and of men—and their minds and souls—can be brought to the ultimate perfection of this world by this art. This occurs, however, only by God granting the discovery of the art which is described by Hermes.

Nothing stronger can be found in the nature of things than this medicine; therefore the author says: *This is the strength of all strength.* <note>Original Latin: *Hæc est totius fortitudinis fortitudo fortis.* This is a famous line from the Emerald Tablet.</note> This is as if he were saying: This is the most powerful force and efficacy of all the powers and virtues of all nature, and as if it were above nature. Therefore, it could not undeservedly be called a metaphysical work arising from natural things through the spagyric mastery. The author gives the reason for such great strength, saying: *Because it overcomes every subtle thing, and will penetrate every solid thing.* <note>Original Latin: *Quia vincit omnem rem subtilem, omnemque solidam penetrabit.*</note> 

Almost all interpreters of Hermes thus far have twisted his meaning in this place toward metals in this manner: "Because," they say, "it will 'overcome'—that is, it will solidify—every subtle thing (namely Mercury, or common quicksilver) and it will 'penetrate every solid thing'—that is, it will bring every hard metal, perfect or imperfect, such as the Sun, Moon, Saturn, Jupiter, Mars, and Venus <note>In alchemical shorthand: Sun (Gold), Moon (Silver), Saturn (Lead), Jupiter (Tin), Mars (Iron), and Venus (Copper).</note>, to the greatest and least spagyric and natural perfection." But because I have undertaken to treat and illustrate this matter from a medical perspective, leaving each man to his own opinion, I will proceed with my duty according to my plan, and I will interpret it in this way: "Because," I say, "it will 'overcome'—that is, it will expel—every subtle thing (meaning the spiritual darkness occupying the mind) and it will 'penetrate every solid thing'—namely, every coarse and hard defect of the body..."

<summary>This page interprets the Emerald Tablet of Hermes Trismegistus as a guide for creating a universal medicine that heals both physical illness and mental disorders. The author reclaims the text from purely metallic or "gold-making" interpretations, focusing instead on the "spagyric" restoration of human health and intellect.</summary>

# THE WRITINGS OF TRISMEGISTUS

<page-num>385</page-num>

<header>OF TRISMEGISTUS.</header>

...[the medicine] will eradicate [all obscurity] even from the most solid parts through spiritual penetration. Just as we previously related the "glory of the world" to riches and "obscurity" to diseases, in this place we take "subtle" to mean the spirit and "solid" to mean the body. After the author of the <term>spagyric</term> <note>Spagyric refers to the alchemical process of separating and recombining substances to achieve a purified state.</note> mastery has completed the practical instructions, and even enumerated its utility, use, and the excellence of its virtues, he did not wish his disciples to be ignorant of where this arduous work is derived from. Therefore, he admonishes them with these words: *In this way the world was created* <note>original: "Sic mundus creatus est"</note>. It is as if he were saying that the spagyric artifice must be learned thoroughly from the creation of the world. He does not mean that he wishes it to be made from nothing, as the world was, but rather he teaches how to bring the highest perfection—which was created in things and placed there by heaven—from potential into act. Therefore, "creation" is to be understood here as the *order* of the world’s creation, so that the meaning of the words is this: The spagyric artifice follows the same order, or one similar to it, by which the world was created. For it must be confessed that this work is divine rather than human or natural; man brings nothing of his own here except his service, and nature brings nothing except that in which it has already ceased to act. It remains for us to look at the sequence of Genesis in this place. We read there: *God created the heaven and the earth* <note>original: "Creavit Deus cælum & terram"</note>. Hermes says it is necessary for you to bring the heaven and the earth—which were created by God and placed in a composite state—back from their potential into act by dividing the higher from the lower, so that one might generate a third from the two through a likeness. *He separated the waters under the firmament from the waters above the firmament, and so on* <note>original: "Separavit aquas sub firmamento ab aquis supra firmamentum, & quæ sequuntur"</note>. To be brief, if you contemplate the whole of Genesis while invoking the divine light, you will find the spagyric art. Nor did it seem enough to Hermes unless he progressed further to the miracles of this work, saying: *From this will come wonderful adaptations, of which this is the manner* <note>original: "Hinc erunt adaptationes mirabiles, quarum modus est hic"</note>. As if he were saying: from the observation of this order, you will see wonderful successions of changes and compositions in our elements and "heaven," the manner of which is found here, namely in the imitation of that divine order of creation. Hermes seems to consider any philosopher to be unrefined and ignorant who understands the creation of the world but is ignorant of these "adaptations." Therefore, one must pray to God that He might deign to reveal the sequence of creation; once this is known, the spagyric artifice can in no way remain hidden. Furthermore, the author, with an insatiable desire to teach his sons and disciples completely, did not want the material from which this divine work is perfected to be hidden from them. *And so I am called (he says) Hermes Trismegistus* <note>original: "Itaque vocatus sum Hermes Trismegistus"</note>. It is as if he were speaking: for this reason I am called Hermes, because I am the interpreter of spagyric wisdom; and <term>Trismegistus</term> <note>Meaning "Thrice-Great."</note>, because the artifice I announce to you lies hidden under a <term>ternary</term> <note>A group of three.</note> concluded into one. For God rejoices in an odd number, of which the sole source and origin is the ternary. The <term>unary</term> <note>The number one or unity.</note>, however, is not counted, because the one, divided into two, overcomes and animates the ternary by its own simplicity through an indissoluble bond. Two by two...

# PHYSICS

<page-num>386</page-num>

<header>PHYSICS</header>

...can by no means be joined, because they are soluble in one and the other by themselves. It would be most necessary in this place to explain the <term>ternary</term> <note>The number three; in alchemy, this usually refers to the three primes: Salt, Sulfur, and Mercury.</note> and the <term>unary</term> <note>The number one, representing primordial unity or the "First Matter."</note> more fully, but because we reserve that for the following sections for the proof of the art, we have thought it best to refrain for now; meanwhile, let us undertake to clarify the remaining clause concerning matter. *Having* (he says) *three parts of the philosophy of the whole world.* <note>original: "Habens tres partes philosophiæ totius mundi." This refers to the three-fold wisdom claimed by Hermes Trismegistus.</note> This is as if he were saying that he knows for certain that the entire world consists of three parts throughout. Even though the whole world appears to be divided into two visible parts, a third, non-conspicuous part nevertheless lies hidden beneath those, dedicated to an equally invisible unity because of its simplicity. However, each of the said parts—namely the ethereal and the elementary—is further subdivided into three parts: body, soul, and spirit, so that these are naturally located in heaven and on the earth.

Of the first division into the ethereal and elemental region, made under a hidden bond, the last member is destined for this reason for the <term>binary</term> <note>The number two; representing duality, opposition, or the division of the elements.</note> because it is more material. From this, it happened that it was subdivided into the four elements. For two generate nothing but four from the first birth. Spiritually, however, one may see any quality divided into four primary qualities under the binary, which will be discussed more broadly below. The philosophy of the whole world can also be called threefold by reason of the coarser and decomposed matter. For there are three most general kingdoms into which everything that falls under the senses is categorized: minerals, vegetables, and animals, the secrets of all of which were most well-known to <term>Hermes</term> <note>Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary founder of alchemy.</note> through experience. As he testifies in the final conclusion of his <term>spagyric</term> <note>The art of separating and recombining substances to purify them.</note> philosophy, he has completed everything with these words: *What I have said concerning the operation of the sun is complete.* <note>original: "Completum est quod dixi de operatione solis." The "operation of the sun" is a code for the creation of the Philosopher's Stone.</note> It is as if he were speaking in this manner: I have experienced what I say, and I have completed what I announce to you—namely, that the mastery of the universal spagyric medicine is true, certain without lie, and most true, so that the last things correspond to the first. Therefore, not without cause does he call this medicine an "artificial sun," for just as the natural sun naturally flows natural life into all things, in no other way does the spagyric sun refresh and recall this failing life, by driving out the diseases that are ready to drive life from its home. This is that true medicine of the ancient fathers, and the root of long life, a universal remedy that heals all diseases indifferently, increases the vital spirits, and thus vindicates and preserves every body from corruption. However many there are who are ignorant of this art, even if they are most learned from the academies, they are accustomed to disapprove of it. What wonder is it, since they have never heard such things in their schools? It does not follow from this that it should be condemned because learned men are ignorant of it. Indeed, many things have come to light in our century which were unknown to many of the ancients, just as many things now lie hidden from us which were most familiar to the ancient fathers.

# OF TRISMEGISTUS

<page-num>387</page-num>

<header>TRISMEGISTUS</header>

<sig>Bb 2</sig>

What does not pass into oblivion through the ravages of time, as well as the laziness of men? Furthermore, truth is suppressed by the ambition of those who, wishing well only for themselves, begrudge others the secret writings which they themselves have stolen from elsewhere. Therefore, truth does not perish entirely; though it may lie buried for a time for some, it will emerge for others by the will of God, in whose heart all praiseworthy and good arts rest from eternity alongside His wisdom. For God, the giver of all good things, distributes His gifts to whom He wills, and even takes them away from the ungrateful who abuse them. There is no doubt that God revealed a certain medicine to the ancient patriarchs through His Holy Spirit, by which they might protect the corruption of their flesh <note>Protect the body from decay or disease.</note>, and especially to those with whom He spoke and entered into a covenant. But after the vain desire of men to be wise by their own power led them to seek knowledge from themselves, and in things other than Him in whom alone is all health, their minds became blinded. Led into a labyrinth, they sought now this herb, now another; tomorrow that root or another; and the day after, some mixture. Thus, by daily experimenting without judgment, they never reached the goal, nor did they possess any certainty in their teaching. What also seems most absurd is that men are never content with their lot. Almighty God gave to every nation what He wished it to possess, as much for nourishment as for medicine. Otherwise, if these things had to be sought from distant lands, they would only be available to the rich, while the poor would have to die from want. On the contrary, God has far greater care for the poor than He ever had for the rich: sacred testimonies to this are found everywhere. But that slandering enemy <note>original: "inimicus ille calumniator." A traditional reference to the Devil.</note> teaches us to despise our own things and always to crave what is foreign—seeking those things that are less at hand—so that he may render our desires insatiable. We have with us, as many as we are and wherever we live—indeed within us, though not of us—everything that we seek from others outside ourselves: in whatever way it is said. Let us see how the Gentiles and infidels, for their part, might accuse us Christians in this matter. "Nature," they say, "seeks nature similar to itself, and rejoices in its own nature; for if it be joined to a foreign nature, the work of nature is destroyed." A marvelous saying to those who do not deeply consider what nature is, but to those who know her, nothing can be more true in this matter. But let us return to where the digression of our speech turned us aside, and let us more fully prove the opinion of our mind: that we assert true <term>Physics</term> <note>In this context, Physics refers to 'Natural Philosophy' or the study of the physical world and its divine laws.</note> originated from Genesis, as did true <term>spagyric</term> <note>The alchemical art of separating, purifying, and recombining substances, particularly for medicinal use.</note> medicine, and from nowhere else, nor in any other way than through divine contemplation alone. Let us see, therefore, how Johannes Trithemius <note>A famous German Benedictine abbot and polymath (1462–1516) known for his works on cryptography, history, and the occult.</note>, the most excellent of the natural philosophers of our age, applauds Hermes

<header>PHYSICS</header>

## ON THE SPAGYRIC ART, 10. <note>The "Io." in the title is likely an abbreviation for Ioannes (Johannes/John).</note>
### The opinion of Trithemius.

->*The Monad <term>Unarius: The number one or "The One," representing absolute unity in Pythagorean and alchemical thought.</term> (he says) is not a number, and from it every number arises.*<-

<image-desc>Decorative initial A featuring intricate foliate patterns.</image-desc>
Before the universal waters of the abyss (which are mentioned in Genesis) were divided, they were one. By this division alone, the Monad produces the Dyad <term>Binarius: The number two, representing duality, division, or the separation of spirit and matter.</term>, the first of all numbers—not through substance, but by accident. *It is a number and it is numbered, and yet it is not a number and is not numbered. It is not numbered because it is simple by nature, and it is numbered insofar as it is composed of accidents <note>In philosophy, "accidents" are qualities that are not essential to a thing's nature, such as its color or size.</note>. However, it cannot be numbered insofar as there is no number before it.* This is understood as the unity which Hermes <note>Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary founder of alchemy.</note> explains with other words, using an analogy taken from Genesis. *That which is superior,* he says, *and those things which follow.* For the Dyad is denoted by Hermes through the *inferior and the superior.* *Let the Dyad be cast aside,* says Trithemius, *and the Triad <term>Ternarius: The number three, often representing the reconciliation of opposites.</term> shall be convertible to unity.* Hermes says the very same thing in other words: *To perform the miracles of the one thing* <note>original: "Ad perpetranda miracula unius rei." A famous line from the Emerald Tablet of Hermes.</note>. It must be especially noted in this place that unity is understood by both men in two ways. Indeed, Hermes counts unity, as we have said, through the "inferior" and "superior." But Trithemius does so through the constitution of the first number from the Monad. By a far different reasoning, both later measure unity: one by the reduction of the superior and inferior to a likeness found in a miracle; the other by the casting away of the Dyad and the conversion of the Triad into the Monad. Both certainly agree in the same opinion by a wondrous reasoning. Therefore, that natural unity is itself divisible, or rather numerable into the Dyad, and the Triad is reversible into that other unity which is called the Second Unity, beyond which it is not permitted to proceed. And so, every operation of wonders consistent within the limits of nature descends from the Monad through the Dyad into the Triad; yet it does not do so before it arises in simplicity from the Tetrad <term>Quaternarius: The number four, representing the material elements (earth, air, fire, water).</term> through the order of steps. For if you wish to count to four, you know you must start with nothing other than one; and so you say one, two, three, four, which when added together make ten <note>The Pythagorean "Tetraktys" (1+2+3+4=10), which was considered the perfect number representing the universe.</note>. This is the perfect completion of all number, because there is then a return to the One, and beyond the ten there is no simple number. Those who do not know the depths of this connection wonder <unclear>by which</unclear> principles we use in the operation of wonders, falsely thinking that we rely on the help of <unclear>demons</unclear> or any sort of superstition contrary to our Christian faith. We, however, do not wonder at those who judge us this way because of their ignorance of <unclear>those things</unclear> which we have set forth. For the most sacred scripture testifies to the internal knowledge of God, which no one understands except he who receives it:

<header>TRITHEMIUS</header>

...begins: thus no one can be imbued with or use these things unless they have received a singular light of understanding as a divine gift, moving from nature into nature. In this person, there must be fire with light, wind with fire, power with wind, and with power, the knowledge of a sound and whole mind. This, therefore, is the root and foundation of all deep creatures. The first natural division produces the root of perfected knowledge, the description of which is this:

> There are four mothers of those things in the final order, and four fathers of those who are at the beginning: the bond of all these—both the first connected thing and the last simple, pure, unique thing—alone dyes <note>original: *tingit*; in alchemical literature, this refers to the "tincture" or the power of a substance to transform and permeate other matter.</note> all things.

Simple Earth is a pure element and the first proceeding from the One. It is not composed, it is not changed, and it does not undergo connection, but remains that which is incorruptible. It consists in the One as one and not-one; it is not a number, and yet it is a number; it is not numbered, and yet it is numbered. Between it and the One, there is no number. It remains one in unity, and through its embrace, it produces the Triad <term>Ternarius: The number three, symbolizing the return to a new unity after the division of the Dyad.</term>. Embracing this eight times with a wonderful nature, it brings all things back to the One. Its power cannot be fully explained by any master in its entirety. This is not the God we worship; it is a creature, an image of the human mind, neither living nor dead, through which a marvelous effect is produced in all knowledge. And I tell you, friend, in the highest truth of God, that whoever is raised up by the simple knowledge of this pure simplicity will be perfected in all natural science, and will perform wondrous works and find astounding effects. 

The Good is simple and unique, and through it flow not only similar things but many dissimilar things as well. Composite Earth is an element pure by nature, simple and unique; but because what is composed necessarily becomes manifold, varied, and impure, it is nevertheless reducible through fire into water, from water into fire, and from that into the simple One. It is a number, and it is numbered, and it is not a number, and it is numbered. It is not numbered because its nature is simple, yet it is composed by accident <note>In philosophy, "accidents" are qualities that are not essential to a thing's nature, such as its state of being "composed" rather than its essence.</note>. Therefore, it cannot be numbered because there is no number before it. It is numbered by the One from unity—not an absolute one, but an included one. It is called the excluded one, the included one, and the one through one from the One—namely, from the World Soul <term>Anima Mundi: The "World Soul," an intrinsic spirit believed by ancient and Renaissance philosophers to animate all nature and connect the physical and divine realms.</term>. Thus it becomes the Triad. It naturally desires to be with the One; it is powerful through itself in the One, yet powerless in the One. It always revolves in a sphere. It remains as one in every fire, but it is not imagined so. If it is purified by fire and reduced to its simplicity by a fitting washing <note>original: *lotione*; a reference to the alchemical process of purification or "ablution."</note>, it can perform all the mysteries of deep science. 

Earth from the composite is an element and is not an element, through which the Dyad <term>Binarius: The number two, representing duality, division, or the separation of spirit and matter.</term> is reduced to the Triad, which is distant from the One by four steps. It contains wonders; it is varied and manifold, corruptible, and yet it does not wander outside the circle of unity. The mastery <term>Magisterium: The "Great Work" or the highest achievement of alchemical practice, resulting in the Philosopher's Stone or total spiritual transformation.</term> of all secrets lies in this thing’s relationship with the Triad through the Dyad in the One. And whatever things the human mind has wonderfully discovered...

...stand, they are subject to its power, and can be accomplished through a perfect operation. It observes number, degree, and order, by which every operation of the wonders of nature is established. Wondrous are the things it is able to do, and many more than are believed, which bring neither injury to God nor stain to the soul. Through it, wondrous works are performed; through it, there is full knowledge of all human inventions, and effective operation in whatever matter is obscure: because its power, proceeding from the intellect, does not permit one working through the three degrees to err. It discerns all things that men say. An operation begun through it can by no means be seduced into error. Whatever Astronomers, whatever Mathematicians, whatever Magi, whatever the envious persecutors of nature—the Alchemists—whatever the Necromancers <note>original: *Necromantici*; those who claim to communicate with the dead, whom Trithemius considers "worse than demons."</note> promise, it knows how to discern, understand, rectify, find, and, having adapted these to its own principles, perfect them without malice. This itself is the element that is not an element, removed from itself by number, and simply reduced into unity with that which is joined to it.

Without the knowledge of this middle, end, and beginning through numbers, degrees, and orders, neither could a magus give power to images without crime (or even be able to give it with wickedness), nor the Alchemist imitate nature, nor man compel spirits, nor the prophet of nature predict the future, nor any curious searcher of experiments grasp the underlying reason. Therefore, every operation of wonders consisting within the limits of nature descends from the unity through the binary <note>The number two.</note> into the ternary <note>The number three.</note>, yet not before it rises up in simplicity from the quaternary <term>Quaternary: The number four, often representing the four elements or the physical completion of a spiritual idea.</term> through the order of degrees, etc., as stated above. Natural wisdom, therefore, which once stood firm in its pure simplicity relying on the principles of nature, has been so confused by many lies and impurities, and by so many deceptions, that no one—unless they are most learned in both natural and supernatural science—is able to discern one from the other or understand it.

> How many men (he says) erring in natural philosophy do I alone know, otherwise most learned, some of whom have lost their time and substance <note>In an alchemical context, "substance" refers to both their physical materials and their personal wealth.</note> by spending them on Alchemy; some lose their lives along with their possessions; others, desiring to draw out medicine from it, accomplish nothing after long labors; others, searching into the secrets of wondrous effects, have been able to reach no successful experience; others, eager to tell the future, speak falsehoods for truths. While these men pour in the windy <note>Empty or puffed-up.</note> opinions of their own heads from the writings of experts long ago which they do not understand, they unskillfully produce good and true things [mixed with] bad and false ones.

Hence, these three principles must first be noted and learned in that natural, spagyric <term>Spagyric: A term for alchemy (often attributed to Paracelsus) involving the separation and recombination of natural elements to create medicines.</term>, and occult philosophy, without a perfect knowledge of which no effect follows for the operator. The first principle consists in the one—not just any one—but that through which every power of natural wonders is brought into effect, about which we have spoken: because the pure proceeding from the one...

For the ternary number, reduced to unity through contemplation <note>original: *aspectum*; in this context, the intellectual or spiritual "gaze" that perceives the underlying unity of things</note>, contains all things in itself and can do whatever it wills.

Through this, the prediction of future events is verified, and the suggestion of hidden things is perceived by nature from no other source than through it. By this single means, the secret of nature is opened to Alchemists, without which neither the understanding of the art is acquired, nor the effect of the practitioner found. They err, believe me (he says), they all err who trust they can work anything in the hidden sciences of nature without these three principles: moreover, the greater cause of error is that the wise men of old, imbued with the secrets of nature, either remained completely silent about these things, or wrapped them in excessive obscurity, so that they can only be truly understood by those like themselves. The philosophy of this institution is celestial and secret; in it, if anyone truly desires to know and understand something, it is necessary that he flee the tumult of men, desert the world, and contemplate heaven not only with his eyes, but also with his mind. The Spirit of God breathes where it wills, illuminates whom it wills, and whomever He has overshadowed with His divine power, He leads into all knowledge of truth: he who has received this, let him give thanks to God and strive to correspond with the fruits of good works according to the strength received, and let him recognize that he has received it, and thus he will find no reason to be proud. 

But he to whom it has not been granted to know these sublime things, let him either understand his own sluggishness, because he did not labor to know, or let him praise the mercy of the Creator who willed that there be impediments for his benefit so that he would not know: or if he has not acquired it, let him confess that God was not a debtor to him for such a great gift, and let him not murmur. You are a friend (he says); listen to a friend advising you, and you will understand what has been done. As a victor over your kinsmen, tread upon the fire of envy, not the air of mortals, by the hatred of the immortal God: levity threatens danger. Flee the gathering of men caring for worldly things, but associate with those meditating on heavenly things. Because the art of divine love is long, but time is short, and it is better always to love the creator in truth than the creature.

Every number consists of unities alone. Do not all things flow from unity by the goodness of the One, as stated above? And whatever is joined to unity cannot be different, but brings forth fruit through the simplicity and adaptation of the One. What is born from unity, if not the ternary? The Unary, therefore, is simple, the binary is composite, but the ternary is indeed reduced to the simplicity of unity. For there is one pure principle. The binary, departing from unity, is composite, because it is impossible for there to be two principles. Therefore, the ternary alone, sacred and powerful in virtue, having overcome the binary, returns to its principle—not by nature, but by the participation of likeness—in which the mind understands, without contradiction, all the mysteries of the most beautifully ordered secret. This is the most beautiful power of all strength, which conquers all worldly things. 

However, for any man wishing to work with utility in this art through natural wisdom, certain subjects are necessary. First, it is necessary that he be not only inclined by nature toward this art, but also disposed to it, or at least made ready by the mastery of a teacher, through a rectification from the ternary into unity by means of the divided binary. Second, he must have sufficient knowledge of language, so that the common people <note>original: "vulgaris"</note> do not grasp the great majesty of this natural wisdom. It is also necessary to know the foundations of astronomical instruction, or at least to have another at his service who knows it. Third, a supply of books in this science is necessary—specifically those that are the most corrected, of which very few are found today—or there must be someone at hand or in readiness who can truly correct their faults, not increase them. Fourth, a most learned and experienced teacher in this art is necessary;

...it is because this science is wrapped in such mysteries that it cannot be grasped without a most skilled teacher, unless Almighty God should wish to illuminate the mind with a singular gift—something which happens very rarely. <margin>(D)</margin> **Fifthly**, there is required a knowledge of the division of the whole universe of superiors and inferiors <note>original: "superiorum & inferiorum", referring to the celestial and earthly realms</note> from the one up to the quaternary <term>quaternary: the number four, representing the material elements</term> resting in the ternary <term>ternary: the number three, representing the spiritual or divine structure</term>. Likewise, one must know the order of ascent and descent, the degree, the number, the inflection and reflection, and being and non-being in the one and the three. Indeed, to know this is most difficult, because the root of all wondrous effects—in whatever way they may occur in both natural and supernatural wisdom—rests upon the foundation of this principle. Wherefore, whoever grasps this order and understands the method itself shall be perfected in all science and the depths of wisdom, and shall achieve wondrous effects in his work. 

But because these things are most difficult to know, very few labor with profit; many, indeed, labor without fruit in the spagyric <note>original: "spagirica", a term for alchemy involving the separation and recombination of substances</note> wisdom. **Sixthly**, it is necessary that he knows the proper way of living, the order of working, the hour of time, the work, and the master of the work—that is, the planet—the suitable place, the form, the matter, and the mixture of matter; the pure and the impure, the simple and the composite, the similar and the diverse, and the bond of things joined together. And after all these things, he must know the measure of his own soul, and the power of entering into virtue and goodness. 

**Seventhly**, he must know under the dominion of which planet the spirit of the hour of the day and of the time may be, and how every thing of the world behaves according to its substance, accident <note>In philosophy, an "accident" is a property that is not essential to the nature of a thing, such as its color or weight</note>, and effect, especially those things through which they operate. For the inferior things are subject to the superior things, and solely through similarity—which consists of substance, accident, power, virtue, number, degree, and property—by the application of one to another in a manner established by the art, a useful operation of wonders in natural wisdom is performed. 

**Eighthly**, it is necessary in this wisdom to know, and for the operator to understand, every property of the intelligences <term>intelligences: spiritual or angelic beings believed to govern the movements of the planets</term>, their degrees, places or locations, names, words, and offices or works, just as they relate to the extremes in the universal order, and how one must work through them in any universal intention. Or first, the science by which they are certainly perfected is necessary, just as meat is preserved by salt so it does not rot. 

**Ninthly**, in those things which he cannot perform alone, he must have companions, either worthy by nature or made dignified by instruction; because the unworthiness of companions hinders the effect of the operation in all works of wisdom, both natural and supernatural. **Tenthly**, the one working in this art must be firm in confidence, and must in no way doubt or hesitate about achieving the result—not because belief itself contributes anything to these things, but <unclear>because</unclear> hesitation breaks the firmness of the working soul through the middle into the extreme and makes it weak. Without the soul's stable virtue, the desired influx from the superiors does not happen. **Eleventhly**, it is necessary to wi—

# OF TRITHEMIUS

<page-num>395</page-num>

...to <gloss>Pr</gloss><unclear>operari</unclear> <note>original: "prooperari", to labor or work forward</note> with fruit in natural wisdom, to preserve all things most secretly, and to reveal to no man either the failure of the operation, nor the operation itself, nor the intent, nor the art, nor the time, except to a teacher or a disciple. This is because this science flees from the public, and once divulged, it rarely produces perfect fruits. 

This philosophy of ours is celestial, not earthly, so that we may faithfully look upon that highest principle which we call God with the gaze of the mind through faith and knowledge. We truly believe in the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit—one principle, one God, and one eternal highest good existing in a trinity of persons—knowing Him purely and always worshiping Him with a cult of most fervent love and service, from whom are all things that can possibly exist. Unless the living mind rises to this, it will understand none of those things which are beautiful, but will waste away in its own ignorance. 

This ascent is not common, nor is the imitation of those who are carried upward by only a single wing sufficient for it; rather, it is familiar to very few indeed—namely, those who have reduced themselves into unity, not rashly nor wrongly. Many indeed attempt it, but the ternary <note>original: "ternarius", the number three, representing spiritual perfection or the Trinity</note> is not in everyone's mind. Do we not, when about to look up at the heaven, necessarily first raise our head, and bring it back down after we have looked? It is permitted to gaze upon the sun with the eyes alone; the ears do not see. Therefore, so that the soul may ascend, let it not become an ear, but an eye and a heart, and let unity be made from the ternary through participation in goodness toward the principle, because there is one almighty good, not two or many. For unless unity is achieved, there will be no joining of likeness in the mind, nor participation in the good, and without these, there is no transcendence. For unless these things come first, no one will be able to attain the understanding of the higher things, nor the proper operation of the lower things. 

Now, things both universal and singular, as well as the conditions of things, are of necessity partly manifest, partly more manifest, and partly most manifest. And others are hidden, others more hidden, and others most hidden both to sense and to reason: a diversity which the nature of things produces. From this it happens that certain men turn out wiser than others. Moreover, he is called more wise who perceives the less perceptible things. It is to the understanding of these things that we open the way. Accordingly, whoever pants for attained philosophy, both natural and supernatural, can prepare a way for himself to either one through the other; yet he will proceed more safely if he reduces himself from the binary <note>original: "binario", the number two, often signifying duality, division, or the material world</note> into the ternary through the steps of the quaternary <note>original: "quaternij", the number four, representing the material elements</note>, before he attempts or presumes to effect that same thing in natural matters. Although one might also reach the supernatural through the reverse, by means of spagyric medicine <note>original: "spagiricae medicinae", the alchemical art of separating and recombining substances</note>, this way is nevertheless <unclear>much</unclear> more error-prone, nor does it happen that one errs in any way more than in that one; wherefore I would rather persuade everyone that they must walk by the other path. To this...

<header>PHYSICS</header>

Come forward, best of readers, and lift up an attentive mind no less than your ears.

## A CLEARER ELUCIDATION
### *of the interpreter.*

**M**an is naturally one and is not counted as more, yet supernaturally he is counted as two—namely, as spirit and body—which constitute a <term>binary</term> <note>original: "binarius", referring to the number two or a state of duality</note> within him. But because of original corruption, the latter overcomes the former; the result of this is that the spirit is unable to produce anything wonderful. In order for the spirit to accomplish wonders in this life, the binary must be overcome by the <term>ternary</term> <note>original: "ternarius", the number three, representing the spiritual reconciliation of a duality</note>; that is, the body must be conformed to the nature of the spirit, and the spirit must be so joined to the body that it may thereafter find peace within it. When this is done, the ternary, now having arisen in a "second unity," rejoices perfectly. For from the two things mentioned, and from the prior states, one third thing is made through their union. However, this conjunction must be achieved through the steps of the <term>quaternary</term> <note>original: "quaternarius", the number four, here representing the four elements</note>—that is, through the transmutation of the elements from which the body consists into a single and purest element, in the following manner.

First, let water be made from the earth of your body; that is: let your stony, earthy, and sluggish heart be rendered soft, and made vigilant for attaining the knowledge of its GOD, as well as knowledge of itself. In this way, the images and contemplations of the spirit can be imprinted upon the heart, not otherwise than characters from a seal are pressed into wax. Afterwards, let air be made from that water; that is, lift up toward heaven to Him who created it your contrite and humbled heart—like air which always tends toward the highest places—and knock by praying so that your intellect may be opened to understand those things which are of GOD. Finally, let fire be made from this air; that is, let every desire of your now-sublimated heart be converted into the love of GOD and of your neighbor here on earth (to which fire is compared because of its heat), so that this flame may never be extinguished. By this very process, it will happen that through likeness your binary—the spirit and the body—is perfectly joined into one ternary, through the three steps of the quaternary as you have heard.

Now, friend reader, you have the key of meditative philosophy, which opens the way of ascent to the heavens, and no one can shut it against you. You shall hear in what follows of the other key, that of descent, which shuts what no one can afterwards open. Since you have already ascended from the earth up into heaven, it is necessary for you to descend from it back to the earth, to receive the power of superior and inferior things. Behold in how few words I have wished to elucidate, through my little nighttime labors <note>original: "lucubratiunculis", small works produced by candlelight</note>, those matters which the ancient and recent <term>spagyrists</term> <note>original: "spagiri", alchemists who focused on separating and recombining the "virtues" or essences of materials</note> have tried to veil in so many and various wrappings of enigmas. I have done this with a liberal mind toward <unclear>myself</unclear> and toward all students of hidden things. Nor, though weary, will I be burdened to reveal more things to you which lead most greatly to this philosophy, provided you remain vigilant and attentive, if indeed this is your concern. Hear now more broadly of the number, order, and steps.

# TRITHEMII 397

Number consists in order and measure. Likewise, order cannot exist without number and measure. Measure, moreover, consists of both number and order. In this context, Unity <note>original: "Unitas"</note> and the Ternary <note>original: "ternarius", the number three</note> do not admit number—meaning multiplicity—but, having cast off all multitude, they stand in the first order by their own innate and simplest purity. This is the path to the heavens, through which the ancient sages, proceeding intellectually under the guidance of reason, perceived many things that are now considered by our contemporary scholars to be beyond human comprehension.

Do you wish to hear more fully? **Study** generates **knowledge**; **knowledge** gives birth to **love**; **love** produces **likeness**; **likeness** brings **communion**; **communion** leads to **virtue** <note>here meaning "efficacy" or "spiritual power"</note>; **virtue** leads to **dignity**; **dignity** leads to **power**; and **power** performs a **miracle**.

This is the unique path to the end of attained perfection in philosophy, both divine and natural, from which everything superstitious, deceptive, and diabolical is kept far away and put to shame. Therefore, since the end of meditative science—or attained science—is Truth, and the end of <term>spagyric</term> <note>original: "spagiricae"; from the Greek words for "separating and recombining," referring to alchemical practice</note> practice is the Work, we know only as much as we apprehend of the knowledge of God Almighty, who alone is Truth: for we truly know only as much as we love.

Indeed, true and salvific science gives birth to the knowledge of God; knowledge brings love; love brings frequency <note>meaning "constant presence" or "repetition"</note>; frequency brings familiarity; familiarity brings confidence; and confidence brings the attainment of all things which you have requested. Certainly, science precedes the cultivation of virtue, because no one can faithfully desire what he does not know. The knowledge of the true and the love of the right prepare the most certain entrance to happiness. However, as we have said, knowledge precedes love, because no one can truly love what is unknown. For this reason, our Lord Jesus Christ said to the Father in the Gospel: *This is eternal life, that they may know thee, the only true God, and Jesus Christ whom thou hast sent.* <note>John 17:3</note> 

What else is that enjoyment of the super-celestial pleasantness of the blessed spirits, if not the knowledge and love of the Divine Majesty? For the knowledge of salvific science has love joined to itself, nor can the intellectual mind have a partnership in eternal enjoyment if either knowledge exists without love, or love without knowledge. 

Indeed, the evil demons have knowledge, but because they do not have love, they by no means reach that enjoyment which is born from both and not from one alone. Some Gentiles <note>non-Christians or pagans</note>, and many today who are placed outside of Christianity, may perhaps seem to have a love for the one supreme truth; but because they do not know the Father of the universe, the only true God, and Him whom He sent, our Lord Jesus Christ, they have "vanished in their thoughts" <note>a reference to Romans 1:21</note> and in no way reach the enjoyment of the supreme goodness. Moreover, our Savior the Lord Jesus Christ says in the Holy Gospel regarding those who do not know through faith that He has come into the world: *He who does not believe is already judged.* <note>John 3:18</note> For true knowledge is from faith, and love is from knowledge. Therefore, a man lacking faith has no knowle...

# PHYSICA

knowledge. But he who does not possess knowledge lacks love, and he who lacks love is denied the fruit of fulfillment. For this is what the Lord Jesus himself, when he was about to ascend into heaven, revealed to his disciples, saying: 

> Go into the whole world and preach the Gospel to every creature. He who believes and is baptized shall be saved; but he who does not believe shall be condemned. 

Therefore, the first way to God is science, or knowledge through faith, without which no one will be saved. To this true knowledge, all other sciences and studies ought to be directed; unless this is done, those "wise men" who separate their studies from the things we have mentioned will be consumed by vain and foolish labor. The true science and wisdom we have proposed deeply moves the one who knows it with compunction <note>original: "compunctione"; a feeling of deep regret or spiritual remorse that leads to humility</note>; it does not puff them up, it does not allow them to be proud, and it makes them mournful, according to the saying of the wise man: 

> He who increases knowledge, also increases sorrow, because in much knowledge there is much indignation. <note>A reference to Ecclesiastes 1:18</note>

Let us therefore provide that our studies may be true while we have the time. So far he has spoken. In order that I may more clearly reveal to you through these words what I explained above regarding the ascent of the ternary <note>the number three</note> from the binary <note>the number two</note> through the quaternary <note>the number four</note>, take note: 

The first step of the ascent to the heavens is the **study of faith**, for this prepares the heart of man for dissolution into water <note>an alchemical metaphor for the softening or purification of the soul</note>. 

The second step is the **knowledge of <term>GOD</term>** <note>original: "DEI"</note> through faith, by which the contrite heart is prepared for an ascent into the elevated air, and for the hope of a better life. 

The third step is **love** arising from the knowledge of **<term>GOD</term>** through faith and hope, preparing our "airy" heart for love and charity, and for the fiery burning of desire through the likeness of union with **<term>GOD</term>**. 

The fourth is **frequency** <note>original: "frequentia"; meaning regular practice or consistency</note>, by which the love that has been conceived is nurtured through continual devotion and frequent contemplations joined with prayers, leading to the increase of the faith, hope, and love already conceived, while the heart dwells in the heights, almost united with them. 

The fifth step is **familiarity**, which is acquired through the frequency of such conversations with the divine. 

The sixth is **confidence**, by which—being now fearless through faith, hope, and charity frequently practiced—we dare to offer our petitions before God, relying on a great and indubitable certainty that we shall obtain what we desire from our Father. 

The seventh is the **attainment** of the desired petition made in the name of **<term>JESUS CHRIST</term>**, which we enjoy for His glory and our own salvation. 

At last, we are fit for the understanding of all secrets, both natural and supernatural, and having become philosophers created by God, we are filled with all wisdom. It must certainly be noted that, just as in the first, second, and third steps our heart ascends upward, receding from the vile, filthy, and corruptible earth, so through the fourth, fifth, sixth, and seventh steps, it descends into a renewed earth—incorruptible, solid, constant, and powerful; able to resist any assaults of the enemy, and no longer separable from the unity to which it is joined. TRITHEMIUS.

Trithemius previously divided this ladder into nine steps, which, as stated above, can be interpreted as either "perfected philosophy" or <term>spagyric medicine</term> <note>original: "spagiricam"; the alchemical art of separating and recombining the components of a substance to create a more potent medicine</note>. Indeed, these two are simply different parts of one and the same wisdom: the Theoretical part concerns higher or supernatural science, while the Practical part concerns lower, natural wisdom. Truly, because all knowledge of natural secrets depends on the knowledge of supernatural things, we shall interpret the aforementioned steps more fully and clearly through "meditative philosophy," in the following manner.

# ON PHILOSOPHY
## *Meditative.*

Meditative philosophy is the voluntary withdrawal of a well-composed mind from the body, so that the soul may more easily engage with the knowledge of truth. For true meditation, a good disposition of the body is also required so that it does not hinder the mind. This state can be acquired in two ways: by nature or by art. That which is natural can be assisted by art; furthermore, what has been denied by nature in this regard can still be acquired, primarily through the use of reason, through sobriety in diet, and through <term>spagyric medicines</term>; using one or all of these remedies together.

The mind is said to be "well-composed" whenever the spirit <note>original: "animus"; the rational or intellectual part of the human spirit</note> is joined with the soul <note>original: "anima"; the vital or life-giving soul</note> by such a bond that it is able to restrain the appetites of the body and the emotions of the heart. The body's "good disposition" is its immunity from the vices of corruption; it is better to the extent that its component parts have obtained or achieved a greater balance <note>original: "temperaturam"; referring to the healthy balance of the four bodily humors</note>. In this state, the body craves its own desires less and becomes more obedient to the mind.

For whatever the body craves is corrupt; indeed, it can crave nothing except through the faculties of the soul, which is its mover. By its original nature, if it had not been corrupted, the soul would move simply, without any conception of good or evil. But because malice entered the soul first, it strives to carry out that malice through the body, unless the spirit resists. The spirit advises nothing but good. Thus, the soul is situated between good and evil, and it has the choice of good—not through itself, but through the good of which it had been deprived and which has now been restored to it—and it has the choice of evil through itself and for itself. Good permits such evil to happen, and not otherwise, because of the continual and diligent resistance which the soul, dragged down by the body, makes against the pull of the spirit, which moves only toward goodness. To better deduce these things from the mind's perspective, it must be noted here why we assert that man consists of three parts. It is certain that "soul" and "spirit" are used interchangeably; however, we place no other difference between them than in respect to <unclear>attainments</unclear> <note>original: "adeptium"; likely referring to things acquired through spiritual success</note>. Thus, when the soul follows the pull of the spirit of the Lord and acquiesces

<header>PHILOSOPHIA</header>

...rests in it, denying itself, we call it the **mind** <note>original: "animum"; the higher, rational spirit</note> and **spirit**, derived from the living spirit to which it clings. Conversely, if it should resist the Holy Spirit—who imprints upon it the testimony of salvation—and if it should love itself and thereby lose itself, we call it simply the **soul** <note>original: "animam absolutè"; the vital life-force of the individual self</note>. Nor do we wish these writings of ours to be understood in any other way, lest perhaps we be accused by some of any impiety—from which our mind is far removed—but rather it strives with all its strength to draw the soul toward the divine. Therefore, the **mind** is to us the breath of eternal life, and the **soul** is the organ of the mind or spirit, just as the body is the organ of the soul. This soul is the life of the body through a natural union, just as the spirit is the life of the soul through a supernatural union.

Hence, if the soul clings more to the spirit through assent or consent than to the body, the **mind** rises up, and the **inner man**—originally created in the image of God through the breath of eternal life and now reborn—is revealed. Conversely, when the soul clings to its body, obeying it more than the spirit, the **outer man** is left behind, along with a bottomless pit of outer darkness, which is contrary to nature.

The mind also delights in three things: namely, **reason**, **intellect**, and **memory**. **Reason** presents the image of contemplation <note>original: "speculationis"</note> to the **intellect**; the intellect then presents it to the secret **memory** to be preserved. **Primary Reason** is the perpetual and inviolable order of the eternal mind, of which man was made a participant by the highest gift of God, along with intellect and memory—which indeed can be called the "preserving ark" of both.

The soul, in turn, consists of two primary faculties: namely, **motion** and **sense**. Motion is either natural or accidental. **Sense** is the perception of a thing heard, tasted, seen, smelled, or touched, through its own proper organ. Indeed, the members of the body through which the senses are perceived by the soul we call the "proper organs" of the senses. Now, the perception of the senses recalls the knowledge of past things to memory by the representation of present things; and brute animals have this in common with humans. For they recollect those same things by sense only when present objects are offered to them.

There is, however, another root of memory, far more excellent, which uses no mediating representation, but rather cultivates said memory by the diligent activity of the never-idle spirit, making it flourish perpetually. This continuation of memory follows the cultivation of reason and belongs to man alone. Therefore, **common sense** belongs to the animal; reason, however, is specifically intellectual. For brutes do not understand anything outside of the present sense; rational animals, however, understand through the intellect moved by reason, as well as through sense, using the latter as a superior end or as a medium.

Again, in rational beings, the mind and the body are opposite extremes and contraries, which cannot be joined except through the soul acting as a medium participating in both, despite their opposition. Because one of these extremes is perfect, while the other is imperfect, if motion first begins from the perfect, it necessarily passes through the medium to the perfection of the imperfect, and vice versa. # MEDITATIVE WORKS <note>original: "MEDITATIVA"</note>

He created all things under the number three, so that they might come together into one. For He Himself is the author of peace, union, and harmony, which cannot exist without the opposition of at least two things. Therefore, two things are always enemies until they come together as one through a **trinity** <note>original: "ternarium"</note>, and through this unity, they become friends. Again, the **spirit** <note>original: "animus"; the higher, rational part of the human being</note> is equal to all, but it is not received equally by all. Thus, the **mind** <note>original: "mens"; here used to mean the functional intellect or awareness</note> is not equal nor shared equally by all. Indeed, there are very few who have their **soul** <note>original: "animam"; the vital life-force</note> joined with their spirit; many share in the mind to a greater or lesser degree; but most people, cherishing the body within the soul and the soul within the body, do not recognize the spirit, nor do they perceive its warnings. To these people, there is no mind, but rather insanity serves them as reason and wisdom. Therefore, the mind is well-received whenever the spirit and the soul, being in agreement, are at the same time so tightly received by the body that out of these three, one harmonious and inseparable thing is formed.

Furthermore, this friendship can be achieved in no other way than through **division**, without which union can by no means be fulfilled. For a thing is one by its own nature alone; if it remains alone, it would be impossible for it to be joined or united with another. If, however, it is to be united to some other, it is necessary that this other be divided from the one, or by the one, since there is nothing besides that one. And since the parts of the one symbolize or have sympathy with the one, they easily come together into unity—the more so, the less they are removed from the one through intervals of similarity in brightness. For this reason, the pulling away <note>original: "distractio"; a drawing away or detachment</note> of the mind from the body is necessary, so that a union of the mind and its dwelling place may occur.

But truly, since union requires the perfection of both parts, a transition must be made from the perfect extreme (which existed before) through the middle to the imperfect, so that the latter may be perfected. Through this kind of pulling away of the mind from the body, which some call **voluntary death**, the soul and the spirit joined together acquire power and dominion over their body—a power which the spirit alone did not have so freely because of the resisting medium through which the supernatural transition had to occur. For enemies do not come together except through a neutral separation from the side of discord, but which is a participant in the reconciliation with both sides.

By this very principle, **judicial astrology** <note>original: "Astronomia judiciaria"; the practice of predicting human character or future events based on the stars</note>, which teaches that the arrangement of the stars inclines our disposition, is weakened. For the stars have no power over the minds of men—for whose sake they were created—since the mind is a far more excellent and leading creature. That which is less noble does not act upon that which is more excellent, even if it tries. If, however, human bodies conquer the soul and reduce it to the slavery of the corruptible body, I will not deny that then the bodies of the stars, being more noble than the bodies of men, can imprint their actions upon them through their influence. For <unclear>indeed</unclear> **the mind of the wise man will rule the stars** <note>original: "mens sapientis dominabitur astris"; a famous medieval maxim suggesting that wisdom and free will can overcome astrological fate</note>; but the mind of the fool is subject not only to those stars, but even to lower things and all kinds of hardships. The wise man, however, is he who, having obtained a mind, cultivates it; the fool, on the contrary,

# PHILOSOPHY

One who loves the body within the soul, or the soul within the body, while neglecting the spirit <note>original: "animo neglecto"</note>, acts according to the word of God: *He who loves his soul (understand: in the body) shall lose it, and he who hates his soul (in the manner stated above) keeps it for eternity.* <note>A reference to the Gospel of John 12:25. The author interprets "soul" here as the lower, vital life-force tied to physical impulses.</note> A person is said to love their soul in the body when they follow all the wicked appetites of their body. Likewise, even if one does not follow those appetites, but nevertheless delights in thoughts of vanities and imaginary things, they are seen to love the body within their soul.

On the contrary, one truly hates his soul in the body who restrains the harmful appetites of the physical form; and he hates the body in his soul who immediately drives out and eradicates the vain thoughts of his imaginations. This is the path to pure union—namely, the union of the soul with the spirit—and to attaining the **mind** <term>mens; here referring to the highest state of human consciousness where the soul and spirit act as one</term>. Whether we finally call this state "spirit" or "soul," by the name of one we do not exclude the other, because of the union already achieved.

Nevertheless, it must be highly noted that no union is perfect unless it is inseparable. Even so, the beginnings of union can be laid down, which might not immediately achieve their full effect; this does not prevent the resulting awareness from being called a "mind," though it be more or less imperfect. Truly, those who have attained a perfect mind are very few; those who have a beginning of it are many; but those who have none are the most numerous of all.

Furthermore, a good disposition of the physical body is very useful for high contemplation, even if it is not strictly necessary. For the body, by its own corrupted nature—by which it has become diseased and weighed down—greatly burdens the soul and hinders it, so that the soul is less able to perceive the actions of the spirit. However, it happens to some by nature to be more fit than others to undergo that separation <note>The "voluntary death" or spiritual detachment mentioned on previous pages.</note>; specifically those to whose natural corruption at the time of their birth, by some chance, no further corruption or at least very little was added.

Those are less fit who, in addition to their original and accidental corruption, hinder their reason through their own impudence and a dissolute way of life. Such people are agitated by worldly cares, neglect the perpetual things that exist outside this world, and use the things nature gave only for necessity far more profusely than is proper. Therefore, just as something is hindered by the addition of an obstacle, it can be helped by the removal of that same obstacle.

For this purpose, several medicines are created through the **spagiric art** <term>Alchemy; specifically the "solve et coagula" process of separating, purifying, and recombining substances</term>, which is most excellent above all others. These medicines, once removed from their own coarse physical bodies, retain the natural power of cleansing which they naturally possessed. After the removal of their active parts, they can perform that same cleansing action within a foreign subject body—indeed, far more excellently than they were naturally able to do within their own original forms. 

Moreover, whatever is found in the nature of things having form and matter desires to be perfected as much as possible within its own kind; this innate appetite is the most powerful cause of perfection for all things. Since nature also rejoices to be joined to a nature similar to itself and delights in it, the mind prevails when it is aided by a similar, incorrupt medicine, in a disposition...

->### MEDITATIVE THOUGHTS<-

[of the] body, this is forced to descend into that same nature, just as previously, on the contrary, when the body prevailed—strengthened by things similar to itself while its corrupters were overcome—the soul was forced. Lest this seem absurd to anyone, I shall add an explanation. Any nourishment is changed into blood of the same complexional nature <note>The "complexion" refers to the specific balance of the four humors—blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile—within a person.</note> as the nourishment itself was. This is shown by the example of those who are constantly fed on the meat of wild animals, who also happen to become most ferocious themselves. Indeed, nature takes nothing for food except that which is subtle, once the coarse and dreg-filled matter has been removed and ejected in the excrement. Furthermore, it ejects any other leftover waste of the nourishment through the pores as sweat, or through the bladder, the nostrils, or tears. 

This moved Paracelsus <note>Philippus Aureolus Theophrastus Bombastus von Hohenheim (1493–1541), a Swiss physician and alchemist who pioneered the use of chemicals and minerals in medicine.</note> to say that every individual limb of the human body has its own "stomach" in which the nourishment is cooked <note>original: "decoquitur," referring to the process of vital heat breaking down substances</note>, and in which the separation of the superfluous from the necessary takes place. If, however, through the weakness of any limb, such waste cannot be conveniently ejected, the waste from poor digestion nourishes the flesh or bones in that place—contrary to the custom of nature—and extends or bends them into a tumor or a growth. 

But truly, in spagyric <term>spagyric: alchemical medicine involving the separation of ingredients into their purest elements and then recombining them</term> medicines, nothing coarse or superfluous is left behind. For this reason, every part of the body absorbs this medicine in its entirety and transforms it into a nature like itself without the need for separation. Conversely, the medicine impresses upon the body the same property that it possesses—namely, being free from corruption and waste, just as all uncorrupted nature is. 

Furthermore, this uncorrupted nature is the natural **balsam** <note>In alchemical thought, "balsam" is an internal preservative fluid that prevents the body from decaying.</note> of long life, naturally implanted in all bodies and similar in nature to spagyric medicine. Through this balsam, the body's natural (or "radical") heat and moisture are preserved from corruption as much as possible. When this balsam is lacking, the entire body becomes "leprous" <note>Here, "leprous" is used broadly to mean diseased, decaying, or corrupted rather than specifically referring to Hansen's disease.</note>; but when it is restored by an increase from external sources, that which had already been corrupted due to the scarcity of the balsam is ejected as waste. 

Therefore, spagyric medicine differs from common and traditionally used medicine. Common medicine, when passed into the stomach along with its "body" and its corruptions, is cooked and separated no differently than any other food—and not without the greatest loathing and nausea of nature. Spagyric medicine, however, is transformed with the highest delight, beyond all need for digestion or separation, immediately into the natural radical moisture, heat, and balsam. For it is necessary that these three most powerful parts of the physical body be both nourished and restored by things similar to themselves. 

Hence it happens that daily food and drink are consumed along with their physical "bodies," because they were ordained by nature for the nourishment of the elements, and not as medicine. For every element is sustained by an element similar to itself; but all things come together and are preserved in their proper balance by the ethereal substance <note>original: "aetherea substantia"; the "Fifth Element" or Quintessence that permeates the universe.</note>, to which our bal-

[First], and its companions, we make as conformable as possible. For there is in the human body a certain substance conformable to the ethereal substance, which preserves the remaining elemental parts within it and causes them to continue. Thus, the spirit of a **spagyric medicine** <note>Spagyric refers to alchemical medicine, specifically the process of separating and then recombining the essential virtues of a substance to create a more potent "spirit."</note>, when joined with its soul and separated from the coarse and impure body—and afterwards reunited to that body once it has been purified through the soul—nourishes and restores the mental, indeed the spiritual or vital, parts into a substance similar to itself. It also corrects the physical body, even if it has been corrupted, and protects it from all further corruption.

We do not deny that our spagyric medicine is corporeal, but we say it has been made spiritual—a state which the spagyricist induces when *the fixed becomes volatile, and the volatile fixed* <note>original: "ubi fixum fit volatile, & volatile fixum." However, the second union—that of the mind with the body—reveals the sage, as he separates himself from the world and awaits that complete and blessed third union with the **First Unity** <note>God or the ultimate source of all being</note>. May Almighty God grant that we all be made such, and that He Himself may be one in all.

Furthermore, one must also know from where the mind is to be sought. For just as faith is truly a free gift of God, so are all the virtues. It does not follow from this, however, that one should not labor to acquire them, since God by no means hears the idle and the sluggish; indeed, He rather rejects their prayers as if they were blasphemies. It would truly be a great insanity for men to ask God for bread yet be unwilling to plow and sow; it would be no less insane to desire a "mind" <note>Here referring to a state of high intellectual and spiritual clarity</note> and wait for it while applying no diligence whatsoever toward acquiring it. It would be the greatest insanity of all if someone were so ignorant as to think this could be acquired by his own labor without first imploring the grace of God.

->### MEDITATIVE [PHILOSOPHY]<-

[In the huma]n body lies hidden a certain substance of a celestial nature known to very few, which needs no medicine at all, but is itself its own incorruptible medicine. But because it is overwhelmed and hindered by the corruptions of its body from exercising its actions, the philosophers, by a certain divine inspiration, recognized that this virtue and celestial vigor can be liberated from its shackles—not by a contrary, as the unfaithful teach, but by its like. Since, therefore, such a thing is found either in man or outside him that is conformable to this substance, the wise concluded that likes are to be strengthened by likes—by peace rather than war—and that contraries are to be driven out by contraries. Therefore, for the artificial good disposition of the body, we use **spagyric medicine** <term>spagyric: alchemical medicine prepared by separating and then recombining the essential components of a substance to purify it</term>, by which remedy we may ward off its corruption toward natural digestion, and thus through expulsion, with nature working this through an internally strengthened form. From this, the studious reader will gather that from meditative philosophy first, through spagyric [philosophy], the safest passage is made to true and attained wisdom. 

Now let us come to the voluntary division. With the body's preparation complete, it is easily separated from the remaining parts, when whatever the body has desired from the soul beyond physical necessity—at the mind's persuasion—has been denied to it. From that separation results the first union of spirit and soul through the continued study of moral philosophy. These things had to be proposed to the student so they might know by what reasoning we have mixed moral matters with spagyric, physical, and meditative ones, and how each is compared to its corresponding parts—lest the reader say we have blocked the entrance to grasping the matter for those stuck in a labyrinth.

Indeed, what is contrary <note>original: "contrarium"</note> to the true essence and ought not to be, and which exists only through the deprivation of true essence, is nothing other than what truly is not. From this, some conclude that sin and death are such "nothings," because they do not proceed from that true being, but from a <term>privation: the absence or lack of a quality that should naturally be present</term> of true essence.
