This was done through His own Son: who asserted and clearly showed Himself to be the way and the life of truth for us, when by His own death—which He did not deserve—He took away from us the perpetual death with which we all deserved to be punished. 

See then, brothers, how great the effect of truth is: that it is beneficial and peaceful even toward its enemies, provided they recognize it. With Adam we have all indeed sinned, yet very few of us—almost none—openly confess our nakedness as he did. Instead, each person desires not only to appear but to be more perfect, although he is the most imperfect of all; and while distinguishedly cloaked in <note>original: "byssoque coccineo & purpura"</note> fine scarlet linen and purple, he is in reality most naked. 

We inherited this vice from the first appetite of our first parent: that our flesh, more than anything else, desires—rightly or wrongly—to know, to be wise, to possess, and to be honored like an idol. This is the primary pursuit of men in this age, which is most destructive to them, just as it was to Adam. Nor are there lacking among us those who, after Adam's fall, betake themselves to the worse side, and no differently than he, fleeing from the face of the Lord, seek out the hiding places of outer darkness. # MEDITATIVE WORKS

The truth and power of a thing lie hidden within it, and it is through this art that they are to be brought into action. For this to occur, it is necessary to divide them—separating the superior from the inferior—and to purify both parts. Only then, through a <term>spagyric<note>The term "spagyric" refers to alchemical techniques, specifically the process of separating a substance into its components and then recombining them in a purified form.</note></term> operation, can they be reduced back into one, or united. Therefore, the study of the spagyric art, and the first step toward a spagyric union, is the division or separation of the matter.

There is, then, a twofold separation of the elements. The first is the separation of the purer from the more impure, and this is truly spagyric. The second concerns the elemental qualities; this is common and familiar to everyone. Nature, however, works through simple mixing under only two operations: namely, alteration and animation. We shall deal with each of these in what follows; for now, we must speak of the separation of the pure from the impure. 

In certain bodies, this separation occurs by itself; in others, it occurs by means of a vehicle. Although a celestial essence—which they call the <note>original: "quintam," referring to the Quintessence or fifth essence</note> **fifth essence**—exists in all bodies produced by nature, philosophers say it does not abound in anything so much as in wine. For this reason, they have preferred wine, also because the separation is easier. This is not because that substance is more excellent when drawn from its own body than when taken from any other; for its power is universal. It only appears diverse because of the variety of subjects in which it still clings; yet, once liberated, it returns to its own unity. This is one of the secrets of nature through which the spagyrists reached higher things.

Furthermore, we must be careful not to be misled by the name "wine," for it is twofold: the **philosophical** and the **common**. Philosophical wine can be drawn from any natural body. Common wine is sold by wine-merchants. Therefore, whenever you wish, you shall separate the spirit and the soul from any body. 

Let us first teach you about "philosophical wine" by way of an example. Take grains of wheat, barley, or rye, and soak them in spring water, rainwater, or any other water until they swell. Let them be piled into a heap and remain there for several days until they grow warm and begin to sprout. Once this is observed, spread them out and allow the superfluous moisture of the water to dry for a while. Afterward, grind them somewhat coarsely in a mill. Place this flour in a wooden vessel, pour boiling water over it, and cover the vessel. 

After this liquor has cooled and settled, strain it through a hair-sieve or a sack so that it is not at all cloudy. Then, finally, pour more boiling water over the same flour as before and strain it again. Repeat this process of pouring and straining until you perceive that the entire substance of the grain has been received into the waters; you can test this by tasting the last strained liquid and the flour itself. Finally, make all the strained liquids boil until, through evaporation, they are brought to the thickness of honey. 

By this path, you have prepared for yourself "philosophical wine" from grain. You can obtain it in the same way from all other seeds, even those that are too dry to be separated by themselves without burning. A separation made in this manner is said to be done "by a vehicle." # PHILOSOPHY

Through distillation, you will separate the soul together with the spirit—which ascend upward—from their body. You shall <term>sublime<note>Sublimation is a process where a substance is heated until it turns into a vapor and then solidifies again, used here to purify the spirit and soul from the "phlegm," or inactive watery residue.</note></term> this spirit and soul repeatedly until they are entirely separated and freed from all phlegm. The body, having been dried in the shade or by a fire, you must then reduce to the driest ashes using a most violent fire. Pour boiling water over these ashes and let it boil for some time so that you obtain a very sharp <term>lye<note>original: "lixivium"; a liquid solution of alkaline salts leached from ashes.</note></term>. Once it has settled, separate the liquid from the ashes by a careful tilting of the vessel, ensuring the liquid is not disturbed but remains clear. Pour more boiling water over the ashes as before to prepare another lye; add this to the first strained batch. Repeat this leaching process until you perceive that no sharpness remains in the ashes. 

Pass the collected lye through a linen sleeve—which they call a filter—until it becomes a crystal-clear liquor. Evaporate this in glass vessels so that you obtain our <term>tartar<note>In this context, "tartar" refers to the purified crystalline salt of the plant or mineral, considered the "salt of nature" and the foundation of the physical body.</note></term> and the salt of the nature of all things. This salt can be dissolved into "tartar-water" if placed on a marble slab in a cold, damp location.

Once you have the <term>fifth essence<note>original: "essentiam quintam"; the Quintessence or the most purified, potent "heavenly" extract of a substance.</note></term> from "philosophical wine"—or from common wine of any color, provided it is pure and very strong—and you have rectified it perfectly as you have heard, you must then reduce this juice to its ultimate simplicity through constant and diligent rotational motions. When the <term>circle of the wheel<note>Referring to "circulation," a process where a liquid is continuously evaporated and condensed in a closed vessel, often called a "Pelican," to refine its energy.</note></term> is complete, you will see the pure separated from the impure once again. It will float on the surface, transparent and shining with a most serene, sky-blue color. Separate this from the impurities by tilting the vessel, and preserve it.

You have now seen the **spagyric heaven**, which you may adorn with "lower stars" just as the heaven above is furnished with "upper stars." Will the unbelievers—who claim to imitate the Natural Philosophers—now wonder that we handle the heavens and the stars with our own hands? Or will they simply deny everything that is unknown to them, as they usually do? It matters little what they do. No malice or envy shall delay our purpose, by which we strive to benefit all good people and students of the truth. Therefore, let us expand further, proceeding in the manner we have begun.

These "lower stars" are any individual things produced by nature in this lower world through the conjunction of the heavens (the superior elements) with the inferior elements. Already I hear the voices of many growling against us, shouting: "Fie! <note>original: "Vah, apage"</note> Away with them! Such men who say they can join heaven to earth should be cast out." But let them shout as loud as they wish; they shall be forced to hear even higher and greater things. For this "heaven" of ours is celestial matter and universal form, containing within itself all distinct forms, yet all of them proceeding from a single universal form. 

Therefore, whoever knows that individual things can be brought back to their most general "genus" through the spagyric art—and can afterwards imprint upon that genus one or many specific virtues—will easily discover the **universal medicine**. Such a medicine will be capable of removing all corruptions and diseases, whether they are specific to one part or universal to the whole. For since there is only one most general origin of all corruptions...

Afterward, if the "lesser perfect" is added according to the proportion of the Great Work, one will arrive by that path at the **Greater Perfect**, which increases its own species ten thousand times over in external substances. 

But because these things are scarcely intelligible unless one has a full knowledge of the terms of the art, we have decided to define these in the second following grade, once we have first completed our **meditative knowledge**. 

**Meditative knowledge**, therefore, is a certain indubitable resolution of opinions conceived about any truth, achieved through experienced certainty. 
*   **Opinion** is a doubtful presumption of truth clinging in the mind. 
*   **Experience** is the manifest demonstration of truth. 
*   And **Resolution** is the laying aside of doubt. 

We cannot become more certain of any doubt than by experiencing it, nor better than within ourselves. Therefore, let us verify what was said above concerning the truth by making the trial from ourselves. We said before that **piety** consists in the **knowledge of oneself**; hence it follows that we should begin to elucidate meditative knowledge from that point. 

No one can truly know themselves unless they first see and know—through diligent meditation and the investigation of the Holy Scriptures—what they actually are, rather than merely who they are; upon whom they depend or to whom they belong; and for what purpose they were made and created; likewise, by whom and through whom. Once these things are known, **piety** itself begins to arise, which is occupied with two things: namely, the **Creator** and the **creature**. For it is impossible for a creature to know themselves perfectly in any other way than through their Creator. Nothing exists of itself: how can anyone be more certain of the effect before the cause? Does not every beginning precede its middle and its end, or shall anyone approach a matter from the end? 

But **God** is without beginning and end, existing by Himself from eternity, filled with all glory, which He did not wish to possess alone. Rather, by His sheer liberality, He determined to make us participants in His glory alongside Himself, and to create us in His image: the first exemplar of His liberality and a mystery that should not be unknown to us, nor...

### ON CHEMICAL PHILOSOPHY
->Compared to Meditative [Philosophy].<-

To begin with, the **spagyric Chaos** <note>original: "Chaos spagiricum"; the term 'spagyric' refers to the alchemical process of separating and recombining substances to achieve a higher state.</note> is a confusion of particular forms and their matters with their universal form and matter. This is indeed considered in various ways. First, as the confusion in the intellect of those men who do not understand this art. Second, as the confusion of the parts that constitute that extreme. Third, as the confusion by which all intermediate things relate confusedly to the extremes, and successively one to another in potentiality—as well as one to all, in any things within any things, and these existing in any whatever. Fourth, just as nature holds a middle ground between the elements and **elementated things** <term>elementated things<note>original: "elementata"; in natural philosophy, these are physical objects composed of the four elements—earth, air, fire, and water.</note></term>, so too in the art, the craftsman is considered a middle ground between chaos, the operations, and the perfect and most perfect medicine. From these four modes, it can easily be understood that the aforementioned medicines are brought from their potentiality into actuality by means of matter, form, heaven, and intermediate operations. For once motion is excited by the craftsman, chaos passes to the second extreme, which is the perfect medicine, and that to the most perfect, according to the order of the intermediates and their disposition toward one another.

To understand the matter more sharply: our Chaos is something universal, enclosing within itself everything we work upon. From its belly, the ingenious craftsman must draw out his matter, form, heaven, and elements, so that from these he may fashion the medicines that have been mentioned. **Spagyric matter** is indeed called the first and universal matter, or **Mercury** <term>Mercury<note>In alchemy, Mercury is not just the liquid metal, but the vital, fluid principle of life and transformation inherent in all things.</note></term> moving toward growth, and extracting the particular first matter of form from the shaper; it is considered in three ways. First, as a passive subject which, under the craftsman’s excitation, undergoes movement through the required means: from the operations of all these, heaven arises from its matter. Second, it is considered as any sick body that undergoes the form of the medicines, just as elementary things [undergo] a vegetable form. Third, as the matter of the shaper, like the first matter subjected to the actions of heaven; for otherwise it possesses the power of form, as [will be seen] below. By this reasoning, heaven—which becomes the subject for the actions of those forms by which it results in the white or red **tincture** <term>tincture<note>The "tincture" is the medicinal or transmuting agent; white for silver or lesser healing, red for gold or greater healing.</note></term>—can also be said to have the character of matter, since by its action it moves the said forms of the shapers toward the perfect or most perfect medicines, which will also be heard more extensively below. From this, the best knowledge of our chaos is obtained, because one and the same substance, though by different reasonings, relates to another substance passively, and to that same substance actively, and vice versa. Very few until now have had knowledge of the spagyric matter from which the spagyric heaven arises. For one must have a regard for the simple,

The **Form** of things, however, is a generative power by which each thing is able to produce its own likeness—just as the form of a human lies hidden within a human and not in another, and the form of a tree in a tree, and likewise the form of a metal in a metal. Raw materials <note>The original contains a small mark here, likely an alchemical symbol or a smudge, before the word "work."</note> must not enter the work, but must be cleared out through **sublimation** <note>original: "sublimationem"; the process of heating a substance into vapor to purify it from "superfluous earth."</note> to the sides of the subliming vessel, so that the matter may be free from its empty and redundant earth. 

In this work, Form is considered in two ways. First, as the directing cause of the means of this art through the intellect; by this governance, perfect and most perfect medicines come into the light. These are brought forth in the manner of intellectual intermediates, which are like certain sensory instruments by which the craftsmanship is led to perfection. The craftsman of this work is said to be of a "similar form." From this, it is clear that the causative means have the greatest harmony with natural things.

Alternatively, we consider Form as the agent that shapes the matter toward the perfection of the **White** or the **Red** <note>original: "ad album, vel ad rubeum"; these refer to the *albedo* (whiteness) and *rubedo* (redness), the final stages of the alchemical Great Work.</note>. By its power, these medicines transmute any other external forms of lesser capacity into their own likeness. However, these two forms we have mentioned cannot fulfill the mastery on their own; rather, they are like the male from whom the seed is cast into the belly and the **womb of our heaven**.

Furthermore, **Heaven** is our **Mercury**, which is of a celestial color <note>The "Mercury of the Philosophers" was often described as having a blue or "sky-colored" hue, signifying its spiritual purity.</note>. This signifies that it is of a heavenly nature, and for this reason—due to its incorruptibility—it is called "intellectual." It is understood in the same way as the physical heaven, acting like a human who is both sensory and intellectual. For it possesses within itself the property of an incorruptible spirit, which is like a soul holding the conditions of a body, since it generates and produces seed from it like a female. In this way, this work differs from other "masteries" <note>original: "magisterijs"; refers to other chemical or medicinal processes.</note> that enter the art. 

And because it is perceived by the senses, Mercury is called "sensory." This Mercury, as a moving cause, draws out the potential existing in the form of either shaping agent into the actual **Red** or **White**. It carries this potential in its womb no differently than a wife carries an infant conceived by her husband. From this, it can be gathered that our "heaven" acts upon both forms, and within this heaven, there is a hidden power to bring all things from potentiality into manifest act. 

For within it consists the power of both generating and nourishing, just as the masculine seed is found in the menstrual blood of the female. For this reason, it is called the **menstruum** <term>menstruum<note>original: "menstruum"; in alchemy, this refers to a solvent that dissolves and "nourishes" the seed of the Stone, compared to the blood that nourishes an embryo in the womb.</note></term> in this art, and "heaven" by reason of its motion. Indeed, just as the heaven above promotes the universal form, prime matter, the elements, and the species composed of those elements, our "heaven" also moves our forms toward the four elements, and eventually toward the perfect and more-than-perfect medicine. Sometimes it is called **blood**, because it is nutritive; it causes the aforementioned forms to vegetate and grow until they reach their perfection, just as menstrual blood nourishes an embryo from a small...

...from a seed into a great quantity, while the distinction of individual parts is preserved, through the nourishment and alteration of any medium into another quantity or form (these mediums and qualities existing in every alteration), into forms different from the first, until some being arises, joined in continuous quantity, formed from various and discrete parts into one body, living with soul and spirit. It happens no differently with the **spagyric offspring** <note>original: "spagirico fœtu"; the alchemical product or "child" created in the laboratory</note>, which is generated from "heaven" <note>original: "cœlo"; in alchemy, this often refers to the quintessence or the volatile, celestial part of the matter</note> possessing a vegetative property. It transfers a likeness of itself into the perfect and more-than-perfect medicine, just as a vegetative womb <note>original: "matrix"</note> does for the son whom she conceives and bears; she also retains this property as his parent. Likewise, the perfect and more-than-perfect medicines retain the property of their parents—namely, of heaven and the elements—and they transfer this likeness of their perfection into external substances and transmute them into their own species. For this reason, **Vegetable Mercury** <term>Mercurius vegetabilis: Not necessarily related to plants, this refers to the refined "spirit" or "life-force" of a substance that allows it to "grow" or transmute other things.</term> is said to be born from two substances, just as from a woman receiving the male seed, taking on another form and a different virtue than it had before the start of conception. From the male seed, the elements are reckoned in this art as four appearing colors; likewise, they are also considered in four other ways. First, as they are broken off from "heaven" in the matter. Second, as the simple elements of heaven are separated from the thicker elements by the circle of rotation. Third, as they exist naturally in forms and are joined with heaven. Fourth, as they are separated from form and heaven through the mediums of alteration, mixing, dissolution, and generation, by the mastery of separating their qualities; from these stated parts, only the "airy" part is taken and enriched through the artifice of rotation, and thus it is mixed with the forms into heaven. It must be noted, therefore, that the elements can be drawn out of forms through heaven before the union, so that their primary matter or heaven—approaching more closely to the most general genus—may be obtained, etc.

**Dissolution** is the spagyric knowledge, or the "intercourse" <note>original: "coitus"; alchemists often described the chemical union of substances using the metaphor of human reproduction</note> of the male with the female, and the female conceiving from the male everything that she ought to conceive. Let this be the beginning of particular generation, by which the effect of our spagyric marriage is perceived through the senses, and the union of the double seed <note>The Latin text reads "feminis," likely a typo for "seminis" (seed), given the context of the embryo.</note> into an embryo.

**Alteration** is the conversion of one thing into another through likeness. It is considered in two ways according to a twofold operation, insofar as it happens by itself. In the first way, forms are altered into heaven, and heaven into forms. In the second way, it is understood that forms and heaven are so simply converted that they can be turned into a third number—namely, into the perfect and more-than-perfect medicine. These alterations or conversions are called "simple." Others are found which occur "by accident," such as when the perfect medicine is made from imperfect things through **projection** <note>original: "projectionem"; the final stage of the Great Work, where the Philosopher's Stone is "projected" or cast upon base metals to transform them into gold or silver</note>, alteration, and transmutation.

### CHEMISTRY ###

<sig>Dd 3</sig>

**Mixture** occurs from two colors, pale yellow and azure blue, so that from these it may be recognized that the **Forms** and the "heaven" <note>original: "cœlum"; in alchemy, the refined, volatile medium or the "quintessence" that acts as a container for the work.</note> are combined in the **Great Work** without any external additive. Just as in the generation of a human being nothing else is mixed in but the man, the woman, or their seeds, in this place a "marriage" takes place between the forms and heaven. Another mixture also occurs, in which air and fire—acting as mediums for alteration, mixture, dissolution, and generation for both the forms and the heaven—are blended with the matter of heaven and the forms.

**Digestion** <term>Digestio: A process of slow, steady heat that mimics the incubation of an egg or the development of a fetus in the womb.</term> is called the nourishment of the seed conceived by the seed; it is by this means that the "perfect medicine" and the "more-than-perfect medicine" arise. For it is necessary that the forms be digested within the heaven for so long until the "prior medicine" is reached, and thereafter, when it seems right to the craftsman, until the "second perfection" is achieved.

From this it can be gathered that digestion is twofold: the first, by which the transition from the forms and heaven to the **perfect medicine** occurs; and the second, by which one must pass from this medicine and heaven to the **more-than-perfect**. Along this path, other necessary mediums are required, not unlike the earlier ones—namely mixture, alteration, dissolution, generation, and operation—except that something more imperfect arises from the first stages than from the later ones. But as soon as a saffron-yellow color <note>original: "croceus color"</note> appears through digestion, it denotes the "forms"; azure blue, however, denotes our "heaven." Those colors that fall between them designate the medium of the union of heaven with the forms, connecting that union to the perfect medicine, or connecting the forms to the most perfect medicine.

**Generation** <term>Generatio: The stage where the "hidden" potential of the matter becomes a "manifest" or visible reality.</term> is considered in various ways. Generally, it is the manifestation of hidden forms. In the first way, it is considered as the step generating the perfect medicine from heaven and forms. In the second way, insofar as it generates the "most perfect" from the "perfect" and heaven. In the third way, when it begins from dissolution and passes through alteration and digestion to the perfect medicine and makes its limit there, reaching the end of the "lesser perfection." Or indeed, when passing from there, it acquires the final degree of the "greater perfection." In this latter stage, it can easily be perceived that the **Mastery** <note>original: "magisterium"; the completion of the alchemical process.</note> of the greater perfection is promoted by nature rather than by artifice; nevertheless, it is stirred up by artifice in the lesser perfection, where artifice was more useful than nature. In the later Mastery, generation happens no differently than a fetus in a womb, or a bird in an egg; for which reason it is called, in its own way, the **Philosophers' Egg**. This artifice can in no way be better understood than by the fact that it results from the mixture of matter with forms to create precious stones—rubies, sapphires, and pearls <note>original: "uniones"; large, singular pearls of great value.</note>—which are in the womb of our philosophical heaven, through the mediation of generation with the same virtues that natural stones receive from nature. It follows, then, that this "heaven" can attract all the virtues existing in stones, by virtue of its unity or its magnetic simplicity. In this way, you, the ingenious craftsman, will be able to [draw out] <note>catchword: "elicere"; the text continues on the next page.</note> virtues from natural bodies...

**Dissolution** is the hiding of the visible form of the aforementioned bodies—not on its own, but by means of the said "key," which is highly compatible with the bodies. Just as we see water being destroyed by fire through the medium of air, without which it would not rise in vapors. It differs from "greater dissolution" in that in this case, only the forms and the less perfect things are resolved, whereas in the former, any metallic bodies are.

**Evacuation** is nothing other than the extraction of hidden spirits from their bodies, so that one of the two forms—the informing oils—may be shaped, and in this way, through fermentation and inceration <term>Inceratio: The process of adding liquid to a dry substance until it reaches a waxy (cereous) consistency.</term>, they may pass into the **perfect work**. What is drawn from the aforementioned bodies by this operation is the matter from which our perfect work must be led from potential into actualization, using the mediums and operations already mentioned.

**Multiplication** is nothing other than the repetition and continuation of evacuations. Through this operation, we provoke the six bodies <note>Refers to the six base metals: lead, tin, iron, copper, mercury, and silver (relative to gold).</note> to the point of nausea, forcing them to vomit our "offspring" <note>original: "fœtum"; the developing alchemical product or the Stone.</note> from their entrails.

**Spirit** is "exuberated" quicksilver <note>original: "argentum vivum exuberatum"; mercury that has been refined or heightened in its energetic potency.</note>, and it is the spirit of the bodies, already separated by a complete evacuation.

**Sulfur of Nature** is the spirit of the bodies exalted through sublimation into a most excellent salt of four colors: namely, pale, green, black, and red. This last color denotes fire, and through this color, the transition is made to the Sulfur of Nature, which arises from exuberated quicksilver. This indicates that it takes its origin from its own spirits, as well as from the multiplication that proceeds from evacuation—and that from dissolution, and that in turn from calcination, which comes from all bodies. This Sulfur is the "son" born from the imperfect things, prepared to put on white and purple garments <note>A reference to the *albedo* (whitening) and *rubedo* (reddening) stages of the Great Work.</note>. He differs from the "son" who is generated from the perfect things through the oil in which the forms of the imperfect sons are contained; likewise, because their sulfur belongs to nature, while the sulfur of others is receptive to moisture because it is dry.

**Tinctures** are the colors appearing in the work in various ways: first, green and saffron-yellow; second, red and saffron-yellow, green and black. First, the colors denote the tincture itself, by which the Sulfur of Nature must be tinged, taking its origin from the Sun <note>Gold.</note> and Moon <note>Silver.</note> through the artifice of the operations set down above. Others, however, signify that the sulfurs of any imperfect bodies must put on those colors, so that from them an offspring may be made, having and possessing the power of its parents from whom it took its origin. The third level of meditative philosophy is called **philosophical love**, produced from knowledge; it is the union of secrets from the one back into the one through peace. Indeed, the "peace of parts" is the harmony within the whole through union. God loves union above all, because He is one, and whatever He ever created, He enclosed under union. From one definite thing made through one indefinite thing, all things proceed that are finite, and again each thing tends toward that "one" by natural instinct. If any should deviate from this, they are judged by philosophers to be held under the **secret of the binary** <note>original: "secreto binario"; referring to the state of duality, division, or opposition, which was often viewed as unstable or imperfect.</note>, and they must be led back to union through the **ternary** <note>original: "ternarium"; the number three, representing the resolution of duality into a new, stable whole.</note>. God created heaven and earth, and all things that are in them, united together in a hidden way, but separated in a manifest way. There is also a particular and reciprocal love of parents toward their children, and children toward parents, which can by no means be compared to philosophical love. For what father for his son, or son for his father, what brother, sister, or friend would be willing to suffer the loss of even the smallest joint of his body? Who is he that would even willingly undergo a deserved death for himself, much less endure it patiently for another? Where, then, is love to be sought? Certainly nowhere else than from whence it proceeded: *For God so loved the world* <note>original: "Sic DEUS dilexit mundum"; quoting John 3:16</note>—meaning humanity—that He willed His own son to be born as a man, who could die for us impious men, and by his death pay the debt of death to the justice of **God**, which we were bound to suffer. For the Son of God could not die, but having been made man, he died as a perfect man, the **Son of Man**, and he alone, being just, fulfilled justice. O, the admirable love of God toward men! Not from worldly wisdom do such happy waters flow, which we—wretched mortals!—pass by while the vain fictions of human studies hold us back. This **divine love** calls our souls to another philosophy, by which, through constant **meditation** on the blessings of God toward us, our soul is joined to the warnings of the divine spirit, so as to acquiesce to them. ### CHEMISTRY.

There is a natural love among the primary parts of inanimate things, and an enmity, just as there is in the three principal parts of man mentioned before. But in those, no more than in these, a true union cannot occur unless corruption is first removed. Therefore, it is necessary that you make peace among enemies, so that friends may come together into one. In all imperfect bodies, and those falling short of their ultimate perfection, enmity and friendship are likewise innate together. If enmity is removed by human wit or industry, it is necessary to arrive at the ultimate perfection of union through art. You shall therefore separate by fire the parts from each body; cleanse the impure ones; afterwards mix pure things with pure, and having first sublimated the heavier things with the lighter, it will happen by this very process that the fixed is made volatile, and the corporeal [made] spiritual. In short, a philosophically natural love exists within the elements; you should embrace this by art if you truly desire to be a Physician <note>original: "Phyſicus"; here meaning a Natural Philosopher or student of nature</note> and not a neglecter of nature, or rather its destroyer.

As we have heard that concord is necessary in supernatural and natural things, in <term>spagyrics: the alchemical art of separating and recombining substances to find their pure essence</term> matters there is also a certain admirable coherence to be observed among the mediating instruments, such as that of intellectual things with sensory things. For the form sometimes represents the person of the artisan existing as an instrument, by which nature generates the particular <term>spagyric egg: a symbolic vessel or the "seed" of the alchemical work</term> out of the intellect, although it must be distinguished from our form (which we otherwise call heaven); nevertheless, one cannot persist without the other in the <term>spagyric</term> art. For the "heaven" form is the principle and sensory medium that generates, nourishes, and causes things to grow or vegetate, moving the elements toward a particular generation—just as the greater heaven [the cosmos] moves the lower things—and from the forming form, which it acquires through the vegetable form and holds joined and bound by an indissoluble knot, it causes the particular sought-after thing to multiply in extrinsic substances. Thus it is with many other hidden things in the progress of the art, possible for the artisan to know and effect.

But the form which is the human intellect is the beginning, middle, and end in preparations: and this is denoted by a saffron <note>original: "croceo"; a yellow-gold color often associated with the sun or the soul in alchemy</note> color, by which it is indicated that man is the greater and principal form in the <term>spagyric</term> work, and a form more powerful than heaven. The remaining forms are lesser than these, and of lesser perfection. Likewise, the equalized mixture of the saffron color with green [indicates] the existence of a greater or lesser concord concerning contrariety in the equality of the ultimate end. For one of the three forms cannot be absent without all failing at once. For if heaven were lacking, the generation of the elements would fail, and there would follow a deprivation of both lesser and greater perfection. Therefore the intellectual form, with the vegetable form and the form of motion, must be so joined by the intellect that one is conditioned by the other: thus it goes for the remaining levels and mediums up to the most perfect. The form which is called "motive" [moving] is a certain universal principle in the levels...

# PHILOSOPHY

<meta>catchword: matured [matus, likely completing 'formatus' or 'formatio']</meta>

of this art, moving each one through all the steps to the next, right up to the very last and the end of the work. Therefore, the motion of the form can be called a motion that awakens all things according to the order of their steps, until perfection is reached. Indeed, form and matter are substantial principles much greater than accidental ones; for those are merely changes in the work, such as colors, alteration, digestion, and so on. The truth of this business is demonstrated more through the lesser and greater degrees of perfection—by the immensity of their transforming power—than by accidental steps. Nevertheless, the beginning, the middle, and the end which have been mentioned are equal, because of the similarity of that same end toward which all things tend, as if through a marvelous chain. However, so that we may have a greater understanding of what has been said, we must necessarily come to the universal practice of this art.

Pour such a quantity of <term>spagyric heaven: the refined, volatile spirit or solvent used in alchemy</term> over either of the forms so that it stands four finger-breadths <note>a traditional measurement of depth, roughly 3 inches</note> above it. Let all this be kept placed in <term>dung: a common alchemical method for providing gentle, steady heat through the fermentation of manure</term> for six natural days, or until the form is converted into water. Afterward, having removed the vessel and placed it in ashes <note>a "sand bath" or ash heat, providing a more intense heat than dung</note>, let that which was dissolved be drawn off by distillation. To the dregs, pour as much of the "heaven" as before, and let them be kept together in dung for a month and a half, or longer, in <term>putrefaction: the breaking down of matter through warmth and moisture to release its essence</term>; finally, let all the liquid be distilled in a secret furnace until it can no longer drip.

Next, let a water thicker than the previous one be distilled in ashes, which they call "air." Again, pour as much "heaven" as before onto the nearly dry dregs, let it putrefy in dung for the same amount of time as before, and let it be distilled through ashes into "air" until it will drip no more. Afterward, let the pouring of the "heaven" upon the "earth" <note>the solid residue or 'feces' remaining in the vessel</note> be repeated like rain, with the same weight and for the same time as above; after it has putrefied in dung, let it be distilled again through ashes until no more "air" comes out. Finally, pour the whole quantity of this "air" onto the dregs—or first grind them thoroughly upon a marble stone—and in a closed vessel, for forty days from the putrefied material, let both "air" and "fire" <note>the most refined and volatile part of the substance</note> be distilled together in ashes; meanwhile, one must take care lest the dregs be turned red by a more violent fire before the proper time.

Then you shall separate the "air" from the "fire" by means of dung, and if the heat of a <term>bath: a water-bath or balneum Mariae</term> is not sufficient, the slow heat of ashes will supply it; let each be kept separately. Then pour the "air" back onto its "earth," and having digested them in dung for fifteen days, you shall distill both "air" and "fire" from there together through ashes, and you shall separate them as above by means of the bath, storing each with its like. Repeat these pourings, <term>inhumations: the act of burying the vessel in dung or earth to maintain heat</term>, and distillations as many times as necessary until no more "fire" comes forth from the earth, and it becomes black or reddish. Finally, from the "air" digested in the dung-bath for eight days, distill whatever is able to rise by that same heat; pour this distilled liquid back onto its dregs, digest as before and distill, pour back again, digest, distill, and so on, repeating the same process seven times. Thus far the for— <note>original: "for-"; the text cuts off here and continues on the next page</note>

# CHEMISTRY

...formed is a triangle out of air, <term>heaven: the volatile spirit or refined solvent</term>, and <term>dung: a source of gentle, steady heat from fermenting manure</term>, in the middle of which is the **soul of air**. With the operations in dung having been performed previously, you will be able to convert fire into the **soul of fire**, and to form another triangle out of heaven, dung, and fire. With all these things accomplished, the **elemental wheel** is finished by fixation, and by their abundance of air and fire through <term>corruption: the alchemical process of breaking down a substance to its base state</term>. 

Afterward, once the earth has been evacuated until it is deserted and converted into the **sulfur of nature**, let a triangle be formed out of earth, dung, and <term>ashes: a sand or ash bath providing moderate heat</term>, in the middle of which will stand the **soul of earth**. Nor is the wheel of corruption finished before this, whose instruments are heaven, dung, the **secret furnace**, the heat of ashes, etc. 

Now at last one must proceed to the **wheel of generation**. So that you may make the composite out of fire and air for the "sun" <note>original: "ad solem" — meaning the creation of gold</note>, take four parts of fire and mix them with fifteen parts of air; once digested together for fifteen days, let them be distilled by means of dung. You shall repeat this digestion and distillation as many times as necessary until there remains at the bottom of the vessel a liquid like a **shining oil**, which is the composite of air and fire, and is called **slime** <note>original: "limus"</note>. 

By the same process, you shall also convert fire and earth into their own composite, so that a double triangle may now be formed: the first out of fire, air, dung, and ashes, in the middle of which the composite of fire and air will thrive; the latter out of fire, earth, dung, and ashes, in the middle of which will stand the composite of earth and fire.

Now finally, take one part of the composite of fire and air, to which you will mix a sixth part of heaven, and keep it in digestion for thirty days: in this way you will have formed a triangle out of heaven, the composite of fire and air, and dung, in the middle of which this **greater perfect thing** is found, transforming toward the **red** <note>The "Red Work" or Rubedo, the final stage of the Great Work resulting in gold</note>, taking its rise and origin from heaven, and from the composite of fire and air, and from dung. 

When you have done this same thing with the composite of fire and earth—by joining to it one and a half parts of heaven—you will have another triangle out of heaven, the composite of earth and fire, and dung, in the middle of which will stand the **lesser perfect thing**, transmuting toward the **white** <note>The "White Work" or Albedo, the stage resulting in silver</note>, etc. 

If, however, you do not wish to mix in the "heaven," in order to avoid the immense labor, you shall <term>cerate: to soften a hard substance until it has the consistency of wax</term> the elements with the composites previously given until they flow like wax. Keep this waxed material in digestion for ten days; afterward, once extracted, you shall cerate it again as before, with the liquid injected drop by drop, until you perceive in it an easy liquefaction. Keep this matter in a <term>philosophical vessel: a specialized glass flask, often called a Pelican or a Bolt-head</term> sealed as well as possible in the secret furnace for one hundred and fifty or more days, until you see the work completed according to the signs described below. 

This process is the best in the **greater practice** <note>The pursuit of the Philosopher's Stone</note>, using the method of the **minor work**. Note that the creation can also be done with fire and air separately before the creation of the slime, while they are not yet reduced into one. Thus far the wheel of generation is completed, through which the artisan acquires the desired result, God granting it. From these two "slimes," various things can be done in the <term>spagyric: the Paracelsian art of separating and recombining the components of substances</term> work, according to its breadth, as first in the royal practice, and in the ceration...

# PHILOSOPHY

...by the craft of its own leafy earth <note>original: "terra foliata" — a purified salt or crystalline substance that appears in thin layers or "leaves"</note>, or of the elements, by first waxing it with air and fire, or with the aforementioned slimes made from air and fire: in which craft the wheel of generation reaches its final end, the sign of which is the red triangle within us. The beginning of the work, therefore, is corruption <note>the breakdown of the initial substance</note>, and the end is generation; through these operations, one quality is corrupted and another is introduced through generation, such as by corrupting water and generating earth. This is done by hiding the earth and making fire and air manifest, until the greater and lesser perfection arise through their intermediaries, which are the heats of dung, of ashes, and of the secret furnace <note>different levels of heat: dung is gentle, ashes moderate, and the furnace intense</note>, by which water is converted into earth, and this into air and fire.

Earth is therefore the medium between water, fire, and air; and dung, ashes, and the secret furnace exist as the medium through which fire and air are converted into the **soul of fire** and **soul of air**. On this account, fire and air are the medium between earth itself, the soul of fire, and the soul of air. Then, dung, ashes, the secret furnace, and heaven <note>referring to the volatile spirit or the highest heat source</note> are the medium through which the soul of fire and the soul of air are converted into the composite of fire and air, and into the composite of earth and fire. For this reason, heaven is the medium between the soul of fire, the soul of air, the composite of air and fire, and the composite of fire and earth. Likewise, dung, ashes, and the secret furnace are the medium through which the composite of fire and air, as well as the composite of earth and fire, are joined to the elements. Similarly, the composite of fire and air, and the composite of fire and earth, are the medium between the soul of fire, the soul of air, and the lesser and greater perfection.

After hearing about the universal practice of the greater **spagyric** <term>spagyric: the alchemical art of "separating and recombining" substances to purify them</term> work, let us come also to a certain general practice of the lesser work. Cast a metallic body into the spagyric key <note>original: "clavem spagiricam" — a powerful solvent, often an acid or "menstruum," used to open the metal</note>, and allow the contents in their vessel to be digested together for one week at the heat of the first degree, or of dung. But before it is cast into the key, it must be reduced to a **calx** <term>calx: a crumbly powder produced by roasting a metal, effectively "killing" its metallic form so it can be reborn</term>, so that the body may be better dissolved and evacuated by means of the key, and by the heat of the first degree from the triangle according to the natural order. 

Once the dissolution of the body is accomplished, let the vessel be set for distillation at the same heat; it will lose the key and be reduced into earth. Allow this earth, having been very well ground upon a marble stone, to be resolved into water by itself. Where the earth is too dry, let it be sprinkled with a little of the key, and after three days it will begin to be resolved into a composite water containing the four elements. Distill this water through a filter, and whatever remains undissolved, let it be dissolved again as before and filtered; do this repeatedly until a sufficiently good quantity of water is obtained. By this operation, the "triangle of evacuation" will have been completed, in the middle of which is the earth, which must drink up its own water as follows: Keep the filtered water in the heat of the first degree for digestion, and it will cast out the key entirely and be converted into small stones, which are not yet the **elixir** <term>elixir: the perfected substance or "medicine" capable of transforming base metals or healing the body</term>. With the aforesaid evacuation, another triangle is completed from the water...

# CHEMISTRY

...with heat of the first degree <note>original: "calore primi gradus" — the gentlest level of heat, often compared to the warmth of the sun or a nesting bird</note>, and with the key, in the middle of which the aforementioned stones exist. Keep them, once crushed into a very fine powder, in a state of putrefaction <note>the process of breaking down a substance to its base components through moisture and gentle heat</note>, until they are converted into a water or a metallic oil, in which the four elements are present. Divide the qualities of these elements as you have heard. Once they are divided, purify the earth, or render it most subtle through the proper sublimations <note>the process of heating a solid until it becomes a vapor and then solidifies again in a purer state</note>; then, finally, let the earth imbibe the elements: first with celestial water, then with aerial water, and lastly with fiery water, as is the custom of the art, and let them be boiled down to the perfection you have heard. Following this process, the extreme principles and the intermediaries of this art are applied to whatever spagyric <term>Spagyric: A term for alchemy focused on separating components and then recombining them to create medicines or purified materials</term> work you desire.

Now that the third step of the spagyric scale is completed—which is called **philosophical love** <note>original: "amor philosophicus" — likely referring to the affinity between substances or the spiritual devotion of the alchemist</note>—we reach the fourth step of the meditative scale, which is called **frequency** <note>or "constancy"</note>, and the perseverance of the love conceived toward the truth. For there is no other path to the virtues than through diligence. If the earth is not diligently cleared of the tares <note>original: "lolio" — a common weed that grows among grain</note> that it produces of its own accord, instead of sweet herbs and flowers, it will produce nothing for us but thistles and nettles.

It is no different regarding the natural man or his bodily soul. For this reason, it [the soul] was given to us as a colony <note>original: "coloniam" — a territory or garden to be cultivated</note>. Whatever grows in it beyond the divine sowing once made in the past must be uprooted. We can tame it no better than by first removing gluttony <note>original: "crapulam" — excess in food or drink</note> itself, which induces sleepiness and laziness. We shall also remove idleness, so that the most powerful root of vices may wither within us. Let nothing be granted to the body beyond necessity, for whatever is superabundant will grow into a vice. The soul that neglects to correct its body will find things go poorly for itself because of it; for reason was given to the soul in the first place to be turned to its proper uses, which is the true knowledge of God.

The soul is, therefore, like a tutor <note>original: "pædagogus"</note> to its body; if it does not correct the pupil, it shall be punished along with him without mercy. Not foreign to the care of gardens is the discipline that must be maintained with a double effort: first, by uprooting the useless weeds that grow over the good ones so they do not stifle their growth; and likewise, by casting out evil thoughts, enmities, and other things of that kind from the soul, and by restraining the body from every evil work. It is not fitting for a teacher to teach one thing and do another different from his own instruction. If he provides the occasion for sinning to his pupil by his own example, why should he rebuke him?

The body contemplates nothing, but the soul carries out the silent operations of the imagination, which the body then attempts to execute in imitation of that model. For conception belongs to the soul, but execution belongs to the body. Let us see to it, then, that we do not ascribe more to the body than it is capable of. Although the body itself is more prone to executing the soul's wicked conceptions and takes more delight in them than in good ones, if we substitute good thoughts in place of those rejected ones, the body will be able to work nothing but good, or at least desist from all evil. This is one method of conquering the body; now hear the other.

In no different way must the body and soul be irrigated with living water <note>original: "aqua viva" — a biblical reference to spiritual life and the Holy Spirit</note>, which is the Word of God. This must be meditated upon day and night, and besides this, nothing but what is good, so that even the body may be able to speak and do nothing other than that very thing. We see, therefore, that the body and soul can be very well compared to gardens and fields. As Christ says in the Gospel, the good seed that falls into well-cultivated earth brings forth good fruit. In the same way, the Word of God that falls upon a soft and contrite heart will make the body fertile for the richest fruit unto eternal life. It is certain that, from the time of the first fall <note>referring to the Fall of Man in Genesis</note> until this day, the hearts of men have always been hardened; unless they are softened by the Word of God, they remain hard. Pharaoh’s heart was hard from his mother's womb (as are the hearts of all men), and because it was not softened by the Word of God, it became and remained hardened. We are all born rebellious and enemies to God, and we remain so until this enmity is rooted out by the Supreme Farmer <note>original: "summum agricolam" — God as the metaphorical gardener of the soul</note>, whose minister you, O Mind, must be. You have the seed, the field, and the water; nothing more is lacking to you but assiduous, uninterrupted labor. You must never cease to revolve in your thoughts those things which you have already heard and will hear; otherwise, through neglect, you will give an opening to your enemy. It should be noted at this point that the mind is first united in love by the Spirit of the Lord and the soul, in which it thereafter makes its dwelling; moved by the guidance of that same Spirit, it is strengthened to move the body further.

This should be understood in no different way in the spagyric art <term>Spagyric: The branch of alchemy focused on the separation and recombination of natural substances to create potent medicines</term>. For it is impossible for any craftsman to become prompt or fit in this art except through frequency and the assiduousness of work, by which he acquires a habit. For just as in meditative philosophy, through the frequent "rumination" <note>original: "ruminatione" — literally "chewing the cud," meaning to deeply and repeatedly contemplate information</note> of those things which we have learned and loved through study, we attain three things: namely, familiarity with that which we love, likeness to it, and communion with it. These three seem to coincide almost as one. For through familiarity, we are rendered similar in both will and character to that with which we are familiar, so that we even share in its individual actions and desires. Likewise, in any art, we are made ready through frequent use, rendered skillful by ease of habit, and find delight through assiduousness. What does it profit someone wishing to learn the art of baking <note>original: "pistoriam artem"</note> to have merely seen a baker working very often, unless he himself, putting his hand into the dough, repeats the work so many times until, having become a practiced and ready baker, he is able to teach others the art he professes? # CHEMICAL STUDIES

...mind, body, and the age of men, it is granted to only one among hundreds of myriads to conquer—that is, to reach the perfect goal of the art. Yet, some secrets of nature and certain mysteries can be uncovered through the greatest study and labor; these serve the <term>medical art</term> <note>original: "rem medicam"</note> far better than any other discovery made outside of this aforementioned art.

But truly, to find that **universal medicine** <note>The "Panacea" or Philosopher's Stone, believed to cure all diseases and perfect all matter.</note> mentioned above has happened to very few—indeed, almost none—to this day, and then only as a miracle. It happens only to those who have first been able to lead themselves back, by the grace of a merciful God, into the very likeness of that which they desire: that is, those who have purged their bodies of impurity through the mind, and have finally cast away all the clouds of the mind and body alike.

I urge all investigators of this art to pray to God continually, to study, and to work; it cannot be that they will fail to achieve what they ask in the name of Jesus from the **Giver of Lights**. But first, let them consider what it means to "ask the Father in the Son": it is nothing other than to demand only that which is for the glory of the Father and the Son. Many are accustomed to wishing for what seems useful to themselves, but they receive nothing from God except what is truly useful. God aids diligent and frequent efforts, and He despises the negligent. Let us therefore love the good in such a way that we do not crave the evil.

It remains for us to pass over to <term>spagyric frequency</term> <note>from the Greek "spao" (to tear apart) and "ageiro" (to gather); the alchemical process of separation and recombination. "Frequency" here refers to the repeated cycles of the work.</note> in this manner: namely, that we ruminate upon those things said above. When Nature corrupts an individual thing, she first makes it putrefy; afterward, she separates from it the "composite elements" that are most closely within it; then she brings each of these to a state of ultimate simplicity; and finally, she returns them to their <term>first matter</term> <note>original: "materia prima" — the formless, primal substance of the universe.</note>. Once this is done, the **wheel of corruption** is complete.

From this first matter, the **wheel of generation** takes its beginning, passing back toward the simple elements. Finally, through the mixing of these, the composite elements arise, from which the "elemented subject" is made according to its own species and form, under which the elements are drawn into the composition of the individual.

The spagyric artist must observe this process so that, where Nature finishes, he himself begins—through the rotation of corruption—in a **backward step**. That is, he moves from the end, through the middle, toward the beginning of the wheel of corruption, employing the means of:
*   **Calcination** <note>Burning a substance to ash to remove impurities.</note>
*   **Dissolution**
*   **Putrefaction**
*   **Division**
*   **Purification**, etc.

Next, one must come to the **wheel of generation**, the means of which are **mixing**, **inceration** <note>original: "inceratio" — processing a substance until it has the consistency of wax.</note>, and **decoction** <note>Boiling or heating.</note>. When these are perfectly arranged, they are the instruments of the **spagyric offspring** <note>The final product or "child" of the alchemical work.</note>. Once these are performed in this manner, the artist will have what he desires.

The **Form** of this work is considered in three ways:
1. As the First Cause.
2. As the Artist.
3. As any of the other intermediate means.

**Matter** is also considered in three ways:
1. As the subject from which the **Mercury of the Art** is drawn.
2. As the elements.
3. As the **Sulfur of Nature**.

### PHILOSOPHY

The **Heaven** <note>original: "Cælum"; in alchemy, this often refers to the "quintessence" or the volatile, spiritual medium within the chemical vessel that influences the material below.</note> also has a threefold consideration: First, as the **greater heaven**; Second, as **vegetable Mercury** <note>original: "Mercurius vegetabilis"; likely referring to a solvent or spirit derived from plant matter, such as alcohol, used to extract essences.</note>; Third, as the **soul of metals**.

The **Elements** are considered in two ways in this place: First, **simply**; second, **compositely**.

**Power** <note>original: "Potentia"</note> or **alteration** differs in as many ways as there are diverse means of operation.

**Mixture** <note>original: "Mixtio"</note> has a fourfold meaning: First, of the heaven with form; second, of air with water; third, of water with fire; fourth, of air with water and the heaven.

**Dissolution** has only one consideration, which is the relationship between the heaven and the forms.

**Generation** has a twofold meaning: the former by which the elements are generated; the latter by which the **spagyric offspring** <note>original: "fœtus spagiricus"; the resulting substance or "philosopher's stone" produced by the alchemical process.</note> is generated from these and the heaven.

**Colors** also have a twofold meaning: the former in the evacuation of bodies and the rectification <note>The process of purifying a liquid by repeated distillation.</note> of elements; the latter in the generation of the spagyric offspring.

The **lesser perfect** <note>Likely referring to base metals or incomplete alchemical stages.</note> has only one consideration, as is evident to the senses.

**Fermentation** has a threefold meaning: First from virtue <note>Inner power or quality.</note>; second from quantity; third from both together.

**Separation** also has a threefold operation: First indeed between the qualities of the elements; second, of their purification and fixation; third, of the vegetable Mercury and the dregs <note>original: "fæcum"; the solid residue left after distillation or filtration.</note>.

**Operation** has as many meanings as there are means existing in this art.

The **greater perfect** <note>Referring to the final, perfected goal of the art, such as gold or the universal medicine.</note> has a single consideration like the lesser, as is evident to the senses.

The principles and means of Philosophy are found in all the principles and means of this art—like the **movement of the sphere**, which must be considered as a form containing all natural instincts and appetites.

The most subtle and powerful means in the work is the **reiteration of the wheel of corruption of metals**, which occurs as follows: Once the forms have been placed in the heaven, buried, dissolved, and evacuated through the practice of the "brief art," until one arrives at the **sulfur of nature** <note>original: "sulphur naturæ"; the active, combustible, and masculine principle of matter in alchemical theory.</note> in the metals, then the wheel of corruption is finished.

**Reiteration** <note>The repetitive cycling of a process to increase purity.</note> occurs when the sublimated earth is placed in the heaven and is dissolved therein by putrefaction and division. After the air, fire, and water have been evacuated, let the craftsman lead the earth back again to its purest sublimation; once finished, the **wheel of generation** follows from there with its principles and means, until it is brought to its end. This operation is more subtle than others—though longer, it is nonetheless more perfect. By this path, the "lesser perfect"—which is the unfermented offspring—is converted into the "greater" and fermented spagyric offspring through the <meta>catchword: separation of the elements</meta>

# CHEMICA.

...their separation and composition, as noted below. Nature in no way permits the elements to be separated by themselves, for in that state each would remain alone, possessing only a single quality, and would have no appetite for generation <note>In alchemy, "generation" refers to the process of growth or the creation of a new substance.</note>, which is contrary to nature.

Therefore, the separation of the elements is the predominance and victory of one in and over another, within a state of mixture, not total division. The color of **fire** is red, and before its sphere is reached, one passes through the sphere of **air**. Before the redness appears, a clear and transparent **citrine** <note>A pale yellow or lemon-like color.</note> color appears, because it consists of fire mixed with air. Furthermore, before reaching the sphere of air, one must make the passage through the sphere of **water**; for this reason, a white color appears, watery and shining. But because **earth** is the center and the principle from which the ascent must begin, while the **spagyric offspring** <term>spagyric offspring: the resulting substance or "philosopher's stone" produced by the alchemical process</term> is still in its sphere, the black color proper to the earth appears in it. Note, therefore, the separation of these elements and their subsequent conjunction into one—that is, into fire. Likewise, if the red or white, or any other color, appears before the black color has appeared, believe for certain that the operation of the "offspring" has been ruined, due to the destruction of the intermediate steps.

A difference must likewise be noted between the **elixir** and the **stone**, based on the "raw" and the "cooked." For the elixir is a medicine composed of air, water, and earth; therefore, it leads only to the **white** <note>The "white work" or *albedo* produces silver, whereas the "red work" or *rubedo* produces gold.</note>. If the body, having been resolved into water, was red, it reflects the color of the most excellent **carbuncle** <note>A glowing red gemstone, often associated with the final stage of the alchemical Work.</note> when it has been converted into a composite of the soul of fire and air, and into a composite of earth and fire. But if it was white, it will bring forth a green color mixed with blackness.

Various errors are also to be noted by the practitioners. The first and most powerful consists in this: when they do not know how to **imitate nature**. The second is that they sometimes judge the beginning of the stone to be the end, and think they have finished where they have barely begun, as in the false opinion of the **red triangle**. For the composition of the **greater stone** lasts two years for those who have never composed it before; but for the expert, it takes a year and three months. There are some branches in the breadth of this art which are completed in four or six months; if the practitioner can find these, it is well indeed; if not, let him deplore the smallness of his own intellectual capacity, since they are described clearly enough everywhere. Now we must come to the greater differences.

**Form** is twofold: simple and composite. **Simple** is absolute unity and the singularity of its thing, consisting in itself and not with another. **Composite** is the union of its four primordial chambers.

**Matter** consists of the four elements: either simply, as signified by the first form, or compositely, as denoted by the latter.

The **vegetable menstruum** <term>menstruum: a solvent used in alchemy to extract essences or dissolve metals</term>, which is named the "heaven" or the "philosophical key," is of two kinds: one is **resolutive** <note>original: "resolutivum"; capable of dissolving or breaking down substances.</note>, but the other is **referable** <note>original: "referabile"; likely meaning it can bring back or restore the substance's properties.</note>.

# ->PHILOSOPHY<-

The **resolving agent** <note>original: *Resolutivum*; a substance used to dissolve or break down materials into their core elements</note> is something celestial; the other kind is not, but is rather more corporeal. The celestial type is the **fifth essence** <note>original: *essentia quinta*; the "quintessence" or purest, most concentrated spirit of a substance</note>, or that of tartar <note>original: *tartari*; a salty crust formed during wine fermentation, highly valued by alchemists as a source of "fire"</note>, from whose nature its own resolvable substance is brought into action. Alternatively, it is defined in this way: it is a **burning water** <note>original: *ardens aqua*; likely a highly distilled alcohol or "spirit of wine" or a strong mineral acid</note> perfectly rectified, by whose power any bodies are dissolved, putrefied, and rendered purer; their elements are separated and exalted into a **miraculous salt** <note>original: *sal mirabile*</note> and into earth, by the highly active power it possesses. Whoever thinks there is any other such water is ignorant and foolish. 

The **resolvable** <note>the material being dissolved</note> is a **solvent** <term>menstruum: a liquid used to dissolve a solid, named for the "menstrual" cycles of time often required for the process</term>, a potential vapor existing in any metallic body, joining sulfur and quicksilver, without which nothing is brought to completion. Finally, it is defined thus: it is the medium joining imperfect and perfect metals into the **stone** <note>The Philosopher's Stone</note>. 

This resolving solvent is hot up to the second point of the fourth degree: for this reason, its power must be increased with "hot" vegetables up to the final point of that same degree. These include:
*   **Wild celery** <note>original: *apium sylvestre*</note>
*   **Monkshood** <note>original: *napellus*</note>
*   **Oleander**
*   **Cashew** <note>original: *anacardus*; specifically the Malacca bean or marking nut</note>
*   **Black pepper**
*   **Pellitory** <note>original: *piretrum*; a root that causes a burning sensation</note>
*   **Euphorbia** <note>a plant with a caustic, milky sap</note>

Without these, it only dissolves over a long period of time. 

Thus far concerning the fourth degree of the meditative scale—namely, **frequency**—which works an intimacy, similarity, and communion of the soul with the divine spirit. We have spoken of the comparison made to it through diligence in the **spagyric work** <term>spagyric: the alchemical process of separating and then recombining substances to purify them</term>, which produces readiness and a physical ease with the highest delight. 

Now, however, we arrive at the **fifth degree**, which is **Virtue** <note>original: *Virtus*</note>; let us therefore hear of this. The virtue of things is both the center and the truth of each thing: the former is an effectiveness known through experience, while the latter is a celestial influence. Whatever does not come from heaven cannot be called a virtue, but rather an image of it, and often a false one. In ancient times, the Philosophers who were ignorant of God wished to depict virtue, but they did so falsely, because they did not understand His Son, in whom all the virtues of God are made manifest. Even their disciples divided "virtue" into Theological and Ethical parts, not considering that these latter virtues should in no way exist or be named as such, except insofar as they are from God. 

The **fortitude** of the Romans against their enemies was actually **stubbornness**; their **magnanimity** was **pride**; their **prudence** was **fraud and deceit**; and their **abstinence** from honors was **ambition**. So it was with the rest: they were vices rather than virtues, because they were performed not for the glory of God, but for the glory of men and for themselves. 

Christian Philosophers of every profession, however, hold only **Truth** as virtue, which they divide into **faith, hope, and charity**. Entire truth and every virtue consists of these three and in these alone; outside of them, there is nothing but falsehood. **Faith**, moreover, is the certainty of those things that are heard and not seen. For this reason, it was said by Paul that "faith comes from hearing," because that which is seen is not faith, but rather a certain knowledge demonstrated as if to the eye. We have the testimony of this matter in the Holy Scripture from the Gospel.

"You believed," Christ said, "because you saw: Blessed are those who have not seen and have believed." <note>original: *Credidisti (inquit Christus) quia vidisti: Beati qui non viderunt & crediderunt*; a reference to John 20:29</note> Hope is the stimulus of faith toward the certainty of future truth and firm constancy. Unless one knows for certain that he will acquire what he pursues, his effort grows quite cold; but when he has confirmed his hope through faith, and vice versa, aided finally by practice and natural talent, there is nothing he cannot achieve. Furthermore, it is certain that in this context faith is proven through **charity** <note>original: *charitatem*; here meaning selfless love or divine grace</note>, just as one can work well or poorly through a good or bad impulse. Charity, therefore, is faith perfected in action. Who should judge true faith other than the one in whom faith alone resides, and who says that it must be known by its works? Some, understanding this matter (as I believe), have said that charity must begin from oneself, which can be interpreted in this way: a Christian man must first acquire a habit of virtue within himself through the frequent practice of love toward God and his neighbor, before he is able to exercise it toward others in action. Therefore, learn, O mind, to work true charity within your own body by restraining its vain appetites—born of the evil one—within the soul; in this way, it will gradually result in your being ready for all good things.

In no different a way, a certain hidden truth exists in the center of natural things, which is not seen by external eyes but is first perceived by the mind alone. The philosophers have experienced this, and they discovered its power to be such that it performed certain miracles. Therefore, it is not surprising that men have performed miracles through faith, since even "senseless" <note>inanimate or unthinking objects</note> things are able to provide similar results through the virtue contributed to them by God. The **Art** <note>the practice of alchemy</note> consists chiefly in this: that the **spirit of things** be liberated from its bodily shackles, just as it was said above concerning man, that his mind must be made free from the body. Every object's body is therefore a prison in which the virtues of the soul of things are held and hindered, preventing their natural spirits from freely impressing their powers and actions upon it. Such is the spirit of these senseless things—and of the same efficacy according to the nature of the subject—as is unwavering faith in man. Thus, the true virtue of men is faith, and for all other things, it is the truth of their efficacy.

The **lodestone** <note>original: *magnes lapis*; a naturally magnetized piece of the mineral magnetite</note> teaches us that a specific virtue and heavenly influence resides in every thing, perceptible to the eyes only by its effect; in it, that magnetic or attractive force of iron is not seen, because the spirit is latent within it and does not fall under the senses. Wine also, both the common and the **philosophical** <note>original: *philosophicum*; "philosophical wine" refers to a highly refined alchemical substance rather than a beverage</note>, has various virtues within itself which have been brought to light through the experience of the Art, by means of **separation**. For its spirit warms and dries, but its body produces the exact opposite, for it moistens with a cooling effect, as can be seen from **burning water** <note>original: *aqua ardente*; distilled alcohol or spirit</note> and **vinegar** <note>original: *aceto*</note>. These faculties of one and the same natural compound are entirely contrary because of separation; before that, they were not so different, because they were then mixed by a natural...
