# 485 #

<center>WITH THE BODY.</center>

It remains in order for us to balance this through weights. We have said before that the order of creation consists of numbers, measure, and weight <note>original: "numeris, mensura, & pondere"; a reference to the Wisdom of Solomon 11:20, a foundational text for medieval and Renaissance science</note>. The two preceding elements we completed through the **unitary** and the **ternary** <note>the numbers one and three</note> alone, without the help of others. Now, let us also weigh out weights to infinity through these same numbers, which can be done by no others better nor more fitly. With only two weights—the first of one pound, the second of three—the balancing proceeds into infinite weights. Thus, one [pound] balanced by these: this and one, they weigh three or three pounds; this weight once, and once one, makes four; three once, and twice one, five; three twice, six weights; three twice and once one, seven; three twice, and twice one, eight; three thrice, nine; thrice three and once one, ten; thrice three and once one, eleven; three four times, twelve; and so on into many thousands of thousands. But if someone wishes to do this with less effort, let him fashion for himself three other odd weights from the **quinary, septenary, and novenary** <note>the numbers five, seven, and nine</note>; or let him add weighted matter to weighted matter as an increase whenever it shall seem expedient. But truly, **spagyric** <term>spagyric</term> <note>the alchemical art of "separating and recombining" elements to reach a state of purity</note> weights remain in unity, and they have no progress toward increase except through unity, like that of a single center toward its first monarchy and circumference—namely, the **denary** <note>the number ten</note>; and from that same center to the second unity, a hundred; to the third, a thousand; to the fourth, ten thousand; to the fifth, a hundred thousand; to the sixth, a million; to the seventh, ten million, and so on to infinity. This progression of order is not so much spagyric as it is natural, and most hidden in the center of nature; yet it is brought forth into the light and manifested through the spagyric art, or rather led from its potentiality into act. These are the things which ought to have been said in this place concerning artificial and natural numerical weights through the unitary, the ternary, and the denary. Nevertheless, let us see what that **binary** <note>the number two</note>, with its **quaternary** <note>the number four</note>, is able to provide in artificial weights. With a weight of two pounds, and another of four pounds, there is no way that the unitary, nor the ternary—in short, no odd weight—can be balanced, but only even ones. In natural things, however, they exercise their tyranny, dragging all parts of nature through sections outside of just proportion and monarchy.

## ON THE STRUCTURE OF PRECIOUS STONES.

Hitherto, the natural order and proportion have been led forth through numbers, measures, and weights; however, so that each thing I have said may be more clearly understood—and lest I seem to have "spoken to stones" <note>a play on words; "lapidibus verba facere" is a Latin idiom for speaking to those who won't listen, but here it also refers to actual stones/alchemy</note> or to have not sufficiently illuminated that famous "Stone of the Philosophers" <note>the Philosopher's Stone, the legendary substance capable of transmuting base metals into gold and granting eternal life</note>—I shall endeavor either to turn my "stony" readers into transparent gems, or rather to transmute them into those metals, so that if I cannot satisfy myself, I may at least satisfy others. Therefore, extracting the **Mercurial water** <term>Mercurial water</term> <note>original: *Mercurialis aqua*; the "universal solvent" or first matter in alchemy, believed to be the key to the Great Work</note>...

# 486 #

<center>### OF GEMS ###</center>

Dissolve the **Mercury of the philosophers** <term>Mercury of the philosophers</term> <note>Not common quicksilver, but a secret, refined "prime matter" used by alchemists as a universal solvent</note> itself into its vegetable **fifth essence** <term>fifth essence</term> <note>original: "quintam essentiam"; the purest, most concentrated spirit of a substance, also known as the quintessence</note>. Divide this into four parts, of which one shall be a quarter, and the other truly three-quarters. From the three-quarters, take one and a half [of those quarters], and from the first quarter part, take a half: which together make half of the whole. In this manner, three-eighths will remain to be buried in the earth, and one-eighth to be exposed to the air with the rest that shall be mentioned later. In some portion of the remaining half part, dissolve a portion of the **moon** <note>original: "lunae"; in alchemical terms, this refers to silver</note>; once dissolved, clarify it through a filter and save it, throwing away the dregs as useless. Dissolve all the remaining **planets** <note>the other six metals associated with celestial bodies: gold, iron, copper, tin, lead, and mercury</note> in a suitable remaining portion of the **Mercurial water** for each, and do as was done with the moon. You shall distill each filtered solution by itself in a vaporous **water bath** <term>water bath</term> <note>original: "balneo maris," literally "bath of Mary"; a method of indirect heating using a vessel of hot water or steam to ensure gentle warmth</note>, until all the moisture has ascended and collected itself in the receiver vessel placed below.

Afterward, return a third part of this distillate to the dregs remaining in the **cucurbit** <note>the lower, gourd-shaped part of a distillation apparatus</note>, and you shall keep this alone by itself. The other two-thirds you shall place into a long-necked vial—seal both vials, however, with the **seal of Hermes** <term>seal of Hermes</term> <note>original: "sigillo Hermetis"; an airtight glass seal made by melting the neck of the glass closed</note>—and expose them to the air in a safe place so they are not broken. The other vial containing the dregs you shall bury entirely in the earth under the open sky, except for the tip of the neck which should stick out a little. You shall do the same thing separately for the other remaining planets. In two other vials, you shall include the saved Mercurial water and seal them as before: in the one which is to be placed in the air, let there be the aforementioned one-eighth; in the other, however, which is to be buried in the earth, let there be three-eighths. By this work, you will have completed the **philosophical solution**; now you may come to the **congealing**.

When a year has passed <note>original: "Anno revoluto"</note>, see that a double vessel is cast for you by glass artisans, which has the shape of a very round sphere divided through the middle; let the upper vessel also be so adapted to the lower one that it can be removed and replaced as often as necessary. When this is finished, make for yourself wax molds, empty like little vessels or boats, which can be filled with liquid and float upon the water. The method for making molds of this kind is this: have an oblong iron rod, filed and polished at one of its ends in the shape of the stone you wish to represent. Let this then be dipped in oil, and afterward immersed by the said end into melted wax, and then into cold water. Once the wax is coated and cut around, let it be freed from the iron, and you will have the molds you desire. 

**Otherwise:** Care for stones to be shaped by a revolving wheel, like natural ones, in whatever round or rough form you wish. At last, remove the vials from the earth and take down the others from the air. Then, you shall moisten the lower part of your spherical vessel with the "earthy" Mercurial water so that it fills half of it, and make the little molds float upon it. Afterward, if you wish to have a **Saturnine, Jovial, Martial, Solar, Venereal, Mercurial, or Lunar stone** <note>stones corresponding to lead, tin, iron, gold, copper, mercury, or silver</note>, you shall fill the wax molds a little less than full with the "heaven" of any of the said planets—that is, the "aerial water"—but not to the top, so the liquid does not flow out. Then finally, [cover] the lower spherical vessel with its upper part...

### STRUCTURE ###

The vessel should be covered, and it should remain closed for several hours, until you see the waters in the molds somewhat thickened. Once this is perceived, uncover the vessel and invert the small molds, so that the **fixative water** <term>fixative water</term> <note>original: "aqua fixativa"; a liquid used to stabilize or "fix" volatile substances so they can withstand heat</note> touches the paste; once the vessel is covered again, let them remain in the shade until they harden into stone. However, this process savors more of the **transmutatory art** <note>original: "transmutatoriam artem"; alchemy focused on changing one substance into another, specifically base metals into gold</note> than the medical art, because of the mixing of the **earth** with its **heaven** <note>In alchemical terminology, "Earth" (terra) refers to the solid, fixed residue or salt, while "Heaven" (caelo) refers to the volatile spirits or distilled vapors of a substance</note>. This results in stones finished in this manner being darker than those prepared by the following artifice: Let a part of any metal, or **earthy water**, or if you wish, the **fixative fifth essence** be placed in the lower part of the vessel; with the small molds floating by themselves while empty, let the vessel be closed at the top, and let the closed vessel be left for a quarter of an hour, so that the molds may be imbued with a certain invisible and fixative vapor. Afterward, having opened the vessel, let the molds be filled only with the **ethereal water** <note>original: "aqua aerea"</note> or heaven, and with it closed again, proceed as above. It is also possible for all the earthy waters to be poured together into the lower vessel, and for the molds to be filled with the mixed heavenly waters; by this same process, a unique stone will be obtained that embraces all the **planets** <note>The seven metals of alchemy: Gold (Sun), Silver (Moon), Iron (Mars), Mercury (Mercury), Tin (Jupiter), Copper (Venus), and Lead (Saturn)</note> within itself. Some mix the aforementioned vapors of two or three planets according to a proportion chosen at will, to prepare the stones listed below and adorn them with their own colors:

**Carbuncle** <note>original: "Carbunculus"; a red gemstone, typically a deep red garnet or ruby</note> is made from the heaven of the **Sun** <note>Gold</note> and from its earth.
**Diamond** <note>original: "Adamas"</note> from the heaven and earth of the **Moon** <note>Silver</note>.
**Sapphire** from the heaven of the Moon and its earth, mixed with the earth of **Jupiter** <note>Tin</note>.
**Topaz** from the heaven of **Mars** <note>Iron</note> and the earth of the Sun.
**Hyacinth** <note>original: "Hyacinthus"; a yellow, orange, or red-brown zircon</note> from the heaven and earth of Mars, mixed with the earth of the Sun.
**Heliotrope** <note>original: "Eliotropia"; also called bloodstone</note> from the heaven of **Venus** <note>Copper</note> and from the heaven and earth of Mars, with the earth of the Moon.
**Almandine** <note>original: "Alamandina"; a type of purple-red garnet</note> is made from the heaven and earth of Mars.
**Pallax** <note>likely "Balas ruby," a type of spinel</note> is made from the heaven and earth of the Moon, with an equal weight of the earth of the Sun.
**Beryllus** from equal parts of the heavens of the Moon and Jupiter, with the earth of the Moon.
**Pearl** <note>original: "Unio"; specifically a large, singular fine pearl</note> is made from one part of the heaven of Jupiter and its earth, with five parts of the heaven of the Moon.
**Solar stone** <note>Sunstone</note> is made from its own heaven and earth. Likewise, the stones of all other planets are made each from its own heaven and earth.
**Emerald** <note>original: "Smaragdus"</note> is made from the heaven of Venus and the earth of the Moon.
**Mixed stone** is made from the heavens and earths of all things, mixed equally.

Many other stones can also be made by this art in imitation of natural ones, which would be tedious to recount. However, anyone may, according to their own experience, manufacture whichever stones they wish, adorn them with their colors and virtues, and engrave **characters** <note>original: "characteribus"; mystical or astrological symbols believed to imbue the stone with specific powers</note> upon them under the **constellations** (provided they are a good **mathematician** <note>original: "mathematicus"; in this period, the term included astrologers and astronomers</note>) in a short space of time, most conveniently before the aspects pass away too suddenly. What else now remains but to diligently investigate the particular powers of all stones and metals and adapt them for medicine?

### THE STRUCTURE OF GEMS ###

In a vessel similar to the first, let the gems be dried in the shade, away from the sun’s rays. Once they are shaped, you shall thread them all with a wire, taking care not to touch them with your hands. Let them be suspended in a glass vessel containing its own clear water, and with the vessel closed, let them be placed in the open air away from the sun's rays for eight days. Afterward, let them be kept in the sun for three days, shaking the vessel very gently every three hours. By the vapor of this kind of liquid, they will be perfected and will harden into a solid state. By the same process, <term>carbuncles</term> <note>original: "carbunculi"; a term used in antiquity and the Renaissance for deep-red gems, usually garnets or rubies</note> and many or even a single ruby can be made in whatever size the craftsman desires, once the perfected <term>Red Mercury</term> <note>original: "Mercurio rubeo"; a highly purified alchemical substance believed to have the power to color and fix stones</note> has been dissolved just once. If you wish to prepare stones of other colors, you shall do as above with white <term>philosophical mercury</term> <note>original: "Mercurio philosophico"; the "living" spirit of mercury used as a base in alchemical work</note>, because the color white is receptive to all others. Any industrious operator will be able to find the <term>congealing process</term> <note>original: "congelationem"; the transition from a liquid or vaporous state to a solid</note> necessary for this work from the preceding pages, which is far superior to what has been said before. Furthermore, when celestial waters impregnated with mineral virtues are exposed to the air through the <term>revolution of a full circle</term> <note>likely referring to a full astrological cycle or a complete seasonal year</note>, they are more broadly and fruitfully impregnated with celestial powers and virtues, by which they become fit and suitable for the dissolving of all things, even the most solid bodies. However, lower celestial waters, when exposed to the "belly of the earth," receive those same virtues at the same time, but through a different medium—namely, an earthy one—by which they acquire the power of congealing all things, and their own <term>quicksilver</term> <note>original: "argentum vivum"; literally "living silver," another name for mercury</note>. Among all the <term>sulfurs</term> <note>In alchemy, "sulfur" represents the active, combustible, and "masculine" principle of a substance</note>, this unique one is the most excellent, as is the quicksilver, which we have taught to be the most outstanding and more "philosophical" than the others. Although there are many other philosophical sulfurs and quicksilvers, they are not of such great subtlety and sublimated virtue. These, therefore, are the waters of the philosophers, the most excellent among the rest: one is formal, celestial, and superior; the other is material and inferior. Yet both are born from one and the same root, and they differ only through the industry and application of this <term>spagyric art</term> <note>original: "artificium spagiricum"; the alchemical process of separating and recombining the components of a substance to purify it</note>, so that what was taught above by <term>Hermes</term> <note>Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary father of alchemy</note> may be confirmed: *What is below is like that which is above, and vice versa.* Therefore, let no one in the future complain (as has been the custom until now) about the obscurity of the "stone" or the <term>Philosopher’s Stone</term> <note>original: "lapidis philosophorum"</note>; I have already presented them as sufficiently clear, transparent, translucent, and illustrious from the darker matters. I have illustrated them and restored them to their own light for you, ingenious readers, so that the last things might correspond to the first, and vice versa—namely, that the artificial and spagyric light might correspond to the light of Nature, which gave its name to this little work and to our newly born offspring. May Almighty God grant that it be useful and healthful to all readers whom He knows to be worthy, for His own glory, to whom alone I bring this accepted light, and not to the schools of Athens, nor to any others. But let Him keep the unworthy from the reading of these things, since they are not of the same "leaven"; for indeed, the entrance is open to the worthy,

->*Preface to the reader.*<-

*Every operation requires its own proper order, without which nothing beautiful or praiseworthy is accomplished that might bring any utility to mankind. What, I ask, can be more ruinous in this life than confusion? Do we not know that this confusion has ruined the world from the beginning? Its traces are still placed before our eyes to the great misfortune of many, so that one may see that there is nothing that is not corrupted among all nations. Therefore, confusion must be utterly rejected and avoided by every good man, and especially by the Christian, chiefly because it proceeds from the enemy of God and man. Do we think that <term>God the Best and Greatest</term> <note>original: "Deum Opt. Max."; an abbreviation for Deo Optimo Maximo, a title originally for Jupiter but frequently used by Renaissance writers to refer to the Christian God as the supreme architect of the universe</note> wished to preserve order in the first place, during the building of the fabric of this world, for no reason? He proposed this order for us to meditate upon, no doubt, and not merely to look at. If it were rightly understood how much utility and how much doctrine could fall to us from this, we would wish for no other books and no other Teachers prior to Him, who alone bears the testimony of truth in our hearts. Here You, who are the author of peace, teach us to seek above all that order in peace, which if it be preserved, all things shall be at once peaceful and tranquil. On the contrary, when order is violated, discord is soon at our doors through confusion. This is why our Lord Jesus Christ, so often instilling peace into his disciples, also left it as a testament when departing from them, and to us in union. Therefore, in all works, whether spiritual or temporal, **order** must be maintained as the strongest root of peace and all harmony, so that all human actions and exercises of any kind look toward this. Accordingly, **Paracelsus**, being about to treat the highest and chief <term>secret</term> <note>original: "arcanum"; in Paracelsian chemistry, an arcanum is a "secret" or "inner power" of a substance that has healing or transformative properties</note> of medicine—the transmutation of natural things to the ultimate degree of perfection—wished first of all to indicate which order must be followed. For whatever nature works, she does so according to the order divinely prescribed for her; she effects this without variation, so that if she is sometimes hindered by an external accident from observing this order, that which is produced turns into a monster, departing from nature. This is not her error, but the error of the hindrance. You will ask, who hindered her? The <term>Author of Confusion</term> <note>a reference to the Devil or the forces of chaos</note> has always striven for this through his ministers from the beginning, and he will not cease until the end.

Furthermore, this is common to all things and elements: that species differ among themselves only by their form. # TO THE READER. 493

[Nature] produces herbs, small animals, and even minerals. Who, I ask, does not see that this is a natural transmutation of forms, and not of matter? We are also taught by this example that if forms are separated from the elements of natural things, these elements become suitable for any form whatsoever. Since the matter of the elements is one and the same, it does not receive just one or another form, but rather all forms in the threefold genus of produced things <note>referring to the three kingdoms of nature: vegetable, animal, and mineral</note>. There is no need to investigate whether the elements of vegetables, stripped of their forms, are able to receive a mineral form; the matter is clear in itself. Furthermore, when the elements of corpses are returned to the earth, they become the elements of vegetables and other things, and so on for the rest. Since, therefore, the element of one genus becomes the element of another genus, how much more can the element of one species become the element of another species within the same genus? For forms do not come from the elements, but from the firmament <note>original: "ex firmamento"; in Paracelsian thought, the "firmament" or "stars" provide the spiritual blueprint or "form" that gives life and identity to physical matter</note>.

Hence, no one of sound mind who sees forms being separated from elements will be able to deny the transmutations of things. Let the proof be in experience: wood consumed by fire and turned to ashes, its vegetable form departing into the breezes; if this form were captured by a <term>spagyric</term> <note>original: "spagiricum"; the alchemical practice of "separating and recombining" to purify substances</note> practitioner so that it does not fly away, and were then poured back again into its own ashes, and they were purified together into a mucilaginous substance and committed again to the earth, they will return to their original form. This is something the ashes by themselves certainly would not have achieved, as the author posits in his book *On the Resuscitation of Things* <note>original: "de resuscitatione rerum"; a famous Paracelsian concept regarding palingenesis, or the chemical "rebirth" of a plant from its salts and essence</note>. Whoever refuses to believe it, let him try it and keep the prescribed order; otherwise, it will not happen due to confusion, whereas without such confusion it would have succeeded perfectly.

Therefore, just as a proper form can be separated from its elements and return to them again, if these elements are imbued with the form of another species (provided it is within the same genus), what will prevent them from taking on that form? For the elements produce no form of themselves, but only that which is in the seed; just as the earth does not produce the form of any particular element, but rather grain from grain and a tree from a kernel. Therefore, the first and most important work of this matter consists in this: that rightfully, according to the <term>spagyric</term> order borrowed from nature, the separation of forms from their ele-

### PREFACE 494

...instruments. The alchemical philosophers <note>original: "spagiri philosophi"</note> did not simply dream this up in the manner of the Greeks; rather, being taught by nature alone, they use glass vessels <note>original: "organis"; literally "organs," implying the equipment functions like biological organs</note> as if they were a stomach. In these, they cook their material with fire, just as nature itself, through natural heat, softens food into <term>chyle</term> <note>the milky fluid formed in the stomach during digestion</note> by cooking it; it refines, dissolves, and putrefies it before separation. Similarly, the Art [of Alchemy] sublimes its matter through <term>calcination</term> <note>heating a substance to high temperatures to reduce it to a powder</note>, dissolves it, and putrefies it before separating it through distillation. Afterward, it sifts the pure from the impure—namely, the <term>firmamental</term> <note>referring to the celestial or spiritual blueprint of a thing, often associated with the stars in Paracelsian thought</note> parts from the elements—and then separates both of these from their own excessive impurities.

Nature itself teaches this process: it divides its putrefied chyle into two parts. One part, being purer, it presents to the liver to be cooked again; the other part, being more impure, it banishes to the intestines for ejection. From the liver, another separation occurs: one part serves to nourish the elements of the body, while the other serves to feed and cherish the vital and firmamental parts, so as to retain the spirit of life within its subject—namely, within the <term>radical moisture</term> <note>the innate, vital fluid that traditional medicine believed acted as the "fuel" for the flame of life</note>.

At this step, one can see the controversy between the Greeks <note>referring to the classical school of Galenic and Aristotelian medicine</note> and the spagyrics. The Greeks claim that the separation in the liver involves only the four <term>humors</term> <note>blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile</note>, which they attribute to the elements. Thus, they make no mention of the "firmament" of things, nor do they make any distinction, as if life were derived solely from the physical elements; they pass down a confused doctrine about these things without discrimination. In contrast, the spagyrics teach that elements are nourished only by things like themselves, and vital parts by vital things.

Indeed, no natural philosopher can doubt that the natural life of things is owed to the firmament (after God) and not to the elements. Likewise, corporeal things are nourished by bodies, and spiritual bodies by spirits; or, to be better understood, material things by material ones, just as <term>formal</term> <note>relating to the "form" or essential identity of a thing rather than its physical bulk</note> things are nourished by formal bodies. We say this lest we be accused by clever critics of proposing "forms" without matter, or vice versa. For we say that the elements have obtained their own specific form and life from the firmament, but that these elements alone can generate nothing at all without other peculiar firmamental influences—no more than a woman can without a man. Furthermore, in the Creation, God gave life to all through light; but for propagation, He gave to each a seed in which the *form*

Therefore, in Physics, the greatest account must be taken of these influences rather than of the elemental <term>humors</term> <note>the four fluids—blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile—traditionally thought to govern health</note> or qualities.* 

*The <term>spagyric school</term> <note>original: "spagirica schola"; the followers of Paracelsus who used chemistry to produce medicines</note> has labored most intensely on this: to always free the vehicle of life from thicker bodies—as if from a prison—so that it may cherish, restore, and long retain life within the human body. It was no less necessary to find a matter which, in its own creation, had drawn in more of these vital and celestial influences. This school discovered that such a matter is that which approaches closest to the center. For in that center, the rays of all the celestial bodies concur, not unlike arrows shot from every direction toward a single target. From this it happens that the compressed force and the confluence of virtues obtain their most intense action and most vehement power in their extension.* 

*Therefore, the further these influences are distant from the center, the more rare and loose they are found to be, and possessed of lesser forces and virtues, as can be seen in the case of vegetables. For this reason, experience following upon meditation has taught that in metals and minerals, which are closer to the center, the most excellent and abundant virtues of all reside. The alchemists therefore preferred these above all others, so that from them they might elicit a certain <term>universal medicine</term> <note>original: "medicinæ quandam universalem"; a theoretical "cure-all" or Panacea derived from the highest alchemical processes</note> in a form most united and tempered, by which individual things might finally be brought to union and a true temperament.*

Hence it happened that, because of such universal power and virtue, what Egyptian antiquity once developed especially for medicine (having been taught, of course, the Mosaic traditions from Genesis by the Hebrews), the greed and ambition of the Greeks perverted into the accumulation of treasures. They do so by the mere meditation of such rarity and such depth of divine wisdom, which shines forth as a spark in this greatest of secrets. To these men, it is especially delightful to dwell in these great works of God, far more than for most others to dwell in their own wealth and pleasures. ...blasted by any celestial influence <note>original: "sideratione"; referring to the belief that planets or stars could "strike" objects and change their nature, such as petrifying them</note>, they were transmuted into true stones. Springs also bubble up in many places which, by a natural property, transform anything thrown into them into the hardest stones. Wise men, having contemplated these and similar works of nature, learned that similar things can be done by art, provided that a similar order is observed, which nature teaches through her own instruments. We see this same thing happening in most mountains, where coals are naturally generated from stones by a kind of Etnean fire <note>referring to the volcanic heat of Mount Etna</note>, which are also very frequently used in blacksmiths' workshops. 

As this last transmutation is done through fire in the earth, the others mentioned above seem to be done through water and air. These, therefore, are the instruments of nature; they also serve as the matter itself, while motion serves as the form. What then, I ask, if the natural composite earth is made through fire, and that water through air, but this fire through fire, and that descending air is made through air, and this again becomes water through water, and finally this returns to earth through fire: what kind of transmutation do you think will result from that? If you experiment, you will know. The ignorant common folk do not see these things, for no other reason than that they do not consider the secrets of nature. 

Therefore, whoever is ignorant of these things along with that common crowd, and denies what nature places before everyone's eyes, however learned or literate he may seem, is not worthy of the name of philosopher or physicist <term>physicist</term> <note>original: "physici"; in this era, a "physician" or "physicist" was a "natural philosopher" who studied the internal workings of the physical world</note>. From where, I ask, does Physics have its first foundation? Is it from appearances alone or the manifest surface of natural things? Not at all, but from the most hidden operations of nature, compared against the most manifest effects. Since nature herself is imperceptible to all senses, her operations are no different. Who, I ask, ever saw a tree grow, or the sun and stars move? No one. Yet everyone notices that they have grown and that those have moved over intervals of time. In physics, therefore, work is needed primarily with the mind, more than with the eyes or other senses. Although the latter serve as signs for us to proceed further, otherwise there would be no difference between a philosopher and a peasant. 

But to return to our purpose: the Scale of Transmutation has seven principal steps, which are: *Calcination, Sublimation, Solution, Putrefaction, Distillation, Coagulation, and Tincture.* Under calcination are contained these members: *Reverberation, Cementation,* and also *Incineration.* By all these operations, all things are turned into lime <note>original: "calcem"; the white, powdery substance left after burning</note> or into ashes. In the first step of transmutation, therefore, natural elemental bodies are converted into earth, using a moderate fire as an instrument. Here, the difference between material elements and instrumental elements must especially be noted, of which we spoke in passing. For the latter are external, while the former are internal. Once the first operation is completed—whether by calcination, reverberation, cementation, or incineration—

...of [nature's secrets]; next in the order of preparations follows **sublimation**, by which earth that has already been calcined <note>burned to a fine powder or ash to remove impurities</note> is converted either into water or into air, according to the nature and properties of the substance being transformed. Indeed, the elevation of volatile parts from fixed parts is most suitable for dry substances; therefore, sublimation is appropriate for things of that condition. If, however, a separation of moist things must be carried out, such as those from plants or animals, then their sublimation belongs to the fifth degree, namely **distillation**. But because we are dealing here primarily with dry things, such as metals and minerals, the order appropriate to them must likewise be observed.

Accordingly, the sublimated volatile part—just as in moist things—reaches such a state of fixation through **cohobations** <note>the process of repeatedly distilling a liquid over its own solid residue to concentrate its "virtue"</note> (that is, the re-joining of separated parts and repeated separations) that it remains below with the fixed parts and no longer rises, but settles in the form of an oil or a stone. For through air, by solution, they pass into oil; but by coagulation through fire, they pass into stone. An example of this is any metal driven into sublimation by sal ammoniac <note>original: "armoniaco sale"; a naturally occurring mineral salt (ammonium chloride) used as a flux in alchemy</note>, for this turns to stone through these successes. By this operation of sublimations, many corrosive things become sweet or mild, and vice versa—though usually with the addition of another substance. Likewise, many sharp things become sweet, and sweet things conversely become sour, some by themselves and others when prepared in this manner with other substances.

After the second stage, the third degree follows: **solution**. This is twofold: one produced by cold, and the other by heat. Salts, corrosives, and any calcined materials are coagulated <note>solidified</note> by fire, and finally resolved <note>melted or dissolved</note> by the cold of the air into a liquor, water, or oil when placed in a damp place like a cellar, or in the air upon a marble stone or glass. Fatty and sulfurous things, however, are resolved by the heat of fire. In summary: what is dissolved by the heat of fire is eventually coagulated by the cold of the air; conversely, what is dissolved by the cold of the air is coagulated by the heat of fire.

Note the reasoning by which we say that air is cold, which seems to conflict somewhat with the opinion of several philosophers; for they maintain that air is hot and moist. But they do not consider what air is actually composed of. Is it not made from fire and water? For what else is air but water resolved by fire? Therefore, it borrows heat and dryness from one of its parts (namely fire), but from the other, it borrows coldness and the moisture of its water. There are only two principal qualities, while the other two are merely their servants. For nothing is naturally hot that is not also necessarily dry by nature; likewise, nothing is cold that is not for that reason moist. Whatever else happens to these should be judged as occurring by accident, not by nature. It is no different with the elements: fire and water hold the chief place. Earth, however, borrows its coldness from its companion, water, and the dryness it has from fire. By itself, earth is never hot or moist, nor even cold or dry, but seems to serve its other two principles no differently than wax serves any [shape...]

...seal. <note>original: "sigillo"; this completes a word from the previous page</note> Likewise, we must judge the nature of air: for it receives its heat and dryness from its father, namely fire, and its coldness and moisture from water, its mother. Thus, they are generated by these parents, fire and water: air—being masculine, or rather a hermaphrodite—and the female earth. 

Thus far we have spoken of natural instruments and matter. The fourth degree is **putrefaction**. By its excellence, this stage ought to deserve the first place, were it not that such an inversion would struggle against the true order and the secret—which is hidden from many in this place and revealed to very few. Therefore, the established series must remain and not be changed, any more than the rings in a chain; if a single ring should fail, whatever is held captive by them would escape. 

The property of **putrefaction** <note>the process of rot or decay which alchemists believed was necessary to release the "seed" or essence of a substance</note> is such that, by consuming the old nature of things, it introduces a new one, and sometimes produces the fruit of a different generation. For all living things die through corruption; once dead, they putrefy, and then, through the transmutation of generation, they acquire life once more. Even corrosive spirits <note>harsh, acid-like substances</note> grow sweet and mild through this process, and all colors are changed into others; likewise, the pure is separated from the impure, which settles at the bottom. The parts of putrefaction are **digestion** and **circulation**.

Finally, the fifth degree is **distillation**, which is nothing other than the separation of the moist from the dry, and the thin from the thick. Its parts are **ascension**, **washing**, **imbibition**, **cohobation**, and **fixation**. **Cohobation** <note>the process of repeatedly pouring a distilled liquid back onto its solid remains and re-distilling it</note>, which concludes the individual parts, is the repeated pouring and distilling of the distilled liquor back onto its own dregs. For example, vitriol <note>a sulfate mineral</note> is fixed by its own water through cohobations, and is then called "sugared alum." When this is dissolved into a liquid, putrefied for a month, and then distilled, it yields a water as sweet as sugar: a secret medicine excellent above all others for extinguishing the "microcosmic fire" <note>likely referring to internal inflammation or fever</note> that afflicts metal miners, which is discussed more fully in the book *On the Diseases of Mineral Miners*. In the same way, any other minerals or watery substances, such as saltpeter <note>original: "sal nitrum"</note>, can be fixed by cohobations.

The sixth degree is **coagulation**. Like its opposite, **solution**, it is twofold: of cold and of heat (that is, of air and of fire). Again, each type of coagulation is double. The first kind of cold coagulation happens from common air outside of a fire; the second comes from the upper firmament through the "winter stone," which congeals all waters into snow and ice. However, the first coagulation of heat is achieved through industriousness in the art [of alchemy], following the observed degrees of fire, and this is "fixed"; the other cold coagulations are not fixed in alchemy. The second kind of heat coagulation is produced by the Etnaean <note>volcanic or subterranean</note> and mineral fire under the earth and beneath the mountains, directed by the natural **Archeus** <term>Archeus: the "internal chemist" or vital force of nature that shapes and transforms matter</term> of the earth. The fire that is stirred up and graded through alchemy for coagulation is not at all unlike this natural fire. Whatever is coagulated by this Etnaean fire remains fixed.

...as can be seen in metals and minerals, each of which consists, from the beginning, of a certain mucilaginous <note>jelly-like or viscous</note> matter, coagulated in the mountains into stones, metals, marcasites <note>iron pyrites or brittle metallic ores</note>, salts, etc., through the *Etnean fire* <note>original: "Ætneum ignem"; referring to the volcanic or subterranean heat of the earth</note> and the *Archaeus of the earth*, the natural craftsman. The seventh and last step of the scale of transmutation is the **Tincture**, the most noble medicine of all, forged from the *chemical art*, by which any metallic bodies, and even human ones, are tinged <note>transformed or infused</note> into a substance far better, more noble, and more excellent than they were naturally before, and are brought to the highest degree of health, color, and perfection—into a more powerful and excellent nature. There are various types of these tinctures, which are not to be listed here. 

First, bodies must be removed from their metallic coagulation by fire and melted; otherwise, they do not receive the active tincture unless they are unlocked and opened. Furthermore, any tinctures of metals must be of a very fixed substance, easily meltable and incombustible in nature, so that when placed on a glowing hot plate, they flow quickly like wax and penetrate the metal without smoke faster than oil seems to enter paper or water enters a sponge; and they tinge it into a white or red color that remains in the fire and withstands any test. 

In the first degree of calcination <note>reducing a metal to powder through heat</note>, therefore, metals reduced to *alcohol* <note>original: "alcohol"; in this era, the term referred to an extremely fine, subtle powder rather than a liquid spirit</note> for such tinctures acquire easy liquefaction—namely in the second degree of solution—and thereafter through putrefaction and distillation, their tinctures must be fixed, become incombustible, and remain unchanging in color. But to recover or preserve the health of human bodies through restoration and renewal, they [tinctures] must be drawn from gold, pearls <note>original: "unionibus"; large, high-quality pearls</note>, antimony, sulfur, vitriol, and the like. 

Different sources of fire also have different operations in alchemy: 
- One is the flame of wood, which they call **living fire**, and by which the bodies of all metals or others are calcined and reverberated. 
- Another is the continuous heat of a candle or lamp, by which volatile substances are fixed. 
- Another is that of coals, by which bodies are cemented, colored, and purged of their dross; likewise gold and silver are brought to a higher degree, *Venus* <note>original: "Venus"; the alchemical name for copper</note> is whitened, and in short, all metals are renewed. 
- A glowing iron plate has another operation, upon which the testing of tinctures is performed. 
- Another is the heat excited by fire through the medium of iron filings. 
- Another in ashes; likewise in sand another. 
- And in the *bath of the Sea* or *of Mary* <note>original: "balneo Maris vel Mariæ"; the *bain-marie* or double boiler, named after Mary the Jewess</note> another, by which various distillations, sublimations, and coagulations are performed. 
- The *bath of dew* <note>original: "balneum roris"</note> has another, which I have elsewhere called the "vaporous bath," by which many solutions of physical things are made. 
- The *horse’s belly* <note>original: "venter equinus"; a warm, fermenting heap of manure used to provide a gentle, steady heat</note> has another, in which the principal putrefactions and digestions take place. 
- And far different from all these is the **invisible fire**, that is, the *rays of the Sun*, which is made manifest through its operations by means of a mirror or crystal, and about which the ancients did not...

## *On the Simple Fire of the Chemists.*
### CHAPTER II.

After we have said enough for the ingenious concerning the artifice of transmutations through the scale and its degrees, so that the order (which was described above) may be preserved, it will be necessary to present the instruments to the initiates before the matter itself, lest the unrefined and unskilled move their feet before their hands. Therefore, let those not approach here who have no mind's eye, and whom the hand cannot serve: for the foot and the eye of flesh, without a sound and uncorrupted mind, are altogether useless. Thus, the most powerful and most required instrument is fire, which is indeed living from its own nature and is brought to life by no other fire. From this, it follows that it has the power and strength to bring to life whatever else is hidden in things. Just as the Sun was created by God in this world to awaken the resting fire in all things, and to ignite with its own fire all the spheres of the Moon, Mercury, Venus, Mars, Jupiter, and Saturn, and the rest of the stars, which otherwise have none of their own, nor can they offer any from themselves: for through themselves they are dead; yet once ignited by the solar fire, they live and perform their own operations according to the property of each. Truly, the Sun receives the light and life which it has—the fire—from no other star; it is ruled solely by God its creator, so that it always and equally burns and shines in itself, illuminating every other natural light. Not otherwise in the spagyric <term>Spagyric: The alchemical art of separating and then recombining the components of a substance to create a more potent medicine.</term> art must we judge the fire of the athanor <term>Athanor: A specific type of alchemical furnace designed to provide a steady, uniform heat for a long time, often called the "picket-furnace."</term> and the secret furnace of the philosophers, which ignites the furnace and the sphere of the vessel and the fire of the matter, just as the sun is seen to operate in the whole world, without which nothing at all can be generated within it. Likewise, in the art, nothing is accomplished without this simple fire, since it is the most powerful part and operation of this artifice, embracing all others within itself and being comprehended by none; it exists by itself, not needing others, but all other operations that occur need this simple fire, from which they receive life along with the matter itself.

...as can be seen from metals and minerals, each of which consists, from the beginning, of a certain mucilaginous <note>slimy or jelly-like</note> matter, which is coagulated in the mountains into stones, metals, marcasites, salts, and so on, by *Etnean* <note>volcanic or subterranean</note> fire and the *Archeus* <term>Archeus: in Paracelsian philosophy, the internal "master craftsman" or vital force that directs natural processes</term> of the earth. The seventh and final step of the scale of transmutation is *Tincture* <term>Tincture: the most potent alchemical substance, capable of "staining" or transforming the very nature of a material</term>, the most noble medicine of all produced by the Chemical art. By this, any metallic bodies—and even human ones—are transformed into a substance far better, nobler, and more excellent than they were naturally before, and are brought to the highest degree of health, color, and perfection, into a more powerful and excellent nature. There are various species of such tinctures, which need not be recounted in this place.

Bodies must first be moved from their metallic coagulation and melted by fire; otherwise, they will not receive an active tincture unless they are first unlocked and opened. Furthermore, any tinctures of metals must be of a very fixed substance, easily meltable, and incombustible by nature, so that when placed upon a glowing hot plate they soon flow like wax. They should penetrate the metal without smoke more quickly than oil is seen to enter paper or water a sponge, and they should dye it into a white or red color that remains permanent in the fire and stands up to any test.

In the first stage of calcination <note>reducing a solid to powder via heat</note>, therefore, metals are reduced to *alcohol* <term>alcohol: in this context, it refers to an "alcohol of wine" style of refinement, meaning a powder so fine it is impalpable, rather than a liquid</term> for these kinds of tinctures, and they acquire an easy liquefaction. In the second stage, namely solution, and thereafter through putrefaction and distillation, their tinctures must be fixed, rendered incombustible, and made unchangeable in color. To restore or preserve the health of human bodies through restoration and renewal, these tinctures ought to be drawn from gold, pearls <note>original: "unionibus"</note>, antimony, sulfur, vitriol, and similar things.

Different sources of fire also have different operations in alchemy:
*   The flame of wood, which they call "living fire," by which the bodies of all metals or other things are calcined and reverberated.
*   The continuous heat of a candle or lamp, by which volatile things are fixed.
*   The heat of coals, by which bodies are cemented, colored, and purged of their dross; likewise, gold and silver are brought to a higher degree, *Venus* <note>The alchemical name for copper</note> is whitened, and in short, all metals are renewed.
*   The ignited iron plate, upon which the testing of tinctures is performed.
*   The heat excited by fire through the medium of iron filings.
*   Heat in ashes.
*   Heat in sand.
*   The *Bath of the Sea* or *Bath of Mary* <term>balneum Mariae: a water bath or double-boiler, named after the legendary alchemist Mary the Jewess</term>, in which various distillations, sublimations, and coagulations are performed.
*   The *Bath of Dew*, which I have elsewhere called "vaporous," by which many solutions of physical things are made.
*   The *Horse’s Belly* <term>venter equinus: a method of providing gentle, steady heat by burying a vessel in fermenting horse manure</term>, in which the principal putrefactions and digestions take place.
*   Far different from all these is the *invisible fire*—that is, the sun's rays—which becomes evident through its operations when using a mirror or a crystal, and of which the ancients did not...

...they have mentioned. By this fire, the three principles <note>In Paracelsian alchemy, these are Salt, Sulfur, and Mercury—the basic building blocks of all matter.</note> of every thing can be separated upon a wooden table without fear of flame or scorching; by it, any metals can be liquefied without visible fire, and even combustible things can be reduced to coals and ashes. Moreover, the transmutations of imperfect metals toward perfection cannot be properly achieved without the Stone <note>original: "lapide," the Philosopher's Stone</note> or the Tincture, which we will treat in their own place below. Furthermore, we will say something below regarding the transmutations of the imperfect into other imperfect things, brought forward only as a proof of transmutations; however, we shall not do so until we have completed the treatment of fire, upon which the hinge <term>cardo: the central point or pivot</term> of the whole art chiefly turns, and have taught several processes for the Stone from Paracelsus.

### *On the Simple Fire of the Chemists.*
#### CHAPTER II.

After we have said enough for the ingenious concerning the artifice of transmutations through the scale and its degrees, so that the order (previously mentioned) may be maintained, it will be necessary to present the instrument to those being initiated before the matter itself, lest the unrefined and clumsy set foot before they move a hand. Therefore, let those not approach here who lack the eye of the mind, and whose hand cannot serve it; for the foot and the eye of the flesh, without a sound and uncorrupted mind, are utterly useless.

The most powerful and most greatly required instrument, therefore, is fire, which is indeed living by its own nature and is animated by no other fire. From this it follows also that it has the power and strength to animate any other fire hidden within things. Just as the Sun was created by God in this world to awaken the resting fire in all things, and to ignite with its own fire all the spheres of the Moon, Mercury, Venus, Mars, Jupiter, and Saturn, and the rest of the stars <note>In the 16th-century worldview, the planets were often referred to as stars that moved within their own celestial spheres.</note>, which otherwise have none of their own, nor can they provide any from themselves; for of themselves they are dead, yet once ignited by solar fire, they live and perform their own operations according to the property of each. 

The Sun, however, receives the light and life it possesses as fire from no other star; it is governed only by God its creator, so that it may always and equally burn and shine within itself, illuminating every other natural light. In no different way must one judge the fire of the athanor <term>athanor: a specialized alchemical furnace designed to maintain a steady, uniform heat over long periods</term> and the secret furnace of the philosophers in the spagyric <term>spagyric: the alchemical art of separating substances into their components and then recombining them to create more potent medicines</term> art; it ignites the furnace and the sphere of the vessel and the fire of the matter, just as the sun is seen to work in the whole world, without which nothing at all can be generated within it. Likewise, in the art, nothing is accomplished without this simple fire, since it is the most powerful part and operation of this artifice, embracing all others within itself while being grasped by none. It stands by itself, not needing others, but all other operations that are performed require this simple fire, from which they receive life along with the matter itself.

Elsewhere Paracelsus speaks of the simple fire in this manner. The most famous opinion of the philosophers (he says) is this: Let fire and *azoth* <note>original: "Ignis & azot"; Azoth was considered the universal solvent or the essential agent of transformation in alchemy.</note> be enough for you, for fire alone is the whole work and the entire art. Furthermore, as many as build their fire simply with coals err, whether they keep the vessel in it or above it. Some have tried in vain with the fire of horse manure. They have sublimated the matter by the fire of coals without any medium, and yet they did not dissolve it. Others have stirred up heat with their lamps, asserting that this is the secret fire of the philosophers for fashioning their Stone. Some have placed it in a bath, and this in heaps of ants; others in juniper ashes; some have sought this fire in quicklime, in tartar, vitriol, saltpeter, and similar things. Others [sought it] in "burning water" <note>original: "aqua ardente," typically referring to distilled alcohol or strong acids.</note>, as Thomas Aquinas falsely speaks of this fire, saying that God and His Angels cannot be without it, but use it daily. What blasphemy is this? Is it not a most manifest lie, that God cannot be without the elementary fire of burning water—indeed, [cannot be without] all His creatures whenever He wishes? All heats stirred up by the means that have been mentioned are utterly useless for our work. See that you are not seduced even by Arnold of Villanova, who wrote of the fire of coals, for he himself will deceive you by this very thing. Almadir says: Only the invisible rays of our fire suffice. Another brings forward an example: that celestial heat, by its reflections, is most effective for the coagulation and perfection of Mercury through its continuous motion. Again, the same [Paracelsus] says: Make a vaporous fire, digesting and cooking, continuous; not, however, flying or boiling, but altering and penetrating. I have already truly told you every way of stirring up the heat of the fire; if you are a true philosopher, you will understand well. Thus he concludes. Salmanazar says: Our fire is a corrosive fire, which draws a mist and a cloud over our vessel, in which cloud the rays of this fire are hidden; if this "chaos" <note>In Paracelsian chemistry, "chaos" often refers to a gaseous state or the atmospheric medium through which spirit acts.</note> of dew and the moisture of the cloud are lacking, an error is committed. Again, Almadir says: unless our fire has warmed the sun with its moisture through the "manure of the mountain" <note>original: "fimum montis," an alchemical metaphor for a specific substance or tempered heat source.</note> by a temperate ascent, we shall not be sharers of the white nor the red Stone. All these things demonstrate clearly enough to us the hidden fire of the wise. In summary, this is the matter of our fire: namely, that it may be kindled by the quiet spirit of sensible fire, which pushes upward like a heated chaos from the opposite side and above our philosophical matter; which heat, glowing above our vessel toward the motion of perfect generation, should press on constantly without intermission and indeed temperately.

### CHAP. III.

After we have spoken of the simple fire, it seems fitting that we should also bring something regarding the multiple <note>original: "multiplici"; also translated as "manifold" or "composite" fire.</note> fire into our discussion, more fully and clearly than before: for we have touched upon this latter type only briefly, as if through a screen. Fire is therefore manifold, varying according to the diversity of the subject into which it flows, and through which it is afterwards excited in other subjects. Examples include the fire of ashes, of sand, of the bath <note>original: "balnei"; referring to the *balneum Mariae* or water bath.</note>, of filings, and so on. These possess a mediated heat, flowing from an immediate source into the subject matter of the instrument, and from there into the material underlying the art. Indeed, in this manifold fire consists the difference of the subject; this is the reason why nothing in the nature of things can be seen to be similar to any other in all things and through all things, even if both are of the same species—indeed, even if they are members of the same individual. 

Just as one metal produces gold, while another generates silver; one brings forth that which is of Saturn <note>Lead</note>, of Venus <note>Copper</note>, or of Mars <note>Iron</note>, and so on; likewise, each of these varies according to the difference of the place from which it was dug and born. Not even two men, nor two members of one body, nor two leaves of the same tree are found to be identical: and so it is with the rest. This dissimilarity does not arise from the first fire of the creatures <note>The "simple fire" or divine spark.</note>, but from the varied governance of the elements through the planets, and not through the Sun alone. For at every moment, the heat in the elements is changed by this arrangement, as is the form of things decomposed from the composite, and not from the simple. Where the mixture of elements is not so very great, there **Gold** <note>original: "Sol"</note> is generated; where it is a little greater and more impure, there **Silver** <note>original: "Luna"</note>; likewise, from the more imperfect comes **Venus** <note>Copper</note>: and so with the rest, according to the changes in the mixtures. The ore of each metal is not like another, nor do their spirits agree with one another in all respects. 

If, however, they were generated from the simple fire alone, without the intervention of the manifold fire, no distinction of properties and forms could occur—not only in metals, but in all other creatures. As for why no more than seven in number come into use—six of which are solid, and the seventh <note>Mercury/Quicksilver</note> fluid and rare—this has its reasons in "attained philosophy" <note>original: "adepta philosophia"; refers to the higher insights of a master philosopher.</note> and not in common alchemy; therefore, these reasons are to be reserved for their proper place, lest we wander from our purpose. Let this suffice for what has been said concerning the manifold philosophical fire, deduced from physical reasons.

Indeed, the first thing is the furnace, called <term>Athanor</term> <note>From the Arabic "al-tannūr," meaning oven; in alchemy, it refers to a self-feeding furnace designed to maintain a constant temperature for long periods.</note> by the chemical name given by the ancients; this takes the place of the womb in <term>spagyric</term> <note>A term often used by Paracelsus to describe alchemy, specifically the process of separating and recombining the essential components of a substance.</note> generation. Hermes Trismegistus, although not the inventor of this art—no less than Paracelsus of spagyric medicine—nevertheless deserves to be called its restorer. He asserts that this spagyric work, in which human philosophy places its finishing touch, took its beginning from the meditative contemplation of the <term>macrocosm</term> <note>original: "majoris mundi"; the "greater world" or the universe as a whole.</note>, hinting that the spagyric Athanor ought to be built in imitation of heaven and earth. But I will not be reluctant to examine this comparison briefly for the sake of exercising the mind, so that I may be of use to the readers. No physicist will deny that the Sun generates a Sun like itself, but not everyone will admit that this offspring exists in the center—especially the disciples of those philosophers who have had no knowledge of <term>Etnean fire</term> <note>original: "ignis Ætnæi"; referring to the volcanic heat of Mount Etna, used here as a metaphor for the central, internal fire of the Earth.</note> other than from the eye of the flesh, like unlearned rustics. This earthly Sun (or that of the lower or elementary machine) is ignited by the fire of the superior Sun; in the same way, the center of our matter is ignited by the center of our world or Athanor (which is fire), acting in this part as the natural Sun through similarity. Who does not see (I ask you, brothers) that the form of the entire created world has the likeness of a furnace, or to speak more reverently, of a containing womb—namely the elements, in which the seeds of the <term>Sun and Moon</term> <note>In an alchemical context, "Sol and Luna" usually refer to Gold and Silver, or the male and female principles of the work.</note>, sent down through the stars by various influences, are corrupted, cooked, and digested into the generation of all things? But these things are clearly manifest even to children, let alone philosophers, wherefore we shall not press them further.

Let us therefore come to the construction of our Athanor. First, let a furnace be built with a height of six <term>spans</term> <note>original: "spithamarum"; a span is the distance from the tip of the thumb to the tip of the little finger, roughly 9 inches or 23 cm.</note>, and an internal round width of one span, so that it is slightly wider at the bottom than at the top on the inside, and polished, so that the coals thrown in do not stick to any roughness but can easily descend while they are burnt below near the grate. At its level, let there be several holes, to which two or three lateral or "womb-like" furnaces correspond, or if you wish, only one: let the width of the small doors be four fingers, and wide ones at that. To each small furnace let a bronze vessel be fitted with water, and let the rest be enclosed, like an egg in a hen, or glass in its womb, according to the skill of the <term>mastery</term> <note>original: "magisterij"; referring to the completion of the alchemical Great Work.</note>. Then, when the work is to be done and everything is most diligently prepared, let the small tower be filled to the top with coals broken to the size of a walnut or a little larger, and let them be lit below at the doors. Let the tower be blocked at the top, lest the coals ignite in the middle or at the top and excite a heat that ruins the whole work, burning everything at once. When the heat seems to exceed what is right, it can be restrained by placing a small brick at the door; on the other hand, if it is too weak, the coals should be stirred beneath the grate with a small iron poker. But the fire will be more suitably moderated by <term>registers</term> <note>original: "regisris" [sic: registris]; these are sliding plates or dampers used to regulate the flow of air into the furnace.</note> (which they call rudders): each thing is taught by...

...use in the preparations of those things which are necessary, before that point is reached. Therefore, with the fire moderated to a just equality of proportion, as nature itself teaches in all things, the heat will excite the ferment, and subsequently, this heat excites the matter lying hidden within the egg <note>The "Philosopher’s Egg" refers to the sealed glass vessel, often oval-shaped, used in alchemical operations to contain the matter being transformed.</note>. Accordingly, not otherwise than the sun shines in the great world, illuminates, and grants life to all the other stars and elements, the **spagyric fire** <note>Spagyric refers to the alchemical process of separating and then recombining the essential components of a substance to create a more potent form.</note> illuminates its **athanor** <note>A self-feeding furnace designed to maintain a constant temperature for long periods.</note> and every instrument; it also warms the **bath of the sea** <note>original: "maris balneum"; commonly known as a "bain-marie," a water bath used to provide gentle, uniform heat.</note> just as a hen hatches her own animated egg. 

But I hear a giant roaring like a lion against the furnace, seeking a Paracelsus whom he may devour. "Behold!" (he says), "how he contradicts himself! Just recently he strictly forbade that a fire be built with coals, and that most severely; but now he teaches that the use of coals is most powerful for this art of his." 

You have touched upon it, indeed, but you have judged the writings of Paracelsus to fight against themselves no better than you have judged all other things. However, there is another eye that you should open, lest you seem until now to have judged colors like a one-eyed man, or one who is altogether blind. Did you not see what this little phrase—**simply and without a medium** <note>original: "simpliciter & sine medio"; Paracelsus likely meant that coals should not be used in direct contact with the vessel, but rather through a mediating layer like sand or water.</note>—added to the prohibition of coals, actually means? 

Do you see how, contrary to your hope, Paracelsus—though dead—is still able to respond to you and the rest of his detractors through his living writings, and to say: "You who judge me to err, you yourself err, being judged by your own self"? Have I not more often warned you, and envious men like you, throughout almost all my writings, that you should not pass over even a little word without chewing it properly? Otherwise, it would happen to you giants, in dealing with my pygmy **homunculus** <note>A "little man" or artificial life-form that Paracelsus famously claimed could be created through alchemy; here used metaphorically for his specialized knowledge or smaller works.</note>, what once happened to Goliath with the little boy David. "Beware," I say, again and again, "lest you collapse by this stone of ours as if by a great mystery, and at the same time descend with it to the pits, where you try in vain to banish me." 

Paracelsus seems to thunder these things from the tomb. Brothers, one must not speak of the dead in this way, contrary to equity—indeed, not even of those who served poorly. Let them all remain in their rest; their own deeds await each of them. It is easy indeed to criticize; to avoid judgment today is difficult, and in the end, it is not possible. What are you that I am not? What am I that you are not? Again, what can happen to both that cannot happen to the other—namely, to err? We are all humans, to whom this happens especially more than to irrational brutes, which are moved only by instinct. I confess error exists in many; you err, and it is your part to confess it, and mine to warn you, not to judge you. Therefore, let it be your duty, as it is mine, not to make public the improper deeds of brothers through envy, before having warned them with some modesty according to the discipline of true philosophy. Otherwise, neither you, nor he, nor I, acting differently, are worthy of the name of philosophy. 

But this philosophical discipline (alas!) is attacked even by the most learned; the dogma of the Gentile philosophers <note>Referring to the classical Greek and Roman philosophers like Aristotle, whose theories Paracelsians often felt were outdated or "pagan" compared to their own "Christian" alchemy.</note>, so highly celebrated in this time, has grown so strong in them that they do not see all of this, whatever it is...

Outwardly and inwardly, they pretend to nothing but a pure ambition for honors; this has been the chief aim of their study and labors. From this, it happens that everyone tries to prepare a reputation for themselves through the weakening or blackening of another. But the miserable wretches do not consider that no injury can be done so great that a far greater one does not await them—provided, however, that we are all equally foolish, and no one is found who wishes to be wise according to his measure. Many are wise more than is sufficient, or most are wise too little, while almost no one keeps to the middle path. Let us see to it, therefore, that the wisdom we pretend to have is not, by the just judgment of God, transformed into manifest foolishness even in this age, and that by our own efforts. Therefore, if we have erred in anything, as our own conscience accuses us, whereby we might be seen to have provided a scandal to others tending toward their deception, let us retract it without shame before God and men, in writing just as it was committed. As we said before, the common error of men is recognized by the wisest, but truly not by the dull and the foolish, for whom every delirium is the true path, and vice versa. But let us dismiss the insane and deal more extensively with the upright and the intelligent. ### CHAPTER V.

Many philosophers, presuming too much of themselves recklessly, have wrongly understood the occult and secret vessel of the philosophers. They have understood even worse what **Aristotle the Alchemist** <note>original: "Aristoteles alchemista"; this refers to various medieval alchemical texts falsely attributed to the Greek philosopher Aristotle, rather than the historical "Academic Greek" himself.</note> (not that Academic Greek) says, stating that the matter must be cooked in a threefold vessel. Likewise, they most poorly understand what is said by another: that the matter in the first separation and the first degree requires a metallic vessel; in the second degree—namely of coagulation and the whitening of its earth—a glass vessel; and in the third degree, which is of fixation, an earthen vessel. Nevertheless, through all these descriptions, they understand only one single vessel in all operations, right up to the perfection of the **Red Stone** <note>original: "rubei lapidis"; the final, most potent state of the Philosopher's Stone, capable of transmuting metals into gold and curing all diseases.</note>. 

Since, therefore, our matter is our root for both the white and the red, our vessel must necessarily be of such a fashion that the matter within it can be ruled by the celestial bodies. For the invisible **celestial influences** <note>original: "Influentiae namque caelestes"; the belief that the movements and positions of stars and planets directly affected the success of chemical transformations on Earth.</note> and the impressions of the stars are especially necessary for the work. Otherwise, it would be impossible for the oriental, Persian, Chaldean, and Egyptian stone—insurmountable by other means—to be fulfilled; through this stone, Anaxagoras <note>An ancient Greek philosopher who famously suggested that the sun was a red-hot stone and that meteorites fell from the heavens.</note> knew the powers of the entire firmament and predicted that a great stone would descend from heaven to the earth, which indeed happened after his death. To the **Cabalists** <note>Practitioners of Kabbalah; here referring to those who applied mystical Jewish traditions and sacred geometry to alchemy.</note>, especially, our vessel becomes known, according to a truly geometric proportion and measure, and from a certain **squaring of the circle** <note>original: "circuli quadratura"; a symbolic reference to the alchemical goal of bringing the four elements into a perfect, unified fifth essence or "quintessence."</note>...

# OF METALS

<margin>The construction of the vessel</margin> ...must be constructed so that the spirit and soul of our matter, having been separated from its body, are able to rise with it to the height of its own "heaven" <note>In alchemy, the upper part of a vessel is often called the 'heaven' (coelum), where vapors condense.</note>. If the vessel is narrower, wider, higher, or lower than the governing and operating spirits and soul require, the heat of our secret **philosophical fire** (which is indeed most sharp) will urge the violently excited matter toward excessive operation. This may cause the vessel to shatter into a thousand pieces, not without danger to the operator’s life and limb. Conversely, if the vessel is more spacious than the heat can proportionally act upon, the work will be vain and fruitless. For this reason, our **philosophical vessel** <term>vas philosophicum: a specially sealed glass container used for long-term heating</term> must be fabricated with the greatest diligence and industry. 

As for the material of this vessel, it is understood only by those who, in the first solution of our fixed and perfect matter, have led it back to its **first essence** <note>The 'prima materia' or original state of a substance before it takes a specific form.</note>; enough has been said of this. The operator should also note most diligently what the matter sets aside and rejects during that first solution. The method for describing this vessel is difficult: nevertheless, its form must be such as nature itself demands. It must be sought and investigated from one source and another. In short, its shape must be such that, from the height of the **philosophical heaven** raised above the **philosophical earth**, it can work upon the fruit of its own earthly body. It should have this form so that the separation and purification of the elements can occur when the fire drives one from the other, and so that each can occupy its own place where it belongs. Furthermore, it allows the **Sun** and other **planets** <note>The Sun and planets here refer to the metallic principles (Gold, Silver, etc.) acting within the vessel.</note> to exercise their operations around the elemental earth, ensuring their circular courses are neither hindered nor driven by too rapid a motion. According to all that has been said, it must have the correct proportion of roundness and height.

Regarding those things which pertain to the first purification of mineral bodies, these include: melting vessels (crucibles), tongs, bellows, cupels <note>Small, porous bowls used to separate gold or silver from base metals</note>, test-dishes, cementing vessels, ash-pots, cucurbits <term>cucurbita: a gourd-shaped glass vessel used in distillation</term>, and phials (boltheads) for **strong waters** and **aqua regia** <note>Strong waters (aquas fortes) usually refers to nitric acid; aqua regia is a mixture of nitric and hydrochloric acids used to dissolve gold.</note>, as well as those things necessary for the final "projection" <note>The act of throwing the philosopher's stone onto a base metal to complete the transmutation.</note> in the work. 

Furthermore, concerning the vessel for this work, Paracelsus speaks in another place in this manner: "For this art, it is necessary that you have a glass of right and just proportion. For if it is more spacious than is proper, the matter—that is, the humidity—is so scattered that nothing is born from it. But if it is too narrow or compressed, the 'seed' will be suffocated, so that it can produce no fruit." It is clear from the example of a plant sown in the shade or under a roof: nothing good or fruitful is produced there. Therefore, it is of great importance to turn one's mind to this glass; for an error committed in it or by it is not easily corrected; indeed, the work is not led to its desired end because of this impediment. Accordingly, for **two ounces of matter**, take **two and a half ounces** of glass or of the **philosophical egg** <note>original: "ovi philosophici"</note>—that is, let it reflect this weight. However, one must also account for the proper thickness of the glass. If these things are observed, an error is not easily committed in this part. Thus, let this be enough concerning the local instruments.
