## On the Subject or Philosophical Matter in General.

### CHAPTER VI.

We have previously spoken clearly enough about chemical instruments; now, however, hear what matter the **spagyrists** <term>spagyrists: alchemists, specifically those following the tradition of Paracelsus, who focus on the "separation and recombination" of natural substances</term> have chosen for beginning their work. After plants have been **mortified** <term>mortified: the process of destroying a substance’s external form—often through decay or burning—to release its internal essence</term>, the currents of two minerals—namely sulfur and salt—are transmuted into a mineral nature, so that perfect minerals eventually result from them. Indeed, in the mineral caverns of the earth, certain plants are found which, over a long passage of time and through continuous heat, have shed their plant-like sulfurous nature and put on a mineral one. This occurs most especially where such plants are deprived of their proper nourishment, so that they are subsequently forced to take their food from the sulfurs and salts of the earth. This continues until that which was formerly a plant turns into a perfect mineral. From this mineral condition, a certain perfect metallic essence sometimes arises, and this happens by progressing one step at a time.

But let us return to the **philosophers' stone** <note>original: "lapidem philosophorum"</note>, the matter of which is most difficult to find and to understand. For this stone, as for any other thing, the most certain method and rule of investigation to determine what they contain and what they are worth is the diligent examination of their root and seed. By this, one arrives at the knowledge of the materials. To this end, a very necessary consideration of principles is of great use: namely, by what path or by what means nature first arrived at the goal of perfection from a state of imperfection. For this consideration, it is helpful above all to have it well-proven that everything created by nature was composed of the **three first principles** <note>These are the "Tria Prima" of Paracelsus: Sulfur (the Soul/flammability), Mercury (the Spirit/volatility), and Salt (the Body/solidity).</note>—namely natural Mercury, sulfur, and salt—mixed into one, so that in some they are volatile, and in others fixed. 

Whenever bodily salt is mixed into one body with spiritual Mercury and animated sulfur, nature then finally begins to work in subterranean places (which it uses in place of its own vessels) by means of a separating fire. Through this fire, the thick and impure sulfur is separated from the pure, and is segregated from the salt of the earth and from the Mercury-clouds. Those prior parts are preserved, which nature cooks again together into one constant **earth-joined** <term>geogamicum: a term referring to a substance formed by the "marriage" of elements within the earth</term> body. This operation is held by the **Magi** <note>The "Magi" here refers to wise men or advanced practitioners of the alchemical and hermetic arts.</note> to be a mixing and joining through the union of the three: namely, of the body, the soul, and the spirit. When this union is fulfilled, a pure Mercury results from it. If this Mercury flows through subterranean passages and veins and meets with **primordial** <term>cahoico: likely derived from "Chaos," referring to a raw, unformed, or chaotic state of matter</term> sulfur, it is coagulated by that very meeting according to the condition of the sulfur. It remains, however, still volatile, so that it is hardly cooked into a metal even a hundred years later. From this comes the common saying that Mercury and sulfur are the matter of metals, as is also evident from the reports of mineral miners. Yet, this is not the common mercury, nor common sulfur...

...are the matter of metals, but the mercury and sulfur of the philosophers are incorporated and innate within the perfect metals and their forms, so that they never flee from the fire, nor are they corrupted by the force of the elements. Indeed, the **spagyric** <term>spagyric: relating to alchemical practice, specifically the art of separating and recombining substances to achieve a higher state</term> philosophers say that our Mercury is mastered through the dissolution of such a natural mixture. Under this form of words, therefore, our Mercury is to be drawn out from perfect bodies and the powers of the terrestrial planets. **Hermes** <note>referring to Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary founder of alchemy</note> asserts this very thing with these words: "The Sun and the Moon are the roots of this art." The son of Hanuel says that the **philosophers' stone** <note>original: "philosophorum lapidem"</note> is water coagulated, namely in the Sun and the Moon. From this, it appears clearer than the sun that the matter of our stone is nothing other than the Sun and the Moon.

This same point is confirmed because every like naturally brings forth and generates its like. And just as we know there are no more than two stones, the white and the red, there are also two matters for the stone: the Sun and the Moon, joined together in their own marriage, both natural and artificial. And just as we see that a man and a woman cannot generate at all without each having their own seed, in the same way, our man—the Sun—and his woman—the Moon—cannot conceive without each having their own seed and sperm, nor can they labor toward generation. From this, our philosophers concluded that a third thing is necessary: namely, the "animated seed" of both the chemical man and woman, without which they judged their entire work to be vain and empty.

This kind of sperm is Mercury, which, through the natural conjunction of both bodies of the Sun and Moon, receives their nature into itself in union. Only then, and not before, is the work fit for the meeting, the entrance, and the generation, through the masculine and feminine force and virtue. Moved by this, our philosophers said that this Mercury is composed of body, spirit, and soul, and that it has taken on the nature and properties of all the elements. For this reason, with the strongest wit and intellect, they asserted that their stone is "animal" <note>original: "animalem," here meaning "living" or "possessing a soul"</note>, even calling it their **Adam**, who carries his invisible **Eve** hidden within his body from the moment they were united by the power of the Supreme Creator of all things.

For that reason, it can rightly be said that the Mercury of the philosophers is nothing other than their most hidden, composite Mercury, and not that common variety. They spoke wisely to the wise when they said: "Whatever the wise seek is in Mercury." Almadir the philosopher says: "We extract our Mercury from one perfect body and two perfect natural conditions incorporated together; here it pushes out its perfection externally, by which it is able to resist fire, and by that external perfection, whatever imperfect thing is already enclosed within it is defended from outside attacks." By this passage of the sharpest philosophers, the matter of the stone is understood as **Adamic**, the **microcosmic limbus** <term>microcosmic limbus: the "border" or essential material of the "small world" (man), mirroring the materials of the universe</term>, and the matter of the philosophers...

...homogeneous, and unique. These sayings of the philosophers, which we mentioned previously, are truly golden and must always be held in the highest esteem, because they contain nothing superfluous and nothing weak. In summary, therefore, the matter of the **philosophers' stone** <note>original: "lapidis philosophorum"</note> is nothing other than a fiery and perfected Mercury extracted through nature and art—that is, artificially prepared—and the true hermaphrodite **Adam** <note>In alchemy, "Adam" often represents the primordial, undifferentiated matter that contains both masculine and feminine principles</note> and **microcosm** <term>microcosm: a "miniature world" that contains the qualities of the entire universe</term>. Asserting this very thing, that wisest of philosophers, **Mercurius Trismegistus** <note>original: "Mercurius Trismegistus," the legendary Egyptian sage credited with the founding of alchemy</note>, called the stone "the orphan." Our Mercury, therefore, is that very substance which contains within itself the perfections, forces, and virtues of the Sun, and which runs through the streets and houses of all the Planets; in its regeneration, it has acquired the power of things above and things below. It is also to be compared to their marriage, as is evident from the whiteness and redness gathered together within it.

The Magi, through their wisdom, affirmed that all creatures are to be led back to a single united substance. They claim that through its cleansings and purifications, this substance ascends to such subtlety and divine nature and property that it works wonders. They also considered that it would return into the earth, and through a supreme **magical separation** <note>This refers to the alchemical process of "solve et coagula" (dissolve and stays), separating the pure from the impure</note>, a certain perfect substance would emerge. Finally, through many industrious and very long preparations, it is raised from vegetable substances into mineral, from mineral into metallic, and from a perfect metallic substance, it is lifted into a **fifth essence** <term>fifth essence: also known as the "quintessence," the purest and most concentrated spirit of a substance, believed to be the material of the heavens</term> that is similar to eternity and divine, enclosing within itself the essence of all celestial and terrestrial creatures.

The Arabs and Greeks, denoting hidden meanings through secret characters and through the hieroglyphic descriptions of the Persians and Egyptians, reached secret and abstruse mysteries. Having attained these and partly understood them—while partly not—they saw certain wonders with their own eyes through experimentation. But because supernatural things lay hidden more deeply than their grasp could reach, they did not call this secret "supracelestial" according to the opinion of the Magi, but called it the "philosophers' secret," and according to the opinion of **Pythagoras** <note>The ancient Greek philosopher; alchemists often cited him as a source of mathematical and harmonic wisdom</note>, they called it "their stone."

Whoever attained this shadowed it with various enigmatic figures, deceptive similarities, comparisons, and fictional names, so that its matter would remain hidden at least from posterity, and no knowledge—or at least very little—could be had of it. Many of the ancients revealed this matter and its preparation openly enough, yet in ingenious parables and enigmatic words and figures, so that they might bar the unworthy from such a mystery of both nature and art. Nevertheless, very few—even among those suited for this art—have sought the perpetual balsam of nature and the perfect stone, because of the immense labor intertwined with difficulty that occurs everywhere during the investigation. Thus it happened that lazy and idle minds ceased from the work. However, the greedy, for whom the [hunger] of gold...

### OF METALS

The hunger for wealth and the poverty of those most wretched <note>original: "fames & argenti vilissimorum"</note> gives them the courage to persist most diligently in this work, so much so that they neglect their own lives and resources in pursuit of it. However, because God has not destined such worldly happiness for them, they have "lost both their oil and their labor" <note>An idiom meaning they have wasted their time, effort, and resources; original: "oleum perdiderunt ac operam"</note>. Therefore, there is a need for study and a most sharp wit in this matter, so that the mind of the authors writing on this art may be uncovered through various comparisons and similarities. 

So that those who are more gifted might understand to some extent, we shall bring forth a suitable comparison, by which the material of the **perpetual balsam** <term>perpetual balsam: a legendary alchemical substance believed to preserve the body from decay indefinitely</term> is prefigured. This balsam is suitable for the human body for recovering the highest health, preserving it, and driving away disease, as **Paracelsus** says. Let common and natural fire be our example: this fire is invisible to us, and therefore it must be sought and found in the air where it lies hidden, by the striking of a stone against **steel** <term>chalybs: a term for hardened steel or the tool used to strike flint</term>. Yet the fire does not reside primarily in those objects, but in the air; nor is it caught except by a dry object used as **tinder** <note>original: "fomite"</note>. 

For dryness immediately conceives a heat similar to itself, and both work together in the subject until all moisture is consumed, leaving only a dry and ashen body subject to death, deprived of the fire of life and its fuel. In no different a way must the philosophers investigate the matter in which the fuel and the fire of life are most present. These must be drawn out through preparations, so that they might increase the life of a human life that is almost failing. For just as wood that is nearly consumed—leaving behind only very few glowing coals or sparks—revives into a flame and the life of the fire when wood is added as a suitable fuel, so too in the human body does the **perpetual balsam**, when added even to a tiny remaining atom of life, rouse this into a flame and its former vigor.

Truly, the question concerns the matter in which this rousing fire lies hidden. It is neither right nor safe, says **Paracelsus**, to speak of this clearly and openly to everyone alike. Is the grace of God not sufficient for the **children of light**, to whom the faculty is given to lead the light out from the darkness of shadows, figures, and riddles? The **children of darkness** are tested by this reasoning; for even from the light, they happen to elicit nothing but mere shadows. For Nature seeks a nature similar to itself and rejoices in it; and just as iron is drawn by a **magnet**, so darkness generates darkness, but light gives birth to light. 

This stone is hard; who can extract the kernel from it? What is harder than a whetstone or steel, unless it be the **diamond** <term>adamas: often translated as diamond, but historically referring to the hardest known substance</term>? Yet even this is worn down. But by what artistry the stone of the philosophers is to be opened, so that fire and life may be supplied to us from it, we do not see. The eyes of the mind must be opened, and first it must be considered which medicine is, above all others, more suitable for human life through nature and art—so that life may be conserved and preserved in health until its predestined end, and be most safe from corruptions. No one, or at least no true **physician** <note>original: "physicus," meaning a natural philosopher or student of nature's laws</note>, will call into doubt the **metallic essences**, especially those of perfected bodies...

# OF TRANSMUTATION

...of all things which nature has produced, metals are the most durable and the least subject to decay. Accordingly, if life is the fire and heat of the natural form, united to the moisture of its matter through light (as is clear from Genesis), and if light lives nowhere more radiantly than in bodies less subject to corruption; what shall prevent the heat of fire and the **radical moisture** <term>radical moisture: the essential fluid believed to sustain life in alchemy and medieval medicine</term>—which are incorruptible within metals—from being awakened from sleep into manifest life? When joined to the organs of human life, they may revive a life that is nearly slumbering. 

For those things only sleep in metallic bodies; they rest just as a man seized by sleep lies as if dead, moving only by his breathing, but not with his body. The spirit of metals, if it is freed from the sleep of its own body, will exercise its movements and actions upon any body presented to it, just as that man does. We must judge human bodies no differently: while they are sick, the vital spirits within them fall asleep, unable to breathe truly or freely because of the drowsiness of their corrupted dwelling-place. 

Therefore, once the corruptions of darkness are removed from the body—not by an outside physician, but by nature itself, strengthened by the physician's help and the addition of the "foreign" incorruptible life of metals—these vital spirits freely exercise their movements in humans. It is no wonder, then, if miraculous cures are performed by **spagyric** <term>spagyric: alchemical medicine involving the separation and recombination of plant or mineral components</term> physicians, which are otherwise impossible through the common medicine of the Greeks. This is why the Greeks judged certain diseases to be incurable, which they themselves were unable to expel because their own medicines were "sleeping" or as if dead. 

Hence the difference between spagyric and Greek medicine is beautifully seen: the latter sleeps with the sleepers, while the former, awake and free from all slumber, rouses the sleeping faculties of life. But to return to the investigation of the matter: this can be understood no better than through the errors committed by seekers in this regard.

### *On the various errors in the investigation of the matter of the perpetual balsam, or the philosopher's stone.*

## CHAPTER VII.

Observing the great difficulty of this art, **Arnaldus** <note>Arnold of Villanova (c. 1240–1311), a famous physician and alchemist; original: "Arnaldus in suo rosario"</note> says in his *Rosary*: "They have assigned various and most hidden names to this matter of the Stone, drawn chiefly from similarities." For they called it vegetable, mineral, and animal, though not according to the literal sense, as those wise in divine secrets and experienced in the miracles of such a Stone easily know how to interpret. 

An example of this is the **Lunaria** <term>Lunaria: literally "moon-plant," used here as a code for an alchemical substance or process</term> of **Raymond Lull** <note>Ramon Llull (c. 1232–1315), a philosopher to whom many alchemical works were attributed</note>, which produces flowers of wonderful virtues that are nonetheless very familiar to philosophers. It was not the opinion of the one who gave it this name that it should be understood as some **projection** <term>projection: the final stage of alchemy, where the Stone is cast upon a base metal to transform it into gold</term> upon metals, or that a similar preparation should be made from them; rather, the hidden mind of the philosophers looks elsewhere entirely. By a similar name they called their matter **Martagon** <term>Martagon: a type of lily (Lilium martagon), used here as a pseudonym for the alchemical matter</term>, to which also from here...

# OF METALS

<note>original header: METALLORUM</note>

...they applied a hidden chemical operation, even though it signifies nothing except a certain secret similarity. A significant error also arose regarding the liquids of plants, with which very many people have attempted to coagulate Mercury, and afterwards to convert it into silver <note>original: "lunam" (the Moon), the alchemical symbol for silver</note> using fixing waters. They believed that whoever could achieve coagulation in this way, without the aid of metals, would attain the greatest mastery <note>original: "magisterium," the successful completion of the alchemist's goal</note>. 

But although the juices of some plants may achieve this, it should be judged as happening for no other reason than the resin, fatness, or earthy sulfur in which they greatly abound. This substance attracts the moisture of the Mercury and mixes with its substance, coagulating it without any actual benefit. For it has been found that the thick and external sulfur found in plants is in no way suitable for perfect **projection** <term>projection: the final stage of the alchemical work, where a small amount of the "Stone" is cast upon a base metal to transform it into gold or silver</term> in alchemy; many have discovered this not without great expense. 

Even though some thought they had coagulated Mercury with the white and milky juice of **spurge** <term>tithymallus: a genus of plants (Euphorbia) containing a caustic, milky sap</term> because of the intense and sharp heat existing within it, the effect was actually achieved by a hidden cold—the manifest opposite. For this reason, they called it **Virgin’s milk** <term>lac virginis: a common alchemical term for various white precipitates or washes</term>, yet this foundation was false. 

One should judge the juice of **celandine** <term>chelidonia: Greater Celandine, prized by alchemists because its bright orange-yellow sap suggested the presence of gold</term> no differently, even if its color deceives the eyes of men as if it were endowed with gold. Collecting this plant at a certain and determined time, they pulled it up by the roots, hoping to hunt for its soul or quintessence, from which they might make a coagulating and transforming **tincture** <term>tincture: a potent liquid or substance capable of transmuting metals or healing the body</term>. But from this, nothing arose except a foolish error. 

Others boiled this juice to a thickness (which they call "consistency") and exposed it to the Sun so that it might coagulate into a hard mass. This mass was later ground into a very fine powder, which they believed would turn Mercury into gold <note>original: "solem" (the Sun), the alchemical symbol for gold</note> by projection, though they found this to be false. Some mixed **sal ammoniac** <term>sal armoniacum: ammonium chloride, used as a flux in alchemy</term> into this powder, others added **colcothar of vitriol** <term>colcotar vitrioli: a brownish-red iron oxide residue left after the distillation of sulfuric acid from vitriol</term>, thinking that by this path they could finally reach the desired goal. 

Afterwards, they reduced these into solutions of yellow water, so that this salt might grant the tincture entry into the substance of the Mercury; yet nothing was achieved by it. Some, in place of the aforementioned things, took the juices of **smartweed** <term>persicaria: a common herb, sometimes called lady's thumb or water-pepper</term>, toad-plant, tarragon, willow leaves, spurge, **caper spurge** <term>cataputia: Euphorbia lathyris, a plant with strong purgative properties</term>, **spearwort** <term>flammula: a species of buttercup known for its acrid, burning taste</term>, and similar plants, and kept them enclosed in a glass vessel in the ashes for several days along with the Mercury itself. It happened that the Mercury was turned into ash, or rather a powder, but wrongly and with no fruit. 

For these men were deceived by the empty rumors of the common people, by which it was spread abroad that Mercury was to be coagulated without metals, as we mentioned before. Many have extracted salts, oils, sulfurs, and so on from plants, but in vain, since through these no true coagulation of Mercury, nor any perfect tincture or projection, can be made. It is by similarity alone, not by substance, that the philosophers compare their matter to a certain golden tree with its branch-

<note>original header: DE TRANSMUTAT.</note>

...they compare it to the seven metals, understanding that it encloses the seven metals within its own "seed" and that they lie hidden within it; for this reason, they said it was **vegetable**. They also called it this because, no differently than natural trees bring forth various flowers in their own season, the matter of the Stone displays the most beautiful colors openly during the production of its "flowers." Likewise, because a certain matter rises up from the **philosophical earth** like a sprout with the appearance of a dark sponge, they said the fruit of their tree tends toward heaven. Therefore, they declared that the hinge of the entire art turns upon the "vegetables of nature," and not upon physical vegetable materials. They also said this because their Stone contains soul, body, and spirit within itself, just as living plants do. 

By a not very different similarity, they called this matter **virgin’s milk** and the **blessed blood** of a rosy color, which however is suitable only for the prophets and the sons of God. From this, the **Sophists** <note>Sophistae: a derogatory term for alchemists who lacked true philosophical understanding and pursued "get-rich-quick" schemes</note> concluded that the philosophical matter consists of the blood of animals or humans; they took this opportunity because animals are nourished by vegetables. 

Some others sought the Stone in hair, in the salt of urine, and in common things. Others searched in hen’s eggs, in the lime of those eggs, in milk, and similar substances, with which they all thought they could **fix Mercury** <term>fixation: the process of turning a volatile substance, like quicksilver, into a solid, stable form that can withstand heat</term>. Some extracted salt from foul washings <note>original: "fœtido lotio," likely referring to aged urine used for its ammonia content</note>, nor were there those who failed to believe that small stones found in the body <note>referring to kidney or bladder stones</note> were the matter. Others macerated egg membranes in a very harsh lye, mixing in eggshells, attributing to these the secret of fixation for the perfecting of Mercury. 

Some, comparing the white of eggs to silver and the yolk to gold, chose them for their matter. Having mixed in common salt, sal ammoniac, and burnt tartar, they enclosed these together in glass and putrefied them in a **water bath** <note>original: "balneo maris," or bain-marie</note> until the white color turned into a deep red like blood. This they distilled into a most foul-smelling liquor, which was entirely useless for the work they sought. Others putrefied the white and yolk of eggs until a **basilisk** <term>basiliscus: a mythical king of serpents; in alchemy, it refers to a deadly or highly potent substance produced from putrefaction</term> was generated, which they burned into a deep red powder, thinking they could "tinge" <note>tingere: to transform the color (and thus the nature) of a base metal into gold</note> with it. The author of this practice was **Gilbertus Cardinalis** in his treatise. 

Many others distilled the gall of oxen and other animals, mixed with common salt, into a liquor. They believed that powders used in **cementation** <term>cementation: a process of refining gold by heating it with granulated materials to remove impurities</term> soaked in this liquor could tinge their metals through a certain mastery they call **"part with part"**; however, nothing came of it. Some, choosing **tutia** <term>tutia: zinc oxide, often used to turn copper into brass, which looks like gold</term> with certain additions like **dragon’s blood** <note>a bright red resin from the Dracaena tree</note> and other such frivolous trifles, were seduced into trying to change copper or electrum into gold. 

Others, following the "Art of the Venetians" (as they called it), enclosed twenty or so **spotted lizards** <note>original: "stelliones," a type of lizard</note> in a jar and drove them to madness through hunger, so that the starving creatures would devour one another until only one survivor remained. They fed this survivor with filings of copper or electrum, believing that this kind of animal could effect the desired transmutation through the power of digestion in its stomach alone. Finally, they burned this animal into a very red

...powder, which when they believed it to be gold, they were miserably deceived. Some finally found gold in fish known as trout, which had been cremated through melting; this occurred for no other reason than because this genus of fish is accustomed—taught by nature—to collect and swallow golden scales and sparks in rivers, which are carried there by torrents and sometimes flow down from the mountains. However, this itself happens only rarely. Such impostors are mostly found in the courts of princes. Certainly, the matter sought by the chemical philosophers is not to be found in animals; I would wish everyone to be warned of this once and for all.

Yet it should be known that the philosophers called their Stone **animal**, because in its final operations, by the power of this most noble fiery mystery, a dark and red liquor like blood drips out from its matter and its vessel drop by drop. From this they brought forth a prophecy: that in the final times, a most pure man would come to earth through whom the liberation of the world would be achieved, and he himself would emit drops of a rosy or red color and blood, by which the world would be redeemed from its stain. <note>The author is drawing a parallel between the "blood" of the Philosopher's Stone and the Passion of Christ, a common theme in 16th and 17th-century Hermetic philosophy.</note> In like manner, the "blood" of their Stone, in its own kind, liberated "leprous" metals <term>leprous metals: base metals like lead or tin, which alchemists believed were "diseased" versions of gold</term> as well as human beings from their contagious infirmities. Therefore, they did not undeservedly say that their Stone was "animal."

Regarding this, **Mercury** <note>In alchemical literature, "Mercury" is often personified as a teacher or a god-like figure revealing secrets.</note> speaks to **King Calid** <note>Referring to Khalid ibn Yazid, an Umayyad prince traditionally credited with being one of the first Muslim alchemists.</note> in this manner: "This mystery," he says, "is permitted only to the prophets of God to know, which is why it is called the **animal stone**. For in the blood of this stone lies its soul; it is also composed of body, spirit, and soul." For a similar reason, they called it their **microcosm**, because it possesses the likeness of all things in the entire world; and for that reason again they say it is an "animal," just as **Plato** calls the great world <note>the Macrocosm</note> an animal. 

Ignorant people followed, believing the Stone to be triple and secret in three distinct kinds: namely, vegetable, animal, and mineral. Because of this, they sought it even in minerals <insert>separately</insert>. But this opinion is far from the view of the philosophers; for they assert that their Stone is **uniformly** vegetable, animal, and mineral <note>meaning it contains the properties of all three kingdoms of nature at once</note>. 

It should be noted further that nature has distributed its mineral seed into various kinds: namely into sulphurs, salts, boraxes, nitres, ammoniacs, alums, arsenics, black-inks <note>original: "atramenta," usually referring to vitriols or ferrous sulfates</note>, vitriols, tutty <note>zinc oxide</note>, hematite, orpiment, realgar, magnesias, cinnabar, antimony, talc, cachimias <note>impure metallic ores or slag-like minerals</note>, marcasites, etc. In all of these, nature has not yet fulfilled our matter. Although in some of these mentioned species, it sometimes reveals itself in a wonderful appearance regarding the transmutation of imperfect metals. Indeed, long experience and practice with fire show manifold transmutation in the matter of minerals—not only from one color to another, but even from one essence to another, and from imperfection to perfection. But although nature itself sometimes, through these mineral means, of such a kind...

-># ON TRANSMUTATION #<-
<meta>catchword: ...ations and</meta>

...even if a philosopher performs demonstrations involving many intervening preparations, they do not, for that reason, intend for the matter of their Stone to proceed primarily from any of the intermediate minerals, even though they call their Stone "mineral." Taking the opportunity from this name, the **Sophists** <note>In alchemical literature, "Sophists" refers to "false alchemists" or "puffers" who took metaphorical instructions literally and failed to find the true secret.</note> have persecuted **Mercury** itself with various tortures: some by sublimations, coagulations, precipitations, and with mercurial "strong waters" <term>strong waters: *aquae fortes*, usually referring to nitric acid or other corrosive mineral acids</term>, and so on. All of these are erroneous paths to be avoided, along with the other preparations of minerals used by the Sophists, such as the purifications and fixations of spirits and metals. 

Furthermore, the many preparations of the Stone—indeed, all those described regarding minerals in this manner, such as those by *Geber*, *Albert surnamed the Great*, and similar authors—are merely sophisticated <note>original: *sophisticæ*; here meaning deceptive or artificial</note> purifications, cementations, sublimations, distillations, rectifications, circulations, putrefactions, conjunctions, solutions, ascensions, coagulations, calcinations, and "incerations" <term>inceration: the process of adding liquid to a substance until it reaches a soft, wax-like consistency</term> that are utterly useless. This applies whether they are performed in a tripod, a **reverberatory furnace**, an **athanor** <term>athanor: a "philosopher's furnace" designed to maintain a constant heat over long periods</term>, a melting-vessel, an acid-bath, or using dung, ash, sand, and the like; as well as in a cucurbit, a **pelican** <term>pelican: a circulating distillation vessel with two side-arms that feed back into the body, resembling a bird pecking its breast</term>, a retort, a vial, a fixation-vessel, and others of that kind. 

The same judgment must be made regarding the sublimations of Mercury through mineral spirits to produce the "white" or the "red" <note>The "White" and "Red" refer to the two main stages of the Alchemical Great Work: the *albedo* (silver) and *rubedo* (gold).</note>, such as through vitriol, saltpeter (or another salt), alum, saffron of Mars <term>saffron of Mars: *crocus Martis*, a red iron oxide powder</term>, etc. Concerning all of these, *John of Rupescissa* tells false fables in his treatise on the white and red philosopher's stone; these are all fictitious dreams along with others, miserably leading good and simple men astray. 

One must also flee those specific "sophistical" methods of *Geber*, such as the seven-fold sublimations, or "mortifications," as well as the "revivifications" of Mercury with preparations made through **Salt of Urine** or through the "sepulcher" <note>original: *sepulcrum*; likely a reference to a specific type of heat-retaining vessel or burial in dung for warmth</note>, every one of which is completely false regarding the Stone. Certain others, having attempted to "fix" Mercury with the sulfurs of minerals and metals, were greatly deceived. I have nevertheless seen Mercury brought into a metallic body by this art through such "fixations," mimicking and representing good silver in every likeness and in every way; yet, when put to the test of the **test** or the **cupel** <term>cupel: a shallow, porous dish used in assaying to separate precious metals from base metals like lead</term>, it appeared as the fraud it truly was. 

Some of the Sophists attempted to wring out a "fixed oil" from this Mercury, sublimated seven times and dissolved as many times, using the medium of "strong waters," by which they hoped to bring any imperfect metals to perfection; but they were forced to abandon that work as fruitlessly as the rest. Others purified **vitriol** seven times by calcination, solution, and coagulation, and with the addition of two parts **sal ammoniac** and by sublimation, so that it might be dissolved into a "white water." To this they added a third part of "living" <note>original: *vivi*; i.e., quicksilver or liquid mercury</note> Mercury, so that it might be coagulated by that water; afterwards, they sublimated the Mercury from the said vitriol and sal ammoniac so many times that it turned into a hard stone. They claimed that this, conceived from vitriol, was the **Red Sulfur of the Philosophers**, the solution of which...

...through various sublimations and coagulations, but in the final **projection** <note>The act of "throwing" the Philosopher’s Stone onto base metals to effect transmutation.</note>, nothing was achieved. Others coagulated **Mercury** <note>Quicksilver</note> using alum water, turning it into a hard mass resembling alum, which they then tried to "fix" <term>fixation: the process of making a volatile substance stable under heat so it does not evaporate</term> using "sharp waters" <note>original: *aquis acutissimis*; likely strong mineral acids</note>, but to no avail. The **Sophists** <note>False alchemists or those who lack true understanding.</note> presume to have many methods for fixing Mercury; however, they labor in vain, as it contains nothing perfect or constant. Thus, they fruitlessly add other minerals to it through their deceptive processes; by these additions, the Mercury is only stirred to a greater "wickedness" <note>In alchemical terms, "malitia" or wickedness refers to the volatile, corrosive, or unstable nature of the substance.</note>, becoming more "living" <note>More volatile and difficult to capture.</note> and impure rather than perfect. Therefore, one should not seek the "matter" of the philosophers from Mercury, as it is an imperfect thing. Even if it could be brought to perfection, it would be extremely difficult—if not impossible—using the methods of the Sophists, since it contains nothing that can be forced or stirred into a state of perfection.

Some have taken **arsenic** that has been sublimated several times and dissolved and coagulated many times in oil of tartar; they claimed to fix this in order to turn **copper** into **silver**. This process brought about nothing but a certain "sophistic whitening" <note>original: *dealbationem*; a surface-level bleaching that makes a metal look like silver without changing its internal nature.</note>. Indeed, this substance can by no means be fixed unless the "tingeing spirit" within it is properly understood—a point on which nearly all philosophers have "dozed off," wasting their efforts trying to produce something good from arsenic. Whoever remains ignorant of this spirit should have no hope of fixing the arsenic or attributing any power to it through other means to achieve the perfection of transmutation. For this reason, I make it known to all who spend their labor on this, that the "whitening" mentioned above is derived from a false foundation; by it, copper is falsely whitened on the surface only, and not truly changed. 

The Sophists have even mixed **Venus** <note>The alchemical name for Copper.</note>, thus masked and painted, with twice its weight of **Luna** <note>The alchemical name for Silver.</note>, and sold the mixture to goldsmiths and minters. In the end, they transformed themselves into counterfeiters—not only those who sold it, but even those who bought it. Some of the Sophists took **red arsenic** instead of the white variety, and this too resulted in the same false art, for however it is prepared, it displays nothing but a surface whiteness.

Others have gone further with **common sulfur**. While it was still yellow, they cooked it in vinegar, lye, or very sharp urine for a day and a night until a white color emerged. Afterward, they raised it <note>Distilled or sublimated it.</note> from common lime and eggshell lime; they cooked and sublimated it many times. Nevertheless, it always remained combustible, even though it was white. With this, they tried in vain to fix raw Mercury into **gold**. However, a most beautiful **cinnabar** <note>A bright red mineral (mercuric sulfide) used as a pigment.</note> resulted from the process—the best I have ever seen. Thinking they could fix this through "cementation" <term>cementation: a process of heating a metal with a powdered preparation to change its properties</term> and fixation using "oil of sulfur," it gained a bit of the desired appearance, but the outcome was quite different from what the work itself required. Others reduced common sulfur into the form of a "liver" <note>original: *formam hepatis*; likely "liver of sulfur" (potassium polysulfide).</note> by mixing it with linseed oil, oil of bricks, or olive oil, cooking it in vinegar, and afterwards upon a marble stone...

...even if one makes demonstrations through many intervening preparations, the philosophers do not, for that reason, intend for the "matter" of their Stone to proceed primarily from any of the intermediate minerals, even though they call their Stone "mineral." Their methods of **cementation, sublimation, distillation, rectification, circulation, putrefaction, conjunction, solution, ascension, coagulation, calcination,** and **inceration** <note>the process of softening a substance to a wax-like consistency</note> are entirely useless. This remains true whether they are performed in a tripod, a reverberatory furnace, an **athanor** <note>a furnace designed to maintain a uniform heat over long periods</note>, a melting-vessel, a vinegar-bath, dung, ash, sand, and the like, or in a **cucurbit** <note>a gourd-shaped glass vessel</note>, a **pelican** <note>a circulatory distillation vessel with two side-arms</note>, a retort, a vial, a fixatory, and other such tools. 

The same judgment must be made concerning the sublimations of Mercury through mineral spirits into the "white" and the "red" <note>The *albedo* and *rubedo*, the final two stages of the Great Work.</note>—such as through vitriol, saltpeter (or some other salt), alum, saffron of Mars <note>iron oxide</note>, and so forth. Regarding all of these, **John of Rupescissa** <note>A 14th-century Franciscan alchemist known for his work on the "quintessence."</note> falsely tells tales in his treatise on the *White and Red Stone of the Philosophers*. These are all fabricated dreams which, along with others, wretchedly lead good and simple men astray. 

One must also flee those specific sophistic tricks of Geber, such as the "sevenfold sublimations" or "mortifications," as well as the "revivifications" of Mercury with preparations made through the salt of urine or the "sepulcher" <note>original: *sepulcrum*; a method of gentle heating by burying a vessel in warm horse manure</note>, every one of which is utterly false regarding the Stone. Certain others, having tried to "fix" Mercury with the sulfurs of minerals and metals, were highly deceived. 

Nevertheless, I have seen Mercury brought into a metallic body through such fixations in this art, mimicking and representing good silver in all respects and by all means; yet, in the test of the **cupel** <term>cupellation: a refining process where ores are heated to separate precious metals from base metals like lead</term>, its falsity was exposed and appeared exactly as it was. Some of the Sophists attempted to wring out a "fixed oil" from that Mercury (having sublimated it seven times and dissolved it as many times) by means of strong waters, by which they hoped to bring any imperfect metals to perfection; but they were forced to abandon that work as frustrated. 

Others have purged **vitriol** <note>sulfate minerals, often green or blue</note> seven times through calcination, solution, and coagulation, and with the addition of two parts of **sal ammoniac** <note>ammonium chloride</note> and sublimation, so that it might be dissolved into a "white water." To this they added a third part of live Mercury, so that the water might be coagulated; and they afterwards sublimated the Mercury from the said vitriol and sal ammoniac so many times that it turned into a hard stone. They affirmed that this substance, conceived from vitriol, was the "red sulfur" of the philosophers, the solution of which—

For even if the operation of these is most powerful in the nature of things, nevertheless their true process is known to very few to this day. One must also abstain from the sophistic preparations of common **Mercury**, **arsenic**, **sulfur**, and other similar things, through **sublimation** <note>turning a solid into vapor with heat</note>, **descent** <note>a form of distillation where the vapor is forced downward</note>, and **fixation** <term>fixation: the process of making a volatile substance stable under heat</term>, with vinegar, saltpeter <note>potassium nitrate</note>, tartar, vitriol, and **sal ammoniac** <note>ammonium chloride</note>: at least in that way or method taught by the books of the Sophists. Likewise, flee the sophistic **tinctures** <term>tincture: in alchemy, a substance capable of infusing its color or quality into a metal to transform it</term> derived from **marcasites** <note>iron sulfide minerals</note> and **saffron of Mars** <note>original: "croco Martis," a reddish iron oxide</note>, and from that sophistication which is called "part with part," of "fixed silver," and similar trifles. For even if they show some superficial appearance of truth (and indeed, this "fixation of silver" is a matter of little labor and effort), nevertheless, such a progression of preparation is void and invalid.

Let us now hear what the true **matter** of the **Philosophers' Stone** is. In the art of **ferments** and **fermentations** (says **Paracelsus** <note>The famous 16th-century Swiss-German physician and alchemist</note>), the philosophers have labored most, which seems the most important among other arts; regarding which, some have even made a vow to God and the philosophers that they would never reveal the secret <note>original: "arcanum"</note> of that matter, except through likenesses and parables. Yet **Hermes** <note>Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary Egyptian sage and father of alchemy</note>, in the seventh book of his treatises, reveals ferments most clearly, saying they consist of nothing but their own dough <note>original: "pasta"</note>: furthermore, that the ferment whitens the confection, prevents scorching, and utterly slows the flow of the tincture, strengthens the bodies, and increases the union. He also says it is the key and the end of the work, concluding that the ferment is nothing else but a dough, just as there is nothing for the **sun** <note>gold</note> but the sun, and nothing for the **moon** <note>silver</note> but the moon. Others affirm that the ferment is the **soul**, which, unless it has been properly and rightly prepared from the **mastery** <term>magisterium: the "masterwork" or the completed alchemical substance</term>, can effect nothing. Some zealots of this art have sought their ferments in various primary and intermediate minerals, but they discovered they had run in vain. Because the substance which is sought is the same as that from which it must be drawn. It must be noted, therefore, that such fermentations by no means succeed according to the wish of the seekers, but rather 

->only<- 

through natural concordances and gradual successes.

## *On the preparation of the spagyric matter in general.*
### CHAPTER VIII.

Nature first requires of the craftsman that the **philosophical Adam** <note>original: "philosophicus Adam"; a term for the "Prime Matter" or the raw, unrefined state of the material used to make the Stone</note> be brought into a **Mercurial substance**, and finally be born as the eastern **solar** and **lunar stone** <note>the gold and silver versions of the Philosopher's Stone</note>. Furthermore, it must be noted that those common preparations of **Geber**, **Albertus Magnus**, **Thomas Aquinas**, **Rupescissa**, **Polydore**, and their like, are nothing other than certain "particular" solutions and **calcinations** <term>calcination: the process of heating a substance to high temperatures to reduce it to powder</term> which do not pertain at all to our "universal" work; for this work requires only the most secret fire of the philosophers. Therefore, let fire and **azoth** <term>azoth: the "universal solvent" or the essential spirit of Mercury believed to be the soul of all matter</term> be sufficient for you.

When you hear the Philosophers make mention of certain preparations—such as **putrefaction** <note>the symbolic "rotting" or breakdown of the matter</note>, distillation, **sublimation**, **ceration** <term>ceration: the process of softening a hard substance until it has the consistency of wax</term>, **fixation** <term>fixation: making a volatile substance stable so it no longer evaporates under heat</term>, and so on—you must understand that in their "universal" work, Nature herself fulfills all these operations within the said matter. It is not the work of a human operator, but occurs only within the **philosophical vessel**, using a fire that is like nature’s own and not a common flame. For the **White** and the **Red** <note>the two main stages of the Stone's perfection</note> spring forth from a single root without any intermediary. The matter is dissolved by itself and joined by itself; it turns white and turns red; it becomes saffron-colored and black by its own power; it marries itself and conceives within itself. It must therefore be boiled, roasted, and melted: it ascends and descends. Indeed, all these operations are a single process, performed by fire alone.

Some philosophers, however, have dissolved the **body of the sun** <note>gold</note> through a highly refined "essence of wine" <note>pure alcohol</note> and rendered it volatile so that it might ascend through the **alembic** <note>a distillation apparatus</note>, thinking this was the true volatile matter of the philosophers—but it is not. Even if it is a secret not to be despised to bring a perfect metallic body into a volatile and spiritual substance, they nevertheless err in the "separation of the elements." This process used by the monks—namely **Raymond Lully**, **Richard the Englishman**, **Rupescissa**, and others—is erroneous. For they believed they could separate gold in this way into a subtle spiritual and elemental power, and afterwards join each part separately through **circulation** and **rectification** back into one; but they did so in vain. 

Indeed, even if one element were somehow separated from another, anything separated in this manner can be further separated again. These parts can by no means come back together into one through circulation in a **pelican** <term>pelican: a specialized alchemical flask with two curved necks that feed distilled vapors back into the base, used for constant circulation</term> or by distillation; instead, they always remain as a certain volatile matter and "**potable gold**" <note>original: "aurum potabile"; a medicinal liquid gold</note>, as they call it. The reason why these men could not reach their goal is this: Nature by no means wishes to be pulled apart in this way, nor to be separated by human "disjunctions" using earthly glassware and instruments. She alone knows her own operations and the weights of the elements, whose separations, purifications, and joinings she executes without the help of any operator.

<summary>This page argues that true alchemy relies on the internal, natural transformations of matter ("Nature herself") within a sealed vessel, rather than the manual chemical experiments of medieval scholars like Lully or Aquinas. It emphasizes that the Philosopher's Stone creates itself through a single, unified process of heat rather than multiple human-led steps.</summary>

...or of manual skill, provided the matter is contained in the **secret fire** and in a hidden vessel. Therefore, the separation of the elements is impossible by human hand; though it may appear to happen, it is not true. This remains the case regardless of what is said about **Raymond Lull** <note>a famous 13th-century polymath and reputed alchemist</note> and his noble **Golden Angel** <note>original: "Angelicus aureus"; a gold coin allegedly produced by Lull through alchemical transmutation for the King of England</note> which he is falsely thought to have manufactured. For nature itself possesses within it its own separator, which joins together again that which it separates without human help. Nature knows the proportion of every element best of all, and not man—despite what writers may fabulate in their erroneous, frivolous, and false recipes regarding this "volatile gold" of theirs. 

This is the opinion of the philosophers: when they have placed their matter in the more secret fire, it is cherished on all sides by this "philosophical heat" so that, beginning to pass through **corruption** <note>the breakdown of the original form</note>, it turns black. They call this operation **putrefaction** <term>putrefaction: the symbolic "rotting" or decomposition of the matter, indicating the death of the old form</term>, and they name this blackness the **raven’s head** <note>original: "caput corvi"; a traditional alchemical term for the *nigredo* or black stage of the process</note>. The rising and falling of this matter they call their **distillation**, ascension, and descension; they say that the drying out is **coagulation** <term>coagulation: the process by which a liquid or dispersed substance becomes solid or semi-solid</term>, and the whitening is **calcination** <term>calcination: here used to mean the purification of the matter until it reaches a white state</term>. And because the matter becomes fluid and soft by continued heat, they make mention of **ceration** <term>ceration: the process of softening a substance until it has the consistency of wax</term>. When, however, it ceases to rise and remains liquid at the bottom, they call this **fixation** <term>fixation: making a volatile substance stable so it no longer evaporates under heat</term>. In this manner, therefore, the names of the philosophical operations are to be understood, and not otherwise. Having thus explained the instruments and the matter with its **ferments** <note>substances that "leaven" the matter to trigger transformation</note>, we must come in order to the weights, without which our work is in vain.

## *On the proportion of the matter and form of the spagyric stone.*

### CHAPTER IX.

The formal part of our "offspring" is the **Mercury of the philosophers** and the spirit or **tincture of the sun** <note>the essential "soul" or coloring principle of gold</note>; the "living" part, however, is the other material part. Accordingly, the composition of this most sacred **Adamic stone** <note>original: "lapis Adamicus"; a reference to the primordial, perfect matter of the first man</note> is made from the **Adamic Mercury** of the wise, joined with their **woman Eve** <note>original: "Evena muliere"; symbolic names for the masculine/fixed and feminine/volatile principles</note> through marriage and the union of one Mercury and the other into a third. There is, therefore, a single matter of the philosophers consisting of a spiritual, a corporal, and an animal Mercury. The corporal Mercury is the subject of the tinctures, while the spiritual and animal provide the medium for joining them. 

Truly, in the conjunction of these, the due proportion must be observed; for if more of one than the other is taken, the seed cast into the field will either be suffocated—so that it cannot live long enough to be perfected by the fire united with the Mercury of the philosophers—or, on the other hand, if there is too little, it cannot be dissolved at all, which will result in it being dried up and bringing forth no fruit. Therefore, listen to how much of the one and the other should be taken, lest the whole work be destroyed through ignorance of this proportion. Let one part of the "female" be taken to two parts of "earth," or three to four, and you will not err; rather, the work will be led to the desired end in this part, provided...

...the rest is moderated. Elsewhere **Paracelsus** <note>Philippus Aureolus Theophrastus Bombastus von Hohenheim (1493–1541), a Swiss physician and alchemist who pioneered the use of minerals in medicine</note> speaks of this proportion in this manner: Weight must be observed in a twofold way—the first is natural, the other is artificial. The natural weight achieves its effect in the earth through nature and "concordance," about which **Arnaldus** <note>Arnaldus de Villa Nova (c. 1240–1311), a famous physician and reputed alchemist</note> wrote. If more or less is added to the earth than nature allows, the **soul** <note>the vital, animating principle of the matter</note> is suffocated, and no fruit is perceived, nor any **fixation** <term>fixation: the process of making a volatile substance stable so that it does not evaporate when heated</term>. The same is to be judged regarding water: if more or less of it is taken, it will bring no less unsuitable damage; an excess of it renders the matter excessively moist, while a lack of it makes it drier and harder than is right. If too much **air** is present, too much of the **tincture** <term>tincture: the spiritual essence or "color" that has the power to transform and ennoble a substance</term> is imprinted; if too little, a pale body will emerge. Likewise, if the fire is too fierce, the matter is scorched; if it is too weak, it has no power to dry out, nor to dissolve, nor to heat the other elements. In these things the elemental weight consists. But the **artificial weight** is most hidden, since it is contained within the magical art of proportions. Between the spirit, the soul, and the body (say the philosophers), the weight is established with **sulphur** acting as the ruler of the work: for the soul desires sulphur above all else, and necessarily observes it by reason of weight. Understand it in this way: our matter is united to **fixed red sulphur**, to which a third part of the governance is committed until the final degree, so that it may perfect the operation of the **Stone** <note>the Philosopher's Stone</note> into infinity, and persist with it together with its fire. Thus it consists of a weight equal to the matter itself, in all things and through all things, without any variation of any degree of **transmutation**. Therefore, after the matter has been adapted and mixed in its proportioned weight, it must be closed most securely in the **vessel of the philosophers** <note>a sealed glass flask, often called the "Philosophical Egg"</note> with its own seal, and committed to the **secret fire**. In this fire, the **philosophical Sun** <note>original: "Sol philosophicus"; a metaphor for the perfected gold or the Stone itself</note> will arise and rise up; it will illuminate all things that await its light and have desired it with great hope. But because these things cannot be rightly understood unless one has a perfect knowledge of the **spiritual tinctures** in metals, we must also discuss these.

It is not consumed by it, nor scorched like all the others; rather, it shines and is made ever more clear. It is subject to no corruption, nor to heat or cold or other qualities, which bring no detriment to it in any way. Thus it happens that the body it once inhabits is protected and defended from all accidental corruptions and diseases, so that the body may likewise endure the fire along with it with-

[...without any] injury. A body does not possess virtues of this kind from itself, but from its spirit alone, which accomplishes this very thing. It is certain that the body of the **Sun** <note>original: "solis"; in alchemy, the Sun represents Gold</note> is **Mercury** <term>Mercury: here referring to the "philosophical mercury" or the fundamental metallic principle of liquidity and shine</term>, which nevertheless can by no means endure fire, but very quickly flees from it. Since, therefore, it exists in gold and persists constantly without fleeing, there is no doubt that such **fixation** <term>fixation: the process by which a volatile substance is made stable and resistant to fire</term> occurred to it because of the spirit. What role and office it holds in Mercury, what will hinder it from performing that same role when freed from its own body and taken into the human body? Indeed, what would stop it from rendering the human body safe from all corruptions, diseases, and whatever accidents, and bestowing a long and healthy life, just as it once did for our first parents? <note>A reference to the biblical patriarchs, like Methuselah, believed to have lived for hundreds of years</note>

For this reason, those who hope and believe in such opinions happen to be both defrauded and led into error.

Thus far concerning the spirit of the Sun and its **tincture** <term>tincture: the spiritual essence or "color" that has the power to transform and ennoble a substance</term>; now let us see what the **Moon** <note>original: "luna"; in alchemy, the Moon represents Silver</note> possesses. In this, a white tincture lies hidden, just as the red one does in the Sun; it is also born from a subtle spirit, yet one not as perfect as that of the Sun. Nevertheless, it far surpasses the tinctures of the other subsequent metals in purity and constancy. For **Lead** <note>original: "Plumbum"</note>, when heated by fire, consumes all other metals and even itself, except for the Sun and the Moon, to which it brings no harm. <note>This describes the process of "cupellation," where lead is used to purify gold and silver because it oxidizes and carries away impurities while leaving the precious metals intact.</note>

Since, therefore, the spirit of the Moon is able to protect the body it has once put on—namely, Mercury—from the injury of fire and other accidents, and to make it constant, it is easy to conclude from this: if it achieves this in the so unstable and volatile body of Mercury, how much more effectively will it work when freed from its body and cast into the human body? Will it not also protect the human body from any corruptions and diseases? Truly, whatever it performs in Mercury, it can do the same in the human body, preserving a long and healthy life and driving away all diseases that fall under its power, according to the degree assigned to it by nature.

Indeed, the more sublime, subtle, and perfect any medicine is, the more perfectly it also cures in its own kind. Accordingly, those physicians are quite unrefined who have founded their art primarily on corruptible medicines, such as vegetables; nevertheless, they attempt to achieve permanent and fixed cures for the most unstable conditions using these means, which is impossible for them to undertake. But what shall I say of these men? They have learned nothing else in their academies until now. Therefore, rather than learning and studying from the beginning, they judge that they must remain with their ancient and masked studies.

The spirit of **Venus** <note>original: "Veneris"; in alchemy, Venus represents Copper</note> arises from a mixture of coarser elements than the preceding ones, wherefore it is subject to them; yet it is more perfect than the other subsequent spirits and tinctures, which it surpasses in fixation and constancy. Copper, whether melted by fire or glowing hot, is not as easily consumed or evaporated as the metals that follow it, nor is it so quickly corrupted by air or moisture as **Mars** <note>original: "Mars"; in alchemy, Mars refers to Iron</note>; for this metal persists more fixedly in the fire. It would be safer, however, to use only the spirits of the perfect metals, were it not that gold and silver are too precious for any common sick person to afford such medicine; or rather, these are more difficult to prepare than the talent and industry of every physician allows. Thus it happens that the physician is forced to do what he can and what he has learned—namely, to treat with vegetables and animals. Yet these are surpassed and left far behind by minerals, no matter how crudely prepared <note>original: "rudi Minerva," a Latin idiom for something done without much art or refinement</note>.

Nevertheless, it surpasses any other metals in hardness and dryness, and it destroys and breaks apart mixtures, perfect and imperfect alike. In the same way, it twists the members of the human body when applied to a disease other than what is appropriate. But for external ulcers, for which it is indeed suited, this spirit when taken cures from the root, removing every cause of contagion equal to its own degree, though not those superior to it. Therefore, it does not lack the powers and virtues granted to it by God and nature in its own special property.

The **Spirit of Jupiter** <note>original: "Spiritus Jovis"; Jupiter is the alchemical name for Tin</note> is born from a white and pale substance of fire; it is unworkable by the hammer by nature, though not as much as Mars. By mixing with others, it corrupts and breaks them, especially **the Moon** <note>original: "lunam"; Silver</note>, so that it can hardly be separated from it; nor does the silver become workable again unless the tin is entirely removed with great labor. It works a similar effect in other metals except for **Saturn** <note>Lead</note>. In the same way that it acts upon its own kind, it acts when taken into another, such as a human being: [distorting] the limbs...

# OF METALS.

Copper, <note>original: "cuprum"</note> whether liquefied by fire or glowing hot, is not so easily consumed or vanished as the metals that follow, nor is it as quickly corrupted by the air or by moisture as **Mars** <note>the alchemical name for Iron</note>; for it persists more fixedly in the fire. Whatever it works for the preservation of its "Mercury" body, it performs the same in the human body, according to the degree granted to it by nature: for it equally protects wounds and ulcers from the accidents that could happen to them from the air or fire; furthermore, it drives out all diseases that are contained under its degree or dominion, and plucks them out entirely by the root. Conversely, it tears apart any metals with which it is mixed—even the bodies of the perfect metals—so that they do not admit the hammer, nor do they remain workable until they are freed from it. It works in no different a way in the human body, especially if it is taken for some disease for which it was not destined by nature according to its degree: it brings about contractions of the limbs. For this reason, let the physician first learn well which diseases the spirits and tinctures <term>tincture: in alchemy, a concentrated spiritual essence or medicine that can "color" or transform a substance</term> of the imperfect metals suit, before he experiments at the peril of his patients.

Yet it would be safer to use only the spirits of the perfect metals, were it not that gold and silver are too precious for just any sick person to afford such medicine, or rather, the preparation of these is more difficult than the genius and industry of every physician can bear; thus it happens that the physician is forced to do what he can and what he has learned, namely to treat with vegetables and animals. These are surpassed and left far behind by minerals, even if the minerals are prepared with only simple skill. <note>original: "rudi Minerva"; a Latin idiom for rough or unrefined workmanship</note>

The tincture of **Mars** consists of a combustible and thick mixture of elements, but beyond the other imperfect metals, it has a harder and less workable substance; it is also barely fusible, and corruptible by the air and water, by which it is consumed through verdigris or rust, and most easily by fire. Nevertheless, in hardness and dryness, it surpasses any other metals, which it destroys and breaks apart by mixture, the perfect no less than the imperfect. In the same way, it twists the members of the human body when it is applied to a disease other than what is proper. But for external ulcers, for which it is indeed suitable, this spirit, once taken up, cures from the root, removing every cause of contagion equal to its own degree, though not superior. Therefore, it does not lack the powers and virtues granted to it by God and nature in its own special property.

The spirit of **Jove** <note>the alchemical name for Tin</note> is born from a white and pale substance of fire, naturally unworkable by the hammer—though not as much as **Mars**—and by mixture it corrupts and breaks apart other metals, especially **Luna** <note>Silver</note>, so that it can hardly be separated from it; nor is the silver workable unless the tin is entirely removed with great labor. It works a similar thing in other metals except in **Saturn** <note>Lead</note>. That which it works in its own kind, it works similarly when taken externally into another, such as into a human: it [tortures] the limbs...

...it tortures with dire sufferings and pains, and eats away at the body with the greatest heat, so that the natural faculties are unable to function. Yet, when applied externally to fistulas, cancers, carbuncles, and similar conditions—which do not exceed the degree of its own nature—it is an excellent remedy, rooting out every evil.

The spirit of **Saturn** <note>the alchemical name for Lead</note> arises from a dark, shadowy, and cold mixture of elements; because of this, it lasts less time in the fire than the others and disappears more quickly along with its body. It cleanses the bodies of **Sol** <note>Gold</note> and **Luna** <note>Silver</note>, and in the trial of the fire <note>original: "examine," referring to the process of cupellation or assaying</note>, it purges them of every excess, yet it leaves them shattered and brittle after this "bath." In a similar way, if taken internally by a human, it twists the limbs with even greater pain than tin or iron; however, because a spirit of this kind is thickened by a cold much more intense than others, it does not agitate the body as sharply. Nevertheless, it possesses great power and ability for healing fistulas, cancer, and other ulcers of this kind, as well as for removing many defects, just as it draws out any impurities from gold and silver. Truly, unless it leaves the body at the same time as the disease after the operations are completed, it will bring far more harm than benefit. Therefore, the physician wishing to use this spirit should first know which diseases it suits and for what purpose it is naturally intended in medicines.

Finally, the spirit of **Mercury** <note>Quicksilver</note>, since it has no determined or certain form of its own, is subject to all others that come before it, just as wax is shaped by a seal. Indeed, it receives into itself whatever spirit is applied to it: thus, when the spirit of **Sol** <note>Gold</note> is impressed upon it, it passes into gold; if the spirit of **Luna** <note>Silver</note>, it passes into silver; and so with the rest. It puts on the nature of whichever metal's spirit it embraces. Therefore, in relation to its body, it is compared to the other aforementioned spirits as a wife is to her husband—not by a simple physical mixture, but when the spirit has been drawn out from its metal and cast into the Mercury after preparation; only then does it reveal its transmutation. In the same way, the "dead" female of the metal—like an uncultivated field or earth—if it is soaked or vivified by the <term>philosophical plow: a metaphor for the alchemical tools or acidic "waters" used to break down and prepare the base matter</term> (which "female" part remains fixed and incorruptible in this work), it is united by the aforementioned bodily spirit through the degrees of fire into that spirit's nature and substance. This occurs together with the dead body of the metal, which can by no means happen with the crude, unprepared spirit of Mercury. 

And even if the body of Gold exists as Mercury or "living silver" <note>original: "argentum vivum"</note> and is fixed, common Mercury is nevertheless not yet fixed, nor has it yet "risen again," even if it has been mortified <note>chemically "killed" or lost its metallic form</note>. For the **resurrection of metals** is an immortal regeneration, and the medium through which such <term>tinctures: concentrated spiritual essences of metals used to "color" or transform other substances</term> are advanced toward their own generation. Therefore, it cannot be united with dead bodies for the purpose of fixation, but only with extracted spirits—those called "bodily" spirits—which are subject to metals in the same way common Mercury is subject to all metallic spirits. For the crude spirit of Mercury by no means generates this tincture in substance, no more than a concubine produces legitimate offspring. Likewise concerning Mercury...

### *On the specific preparations of the matter of the stone, and*
### *first through Electrum.*
### CHAPTER XI.

Nothing exists in the nature of things that lacks its own form: for everything that exists is generated, multiplied, and destroyed in its own concordance <note>a state of harmony or proper proportional relationship between elements</note>, and it reveals its own beginning, from which it is perceived through the senses that that very thing which was at the beginning must also be at the end. Whatever is interrupted seems to be something like an imperfection which nature urges toward generation by accident. Since, however, accidents can be removed by Vulcan <note>the Roman god of fire, used here to represent alchemical fire or the art of chemistry</note> so that they have no effect, nature can to that extent be improved, which is what happens in that stone. For if you wish to fashion this from true matter (which you have easily learned from the preceding instructions), it will be necessary above all to remove superfluities, so that it may be formed, multiplied, and increased in its own concordance. Indeed, Nature has left it imperfect, since she herself does not form the stone, but only its matter, from which it is quite impossible for that to be made which is made after its preparation through the stone, because accidents hinder the matter. Therefore, the matter without preparation, in respect to the stone, is nothing but a semi-perfect thing, not consisting in any concordance that could be called perfect, or suitable for the health of the human body.

Let the Microcosm <note>literally "the little world," referring to the human being as a reflection of the greater universe</note> be an example: here, through its architect, only a man was fashioned, not a complete work, since he does not stand in his own concordance, but is only a medium until a woman <note>original: "virago," here referring to the biblical Eve created from Adam</note> similar to himself is added, fashioned from him; then at last they produce a whole and complete work. Both are earth, and two earths constitute one whole human, who can be increased and grown, once this formed concordance is brought about. In the same way, the Philosopher's Stone (which must restore man no less than the metals themselves), when purged and liberated from superfluous accidents, and placed in its own concordance, works certain miracles in all infirmities; otherwise, the labor undertaken in the philosophical work of the balsam <note>a healing or preservative essence</note> and the perpetual stone outside of concordance is in vain. Therefore, so that it may come to its concordance, it must be reduced to the first matter, whereby the male can act upon the female, and its manifest part <note>the visible qualities</note> may be hidden, and this manifest part may become... so that the seed of both, namely the male and the female, enclosed in their concordance, and made more than perfect by the medium of Vulcan, and exalted in its highest degree, [attains] qualified virtues... <note>The text cuts off here at the catchword "virtu-" to be continued on the next page.</note>

...all these things, together with the tempered and clarified essence, may be able to exert their power upon the human body, as well as upon metals, by expelling impurities through the pulse, and by arranging and preserving what is good in the human blood in its proper place. Through this medicine, the Microcosm <note>the human being, viewed as a miniature reflection of the universe</note>—dwelling in the borderland of the earth <note>original: "limbo terrae"; in Paracelsian thought, the "limbus" is the primordial matter or "chaos" from which the human body was formed</note> and formed from it—may be radically and truly brought to health and preserved in the same. No physician, at least one born of astral medicine <note>medicine that accounts for the influence of celestial bodies and spiritual forces</note>, should be ignorant of such a great mystery and supreme secret. 

Therefore, so that we may more and more clearly reveal the matter and preparation of such an admirable medicine to the sons of doctrine: let it be known that one thing has been given and produced by nature, in which (as if in a chest) the numbers 2, 3, and 4 are mysteriously enclosed and rest hidden.
