Hence, it is first necessary to know in which subject Nature has placed these numbers. You will find its virtues described at great length in my *Archidoxes* (he says), in the book on renovation and restoration. Furthermore, I will now demonstrate the matter quite openly to the disciples of the stars, along with the preparation of the entire work. Let him who has ears to hear, and mental eyes to see, hear and see what Paracelsus teaches before he judges unfairly with the rest.

Immature mineral electrum <note>original: "Electrum minerale immaturum"; electrum was traditionally an alloy of gold and silver, but here refers to a specific mineral starting material</note> should be placed in its sphere <note>the alchemical vessel</note>, so that filth and superfluities may be washed away. Let it be highly purified through stibium <note>antimony</note> according to chemical use and custom, lest it suffer damage because of its impurity. Afterward, let it be dissolved in the "stomach of the ostrich" <note>original: "stomachus struthionis"; an alchemical metaphor for a powerful corrosive acid or solvent</note> which grows in the earth, fortified by the "sharpness of the eagle" <note>original: "acritudinem aquilae"; the "eagle" usually refers to sal ammoniac or a sublimated spirit</note>. 

Once the electrum has been absorbed and has acquired yellow flowers, or a likeness to the flowers of the heliotrope in the solution, do not forget to lead this same substance toward a certain spiritual and transparent essence, which should have the appearance of white vitriol. Then, finally, add half the weight that the corporeal electrum had before preparation from the "extended eagle" <note>original: "aquila extensa"</note>, and from there, let the "stomach of the ostrich" be distilled off <note>original: "abstrahatur"; a process of removing a solvent by heat</note> several times; this is done so that the electrum may emerge more and more spiritual. 

When the "stomach of the ostrich" has become weaker in its operation, it must be renewed and strengthened again, distilling it off each time. Finally, when it has again lost its sharpness, let the "tartarized quintessence" <note>original: "essentia quinta tartarizata"</note> be added until it stands four fingers above the matter, and let it be deprived of its redness, which should ascend at the same time. This must be repeated until it becomes sufficiently white by itself (which indeed appears to the eyes as it gives itself over more and more to sublimation). Once this sign is perceived, let it be sublimated, and the electrum [is turned] into the whiteness of the sublimated eagle...

...turned into filings, and with little and light labor it will be brought and transmuted to that state: which indeed we seek for the use of our medicine. By this very means, you will be able to proceed against many ailments which do not yield at all to common medicines. In medicine, no greater foundation can be found than that which lies hidden in <term>electrum</term> <note>original: "electro"; in Paracelsian alchemy, this is not just amber or a natural alloy of gold and silver, but a specific "magical" alloy of the seven metals corresponding to the planets</note>. I confess, however, (he says) that in other minerals great secrets are similarly hidden, but they are subject to a greater and more prolonged labor, the use of which is turned into abuse by unskilled artists, whose hands destroy more in this medicine than they build. For this reason, it is by no means to be praised for every chemist to take up the role and duty of a physician, of which he is ignorant and for which he is unfit. It would be rightly noted that the rash, imaginary, and presumptuous physicians of that sort—who soon think themselves chemists and doctors by reading alone, and who rush into these arts through the window and not through the door—should be punished. I do not wish the blame to be cast on me because of my writing, nor do I recognize all those as disciples who proclaim themselves to be mine, or who read my writings; I recognize only those who both understand me and follow the truth. The others I pronounce to be voluntary deceivers and vagabond men, who snatch the bread from the mouths of true disciples, harming everyone under my name because they have no care for any art that is certain and true.

But let us return to the purpose. So that the broken electrum may finally be led to the desired end, the artist must take only as much of it rendered volatile (as described before) as he wishes to complete, and it must be enclosed in a <term>philosophical egg</term> <note>an oval glass vessel used in alchemy</note> <term>Hermetically sealed</term> <note>original: "Hermetice sigillato"; airtight, usually by melting the glass neck of the bottle</note>, so that it cannot breathe out in any way. Let this be placed in an <term>athanor</term> <note>original: "athanore"; a furnace designed to maintain a uniform and constant heat over a long period</note> and held there until it dissolves of its own accord gradually on the surface; then at last a certain island may be seen in the middle of this sea, which, gradually decreasing, passes away into blackness like <term>shoemaker's ink</term> <note>original: "atramenti sutorij"; often a reference to vitriol or iron-based blacking, signifying the *nigredo* or black stage of the work</note>. This is the "bird flying at night without wings," which the first dew of heaven, by continued decoction and by ascending and descending, converts into the <term>raven’s head</term> <note>original: "caput corvi"; the symbolic name for the black stage of the alchemical process</note>, and finally into the <term>peacock’s tail</term> <note>original: "caudam pavonis"; a stage where many iridescent colors appear in the vessel</note>, and afterward it acquires the whitest swan-like feathers, and lastly the highest redness, a sign of its fiery nature. Through this fire, it expels the accidents of all diseases out of the human body and restores members deadened by cold or paralysis. This kind of preparation is made (according to the opinion of all philosophers) in only one vessel, one furnace, and one continuous vaporous fire. When all these things are finished, the medicine is made and perfected as if celestial—which can be made more than perfect through its own flesh and its own blood, and through its internal and hidden fire brought into the manifest, by which likewise metals...

God, the Best and Greatest <note>original: "D.O.M." for "Deo Optimo Maximo"</note>, wished this mystery of nature, which is above nature, to become known to some men for His glory. It will be your part to imitate with understanding what I have prescribed to you at the beginning; do not flee from the labors, let the coals not terrify you, nor the laborious diligence and industry necessary in this place. But you must propose in your mind that, through constant speculation and meditative prayers intervening, all the most hidden things can be uncovered..."

be covered by pious minds, nor will that labor return to you without most abundant fruit.

In order, therefore, to bring some light to those reading these writings of Paracelsus, it seemed fit to add something that might open up the <term>electrum</term> <note>original: "electrum"; in this context, the magical alloy of the seven planetary metals</note> lying hidden within its hard shell. Everyone knows that metallic or mineral electrum is a mixture of two or more such bodies. Therefore, we must first seek an immature mineral of this kind—that is, one compacted by nature—which contains several elements, just as an alloy is made by art from various things, such as <term>latten</term> <note>original: "lato"; a brass-like alloy of copper and zinc</note> and bell-metal, and the like. But see what will be said below concerning cinnabar. Truly, so that these things may become clearer, I wished to collect for you in order those things which are more closely related rather than distant; therefore, let us now subjoin that <term>spagyric</term> <note>original: "spagiricum"; the alchemical art of separating and recombining substances to achieve a higher state</note> marriage, which we touched upon briefly above when dealing with the spirits and tinctures of metals.

->*On the marriage of the spagyric or philosophical stone.*<-

### CHAP. XII.

The Mercury of the philosophers should be carried into corporal Mercury, just as a seed is cast into its living field; that is, the Mercury of the Sun <note>original: "Mercurius solis"; referring to the philosophical essence of Gold</note> should be projected into the philosophical earth for the generation of tinctures. This living field will dissolve the Mercury of the wise, conceiving its powers within itself, and the field will "kill" that living thing—namely, the living corporal spirit—and from this, a constant and inviolable marriage will be made through fire and within the fire itself. For the philosophical Mercury (that of the Sun) is compared to the corporal spirit of Mercury in their conjunction just as a husband is to his wife, since both are from one and the same root or origin. Although the body of the Sun remains fixed in the fire, while the <term>metallic woman</term> <note>original: "metallica mulier"; the volatile, mercurial principle that must be "fixed" by the male gold principle</note> is not fixed, nonetheless the former is compared to the latter no differently than a seed to a field or the earth. Whatever is sown must be harvested: as barley from barley, wheat from wheat, and so with the rest. Likewise, in the art, if gold is sown, gold shall also be harvested; if silver, then silver; if copper, then copper, and so on. For this reason, tinctures arise from metals, each in its own degree, brought about by the Mercury of the wise and not by common <term>quicksilver</term> <note>original: "Mercurio vivo"</note>. However, common mercury serves as the augmentation, producing fruit just as the earth does from a seed. After you have enclosed the matter in its vessel, let it be placed in natural heat, so that the external heat does not exceed the internal; otherwise, no union will follow. For excessive heat scatters and burns the matter, so that nothing is generated from it. Consider the aerial part of the world, halfway between heaven and earth; without this medium, all creatures would be burned up by the heat of the Sun and the other stars and would produce nothing. Therefore, an ethereal medium is made between the fire and the matter, lest the work be destroyed. Conversely, if the living fire is weaker than is proper, the spirit of the matter will rest, doing nothing to its moisture other than causing its sudden drying out and fixation.

For the metallic spirits are dead and dormant, so that they can do or work nothing unless they are awakened to life by living fire. In the great world <note>The macrocosm, or the universe at large.</note>, it seems not dissimilar to seeds cast into the earth; they lie there as if dead, so that they are quite unable to grow by themselves unless they receive life and motion from the Sun. Therefore, let the craftsman see to it at this stage that he maintains a middle path in the regulation of his fire; otherwise, he will never be able to obtain his wish.

Once set in motion by the proper heat, the matter soon begins to turn black <note>The *nigredo* stage, representing the initial "death" and purification of the substances.</note>, and as dryness subsequently acts upon the moisture, the <term>philosophical garden</term> <note>original: "hortus philosophicus"; a metaphor for the chemical reactions taking place inside the vessel.</note> begins to flourish in the "egg" <note>The *ovum philosophicum*, a round, sealed glass flask.</note> with diverse and various colors in the manner of a <term>peacock's tail</term> <note>original: "caudæ pavonis"; an iridescent stage of the alchemical process where many colors appear.</note>, the likes of which a worker never happens to see in his whole life. Sometimes the glass will appear coated with gold inside, which is indeed a sign of the husband's action upon the woman’s seed—that is, the seed of the sulfur acting upon the <term>menstruum</term> <note>original: "menstruum"; a solvent or medium, here referring to the philosophical Mercury.</note> of Mercury—and of their mutual alteration and mixing. 

Afterward, as the moisture gradually fails through successive drying, these flowers and colors pass into a sprouting whiteness, until the matter reaches the degree ordained by nature's thread. Meanwhile, it should be noted that the work must not be rushed, as many do, desiring this "offspring" to be born in the space of a single year or nine months, like grain or a human in the mother's womb. Gold and silver are not born as quickly as those things. Indeed, the more excellent and perfect something is by nature, the more time it needs to be born; for what is made quickly seems to perish quickly, like grass, man, and similar things, whose life is brief for that reason. It is not so with gold and silver, which are more compact by nature and made of more constant things than flesh or blood; therefore, they offer long life to humans more than other things and preserve their health against corruptions, just as they do for <term>common Mercury</term> <note>original: "Mercurio vulgi"; ordinary quicksilver as opposed to the refined "Philosophical Mercury."</note>.

When the whiteness is at its highest degree, the vessel can be opened and the White Stone taken out. Let this be the test of its perfection: if a small particle placed upon a red-hot plate of <term>Venus</term> <note>original: "Veneris"; the alchemical name for copper.</note> gives off no smoke, it is well; otherwise, it must be digested longer until you learn the exact point of birth and fixation. You must do the same when you have progressed to the Red Stone.

This is the <term>ferment of multiplication</term> with common Mercury, following the same weight, place, and moderation as was said before concerning the philosophical Mercury. By this process, one part will eventually tinge a hundred parts more perfectly than before, and if this is repeated more often, it will provide as much material as you wish, so that one part may bring a thousand parts of Mercury to the best <term>Moon</term> <note>original: "lunam"; the alchemical term for Silver.</note>. For a greater declaration of this work, Paracelsus breaks out more broadly into these words, saying: "So that you may understand better, I say, let the highly purified Mercury of the philosophers be dissolved by its spouse—namely, the corporal spirit or living Mercury. The woman shall dissolve her husband, and the husband likewise his wife."

### *Regarding another process for the stone, by Paracelsus.*
# CHAPTER XIII.

The ways of philosophy are various, all tending toward one and the same goal and stone, as is evident from the preceding and following pages. Therefore, this art is described in various ways by the author. Let us hear, therefore, what he teaches in another place about this stone. "The nature of minerals," he says, "has produced one admirable genus in the bowels of the earth, and that a twofold one; this is found in various places in Europe. The best which was offered to my hands, and proven by experiment, from the figure of the <term>macrocosm</term> <note>The "greater world" or the universe at large, which alchemists believed was mirrored in the "microcosm" of the laboratory</note>, is a star from the beginning of the sphere of the sun: the other consists in the southern star in its first flowering; it is the viscous matter of the earth brought into the light by its own star, and in its first coagulation adorned with redness; in it all the flowers of minerals and colors are included, about which there is much written by the philosophers. As far as its moist and cold nature is concerned, it was adapted to water by a certain comparison. But the perfect knowledge of it, when compared to experience, has hitherto remained hidden from most—indeed almost all—philosophers, as many as have aimed their arrows at the target before me; striving in vain, they have turned very far away from the true and complete goal. They were of the opinion that **Mercury** and **Sulfur** were the mother and father of all metals, but indeed they did not remember the third <note>Paracelsus is referring to "Salt," completing his famous *Tria Prima* or three primary principles of matter</note>. Indeed, what is more, none of these has yet been able to take up the fishing net which belongs to the true water—the mother of metals—which when separated by the <term>spagyric art</term> <note>The alchemical process of separating a substance into its components and then purifying and recombining them</note> makes its "fish" manifest. These are fish which neither the fishing of **Galen** <note>A famous Greek physician whose theories dominated medicine for over a thousand years</note> nor the torn net of **Avicenna** <note>The influential Persian polymath and physician Ibn Sina</note> were ever able to catch. If I had to demonstrate to modern physicians even the name alone of the conjunction, solution, and coagulation which nature itself has revealed and demonstrated in this, its creation, from the beginning of the world, a year would fail me, and all the paper, however much there might be, would be insufficient to instruct them."

... Indeed, I say that in this mineral there are three substances, namely Mercury, sulfur, and mineral water, from which it is composed and separated by the <term>spagyric art</term> <note>The alchemical practice of separating and then recombining the essential components of a substance</note>: it is dissolved in its own not-yet-mature liquor, just as a pear is hidden within its own tree. The "hider" of the pear is the tree; when the stars and nature come together within it, the tree puts forth green branches. Later, in March, it reveals its atoms, leaves, and flowers, progressing toward the fruit and the production of the pear, which finally emerges in autumn. We must think in a similar way regarding the minerals in the bowels of the earth, which are thrust out into the light by the influence of the stars. This is the primary thing to be considered by the alchemist who longs for the treasure of nature. I shall now reveal the method of this craftsmanship—its beginning, middle, and end—together with its own water, sulfur, and balsam. By the solution of these three, and their subsequent conjunction into one, the entire business of the Work is completed in the following manner.

Let a mineral of <term>cinnabar</term> <note>original: 'cinabaris'; mercury sulfide, the most common ore of mercury</note> be taken and washed with celestial water <note>usually rainwater or dew</note> for three hours; finally, let it be strained and dissolved in <term>aqua regia</term> <note>original: 'aqua regia', or 'royal water'; here made from vitriol, saltpeter, and common salt</note>. Let it be drawn off through an <term>alembic</term> <note>a distillation apparatus</note>, poured back again, and treated by <term>cohobation</term> <note>repeatedly distilling a liquid from its solid residue to increase its potency</note> so that the pure may be separated from the impure which remains below. Let it putrefy in horse dung for a month, and afterward let the elements be separated: when they have manifested their signs, let them be distilled through an alembic at the first degree of heat. By this, the water and air ascend first, and finally the fire; this occurs at the remaining degrees of heat, which can be discerned by an experienced operator. 

At the bottom of the vessel the earth remains, in which lies hidden all that has been sought by many, yet found by very few. You shall artificially calcine this earth, enclosed in a reverberatory furnace, proceeding from the first to the fifth degree, allowing five hours for each degree. This is done so that you may have a volatile salt, as subtle as <term>alcohol</term> <note>In this context, 'alcohol' refers to an extremely fine, purified powder rather than a liquid spirit</note>, and a constant "star" of fire and earth, which you shall separate by means of the elements of water and air that you preserved earlier. 

Finally, place it in the digestion of a <term>bain-marie</term> <note>original: 'balnei maris'; a gentle water bath</note> for eight hours, and you will see that which has been unknown and least considered by many alchemists until now. Separate it skillfully and in a spagyric manner according to your experience, and the earth itself will be rendered wonderfully white, from which the tincture has been extracted. Next, join the element of fire with the "alcoholized" salt of the earth. Through digestion and the artifice of the <term>pelican</term> <note>A circulatory distillation vessel with arms that return the condensed vapors to the base</note>, this substance will deposit yet another sediment, which you shall separate from the pure. 

Then at last, take the "pelicanized lion" which was found from the beginning. When you see its tincture and the element of fire above the water, air, and earth, separate it using a <term>tritorium</term> <note>a separation funnel or vessel</note>, and strain such a "Sun" <note>gold</note> by tilting the vessel; for this is **potable gold**. Let it be drenched with the sweet alcohol of wine <note>ethanol</note> and drawn off until no more sharpness of the *aqua regia* is perceived. Separate this **Oil of the Sun**, and place it in a retort vessel with the Seal of Hermes <note>an airtight or 'hermetic' seal</note>...

...closed, for elevation—that is, for exaltation—so that it may be doubled in its degree. This glass, very well closed, should be placed in a cold place; it will not dissolve there, but will be coagulated, and this is to be repeated three times by dissolving and coagulating. By this artifice, the <term>Tincture of the Sun</term> <note>original: 'tinctura Solis'; the essential essence or "dye" of gold used to transform other substances</note> is perfected in its degree. Finally, take a double amount of this <term>Venus</term> <note>copper</note> at its highest level and prepared in the <term>spagyric way</term> <note>the process of separating, purifying, and recombining chemical components</note>, upon which you should pour the elements of water and air which you had saved; dissolve and putrefy it for a month, as before.

Separate this from the white; for the red tincture is so powerful that it dyes all white bodies into redness, or red ones into whiteness, which is truly wonderful. Drive this tincture through a retort; you will see a blackness arise, which you will drive again through the retort, and that quite often until it becomes white. Pursue this work of yours, and do not lose heart because of the great labor. Do not desist (I say) from the work I have mentioned, until you have the signs and see the lion and the indissoluble treasure. Blessed is he who finds it and knows how to apply it to the tincture.

This is the true <term>balsam of the celestial stars</term>, which allows no body to pass into putrefaction, and leaves no leprosy, gout, or dropsy unexpelled by the administration of a single grain, if it be fermented with the <term>sulfur of the Sun</term> <note>original: 'sulphure solis'; the active, combustible principle extracted from gold</note>. The nature of water will teach and reveal everything, and everything I have written.

Take, therefore, as much of the <term>liquor of minerals</term> as you wish, two parts of the <term>salt of the red earth</term>, and one part of the sulfur of the Sun. Let them be dissolved and coagulated in a <term>pelican</term> <note>a specialized alchemical vessel with two curved "arms" that allow condensed vapors to flow back into the main body, ensuring constant circulation</note>, and that for the third time. In this way, you will have the tincture of the alchemists, whose weight is by no means to be described here, but reserved for its own place. 

Whoever possesses one ounce of the <term>Star of the Sun</term> <note>the quintessence or "Astrum" of gold</note> and projects it over several ounces of gold, will dye his own body. If he has the <term>Star of Mercury</term>, he will similarly dye the whole body of common mercury. If the <term>Star of Venus</term>, in no dissimilar way he will dye the entire body of Venus into the best gold, and into the highest and constant perfection; so must it be judged concerning the "stars" of the remaining metals, such as <term>Saturn</term> <note>lead</note>, <term>Mars</term> <note>iron</note>, and the rest. From these also, by the same reasoning, tinctures are drawn, which are not to be described here because they are contained in the books *On the Nature of Things* and the *Archidoxis* <note>Two seminal works by Paracelsus</note>.

With these few words, I wish the <term>first entity</term> <note>original: 'primum ens'; the fundamental, primordial essence of a substance</note> of metals and minerals of the earth to be declared sufficiently and abundantly to true alchemists, along with the tincture of the alchemists. Nor should any of the operators be deterred by a span of nine months, but should proceed without weariness under spagyric guidance, by which, in forty alchemical days, he will be able to fix, extract, exalt, purify, ferment, and coagulate the <term>Stone of the Alchemists</term>, to the honor of God, to whom be praise, honor, and glory.

The exposition of the Cabalists <note>mystical scholars who sought hidden meanings in texts and nature</note> holds, under the name of the Phoenix, that the eagle is a volatile thing whose feathers fly without wind, and which lift the body of the phoenix with them into its nest. In that nest, it is nourished by the element of fire; its chicks pluck out the mother’s eyes with their beaks, and a "whiteness" <note>original: 'albedo'; the second major stage of the alchemical Great Work, symbolizing purification</note> is produced in its own separate sphere. In this whiteness consists the life of its heart and the balsam of its intestines. According to the Cabalistic sense, sulfur is interpreted as cinnabar <note>original: 'cinabaris'; mercury sulfide, a bright red mineral</note>, about which Paracelsus has spoken above. Very recently, when discussing electrum <note>an alloy of gold and silver, or more broadly, a potent medicinal mixture of metals</note>, I referred the reader to cinnabar for good reason; for they have the greatest affinity. What else is cinnabar but a composition or mixture of two minerals, sulfur and quicksilver? What also is electrum, if not a mixture of two or more minerals or metals? Therefore, if the **Sulfur of the Sun** <note>original: 'Sulphur Solis'; alchemical gold</note> is joined by artifice with the **Philosophical Mercury of the Moon** <note>original: 'Mercurio lunæ philosophico'; alchemical silver</note>, why shall it not be electrum, and why shall it not be cinnabar? Whether it is made by nature or through chemistry, the component parts do not differ. But this will be clearer in what follows.

### *Regarding the fourth Paracelsian process for the Stone.*

## CHAPTER XIV.

Before we speak of the **physical tincture** <note>the 'medicine' or agent used to transform base metals into gold or heal the body</note>, it will be worthwhile first to know what its subject is; for this has always been hidden until now. The matter of the tincture is, therefore, a certain thing (provided you understand me according to the spagyric sense) which indeed passes from three into one essence by the chemical art, or is able to remain so. Indeed, to declare it by its own name according to ancient use and custom, it has been called the **Red Lion** <note>original: 'Leo rubeus'; a term often referring to the final stage of the matter or a specific prepared mineral</note> by many, but truly known by very few. This, by the help of nature and art alike, can be transmuted into the **White Eagle** <note>original: 'aquilam albam'; often a symbol for the process of sublimation or the purified white stage of the matter</note>, so that from one, two are made, which shine for the spagyrist <note>an alchemist who practices the art of separation and recombination</note> even beyond the splendor of gold; when preserved in one, they shine even more. 

Now, if you do not understand the accustomed speech of the Cabalists and the ancient Astronomers <note>astrologers</note>, you are by no means called by God to the spagyric art, nor chosen by nature; indeed, you are not fit even to open your mouth in this art. Therefore, the matter of the tincture is the greatest pearl and most precious treasure, and the most noble thing of all that can fall to the meditations of men through the manifestation of the Most High Creator. This is the **Lily of Alchemy** and Medicine <note>original: 'Lili Alchemiæ'</note>, which philosophers have sought so accurately, but because of a lack of complete knowledge and its perfect preparation, they have not yet been able to lead it to the most absolute end. Through their investigations and experiences, only the beginning of the tincture has been given to us; yet the true foundation, which it behooves my disciples to imitate, was left to me, so that no one should mix their own masks <note>false theories or "larvae"</note> with our inventions. I (says Paracelsus) shall rightly correct the spagyrists after my long experiences, and separate the false and erroneous from the truth—

<meta>This page continues the technical discussion of the preparation of the alchemical "subject," transitioning from the general theory of electrum and cinnabar on the previous page to the specific "Lili" process and the practical methods used by ancient and modern spagyrists.</meta>

<page-num>536</page-num>
<header>OF TRANSMUTATION</header>

I will indeed separate [them], since I have found through very extensive investigations how I might justly reprove similar [imitations] and—if the experiments of the Ancients are nevertheless more excellent—I would by no means have undertaken such great labors, which I have willingly assumed for the sake, utility, and honor of all honest alchemists. Since, therefore, the subject of the tincture has been sufficiently declared, so that it could or should hardly be done more faithfully for the brothers, I shall approach its preparation; beyond the experiences of the first age, I shall also add my own inventions. 

The ancients putrefied their *lili* <note>original: 'lili'; a Paracelsian term for the matter of the Tincture, often associated with the 'Lily' or the purified subject</note> for one philosophical month <note>traditionally forty days</note>. Then they distilled the moist spirits from it until the dry spirits were raised. They imbued the *caput mortuum* <term>dead head; the dross or metallic residue remaining after distillation or sublimation</term> with the moist spirits and drew it off again through distillation quite often, and they did this for so long until the dry parts were raised up entirely. Afterward, they united the drawn-off humors and spirits together in a pelican <term>a circulating distillation vessel with two side-tubes that return condensed liquid to the body, resembling a bird pecking its own breast</term> three or four times, until the whole of the *lili* settled at the bottom in a dry state. 

Although experience gave this process before fixation, nevertheless our predecessors often perfectly attained their desire by it. They would have had an easier way, however, to arrive at the treasure of the **Red Lion** <note>a symbol for the final stage of the Great Work or the solar principle</note>, if they had learned the concordance of Astronomy with Alchemy, which I demonstrated in the *Apocalypse of Hermes* <note>a famous alchemical text attributed to Hermes Trismegistus but often associated with Paracelsian thought</note>. But since every word (as Christ speaks for the consolation of the faithful) has its own essence, the spagyrists <note>alchemists who specialize in the separation and recombination of natural essences</note> who labored before my time—a heavy and difficult task—can now, by the help of the flowing Holy Spirit, find their theory and practice relieved in this century by my own. 

While the first age gave the first experience of the tincture, two spagyrists made it from a single simple substance. But because this discovery would have perished in this second age, their successors, by diligent scrutiny, afterward happened upon two names for the same simple thing and named it with a single word; namely, *lili*, the subject of the tincture. Finally, the imitators of nature putrefied this matter in its own time, not otherwise than a seed in the earth, since before this corruption <note>in alchemy, 'corruption' refers to the breakdown of a substance's form so a new one can emerge</note> nothing is born from it, nor can any secret be extracted. Afterward, they drew off the moist spirits from the matter, and finally, by the violence of fire, the dry spirits were likewise raised and sublimated. By this path, not otherwise than a farmer following the seasons of the year, one arrives at maturity. 

At last, when their "spring" was finished, it came forth at the time when they incorporated those fruits and dry spirits, and they brought the magistery <note>the successful completion of an alchemical process</note> of the tincture to the point where it reached the harvest and disposed itself to extreme maturity. The ancient spagyrists would not have needed such long labor and tedious reiteration if they had learned the work in the school [of nature]; they would have attained it far more quickly and with less expense. 

Accordingly, I say to you (says Paracelsus): take only the blood of the color from the lion, and the gluten from the eagle; after you have joined them together, coagulate them according to the ancient process.

You will possess the tincture of the philosophers, which an infinite number of men have sought, but only a very few have found. Thus, the alchemist compounds certain simple substances, which he breaks down according to the rules of the art, and from them prepares something else, continuing until they become one: this achievement effects more than nature itself could do on its own. So that you may understand me rightly and properly, seek your **lion** in the East, and the **eagle** toward the South <note>In alchemical symbolism, the "Lion" often represents fixed solids or acids (like antimony or gold), while the "Eagle" represents volatile substances or spirits (like sal ammoniac or mercury)</note> for the undertaking of this work of ours. You will find no better instruments than those produced in Hungary and Istria. But if you desire to lead it from unity through duality into trinity, with an equal permutation of each, you must direct your journey toward the South; thus in Cyprus you will obtain your wish, of which no more need be said. 

Many secrets exhibiting transmutations are found, though known to few; and although they may be manifested to someone by the Lord God, a rumor does not immediately break out alongside the art, but the Almighty gives with the secrets themselves an understanding to hide these and other things until the arrival of **Elias the Artist** <note>original: "Heliæ Artiſtæ"; a prophetic figure in Paracelsian thought expected to appear in the future to reveal all hidden knowledge and the ultimate secrets of alchemy</note>, at which time nothing shall be so hidden that it will not be revealed. For we see that in the **sulfur of Jupiter** <term>original: "sulphure Jovis"; likely referring to a specific preparation of tin, as Jupiter is the planetary symbol for tin</term> there is a very great tincture of gems, which indeed brings them to a higher state than nature is able to do by itself; but enough of these things, let us finally return to the physical tincture.

Lastly, the ancient spagyrists <term>alchemists who focus on the separation and recombination of substances</term> "pelicanized" <note>subjected to circular distillation in a "pelican" vessel, as described on the previous page</note> their *lili*. By a certain orderly increase of the fire, they fixed their matter for so long until, after the disappearance of all colors, it took on a redness like blood, and with it the condition of the **salamander** <note>The salamander was a mythical creature believed to live in fire; here it refers to the substance becoming "fixed" and able to withstand the heat of the furnace without evaporating</note>. Their process was indeed correct, and it is right and proper for every person seeking this **pearl** <note>original: "magaritā"; used metaphorically for the Tincture</note> to proceed in the same manner. It would be very difficult for me to declare this more clearly to you, yet once you have learned in the school of the alchemists to observe the degrees of fire and to change the vessels, you will finally see—as soon as your *lili* has been heated in the **philosophical egg** <term>an oval-shaped glass vessel used for long digestion</term>—that it appears with wonderful demonstrations. It becomes blacker than a crow, then in the success of time whiter than a swan, and finally, passing through yellowness, it becomes redder than any blood. 

Therefore, when we have the **treasure of the Egyptians** <note>A common alchemical metaphor for the secret wisdom of transmutation</note> in our hands, we must turn it to our advantage, and that through a double mastery: the first for the restoration of health in the human body, and the second for the transmutation of metals. For it to come into this [latter] use, one weight of it must first be projected upon a thousand weights of molten **Sun** <note>original: "solis"; the alchemical term for gold</note>; only then will the Medicine be prepared to take away the **leprosy of metals** <term>original: "lepra metallorum"; the impurities or "base" qualities of metals like lead or tin that prevent them from being gold</term>. 

Likewise, some of the physicians in Egypt lived one hundred and fifty years through this tincture. The lives of others were longer by this means, as is evident from histories. The tincture of the physicians is therefore a certain universal medicine, which consumes all diseases no differently than fire consumes all wood. Its dose is very small, but its operation is most powerful. Through it (says Paracelsus) I have cured leprosy, dropsy,

### *Concerning the fifth, very brief process of the Stone discovered by the same author.*

### CHAPTER XV.

I am not, nor do I wish to be, a teacher or follower of that Stone which is taught in various ways by many others. Therefore, leaving that Stone and its process aside, I have proposed to write down very briefly that which was discovered by me through both use and experience. This process tints the bodies of men no less than the other, even if it is not prepared according to a similar procedure. Take, therefore, **Mercury**, otherwise known as the element of Mercury, and separate the pure from the impure; afterward, let it be reverberated <note>heated in a furnace where the flame is "turned back" or reflected onto the substance</note> until it reaches whiteness <note>original: "albedo"</note>. Sublimate this with **sal ammoniac** <note>ammonium chloride</note> until it is resolved; let it be calcined and dissolved again, and then digested in a **pelican** <note>a specialized alchemical flask with two side arms that return condensed vapors to the body of the vessel, allowing for continuous "circulation"</note> for one month. Finally, let it be coagulated into a body. This is no longer burned, nor consumed in any way, but remains in the same state. The metals it penetrates become permanent in the ash-cupel <note>original: "cineritio"; referring to the cupellation process used to test the purity of precious metals</note>, so that they can in no way be reduced to nothing or altered; rather, as has often been told, it removes all superfluous qualities from things both sensible and insensible. And although I have set down a very brief way and process, it nevertheless requires long labor and is entangled in many circumstances; it requires an operator who is not easily affected by weariness, but who is supremely diligent and expert.

### *Concerning a certain particular secret of a white tincture through arsenic.*

### CHAPTER XVI.

Some wish arsenic to be composed of Mercury and sulfur; others of earth and water; many of the nature of sulfur. In whatever way it may be, its nature is such that it transmutes red copper <note>original: "rubeum cuprum"</note> into white. It can also be brought to such perfection of preparation that it may truly and perfectly tint; however, not by that way taught by many **Sophists** <note>here meaning "deceptive practitioners" or "pseudo-alchemists"</note>, such as **Geber** in his *Sum of Perfection*, **Albertus Magnus**, **Aristotle** the Chemist in his *Book of the Perfect Mastery*, **Rhazes** <note>original: "Rafis"</note>, and **Polydorus**. For these writers, as many as there are, err; or else out of envy for the study, they write and propose false things, received opinions, and their own whims, which they themselves sometimes did not even understand. **Arsenic** truly contains three natural spirits: the first is combustible, corrosive, volatile, and penetrating of all things. This spirit whitens **Venus** <note>the alchemical name for copper</note> and, after a few days, renders it spongy. This artifice belongs properly only to those who practice the **caustic art** <note>the chemistry of corrosive or burning substances</note>. The second spirit is crystalline and sweet. The third

...but the tingeing <note>the part capable of changing the color/nature of a metal</note> part is separated from the others mentioned above. > *I have nine letters, I am of four syllables, understand me.*
> *The first three have two letters each,*
> *The others have the rest, and five are mutes;*
> *Of the total number, the hundreds are two, [plus] eight,*
> *And three times thirty, along with seven. He who understands who I am,*
> *Will not be unrefined or ignorant of the wisdom that is in me.*

All these things agree in this Greek word, numerically calculated in Greek: <term>ἀρσενικὸν</term> <note>original: "arsenikon"; arsenic</note>, as far as it pertains to the white tincture. But the red [tincture] is not found in arsenic, in whatever way it may be prepared. When unprepared and crude, by melting it with copper alone, it tints this to a very great whiteness, but it is not fixed <note>stable under heat</note>, because the crude tincture is likewise volatile; if it were fixed, there is no doubt that it would also exhibit a fixed tincture. For nothing penetrates metals in their crude state more easily than this spirit. The most important part of the business consists in its separation and fixation.

Pythagoras, for 그 reason, did not wish to be called a "wise man" <note>original: *sophus*</note>, because in his time the priesthood of the Egyptians and their wisdom were by no means taught perfectly as was fitting, even though he nonetheless brought back many hidden mysteries from there; Anaxagoras likewise brought back many, as is evident from the disputes he held concerning the sun and its stone, and which he left behind at his death. Therefore, we leave behind the philosophical wisdom of these Greeks as a sophisticated speculation <note>meaning a logic-heavy, overly theoretical approach</note>, degenerate from other true arts and sciences, and standing far and wide apart from them. Very many have attempted to both scrutinize the most secret magic of those wise men and to put it into use, yet that very thing has not yet been achieved. 

Many in this time of ours exalt Trithemius, others Bacon and Agrippa, for their Magic and Cabala; which, however, do not seem to agree in all things through every point. For **Magic** is the art and faculty through which one arrives at the knowledge of the elements, of bodies and their fruits, and of properties, powers, and hidden operations. But **Cabala** <term>Cabala</term> <note>here referring to "Christian Kabbalah," a mystical method of interpreting divine secrets and the names of God</note> seems to build a path for men to God through spiritual elevation <note>original: *Anagogia*</note>, and to teach how one must live with Him and prophesy from Him alone. For Cabala is full of divine mysteries, just as Magic is full of natural secrets. Indeed, Magic teaches one to speak of the omens of the future from the nature of past and present things; its operation, however, consists in knowing all creatures internally—both celestial and earthly bodies—what is hidden within them, what forces and virtues lie concealed, for what they were destined from the beginning, and with what properties they were endowed. These and similar things provide the bond by which celestial things are joined to earthly things, as is even perceived sometimes by the eye and the senses through their operations. Such a conjunction of celestial influences, or impression, by which celestial virtues operate upon inferior bodies, was of old called the **Gamaheum** <term>Gamaheum</term> <note>a term used by Paracelsus and others to describe a "marriage" or union of heavenly powers with physical objects, often resulting in talismans or stones with supernatural properties</note> marriage of celestial powers and properties with elemental bodies by the Magi and Wise Men. ## *On the cements and cementations of metals.*
### CHAPTER XX.

We have heard before about the most excellent and greatest tinctures of the philosophers; now it is time for us to bring the lesser ones into the light, because they are not used for medical purposes for the bodies of men, but only for removing the "clouds" from metals.

1. The first cement, therefore, is the **Royal Cement** <note>original: "cimentum regale"; a process used to separate gold from silver and other base metals</note>, described by Paracelsus not according to the common manner, but from the experience alone which he gained, not following the custom of the ancients. Take a half pound each of <term>flowers of copper</term> <note>original: "florum æris"; likely copper acetate or verdigris</note>, <term>antimony</term>, brick dust, and common salt. Let them all be ground very finely and mixed together, and afterwards soaked in wine and dried; this must be done twenty-four times. With this powder, let the **Moon** <note>Alchemical term for silver</note> in the form of thin plates be "cemented" at a medium level of fire for four hours, then for the same number of hours at a moderate fire, and finally at a melting fire for twelve hours. Then at last, take out the <term>regulus</term> <note>The metallic mass found at the bottom of the crucible</note>, and having made it into plates as in the prior process, you shall cement it with the same materials, the same levels of fire being observed, repeating this same thing four or five times. Finally, let it be refined by <term>cupellation</term> <note>original: "fulminetur per cineritium"; a refining process using a vessel of bone ash</note>, and the <term>slag</term> <note>original: "loppa"</note> reduced back into Silver. The instruments, namely the vessels, must be very well sealed with clay and very firmly closed. Think of me as setting down a lengthy process in this place for this reason: because in short stages of fire, experience has wished to teach nothing good. Indeed, the duration and violence of the fire are the most powerful fixation of the Royal Cement; indeed, it would be much better if the things which have been mentioned were contained in such a cement for four natural days. It should also be noted that the "flowers of copper" must first be extracted from the copper by means of vitriol; for in that, a certain nature of fixation is held for many reasons. Antimony is similarly to be "fixed"—retaining those virtues which it possesses, however—through putrefaction and purification; for its powers cannot be sufficiently known. Likewise, the bricks ought to be taken from a good roof; for there is in the roof itself a certain capacity for the constriction and fixation of the veins or pores in metals. Salt also fixes and corrects the **leprous Moon** <note>Impure or clouded silver</note> from its cloud. It is necessary, therefore, for these four things to come together in the composition of this cement. Furthermore, the fire must be observed, and nothing else added, nor any other metal; for it is sufficient by itself.

2. The second cement is suitable only for the **Sun** <note>Alchemical term for gold</note>, in which three "accidents" especially are to be noted. Sometimes it is found...

<header>OF METALS.</header>

**Gold** <note>original: "sol" (the Sun), the alchemical name for gold</note> that fails in the <term>cement</term> <note>A process of heating metal with dry chemical powders to purify it</note> by a fourth or a half part does so because it is not sufficiently "fixed" by nature, but exists as yet in an immature state. Therefore, it must be cemented so that it can retain the volatile part of its body along with the fixed part; otherwise, this immature portion is separated from its fixed body either in the cement, or in the <term>cupellation</term> <note>original: "cineritio"; the process of refining gold or silver by melting it on a bed of bone ash (the cupel) which absorbs base metals</note>, and sometimes in <term>aqua fortis</term> <note>Nitric acid, used to separate gold from silver</note>. Second, an accidental defect is seen in most gold when it has a paler color and a faint yellowness; such a color must be introduced by the cement in this way, so that it remains without any loss of the metal's body in any test. The third defect concerns the weight; because of a lack of weight, gold is considered cheaper the lighter it is: for it ought to be heavier than lead, and (as many maintain) even heavier than <term>quicksilver</term> <note>mercury</note>. By this indicator above all is gold proved or rejected, for it is the one by which it can least deceive others: for it is easier to impose upon the eyes with color and constancy than to deceive the sense of touch with weight. All these things are to be corrected in this manner: Take a half pound each of <term>flowers of antimony</term> <note>A white powder of antimony trioxide produced by sublimation</note> and <term>flowers of copper</term> <note>original: "florum aeris"; copper oxide or acetate</note>, and one drachm of fixed, coagulated Mercury. Let all be mixed together and soaked in the red <term>oil of antimony</term> <note>Antimony trichloride or a similar preparation</note> until they become entirely red. Afterwards, let the gold—thinly laminated into sheets or granulated—be cemented with these for twenty-four hours in the heat of a furnace, without any decrease in heat, in a melting vessel <note>a crucible</note> which is very well sealed. When this time has passed, take out the <term>regulus</term> <note>The "little king"; the metallic mass found at the bottom of the crucible after smelting</note>; let it then be melted through a process with crude antimony, with <term>borax</term> <note>original: "chrysocolla"; a flux used in soldering and melting</note> added, and poured out into an oblong mold. This is the best cement of "the Sun" for all the aforementioned degrees.

3. The third cementation is as follows. We have previously set down two fixations of cements necessary for multiplying gold and silver; now we must also take account of the imperfect metals in that regard, so that they may likewise be rendered fit by their own cement to receive the "cementary tincture" into themselves—which they cannot receive unless first prepared in this manner. Only four imperfect bodies <note>Lead, tin, copper, and iron</note> are to be included under this cement; Mercury, however, is to be excluded and reserved for its own peculiar cement. Take one pound of <term>saltpeter</term> <note>Potassium nitrate</note>, two pounds of saltpeter <note>Note: The text repeats saltpeter, likely meaning two different grades or a transcription error for another salt</note>, and a half pound each of common salt and <term>salt of tartar</term> <note>Potassium carbonate</note>. Let all be mixed together and placed in a melting vessel, arranged layer upon layer with plates or filings of the metals. Let them be cemented, being very well sealed, for twelve hours with a most violent fire, which should be light for the first two hours. When this time is finished, let what remains be taken out—namely, the <term>slag</term> <note>original: "loppa"; the dross or waste material</note> together with the regulus. 4. The fourth cementation concerns ores <note>original: "minerarum"</note> that possess perfect metal within themselves but lose it through common smelting <note>original: "liquationem"</note>. It should be noted in this place that metals cannot be better "fixed" than while they are in their crude <note>unrefined</note> state. In this way, metals are found in ores that never appear otherwise. This kind of transmutation takes place in ores and metals before smelting, so that the metals may be able to be strengthened in their own proper nature, or be transmuted into another metal. Therefore, two cements are to be understood here as one: the first for fixing the metal in the ore without transmutation; the second for transmutating the ore of **Venus** <note>Copper ore</note> into **the Sun** <note>Gold</note>, or into another metal. For more excellent spirits are present in the ores than in the metals themselves; they greatly assist in the gradations and fixations of metals, since they contain within themselves colors and the <term>tincture</term> <note>The transformative essence or color-giving property</note> in their own material, not yet changed by fire.

Therefore, the description of the fixation of a metal in its ore is as follows: Take one pound of the ore of **Mars** <note>Iron ore</note>; to this, being very well ground, add two pounds each of antimony and saltpeter <note>original: "salis nitri"</note>. Let them be strongly heated for smelting in a closed vessel, well sealed with lute <note>original: "lutata"; a clay paste used to make vessels airtight</note>, and let them remain so for twenty-four hours. Afterwards, having been removed and reduced with **Saturn** <note>Lead</note>, let them be <term>cupelled</term> <note>original: "fulminentur"; literally 'to be struck with lightning', referring to the bright flash seen when the metal becomes pure</note>, and you will find the metal fixed in its proper color; the same is to be understood for the remaining ores. For the spirits of metals still existing in their ores proceed in their colors and essences while they are yet crude.

The description of the transmutation of ores is this: Take saffron from the flowers of Mars <note>Iron oxide</note>, flowers from the saffron of Venus <note>Copper oxide or a similar prepared sublimate</note>, vitriol, and alum, a half pound of each; one pound of prepared common salt, and two pounds of ore. Let them all be melted and deprived of moisture, and let them be cemented for twelve hours. Afterwards, let them be melted in **Saturn** <note>Lead</note> and cupelled <note>original: "fulminentur"</note>, which being done, the transmutation will be found in the cupel <note>original: "cupella cineritij"</note>. To this kind of transmutation, a mixture of metals can also be added, considering however the greater aptitude of one over another, by which the transmutation may happen more easily.

It is necessary that both forms of **Mercury**—the physical and the common—be solidified <note>original: "coagulandum"</note>, so that they may withstand the cement <note>A dry chemical mixture used to treat metals at high heat</note> and receive a physical substance along with a tincture and color, as befits the finest metals. The solidification of **Mercury** is as follows: Take **strong water** <note>original: "aqua fortis"; nitric acid</note> that has been entirely stripped of its power and sharpness after being used to dissolve **the Moon** <note>Silver</note>, and which has lost its ability to dissolve further. Once removed from the water, let it be washed repeatedly until it becomes "sweet" <note>Neutralized of acid</note>, and then let it be cemented as described below. Take two and a half ounces of borax, half an ounce of **sal ammoniac** <note>Ammonium chloride</note>, and one ounce each of **flowers of copper** <note>original: "florum aeris"; copper oxides or carbonates</note> and **saffron of Mars** <note>original: "croci martis"; iron oxide</note>; then take half an ounce each of calcined vitriol, calcined alum, **hematite** <note>Bloodstone</note>, and **Armenian bole** <note>A medicinal red clay used as a binder</note>.

Arrange them layer upon layer in a melting vessel. Afterward, let them be heated slowly for the first six hours; for the next six hours, let the fire be increased; and finally, for twelve more hours, let it be most violent. When this is done, sublime and cement it again as before; by the fourth or fifth cementation, you will find the **cinnabar** is "fixed" <note>Stable under heat</note>. Reduce this through **Saturn** <note>Lead</note> and let it be cupelled, and its transmutation will be achieved. The same must be done with other volatile metallic bodies.

We have completed our little book on cements, in which we have taught the methods of cementation sufficiently amply and clearly. Although many other descriptions by different authors are available, we have excluded them from our own, setting down only those which I have found to be more useful through practical experience. ## On the gradations of metals.
### CHAPTER XXI.

It has seemed fit to set down fourteen gradations of metals in this place; although far more others may be found, we have collected only those which stand upon certain experience and which we know to be worthy of recording. They are prepared under a triple distinction: namely, those made through **strong waters** <note>original: "aquas fortes"; typically nitric acid or mixtures of acids</note>, those through oils, and the remainder through liquors.

1. The first gradation is made through the first strong water in this manner: Take two pounds each of **vitriol** <note>Sulfuric acid precursors, like iron or copper sulfate</note>, alum, and **saltpeter** <note>original: "salis nitri"</note>. Take one <term>verto</term> <note>A specific unit of weight; the text defines it here as a fourth part of a pound (approx. 3 ounces)</note> each of **flowers of copper** <note>Copper oxides</note>, **saffron of Mars** <note>Iron oxide</note>, and **hematite**; take half a pound <term>℔. ß.</term> <note>original: "libra semis"</note> of cinnabar; one and a half *vertos* of antimony, and half a *verto* of arsenic. Let all be distilled together into a strong water, which should be purified and rarefied according to the use of similar waters. In this water, dissolve **cemented Moon** <note>original: "lunam"; silver that has undergone heat treatment</note> or "part with part" <note>An alloy of equal portions</note>, namely **Moon** and **Venus** <note>Silver and Copper</note>, and keep them in digestion <note>Gentle, steady heat</note> for one month. Afterward, let the residues be refined by **cupellation** <note>original: "fulminentur"; literally "struck with lightning," referring to the bright flash seen when precious metal is purified in a furnace</note>, and the transmutation will be achieved. Whatever residue remains in the strong water should be precipitated and refined as above: thus the remainder of the silver is obtained. Note meanwhile that each ingredient ought to be prepared before they are used in gradations; otherwise, every transmutation is greatly hindered by impurity.

2. The second gradation is through the second strong water. The process of this second gradation is especially to be noted, as it is performed with greater profit and subtlety than all others made through waters. Take, therefore, one pound each of **saltpeter** <note>original: "salis petræ"</note> and cinnabar; let them be ground together, and let a water be distilled from them, which you should save. You shall do this same thing also, using the same weight, with antimony and arsenic. Mix both waters together, and add one pound each of saltpeter and alum. Again, let all be distilled together in the manner of strong water. For all metals that are dissolved in this water and remain in digestion longer than is believable, the operations, powers, and virtues of perfection are fulfilled; for within a composition of this kind, the full faculties of the true transmutation of metals—which possess bodily matter within themselves—lie hidden. For these three distillations, by the strength of their water, dye <note>To "dye" or "tincture" a metal meant to permanently change its color and nature, usually toward gold.</note> so vehemently that no greater or more vehement operation can be found among strong waters.

3. The third gradation is through the third strong water. Take cinnabar

## *On the Vexations of Alchemists.*
### CHAPTER XXII.

Having completed the gradations and cements of metals, we have decided to come in the last place to the **vexations of the Alchemists** <note>The "vexations" or "labors" refer to the specific chemical challenges, trials, and theoretical puzzles faced by practitioners</note>, with which we shall conclude the Alchemy of **Paracelsus**. What Alchemy may be, therefore, must first be stated: it is certainly nothing other than a perceptible—yet industrious—conceived true discourse, by which the types of metals are taught to be transmuted from one into another. Of all the celestial stars, **Gold** <note>original: "Sol"</note> and **Silver** <note>original: "Luna"</note> are but one stone in themselves; and the earthly stone proceeded from the celestial stone through the same fire, the same coals, ashes, expulsions, and the same purifications by which that celestial stone—clear and pure in its splendor—was separated and brought back to its essence. Indeed, the entire globe of the earth is nothing else than something cast off, congealed, mixed, corrupted, crushed, and again coagulated; it is a stony work partly melted into one mass, which holds its seat and rest in the very center of the sphere of the firmament. 

It should further be noted that those precious stones, which are called by their own names after the celestial stones or stars, hold the place closest to perfection, purity, beauty, clarity, virtue, incorruptibility, and constancy in fire, yet they lie hidden within other earthly stones. They have the greatest affinity with the stars or celestial stones and are of the same nature, for they derived from them into the stones in which they are now found. 

The same must be judged concerning metals. For **Alchemy** <note>The art of transforming and purifying materials</note>, therefore, there is primarily no need for other instruments than a smelting workshop, bellows full of air, tongs, hammers, crucibles, pots, and **cupels** <note>shallow porous cups used in assaying to separate precious metals from lead</note> constructed from beech ashes. Afterward, let **Lead** <note>original: "Saturnus"</note>, **Tin** <note>original: "Jupiter"</note>, **Iron** <note>original: "Mars"</note>, **Gold** <note>original: "Sol"</note>, **Copper** <note>original: "Venus"</note>, **Quicksilver** <note>original: "Mercurius"</note>, and **Silver** <note>original: "Luna"</note> be placed therein, and let them be worked even until the end of the **Lead** <note>original: "Saturni"; refers to the process of cupellation where lead is used to purify the other metals</note>. 

If, however, metals remain buried in the earth for a very long time, they are not only consumed by rust, but through perseverance they are transmuted into natural stones, of which the number is infinite; yet this secret is known to few. Sometimes there is found in the earth the old stone money of the **Gentiles** <note>Referring to ancient Roman or Greek coins</note> impressed with their images and characters, which was previously metallic, but was turned into stone through a transmutation performed by nature.

### *On the manner and place of seeking metals.*
### CHAPTER XXIII.

In the earth and in stones, the hope of finding metals is most uncertain; yet, because this is the primary method of acquisition, it should by no means be despised, but rather greatly praised. Such human desire and appetite should no more perish than the lawful love of young people for marriage. For just as bees desire flowers for the sake of honey and wax—yet not for themselves—so it would be right for men, like the bees, to long to extract metal from the earth without greed or regard for their own advantage. For he who seeks too much usually finds the least. God grants to men not only gold or silver, but also poverty, filth, and misery. He has also called some to a singular knowledge of metals and minerals, who have attained a shorter and easier way of manufacturing **Gold and Silver** <note>original: "solem & lunam"</note> without the need for digging or smelting. This is done by means of metals prepared by art, such as **Lead** <note>original: "Saturno"</note>, **Tin** <note>original: "Jove"</note>, **Copper** <note>original: "Venere"</note>, **Iron** <note>original: "Marte"</note>, and **Mercury** <note>original: "Mercurio"</note>, from which—and from any of them separately—they manufactured Gold and Silver, though more easily from one than another.

# OF METALS.

...from deep speculation result wonderful works, which many times—though contrary to the opinions of ancient natural philosophers and quite different from them—are nevertheless found to be true through proof and experiment. First, nothing in this art is more true than that which is least known, and to which the least faith is given. The sole occasion and cause of all difficulty in **Alchemy**, because of which many are reduced to poverty and the rest labor in vain, is the ignorance of the operators, and the too great or too small quantity (or even the [incorrect] equality) of the materials. Because of these errors, the substances in the operations are either destroyed or reduced to nothing. 

But if the true process has once been found, the thing, changing itself daily, approaches more and more toward perfection. The right way is easy, but it is found by very few. At times it happens that some speculative artisan devises an art in **Alchemy** through his own delirium, as if positioned in a labyrinth, whether anything or nothing is actually achieved by it. For he must do nothing by which a thing is introduced into nothingness, so that something may again arise from nothing: this is an incredible proverb, yet not at all false. 

Destruction perfects the good, for the good can in no way appear because of its "concealer." <note>original: "occultatorem"</note> For the good is hardly good while it is hidden. The concealer, therefore, must be removed so that the good may be able to appear freely with clarity. The concealer consists of the mountain and stone, the sand of the earth, the paths of the sun, and the veins in which the metal grew. But each one of the visible metals is the "dross" <note>original: "fex," meaning dregs, scum, or sediment</note> that conceals the other six metals. 

And because every imperfect thing is corrupted, burned, and reduced to nothing by the element of fire—such as these five metals: **Mercury** <note>term: Mercury (Quicksilver)</note>, **Jupiter** <note>term: Jupiter (Tin)</note>, **Mars** <note>term: Mars (Iron)</note>, **Venus** <note>term: Venus (Copper)</note>, and **Saturn** <note>term: Saturn (Lead)</note>—on the contrary, perfect metals are not consumed by such a fire, namely **Sol** <note>term: Sol (Gold)</note> and **Luna** <note>term: Luna (Silver)</note>. Thus it happens that they remain in the fire, and from the other imperfect metals in which they are corrupted, they simultaneously assume their own body and appear to the eye. 

How and by what skillful method this is done can be gathered from the **Seven Canons** set down below; likewise, one may learn the nature or property of each metal, how it works with others, and what it is capable of achieving in their mixture. But this must be especially noted: those seven canons cannot be understood at first glance or by a light reading, even by a reader who is commonly considered very sharp. For a shallow intellect does not easily admit hidden things; therefore, each of these canons requires no small amount of discussion. There are many elitist and proud spirits who rashly persuade themselves that they understand everything this little book contains; they believe they possess better things and are accustomed to scorn these matters—namely, the "sun between two moons" and the "sun in parentheses." <note>These are likely symbolic alchemical diagrams or notations representing specific planetary/metallic alignments or chemical states.</note>

This, therefore, is the method of transmuting **Iron** into **Copper**: let filings of <term>Mars<gloss>Iron</gloss></term> be boiled in water of vitriol <note>Vitriol usually refers to sulfate minerals, like iron or copper sulfate.</note> for a very long time, or let its small plates be cemented with calcined vitriol, or let them, when glowing hot, be extinguished in oil of vitriol.

Once the vessel has cooled, you will find at the bottom a <term>regulus<gloss>A metallic mass or "button" that settles at the bottom of a crucible after smelting.</gloss></term> of lead that is malleable without being heated, but not to such an extent that it is as quickly fusible as other lead. 

**Copper** is transmuted into **Lead** in this manner: first, let <term>Venus<gloss>Copper</gloss></term> be whitened with sublimated **Mercury** and fixed arsenic so it resembles <term>Luna<gloss>Silver</gloss></term>. Afterward, let it be granulated and have added to it an equal weight of fusion or reduction powder, with which it should be cemented for some time. Finally, let it be melted into a leaden regulus. 

Conversely, **Lead** is turned into **Copper** if plates of <term>Saturn<gloss>Lead</gloss></term> are cemented with calcined vitriol or <term>crocus of Venus<gloss>A reddish-brown copper oxide powder.</gloss></term> as above, and finally melted; a copper and malleable regulus will be obtained. 

**Lead** is easily turned into **Tin**, its plates being stratified with <term>sal ammoniac<gloss>Ammonium chloride, frequently used as a flux in alchemy.</gloss></term>, cemented, and finally melted, as with the others above. Although transmutations of this kind may be done with little or no profit—or even at a loss—they are nevertheless sometimes useful in many applications. It seemed fit to weave these in here, so that it might be seen how under every manifest <note>Visible or obvious.</note> metal, others lie hidden through the concealment of that which is manifest. 

Who doubts that under the light, darkness has been secretly suppressed and held back? When these finally emerge with the <term>malice of light<gloss>original: "lucidi malitia"; likely referring to the corruption or harsh manifestation of physical matter.</gloss></term>, that which was good is turned into evil, since these two joined together wage war against each other from that time when light was first hidden by the emerging shadows: but enough of these things for the wise and for our own people. I see that I must hasten to the **Canons**, by which both the hidden vices and the virtues of metals may become known, into which they must be turned by a most fixed concealment.

### On the nature and property of Jupiter.
#### The second Canon.

That which is manifest of <term>Jupiter<gloss>The alchemical name for Tin.</gloss></term> (understand here the physical body) contains six metals within itself spiritually hidden, one deeper and more tenacious than the other. It participates in nothing of the fifth essence, but is of the nature of the elements; for this reason, its melting is manifested immediately by the application of a light fire, and it is coagulated by the approach of a similar cold. It has an affinity with the melting of all other metals. For the more similar a thing is to another in nature, the more easily it is united to it through conjunction; also, the interaction of things near to each other is easier and more natural than those far apart. A remote thing tends to deceive, because the greatest part of it is least seen. 

Hence it happens that men do not pant after the heavenly beings, because they are very distant from them, and they do not see their glory; likewise, they do not fear the infernal beings so much because they are remote, and no living person knows or has actually experienced the misery of their state and punishment; for this reason, hell is treated as if it were nothing. In no different way, more remote things are considered more vile the more crude a place they occupy, because according to the property of its location, every thing turns out better or is changed, which can be demonstrated by various examples. 

Therefore, the further **Jupiter** [Tin] is from <term>Mars<gloss>Iron</gloss></term> and <term>Venus<gloss>Copper</gloss></term>, and the closer it is found to the <term>Sun<gloss>Gold</gloss></term> and <term>Moon<gloss>Silver</gloss></term>, the more it seems to approach the nature of gold and silver in its body—becoming larger, stronger, more visible, more tangible, more perceptible, more lovable, more acceptable, more known, more true, and whatever else can be said, than when it is remote. Again, the more remote any thing is, the more vile it is esteemed in all the aforesaid qualities, for no other reason than that the present thing is always preferred to the absent one. Therefore, the closer the manifest nature is, the further the hidden nature resides. Wherefore, the spiritual, hidden, and remote place must be considered and noted by <term>Alchemists</term> with the greatest diligence—that place in which the Sun and Moon exist. Whichever they have desired, let them seek it in the distance; likewise, let them see in the near, at the place where **Jupiter** stood physically; let them not doubt that the Sun and Moon truly exist there, and may be seen by the eye according to the test. ## On the nature and property of Mars.

### The third Canon

Six hidden metals expelled the seventh, **Mars**, and rejected him from themselves, making him corporeal; they left him the least value, while imposing upon him the greatest hardness and the burden of labors. Each metal cast off and manifested its own strength of coagulation and hardness into him, while they retained for themselves their own color, melting point, and nobility. It is a work most difficult and far too laborious to make a prince or a king out of a foolish and common man. But **Mars** acquires dominion with a strong and fighting hand, and occupies the place of the king. Yet there is reason for him to beware of snares, lest he unexpectedly becomes a captive. It must therefore be considered by what means **Mars** may obtain the place of the king, and how the **Sun** and **Moon** with <term>Gemini<gloss>The Twins; likely a reference to the 'mercurial' or dual nature required for certain chemical unions.</gloss></term> may hold their place.

## On the nature and property of Venus.

### The fourth Canon

The other six metals fabricated an external body from all their color and the medium of their melting impermanence. Whatever is naturally combustible, then, and subject to fire, can be transmuted from one form into another: namely into <term>lime<gloss>The powder (oxide) remaining after a metal has been roasted or 'calcined.'</gloss></term>, soot, ashes, glass, colors, stones, and into earth; which last can, in turn, be reduced back into many new metallic bodies. ## *On the nature and property of the Moon.*

### The sixth Canon.

To wish to produce Saturn or Mars from the <term>Moon<gloss>Silver</gloss></term> is no lighter or easier a work than to produce Moon from Mercury, Jupiter, Mars, Venus, and Saturn with great profit. Yet it is not useful to transmute perfect things into imperfect ones, but rather the latter into the former. One must therefore know what the matter of the Moon is, or from whence it originates. Whoever is unable to consider this will never be able to manufacture Moon at any time. But if it be asked, what is the Moon? It is indeed made from six spiritual metals hidden within itself, the seventh being manifest, as has often been said before; put another way, [it is composed of these] outwardly and materially; for always the seventh contains the other six hidden within itself. Furthermore, the six spiritual metals do not persist without some outward and material metal; so also no corporeal metal can have a place or essence without those six spiritual ones. The seven corporeal metals mix well by melting, but this mixture is useless for the Sun and Moon; for in it, everything either remains fixed in the fire or flees from it. For example: mix Mercury, Jupiter, Saturn, Mars, Venus, the Sun, and the Moon in whatever way you can—all these together—from that, the Sun and Moon will indeed be made, yet the other five will not be transmuted, so that from those, through the Sun and Moon, Sun and Moon may be made; although all have been melted into one mass, nevertheless each remains in its own nature exactly what it is: these are the things to be judged concerning corporeal mixture.
