### ON TRANSMUTATION

...that there is no separation or mortification <note>In alchemy, "mortification" refers to the process of breaking down or "killing" a substance's current form so its essence can be reborn in a more perfected state.</note> of the spirits, because spirits of this kind are such that they can never persist without bodies; even if the body were taken from them and mortified a hundred times in a single hour, they would nonetheless always acquire another more noble than the first. And this is the transposition of metals from one death to another, from a lower degree to a greater and higher one—that is, into the <term>Moon<gloss>Silver</gloss></term>—and from the better into the best and most perfect, which is the <term>Sun<gloss>Gold</gloss></term>, the most brilliant king of all other metals. It must be said further that metallic spirits of this kind acquire a body in their primary generation through celestial influence—namely, a stone <note>Likely referring to raw ore as it is found in the earth.</note> of vile appearance, which the master metallurgist completely melts, corrupts, and mortifies with fire. Then, finally, in that very mortification, the metallic spirit receives a better and nobler body, not brittle, but liquable and malleable. Then the Alchemist approaches, who again corrupts, mortifies, and skillfully prepares such a metallic body, so that the spirit of the metal may once again put on an even nobler and more perfect body, manifesting itself clearly in the light of the Sun or the Moon. Then at last, the metallic spirit and body, perfectly united together, are safe from the corruption of elementary fire, and are indeed incorruptible. It is therefore most true, as has been said very often above, that the six metals always generate the seventh, or produce it from themselves into manifest being.

**Question:** If it be true that the <term>Moon<gloss>Silver</gloss></term> and every other metal derive their origin from and are generated by the other six, what then is the property and nature of the Moon? 

**Response:** From <term>Saturn<gloss>Lead</gloss></term>, <term>Mercury<gloss>Quicksilver</gloss></term>, <term>Jupiter<gloss>Tin</gloss></term>, <term>Mars<gloss>Iron</gloss></term>, and <term>Venus<gloss>Copper</gloss></term>, nothing else nor any other metal can be made but the Moon. The cause of this is that every one of the other six metals has in itself two virtues, which are properly the spirits of the Moon, which (in brief words) are acquired by it in this way: For the Moon consists of six spiritual metals and their virtues, each of which has two; thus, in total, twelve exist in one body, placed in this metal, which are compared to the seven planets and the twelve celestial signs. 

For the Moon has from the planet **Mercury**, and from **Aquarius** and **Gemini** (or from **Aquarius** and **Pisces**), its liquidity and its white splendor. 

The Moon also has from **Jupiter**, **Sagittarius**, and **Taurus**, its white color and its great constancy in the fire. 

The Moon has from **Mars**, **Cancer**, and **Aries**, its hardness and its good ring <note>original: "clangorem," referring to the clear sound silver makes when struck.</note>. 

The Moon has from **Venus**, **Gemini**, and **Libra**, its measure of coagulation and its malleability. 

The Moon has from the **Sun**, **Leo**, and **Virgo**, its sincere purity and great constancy against the forces of fire. 

The Moon has from **Saturn**, **Virgo**, and **Scorpio** (or **Capricorn**), a homogeneous body, pure cleanliness, and constancy against the violence of fire. 

Such is the natural knowledge of the exaltation and the cause of the spirit and body of the Moon, with its composite nature touched upon in brief.

OF METALS.

## *On the nature and properties of the Sun.*
### The seventh canon.

The seventh <note>The author counts the Sun (Gold) as the seventh metal, crowning the group of six "spiritual" metals previously discussed.</note> among the six spiritual metals in bodily form is the <term>Sun<gloss>Gold</gloss></term>, which in itself is nothing other than pure fire. As for why it possesses a body that is more beautiful, yellower, more visible, more perceptible, heavier, colder, and more uniform in appearance and touch than the others; the entire cause of this is that it contains within itself the solidifications of the other six metals, by which it has been compacted into a single, most dense external body. 

Its melting by means of elementary fire, however, proceeds from <term>Mercury<gloss>Quicksilver</gloss></term>, Pisces, and Aquarius <note>In alchemy, Mercury represents the principle of fluidity. Pisces and Aquarius are zodiac signs associated with water, here linked to the "hidden liquefactions" that allow Gold to melt.</note>, which hold these liquefactions spiritually hidden within themselves and work upon the Sun. A most clear example of this is seen when Mercury itself most easily mixes with the Sun physically through an "embrace" <note>This refers to amalgamation, where mercury dissolves gold at room temperature.</note>. 

But the fact that the Sun—after melting and as the heat recedes and cold arrives from without—coagulates and becomes hard and solid, is caused by the remaining five metals whose natures it embraces within itself: namely <term>Jupiter<gloss>Tin</gloss></term>, <term>Saturn<gloss>Lead</gloss></term>, <term>Mars<gloss>Iron</gloss></term>, <term>Venus<gloss>Copper</gloss></term>, and the <term>Moon<gloss>Silver</gloss></term>. In these five, "cold mansions" <note>Astrological positions or inherent elemental qualities associated with coldness and stability.</note> are primarily found along with their governing influences. From this it also happens that the Sun can hardly be melted except by the application of fire, because of the aforementioned cold. 

Nor can Mercury assist with its own natural heat or fluidity, nor defend the Sun against the coldness of those five metals; for Mercury is not powerful enough to keep the Sun in its liquid state, since the Sun must obey the five metals more than the single one <note>Mercury</note>, whose sole duty by its nature is to always flow. Hence it also happens that Mercury is unable to act during the solidification of other metals, for its nature is not to make things hard or solid, but liquid. 

To make something fluid belongs to the nature of heat and life, while coldness possesses the nature of hardness, consolidation, and immobility, which are compared to death. For example, if the six metals—Jupiter, Venus, Saturn, Mars, the Moon, and the Sun—are to be melted, it must be done by the heat of fire. Snow or ice, which are cold, will not accomplish this, but will rather coagulate them or make them hard. As soon as a metal melted by fire is removed from the flame, the cold rushing into it makes it congealed, hard, and immobile by itself. 

But as for Mercury flowing and remaining always "living" <note>The term "quick-silver" (living silver) refers to its liquid state at room temperature.</note>, tell me, I pray: is this caused by heat or cold? Whoever responds that this happens by a cold and moist nature (as has been judged until now), and that it derives its life from coldness—the proponent of such an opinion has no knowledge of nature, but has been led astray along with the common crowd. For the ignorant crowd judges nothing but falsehoods from outward appearances in natural matters; they firmly hold only to what they see with their fleshy eyes. Therefore, anyone who desires to know the truth in these matters should depart from such views. Mercury...

# ON TRANSMUTATIONS

Indeed, [Gold] does not live from a cold nature at all, but from a hot and fiery one; for every living thing is fire, by this reasoning: that heat is the occasion of life, but cold is the occasion of death. Likewise, the <term>Sun<gloss>Gold</gloss></term> in itself is pure fire, yet not "living" <note>The author distinguishes between biological life and the "vitality" or "spirit" of a metal.</note>, but hard, and displays only the color of sulfur, like white mixed with red in a certain proportion.

The five cold metals, however—namely <term>Jupiter<gloss>Tin</gloss></term>, <term>Mars<gloss>Iron</gloss></term>, <term>Saturn<gloss>Lead</gloss></term>, <term>Venus<gloss>Copper</gloss></term>, and <term>Luna<gloss>Silver</gloss></term>—contribute their own virtues to the Sun. According to their coldness, they give the body itself; according to fire, they give color; according to dryness, hardness; according to humidity, the weight itself; and likewise, from their brightness, they give it its resonance <note>The "clagor" or ring of the metal when struck.</note>. 

The reason that the Sun is not burned up in the element of terrestrial fire, nor even corrupted, is the result of the harmony of the Sun with fire; for one fire cannot burn another, nor consume it. Rather, when fire approaches fire, it increases and becomes stronger in its operations. To be sure, that celestial fire which the Sun pours into the earth to work among us is not the same kind of fire as that in the heavens, nor is it similar to our fire existing upon the earth; rather, that celestial fire among us is a cold and congealed fire, which is the body of the Sun. For this reason, the Sun can in no way be overcome by our fire; it only happens to it that it melts, just as snow and ice melt from that same celestial Sun. Therefore, fire does not have the power to burn fire, because the Sun is fire, which exists as a liquid in the heavens but as a solid among us. Gold, likewise, is threefold in its essence: the first is the celestial dissolved [gold], the second is the elementary fluid [liquid gold], and the third is metallic and corporeal [solid gold].

The readiness of manufacturing through <term>Alchemy</term> is easier than is necessary to make extensive mention of in any document or writing, much like those things which are usually made from "annual snow" <note>This may refer to a common but temporary substance, or perhaps a specific alchemical metaphor for a white precipitate.</note>. Indeed, whoever judges <term>Mercury<gloss>Quicksilver</gloss></term> to be of a moist and cold nature is deceived, convicted by their own manifest error; for by its own nature it is nothing but supremely hot and moist, for which reason it is naturally forced to be liquid in its flow and "life." For if it were moist and cold by nature, it would have the appearance of frozen water, and would always exist as hard and solid; and like frozen metals, it would require fire to liquefy it. Yet it needs no [external fire], since it possesses liquefaction and flow from its own heat naturally implanted within it, which keeps it in perpetual flow and makes it "living," so that it can neither die nor be coagulated on its own. 

But in these matters, it is especially necessary to know that the seven spirits of the metals, or however many of them come into the fire mixed together, wage a battle among themselves—especially <term>Mercury</term>—so much so that each exerts its own virtues and powers upon the other out of a desire for conquering, liquefying, and transmutating. One plunders the virtue, life, and form of another, and bestows another nature and form. For by heat, spirits of this kind are set in motion, and through their vapors they are excited to work a mutual transmutation upon one another, from one virtue into another, until they reach perfection and purity. 

But what, finally, should be done with <term>Mercury</term> so that—its humidity and heat being entirely removed, and in their place the greatest coldness being thoroughly introduced—it might be congealed, consolidated, and entirely "mortified" <note>In alchemy, "mortification" refers to the process of stripping a substance of its outward form or "life" (in this case, Mercury's fluidity) to prepare it for a new state.</note>? Furthermore, it should be noted that the coldness (which <term>Mercury</term> requires for its consolidation and mortification) is not at all perceptible to the outward senses, like that of snow or ice, but rather appears outwardly as something hot. We must judge the heat of <term>Mercury</term>—by which it flows naturally—in no different a way; it is not a heat perceptible from the outside according to the likeness of our qualities, but rather it appears as the greatest cold. Hence the <term>Sophists<gloss>false philosophers</gloss></term> (an inexpertly talkative race) assert that it is of a cold and moist nature. Because of this, they also strive to coagulate it with nothing but hot things; however, they find daily to their own loss that it is made more fluid than the solid they desire.

# ON THE GENERATION
## of Minerals.
### CHAPTER I.

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'C' containing foliate scrollwork patterns.</image-desc>When I had read the writings of the ancients concerning the generation of minerals with the greatest care, I discovered that they did not understand the **ultimate matter** of them, and consequently, they understood the **prime matter** <note>In Aristotelian and alchemical philosophy, *materia prima* (prime matter) is the raw, formless base of all things, while *materia ultima* (ultimate matter) is the final, perfected form of a substance.</note> much less. For indeed, so that the beginning of any thing may be properly known, its end must be especially well understood. Therefore, I have decided first of all to propose the ultimate matter of minerals to us, from which you will easily understand the prime matter from which they take their origin. 

Let us first bring forward an example from medicine, in which a disease is to be known by its outcome, and not from its beginning (in which there is no certain knowledge); because that which is introduced through blindness must itself be blind. However, the end is visible from the outcome, toward which the disease is perceived to tend as toward a target set for itself. Hence, no thing can be better known than when it is best understood for what end it was created by God; otherwise, it will easily happen that the true use of God's creature turns into an abuse. Whoever, therefore, undertakes any work from a certain substance must know that very substance from its roots, so that he may complete it in the order prescribed by God. If he lacks a perfect knowledge of the matter, or has none at all, it may turn out otherwise, and the work of the devil might be performed instead through the abuse of matter and instruments. 

Let this be a sufficiently plain example: of what use is an axe or a pick-axe, or wood or any other material, in the hand of one who does not know how to use them? In such hands, they can...

#### On the plain manifestation of this art.
#### CHAPTER XXVII.

When you have caused the heaven or the sphere of Saturn <note>Saturn is the alchemical name for the metal lead. The "sphere" or "heaven" refers to its celestial influence or its volatile, spiritual state during a chemical process.</note> to run with life upon the earth, place upon it all the planets <note>In alchemy, the "planets" refer to the seven known metals: Gold (Sun), Silver (Moon), Mercury (Mercury), Copper (Venus), Iron (Mars), Tin (Jupiter), and Lead (Saturn).</note> or whichever ones you wish, yet let there not be too much of the Moon, but let less of her be added than the others. In this way, all the planets remain consistent so that, their old and corruptible bodies being dead, they have put on a new, perfect, and incorruptible body. This very thing is the spirit of heaven, from which the said planets become corporal and living again, as before. Take this new body from life and from the earth, and keep it: this is the Sun and the Moon <note>Gold and silver</note>. You have, in this manner, the art entirely manifest and complete. If you do not yet understand or know it, it is well: for it must remain so, and not be made commonly and openly known to all indifferently.

# ON THE GENERATION
## of Minerals.

### CHAPTER I.

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'C' featuring floral patterns and stylized foliate scrollwork within a square frame.</image-desc>
When I had read most accurately the writings of the ancients regarding the generation of minerals, I discovered that they did not understand their ultimate matter <note>The final, completed form of a substance after it has been fully processed or matured</note>, and consequently, much less the first matter <note>original: *primam materiam*; the raw, unformed substance from which a thing originates</note>. Indeed, so that the beginning of any thing may be rightly known, its end must especially be understood. Therefore, I have decided to set before us first of all the ultimate matter of minerals, from which you will easily understand the first matter from which they take their origin. Let us first bring forward an example from medicine, in which a disease is to be known by its outcome, and not from its beginning—in which there is no knowledge. Because that which is introduced through blindness must also itself be blind; the end, however, is visible from the outcome, toward which it is perceived to strive as if toward a target set for itself. Furthermore, no thing can be better known than when it is best understood for what purpose it was created by God; otherwise, it will easily happen that the true use of God's creature turns into an abuse. Whoever, therefore, undertakes any work from any substance, must know that very substance from which it comes radically <note>from its roots or foundations</note>, so that he may complete it according to the order prescribed by God. Otherwise, because of an imperfect knowledge of the material, or sometimes none at all, it may happen differently, and the work of the devil might rather be performed through the abuse of the material and the instruments. A crude enough example is this: what use is an axe or a hatchet <note>original: *dolabra*; a tool used for cutting or masonry</note>, and wood or any other material, in the hand of one who does not know how to use them? They can tend elsewhere,

...can be put to use, rather than toward their destruction. Moreover, he who knows how to fabricate a lawful and honest work from instruments and matter can and ought to take it into his hands, so that it yields to the utility of his neighbor, while keeping for his own use that purpose for which the matter was given by God. For God willed that he, to whom He gave true knowledge of the use of a thing, should also have and possess everything He created. To this, everyone who perceives in his own conscience that he is called to it must apply himself, learning this likewise, and not usurping something foreign or fantastic suggested by the devil.

Learn, then, the ultimate matter <note>The final, perfected state of a substance</note> and the first matter of things from fire; for fire, like a key, unlocks the chest, and makes manifest whatever is hidden in anything. Therefore, in this place, the ultimate matter of things is that into which they are completely resolved through fire, so that finally, among the three universal firsts <note>term: *tria universalia prima* — The Three Principles: Mercury, Sulfur, and Salt, which alchemists believed composed all matter</note>, about which I have discussed in various places, the first and predominant principle may be recognized.

Let a metal dissolved by fire be an example: it immediately reveals its first beginning to be **mercurial water**, and not sulfur, because its resolution does not burn like resins. It is also demonstrated not to be salt because the first sign of its resolution is not a crumbling <note>original: *friatio*; the act of breaking into small pieces or grains</note> apart from its liquefaction and burning, as is seen to be the case with earthy things and stones. Nevertheless, every metal has sulfur and salt in it, but **Mercury** holds the principal place; so it is with the other minerals.

But it seemed right to God to create the element of water, and that daily any minerals for the use of men should be produced from it, so that it might be their **mother**. In water—as if in its own womb <note>original: *matrice*</note>—the mineral fire, and likewise salt and Mercury, are cooked into metals, stones, and every mineral substance, even if the offspring exists unlike the mother. In this way the Most High created all things in their own nature, just as birds are for one purpose in the air and fish for another in the waters; so it is for all the rest, which are to be committed solely to His divine will, who makes all things as they are, and willed from eternity that those things He makes should be.

Just as water is not similar to its metallic offspring, nor the son to the mother, in the same way the earth itself is wood, and yet not wood, which nevertheless comes from it. By the same reasoning, stone and iron are made from water—which becomes such a water as it itself was not—and earth similarly becomes that which it is not in itself. So also it is necessary for man to become what he himself does not presently exist as. In short, whatever must pass into its ultimate matter must become something other than what its beginning was, each thing being various and diverse in its kind, even from a single mother.

Thus God willed to be one in all things, and likewise that there be one first and ultimate matter of all things; such, and so admirable, is the first Architect of things, as there never was before, nor ever shall be another. But as you have heard thus far concerning the mother of minerals—namely, water—in what follows we will further teach how the ancients wrote wrongly and erroneously that it is earth, which they have not yet been able to truly demonstrate.

# OF MINERALS

## *On the ultimate and first matter of minerals.*

### CHAPTER II.

The first principle with God was the **ultimate matter** <note>original: *ultima materia*; in this philosophy, it refers to the final, perfected form God intended for a thing</note>, which He himself made into the **first matter**, like a fruit that produces another fruit. This matter itself possesses a seed, and this seed resides in the first matter. Similarly, in the ultimate matter of minerals, the first matter was created—that is, it was made into a seed. This seed is the **element of water** which resolves so that it becomes water. For this purpose, God entrusted it to nature, or ordained within it, that it should produce the ultimate matter; indeed, that matter is contained within the water. 

Nature, therefore, takes what is in the water under its own power and process of separation. Whatever belongs to a metal, it separates into a metal, each according to its own kind; so it does with gems, stones, the **magnet**, and other things of that type, each in its own nature and species. For just as God ordained for wheat its own time for harvest, and autumn for sweets <note>original: *bellariis*; refers to treats or fruits and nuts harvested late in the season</note> and similar things within their own elements, He willed that the element of water should have its own proper time of harvest and autumn. He also prefixed the times for the collection of fruits for all other things according to their kind. 

The element of water is therefore the mother, the seed, and the root of all minerals. The **Archeus** <note>term: *Archeus* — the internal "master craftsman" or vital force that Paracelsus believed directed the growth and functions of all natural things</note> within the water is the one who arranges each thing in a specific order, so that every single thing reaches its natural ultimate matter. Finally, man receives this as his own "first matter" for art <note>meaning: the raw material used by the alchemist or craftsman</note>. That is: where nature ends, there the art of man begins; for nature's ultimate matter is man's first matter. Conversely, the corruption <note>in the sense of breaking down or transforming</note> of nature through art becomes man's ultimate matter. 

With such wonderful workmanship, God created water as the first matter of nature—such a soft and weak substance—and yet from it comes the most solid fruit: metal, stones, and so on. Thus, from the softest comes the hardest, and from water comes fire <note>likely referring to the "igneous" or sulfurous properties within minerals</note>. This is beyond the grasp of human intellect, yet it is not beyond nature. Indeed, God created marvelous offspring from that mother [water], as is apparent in humans; if they are observed even in their own mother, each will be found to have a peculiar talent and property, not according to the body, but according to the condition of their temperament <note>original: *complexionis*; the specific balance of humors and qualities in an individual</note>.

---

## *On the field, roots, and trees of minerals.*

### CHAPTER III.

The Most High created the element of water to be like a field in which the roots of mineral trees, arising from their seeds, might be fixed. From there, the trunk and branches are pushed forth into the earth, as will be discussed more broadly below. He therefore separated water from the other three elements, so that it would exist as a body free by itself—not in the air, nor in the earth, nor in the heavens—but placed in the lower globe. It exists upon the earth and has its center within it, where it is founded. It was created with such wonderful order that, together with the earth, it must carry man, just as one is carried upon the water as if in a ship...

->*Of the natural dispenser of minerals, and his subordinates.*<-
->CHAPTER VIII.<-

Just as in the craft of minerals performed by men—to prepare them and then bring them into use—not just one, but many are required in succession; yet each of them has a specific gift for his office. For what good are the gifts dug out from the bowels of the earth without their separator, preparer, or smelter? What is the smelter again without the smith? Likewise, he can do nothing without a buyer, nor can the buyer do anything without the one who knows how to adapt the metals for use. Nature herself does not need all these, but only her own [ministers], such as first, the **Archeus** <note>term: Archeus — the "internal chemist" or vital force that directs the growth and transformation of matter</note>, the dispenser of minerals. He, being the minister of nature himself, has these subordinates: first, one who provides the bodily matter upon which the operation may fall—namely, mineral **Sulphur** <note>In Paracelsian thought, Sulphur represents the principle of combustibility and structure</note> of this or that condition and nature; second, one who fashions properties and virtues and works upon the pre-existing matter, such as **Mercury** <note>In alchemy, Mercury represents the principle of volatility and the "spirit" of a substance</note>; and third, one who through compaction and coagulation joins the individual parts together into one body, namely **Salt** <note>In alchemy, Salt represents the principle of stability and physical solidity</note>, the confirmer of the work. All these, heaped together into one and enclosed in his **Athanor** <note>term: Athanor — a self-feeding alchemical furnace designed to maintain a steady, uniform heat</note>, the Archeus digests <note>original: *decoquit*; literally "cooks down," referring to the alchemical process of maturation through heat</note> just as a seed in the earth; and not only into themselves, but they are also mutually digested among one another in this manner. Sulphur submits its body to the other two, so that they may work upon it whatever they wish and lead it to that end for which that which must be made from it is destined. Mercury comes with the properties of its virtues; this is digested from the other two. When such digestions of all things are completed, then finally it begins to work itself into its other associates and into itself, first by condensing, then...

## *On the Virtues and Properties of Salts in Alchemy and Medicine.*

### CHAPTER IX.

God the Best and Greatest <term>O.D.M.</term> <note>original: *O.D.M.*, an abbreviation for *Optimus Deus Maximus*, a common honorific for the Divine</note> wished to bring man to such a state of necessity through nature that he cannot live naturally without natural salt. Consequently, he has need of this in all foods. Indeed, <term>salt is the balsam of nature</term>, which prevents the corruption of hot <term>sulphur</term> and moist <term>mercury</term>, from which the natural man is composed <note>Paracelsus taught that all matter, including the human body, is made of three principles: Sulphur (the combustible/soul), Mercury (the fluid/spirit), and Salt (the solid/body)</note>. Since it is necessary that these primary seasoned components be nourished by things similar to themselves, it follows necessarily that man must use "burning" foods to sustain his internal sulphur; "moist" foods to nourish his mercury; and likewise "salty" foods to preserve the salt in its capacity as a seasoning. The power of this preservation is most clearly seen in how it keeps dead flesh from rot for a very long time; it is easy to judge how much more it will preserve living flesh. To come at last to its types, three are considered especially suitable for human use. The first of these is <term>sea salt</term>, the second is <term>spring salt</term>, and the third is <term>mineral salt</term>. Spring salt is most conducive to health, mineral salt takes second place, and finally sea salt. Both the first and second types are boiled by human art, while the remaining one is cooked by nature alone. This mineral salt and sea salt are not categorized under the nature of <term>brine</term> <note>original: *muriæ*; brine or pickling liquor</note>, but that which is boiled is first turned into brine before it is separated from the water and coagulated into salt. Two descriptions of salt must therefore be proposed to us: one concerning brine, the other concerning fully finished salt. First of all, however, a certain common method of correcting any salt must be considered, in this manner: Wherever salt does not intervene in foods, there is no correction in them...

->*On the virtues of vitriol in medicine, raw or calcined.*<-

### CHAPTER XVI.

For the most grievous stomach pains and sicknesses arising from the immoderate consumption of food and drink, or for its bad digestion, vitriol administered raw—in the quantity of six <term>cometæ</term> <note>likely a specific small measure or drop used by Paracelsus</note> or three drops, that is, three grains—in wine or water for the weak, or in distilled wine for the robust, thoroughly purges every vice, driving it out from above and below <note>referring to its effect as both an emetic and a laxative</note>. In the <term>arcana</term> <note>the hidden or secret medicinal teachings</note>, vitriol is called *grillus* or *grilla*. Neither hellebore, nor <term>colocynth</term> <note>bitter apple, a powerful and often harsh purgative</note>, nor <term>diagridium</term> <note>a purified form of the resin scammony</note> purge as vehemently or cure as perfectly as this; nor do they have the power to expel worms. Vitriol is also the best purgative above all others for treating the "falling sickness" <note>epilepsy</note>. Such properties come to it from a twofold nature: namely, of acidity and saltiness; for this reason, it is a much nobler medicine than others. Its <term>colcothar</term>, or what they call the red <term>caput mortuum</term> <note>literally "dead head"; the useless dregs remaining after a chemical process</note>, is not to be taken internally; it is suitable only for surgical treatments, such as for putrid ulcers of the first degree of malignancy; however, the oil of vitriol should be used for those that have reached the second and third degrees.

Its medicinal virtues are contained in other books of medicine, such as in the *Bundle of Paracelsian Flowers*; in this place, we proposed only to treat and gather into one those things which pertain to transmutatory Alchemy, even if medicinal matters sometimes compel us to digress from our purpose. Hence, we must see what vitriol provides in chemical matters, beyond the transmutation of iron into copper as we said above, the formula of which we have thought best to set down first. Although the work is not as difficult as transmuting iron into gold, God wants the lesser things to be made public first, and the greater to remain hidden for a while, until the <term>Elias of the Art</term> <note>original: *Helias artis*; a messianic figure in alchemical lore, specifically *Elias Artista*, who was prophesied to reveal the ultimate secrets of nature in the final days</note> arrives; for all arts have their own peculiar [spirit], as in other intelligences—

In vitriol, so great and so powerful a <term>tincture</term> <note>a transformative essence or concentrated color</note> lies hidden that it is scarcely believable to anyone not experienced, though well understood by him who understands its secrets. Whenever the oil of vitriol is mixed with the oil of Mercury, and both are coagulated together, they pass into a stone of wonderful tincture and condition, similar to a sapphire. Having finished with the salts, we must come to the sulfurs.

->*On the triple sulfur of minerals.*<-
->CHAPTER XVII.<-

Sulfur ought properly to be called the "resin of the earth," in which innumerable virtues lie hidden in both faculties <note>meaning both the medicinal and the alchemical arts</note>; however, the raw form is powerful in neither. Only its <term>arcanum</term> <note>the pure, secret essence of a substance</note>, rescued and freed from impurities, performs wonders: first washed to an excellent whiteness, like that which is seen in snow, through the <term>Isopic art</term> <note>original: *Isopicam artem*; likely referring to a purification process, possibly derived from 'hyssop' (cleansing) or a corruption of 'Aesopic'</note>. It has as many diverse virtues as it has various origins. For any metal or mineral contains a sulfur within itself that differs from another. As we said above regarding the likeness of chestnuts and nuts: minerals are likewise wrapped in their shells, yet in the kernel <note>original: *nucleo*</note> lies the most excellent virtue, which is nourished and sustained by external things. And there is a third kind, which is extracted from the kernels of minerals or metals, which can be called nothing better by the art than "animated" and "spagyric": and which must be applied to anything similar to itself in both faculties. Two conditions of embryonated sulfur are to be noted: one becomes volatile from the fixed; the other is pure and living fire, both invisible and visible. In a similar way, it passes through the consumption of wood and of disease. The extraction of embryonated sulfur is performed either by <term>sublimation</term> <note>heating a solid until it becomes a vapor and then a solid again to purify it</note> or by <term>descent</term> <note>original: *descensum*; a method of distillation where the substance is melted or vaporized downwards into a receiver</note>. In such cases, it must be extracted from its mineral bodies with <term>aqua fortis</term> <note>nitric acid</note> and then coagulated. 

All this, when separated according to true harmony, contains within itself a golden nature, which is why it is to be sought in <term>Alchemy</term> above all else, because it easily accepts fixation. Indeed, it fixes gold in <term>cements</term> <note>dry heat treatments used to purify or color metals</note>, and in other metals that are not yet mature or are still volatile. However, gold is sought from it in vain unless it is first present by nature: it contains no silver, but only gold—one more than the other, as in the embryonated form of <term>Venus</term> <note>copper</note>, red talc, and golden or iron <term>marcasites</term> <note>a mineral often confused with pyrite (fool's gold)</note>, which rarely lack gold. 

Whoever wishes to apply their hand to these things should remember and note well to separate such sulfur from gold with the greatest industry, and so skillfully that nothing of the gold is lost. Many could be helped at this point; it is true that I remain silent. However, since riches lead the poor entirely away from the true path, taking away humility and piety and bringing in their place pride, arrogance, petulance, and incontinence, I must remain silent, leaving poverty as a bridle for the poor and the greedy.

Not content with this, they made a most obstinate progression to reach <term>fixation</term> <note>the process of making a volatile substance stable under heat so it does not evaporate</note>, continuing until no house or possession remained for these poor wretches, who experienced "transmutation" in their own lives <note>i.e., falling from wealth to poverty</note> rather than in the metals. From the time that "electrum"—a name bestowed by the ancients—fell into oblivion, ruin soon followed for those who falsely changed this name to gold and silver; that is to say, the perdition of modern chemists. 

To define electrum: it is a metal forged from another by art, which is no longer similar to that from which it was made. For example: an arsenical metal, prepared according to the ritual of metallic preparation and <term>cemented</term> <note>heated while surrounded by a powdered chemical mixture</note> with <term>Venus</term> <note>the alchemical name for copper</note> in the usual manner, converts the copper entirely into white electrum, which is of less value than the copper itself. What need is there, then, to debase metals at great expense? Would it not be better to leave copper in its natural state, saving the money, time, and labor to be applied to a more useful work? The ancients called electrum by its proper name; the more recent workers falsely call it silver. The ancients suffered no loss because they recognized electrum for what it was; the moderns, because they have no knowledge of electrum, suffer the loss of their wealth, labor, and time.

Subsequently, through descent and precipitation, they achieved nothing more than their own <term>calcinations</term> <note>reducing a metal to powder through heat</note>. Thus it happens that obstinate men are deceived in Alchemy when they do not exactly understand the vocabulary of their art’s impositions from the very foundation.

It is frequently found to contain gold, and only very rarely does it lack gold, like many other things. ## *On Quicksilver.*
### CHAP. XIX.

Having finished our discussion of salts and sulfurs, we come now to quicksilver <note>original: *argentum vivum*, literally "living silver"</note>. This cannot properly be called a metal, but rather a metallic water; yet it is called a metal for this reason: that through Alchemy it can be brought into a solid substance and into the color of metals—sometimes being <term>fixed</term> <note>rendered stable and resistant to evaporation by heat</note>, and other times not. It can be recognized as the "first matter" of the Alchemists, who are able to manufacture from it gold, silver, copper, and so on, provided they persist through the trial of the assay; likewise perhaps tin, lead, and even iron. Indeed, it is of a wondrous nature and cannot be thoroughly understood except through the greatest labors. In short, it reveals itself to be the primary material of the Alchemists within the metallic degrees, and a supreme <term>arcanum</term> <note>a deep secret or powerful medicinal mystery</note> in medicine. It is a water that does not wet what it touches, and a "running animal without feet," heavier than all other metals. It consists, like all individual things, of sulfur, salt, and mercury. It reveals the first and last matter in the smelting of metals, especially in those which melt by color before they reach a glow, and in others by their flow.

## *On Cachymia and Imperfect Bodies.*
### CHAP. XX.

There is another kind of mineral body which is neither a salt nor a metal, but is "metallic" in character. These include <term>marcasites</term> <note>often referring to iron pyrites or similar glittering ores</note>, <term>chiseta</term> <note>likely another term for pyritic or copper-bearing ores</note> (both red and white), various forms of antimony (perfect and imperfect), arsenical minerals, <term>orpiment</term> <note>original: *auripigmenta*, a yellow arsenic sulfide used as a pigment</note>, various talcs, cobalt, garnets, gems, and so forth. I say they are metallic because they possess the "first matter" of metals in the highest degree and take their origin from the three metallic principles. It is to these minerals that the metals—such as gold, silver, copper, and iron—flee and in which they are incorporated. Truly, because a "metallic enemy" is incorporated with them at the same time, they cannot be separated and liberated from the tyranny of that enemy except through Alchemy. There are various such enemies who practice "robbery" against the metals, just as if someone seeking refuge in a companion's house were to be plundered and killed by the very person whose help they implored. Some of the aforementioned consist mostly of sulfur, such as marcasites, chiseta, and cobalt; others indeed consist of the "body of Mercury," such as arsenical minerals, orpiments, and antimony; while others consist of salt, such as all the talcs. Marcasites are found in two colors, white and yellow, according to the metallic...

### *On the metals completed by nature, both perfect and imperfect; and first, of Saturn or lead.*

## CHAPTER XXI.

**Saturn** <note>The alchemical name for lead.</note> has obtained the blackest and thickest body of all, a mercury similar to it, and a salt that is the most easily melted of all. Through "corruption" <note>chemical breakdown or oxidation</note>, it is easily reduced into its spirit: into white **ceruse** <note>white lead, used as a pigment</note>, into yellow, into **minium** <note>red lead</note>, and finally into glass, like the rest. **Tin** <note>original: *stannum*</note> is made from a fixed white sulfur and a fixed salt, but from a mercury that is not fixed. Because it is fixed in its body but not in its mercury, it easily loses its metallic fusion when the spirit flies away through fire; indeed, when that spirit is absent, it is no longer a metal, but a vanished body. **Iron** and **steel** <note>original: *chalybs*</note> are made from non-melting sulfur, salt, and mercury, which are the opposites of tin and lead. ...from the purest sulfur, highly sublimated by nature and cleansed of all dregs and impurities, raised to such transparency that no other body among the metals can ascend higher. This sulfur is one part of the **prime matter** <note>original: *materiæ primæ*; the foundational substance of all things</note> of gold. If alchemists were able to obtain this—as it is easily found within its own tree and root—they would have every reason to rejoice. For this is the true **Sulfur of the Philosophers** <note>a spiritualized, non-combustible form of sulfur believed to be a constituent of the Philosopher's Stone</note> from which gold is made, and not that other common sulfur from which iron and copper are formed, and so on. This is the weight of its universal nature. Its **Mercury** <note>quicksilver, as a philosophical principle of fluidity and spirit</note> is also highly separated by nature from all earthly and accidental excess, transformed separately into its own Mercurial part and into extreme clarity. This Mercury of the Philosophers is the second part of the prime matter of gold, from which gold ought to be born just as roses are born from rose seeds. It is set apart for the highest crystalline clarity and purified from all saltiness, bitterness, acidity, aluminosity, and vitriol-like qualities <note>the harsh, corrosive properties of mineral salts</note>, so that nothing at all clings to it as it now rejoices freely in the highest brightness and transparency. When these three <note>Sulfur, Mercury, and Salt</note> come together into one, gold is processed <note>original: *decoquitur*; literally "boiled down"</note> into a mass, though not always of the same condition or grade. For nature exhibits thirty-two grades of gold, which in the Art <note>the practice of Alchemy</note> become twenty-four in the highest degree of perfection. The reason for this is that gold is nourished in its own "tree," just as a cow is in its pastures, or an **Epicurean** <note>a follower of Epicurus; here used to mean someone who delights in fine food</note> in his tavern and larder. As soon as either of these leaves their pasture, they grow thin; it happens no differently with gold: as soon as it becomes the "prime matter of man" <note>likely referring to gold's use in medicinal "potable gold" or its transition from a mineral state to a human-applied state</note>, it is diminished by eight degrees. Indeed, such pastures are sometimes worse, which results in poorer grades of gold or fewer being produced, so that nature’s highest might descend from twenty-six to ten in the Art. The accidents or rather the influence of the stars or the elements sometimes hinder the generation of gold, so that nature becomes rougher or more unmanageable. But it is especially the inequality of the weights of the first three principles—such as an excessive portion of **Salt**—that makes it paler; with too much Mercury, it turns more yellow than is right; and with a more abundant **Sulfur**, it is rendered too reddish. Among nature just as among men, errors occur through these impediments, which can be removed by **antimony**, **cementations**, and **quartations** <note>various metallurgical refining processes used to separate gold from other metals</note>. Furthermore, in sulfur one should seek nothing other than the "body"; in salt, the "confirmation" <note>stability or firmness</note>; but in Mercury resides all virtue, property, essence, and medicine. These do not exist in the others as they do in Mercury, which are like a dead body lacking a spirit; in such a body, we still experience some elementary virtues—just as we find in vinegar the remnants of the fire of wine, still possessing consuming and corrosive powers, yet not nourishing or strengthening ones as we find in wine. Natural things are judged in their manifest <note>visible</note> state to be composed of the four elements, but in their hidden state, the matter is quite different:

For they are composed of only the three aforementioned things having a common **magnet** <note>the attractive force or "magnetic virtue" that binds the three principles together</note> between them, which in the **decoction** <note>original: *decoctione*; the alchemical process of heating or "cooking" a substance to maturity</note> of preparation draws the trinity of essence to itself. Ancient natural philosophers called this a "state," because the trinity acquires a state of unity in which natural motion rests and stops at a specific degree. Indeed, that magnetic virtue which attracted the medicine into **Mercury** <note>quicksilver</note>—where it is also found—should rightly be called a fourth principle, though not an element. In the final separation, however, Mercury loses most of its weight. With all these things arranged by nature in this manner, gold grows into a tree, extending from the root through the trunk into its branches and **twigs** <note>original: *locustas*; here referring to the outermost clusters or shoots of the metallic "tree" in the earth</note>, in which flowers bloom (just as is seen above the ground). Even when these flowers fade, fruit is not always found at the ends of the twigs; sometimes it is found several hundred paces deeper in the tree, sometimes in the middle, or several degrees toward the surface of the earth.

It sometimes happens that nothing grows except Mercury, where it has suppressed the other principles through its own excess. If, however, the **corrosive salts** dominate by their nature, they eat away the flowers of the tree like worms. Under the dominion of sulfur, everything is burned, just as things above ground are scorched by the excessive heat of the sun.

**Copper** <note>original: *cuprum*</note> is made from reddish-brown sulfur, red salt, and yellow Mercury, cooked into a metal. This contains its own "male" within it—that is, the **slag** <note>original: *scoriam*; the dross or impurities separated from metal during smelting</note>. If this slag is reduced back into its metal after being separated, it returns to a "masculine" copper that will no longer be corrupted, and the "female" part will provide no further slag. In hammering and melting, they differ no more than steel and iron, and they can be separated in the same way so that two distinct metals are produced from them.

**Silver** is composed of white sulfur, salt, and Mercury, prepared and fixed by nature to the highest degree of purity and transparency. It follows closely after gold in the **cupel** <note>original: *cineritio*; a refining process using a vessel of ash to separate precious metals from lead</note>, but not in antimony, nor in the **royal cement** <note>a dry refining process used to purify gold by removing silver</note>, nor in **quartation** <note>original: *quartatione*; the process of refining gold by alloying it with three parts silver so that acid can dissolve the silver and leave the gold pure</note>.

The difference in **fixation** <note>the quality of a substance that allows it to resist the fire without evaporating</note> between gold and silver is recognized by the fact that gold is male, possessing very fixed masculine powers, while silver, as the female, is weaker. They are made of one and the same **prime matter**, and differ in color and fixation only as male and female. There are, therefore, only seven metals in number, excluding Mercury itself: **Gold, Silver, Tin, Lead, Iron, Steel, and Copper.** Although this last one [copper] contains both male and female within itself, since both are cast together for use and are not separated by nature like steel and iron, they are considered as one. This is because they have the same hammering properties and are equally workable; they are not commonly separated unless done chemically for the purposes of the alchemical art. It should also be noted that in metals, the male is not always found produced by nature alone without its female,

### CONCLUSION.

Therefore, this detailed treatment of the natural generation of minerals was highly necessary; once this is properly understood, one may more easily grasp what the **regeneration** <note>original: *regeneratio*; in alchemy, this refers to the purification and "rebirth" of a metal into a higher state, such as through transmutation</note> of metals—achieved through chemical artifice—truly is, as discussed in the previous section. For it is the opinion of all who philosophize in this art that, first and foremost, the practitioner of this profession must imitate nature in all things most exactly. Accordingly, it was equally necessary to speak of and to understand what and how she works within the depths of the earth while managing her **mineral economy** <note>original: *mineralem œconomiam*; the orderly natural system by which minerals are produced and distributed</note>, as well as what matter and what instruments she uses. Whoever does not understand by this path will by no means reach the goal toward which his mind’s effort is directed. Let him, therefore, who scrutinizes such an arduous and secret matter, become a student of **nature** no less than of **art**.

...[the] salvation of God, greater benefits toward the human race? Absolutely none. But, alas, there are very few who care for these things. For this <term>iron age</term> <note>original: "ætas hæc nostra ferrea." Once, sublime geniuses and noble royal minds were occupied with the diligent investigation of the most excellent matters of secret philosophy and natural mysteries, by which they served as a protection to all their people in times of both war and peace. The ancients sought those nobler arts with the greatest desire and love, and for their sake, they threw themselves into many waves and dangers, so that by possessing them, they might render themselves and their fatherland more famous. 

In our time, however—among kings and princes as much as among subjects and private citizens, among the learned and the unlearned—not only does negligence and contempt for this art increase, but even hatred and anger against such a brilliant light rages. Thus it happens that those who, with a higher mind, attempt to recall those <term>spagyric</term> <note>The alchemical art of "separating and recombining" elements to create medicine.</note> arts of the ancients into the light are left ignoble and in obscurity, and experience the enmity of all, since they have no patrons or <term>Maecenases</term> <note>original: "Mæcenates." Hence, brilliant geniuses (of which our century brings forth many) are suppressed, and they are not allowed to reach their proposed goal; for, while destitute of patrons, they are forced to give their attention to cheaper matters and, in their misery, are compelled to serve the dull and the foolish. # ON PHILOSOPHICAL MINERALS AND METALS: AND
## FIRSTLY ON THE MERCURY OF THE PHILO-
### sophers, its subtle preparation and various virtues.

From Mercury or quicksilver, all sulfurousness—or all parts of sulfur—along with the leaden and earthy parts, must be removed, even if this seems absurd to many philosophers and those who do not closely understand the reasoning of the philosophers.

Mercury purifies the Sun <note>original: "solem." In alchemical texts, "the Sun" is the standard term for Gold.</note> from all other metals, and all things except for the Sun float upon it.

Gold sinks because it is heavier and immediately liquefies; so it is also with men <note>This is likely an alchemical analogy suggesting that just as gold is "tested" and refined by mercury, the human spirit is refined through trials.</note>.

Philosophical mercury is accustomed to cleanse itself of its depraved qualities, and to powerfully drive away and cast out excesses to the organs of excretion, as follows below.

<margin>Its use in Epilepsy.</margin>
<margin>In Dropsy.</margin>
<margin>In Cancer.</margin>
<margin>In Scabies.</margin>
The philosophers say: Our Mercury is not at all poisonous; rather, it takes away whatever is in excess and adds what is lacking. Furthermore, for those with epilepsy, abdominal pains, those intoxicated, or those infected by poison, it serves greatly as that "Great Theriac" <note>original: "theriaca." A famous ancient medical concoction used as a universal antidote and panacea.</note>. For by its subtlety, it is able to penetrate all the veins of the body in an instant; it also checks growths in the flesh. It heals those corrupted by dropsy <note>original: "hydrope." A historical term for edema or swelling caused by fluid accumulation.</note> or other infirmities, purifies the blood, and is marvelously useful for various abscesses. It knits together old wounds as well as recent ones along with putrefying ulcers. It opposes dysentery and all contagious diseases; it stops bleeding and the flow of humors coming from the membrane of the brain. It leads ulcers to scarring and clears away the filth and sores of the eyes. In a moderate dose and quantity, it expels cancer and cancerous fistulas. It cures scabies <note>original: "scabiem." A contagious skin infestation, often called "the itch."</note> without harm. A scented ointment <note>original: "smegma." Here used in the classical sense of a detergent or medicinal salve.</note> can also be made with Mercury against scabies. In place of pure Mercury, one can also use a certain <term>amalgam</term> <note>A mixture or alloy of mercury with another metal, in this case, gold.</note> made from six parts Mercury and one part Sun [Gold]. This Mercury resists pains of the colon and the flanks; and it performs not only what has been mentioned, but even certain greater miracles. It heals many other various conditions, as any physician according to his learning will very easily recognize and admit. But let 10 grains be given to a stronger body, 8 to a moderate one, and at most 5 to a weaker one (provided the digestion is not too weak). It heals quartan fevers <note>original: "quartanis." A form of malaria where the fever recurs every four days.</note>. It also opposes the plague, both by preserving against it and curing it.

<header>ON MEDICINES</header>

Therefore, many benefits arise from Mercury, as is established by countless experiments. Common Mercury or Quicksilver is fourfold. The first is collected from water springs, which Pliny (Book 33, Chapter 6, and also Book 3) calls a certain "perpetual and eternal vomit" <note>original: "vomica". In classical Latin, this refers to an abscess or discharge; Pliny used it to describe native quicksilver found in its pure liquid state.</note>. It is a poison to all things, and this is in very frequent use. Regarding the disadvantage of quicksilver, read Dioscorides in Book 5, Chapter 60. Taken as a drink, it has a destructive power; for by its weight, it corrodes the intestines and other organs. The same author in Book 6, Chapter 2 [notes]: The common crowd of physicians and unlearned people, such as Jews, monks, petty priests, barbers, tooth-pullers, and old women—understanding little or nothing of philosophy—with a certain insolent boldness, contend to attribute the power of healing any afflictions whatsoever to quicksilver or common Mercury, at the risk [of the patient]. By their error, many are destroyed rather than cured, as is openly taught by Theophrastus Paracelsus and other spagyrics <note>original: "spagyros". This refers to alchemists who followed the Paracelsian tradition of using chemical extractions for medicine.</note>. For [the unlearned practitioner] is accustomed to burn quicksilver into ash, and to offer it in potions mixed with certain other substances for colic and iliac <note>Severe abdominal pain or intestinal obstruction.</note> or dysentery; likewise for killing worms in infants, and similarly for the Neapolitan disease <note>original: "morbum Neapolitanum". A common 16th-century term for Syphilis.</note>. For external afflictions indeed, when prepared and precipitated with *aqua fortis* <note>Nitric acid.</note>, it can be effective, especially for malignant ulcers and the venereal plague. Likewise, for removing boils of the bladder neck, it is accustomed to erode and dry out the flesh even without pain. It draws out excrement through the bowels and expels wicked humors through the pores.

## BERNARD G. PENOT OF PORT-SAINTE-
### *Marie of Aquitaine on Mercury.*
#### ADDITION.

<margin>Mercury receives into itself all faculties.</margin>
Mercury is nothing other than the corporeal "spirit of the world" <term>spiritus mundi: a vital, celestial force believed by alchemists to permeate the universe and act as a bridge between the physical and spiritual realms.</term> formed in the womb of the earth, which receives into itself all faculties, whether animal, vegetable, or mineral. Just as some wax receives into itself the impression of all forms, so Mercury receives into itself the properties of all natural things. If it has been cleansed and prepared as it ought to be, then, being most perfect and pure, it receives into itself the impression of the purest gold and silver. Just as the Moon is the universal receptacle of all things, especially of the Sun, so also Mercury is the universal receptacle of the virtues of all natural things, especially of gold. Therefore, by comparison, the philosophers call it the Moon of the Earth, just as gold is the [Sun] of the earth. And just as the Moon is the first gate in heaven, so Mercury, compared to the Moon, is the first gate to the art <note>The "Art" refers to the practice of Alchemy or the Great Work of transmutation.</note>. Just as when the earth is placed between the Sun and the Moon, it hinders the Moon so that it does not receive the influence of the sun's light, and thus remains dark; similarly, the earthly impurity hidden within Mercury hinders it from receiving the perfection of the nature of the Sun. Therefore, many benefits come from Mercury, as is established by countless experiments. The common Mercury, or Quicksilver, is fourfold. The first is collected from the springs of waters, which Pliny (Book 33, Chapter 6; also Book 3) calls a certain perpetual and eternal "sore" <note>original: "vomica." In ancient medicine, this referred to a discharging abscess or ulcer; Pliny used it to describe the "oozing" nature of liquid mercury found in nature.</note>, and it is a poison to all things; this is the type in most frequent use. Regarding the harmfulness of quicksilver, read Dioscorides in Book 5, Chapter 60. As a drink, it has a ruinous power; for by its own weight, it corrodes the intestines and other organs. The same author says in Book 6, Chapter 28: The common crowd of doctors and unlearned fools <note>original: "idiotæ." Used here to mean those without formal academic or alchemical training.</note>, such as Jews, monks, petty priests, barbers, tooth-pullers, and old women—as well as philosophers who understand nothing or certainly very little—contend with a certain insolent boldness to attribute the power of healing any dangerous affliction to quicksilver or common Mercury. By their error, many are destroyed rather than cured, as is openly taught by Theophrastus Paracelsus <note>Philippus Aureolus Theophrastus Bombastus von Hohenheim (1493–1541), the Swiss physician who pioneered the use of minerals and chemicals in medicine.</note> and other spagyrists <note>term: spagyri. Alchemists who follow the Paracelsian method of "separating and recombining" substances to create potent medicines.</note>. For it is common to burn quicksilver into ash, and when mixed with certain other medicinal types for the stomach, the intestines, or dysentery, it is administered in potions; it is likewise used for killing worms in infants, and similarly for the "Neapolitan disease" <note>A common historical name for syphilis.</note>. Indeed, for external afflictions, when prepared with *aqua fortis* <note>original: "aqua forti." Literally "strong water," refers to nitric acid, used to dissolve metals.</note> and precipitated, it can be effective against malignant ulcers and especially the venereal plague. Likewise, for destroying boils on the neck of the bladder, it is accustomed to erode and dry out the flesh even without pain. It draws out waste through the bowels and expels corrupt humors through the pores.

Mercury is nothing other than the corporeal "spirit of the world" formed in the womb of the earth, which takes into itself all faculties—animal, vegetable, and mineral alike. If it has been cleansed and prepared as it ought to be—at its most perfect and pure—it then receives the impression of the purest gold and silver. Just as the Moon is the universal receptacle of all things, especially the Sun, so also Mercury is the universal receptacle of the virtues of all natural things, especially of gold. And just as the Moon is the first gate in the heavens, so Mercury, compared to the Moon, is the first gate to the Art <note>The "Art" refers to the Great Work of Alchemy.</note>. ## FOR THE VENEREAL BLIGHT AND OTHER
### *diseases, the best preparation.*
### AN ADDITION.

<margin>Mercury is perfected by gold.</margin>
Take 1 pound of quicksilver; dissolve it in <term>aqua fortis</term> <note>Nitric acid, literally "strong water."</note> so that a precipitate is formed. Then take distilled vinegar and dissolve the precipitate in it by boiling for four hours. Afterward, pour what has been dissolved into a glass vessel and again pour in more vinegar; repeat this until the vinegar has dissolved all the Mercury. Then distill all the vinegar in a <term>bain-marie</term> <note>original: "balneo Mariæ" or Mary's Bath; a water bath used for gentle, even heating.</note>, and at the bottom there will remain a mass like salt. Pour rainwater, distilled four times, upon this mass, and let it be cooked for half a day in a closed glass vessel. Afterward, let it settle; pour off the clear liquid and distill it by the [water] bath, and you will have a clear mass. Dry it and divide the mass into two parts. Over one part, pour <term>spirit of wine</term> <note>Ethanol or high-proof alcohol.</note> and let it remain for eight days to digest. Drive it through a <term>retort</term> <note>A glass vessel with a long, downward-pointing neck used for distillation.</note> in a bed of ashes with a large receiver attached; first the spirit of wine will come out, then the "spirit of Mercury," and a very black dross will remain at the bottom. Do not open the joints of the receiver for 24 hours; the crystalline spirits of Mercury cling to the sides of the vessel and do not dissolve except after 12 hours. Then, once the receiver is open, extract the liquids in a very gentle bath; the spirit of wine will come out, and the <term>essence of Mercury</term> will remain at the bottom of the vessel in the form of an ash-gray oil. Place this liquor in a small glass vessel with very gentle heat; then, in the same vessel, gradually dissolve the other reserved part of the Mercury, which has been ground into powder. Add as much as can be dissolved until it becomes a softish mass. This done, seal the vessel <note>Hermetically seal the glass.</note> and cook it in ashes, increasing the heat by degrees until it turns into a red powder. One grain of this, administered in wine or another liquid, drives out the <term>Neapolitan disease</term> <note>original: "morbum Neapolitanum"; a common early modern name for syphilis.</note> and performs other wonders. It is administered three times a week; let the patient beware of [cold] air and drink sugared wine. It purges only through the stool. It performs many other things which I omit for the sake of brevity.

### ON SULPHUR AND THE USEFULNESS OF SUL-
### phur, which is varied.

Oil of sulphur <note>original: "Sulphuris oleum." In this context, this likely refers to a concentrated sulfuric acid produced by the "bell" method or a similar alchemical distillation.</note> opposes both internal and external ailments, as follows. Moreover, this oil has a peculiar power and capacity for drawing out impurities. It heals anal fissures, fistulas, <term>apostemes</term> <note>inflammatory swellings or abscesses</note>, itching, prolapses, <term>mariscae</term> <note>hemorrhoidal swellings resembling figs</note>, and other ailments by light contact or anointing. Likewise, it cures the stomach, liver, spleen, womb, bladder, intestines, and joints—specifically those parts affected by an abundance of humors or putrefaction. 

A small amount of this oil is given with a distilled liquid or a decoction of a suitable herb, according to the quality of each part and condition: a chicken feather is dipped into the oil, then immediately withdrawn, and what clings to the feather is diluted in the liquid or decoction and given to the patient to drink for stomach pain and colic from "wind" <note>gas</note> with chamomile water. Likewise for <term>orexia</term> <note>here referring to indigestion or a disordered appetite</note> arising from a redundancy of phlegm, with wormwood water; against worms with grass-water or wormwood water. In "coldness" of the liver and <term>dropsy</term> <note>edema or swelling caused by fluid retention</note> with cold water; in pain of the womb with wine from a decoction of betony and <term>matricaria</term> <note>feverfew</note>; in the suppression of urine with wine of boiled garlic. 

Likewise for <term>phthiriasis</term> <note>infestation of lice</note> by dipping a certain woolen cloth into the oil. It aids ear pain and ringing, ulceration, worms, and other ailments, as well as bruised ears; it also helps arthritic diseases. For <term>buboes</term> <note>swollen lymph nodes, often associated with the plague</note>, by placing a moistened woolen cloth over them; it does not have an exceeding power of heating, yet by reason of its mixture and composition, it binds together, wonderfully consolidates ulcers and wounds, and generates flesh most quickly. 

Through contact and anointing, it heals <term>cancer</term> <note>original: "Cancrum," which could refer to malignant tumors or severe canker sores</note>, graying of hair <note>perhaps referring to scalp conditions</note>, ulcers of the head and affections of the brain, colic, skin foulness, along with all conditions of bruised limbs. It draws out a fractured skull [fragments], thins and softens hard things by anointing, heals pains and dislocation of limbs, <term>serpigo</term> <note>creeping skin eruptions or ringworm</note>, and all kinds of scabies. It cures spasms and has a power of drying tumors and tubercles by placing a moistened woolen cloth over them; it treats ulcers of the shins, any wounds—especially hollow and deep ones—<term>vomicæ</term> <note>pus-filled cavities</note>, varicose veins, pimples, ulcers both fresh and old and putrid: finally, any burn arising from whatever cause. 

In ulcers and pustules of the mouth, a moist feather or cotton is applied to the ulcerated place lightly, and so by repeating the contact of the oil several times the evil is healed; it whitens teeth by light touching. If all the teeth ache, a warm decoction of mint in which one, two, or three drops of the oil have been mixed should be held in the mouth. It extracts warts; it cures ailments of the spleen with water of tamarisk or maidenhair fern. Against swelling under the tongue of infants: likewise against the suffering of the colon and griping of the intestines with rue-water or similar, two drops are given in summer, and in winter with <term>aqua vitæ</term> <note>literally "water of life," referring to concentrated alcohol or brandy</note> or muscatel wine.

### ON VITRIOLIZED SULPHUR.

You will recognize vitriolized sulphur <note>original: "Sulphur vitriolatum," likely referring here to a preparation of "sweet vitriol" or an early form of ether</note> when a disease must be cured by <term>anodynes</term> <note>pain-relieving medicines</note>; it effects this then without any danger. This same Sulphur is fixed by its own nature and possesses a sweetness; and even chickens, having devoured it, will sleep for a time without harm, and are afterwards revived. This Sulphur settles all <term>passions</term> <note>in this context, painful physical conditions or "suffering" of the body</note> without danger; it binds all pains and every colic passion, and this medicine ought to precede all preventative treatments.

### ADDITION.

℞ <note>Take</note>. Take <term>vitriol</term> <note>a sulfate mineral, usually iron or copper sulfate</note>, dissolve it in water, and make it boil. Place iron plates into it, and you will find them loaded with a red powder; scrape this off. Do this for as long as it takes until you have extracted all the Sulphur. This you shall <term>circulate</term> <note>a process of continuous distillation or reflux</note> with the best spirit of wine <note>alcohol</note>; leave behind what is black, and save what is very red: it works most powerfully both internally and externally.

### ON SALT AND THE POWERS OF SALT.

Salt is a certain very strong remedy and, according to that proverb, it is the most excellent seasoning of all seasonings. For the common power of all salt is to heat, to dry, to thin out, to dissolve, to disperse, to cleanse, to bind, and to consume superfluous <term>humors</term> <note>the bodily fluids thought to control health in medieval medicine</note>.

However, salt that is drier is more fit for salting <note>preservation</note>, and therefore its power is also to turn away the loathing of poisonous humors, to prevent nausea, and to incite and stir up a craving for all foods, while consuming what is harmful. The same is provided by pickled olives, lemons, caper flowers and fruits; the same is provided by grapes, apples, pears, figs, and turnips. Furthermore, the power of salt is to protect the meat of both fish and other animals which we eat from putrefaction—lest they by chance be corrupted even in the stomach and "cheese" be curdled there—and to defend them most conveniently. Truly, it also guards any wine from mucus and sourness, and clarifies it more quickly, and even tempers their sharpness so that they have less power to cause drunkenness. Likewise, it makes softened skins more loose and capacious through washing, and by its sharp quality, it improves and betters the thickness of leathers, strengthens their flavor, and makes them better. Likewise, it makes sterile, marshy, and wet fields fruitful; it peculiarly heals the olive tree on the sea shore, and the Radish, Beet, Rue, and Cumin, such that they are much sweeter and much more fertile...

<page-num>605</page-num>
<header>ON CHEMICALS</header>

As Pliny testifies, these things are done <note>original: "res Plinio teste fiant," referring to the properties of salt</note>. In flocks, herds, and beasts of burden, as they return to the pastures and perceive the taste by licking, it corrects their loss of appetite and greatly provokes an eagerness for food and drink, so that they provide milk much more abundantly, and that milk yields a much more pleasant cheese. Likewise, according to the testimony of Plutarch, it is most convenient for making livestock pregnant and for removing excessive fat that is harmful to them. On the advice of Aristotle, it is used to stir sheep to mate by having them lick it before and after, and it heals various diseases in flocks, herds, and beasts of burden. 

Likewise, it purifies muddy water by a certain injection, just as Elisha did by the word of God in the Fourth Book of Kings, chapter 2 <note>This refers to 2 Kings 2:21 in modern Bibles, where the prophet Elisha purifies a spring with salt</note>. It resists the diseases of beasts when rubbed into a certain linen cloth and dipped in vinegar, so that the areas are bound with bandages; it also works against the diseases of crocodiles. A drink of the same salt with honey and vinegar works against the ailments caused by the centipede <note>original: "scolopendræ"</note>. 

The same salt, smeared on with vinegar, cures the bites of hornets or wasps and scorpions; or, when mixed with vinegar or a fourth part of oil and oregano, pitch, wax, or honey, it cures the bites of serpents. It resists poisonous fungi and the ingestion of opium when taken with honey-water and vinegar. Such is the power of this salt that by a certain injection it partly removes the pestiferous malice of burning coals. 

The power of the same salt, when smeared and applied with vinegar or hyssop, is to resist <term>holy fire</term> <note>original: "igni sacro," likely referring to erysipelas, a skin infection also known as St. Anthony's Fire</note> and creeping ulcers. The power of the same salt, when applied with oil or chewed, is to prevent the pustules of those burned by fire from breaking out. Mixed with other medicines having similar faculties, it settles itching. 

Likewise, it corrects leprosy, boils, <term>lichens</term> <note>a general term for skin eruptions or scaling</note>, and <term>psora</term> <note>itchy skin conditions like scabies</note> when used with raisins (with the stems removed), beef tallow, and leaven or bread itself. Likewise, it treats <term>carcinomata</term> <note>malignant or cancerous ulcers</note> when applied with black briony <note>original: "uva taminia"</note>. Likewise, the same salt, ground with barley flour and applied on a linen cloth moistened with wine, heals <term>phagedenas</term> <note>original: "phagedænas," referring to rapidly spreading or "eating" ulcers</note>. 

The power of the same salt with local soot is to drive away the warts of children by friction. The power of the same salt, by dipping a linen cloth, is to cure the growing or putrefying ulcers of many. Likewise, when applied with spider webs, it commonly heals lighter wounds. Likewise, when applied with honey and flour, it treats dislocations. By adding it to a <term>smegma</term> <note>here meaning a cleansing detergent or ointment</note>, it extends and smooths the skin. 

Thus Galen sprinkled the body of a newborn infant with a modest amount of salt, by which its skin was rendered thicker and more solid, so as to be less subject to external injuries. The power of the same salt, when mixed with medicines for the face, is to create a brightness of the skin, and it is also beneficial for facial bruises. It disperses boils when used with raisins or hog’s lard, as well as with honey. 

The power of the same salt, when added to medicines according to the opinion of the ancients, is to preserve those who are drunk from intoxication when they are anointed with oil. Likewise, it restrains excrescences in the eyes. It consumes <term>pterygia</term> <note>wing-shaped growths of tissue on the white of the eye</note> and removes other exuberances of the flesh; therefore, its addition to eye-salves and plasters is very useful. Indeed, for eyes bloodshot from a blow or bruised, its power—along with an equal weight of myrrh and honey, or with hyssop in warm water—[is beneficial].

Likewise, the power of common salt mixed in wine is even to soften the bowels. Furthermore, in a drink of wine, it expels intestinal worms and tapeworms; and by the admixture of other things, it purges thick and sluggish humors, "glassy" phlegm, and melancholy. 

The power of this same salt, when drunk and applied in a glowing-hot bundle <note>original: "faccis... candentis," likely a heated compress or poultice</note>, is to relieve colic and griping pains. Likewise, with an application of vinegar and oil for those laboring under the "Royal Disease" <note>original: "morbo regio," a historical term for jaundice</note>, it provokes sweat when near a fire and cures perceptible itching.

Likewise, with oregano and leaven (and also butter, as Avicenna <note>Ibn Sina (c. 980–1037), a Persian polymath and influential physician</note> prefers), it ripens tumors of the testicles. 

The power of this salt, when drunk and applied in a glowing-hot bundle, is to mitigate pains of the hips, and with the grinding of flour, honey, and oil, it relieves those with gout. Furthermore, with a very thin rubbing of oil and a morning massage after the gouty pains have subsided, it preserves one from such afflictions. Likewise, it removes corns on the feet and chilblains. Likewise, it aids the weary by a certain liniment of oil. Pliny <note>Pliny the Elder, Roman author of Natural History</note> says that when rubbed on, it corrects the heat and burning of fevers. 

Likewise, the power of salt dissolved in water and taken daily is to preserve one from the pestilence, as the inhabitants of the Kingdom of Mali <note>original: "regni Mellis," referring to the West African empire famous for its trans-Saharan salt trade</note> do. The power of salt is not only to preserve the flesh of animals and vegetables for a longer time, but also to test and refine the veins of metals by a certain addition; for it melts easily, and therefore has a certain peculiar faculty in the process of smelting.
