### For iliac passion.
<note>original: *passio iliaca*; a severe and painful intestinal obstruction, often what we would now call a bowel blockage.</note>

Take a decoction of saltpeter, chamomile flowers, marigold <note>original: *caltharum*</note>, hyssop, mint, lemon balm, powdered orris root <note>original: *radicis Ireos*; the fragrant root of the iris flower</note>, galangal, sweet benzoin <note>original: *asæ dulcis*</note>, and the seeds of parsley, fennel, anise, dill, and cumin. Mix this with sweet almonds to make a medicinal milk.

### For the same.

Let the area be bathed with the same decoction, first anointing the parts with oils of chamomile, dill, and bitter almonds.

### For the colic passion.
<note>A term for severe abdominal cramping or colic.</note>

The same decoction is to be taken, and the same bathing <note>original: *fomentatio*</note> applied, as described for the iliac passion.

### Against dropsy.
<note>original: *hydrops*; an accumulation of fluid in the body's tissues or cavities, now known as edema.</note>

Saltpeter eaten with figs and hyssop.

### For the same.

Saltpeter crushed with figs and hyssop, applied to the stomach <note>original: *ventriculo*; here referring to the external abdominal region</note>, cures dropsy.

### For the same.

Let saltpeter be dissolved in a decoction of dwarf elder <note>original: *ebuli*</note>, elderberry, and orris root; let an enema be made.

### For inflammation of the testicles.

Crushed saltpeter with raisins, mixed with oil of violets and roses, is applied warm in the form of a poultice <note>original: *cataplasmatis*</note>.

### For fleshy growths and excrescences of the penis.
<note>original: *Virgæ*</note>

Saltpeter mixed with the ashes of vine shoots or vines and iron-enriched vinegar <note>original: *aceto chalybeato*</note> is applied externally with great effect.

### For stones of the kidneys and bladder.

Let saltpeter be eaten with <term>oxymel</term> <note>A traditional medicinal syrup made of honey and vinegar</note> and radishes, with rose honey added.

### For the same.

Let the kidneys be anointed externally with rabbit fat mixed with saltpeter.

### For the same.

Use enemas made of saltpeter, purging cassia <note>original: *casia fistulari*</note>, a decoction of rabbit with chamomile, maidenhair fern <note>original: *capillo Veneris*</note>, parsley, and saxifrage, with violet or rose honey added, along with goat fat.

### To dissolve a "mole" in the womb, and for suffocation and other accidents of the womb.
<note>A "mola" or uterine mole was a term for a non-viable mass or tumor in the uterus. "Suffocation" refers to the historical concept of "suffocation of the mother," often associated with uterine displacement or severe cramping.</note>

Let saltpeter be administered <note>original: *propinetur*; literally "offered as a drink"</note> with the juice of chamomile, mercury <note>original: *mercurialis*; a common herb in the spurge family</note>, hyssop, and mugwort <note>original: *artemisiæ*</note>.

### For the same.

Let a pessary be made from saltpeter dissolved in the juice of hyssop, marigold, chamomile, mugwort, and mercury, with almond oil; add galbanum <note>a bitter aromatic gum resin</note>, sweet benzoin, and a little ambergris <note>original: *ambræ griseæ*</note>, or musked alipta <note>a fragrant medicinal paste or ointment</note>.

->*To recover weakened strength.*<-

Take of black pitch, wax, and colophony <note>original: *colophoniæ*; a type of pine resin or rosin</note>, 3 ounces <note>original: *℥ iij*</note> each; let them be melted. Add 1 drachm <note>original: *ʒ j*</note> of tartar, 1 ½ drachms <note>original: *ʒ j ß*</note> of saltpeter <note>original: *nitri*</note>, 3 drachms of native sulfur <note>original: *sulphuris vivi*</note>, 2 drachms of powdered pepper, 2 drachms of benzoin <note>original: *benioni*</note>, half a drachm of euphorbium <note>original: *euphorbij*; a potent plant resin used as a skin irritant</note>, 1 drachm of laudanum <note>In this period, laudanum often referred to the resin of the rockrose (Cistus) when used in plasters</note>, and 1 drachm each of oil of bitter almonds and oil of Cyprus <note>original: *olei ciprin.*; oil made from henna flowers</note>. Let them be mixed to make a plaster.

->*To induce sweating.*<-

Saltpeter taken with the juice of chamomile and marigold <note>original: *calthæ*</note> in broth.

->*To restrain excessive sweating.*<-

Let saltpeter be dissolved with powdered orris root <note>original: *Ireos*</note> in omphacine rose oil <note>original: *oleo rosato omphacino*; oil made from unripe olives and roses</note>; with rose vinegar added, let the body be anointed.

->*To make the parts of the body flexible.*<-

Let the shins or other parts of the body be anointed with saltpeter dissolved in chamomile oil.

->*To turn away the shivering of fever before an attack.*<-

Let saltpeter be dissolved in olive oil, or better yet, in oil of bitter almonds, or dill, or radish seed, or nettles, or castor <note>original: *castorei*; a secretion from beavers used in medicine</note>, or spikenard <note>original: *spicæ*</note>. Let the patient's neck, shoulder blades, and spine be anointed, as well as the tendons of the hands and feet.

->*To loosen the bowels.*<-

Let saltpeter be drunk with powdered orris root in the juice of raw cabbage. Likewise, let one spoonful of powdered saltpeter be drunk in warm whey, or white wine, or a decoction of raisins.

->*For burns.*<-

Saltpeter roasted until it turns black and reduced to a powder is effectively applied to burns <note>original: *combustionibus*</note>.

->*Against the bites of rabid dogs and other venomous beasts.*<-

Saltpeter melted with turpentine, with vinegar and goose or pig fat added, cures venomous bites when applied. Meanwhile, let vinegar be strained through quicklime and mixed with saltpeter, and with this let the wound be washed frequently.

->*For one who has eaten henbane.*<-

Saltpeter dissolved in warm water should be drunk; afterward, vomiting should be induced with a feather or a finger.

->*For one who has eaten mandrake.*<-

Vomiting should be frequently induced with saltpeter, warm water, and honey; then let a decoction of wormwood <note>original: *absynthij*</note> in Malmsey wine <note>original: *malvatico*; a sweet Mediterranean wine</note> with saltpeter dissolved in it be drunk. Let the patients' heads be sprinkled with vinegar and rose oil while using strong-smelling substances; let the patient exert themselves vigorously and induce a sweat.

->*If anyone has eaten [poisonous] mushrooms.*<-

Let lemon balm <note>original: *melissa*</note> be crushed with *posca* <note>a mixture of vinegar and water</note> or vinegar, water, and salt. In this mixture, let saltpeter be dissolved; let it be swallowed warm, and then induce vomiting.

<header>FOR CHEMISTS</header>

### *If someone should eat a buprestis beetle or Spanish flies.*
<note>original: *buprestem vel cantharides*; these are types of toxic beetles used in medicine as blistering agents, but they are highly poisonous if ingested.</note>

Take saltpeter with benzoin <note>original: *asa dulci*; a balsamic resin from trees in the *Styrax* genus</note> dissolved in warm water and honey; so that you may afterwards vomit frequently, then use lozenges <note>original: *trochiscis*</note> of winter cherry <note>original: *alkekengi*</note> with almond milk.

### *Against the drinking of bull’s blood.*
<note>In antiquity, bull’s blood was famously (though incorrectly) believed to be a rapid-acting poison that would congeal in the stomach.</note>

Let saltpeter be drunk with vinegar-water <note>original: *posca*; a common drink of water and wine vinegar</note> and salt, and let frequent vomiting be induced.

### *Against all strangulations, suffocations, and obstructions in general.*

It is established by experiment that saltpeter is a most excellent remedy for all these things, whether it is taken internally or applied in fomentations <note>warm, moist compresses</note>, baths, or plasters; it divides, thins, relaxes, rarefies, expands, attenuates, opens, lubricates, evaporates, expels, and cleanses.

### *For soldering gold or silver, and likewise for coloring gold and silver.*

Let saltpeter and feather alum <note>original: *alumen plumæ*; a fibrous form of alum, though sometimes used to refer to asbestos in historical texts</note> be stirred with the urine of a boy in a copper mortar with a pestle of the same metal in the sun, or in hot ashes, for as long as it takes until it is nearly dried and thick; afterwards let it be removed and dried in the sun in a leaden vessel, and reduced to a powder.

### *For whitening linens and fabric with it.*

Let saltpeter be dissolved in hot lye <note>original: *lixivio*</note>, and in that let the linens be soaked, having been wrung out from water several times, and then let them be dried in the sun.

### *For purifying wool, cloth, and thread.*

Let saltpeter be applied, as above, with hot lye.

### *For preparing leather.*

Saltpeter taken in this way with lye, and afterwards with hot water, cleanses leather and renders it manageable.

### *For lubricating hides.*

Let them be washed in hot water with the essence <note>original: *sapore*; literally "taste" or "character"</note> of saltpeter.

### *For restoring a lost appetite in horses.*

Mix up to 1 ounce <note>original: *℥ j.*</note> of powdered saltpeter into their fodder.

#### ANOTHER SECOND REMEDY, MORE EXCELLENT.

Take the aforementioned material, calcined <note>heated to a high temperature to reduce it to a powder</note> to perfection, which you shall test upon a cupel <note>a small, porous bowl used for refining precious metals</note> just like pure silver; and when it has given the sign of its purity, take it up after it has cooled. Pour the same spirit back on, and repeat this four times, or until they pass through the retort <note>a glassware vessel with a long downward-pointing neck</note> together; you will then have a perfect essence, which you shall circulate <note>a process of continuous distillation and reflux</note> for a period of 14 days in a water bath <note>original: *balneo*</note>. Enjoy these and be well.

### ELIXIR OF HONEY.

Take 6 pounds <note>original: ℔ vj.</note> of the best honey and dissolve it in water distilled three times; filter it and repeat this four times, then finally evaporate the water; dissolve it again and again. This must be done until it is cleansed of all filth and dross. This being done, place the honey itself in a pelican <note>an alchemical vessel with two side-arms for continuous circulation</note> for a month; then, using an alembic <note>a distillation apparatus</note>, you will separate the lighter part in a water bath, while you will distill the other part in an ash fire <note>a method of heating using hot ashes for more uniform temperature</note>. Calcine the earth remaining at the bottom and dissolve it in pure water, removing the dross through a filter; finally, let it be calcined by this method in a slow fire for an hour once all moisture is removed. Gradually soak this again with the previous water and coagulate it in a water bath; then add just as much of its own oil previously extracted in the ash fire, digesting and coagulating it into a thick gum; when you have added the rest of its oil, digest it again as before, and it will be firm and thick. It universally preserves and cleanses the human body from every imperfection, both internally and externally.

## ON THE POWERS OF POTABLE GOLD, AND ITS
*preparation.*

There are various opinions concerning potable gold <note>original: *auro potabili*; gold processed into a liquid form for medicinal use</note>: some hold it in high regard, others despise it; therefore, it is advisable to state the facts of the matter. This will be more easily accomplished if we first consider the powers and properties that learned and experienced men attribute to gold in their books: secondly, if we weigh whether those properties attributed to gold by these authors can also be demonstrated by reason to exist within gold itself. Therefore, as for the first point—namely, the authorities...

<page-num>645</page-num>
<header>### ON CHEMICAL MATTERS</header>

Avicenna <note>the Latinized name of Ibn Sina, 980–1037 AD, a Persian polymath and one of the most significant physicians of the Islamic Golden Age</note>, in his treatise on gold, says that it is temperate by nature; and if it is reduced to filings, it may be usefully mixed into medicines against leprosy <note>original: *lepram*</note>, hair loss <note>original: *profluvium capillorum*</note>, and melancholy <note>original: *melancholiam*</note>. It is said to comfort the heart and prevent its trembling, and to strengthen the eye if it is reduced to the finest powder. In this, nearly all physicians who describe the powers of simple medicines agree. It would be long and tedious to repeat the authorities and opinions of everyone. If, therefore, they attributed such great powers to gold filings, what might happen if it were reduced into a liquid and drinkable form?

Those who have learned the proper preparation to reduce it into a liquid form, and have used it in removing diseases, affirm that it has the power of purifying and purging superfluous humors, removing discharges <note>original: *fluxus*; catarrh or fluid buildup</note> of the head, and liberating the heart from malignant and foul vapors <note>original: *tetris vaporibus*; in early medicine, "vapors" were thought to rise from the gut to affect the heart or brain</note>, driving away melancholy, preserving one from leprosy, sharpening the spirits, and healing epilepsy.

<margin>7</margin>
Arnald of Villanova <note>a 13th-century physician and alchemist</note>, in his treatise on wine or the elixir, says that it cures the suppression of urine. Archelaus the philosopher says that gold is a treasure of human life, healing the infirmities and diseases of men if some of its liquor is consumed. Furthermore, he adds that if its powers were known, people would no longer place their faith in physicians who deny it—either because those doctors fear their own profit might perish, or because they are ignorant of the method of preparation.

Raymundus <note>Ramon Llull, 1232–1316, a Majorcan philosopher and mystic to whom many alchemical works were attributed</note>, near the end of the *Practice* of his *Testament*, says that the water of gold <note>potable gold</note>, when presented as a drink in the proper manner, heals the human body of every infirmity, however old it may be. He claims the physician does not even have need to inspect the urine <note>uroscopy was the standard diagnostic tool of the era</note>, nor other excrements, nor explore the pulse, provided he uses this medicine at least once, with a light diet or regulated lifestyle.

Regarding these great and mighty powers found in gold, Avicenna, in his treatise *On the Powers of the Heart* in the chapter on gold, says that they arise from its "property." In the same treatise, in the chapter on the Hyacinth <note>a precious gemstone, likely zircon or sapphire</note>, he says that such a property should not be attributed to the matter from which it is composed, but to a unique virtue resulting from it, just as appears in the magnet. Therefore, a certain philosopher says that this virtue proceeds from the "whole species," which we commonly call the specific virtue <term>specificam virtutem; a hidden power inherent in the total essence of a substance rather than its individual elemental components</term>. Others think that this virtue is a heavenly gift flowing into any mixture according to a greater or lesser proper proportion of the elements.

Avicenna judges that this specific power is bestowed upon things after the first complexing of the elements. But because we are ignorant of these kinds of proportions, and because it has not been granted to us to know further, we therefore take refuge in experience <note>original: *experientiam*; here meaning experimental observation and clinical results</note>. In such medical matters, it is more profitable to experience and test than to argue—even if we do not deny that the investigation into the causes of such powers can be of the highest value.

...to be greatly aided by the light of nature. And if we consider the excellent composition and temperament of gold, it is well known to be endowed with many powers. For, as Rhasis <note>al-Razi (865–925 AD), a Persian physician and one of the most influential figures in medieval medicine</note> says, in gold there are 10 parts hot, 10 cold, 10 moist, and 10 dry—or if you prefer, ten proportions of each. For this reason, it is almost incorruptible, because just as much as the heat warms it, the cold cools it; the same judgment applies to its dryness and moisture. Since it is therefore balanced in its own temperament, it also has the power of balancing the body, because its matter is purified from two superfluous moistures: namely, the inflammable sulfurous moisture and the evaporable phlegmatic or watery moisture, as <term>Albertus</term> <note>Albertus Magnus (c. 1200–1280), a Dominican friar and polymath who wrote extensively on alchemy and minerals</note> says in his *Book of Minerals*. For this reason, it has great power to purge excess humors and to comfort its like, namely the <term>radical moisture</term> <note>the "vital spark" or innate fluid thought to sustain life and youth</note>. Furthermore, because it enters into all metals, it is "fixed," and it opposes that which is not fixed and vanishes into smoke. Moreover, it has the property of blunting the vapors that rise from the lower parts of the body. Because it is of a refined substance, it has the power to clear out excess fluids; and since it is incorruptible, it can expel corrupt humors, leprosy <note>original: *lepram*</note>, cancer <note>original: *cancrum*</note>, and similar diseases—not to mention gout <note>original: *podagram*</note>, quartan fever <note>original: *febrim quartanam*</note>, and dropsy <note>original: *hydropem*</note>. Finally, because it is bright, it has the power to repel melancholic humors and vapors that are dark and gloomy, by which some patients are clearly afflicted; and while it does this, it grants good understanding. In a word, the goodness of the substance found in gold demonstrates the value of its virtue, and the greatness of its virtue shows the excellence of its operation. This is clearly shown to us through its essential parts: namely, its matter and its form. For noble, pure matter deserves a noble, excellent, and divine form. And we may be permitted to estimate with <term>Plato</term> that forms are given according to the merit of the matter. Albertus Magnus, in the third book of his *Minerals*, proves the same. And as a certain man said: the more the matter is sublimated and refined by nature, the more capable and worthy it is to receive a noble and excellent form. But the excellence of the matter of gold reveals itself in this: that fire, which consumes and devours all other things, brings no harm to it, nor diminishes it. If we consider its divine form, we shall find incredible and almost divine effects. If these things are examined diligently, we shall rightfully compare gold to the celestial sun; for just as the sun animates almost the entire universe and the <term>macrocosm</term> <note>the "great world" or the universe at large</note> with its heat and light, so the terrestrial sun—which we say is gold—has the power of bringing life to the <term>microcosm</term> <note>the "little world," referring here to the human body as a reflection of the universe</note>, which is man.

### ON THE POWERS OF THE HIDDEN SPIRIT.

->TO THE MOST NOBLE, SUPREME PHILOSOPHER<-
->and Mathematician, Lord Petrus Winzius of Olomouc,<-
->celebrated Physician, Bernhardus G. Penotus of Port-Sainte-Marie<-
->of Aquitaine sends many greetings.<-

Whatever is understood to be actually diffused within the circumference of any circle is simultaneously contained, collected in potential, within the center of that same circle. And when that which is collected in potential within the center is unfolded into action, then that which was actually diffused in the circumference is hidden in potential. For example, the light of heaven is dispersed among infinite and many stars, and yet it is also collected all at once in the one **Sun**; and that in which it is dispersed among the many is the "circle" of the light of heaven, but that in which it is collected into one is the "center" of the light of heaven. The light of heaven is twofold: masculine and feminine. The masculine is dispersed in one half of the stars of the summer sky. The other, the feminine, is dispersed in the other half of the stars of the winter sky. Furthermore, all the masculine light of heaven is collected into one, namely in the Sun; all the feminine light of heaven is collected into one, namely in the **Moon**. Just as it is with the dispersion and collection of the light of heaven, so it is also with the dispersion, distinction, and collection of all other things. Thus, all animal virtues dispersed among the infinite animals of the earth are collected into one center in a single **Lion**. And all the animal reasons or intelligences dispersed among all the animals of the world are collected into one in the single head of a **Man**.

In like manner, the Earth is the womb <note>original: *matrix*</note> and the receptacle of all the elements: in which all the powers of hidden things are actually concealed, which can break forth in potential into specific forms...

<header>### ON CHEMISTRY.</header>

Rhazes <note>original: *Rhasis*; referring to the Persian physician and alchemist Abu Bakr al-Razi</note> says in his *Book of Divinity*: know that the things of nature are so bound together by subtle artifice that in any thing, every other thing exists potentially, even if it is not seen in its active state. Albert <note>Albertus Magnus, the 13th-century scholar and patron saint of scientists</note> says in his *Book of Minerals* that gold is found everywhere: because there is no thing composed of the four elements in which gold is not naturally found in its final affinity; and therefore he says the material of the "stone" <note>The Philosopher's Stone, the goal of the Great Work</note> is found everywhere. Likewise, he proves that the greatest mineral power <note>original: *virtus*</note> exists in any man and especially in the head between the teeth, as in its time gold was found in tiny and oblong grains, which could not be unless that mineral power were in man—the same mineral power that is in our Elixir.

Furthermore, a certain "virgin earth" lies hidden in the center of the earth, which must be investigated with the greatest zeal. You (O prince of all philosophers of our age) know her best: You know that one earth is better than another, and therefore more desirable. Therefore, let the seekers of hidden things learn to recognize her; once she is known, she is to be liberated from original sin through fire and water. And let us celebrate the Creator of things, who wished to reveal the riches of such a treasure to mortals, through the only-begotten Jesus Christ. I have written these things as a monument of our duty to you. You indeed are the glory and ornament of both the writing and the author. Fare most blessedly. Frankenthal, on the Kalends <note>The first day</note> of January 1594.

### THE USE AND DOSAGE OF CERTAIN SPAGYRIC MEDICINES.

->**LIQUOR OF PEARLS.**<-

The greatest secret exists in Pearls against consumption <note>original: *phthisim*; a wasting disease of the lungs</note> and the wasting of the body. There is nothing that preserves the radical moisture <note>original: *humidum radicale*; the vital fluid thought to sustain life and youth</note> more than pearls. They restore lost strength and comfort the principal organs. The dose is from <term>half a scruple</term> <note>original: *℈ ß.*</note> to <term>one scruple</term> <note>original: *℈ j.*</note> in a suitable carrier such as wine, water, or a preserve.

->**LIQUOR OF MOTHER OF PEARL.**<-

This has a specific power for strengthening the womb <note>original: *matricem*</note>, it promotes conception, and is also useful for fevers: these essences are always to be administered with a suitable liquid: its dose is from <term>half a scruple</term> <note>original: *℈ ß.*</note> to <term>one scruple</term> <note>original: *℈ j.*</note>.

It rectifies the blood and miraculously consumes all its excess or harm: for women it also promotes the menstrual blood if it does not flow at the right time, and brings it back into balance;

## LIQUOR OF CRAB’S EYES.
<note>original: *Liquor Oculorum Cancri*; "Crab's eyes" are not actually eyes, but stony calcium deposits (gastroliths) found in the stomachs of crayfish, highly valued in early modern medicine as an antacid.</note>

## LIQUOR OF CRYSTAL.

It heals the stone of the kidneys and bladder, and dissolves all **Tartar** <note>original: *Tartarum*; in Paracelsian medicine, this refers to stony or calcified metabolic waste that adheres to organs, causing disease</note> adhering to any part of the body. For this reason, it is very beneficial for those suffering from gout <note>original: *podagricis*</note>, even when applied as an external ointment: it is especially useful for fainting <note>original: *Syncopi*</note> and other diseases of the head, and it strengthens the brain: it is given in doses of 15 to 16 drops in some appropriate water or wine.

## OIL OF GARNETS.
<note>original: *Oleum Granatorum*; while *granatum* can mean pomegranate, in this context of precious stones and "crystals," it likely refers to the gemstone garnet.</note>

It strengthens the heart: it resists poisons: and it also dissolves Tartar. It is given in Malmsey wine <note>a sweet, high-alcohol Mediterranean wine</note> in doses from half a scruple to 16 drops.

## SPIRIT OF TARTAR.

It heals pleurisy when taken with theriacal water <note>water infused with Theriac, a famous ancient "universal" panacea containing dozens of ingredients</note>, or if one drachm <note>symbol: З j; about 3.9 grams</note> of the spirit is given with half an ounce <note>symbol: ℥ ß</note> of Theriac; let it be repeated after six hours, and let sweating be provoked. In the same manner, it also cures the plague, carbuncles, and Anthrax <note>referring to the "burning" skin ulcers associated with the plague</note>; it resists all putrefaction of the entire body and expels them, and dissolves Tartar. Its dosage is from half a scruple to one scruple.

## THE PREPARATION OF CRYSTALS
## and other stones.

Calcine the crystal <note>heat it to a high temperature until it becomes a powder</note>: and grind it into a very fine powder upon a marble slab: calcine it again with sulfur and saltpeter: and let it be "reverberated" <note>heated in a furnace where the flames are reflected down onto the material</note> for a day and a night. Let it be put into a glass vessel with a long neck: and let turpentine-distilled vinegar be poured over it: with the vessel sealed, let it sit overnight upon warm ashes; on the following day, pour off what has been dissolved and keep it; let new vinegar be added again, as was said before. Repeat this until you have the Crystal reduced to a paste. Filter the vinegar in which the Crystal was dissolved: evaporate it in a water bath <note>original: *balneo*; short for balneum Mariae</note>, and the salt of the Crystal will remain at the bottom. Take it, grind it, and sprinkle it upon a marble slab: it will dissolve into a liquor, and do likewise for the remaining precious stones.

## ON THE POWERS OF THE SPIRIT
### *of white amber.*
<note>original: *succini albi*; White amber was highly prized in pharmacy for its high concentration of succinic acid.</note>

It is a most ready remedy and preventative for those who fear they are prone to paralysis, epilepsy, or diseases of that kind. For if every other day, or two or three times a week, some drops of this spirit are taken in lavender water, lily of the valley water, or Betony water, they safely protect against the aforementioned diseases. It also protects against pestilential air and its infection if 2 or 3 drops are taken daily with wine, and one drop is rubbed into the nostrils. The same is achieved if lozenges are made from the whitest sugar and a little spirit of amber, and one or two drops of it are taken daily.

In cases of paralysis, 4 or 5 drops are administered morning and evening in lavender water, and one drop is placed under the tongue with a small feather <note>original: *pennula*; likely a quill used to apply the potent liquid precisely</note>. For it restores speech wonderfully and comforts the brain. It is also very useful when rubbed into the nape of the neck; it restores nerves and contracted limbs excellently, especially in paralysis, whether used by itself or mixed with other balms. It is extremely beneficial for those suffering from stones <term>Calculosis: the formation of stony mineral deposits in the kidneys or bladder</term>; it expels that stony matter through the urine and dissolves the **Tartar** <note>original: *Tartarum*; in Paracelsian medicine, this refers to stony metabolic waste that calcifies and causes disease</note> adhering to the veins. It facilitates childbirth if three drops are given in white lily water in time of need. The same is achieved if it is mixed with a little snake fat <note>original: *axungiæ serpentis*</note> and the woman's navel is anointed. For women suffering from "suffocation" or "strangulation of the womb" <note>original: *suffocationem aut strangulationem uteri*; a historical diagnosis for various physical and emotional symptoms once believed to be caused by the uterus moving upward in the body</note>, it is a most excellent remedy. Rubbed on the nostrils and the chest, and if possible, taken by mouth, it is beneficial for heart palpitations and fainting <note>original: *deliquio animi*</note>; for it strengthens all the principal organs by a certain secret power.

## OPIATE LAUDANUM.
<note>original: *Laudanum Opiatum*; while "laudanum" originally meant any "praiseworthy" medicine, by this time it usually referred to an opium-based tincture or pill.</note>

This is the safest and most healthful medicine for soothing and curing all kinds of pains existing throughout the whole body without any harm. For it settles and removes—wonderfully and within a few hours—the "resolutions of minerals," which sometimes cause strange symptoms in the body. It cures painful catarrh <note>original: *Catarrho*; an excessive buildup of mucus</note>. It cures the cough caused by distillations reaching the lungs; it also heals "lientery" <term>Lienteria: a type of diarrhea where food is passed undigested</term> and diarrhea. It immediately settles colicky pains. It is given in the form of a small pill, three grains in weight, or from 3 to 5 grains.

Against gout and inflammations.

### HOW THE LIQUID OF MERCURY IS MADE

<margin>
It thoroughly heals ulcers of the bladder, throat, and kidneys.

Taken by mouth, it heals ulcers of the bladder, throat, and other hidden parts, and it clears away diseases of the kidneys through sweat and urine.

### OIL OF PINE WOOD.
<note>original: *Oleum Ligni Pini*</note>

It resists poisons and greatly promotes sweating, expels fevers, and is useful for all "cold" diseases <note>In the humoral theory of the time, "cold" diseases resulted from an excess of phlegm or black bile</note>, if 5 or 7 drops are drunk in wine or some distilled water.

### BALSAM OF ST. JOHN'S WORT.
<note>original: *Balsamus Hyperici*</note>

It follows the description by Paracelsus <note>Philippus Aureolus Theophrastus Bombastus von Hohenheim (1493–1541), a famous Swiss physician and alchemist</note> in his *Great Surgery* <note>original: *Magna Chirurgia*</note>. It heals wounds most successfully: it disperses tumors and blood clotted by a fall, etc.

### COMPOUND BALSAM OF SULFUR.
<note>original: *Balsamus Sulphuris compositus*</note>

The dose is half a dram <term>ʒ ß: a dram is about 3.9 grams, so half is roughly 2 grams</term> or as much as can be held on the tip of a knife; it is a most safe preventative against the plague.

### SIMPLE BALSAM OF SULFUR.
<note>original: *Balsamus Sulphuris simplex*</note>

One scruple <term>℈ j: a scruple is about 1.3 grams</term> by weight is given with half a dram of theriac <note>original: *theriacæ*; a famous ancient "universal" herbal paste used as an antidote for poison and a general cure</note>; it cures the plague, pleurisy, etc.

### METHOD OF COMPOSING BALSAM OF SULFUR.

Take ℞ 4 ounces of oil of turpentine and 2 ounces of flowers of sulfur <note>A fine yellow powder produced by heating sulfur until it turns to vapor and then collecting the solid crystals</note>. Let the flowers be added so they may be better dissolved; let the glass vessel be placed over hot coals and moved often. Leave all of this in a sand bath <note>A container of sand heated by fire to provide a gentle, even heat</note> until it becomes like pitch, which will happen in the space of eight or ten hours: let the fire be slow. Finally, pour spirit of wine <note>Concentrated ethanol or distilled alcohol</note> over this material to the height of three fingers, and leave it over a slow fire until the spirit of wine turns red. Pour this off into another glass and pour new spirit over the dregs: and it will be tinted again. Gradually separate these and join both spirits together. Place the tinted spirit of wine in a cucurbit <note>A gourd-shaped glass vessel used in distillation</note> and, with an alembic <note>A distilling lid or "helmet"</note> attached, draw off a portion of that spirit. The tincture of sulfur will remain at the bottom; keep it for use. It is given to those suffering from shortness of breath and those troubled by coughs due to a lung affection, taken in hyssop water or syrup of licorice. This is the famous simple balsam of sulfur.

### COMPOUND BALSAM OF SULFUR.

Take 2 ounces of flowers of sulfur three times sublimated, 1 ounce of camphor, and 4 ounces of turpentine. Grind and sift the flowers and camphor together, place them in a narrow-mouthed cucurbit, and pour your turpentine over them. With everything well-sealed, place the vessel in sand; apply a slow fire for two hours so the sand grows warm, then increase the fire until it begins to bubble in the glass: thus the sulfur will be turned into oil.

This is an admirable balsam for cleansing ulcers and wounds; likewise internally for fevers, the plague, colic, and against poisons...

...on the [se]cond and third [day?], and as the cold recedes, and even for those growing warm, from 5 to 9 drops in syrup of quinces or pomegranates, I have cured many with only a single administration. It is beneficial for the stomach in water or mint syrup for those who are nauseated by food or retain it poorly, provided that a light vomiting precedes it.

For young women who are pale and discolored <note>A condition likely referring to chlorosis or "green sickness," often attributed in the past to anemia or poor digestion</note>—which they mostly contract from poor digestion and a chilled stomach—after a vomit-inducing draft <term>vomitum: an emetic used to clear the stomach</term> is taken, the dose is six to seven drops at one time in syrup of quinces or meadowsweet water <note>original: *aquæ ulmariæ*</note>; it is very helpful after an emetic made from Antimony.

### OIL OF CINNAMON

It strengthens the stomach, the brain, the heart itself, and all the principal members. It immediately stops vomiting caused by Antimony if it is excessive, provided it is taken in its own water <note>distilled cinnamon water</note>. The quantity of oil should be four drops, and of the water, two spoonfuls. If you desire Hippocras <note>A traditional spiced wine</note> in an instant, add several drops of this oil to any noble wine previously sweetened with sugar, along with several drops of oil of nutmeg and cloves; if you like, a little rose water will make it a most pleasant wine. This oil is also taken in sugar tablets called "Hand of Christ" <term>manus Christi: a common sugar-based lozenge used as a vehicle for potent medicines</term>, such that a single drop is instilled into each tablet.

### OIL OF NUTMEG

It aids the memory, dissipates wind <note>gas or flatulence</note>, and repairs a chilled stomach if it is rubbed with it. The dose is from 4 to 6 drops in broth.

### OIL OF CLOVES

It is hot in nature and cheers the stomach, liver, and heart. It stops a flux of the belly <note>original: *fluxum ventris*; diarrhea</note> arising from a cold cause, dissipates melancholic humors, cures vertigo, and likewise "suffocation of the womb" <term>suffocationi matricis: a historical diagnosis for various physical and emotional symptoms in women, then believed to be caused by a displaced uterus</term>. The dose is from four to 6 drops in the morning in broth, or with one spoonful of wine. It has the powers of a balsam if applied to wounds, for it joins them together without pain and cleanses putrid ulcers; when smeared on with camphor, it soothes the pains of ulcers. It also cures toothaches.

### OIL OF ANISE

It is a most excellent remedy for the lungs, coughs, and obstructions; it dissipates all winds, stops catarrh <note>the flow of excess mucus</note>, and strengthens the brain, if 5 to 7 drops are given in wine or syrup of quinces or an appropriate water. Tablets are also made upon which several small drops are placed.

### OIL OF CUMIN

It is very useful for all types of hardness <note>Likely referring to hardened swellings, tumors, or stiff tissues</note>, for it softens them and soothes pains; it stimulates suppressed urine if three or five drops are administered with white wine and fern water <note>original: *aqua filicis*</note>.

### OIL OF JUNIPER

It is effective for the same conditions as oil of turpentine; it preserves the body from decay remarkably well according to its balsamic nature. It cleanses the kidneys and expels kidney stones <term>calculum: a mineral deposit or "stone" formed in the gallbladder or kidneys</term> through the urine, and it promotes sweating. It also extracts the tincture of calcined gold <note>A reference to alchemical processes where oils were used to "draw out" the essence or color of metals</note>. The dose is from six to eight drops in a suitable syrup or broth.

### OIL OF TURPENTINE

It possesses the same virtues as oil of juniper. If it is distilled with water three times or more, it will be as clear as "water of life" <term>aquæ vitæ: a term for high-proof distilled alcohol, literally "water of life"</term>; then it is fit for extracting all tinctures, both of herbs and other things. It is highly penetrative and breaks down stones in the kidneys when taken with parsley water.

### OIL OF GREATER BURDOCK

An excellent remedy for kidney stones. The dose is from 8 to 12 drops in white wine or maidenhair fern water <note>original: *aqua capillorum Veneris*, a common botanical remedy for respiratory and urinary issues</note>.

### *A Secret for Kidney Stones*

Take two pounds of the bark of ash tree root, three pounds of juniper seeds, and two and a half pounds of clear turpentine. Let the things that need grinding be ground and then mixed with the turpentine. Place them all together in twelve pounds of water in a well-sealed vessel to putrefy <note>In early pharmacy, "putrefaction" referred to a controlled process of warm maceration or fermentation to break down plant matter</note> for three months. When the time has passed, distill it in the manner of other oils. A most excellent oil will drip forth; nothing similar is found for such a condition. The dose is 8 to 12 drops; it breaks the stone and expels it when taken with white wine.

### OIL OF WAX

It is recommended for bruises <note>original: *confusionibus*, likely a scribal error for *contusionibus* (contusions)</note> if applied topically; it is a supreme remedy for colicky pains if given in spirit of wine <term>spiritu vini: distilled alcohol or brandy</term>. The dose is from 8 to 12 drops. I also usually place from one to one and a half drams <term>ʒ: the symbol for a dram, a unit of weight roughly equal to 3.9 grams</term> in enemas; it does much for ulcers of the intestines and for pains. If you rectify <note>To "rectify" is to purify a substance by repeated distillation</note> it several times over washed and dry sand, it will acquire a miraculous power of penetration.

### ON COLD OILS

Let the greater or lesser "cold seeds" <note>In Galenic medicine, the "four greater cold seeds" were typically cucumber, melon, gourd, and watermelon; the "lesser" were lettuce, purslane, poppy, and endive</note> be mixed together and placed in water. Let them boil a little; collect the foam and place it in a glass vessel. Let it be digested in a water bath <note>original: *balneo*, referring to a *balneum Mariae* or bain-marie</note> overnight, and it will turn into a most pleasant oil.

### ON JUNIPER.

Place crushed juniper berries in a sufficient quantity of water in a bladder <note>original: *vesicam*, a traditional animal-bladder vessel or a similarly shaped copper vessel used for fermentation and distillation</note>, and add a good amount of yeast: after a proper soaking <term>maceration: the process of softening or breaking down a substance by soaking it in liquid to extract its virtues</term>, it will give you a very abundant burning wine <note>original: *vinum ardens*, a term for high-proof distilled alcohol or spirits</note>.

### *To extract the life of Plants.*

First grind the herb, then distill the water with a glass distilling head <term>alembic: a classic chemical apparatus used for distillation, consisting of a gourd-like container and a cap with a beak</term>, over ashes <note>An "ash bath" or "sand bath" used by early chemists to provide even, indirect heat without breaking the glass</note>: then grind more of the same herb: incorporate this body with the aforementioned water, and place it to rot <term>putrefaction: in early chemistry, a controlled stage of decomposition thought to release the "inner spirit" or "life" of a substance</term> with the joints of the vessel sealed for eight days: then squeeze out all the juice and distill it again: you will have an excellent water, and you will find a powder in the bottom more precious than the water; keep both.

### *A PERFECT CURE FOR CATARRH CONSISTS IN*
### *Black Hellebore, collected in the month of October.*

An extraction of black hellebore <note>original: *Helleborus niger*, a plant used historically as a powerful, though potentially toxic, purgative</note> with anise water to the consistency of honey, to which add bread crumbs in the same amount as the extract: once mixed, let them be placed in a glass flask <term>retort: a glass vessel with a long, downward-pointing neck used for distilling or fermenting substances</term> well-sealed, in horse manure <note>Used as a natural, steady source of gentle warmth for weeks at a time</note> for three weeks. Take the liquid from the dregs and distill it over ashes until you find it has become oily. Take that and place it for digestion in a bath or in manure for 14 days: then separate that which is phlegmy <note>the watery or mucus-like residue</note> from it, and what remains is the essence of Hellebore; which purges the body very gently at a dose of six to eight grains.

### *Another preparation.*

Let the roots be gathered in the month of October and cleaned with the best wine: the outer barks should be selected, as the inner parts are of no importance: let them be soaked (or rather sprinkled with Malmsey wine <note>a sweet, fortified Mediterranean wine</note>) and dried in the sun or other similar heat: repeat this process six times: grind very finely: place this powder in a wide glass vessel, and pour over it the juice of laxative roses <note>original: *rosarum solutivarum*, roses chosen for their mildly laxative properties</note> as much as is needed. Dry it again, and repeat this five times: finally, grind it and keep it in glass: you have an incomparable medicine for almost all diseases, and it is given in doses of 8 to 12 grains with syrup of violets or another approved liquid.

### *Another wonderful recipe taken from a very ancient book.*

Take <note>original: $\mathcal{R}$, the traditional symbol for *recipe*</note> of Black Hellebore roots, and also the herbs, cleaned of all impurities with wine, 4 handfuls <note>original: *m. iv*, where *m* stands for *manipulus*, a handful—a standard unit of measurement for herbalists</note> of each. Let them be crushed and placed in red wine or Muscatel in a glass vessel well-sealed, up to two measures, and leave it in a cauldron in boiling water for a day and a night: afterward, take it out, and strongly squeeze out the juice and filter it. Place this filtrate over 1 handful of fresh crushed Hellebore roots, 5 handfuls of red roses, and 6 drams <note>original: *ʒ. vj*, using the apothecaries' symbol for drachms</note> of Cloves, previously crushed; place them together for digestion...

# TREATISE ON VARIOUS *preparations* OF TARTAR.

Crude Tartar <note>The sediment or "wine-stone" found in wine barrels, prized by alchemists for its chemical properties</note> is taken, ground, placed in a retort, and distilled according to the process for oil of vitriol. Oil and water emerge: separate the water from the oil using a water bath. Rectify the water over <term>colcothar</term> <note>The red iron oxide residue remaining after the distillation of vitriol</note> until the foul smell is gone. It is of the greatest benefit for putrefactions and blockages; it dissolves internal <term>abscesses</term> <note>original: apostemata; localized collections of pus or swelling</note> and consumes defects of the internal chest organs. It heals all scabies <note>A contagious skin disease causing itching and sores</note> when drunk without any other mixture; the dose is one spoonful morning and evening by itself, or with a decoction of <term>guaiac wood</term> <note>A tropical wood used historically to treat syphilis</note>. It strongly induces sweating in cases of the "venereal plague" <note>original: lue venerea; syphilis</note>, and it is a ready remedy for dropsy <note>original: hydrops; swelling caused by excess fluid</note> and long-standing obstructions.

## *ANOTHER PREPARATION OF TARTAR.*

Tartar is calcined <note>Burned to a white ash</note>, ground, and spread upon a marble slab. It is placed in a damp location to dissolve <note>The process of deliquescence, where a salt absorbs enough moisture from the air to become liquid</note>, then filtered and dried; this is repeated three times. Take 1 pound <note>original: ℔ j.</note> of this liquor and 4 drams or more of the best oil of vitriol <note>Sulfuric acid</note>, and drip it drop by drop onto the liquor of tartar. A very white curd forms. If you draw off the moisture to dryness using a <term>B. M.</term> <note>original: Balneum Mariae; a Mary's bath or double boiler</note>, you then have "fixed tartar" for dropsy, stones <note>original: calculum; kidney or bladder stones</note>, and various diseases. It provokes sweating and purges through the bowels, provided it is mixed with honey of roses or another syrup. The dose is from half a scruple to one full scruple <note>original: à ℈ ß. ad ℈ j.</note> in white wine or parsley water.

### *ANOTHER.*

Dissolve calcined tartar upon a marble slab; save the liquid part, calcine the remainder again, pour its own water back over it, and distill in a <term>B. M.</term> Pour its water over it again, distill, and save. Calcine it once more and let it dissolve as before upon the marble: distill it and pour it off. Do this until it no longer coagulates but remains as an oil. With this oil, you can fix <note>To make a volatile substance stable under heat</note> all sublimated spirits, and you shall dissolve corals and pearls. You shall heal all wounds and expel "tartarous" wastes <note>Metabolic wastes or stones thought to resemble the crust in wine barrels</note> from the body. The dose is from 4 to 6 drops in a suitable liquid.

## TINCTURE OF TARTAR.

Let spirit of wine <note>Alcohol</note> impregnated with the tincture of tartar be evaporated to the consistency of honey. Put this liquor into a retort and, observing the proper stages of the fire, distill it. You will have a white, acidic liquor, like oil of vitriol, which is a supreme secret <note>original: arcanum; a deep mystery or highly potent alchemical remedy</note> for all abscesses of the lungs...

### LIQUOR OF TARTAR.

Liquor of tartar is Tartar that has been <term>calcined</term> <note>reduced to a powder by high heat</note> and dissolved upon a marble slab in a cold place. If you place some of this into distilled water, in the course of time, the salt will separate itself from the water like a crystal, the effects of which are varied: the dose is half a scruple <note>original: ℈ ß.; approximately 0.65 grams</note> in its own proper distilled water.

### CREAM OF TARTAR.

Take washed tartar of white wine: grind it into small pieces: throw it into pure water and make it boil in a kettle. By boiling, a crust or "skin" will form; remove it and save it. Take 1 dram <note>original: ʒ j.; approximately 3.9 grams</note> of this, and 8 grains of prepared <term>diagridium</term> <note>A medicinal preparation of scammony, a potent plant-based purgative</note>. Mix these and provide them in a broth; it purges gently. It is a secret remedy for afflictions of the spleen.

### A MASTERY OF TARTAR NOT TO BE DISDAINED.

Dissolve tartar that has been highly calcined in the <term>phlegm</term> <note>The watery, non-alcoholic part of distilled spirits</note> of the "water of life" <note>original: aqua vitae; high-proof alcohol or brandy</note>, filter it, evaporate it, and the salt will remain at the bottom. Dissolve it again in the purified watery part, filter as you did before, and repeat this three times until it leaves no dregs behind. Calcine it well until it reaches a perfect whiteness. Take 1 pound <note>original: ℔ j.</note> of this salt and 4 pounds <note>original: ℔ iiij.</note> of rectified water of life; mix them and distill in a <term>water bath</term> <note>original: B. M. (Balneum Mariae); a vessel of boiling water used to provide gentle, even heat</note>. Two parts will distill without any taste; repeat the process until the said water is "congealed" with the said salt. For every dry thing, by its nature, drinks up its own moisture. Again, dry the salt very well, mix in new spirit of wine, and distill: it will retain some part of the spirit of wine. Place this salt in a glass <term>sublimator</term> <note>A vessel used for sublimation, the process where a solid turns into gas and back to solid, purifying it</note>: it will be sublimated like camphor. Take this sublimated salt and guard it preciously: it performs wonders in the <term>spagyric</term> <note>The alchemical art of separating and recombining the essential components of plants and minerals to create medicine</note> art, for by its mediation, "the light of day" is reduced into the <term>prime matter</term> <note>original: lux diei in primam materiam; a philosophical concept referring to the fundamental substance of the universe</note>. By administering 3 grains in a suitable liquid, you shall heal whatever sicknesses there may be. Fear God and give thanks to Him through Him who lives forever, Amen. We shall deal with this subject more fully elsewhere, God willing; meanwhile, take this in good part.

-> ON MEAD. <-
<note>original: DE HYDROMELITE; literally "honey-water"</note>

I cannot wonder enough how certain men, casting aside all shame, claim the labors and inventions of others as their own, and sell mead to princes and states as if it were some divine mystery, when it is of almost no consequence. But ignorance is the mother of such admiration. Pliny <note>Gaius Plinius Secundus, Roman naturalist</note> makes mention of it in his chapter on honey, and teaches the method of its preparation. In these times, a disagreement has arisen among men and certain women concerning the excellence and use of mead; they prepare it so secretly that not even a mother or father is willing to reveal it to their son. I know many who are not ashamed to ask fifty thousand crowns <note>original: coronatos; a high-value gold coin</note> for the formula of its composition. But when I had traveled to various regions and sold it there publicly and at a low price, I could not help but laugh at their impudence. 

For this reason, I thought it would not be inconvenient if I described some methods of composing it in the present treatise, so that everyone may prepare it as they please and beware of such pharmacists. There are those who simply use no additives in its composition, adding only a bit of tincture of tartar near the end, as Paracelsus <note>Philippus Aureolus Theophrastus Bombastus von Hohenheim, the famous Swiss physician and alchemist</note> teaches in his book *On the Nature of Things*; I approve of this simple preparation. Others, however, use fragrant roots and spices, and from this it happens that the head often suffers from heaviness <note>likely referring to a hangover or congestion</note>. Still others prepare it from purgatives, and it purges no differently than the wine described by Arnaldus <note>likely Arnaldus de Villa Nova, a 13th-century physician</note>. But it is in vain to do through many things what can be done through fewer. As I have experienced it, I will teach two ways of preparing it here. But I do not want this to be hidden from you: it is made more excellently during the Dog Days <note>original: pendente canicula; the hottest period of summer, associated with the star Sirius</note> than at any other time. For the sun impresses its power more upon all things than the heat of the elements...

## ON HYDROMEL.

I cannot marvel enough how certain men, putting aside all shame, claim the labors and discoveries of others as their own, and sell <term>hydromel</term> <note>original: hydromel; honey water or mead</note> to princes and public officials as if it were some divine mystery, when it is of almost no importance. But ignorance is the mother of admiration. <term>Pliny</term> <note>Pliny the Elder, the Roman naturalist</note> makes mention of it in the chapter on honey, and teaches the method of preparation. In these times, a disagreement has arisen between men and certain women concerning the excellence and use of hydromel, and they prepare it so secretly that not even a mother or father wishes to reveal it to their own son. I know many who are not ashamed to ask fifty thousand crowns for the formula of its composition. But when I traveled to different regions and saw it sold there publicly and at a low price, I could not restrain myself from laughing at their impudence. For this reason, I thought it would not be inconvenient for me to describe some methods of its composition in the present treatise, so that everyone might prepare it as they please and beware of such pharmacists. 

There are some who simply use no additives in its composition, only adding a bit of <term>tincture of tartar</term> <note>a solution derived from potassium bitartrate</note> near the end, as <term>Paracelſus</term> <note>The famous Swiss physician and alchemist</note> teaches in his book *On the Nature of Things*, a simple preparation which I approve of. Others, however, use fragrant roots and spices, and from this it happens that the head often suffers from heaviness. Yet there are those who prepare it from purgatives, and it purges no differently than the wine described by <term>Arnaldus</term> <note>Arnaldus de Villa Nova, a medieval physician</note>. ### ON HYDROMEL <note>original: Hydromelite; a fermented drink made of honey and water, commonly known as mead</note>.

I cannot wonder enough how some men, casting aside all modesty, claim the labors and inventions of others as their own. They sell hydromel to princes and the public as if it were some divine mystery, when it is of almost no significance at all. But ignorance is the mother of admiration. Pliny <note>Gaius Plinius Secundus, the Roman naturalist</note> mentions it in his chapter on honey and teaches the method of preparation. In these times, a disagreement has arisen among men and certain women concerning the excellence and use of hydromel. They prepare it so secretly that a mother or father will not even reveal it to their son, and I know many who are not ashamed to ask fifty thousand crowns for the formula of its composition. But when I had traveled to various regions and seen it sold publicly and at a cheap price, I could not help but laugh at their impudence. For this reason, I thought I would not be doing anything inconvenient if I described some methods of composing it in the present treatise, so that everyone may prepare it as they wish and beware of such pharmacists <note>original: pharmacopolis; often implying "quacks" or "medicine-sellers"</note>. There are those who simply use no additives in its composition, only adding a bit of tincture of tartar <note>original: tinctura tartari; a chemical preparation made from the crust left in wine barrels</note> toward the end, as Paracelsus teaches in his book *On the Nature of Things*, which simple preparation I approve of. Others, however, use fragrant roots and spices, and it follows from this that the head often suffers from heaviness. Still, there are those who prepare it from purgatives, and it purges no differently than the wine described by Arnaldus <note>Arnald of Villanova, a famous medieval physician</note>. But it is in vain to do with many things what can be done with few. Based on my experience, I will teach two ways of preparing it here. But I do not want this to be hidden from you: it is made more excellently during the Dog Days <note>original: canicula; the period between early July and mid-August associated with Sirius, the Dog Star</note> than at any other time. Indeed, the Sun impresses more of its virtue into all things than the elementary heat—

<page-num>664</page-num>
<header>ON MEDICINES</header>

[hea]t <note>original: calor; the OCR "lor" is a partial transcription of 'calor' (heat)</note> elementary, or from a hearth or a hypocaust <note>original: hypocauſti; an ancient Roman underfloor heating system, here referring to a stove-heated room</note>, as has often been found through experience. We also see that water in the month of March achieves more than at any other time, as beer brewers <note>original: cereviſiæ coctores</note> know well. For beer brewed in that month is preserved longer and increases in both quality and pleasantness. But lest I seem too long-winded in my writing: you shall begin thus.

### FORMULA.

Take one part honey and eight parts rain or river water; let the honey be dissolved in that water. Afterward, let them boil moderately in a cauldron of sufficient capacity until a third part is consumed, skimming off the foam. The sign of the perfect ratio is if you place a raw egg in it and it floats; then it is ready. If not, boil it down until it gives its sign. You may purify it through a clean linen cloth, then place it in a dry wooden vessel that has been previously seasoned with Malmsey wine <note>original: vino malvatico; a sweet, potent Mediterranean wine</note>. Immediately put in a small bag filled with mustard seed <note>original: grano ſinapi</note> tied with a string, so that you can pull it out when needed. This done, expose your vessel to the hottest sun, and your hydromel <note>original: hydromel; mead</note> will bubble just like new wine <note>original: muſtum</note> at harvest time. When the time has passed, remove the mustard seed and place the vessel, very well sealed, in a cellar. This hydromel is the base from which you can make more at any time.

### HYDROMEL THAT TASTES LIKE WINE.

When you have prepared it once, add one measure of the juice of hop flowers <note>original: florum lupuli</note> to thirty measures of the mead; it will immediately begin to bubble without any heat. The vessel must be kept full continuously, and when it has finished fermenting, you have a hydromel so potent that if you pour it over honey-water that has been boiled, you will have the best hydromel in a short time. Every time you add new hop juice, you will increase its strength by that much more. The rest must be gathered by philosophizing; I should not have to chew everything for you beforehand <note>A proverbial expression meaning the reader should use their own intellect to figure out the remaining secrets</note>. Others add Clary sage flowers <note>original: Ormini flores</note> after the first boiling. But I have another way: I am accustomed to impregnating the honey before I add the water. I have said enough of these things. Let us turn to other matters.

### ANOTHER HYDROMEL WHICH IN ITS OWN TIME *is turned into the sharpest vinegar, one spoonful of which transforms a measure of wine into the sourest vinegar.*

Take: Long pepper, round pepper, nutmeg, and cinnamon, 3 drachms <note>original: ʒ iij</note> of each. Let them be ground. Mix with 1.5 pounds <note>original: ℔ j. ß</note> of rye flour <note>original: farinæ ſiliginis</note> and thin it with hydromel. Make a leaven <note>original: fermentum</note>, of which you should take a piece the size of an egg, and it will bubble by itself. Leave the vessel open in a warm place, and in a short time, it will turn into the sharpest vinegar, with which I myself have dissolved flints. May you favor and enjoy these, my late-night labors.

### MEAD THAT TASTES LIKE WINE.

Once you have prepared it, add one measure of the juice of hop flowers <note>original: succi florum lupuli</note> to thirty measures [of the mead]. It will immediately begin to bubble without any heat, and the vessel must be kept full. When it has finished fermenting, you will have a potent mead. If you pour this over boiled honey-water, you will have excellent mead in a short time; and every time you add new hop juice, you will increase its strength that much more. The rest must be gathered through philosophical reasoning; not everything should be pre-chewed for you. Others add Clary Sage flowers <note>original: Ormini flores</note> after the first boiling. But I have another way: I am accustomed to impregnating the honey before I fill it with water. I have said enough of these things. Let us turn to others.

### ANOTHER MEAD WHICH IN ITS OWN TIME
### *is turned into a most sharp vinegar, one spoonful of which*
### *transforms a measure of wine into the most bitter vinegar.*

Take long pepper, round pepper, nutmeg, and cinnamon, 3 drachms each. Let them be ground. Mix with 1.5 pounds <note>original: ℔ j. ß</note> of rye flour <note>original: farinæ siliginis</note> and temper it with mead to make a leaven <note>original: fermentum; a starter dough</note>. Of this, add a piece the size of an egg. It will boil by itself. Leave the vessel open in a warm place, and in a short time it will be turned into the sharpest vinegar, with which you may even dissolve flint-stones <note>original: silices</note>. Finally, may you favor and enjoy my late-night labors.

Salt of gentian <note>Gentiana; a bitter root used for digestion</note> resists all fevers, opens and clears obstructions of the internal organs, and promotes urine and menstruation. It is also effective against serpent bites when taken with salt of rue and pepper.

### ON THE SALT OF GRATIOLA OR
#### *Grace of God.*

Salt of gratiola <note>Gratiola officinalis, or hedge hyssop, historically nicknamed "Grace of God" for its potency</note> cures dropsy, and is also for those with melancholy, those whose skin is flushed with blood <note>original: sanguini suffusis</note>, and those who are terrified. ### *FORMULA.*

Take one part honey, eight parts rain or river water, dissolve the honey in that water, then let them boil moderately in a cauldron of proper capacity until a third part is consumed, while skimming it <note>original: spumando; removing the impurities that rise to the surface during boiling</note>. The sign of the perfect ratio is if a raw egg is placed in it and it floats; then it is ready. If not, boil it until it gives its sign. You can purify it through a clean linen cloth, then place it in a dry wooden vessel that has been previously seasoned with Malmsey wine <note>original: vino malvatico; a sweet, potent Mediterranean wine often used to flavor or "prepare" storage barrels</note>. Immediately put in a small bag filled with mustard seeds <note>original: grano sinapi</note> tied with a thread, so that you can pull it out when needed. Having done this, expose your vessel to the brightest sun, and your hydromel <note>original: hydromel; a fermented drink made of honey and water, commonly known as mead</note> will boil just like must <note>original: mustum; freshly pressed grape juice undergoing fermentation</note> during the time of the vintage. When the time is completed, take out the mustard seeds and place the vessel, tightly sealed, in the cellar. This hydromel is the base from which you can make it at any time.

### *HYDROMEL THAT TASTES LIKE WINE.*

Once you have prepared it, put one measure of hop flower juice <note>original: succi florum lupuli</note> over thirty measures [of the base]; it immediately begins to boil without any heat, and the vessel must be filled continuously. When it has finished fermenting, you will have such a powerful hydromel that if you pour it over boiled honey-water, in a short time you will have excellent hydromel; and as often as you add new hop juice, so much more will you increase its strength. The remaining things are to be inferred by philosophizing; they are not all to be pre-chewed <note>original: praemasticanda; a metaphor for being explained in tedious detail</note> for you. Others, after the first boiling, put in Clary Sage flowers <note>original: Ormini flores; a herb often used to flavor ale and wine</note>. But I have another way: before I add the water, I am accustomed to impregnate the honey; I have said enough of these things. Let us turn to others.

### *ANOTHER HYDROMEL WHICH IN ITS OWN TIME*
### *turns into the sharpest vinegar, of which one spoonful*
### *transforms a measure of wine into the most bitter*
### *vinegar.*

Take: Long pepper, round pepper, nutmeg, and cinnamon, 3 drachms <note>original: ʒ iij; approximately 11.7 grams</note> each. Let them be ground. Mix with 1.5 pounds <note>original: ℔ j. ß.</note> of rye flour and blend with hydromel. Make a ferment <note>original: fermentum; a starter culture or leaven</note>, of which you should use a piece the size of an egg. It will boil by itself. Leave the vessel open in a warm place, and in a short time it will turn into the sharpest vinegar, which could even dissolve flints. Finally, favor and enjoy my nightly labors.

### QUESTION.
### IS MAGIC PERMISSIBLE?

Many Babylonians write that he who knows how to count knows everything. It is asked: why is man the wisest animal? The answer is: because he knows how to count. True philosophers have not been ignorant of the fact that natural magic depends on numbers. However, it is well known that magic is twofold. One is entirely of demons, [achieved] by their work and authority—a thing, by my faith <note>original: "medius fidius"; an ancient Roman oath to the god of trust, used here to mean "truly" or "in all honesty"</note>, that is cursed and monstrous. The other, when it is properly examined, is nothing else than the absolute completion of natural philosophy, which they call perfect and supreme wisdom. For in the Persian language, a "Magus" <term>Magus: Derived from the Old Persian 'maguš', originally a member of a priestly caste; here the author emphasizes the scholar-priest aspect rather than a sorcerer</term> signifies what we call an interpreter and a worshiper of divine things.

Between these two arts—or "magics"—there is the greatest disparity and difference. That demonic version is condemned and cursed not only by the Christian religion but by all laws and every well-governed republic. Whoever practices this always hides it, for it would lead to the shame and disgrace of the author. No philosopher or person eager to learn the good arts was ever a student of this. This magic seeks out darkness and deserted places; for all science that flees the public eye is suspect, just as that which takes its origin from the spirits of darkness. But the other [magic], all wise men and all nations devoted to celestial and divine things approve of and embrace. This is a higher and holier philosophy. From this, the greatest brilliance of literature and glory has been sought since ancient times, and almost always. Pythagoras, Democritus, and Plato sailed abroad to learn this; having returned, they preached it and held it as their most precious secret.

<margin>It is not granted to everyone, nor always, [to speak] of God—</margin>
Just as that magic of evil demons <note>original: "cacodæmonum"; from the Greek 'kakos' (bad) and 'daimon' (spirit)</note> can claim for itself neither the name of art nor science, so this true magic, full of the deepest mysteries, encompasses the most profound contemplation of the most secret things, and of God, and the knowledge of all nature. This calls forth into the light—from their hiding places—the virtues scattered and sown throughout the world by the grace of God. And just as a farmer joins elms to vines <note>original: "ulmos vitibus... maritat"; a classical metaphor for marriage or close union, referring to the Roman practice of training grapevines to grow up elm trees</note>, so the magus joins the earth to heaven; that is, he connects the lower things to the gifts and virtues of the higher things, and, so to speak, "marries" them. This stirs up such admiration for the works of God that a ready charity, faith, and hope most certainly follow. For nothing promotes religion and the worship of God more than the constant contemplation of God's wonders, than that natural magic by which we are compelled to sing: *The heavens are full, and all the earth is full of the majesty of your glory.* And this is enough regarding the magi. I know there are many who, like dogs that always bark at strangers, often condemn and hate what they do not understand. For this reason, it is not granted to everyone, nor always, nor concerning all things, to philosophize about God...

Many Babylonians write that he who knows how to count knows everything. The question is asked: why is man the wisest animal? The answer given is: because he knows how to count. ### ON THE SALT OF CELANDINE.

Salt of celandine <note>original: Sal chelidoniæ; the Greater Celandine, often used in traditional medicine for liver and eye issues</note> provokes the menses; its dose is one scruple <note>original: ℈ j; a unit of weight in the apothecaries' system</note>, which usually weighs 20 grains of barley. A solution of this salt clears the eyes. This same salt, drunk with wine and salt of anise, cures the "royal disease" <note>original: regio morbo; a historical name for jaundice</note>; the liquid is also effective for ulcers. It also benefits asthmatics and those with obstructions of the chest, cleanses the liver, and is effective against the plague, the pains of colic, and pain and swelling of the womb. It is used for hemorrhoids <note>original: mariscas</note> when mixed with an equal weight of phlegm of vitriol <note>original: phlegmati vitrioli; a dilute acidic distillate of sulfate minerals</note>. <margin>Cancerous ulcers.</margin> For "the wolf" <note>original: Lupum; a term for devouring or corrosive ulcers like lupus or skin cancers</note> and other cancerous or poisonous ulcers, and for chilled limbs that would otherwise have to be amputated, apply salt water with a woolen cloth several times. Anyone who has fallen from a height or from a horse should apply this salt water over the injury. <margin>Note the property of this salt.</margin> It is also effective against the bite of a rabid dog; mix this salt with rose honey <note>original: melle rosato</note> to make an ointment, which prevents ulcers from rotting. Likewise, placed over buboes <note>original: bubones; the characteristic swellings of the bubonic plague</note>, it draws out the poison. Those with the itch <note>original: scabiosi</note> should wash themselves with the water of this salt.

### ON THE SALT OF WORMWOOD.

Salt of wormwood <note>original: Sal absynthij; derived from Artemisia absinthium</note> is usefully administered for almost all diseases, especially in the plague; it draws out water from under the skin <note>referring to edema or dropsy</note>. It promotes urine, strengthens the stomach, and induces sweating. If used from the internal to the external, it expels the "French disease" <note>original: morbum gallicum; a common historical name for syphilis</note>, heals hemorrhoids, and other internal defects. It cleanses and heals abscesses and any putrid wounds by sprinkling it upon them. This salt, dissolved in water, removes warts, varicose veins or pimples, and scars, and restores the flesh. It is used against dropsy, putrid fevers, and both daily and four-day fevers <note>original: febres putridas, quotidianas & quartanas; types of malaria-like fever cycles</note>, following a methodical process after first using evacuants and other appropriate remedies. Combined with the waters of lemon balm, sorrel, and rue, it strengthens the liver and stomach and grants the stomach good digestion. It is also used against the pains of colic and griping of the gut; it heals defects of the anus and rectum, and by irrigation and application, it treats a prolapsed womb. The liquid of this salt, applied with a feather, cures defects of the head such as dandruff, ringworm, freckles, and skin eruptions <note>original: furfures, serpigenes, lentigines, impetigines</note>. Applied with water, it dispels lice, leprosy, and other types of dry or parched scabies. Not only for these, but these mentioned salts also cure other ailments or afflictions.

### ON THE SALT OF MASTERWORT.

Salt of masterwort <note>original: Sal imperatoriæ; a plant once considered a "cure-all" for its warming properties</note> is able to warm cold and numb limbs, to dissolve thick and viscous humors stuck to the sides and linings of the stomach, and to correct other defects of the same, as well as those of the intestines and bladder; furthermore, it can increase the male seed and strengthen "Venus" <note>a euphemism for sexual potency or desire</note>. Salt of masterwort is effective against the plague and promotes sweating if it arises from coldness; it promotes childbirth and drives away miscarriages <note>original: abortus abigit; likely meaning it helps expel a dead fetus or prevents the conditions leading to miscarriage</note>. ### ON THE SALT OF BEAR’S BREECH.

### ON THE SALT OF ANGELICA.

Salt of angelica wonderfully purges the blood, and especially the brain, if twenty drops are dissolved in fennel oil and taken in the evening during a waning moon, with the treatment repeated often at intervals.

### ON THE SALT OF LOVAGE, OR LIGUSTICUM.

Salt of lovage <note>original: "levistici"</note> or ligusticum is suited for the bladder, the kidneys, and a stomach with poor digestion; it is especially appropriate for women and the intestines. It dissolves "sand" <note>small stones or sediment</note> collected from the bladder and kidneys. ## ON THE SALT OF PIMPINELLA
->Stone Pepper<- <note>original: "Steinpfeffer"; likely referring to Burnet-saxifrage, a herb often used to break up kidney stones</note>

<margin>German Pimpinella, or French Saxifrage</margin>
The salt of pimpinella is very beneficial and healthful for the stomach and all the intestines. Indeed, if it is properly prepared and a person consumes it for three days every three months in place of common salt (lest the stomach become too accustomed to it and treat it as a familiar food), and if they do this throughout their life, they will undoubtedly be safe from dropsy <note>edema or swelling</note>, phthisis <note>a wasting disease like tuberculosis</note>, and apoplexy <note>stroke</note>. This salt purifies the blood, opens the arteries, liver, and lungs, and protects against hectic fever. If it is dissolved in choice endive water and applied as a compress to the region of the liver—especially at night when excessive thirst troubles women in childbirth—it is highly effective. The elderly and anyone of a colder temperament <term>Complexion: In historical medicine, the balance of "humors" or qualities (hot, cold, moist, dry) that determined a person's health and personality</term> ought to use this salt. It is useful against cold sweats and expels the plague; or, during a time of plague, it induces sweating. It also relieves headaches caused by coldness, the pains of colic, the "rising of the womb" <note>original: "ascendentem matricem"; a historical condition where the uterus was thought to move upward, causing respiratory or emotional distress</note> in women caused by cold, stones in the kidneys and bladder, vertigo, muscle contractions, and painful urination.

## ON THE SALT OF BLACK PIMPINELLA

<margin>French Pimpinella</margin>
The salt of black pimpinella cleanses and heals any open or corroding ulcers; it prevents the generation of worms and putrid flesh within them and remedies any foul stench.

## ON THE SALT OF CRETAN CARROT
->Commonly known as Spignel<- <note>original: "Behrwurz"; refers to Meum athamanticum, though the Latin identifies it as Daucus Creticus or Candy-carrot</note>

If the salt of Cretan carrot is consumed frequently, it effectively expels a miscarriage or a "menstrual birth," such as a uterine mole <term>Mole: A historical term for a non-viable mass or tumor-like growth in the uterus</term>.

## ON THE SALT OF MOUNTAIN FENNEL

If the salt of mountain fennel is sprinkled into ulcers and deep wounds, it prevents them from smelling foul, generating worms, or producing putrid flesh; however, it should be noted that it usually draws blood from the affected area when used in a weight of two drams. When dissolved with alum in warm wine and used as a gargle, it drives away scurvy <note>original: "stomachacen"; inflammation or ulcers of the mouth often associated with scurvy</note>, restores the natural redness of the gums, and helps the flesh to regrow.

## ON THE SALT OF COMMON FENNEL

The salt of fennel, when mixed with butter into an ointment and applied in a similar way, dries and heals scabby ulcers of the head and ringworm <note>original: "serpigines"</note> of the body. Likewise, it promotes menstruation and urination, and is suitable for those with jaundice <note>original: "arquato"</note>.

### ON THE SALT OF PARSLEY.

The salt of parsley <note>original: "petroselini"</note> dissolves tumors of every kind. If taken regularly with wine, it expels stones from both the bladder and the kidneys. ### ON THE SALT OF CHERVIL, OTHERWISE *Gingidium*.
