Finally, if it is administered with "blessed thistle" <note>original: "cardui benedicti"; a plant famous in the Renaissance as a "cure-all" for its bitter, tonic properties</note> water, it drives away worms from the belly and soothes griping pains around the navel.

### ON THE SALT OF SPEEDWELL.

The salt of speedwell <note>original: "veronicæ"</note>, when taken with theriac <term>Theriac: A famous poly-pharmaceutical "universal antidote" containing dozens of ingredients, including opium and viper flesh.</term> and Malmsey wine, is effective against the plague. If it is reduced into an oil or liquid form, use it as an ointment for pustules, scabies, abscesses, fistulas, and morphoea <note>a skin condition involving discolored, hardened patches</note>. It is also effective against "French pustules" and abscesses <note>referring to symptoms of syphilis</note> when dissolved in rose vinegar, provided they are washed with it frequently.

### ON THE SALT OF IRONWORT.

<margin>It is Ironwort, I believe. <note>original: "Sideritis est, ut puto."</note></margin>
The salt of Ironwort <note>original: "herbæ fortis"</note>, when drunk with wine, treats internal French sickness <note>syphilis</note>; for hot and burning fevers, however, it should be taken in the morning with rose honey. Likewise, it is effective against rot in the mouth and inflammations of the throat. It promotes menstruation in women. Anyone who has an ulcerated neck or putrefied gums should gargle with that salt dissolved in water with rose honey mixed in. Use the same water to wash pustules. This same water, mixed with "essentialized" antimony <note>a purified or alchemically processed form of the mineral antimony</note> and drunk, is effective against the Spanish sickness <note>another contemporary name for syphilis</note>.

### ON THE SALT OF PURPLE LOOSESTRIFE.

The salt of purple loosestrife <note>original: "salicariæ purpureæ"</note>, frequently drunk with wine on an empty stomach, is effective against fevers and "phrensy" <note>original: "phrenesin"; a state of delirium or brain fever</note>. Likewise, it is effective against insanity and the contraction of limbs when used as a fomentation with water. Mixed with vinegar, it counters pestilential fevers. Furthermore, it cures jaundice when taken with betony water, and also treats fistulas.

### ON THE SALT OF FUMITORY.

Let the salt of fumitory <note>original: "fumariæ"</note> be dissolved in water to make a gargle; it is effective against the rot of the mouth, and the same should be used to wash French ulcers <note>syphilitic sores</note>.

### ON THE SALT OF HEMP-NETTLE OR WOOD BALM.

The salt of hemp-nettle <note>original: "galyopsis"</note> or wood balm <note>original: "melissæ sylvestris"</note>, taken in the morning with its own distilled water, is effective against asthma and pain of the heart. Likewise, in wine, it heals fistulas of the breasts. It also promotes menstruation in women, encourages childbirth, and heals tremors of the limbs.

### ON THE SALT OF AGRIMONY.

<margin>Agrimony.</margin>
The salt of Agrimony <note>original: "Eupatorij"</note> is used with rose honey against inflammation of the neck; likewise, it is drunk against pleurisy, other internal abscesses, internal heat, and burning fevers. It is also used against *alcola* <note>white sores or ulcers in the mouth</note> with rose honey. Furthermore, it is effective against intestinal worms, the plague, scabies, dandruff, and the "lousy disease" <note>original: "phthiriasin"; an infestation of lice</note>. By applying or washing with this salt in warm water, it heals the bites of a rabid dog. Likewise, it is beneficial for blisters or ulcerated sites caused by the French sickness. It also assists burnt limbs.

### ON THE SALT OF GREATER CENTAURY.

The salt of greater centaury <note>original: "centaurij majoris"</note> helps those suffering from dropsy <note>edema or swelling caused by excess fluid</note> and pestilential diseases. It is also used against poison, melancholic blood, "the falling sickness" <note>epilepsy</note>, dullness of vision and the eyes, the Hungarian disease <note>original: "morbum Hungaricum"; typically identified as typhus</note>, hot fever, and jaundice.

### ON THE SALT OF PELLITORY-OF-THE-WALL.

The salt of pellitory-of-the-wall <note>original: "parietariæ"</note>, when reduced into a liquid and applied, heals "holy fires" <note>original: "sacros ignes"; likely erysipelas, a painful bacterial skin infection</note>, inflamed growths <note>original: "condylomata"</note>, tumors, and swellings. It is used against stones <note>kidney or bladder stones</note> when taken with the liquid of "crabs' eyes" <term>Crabs' eyes: Small, stony concretions found in the stomachs of crayfish, used in early medicine as an antacid and absorbent.</term> and mugwort water; against colic, much like the salt of Roman chamomile; against all obstructions of the liver and spleen; against rot <note>decay or sepsis</note>, like the salts of wormwood and chicory; and against gas of the stomach and intestines when taken with suitable preserves and medicinal waters.

### ON THE SALT OF CINQUEFOIL.

The salt of cinquefoil <note>original: "pentaphylli"; literally "five-leaf"</note> is effective against diseases of the liver and lungs, as well as poisons, and it heals fistulas when sprinkled upon them.

### ON THE SALT OF BIRTHWORT.

The salt of birthwort <note>original: "Aristolochiæ"</note> resists poisons, hiccups, and even shudders, convulsions, and pains in the side. Likewise, it is suitable for the spleen and for those suffering from asthma; when used as a gargle, it cleanses the gums and teeth.

### ON THE SALT OF VALERIAN.

The salt of valerian promotes menstruation, moves the urine, and benefits pain in the side.

### ON THE SALT OF TORMENTIL.

The salt of tormentil suppresses urinary incontinence and stops excessive menstruation.

### ON THE SALT OF PLANTAIN.

The salt of plantain is given in a drink for ulcers of the kidneys and bladder. It also assists in cases of tertian fever <note>a fever that recurs every third day, historically associated with malaria</note>.

### ON THE SALT OF LESSER PLANTAIN.

The salt of lesser plantain is used for pestilential fevers and pains of the heart; it is also applied to ulcers of the bladder and kidneys when mixed with good wine. Likewise, it works against melancholic delusions, pain and swelling of the womb, and against frenzy and "the falling sickness." It heals internal wounds and abscesses resulting from the "French Sickness" <note>original: "morbo Gallico"; syphilis</note>, as well as old ulcers. It is effective against headaches caused by the "Hungarian disease" <note>typhus</note> when used frequently. Likewise, when mixed with rose honey, it is effective for cleansing or gargling against rot of the mouth and throat, or "alcola" <note>a historical term for mouth ulcers or thrush</note>. Also, when mixed with vinegar, it "extinguishes" burns.

### ON THE SALT OF GREATER PLANTAIN.

The salt of greater plantain cleanses "burnt blood" <note>original: "sanguinem adustum"; a concept in humoral theory where blood becomes overheated, leading to various illnesses</note> and benefits those of a choleric temperament. It also heals "alcola" <note>mouth sores</note>, ulcers of the throat, or abscesses...

### ON THE SALT OF SMARTWEED.

### ON THE SALT OF SMARTWEED.

The salt of smartweed <note>original: "persicariæ"; also known as water-pepper</note> is given to those with fevers, and it corrects defects of the lungs, liver, and spleen when taken with suitable medicinal waters. Likewise, it removes the plague, swellings of the neck <note>original: "alcolam"</note>, tumors, foul breath, cough, bladder stones, and heat in the head. Also, when boiled with honey in the manner of a plaster, it heals growths on the limbs, bruises, impacts, and pleurisy. Dissolved in plain water and applied with a damp cloth, it treats swollen genitals and buboes <note>swollen lymph nodes</note> through washing. If the body is washed with this same water, it wards off mange <note>original: "serpigines"</note> and the pustules of the "French disease" <note>syphilis</note>. It is also very useful for horses and livestock for tumors, fractures, and dislocations of the legs, especially by applying it warm and continuously bathing the area until restored. If the head is washed with this water, it prevents hair loss, stops catarrh <note>excessive mucus</note>, and keeps away skin eruptions <note>original: "impetiginem"</note>. Licorice juice dissolved in this water, or a decoction of the root mixed with honey of roses and drunk, removes swelling of the neck and distress of the chest and heart; it is also beneficial for asthma. It is effective against stones and dysentery when taken with "dianisum" <note>a medicinal preparation made of anise</note> and other ingredients.

### ON THE SALT OF DWARF ELDER.

Salt of elder <note>original: "sambuci"; the common elderberry tree</note> heals dropsy.

### ON THE SALT OF THE ASH TREE.

Salt of ash <note>original: "fraxini"</note> drunk with its own distilled water heals those with spleen disease <note>original: "lienosis"</note> and resists poisons: it also helps against the plague, provided it is administered in the water of blessed thistle <note>original: "cardui benedicti"</note>: the dosage is 1 to 2 scruples <note>approximately 1.3 to 2.6 grams</note>.

### ON THE SALT OF THE GRAPEVINE.

Salt of the grapevine <note>original: "vitis viniferæ"</note> is effective during times of plague; it is a certain diaphoretic <note>a substance that induces sweating</note>: its lye <note>original: "lixivium"; a solution of the salt in water</note> drunk by itself provokes sweat.

When washed, it is mixed into eye medicines and wipes away dimness of vision.

...scholars call these Mercury, Sulfur, and Salt <note>The "Tria Prima" or three primary substances of Paracelsian alchemy: spirit, soul, and body</note>: some are cured much more safely by this preparation from the venereal plague <note>syphilis</note>. Andernach <note>Johann Winter von Andernach (1505–1574), a prominent physician and translator of Galen</note> and other doctors have drawn from the books of Theophrastus Paracelsus, where he writes about the correction of guaiacum wood <note>a resinous wood from the Americas, often called "Holy Wood," used as a standard treatment for syphilis in the 16th century</note> and its preparation; he teaches how to make a gum liquor and an alkali from this wood, with which that venereal plague is cured better than with its decoction or broth, as is the custom among many. In the same way, boxwood <note>original: "buxus"</note> is also to be prepared to cure the venereal plague, nor is any symptom or other danger to be feared from its decoction and method. Thus also pine can be prepared for that "Spanish disease" <note>another contemporary name for syphilis</note>. Likewise, ash and mistletoe; its alkali is used for the evacuation of hepatic flux <note>a discharge or "flow" associated with the liver</note>, and for the "French disease" <note>yet another term for syphilis</note> with its pustules. In expelling these, no regimen of starvation is observed—as is often the case—but patients should be nourished with good food and salt; the guaiacum liquor is their drink, and guaiacum gum serves as a certain ointment for the pustules.

### PREPARATION OF ROCK SALT AGAINST *dropsy and jaundice.*

Take of rock salt <note>original: "salis gemmæ"</note>, juice of Titymalus <note>spurge</note>, that is, the lesser spurge, 1 dram each; cherry gum to the weight of all the ingredients; let a bolus be made and reverberate <note>heat in a furnace</note> in the third degree for two hours, and extract the alkali: the dosage is from 8 to 12 grains. In place of scammony <note>original: "diagridii"; a harsh plant-based purgative</note>, you may take troches of colocynth <note>original: "trociscos alhandali"; a potent medicinal lozenge used as a laxative</note>. **Addition.** Of this rock salt take 5 scruples; of Rebolus <note>an alchemical term, likely referring to a specific Paracelsian preparation</note>, that is, the liquor of true mummy <note>original: "mumiæ liquoris"; a substance made from bitumen or preserved remains, highly valued in early modern medicine</note>, and centaury, 4 scruples each; let them be mixed; the dosage is from 4 to 12 grains taken in an egg; prepare it in the same way for the same diseases. Of this rock salt take 1 ounce; juice of spurge <note>original: "cataputiæ"</note> 2 ounces; wheat flour to the weight of all; let a well-baked bread be made from it, of which 1 to 2 drams should be given.

### ON THE SALT FROM THE ANKLE-BONES OF OXEN OR *pigs.*

This salt, when drunk, helps those with celiac disease <note>original: "cœliacos"; in this context, it refers to general abdominal distress or intestinal disorders</note>; mixed with honey, it kills intestinal worms. Likewise, with oxymel <note>a medicinal drink made of honey and vinegar</note>, it is effective against disease of the spleen.

### ON THE SALT OF HARTSHORN.

Salt of hartshorn <note>original: "cornu cervi"; deer antler, a common source of ammonia and calcium</note> is beneficial for those with celiac disease and dysentery.

Salt of deer blood cures joint disease, gout of the feet <note>original: "podagram"</note>, gout of the hands <note>original: "chiragram"</note>, and gout of the knees <note>original: "gonagram"</note>.

### ON GOAT SALT AND ITS BLOOD.

<margin>What Galen thinks about salt.</margin>
Salt derived from the blood of a goat heals diseases of the joints, including gout in the hands <term>chiragra</term>, gout in the knees <term>gonagra</term>, and gout in the feet <term>podagra</term>. Let what has been said so far regarding salts prepared from herbs, wood, stones, and animals suffice, for their use is very ancient. Indeed, before the year 1500 <note>The author likely means 1,500 years ago, referring to the era of Classical Antiquity</note>, purgative salts were in use among the Greeks. Aetius <note>Aetius of Amida, a 6th-century royal physician in the Byzantine court</note> makes mention of salt of anise. Galen, in Book 2 of *On the Properties of Simple Medicines*, speaking about salt, reports the following: "Burnt salt," he says, "digests more powerfully than salt that has not been burnt, specifically because the body of the salt is rendered finer by the quality it receives from the fire." In the same book, he writes that substances made of fine parts have more efficacy, even if they possess little inherent power, because they penetrate better—especially for dissolving waste and "tartaric" humors <note>In the medical theories of Paracelsus, "tartar" referred to stony deposits in the body, such as kidney stones or the uric acid crystals of gout</note>. For through calcination <note>burning a substance to ash</note>, the salt of things is extracted. However, salt can only be dissolved by salt alone, if you understand this well; thus you may know that opposites are not cured by opposites, but rather "likes are cured by likes" <note>original: *similia similibus curari*</note>. And although salt can even be made from the urine of boys, from animals, and even from old shoes, and can be used without danger for both external and internal medicine, I wish to omit their use because of how loathsome they are. Finally, note this: the more salts are dissolved, filtered, and purified, the more they lose their stench and the more strength they acquire.

### CONCLUSION OF THE WHOLE WORK

*SALTS* are manifold. Some are mineral and fixed <note>In alchemy, "fixed" means a substance that remains stable and does not evaporate when heated</note>, some are vegetable and fixed, and some are animal and fixed; however, fixed forms are found among all these species of salts, both vegetable and mineral (as will be shown below). Fixed minerals include "bread salt" <note>common table salt or sodium chloride</note>, which is extracted from the sea or from well water. Then there is Rock Salt <note>original: *sal Gemmæ*</note>, which is clearer than all others and transparent like crystal; it is better than those mentioned above. There are two species of it: one is crystalline, the other is a transparent red. It is born in mines and sulfurous places, found as a substance within both large and small stones; it is found especially in Spain in a place called Cardona <note>a famous salt mountain in Catalonia</note>, and also in Hungary. Vegetable salts are also either fixed or non-fixed; these are made from the ashes of trees and herbs. When boiled in the strongest lye <note>original: *capitellis*</note> and the water is evaporated, the salt remains at the bottom of the vessel. According to the nature of the ash, it remains as either a fixed or a non-fixed salt; experience will teach you the difference. I tell you one thing: alkali salt <note>usually potassium carbonate derived from wood ash</note> is worthier than all other salts, especially the vegetable ones. It is a "fixed oil" that the dryness of fire has congealed. There are some who make alkali salt from soda and say it is fixed and that it fixes other substances. Therefore, set your heart upon alkali salt, for it is a most excellent secret. Since everything fixed is turned into a fixed na—

## TO FAITHFUL AND PIOUS PHYSICIANS.

I recall (most learned men) having poured over many books by erudite physicians, in which—to my frequent surprise—I found no mention of the supreme Artisan of all things <note>A common early modern reference to God as a craftsman or architect</note>, much less any invocation of divine help before they administered medicines to their patients. Yet it is more certain than certainty itself that the piety of a Physician sometimes achieves more than the admirable knowledge of many others. For this reason, since bodily infirmity sometimes arises from sin, it was the duty of Physicians, when called to the sick, to warn and persuade them above all else to call upon "physicians of souls" <note>Referring to clergy or confessors</note>. In this way, after the patient's spiritual health had been provided for, they might proceed more effectively to the bodily remedy of medicine. At least three most excellent Physicians, as far as I know, entered upon this laudable path and practiced their art with the highest praise: I speak of Arnaldus <note>Arnaldus de Villanova (c. 1240–1311), a famous Catalan physician and alchemist</note>, Gordonius <note>Bernard de Gordon (c. 1270–1330), a notable professor of medicine at the University of Montpellier</note>, and Raymond Lully <note>Ramon Llull (c. 1232–1315), a philosopher and mystic to whom many later alchemical works were attributed</note> in the operative art. These men, by visiting their patients more frequently, exhorted them to repentance; and having first implored the help of the divine power, they experienced God’s greatest blessing in their healing.

The following formula of prayer was familiar to Raymond, which I have chosen to record here, and which ought to remind all true Physicians of their duty.

### THE PRAYER OF RAYMOND LULLY BEFORE the administration of medicines.

> *Lord Jesus Christ, who are the true salvation of all, O Lord, you are the one who created all things "very good" in your goodness and wisdom; without you I know nothing of good in this world. Therefore, Lord Jesus Christ, I humbly adore your majesty, because I know and firmly believe that there is nothing good without your goodness, nothing great without your greatness, nor anything enduring without your duration, nor powerful without your power, nor wise without your wisdom, nor loving without your love, nor virtuous without your virtue <term>virtus</term> <note>In this context, "virtus" refers both to moral virtue and the "potency" or "active power" of a medicine</note>, nor true without your truth, nor glorious without your glory, nor just without your justice. I know also that you wonderfully created man, and even more wonderfully restored him; you who gave medicine for the repair of the health of human bodies: give a blessing to this medicine, so that all the powers you placed within it at the beginning may be brought to their intended purpose. May it merit to bring about health of mind and body in the person whom it enters, through Lord Jesus Christ your son, Amen.*

# THE BOOK OF THE MOST NOBLE LORD
## BERNARD, COUNT OF THE TREVISAN MARCH.

->*On the most secret chemical work of the Philosophers, to be elaborated by nature and art.*<-

---

<image-desc>A decorative woodcut initial 'Q' featuring two figures intertwined with floral and vine motifs.</image-desc>In order to draw back true seekers of this art from common errors into the true path—lest they squander their resources and suffer the loss of their labor, name, and reputation by insisting on the false recipes of books such as those of Geber <note>Jabir ibn Hayyan (c. 721–813), the most famous figure in early alchemy, though many "Geber" texts were later Latin pseudepigrapha</note>, Rasis <note>Al-Razi (865–925), a Persian physician and alchemist</note>, Albertus Magnus <note>The famous 13th-century Dominican scholar to whom many alchemical works were falsely attributed</note>, *The Path*, *The Light*, *The Canon of Pandects*, Demophontus, *The Summa*, and other seductive men—I will first recount my own errors, and then how I reached the desired end, and how four times I fabricated and completed the stone <note>The Philosopher's Stone, the legendary substance capable of transmuting base metals into gold and curing all diseases</note> with these very hands. So that finally, those who read my process may be able to achieve the same result through contemplation and the imitation of nature. 

It would be foolish to judge with the common crowd that this art is false because of the Sophists <note>In this context, fraudulent or deceptive practitioners</note> and imposters we see daily engaged in it, or to believe that its true authors and sages wished to deceive others with their writings because they themselves were deluded; rather, they wished to leave behind a reputation after death, not infamy or disgrace. But the ignorant commoner has this foolish trait: as soon as they read something they do not understand, they condemn it. Therefore, whoever follows the principles of nature through steadfast mental images will profit far more than from the vain and dead letter found under countless figures of riddles and the words of sophists. 

In order to collect for you the opinions of honest men who treat the subject sincerely and purely, I wished to write this little book and divide it into four parts. The first will describe the inventors of the art, and especially those who attained it according to their desire, and through whom I obtained it. In the second, telling my own history, I will speak at length about whatever happened to me in my search over time, and the burdens of my labors, without any envy <note>original: "citra ullam invidiam." In alchemical literature, "writing without envy" meant the author promised to reveal the truth plainly rather than hiding it behind metaphors</note> from beginning to end. The third will discuss the roots and principles of metals with the most evident and philosophical demonstrations. The fourth will contain the practice itself, under a parable <note>An allegory or symbolic story</note> that is not so obscure that it cannot be perfectly understood. 

Indeed, each part is written in such a way that, unless you, the reader, understand through this my book, I do not easily believe you will ever perceive it through any other. Nor should you think you can understand it at first glance; hardly even by the tenth reading. The more often you repeat it, the better you will be able to uncover the matter day by day. No one should grow weary of the labor or regret it, if they believe that by these means intolerable poverty and all diseases can be avoided.

...all diseases of the mind and body, as I myself have experienced in many lepers, those with the falling sickness <note>epilepsy</note>, the dropsical, the hectic <note>those suffering from wasting diseases or consumption</note>, the apoplectic, those with intestinal colic, the demon-possessed, the senseless, the raging, and many others. To learn any mechanical or liberal art, one must spend at least six or seven years; but in this art—which excels all others as much as the Sun excels all stars—one need not endure more than a month, or even five or six days if one is willing. It is quite easy; so much so, that if I were to describe it in clear words or demonstrate it to your eyes, you could hardly believe it. The entire difficulty consists in our language and our intention.

### *THE FIRST PART OF THE CHEMISTRY OF LORD BERNARD, Count of the Trevisan March: Concerning the first inventors of this art.*

The first restorer of the Chemical Art, after it had been forgotten following the Deluge <note>the Great Flood</note>, was HERMES TRISMEGISTUS, as is read in the historical books recording ancient deeds, in the *Imperial Gests*, and in the commentary on the *Emerald Tablet* <note>original: "Tabulæ smaragdina"; a foundational Hermetic text said to contain the secrets of the "prima materia"</note> by Clavetus. He was called HERMES or MERCURY because he was the wisest of all in his time; and "Trismegistus" means "Thrice-Great" or "Thrice-Wise," because he mastered and taught all worldly wisdom, or the triple natural philosophy: the vegetable, the mineral, and the animal—which are one stone. He is called the "Father" in this art due to its restoration, as is held in all the books of the *Hermetic Assembly* <note>original: "Hermeticæ Turbæ," likely referring to the *Turba Philosophorum*, one of the oldest Latin alchemical texts</note>, in which he is mentioned even before Pythagoras. Moreover, as many as hold to this art shall be called the "Sons of Hermes." We read of this man in the Bible that he was the first to enter the Valley of Hebron, and there he found seven stone tablets. Upon these, the Sages had inscribed the seven liberal arts before the flood of waters occurred—each containing only its basic principles—so that they might not fall into oblivion. For at that time, although they were instructed enough to foresee that the world would not perish entirely but would be preserved, they nevertheless did not have such perfect wisdom as to consider that God, who had given it to them at that time, could have given it to others and to another as often as He willed.

He is said to have lived before the Law <note>The Mosaic Law/Ten Commandments</note> and after, during a time when many wise men lived. Aros relates in a certain letter to King Meffohe that this art was revealed by God to several of the children of Israel for the purpose of decorating the Ark of the Lord with gold and completing it, as is found in the prophets Ezekiel and Daniel, and likewise in Josephus <note>Flavius Josephus, the 1st-century Jewish-Roman historian</note>. Some reached it without manifest revelation or books, but through secret meditation on the visible works of God in His creatures—such as Phithomea, Rebecca, Solomon, and Philip of Macedon—all of whom, however, Hermes preceded after the Deluge in the in-

...discovery, through the tables said to have been found by him in the valley of Hebron, the place where Adam had been placed after his exile from the Paradise of Eden. From Hermes, it passed down to many others through a little book which he titled the *Emerald Tablet* <note>original: "Smaragdinam tabulam"; the foundational text of Hermeticism</note>, in these words: *It is true, certain, and most true: That which is above has the nature of that which is below, and that which ascends has the nature of that which descends. Join them by a single way and arrangement. The Sun is the father of this marriage, and the white Moon is the mother; the third, fire, follows as the ruler. Make the coarse subtle, and return this to the dense; in this manner, you shall have the glory of this world.* In this brief book, the entire work is contained. Many followed this art, as we read of King Calid <note>Khalid ibn Yazid, an early Umayyad prince and reputed alchemist</note> of the middle Bendagid Ternary; Aristotle the Chemist, Plato, and Pythagoras (a disciple of Hermes), the author of the *Codex*, in which book the truth of this matter is contained without excess or deficiency, though obscurely enough. In Arabia, King Haly, the greatest astrologer, is said to have had knowledge of it; he taught Morienus, and he in turn taught another King of Arabia called Calid, mentioned before. Likewise, Aros taught it to his brother Nephandin, and Saturnus to Luncabur and his sister Medera. The number of them is infinite, and it is vain to recount them; there is a huge abundance of books written on this art under metaphorical words and figures, so that they cannot easily be understood by any except the sons of the art <note>original: "filiis artis"; those initiated into the secrets of alchemy</note>, whose reading leads one into various errors away from the right path rather than directing one toward the goal. Among their number are Scotus, Arnaldus, Raymond, Jean de Meung <note>French author of the *Roman de la Rose*</note>, Hortulanus, Veridicus, etc. Therefore, so that I might be able to lead students back to the right path, I wished to write this little work for them.

### THE SECOND PART, IN WHICH ARE DESCRIBED
*the immense labors of the author, and his greatest expenses, with the individual operations from the beginning until the end, resulting from the truth of most persistent success.*

When I first undertook this work, there fell into my hands the book of Rhazes <note>Al-Razi, a famous Persian physician and alchemist</note>, in the testing of which I lost four years and eight hundred crowns. Likewise, in the books of Geber <note>Jabir ibn Hayyan</note>, I made a loss of more than two thousand crowns at the start, with many impostors urging and inducing me to do so, in order to exhaust my substance. Afterward, I studied the books of Archelaus for three years, in which I worked together with a certain monk, and in the books of Rupescissa <note>John of Rupescissa, known for his work on "quintessence"</note> and John of Sacrobosco, through "waters of life" <note>original: "aquas vitae"; high-proof distilled alcohol</note> rectified thirty times with the dregs, until it reached such a sharp acidity that it could be contained by no glass; in that labor, another three hundred crowns were lost. Having consumed twelve or fifteen years in this manner, and countless gold pieces, without fruit, after many experiments with recipes in dissolving and congealing, with common ammoniac—

...boiled <note>original: "interco[ctis]"; referring to salts processed through heat and liquid</note>, pine, Saracen, and metallic salts, then calcined more than a hundred times over a space of two years; likewise in rock-alums of ice, scagliola <note>crystalline gypsum or plaster</note>, and feather-alum; in marcasites <note>pyrite minerals</note>, blood, hair, urine, human dung, semen, animals and vegetable herbs, copperas <note>metallic sulfates</note>, vitriols, black-inks, and eggs; by the separation of elements in an athanor <note>a self-feeding furnace designed for constant heat</note>, by alembic and pelican <note>specialized glass vessels for distillation and circulation</note>, by circulation, cooking, reverberation <note>heating by reflecting flames downward onto a substance</note>, ascension, descension, fusion, ignition, reduction to elements, rectification, evaporation, conjunction, elevation, and refinement; by mixing and infinite other regimes of sophistry in which I had already been engaged for twelve years. Having reached the age of thirty-eight, still persisting in the extraction of Mercuries from herbs and animals, I had up to that point uselessly squandered—partly through my own foolishness, partly through the deceptions of impostors—about six thousand crowns <note>a massive fortune, illustrating both the author's wealth and his desperation</note>, so that I had almost lost heart.

But in truth, throughout this time, I did not forget to pour out my prayers to God, that He might deign to assist my endeavors. Next, I happened upon a certain Prefect of our country, who was likewise investigating; he attempted to construct the Stone from common salt <note>original: "sale communi"</note>, dissolving it in the air and congealing it in the Sun, and many other things most lengthy to relate. In this work, a year and a half <note>original: "sesquiannus"</note> passed with others in vain labor, because we were not working upon the true matter. "It is sought in vain in that which does not contain what is sought," as it is read in the truthful *Codex of the Assembly* <note>original: "Codice Turbæ"; the *Turba Philosophorum*, an influential alchemical text composed of dialogues between ancient philosophers</note>. Since, therefore, common salt by no means possesses what we desire—even after being taken through fifteen repetitions—it never showed us any alteration of its natural property; for which reason we left it, attempting it no further.

Furthermore, we saw others dissolving the finest silver, copper, and other metals in very strong water <note>original: "aqua fortissima"; nitric acid</note>; likewise quicksilver, each separately in a particular vessel with the same water, and finally pouring all such solutions together into a single vessel after they had rested for twelve full months. They claimed that this mixture was the "marriage of spirit and body." They kept such a vessel over hot ashes until a third part of the water had evaporated; the remainder they exposed to the rays of the Sun, believing that crystalline stones would be produced from it—white ones, congealed and meltable, for the White Work from the white metal, and red ones from the red metal for the Red Tincture <note>The "White" and "Red" works are the two main goals of alchemy: the creation of silver and gold, respectively</note>. Of twenty-two vials half-filled with such liquid, they gave three to us. We all waited for the outcome of the generation of such small stones at the bottoms of the vessels for five years, but in vain; for indeed, as is said in the *Assembly*, nothing foreign is needed for this stone: for it is perfected by itself in its own metallic matter. At that time, I had completed the forty-sixth year of my age, when I, together with a doctor and monk named Geoffrey Le Lièvre <note>original: "Gotofredo Lepore"</note>, the stone from his...

->**A BOOK ON ALCHEMY.**<-

I approached the work with premeditated intent: for we knew that any other work besides the Stone <note>The "Philosophers' Stone," the legendary substance capable of turning base metals into gold and granting long life</note> was vain and useless. For this reason, we endeavored to fabricate it in the following manner: We bought chicken eggs to the number of two thousand; these we boiled in water until hard and then separated them, calcining <term>calcining: heating a substance to high temperatures to reduce it to a powder</term> the shells until they reached a state of extreme whiteness. As for the yolks and the whites, we allowed each to putrefy separately in horse dung <note>original: "equino fimo"; horse dung was a standard alchemical tool used to provide a gentle, consistent heat for fermentation or "putrefaction"</note>, and afterward, we distilled them thirty times to produce a "white water" and a "red oil" separately. We performed many other operations which I will omit for the sake of brevity. In this vain work, two and a half years of our lives similarly slipped away without any benefit—indeed, at the greatest expense. This resulted in us almost abandoning everything in utter despair, had we not been supported by a new hope. We began again to learn the sublimations of spirits, the distillations of <term>aquas fortes: "strong waters," usually referring to nitric acid or other corrosive mineral acids</term>, the separations of elements, and the various structures of furnaces and fires, in which we were occupied for eight years.

Then there arrived another man, a theologian and a scholar, the Prothonotary <note>A high-ranking official in the ecclesiastical court</note> of Bergen. With him, we also wished to construct the Stone. By his instinct alone, we believed the matter could be accomplished using only vitriol <note>metallic sulfates, often green or blue in color</note>. First, we distilled the sharpest vinegar eight times, in which we dissolved the aforementioned calcined vitriol and then drew it off. Again, we poured it back and drew it off fifteen times every day for a space of two months. On account of the most violent stench of this process, I suffered from a quartan fever <note>a recurring fever, often associated with malaria but here likely caused by inhaling toxic chemical fumes</note> for fourteen months. We allowed this mixture to rest for an entire year, but with no fruit; for it was a foreign matter.

It was later reported to us by a certain learned man that the Emperor's Confessor, whose name was Master Henry, most certainly possessed and held the mastery of the Stone. Therefore, so that we might gain his acquaintance, there was need for the greatest mediation of friends and an expense of more than two hundred crowns <note>a significant sum of gold coins</note> before we could make ourselves familiar to him. He, however, operated in this manner: He mixed a paste made of silver and Mercury with sulfur and olive oil, cooking them together over a slow fire in a "pelican" <note>a specialized glass vessel with two "arms" that allow distilled vapors to circulate back into the main body</note> fortified with heavy clay, incorporating them with a wooden spatula. But the matter could never be mixed into a single body, even in the space of two months. 

At last, we placed this matter into another vial, similarly fortified with clay and sealed; we kept it entirely buried in hot ashes and warmed it with fire all around, believing that in the space of fifteen or twenty-one days, the Mercury—by the power of the sulfurous body—would be converted into the finest silver. When the decoction was finished, he placed lead into the vial at his discretion and melted everything together into one mass with a most violent fire. Once this was "refined" <note>original: "fulminata"; referring to the process of cupellation where base metals are oxidized away to leave pure precious metal</note> through a cupel made of ash <note>original: "capellam cineritij"</note>, we were supposed to find the silver multiplied by a third part. For my share, I had given ten marks <note>a mark was a unit of weight for precious metals, roughly 8 ounces</note> of silver, while others had given thirty-two, from which we expected to receive one hundred and thirty <note>the text ends mid-word: "tri-ginta"</note>...

### BERNARD OF TREVISO

...thirty <note>The text begins mid-word with "-ginta," completing "triginta" (thirty).</note> marks. But it turned out otherwise, since out of thirty-two marks, only twelve were obtained from the companion’s assay; I, however, received fourteen marks from my ten. Because of this, believing I possessed the secret of the stone <note>The "Philosophers' Stone," the goal of the Great Work</note> from a Father Confessor <note>original: "patre Confessore"</note>, I was made poorer by another four hundred crowns <note>original: "coronatis"</note>. Gripped by grief, I abstained from the work for two months, utterly loathing it, especially because all my relatives never ceased to rebuke and torment me daily. I could scarcely eat or drink for sorrow, and was reduced to such a state of emaciation <note>original: "maciem"</note> that everyone thought I had been infected by some contagious poison.

Nevertheless, shortly thereafter, the fire within was suddenly rekindled a thousand times more than before, chiefly because I was weary of the time that had slipped away in vain: for I was then in my fifty-eighth year. The cause of all my errors (alas!) was this: that wandering astray, I was not working with the suitable material <note>original: "materia congrua"</note>. For as **Geber** <note>The Latinized name of Jabir ibn Hayyan, a foundational figure in alchemy</note> himself says: *Any imperfect bodies mixed with bodies that are simply perfect by nature are in no way perfected, because they have already attained from nature a simple form for themselves alone, in the first degree of perfection, and they are "dead." They can bestow none of their own perfection—which is not superfluous—upon others.* This is for two reasons: first, because by the admixture of imperfection they are rendered imperfect, since they have no more perfection than they need for themselves; and second, because their principles cannot be mixed in this way by their smallest parts <term>per minima: a medieval physical concept referring to mixing at the level of the smallest possible particles, similar to atoms</term>.

This is held in the thirteenth book of the *Digests* in the *Pandects* <note>original: "Pandectis," likely referring to a compendium of knowledge or legal texts</note>, and likewise in the first book of **Geber**, and in the *Natural Work* by Master **Raymond** <note>Raymond Lull, a major figure in medieval logic and alchemy</note> and **Arnaldus de Villanova**; in the *Mirror of Alchemy*, in the *Opinions of the Errant* written by **Plato**, in the *Letter of Euvaralus*, in the *Great Rosary*, and in **Euclid’s** brief treatise and other non-sophists <note>In this context, "sophists" refers to fraudulent alchemists or those who use misleading logic</note> in this manner: Common bodies, being absolute in color through nature alone, are dead, so that they cannot perfect the imperfect—unless they are brought by art to a sevenfold, tenfold, or twelvefold multiplication of their perfection; only then do they tinge <term>tinge: to transform or "dye" a base metal into gold or silver</term> unto infinity.

For then at last they are made penetrating, entering, and a tincture more than perfect and "living" with respect to the common ones. Thus, according to **Rhazes**, **Aristotle** the chemist, **Alphidius** in his *Pandects*, and **Daniel** in the fifth chapter of his *Retractations*: *Our completed gold* (they say) *is more than gold.* Likewise, our gold and our white silver are not one and the same as common metals; for in the latter, they are truly dead and devoid of power, as is read in the golden book of the *Codex* and many others. We have certainly seen countless men working in sublimations and multiplications for the white and the red <note>The "White Work" and "Red Work" refer to the two stages of creating silver and gold, respectively</note>, using every kind of material that can be imagined, with the greatest labor and such constant perseverance that it could not be greater.

For which reason, by running here and there, investigating, and experimenting, I had already consumed thirteen thousand and three hundred gold crowns <note>original: *coronatos aureos*</note>; for I had sold a certain property which was worth eight thousand florins <note>original: *florenorum*</note> of German money, so that I fell into the greatest contempt of all my relatives, because I was reduced to such poverty that only a little money remained to me, being then sixty-two years of age and more. Nevertheless, though quite broken in body by such great adversities, I was not so broken in spirit that I would desist from what I had conceived; rather, trusting in the mercy of God, who never fails men of goodwill and diligence, and leaving my fatherland not without the greatest disgrace, I betook myself to *Rhodes*. I was known to no man there, so that I might seek if I could somehow find anyone who might console the afflictions of my desires.

One day I heard of a certain highly religious man of great name; the rumor was that he possessed the Stone so greatly sought after. At very great expense, I entered into a friendship with him. I borrowed eight thousand florins from someone who knew my parents very well. # BERNARD OF TREVISO

...be able to mix, or to bring it about that it should always float upon the earth <note>This likely refers to a substance failing to "fix" or sink into the base metal, remaining separate</note>, even though we kept it in continuous heat for a space of seven months. There was no conjunction nor alteration, even with the fire increased, which resulted in us abandoning that frivolous work; because of it, I once again suffered a loss of three years of time and five hundred crowns. 

This religious man possessed most excellent chemical books, such as the <term>Rosarius magnus</term> <note>The "Great Rosary," an influential alchemical treatise often attributed to Arnald of Villanova</note>, <term>Arnaldus de Villanova</term> <note>A famous 13th-century physician and alchemist</note>, and the <term>Book of the Words of Mary the Prophetess</term> <note>Maria the Prophetess was a legendary figure in alchemy, credited with inventing laboratory apparatus like the bain-marie</note>, in which I began to study anew, abstaining from the work <note>The "work" refers to practical laboratory experimentation</note> for a space of eight years. Then for the first time, I recognized by philosophical and evident reasons that whatever I had worked on before was nothing but foolish and vain labors—especially when I considered this saying from the <term>Codex of All Truth</term>: 

> Nature, it says, is not improved except in its own nature; nature rejoices in its own nature, nature overcomes nature, and nature retains nature. <note>original: "Natura non emendatur nisi in sua propria natura, natura sua natura gaudet, natura naturam vincit, & natura naturam retinet." This is a foundational axiom of "natural" alchemy, suggesting that gold can only be made from things that share its nature.</note>

Having finally been taught by this book, I escaped free from all my sophistries <note>Deceptive or "fake" alchemical methods</note> and erroneous labors. I wished to study first, rather than to work again at great expense and without fruit. I spent many nights sleepless, constantly arguing with myself and concluding with this sentiment: "Why is it necessary," I said, "that I seek this art from men, tormenting myself in vain in this way? If they know the art, they will never reveal it; if they do not, I occupy myself with them in vain, and at great expense I try to capture their familiarity and friendship." 

I considered instead in which places the books most agreed in the same sense; I judged that the truth lay hidden there most of all, for truth cannot exist in many ways, but in only one. By this path, truth itself met me; for in those things where I saw the authors agree most into one, this very thing was what I had so anxiously sought. Although one author calls it by this name and another by that, nevertheless it is one and the same substance; error is committed only in the diversity of words, and not in their concordances. 

Therefore, my son, I wished to write this little book for your sake, so that you do not lose heart, nor be deceived as I was most miserably led astray for a long time. It is the safest precaution to learn by the example of others' dangers. I truly believe (so may God love me) that those men who write such things figuratively or in parables—mentioning hair, urine, blood, sperm, herbs, vegetables, animals, plants, or mineral stones such as <term>salia</term> <note>salts</note>, <term>alumina</term> <note>alums</note>, <term>cuperossas</term> <note>copperas or vitriol</note>, <term>atramenta</term> <note>metallic inks or black salts</note>, <term>vitriola</term> <note>vitriols</note>, <term>boraces</term> <note>boraxes</note>, <term>magnesias</term> <note>magnesium or manganese ores</note>, and whatever stones and waters they propose in this "water" to the readers—I say that they have spent very little or nothing on it, nor sustained any labor, or they were moved to it by sheer cruelty. For I pity all those who are entangled in this labyrinth, or who might fall into it in the future, as often as the intolerable punishments of miseries and calamities which I suffered come to mind. Whoever, therefore, wishes to give faith to me, should not...

...he might have done to his own great advantage, I can only bring back the labor of it from there by instructing others. But whoever refuses to believe will eventually find through his own loss how great a folly it is to be unmoved by the examples of others and to refuse to learn. Flee the <term>sophistications</term> <note>In this context, "sophistications" refers to fraudulent or adulterated chemical processes used by "sophists" or fake alchemists to mimic gold</note> of wicked alchemists, and any others who place their faith in them. For if your reading of books has taught you anything good, they will attempt to take it away with false oaths and assertions, leading you away from the right path. Having nothing with which to excuse their errors, they say: "I have done it often," or "but now I did not have what was necessary for this matter," or "if this and that were added," etc. Unless you flee these impostors and scoundrels as you would a plague, you will never taste anything good in this art. 

Before I had completed this work by <term>experiment</term> <note>The "Great Work" or the creation of the Philosopher's Stone</note>, I had studied the art exactly from books for two years; nevertheless, when such detestable men and most wicked thieves came to me, they asserted manifest errors as true experiments with oaths—even perjuries—which I, in my former delusions, had nonetheless experienced at the greatest expense. Nor could I be confirmed in my own good opinions until I left them behind entirely, and turned my whole study toward that material, pursuing it most vigilantly. 

Whoever desires to learn the true art should converse with the wise: that is, he should read their books, and not those of impostors, even though they teach it in obscure words. Nowhere will you find such books written in clear and open terms; therefore, the possibilities must be considered from the works of nature by comparing the books to nature, and vice versa. 

All sophistications are to be fled: likewise all <term>sublimations</term>, conjunctions, separations, <term>congelations</term> <note>The process of turning a liquid into a solid, often through cooling or chemical change</note>, preparations, disjunctions, connections, and all other deceptions. Let all those be silent who affirm a <term>tincture</term> <note>The substance—often the Philosopher's Stone—capable of transmuting base metals into gold</note> other than ours, and a <term>sulfur</term> other than our own which is hidden in <term>magnesia</term> <note>In alchemy, "Magnesia" does not refer to the modern chemical, but to the "Mother of Metals" or the raw material of the Stone</note>. Likewise those who seek to extract another quicksilver except from the <term>red servant</term> <note>original: "servo rubeo"—an alchemical metaphor, often interpreted as iron or a specific state of matter</note>, and another water from ours which is <term>permanent</term> <note>original: "aqua permanens"—a solvent that does not wet the hands and is central to the alchemical process</note> and is joined to nothing except its own nature, and moistens nothing else except that which is of the unity of its own nature. For there is no other <term>vinegar</term> than ours, no other regimen, nor other colors; likewise no other sublimation, solution, congelation, or <term>putrefaction</term> <note>The stage of "blackness" or decay (nigredo) believed necessary for spiritual and physical rebirth of the matter</note> than ours.

He cites several high scholastic and ancient authorities to support his claim that the "first matter" of metals is specifically mercury and sulfur, not the raw four elements.</meta>

...in the *Abridgment* of Saint Thomas <note>original: "S. Thomæ Breviloquio," referring to a work attributed to Thomas Aquinas</note>, the *Path* of Albert <note>Albertus Magnus</note>, the *Summary* of Scotus <note>Duns Scotus</note>, the *Letter of Seneca to Aros, King of Arabia*, and Hemus <note>Possibly Hermes Trismegistus</note>, Euclid in the seventieth chapter of the *Retractations*, and **the Philosopher** <note>In the Middle Ages, "The Philosopher" almost always referred to Aristotle</note> in the third book of the *Meteorology*. By all of these, it is affirmed that metals are nothing other than **quicksilver** <term>argentum vivum</term> <note>Literally "living silver"; the common term for mercury</note> congealed by the various stages of cooking <note>original: "decoctionibus"</note>. Notwithstanding all these affirmative reasons, these metals are not our **Stone** as long as they remain in their metallic form; for it is impossible for one and the same matter to possess two forms at once. By what logic could they be the Stone—which possesses a noble and intermediate form between metal and mercury—unless the metallic form is first destroyed and removed?

For this reason, the Philosopher and Democritus, in the third book of *Physics* and the third chapter of the *Meteorology*, say: "Let the Alchemists boast as they will, they shall never transmute the forms of metals, unless they first reduce them into their **primary matter**" <term>materia prima</term>. This same point is held by all books that treat the metallic form. 

However, so that it may be understood what is meant by "reduction into the primary matter," it must first be known that the primary matter is the very thing into which a specific form is immediately and most closely introduced. For example, the primary matter of a human being is the seed of both the man and the woman. Many ignorant people, thinking they understand this reduction, wrongly interpret it as the **four elements** <note>Earth, Air, Fire, and Water</note>. For (as they say) all created things consist of these without doubt. But those elements are the primary matter *of* the primary matter. That is to say: quicksilver and sulfur consist of the four elements, and these two are ultimately the primary matter of metals.

Indeed, the four elements are just as suited to forming a donkey or an ox as they are to metals. Nature must first create quicksilver and sulfur before they can become the primary matter of metals. For example, a human being is not composed of the four elements while they still exist in their simple, elementary nature, but only after they have been transmuted by nature into the nature of the primary matter of a human. In no different way, nature—transmuting the four elements into mercury and sulfur—only then creates the primary matter of metals. Whatever nature works upon that matter beyond that point can result in nothing else but a metallic form. 

But previously, while they were still elements and not yet quicksilver or sulfur, nature could have procreated from those same elements an ox, a plant, a human, or anything else differing from a metal. From the preceding points, it is most clearly evident that the four elements are not the primary matter of metals, but rather **quicksilver and sulfur**. Otherwise, according to the opinion of those others, it would follow that humans, metals, herbs, plants, and brute animals—in short, everything—would exist as only one single thing without any difference, and nothing more absurd than that could ever be said. It would also follow that humans could be generated from metals, since humans, like metals, consist of the elements, and beyond that...

<meta>This page continues Bernard of Treviso’s discourse on "primary matter" (materia prima). Having established that metals must be reduced to their primary state before transmutation, he now argues that this matter is specific to each species. He uses biological analogies—human and animal generation—to prove that "like only produces like," a fundamental principle in his alchemical theory.</meta>

# A BOOK ON ALCHEMY #

...otherwise, anything could be made from anything, and like would not produce its like; there would be no generation, no female, and no difference between things if all were, in actuality, one single substance. To return to the subject of **primary matter** <term>materia prima</term> <note>The fundamental, formless "stuff" from which specific things are made</note>, let us use this example: the seed of a man by itself, and the seed of a woman by itself, are not the primary matter of a fetus. This is because nature, acting upon these seeds when they are thus separated, might produce something else entirely—a monstrous thing, such as a **verminous substance** <note>original: "substantiam verminosam"; a reference to the medieval belief in spontaneous generation, where decaying matter produces worms or insects</note>. 

But from the conjunction of both into one, so that the virtue of one receives and embraces the virtue of the other, nature can then produce nothing else except the form of an infant; for this is the final goal of that matter and no other. Nature, therefore, cannot introduce any other form into matter except the one toward which it is finally inclined and disposed. Thus, the **spermatic union** <note>The combined reproductive material</note> alone is the primary matter of that being, or of those from whom the seeds were shed or separated; it can receive no other form than that of its own **species** <term>speciei</term>, for which it is disposed. 

Regarding this "disposition toward a goal," let this crude example suffice: If someone hurries on a journey to a certain place, many paths may appear branching here and there before he arrives; however, once he has directed his step onto the right path and perseveres in it, he will eventually reach the place where he intended to go. In this same way, individual things have their own proper path and matter through which and from which they are made; not just anything is perfected from any matter, nor in any random way. 

It is certainly manifest that every thing has a similar precursor from which it is naturally produced, so that nothing else can be made from it. For instance, in the formation of a horse, there is required a certain equine nature transformed into a spermatic substance, united from two contrary matters (yet under that same equine species). Likewise, for a man, nature itself does not primarily take an equine substance; for every single substance has its own proper and principal seed from which it is made, and it multiplies itself within that seed, and through no other thing nor in any other way. 

This is clear from the Word of God; when He had created man as male and female, He said, "**increase and multiply**" <note>Genesis 1:28</note>—meaning from your own substance, which is similar to you. Indeed, He had said to His other creatures before: "**Let each one produce its own fruit and seed within itself, and let it be multiplied, etc.**" <note>Genesis 1:11–22</note> If God had wished for everything to be generated from one single thing, He would not have made so many and such great creatures, nor such diverse ones; there would have been no need for heaven or light, but the four elements would have always brought forth one and the same thing, which would be most absurd. 

Therefore, out of all things He made various kinds, so that each might generate its own like. Did not the Lord God say to Noah before the flood: "Take with you into the Ark pairs of all animals, male and female, so that afterwards each may be multiplied in its own species"? And do we not see that it happens in no other way? It is clear, then, from the preceding arguments, that for the generation of anything, there is a need for its own like, so that by the command of God, diverse things...

<meta>This page continues Bernard of Treviso’s argument that metals, like all living things, possess specific "roots" or seeds created by God. ## BERNARD OF TREVISO ##

...their roots, created by Him, might be multiplied into diverse forms, each within its own proper substance. This is proven through the authorities of the Philosophers. For **Scotus** <note>likely Michael Scot, a 13th-century mathematician and scholar known for his interest in alchemy</note> speaks openly: from coagulated **quicksilver** <term>argentum vivum</term> and from sulfurous quicksilver, the primary matter of all metals is made. Likewise, in the *Assembly of the Philosophers* <note>original: "Turba [Philosophorum]"; one of the oldest Latin alchemical texts, presented as a transcript of a meeting of ancient sages</note>, a certain Noscus, King of Albania, speaks in this manner: from man nothing is made but man; from a bird nothing but a bird; similarly, from any brute animal nothing but a brute beast. For nature is not improved in another nature, but only in its own nature. 

The same is said by **Jean de Meung** <note>original: "Joanne Mechungo"; author of the "Roman de la Rose," to whom several alchemical "Testaments" were attributed</note> in his testament: Every tree produces its own fruit, such as pears from a pear tree and apples from an apple tree; likewise, metal is generated and multiplied from metal, and from nothing else. Also **Geber** <note>the Latinized name of Jabir ibn Hayyan, the most influential figure in medieval alchemy</note> in his *Summa* has written well in many places to this effect, although in nearly all his books he is entirely rough and deceptive <note>original: "sophisticus"</note> in his teaching; yet he says: "We have experienced every single thing most exactly in its own way, and by proven reasons we have never been able to find anything permanent in the fire except for a **viscous humidity** <note>a thick, oily moisture</note> alone, the root of all metals." All other humidities easily flee from the fire through evaporation and through the separation of one element from another, just as water does through fire: one part goes off into smoke, another into water, and another into earth remaining at the bottom of the vessel. So it is in all things, because in their generation they were not well united; they are consumed by the smallest fire and separated from their natural composition. 

But this **viscous humidity**, namely **Mercury**, is never consumed in it, nor is it separated from its earth, nor from its other elements. For either all remain together, or they depart together, so that nothing at all of their weight is lost. By these words, therefore, Geber concludes that for this precious stone <note>the Philosopher's Stone</note> there is no need for anything else than the sole substance of Mercury, cleansed by the best art, penetrating, staining, "standing in the battle" <note>an alchemical metaphor for remaining stable and unchanging when exposed to the intense heat of the furnace</note> against the fire, and not permitting itself to be separated into different parts, but always persisting most constantly in its substance of "mercuriality." Then at last (he says) it is joined to metals radically in their depths, by destroying their form and introducing another, according to the virtue and color of the **elixir**, or the staining medicine. 

Likewise, that great and most learned King <note>possibly referencing Geber again or Hermes Trismegistus</note> says: "Our medicine is made from two things of one essence, namely from the mercurial union of the fixed and non-fixed nature, the spiritual and the corporal, the cold and moist, the hot and dry; and it can by no means be made from anything else." For the industry of Art introduces nothing new, nor does it bring anything to Nature in its root; rather, Nature is assisted by Art—as is proper—by loosening its bonds. Likewise, Art, assisted by Nature, by learning from her operations and in the supply of matter, both together fulfill the desire according to the wish of the diligent worker. To this **Morienus** <note>a legendary 7th-century hermit and alchemist</note> says: "Mix and cast the **medicine** <note>The catchword at the bottom of the page "dicinam" completes the word "medicinam" (medicine)</note> upon bodies diminished in perfection, or imperfec...

...says that this is nothing else but **quicksilver** <term>argentum vivum</term> exalted by art above imperfect quicksilver: from these they teach openly that [the Stone] is nothing other than quicksilver. **Arnold of Villanova** <note>original: "Arnaldus Villanovanus"; a famous 13th-century physician and alchemist</note> adds:

To refute this as erroneous and false: from that vain opinion, it would easily follow that Nature is superfluous if the "seeds" <note>original: "spermata"</note> of things could be made by art. In such a case, a human could be generated without a human, solely from the four elements without any intermediate nature or alteration; likewise, the principles of compositions would be made [by art], which fights against all natural reason. For in this art, Nature has produced the matter, in which it is afterward assisted by Art. 

It would also follow from that falsehood that a physician could, by his art or herbs, resuscitate the dead, or heal a dying man against the saying of **Avicenna** and **Rhazes** <note>two of the most influential Persian physicians of the Middle Ages</note>. Medicine only assists Nature; when Nature is absent or failing, Art can perform nothing—just as if a laxative is cast into a dead body, it does not purge, because the action is not received by Nature. Which **Hippocrates**, in his *Aphorisms* and *Natural Principles*—a man more divine than human, and like a spirit lacking a body—testifies, saying:

> Art presupposes some thing created by Nature alone, in which [Art] provides help to Nature itself, and Nature to Art.

Therefore, it is clear that Art requires matter which has been created by Nature, and not by Art. For if the work were from Art, what need would there be for Nature in those things where she has not operated, since nothing of hers would be present? Art alone could perfect it without any other extraneous thing, and beyond Nature. It is evident by many irrefragable and most obvious testimonies that Nature procreates and prepares the "spermatic" <note>seed-like</note> natures from herself; finally, Art operates upon them through conjunction, tending toward the end for which Nature had created them. 

Furthermore, even if it were possible for metals to be reduced into the four elements, it would necessarily be required that they be separated into Mercury and sulfur before they could be separated into elements; and afterward, those elements would have to be turned back into sulfur and quicksilver to become the immediate metallic nature. # BERNARD TREVISAN #

<page-num>696</page-num>

...reductions; instead, only that which was there before remains. Why then do we require these futile labors, if the same amount of substance was held when they were in the form of the **seed of quicksilver and sulfur** <term>spermatis argenti vivi & sulphuris</term>, and remains after their reduction into the **four elements**? They acquire nothing new—not in power, nor in weight, nor in quantity or quality. The reason for this is clear: no material was joined to it that would have made it more worthy or would have been exalted with it. Instead, a single material alone was led here and there without any addition. Therefore, it is just as valid in the form of its own seed as it is in the form of the elements. 

If the same objection is raised against our **Stone** <note>The Philosopher's Stone, the goal of the alchemical "Great Work."</note>—namely, that nothing is acquired for it—we deny it. For we reduce it so that in that reduction a conjunction of a new matter of one and the same root may occur; without this reduction, it cannot be done, and indeed an addition of matter occurs. One of the two matters certainly assists the other, so that a far more worthy matter results from it than they were individually before the conjunction. 

Therefore, our reduction is necessary because through it the materials acquire a new form and power due to the addition of new matter. This does not happen in those other "reductions of elements" practiced by others, in which nothing else appears to happen but the movement of bare matter without form, without any innovation, exaltation, or acquisition of any new form or matter. From this, it is clear that the reductions of those men are mere fantasies, vain and erroneous. 

In confirmation of this, a certain man named **William of Paris** <note>original: "Guilhelmus Parisiensis"; likely William of Auvergne (c. 1180–1249), a Bishop of Paris and philosopher who wrote on the intersection of theology and natural science.</note>, a man learned in this art, speaks most openly: 

> In the creation of man (he says), first two **seeds** <term>spermata</term> concur and unite, differing in their qualities. One of these qualities is cold and moist, and in the other, it is hot and dry. These are digested in the mother’s womb by the mixing of the power of both seeds, and by the increase through the moisture of the blood, which is of the same substance as the female seed. Through the intervening action of the power of the male seed, the material of said mixture is nourished until it becomes a middle substance participating in the nature of both, without any diminution or excess.

Furthermore, seeds are created by **Nature** and not by **Art**. Art could not do this in any way; it only effects this: that it joins both together in the mother’s womb. Although Art can also assist in the mixing through the fostering of external heat, rest, the selection of the best and easily digestible foods, and through temperance and moderation in taking them—in all these things, Art does nothing else than assist those things already created by Nature.

The same author adds: 

> To create seeds is not the work of Art. But after they have been created by Nature, then finally Art—acting as the servant of Nature—assists the thing through the natural power existing in the seed-materials already created by Nature, by joining them together...

<meta>This page continues Bernard of Trevisan’s argument regarding the relationship between nature and art in the creation of the Philosopher's Stone. He is specifically addressing the "seed" of metals and refuting the idea that alchemists can create this seed from scratch using the four elements alone.</meta>

# A BOOK ON ALCHEMY. 697 #

...existing, but not yet perfected; yet it adds nothing to the form, nor the matter, nor the power. Therefore, nature is the **first cause of generation**, and art is only the **secondary cause**, which, following after, achieves nothing without the former. For the earth is cultivated for the harvest in vain unless the natural matter created by nature is present—namely, the grain of wheat. It is certain, therefore, that each is helped by the other: nature by art, and art by nature; and in turn, both work toward the task, both that of nature and that of art.

Since, therefore, seeds <term>spermata</term> <note>original: "spermata"; referring here to the reproductive "seed" or "essence" of a substance</note> can in no way be created by art, nor can the matter of metals, it would be impossible for a man by any artifice to reduce the four elements into a "spermatic" form—be it reductive, alterative, or attractive—for the purpose of receiving a form, or an action tending toward or disposing it. 

But if someone should argue that the **Philosophers** say the four elements must exist in our art, their meaning is this: that in their two seeds, the four primary qualities of the elements are held. Namely, **heat and dryness**—which are **Fire and Air**—are in the **mature quicksilver** <note>original: "argento vivo maturo"; mercury that has been "digested" or purified</note>, which is the **male seed**. And **coldness and moisture**—which are **Earth and Water**—are in the **raw and imperfect quicksilver**, which is the **female seed**. It is not that these four elemental parts are actually separated from one another in those seeds, as are the four elements we see with our eyes. Indeed, if they were, they would no longer be the **first matter of metals**, nor could they be altered by any human ingenuity or artifice into the form of the two seeds of the metals' first matter. As the philosopher **Calid** <note>Khalid ibn Yazid, a semi-legendary Umayyad prince and early alchemical authority</note> and the **King of Albania** openly teach in this manner:

> Know that from the beginning of our work, we require only two materials; only two are seen, and only two are touched. No more than two enter into the beginning, middle, and end of the **Mastery** <term>magisterii</term> <note>The "Grand Mastery" or the "Great Work" of creating the Stone</note>. But in these two, the four qualities are present virtually. For in the **greater seed**, as in the more worthy one, the two more worthy elements are contained by their qualities—namely, **Fire and Air**. In the other seed, which is by its nature raw and imperfect, the remaining two qualities are held, and the other two less worthy elements, which are **Earth and Water**.

Through Calid, it is made clear enough that in this art there are only two "spermatic" materials of one and the same root, substance, and essence—namely, a **mercurial** substance, a substance solely viscous and dry, which joins itself to nothing in this world except to **bodies** <note>In alchemy, "bodies" usually refers to the solid metals</note>. **Morienus** <note>Morienus Romanus, a legendary hermit and alchemist</note> asserts this very thing clearly in his book, saying:

> Return the hard, the watery, and the soft to being hard, so that water may be joined to it; hide—or rather conceal—the fire under or within the cold water.

This means: join the **male seed**, which is nothing else than **cooked and mature Mercury** containing the element of fire within itself through digestion, with the **female seed**, which is **living water**. Likewise, **Isidore** <note>Likely referring to a speaker in the "Turba Philosophorum" (The Assembly of the Philosophers)</note> speaks to the same effect in the *Turba Philosophorum*:

# BERNARD OF TREVISAN #

Mix water with fire; this is the **spermatic union** <term>unio spermatica</term> <note>A "spermatic union" refers to the mixing of the essential "male" and "female" principles of matter in a way that allows them to reproduce or grow, similar to biological conception.</note> in potential, which is closest to the noble perfection of the stone for receiving its form. And in the *Codex of All Truth*, a certain Philosopher named **Artephius** <note>Artephius (c. 1150) was a famous alchemist to whom several influential medieval texts were attributed.</note> says: "Join the red man to his white woman in a round bed surrounded by the fire of husks <note>original: "corticum igne"; this refers to a gentle, steady heat, often achieved by burying the vessel in fermenting organic matter like husks or horse dung.</note>; let it be warmed there by a continuous heat until the union of the man with the **philosophical water** is made." This is not common water; rather, in this container dwells everything required for its own perfection. Then at last this union is called the **first matter of the stone**, and not otherwise. For it contains in itself the nature of the **fixed** <note>The "fixed" part is the solid, fire-resistant substance (often associated with sulfur or the "red man").</note>, by which it is stabilized, and a **spiritual nature**, which is the worthy substance of the most noble stone.

In short, he who rightly understands all the Philosophers sees that they agree perfectly in all things; but those who are not **sons of the art** <note>A traditional term for initiated alchemists who understand the true meaning behind the allegorical language.</note>, but are instead ignorant, wrongly judge that the authorities disagree. After I have spoken sufficiently about the **first matter of metals**, and proved with the firmest arguments and worthy authorities that it is **Mercury and sulfur**, I will proceed further for the benefit and utility of the listeners. In this following third part of my book, I shall say what Mercury and sulfur are, how metals are generated in the earth, and their differences, citing the authorities of the Philosophers from whom I learned what I know about the stone, God giving grace and understanding.

***

### THE THIRD PART OF THE BOOK OF MASTER BERNARD, COUNT ###
#### *Of the March of Trevisa, in which he treats of the roots* ####
#### *and principles of Metals, using the most evident reasons,* ####
#### *authorities, and philosophical arguments.* ####

FIRST, it must not be ignored that this is the divine work of **Genesis**, by which God in the beginning created matter confused and unordered: yet full, by His will, of many and infinite materials, from which He drew the **four elements**. From the mixing of these He created living things and diverse creatures; some He willed to be **intellectual**, some **sensitive**, others **vegetative**, and others **mineral**. 

**Intellectual beings** [humans] were created from the four elements, but **Fire and Air** dominate in them more than the other two. In **sensitive beings** [animals], however, the power of Fire is diminished, because Air dominates just as much as Fire does—as seen in brute animals, horses, donkeys, dogs, birds, and so on. **Vegetative beings** [plants] likewise consist of the four elements; in these, **Air and Water** dominate, but the dignity of Air is diminished by the Water, and the Water is governed by a certain earthly and vaporous substance. **Mineral creatures**, although they also consist of the four, are nevertheless dominated by **Earth and Water**; but the quality of the Water is more earthy than aquatic. They are of diverse forms, but can never be multiplied except by reduction to their first...
