### A BOOK ON ALCHEMY ###

matter, with the others previously mentioned having their own seed within themselves, in which lies hidden all the power of their multiplication and final composition. Metallic matter consists solely of **Mercury** <note>In alchemy, "Mercury" often refers to a "philosophical" or primal mercury—the fluid, heavy essence of all metals—rather than just the common liquid metal found in thermometers.</note>, which is cold, moist, and crude, and in which the four elements are also present: namely, the hot, the moist, the cold, and the dry. Of these, two are dominant—the cold and the moist—while the hot and the dry are subject to them. 

The heat of celestial motion, penetrating around the earth and into its veins, is so faint and tempered that it is barely perceptible, yet it is continuous: equal by night and by day. This heat does not come from the **Sun** (as some fools claim) but from the reflection of the **sphere of fire** <note>According to the medieval geocentric model, the Earth was surrounded by concentric spheres of the elements, with the sphere of fire being the highest, just below the moon.</note> surrounding the air, and also from the continuous movement of the celestial bodies, which stirs up an almost unimaginable continuous and slow heat. Even if the heat of minerals did come from the Sun (according to the opinion of **Raymond Lull** <note>Ramon Llull (c. 1232–1315), a Majorcan philosopher and mystic to whom many alchemical works were later attributed.</note> and **Aristotle**), the heat would still be continuous, because the Sun moves incessantly around the earth day and night. 

However, their opinion is false, because the Sun is neither hot nor cold, but its motion is naturally hot. Therefore, the heat proceeding from the motion of the celestial bodies is constantly active in the veins of the earth. Yet it does not "heat" the minerals (as some people speak foolishly); for if it heated them even slightly with this small amount of active heat, in a span of time less than ten years, Mercury would be cooked into the perfection of **Gold** <note>original: "Solis" (of the Sun). In alchemical shorthand, the Sun always represents Gold.</note>—a process which usually takes barely a hundred years to occur. 

Since the Earth is cold and dry, and minerals are located in the center of the earth, if they were to actually perceive even a tiny bit of heat from the Sun, we who are closer to it would be burned up entirely. For the heat would have to be most intense if, while penetrating the coldest bodies of earth and water, it still retained its heat when it reached the center, rather than being entirely extinguished. 

In truth, however, these things ought to be understood more naturally in this way: Since Mercury itself is composed of the four elements, when these elements are heated by the common and general influences through their own proper motion, a natural heat is excited by that very movement. Likewise, the fire and air existing within the Mercury are moved and gradually raised, for they are "worthier" <note>In the hierarchy of elements, Fire and Air were considered "noble" or "active" because they rise, while Water and Earth were "passive" because they fall.</note> elements than the water and earth of Mercury; nonetheless, humidity and coldness still dominate. 

But because heat and dryness are worthier elements, they strive to conquer the other two—namely, the coldness and humidity dominating in the Mercury. For the celestial motions excite other motions of natural heats, through which the qualities of Mercury are moved. Afterward, through a long succession of time, the dryness of Mercury overcomes one degree of its humidity, and it becomes **lead**; then it overcomes another degree, and it becomes **tin**. Finally, the heat of the Mercury again overcomes a little bit of the humidity stemming from its coldness, and it becomes **Silver** <note>original: "luna" (the Moon).</note>. With heat dominating even more, it becomes **copper** (or **Venus**), and afterward **iron**...

...and perfect **Gold** <note>original: "sol" (sun), the alchemical symbol for gold</note>. In this way, the two qualities that previously succumbed, being overcome by coldness and moisture, now conquer the others; heat and dryness dominate, which in their state of activation are **Sulphur**, while the coldness and moisture of the Mercury are **Mercury** itself. 

It is not that this Sulphur is something divided or separated from the Mercury; rather, it is solely the heat and dryness that [previously] did not dominate over the coldness and moisture of the Mercury. This Sulphur, once digested <note>In alchemy, "digestion" refers to the slow maturation of a substance through steady heat, much like ripening fruit or a body processing food.</note>, holds dominion over the two other aforementioned qualities—coldness and moisture—and imprints its virtues upon them. Through these various degrees of **decoction** <note>The process of boiling or heating a substance to extract its essence or mature its form.</note>, the diversities of metals are created. 

**Lead** <note>original: "Plumbum"</note> continually flees and flies away from the fire for no other reason than because the coldness and moisture of its Mercury have not yet been altered by the heat and dryness of its Sulphur, which in no way dominate within it. Otherwise, lead would not be consumed by fire, no matter how intense; on the contrary, its Mercury would "rejoice in its like" <note>A reference to the ancient principle that "like attracts like." If lead were fully matured, its internal fire would harmonize with the external fire rather than being destroyed by it.</note>. 

Likewise, every other metal flees from the fire except for **Gold**, because they are still cold and moist—one more than another, according to their greater or lesser participation in said qualities. They flee (I say) from what is contrary to them and which they cannot endure. For everything naturally flees from its adversary but delights in its like. From this, it follows that Gold is nothing else than pure fire within Mercury, since it does not retreat from fire, however intense it may be, while all others cannot endure it—some less, some more, as they approach or recede from the "complexion" <note>The specific balance of the four qualities—hot, cold, moist, and dry—that determines a substance's nature.</note> of fire. 

For Sulphur is nothing other than pure fire hidden within Mercury, which over a long passage of time is stirred up in the mines and moved by the motions of the celestial bodies (as I said above); it matures the coldness and moisture in Mercury through various degrees of decoction and alteration into different metallic forms: 
1. The first is **Lead**, being less hot and [more] moist; 
2. The second is **Tin**; 
3. The third is **Silver**; 
4. The fourth is **Copper**; 
5. The fifth is **Iron**; 
6. The sixth is **Gold**, which indeed, in the perfection of its metallic nature, is pure fire matured by the Sulphur existing within the Mercury. 

From this, it is clearly evident again that Sulphur is not something separate by itself outside the substance of Mercury, nor is it common sulfur; otherwise, the matter of metals would not be **homogeneous** <note>Consisting of parts all of the same kind; the alchemists argued that if metals were made of two different substances—mercury and sulfur—they could not be a single unified nature.</note> (which contradicts the assertions of all philosophers). These philosophers called these dominant qualities "Sulphur" by way of analogy, because they possess an inflammable substance, hot and dry like the sulfur in which they reside. 

Therefore, it is most clearly evident that metallic forms are created by nature solely from the pure Mercurial substance, and nothing foreign, as **Geber** <note>Latinized name of Jabir ibn Hayyan (c. 721–815), a foundational figure in alchemy. He is often cited to prove that metals share a single root.</note> attests: "In the depths," he says, "of the nature of Mercury is Sulphur, which is produced over a long passage of time in the veins of the earth's minerals." **Morienus** <note>A legendary hermit-alchemist said to have lived in the 7th century, famous for his dialogues on the transformation of matter.</note> and **Aros** <note>An alchemical authority often cited alongside Morienus; likely a corruption of a Greek or Arabic name.</note> speak even more clearly on this matter: Our...

...our sulphur (they say) is not the common kind, but is fixed and not volatile <note>In alchemy, "fixed" substances resist fire and do not evaporate, while "volatile" ones vanish into vapor when heated.</note>, being of the nature of Mercury and not from any other thing. We imitate nature most exactly, which in its own mines has no other material upon which to work except the pure Mercurial form, as is evident through the best reasoning, the authorities, and experience. Within this Mercury is a fixed and fire-proof <note>original: "incombustile"</note> sulphur, which completes our work without any substance other than the pure Mercurial substance. 

Calid <note>Likely referring to Khalid ibn Yazid, an early Umayyad prince associated with alchemy.</note>, Bendegid, Jesid, and Maria <note>Maria the Jewess, an ancient alchemical authority credited with inventing the bain-marie.</note> speak no differently, but clearly in this manner: Nature procreates its metals from the heat and dryness of Mercury when they overcome its coldness and moisture, altering it; and they are perfected by no other essence, as is affirmed in all the books of the Philosophers, though it would be tedious to cite them all.

Truly, it does not dominate within it except through the movement of heat, by which the said sulphur is altered, and simultaneously the other two qualities of the Mercury are changed. In this way, nature—through this sulphur in the veins of the earth—generates the diverse forms of metals according to the different degrees of these alterations. 

In this, we likewise imitate nature, since we take nothing foreign into our material; rather, within our quicksilver <note>original: "argēto vivo," or Mercury</note> there is an incombustible Mercurial sulphur. This sulphur does not yet dominate, however; instead, the coldness and moisture of the volatile Mercury prevail until, by the action of continuous heat persevering upon this quicksilver of ours, the "fixed" quality dominates and is mixed throughout the whole volatile substance. It conquers the coldness and moisture of the Mercury, and finally, the heat and dryness of the fixed part (which are its qualities) begin to dominate the others. 

According to the degrees of this alteration of Mercury through its own sulphur, different colors arise, just as they do—and in no other way—by nature itself in the mines. The first of these colors is **Saturnine blackness** <note>Associated with Lead.</note>; the second is **Jovial whiteness** <note>Associated with Tin.</note>; the third is **Lunar** <note>Associated with Silver.</note>; the fourth is **Venereal** <note>Associated with Copper.</note>; the fifth is **Martial** <note>Associated with Iron.</note>; the sixth is **Solar** <note>Associated with Gold.</note>. 

The seventh degree, however, is brought by us one step higher than it is by nature. Indeed, we perfect it and render it "more than perfect" with a most exalted red or blood-like color. Therefore, since it becomes more than perfect, it is able to perfect other things to that extent. For if it were not perfected further than its own simple nature, what need would there be to spend so much time—namely nine months **and a half**—when we could already have such bodies created by nature without such great labors? 

But it is necessary, as I said before, that the masculine body be made "more than perfect" through art imitating nature, so that by its "more-than-perfection" and abundant radiation, it can perfect other imperfect things in weight, color, and substance, within their mineral roots and principles. ...is so presumptuous that he believes he can perfect this matter, and make it such as we desire, by using some foreign thing in which no radical mixture is held? In the *Assembly of the Philosophers* <note>original: "Turba [Philosophorum]," one of the oldest and most influential Latin alchemical texts, written as a dialogue between Greek philosophers.</note>, a certain man named *Aristeus*—who governed the whole world for sixteen years by his wisdom and was the most excellent after *Hermes* <note>Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary founder of alchemy.</note>, and of whom it is read in the *Chronicles of Solomon* that he gathered the disciples of *Pythagoras* and was never known to lie (for which reason he was called "the truth-teller" by the Astrologers)—says:

Therefore, our matter cannot be improved in any way other than in its own proper nature. *Parmenides* says the same thing, who first withdrew me from errors and directed me onto the right path. It is certainly clear that the metallic nature is not improved except in its own metallic nature, and not in any other, so much so that by this way, through our art, we may perfect in a few months what nature itself could scarcely do in a thousand years. For in the mines there is almost no heat, and if even a little were present, the work of nature would be very swift. Thus, in our art, we have a double heat: namely, of sulfur and of fire, so that the one may assist the other. Fire is not (as *Constantine* and *Empedocles* would have it) part of the substance of the matter, yet it increases the work; otherwise, it would follow that such heat would penetrate more and more every day, which is erroneous. Truly, fire alone rules the entire art, which nature uses, and we can introduce nothing else. By a violent fire, however, things are not altered by one another, nor are they moved. Let there be, therefore, a continuous, digesting fire—not violent, but subtle, enclosed, airy, surrounding, altering, and not burning. As God loves me, I have now told you the whole method of constructing the fire; consider, therefore, and chew over my words piece by piece: for indeed, fire encompasses the whole art, as is clear from all passages of the *Book of Truth*. Consider likewise what the *Great Rosary* <note>The "Rosarius Magnus" or "Rosarium Philosophorum," a famous 16th-century alchemical treatise.</note> brings to this opinion:

> Beware (it says) lest you hasten your solution, wishing to perfect it before the required time: for this precipitation is a sign of the deprivation of the unions. Let your fire, therefore, be persistent and gentle, according to the degree of nature: mild to the bodies, digesting, and excluding the cold.

Likewise, *Maria the Prophetess* <note>Also known as Mary the Jewess, an early alchemical authority often credited with the invention of the "bain-marie" or water bath.</note> adds to this:

> A violent fire hinders the union, and tints the white into a red the color of wild poppy flowers; this you can imagine for yourself and learn from the work, just as I did. Decaying manure was used as a source of low, steady heat in early chemistry.</note> I held it in vain, and in a fire of coals without a medium, my matter was sublimated <note>turned into vapor and solidified again</note>, not dissolved. But in the fire I have described—vaporous, digesting, continuous, not violent, subtle, surrounding, airy, clear, closed, non-burning, altering, penetrating, and living—it succeeded well.

# BERNARD TREVISAN

...curiosity. Indeed (as I said before) the element of fire, which does not dominate in crude Mercury <note>The base metal/spirit central to alchemy, symbolizing fluidity. "Crude" Mercury refers to it in its natural, unpurified state.</note>, is the very thing that digests the matter. Therefore, every true Philosopher will know perfectly how much subtler the element of fire is than the other elements, and in what proportion it is able to overcome them. The weight, therefore, is in the first elemental composition of Mercury, and not in any other work. Accordingly, composition must occur in the first place, or conjunction; afterward alteration, then mixing, and finally, union will be achieved. Whoever wishes to imitate nature in these things should observe only its order and weights, as the *Book of All Truth* holds. If the preparation is made without weight, the work will be delayed, which will easily cause you to lose heart. On this subject, Albugazal <note>original: "Albugazal." Likely Al-Ghazali (c. 1058–1111), a Persian philosopher, though alchemists often attributed their own theories to famous ancient figures.</note>, the teacher of Plato, speaks excellently: *Earthly power, resisting that which is above it, delayed by resistance, is the action of the agent in this matter.* <note>original: "Terrena potentia super sibi resistens, pro resistentia dilata, est actio agentis in ista materia." This refers to the struggle between the "fixed" earth and the "volatile" spirit.</note> These are truly golden words, opening to us the foundation of weights, which you will not easily understand unless you are learned, or they have been explained by someone remarkably skilled. I would have gladly explained them to you, were it not for a vow I made to God, to justice, and to previous Philosophers, that I would never explain the weight, the matter, or the colors in naked words or common speech, but only in parables (as you will soon hear below)—true and perfect ones, without subtraction or excess, in imitation of the wise.

I spoke before of the inventors of this art, and those who possessed it; I also confessed that I myself have possessed and perfected the Stone from beginning to end. Likewise, I spoke of the deceptions I endured, and because of them, the huge expenses and intolerable labors from the eighteenth year of my age until my sixty-fourth year, before I attained the art. But if I had possessed from the beginning all the books I later obtained, I would have reached it sooner without a doubt: yet I read nothing but the most false recipes and erroneous books; furthermore, it happened that I associated only with the most perverse thieves, wicked men, and impostors. But after I knew [the art], I had close acquaintance with fifteen good men who likewise knew the craftsmanship of the Stone, and especially with a certain Barbarini <note>This may refer to a member of the influential Italian Barberini family, or a specific alchemical associate of Trevisan.</note>. (I had nevertheless known the art for two years before I had worked it out or perfected it). This man, during a dispute (when I had unexpectedly said I had not yet tested it), tried to turn me away from the true purpose, wherefore I left his company. We disputed chiefly about the method of hiding and concealing the art from unworthy men. In truth, writers differed from one another regarding the structure of the fire, although they all aimed at the same goal: namely, that it should be done in such a way that the "fleeting" one <note>A common alchemical term for volatile substances that evaporate easily.</note> does not fly away before the "pursuer" <note>The "fixed" substance that stabilizes the volatile one.</note> catches it, regardless of how the fire is prepared. Therefore, so that you may understand my conclusion, prick up your ears more attentively: Our work is made from a single root, and from two Mercurial substances, crude...

# BOOK ON ALCHEMY

...having taken them, drawn from the mineral, pure and clean, joined by the fire of friendship <note>original: "conjunctis amicitiæ." A term for a gentle, balanced heat that allows substances to combine without being destroyed.</note>, as the matter itself requires, and constantly cooked until one thing is made from the two. In this one thing, indeed, the body has become spirit, and the spirit has become body through their mingling.

Afterward, let the fire be increased until the fixed body <note>The "fixed" (fixum) refers to the stable, non-volatile substance that resists the fire.</note> tints the non-fixed <note>The "non-fixed" (non fixum) or volatile substance that usually evaporates.</note> with its own color and nature: for where it is rightly mixed, it overcomes all things, brings them to its own nature and virtue, and finally surpasses and tints a thousand thousand, and ten thousand times ten thousand: he who has seen it, likewise believes it. In this way, therefore, it is multiplied in virtue and quantity, as that venerable Pythagoras, Isudrius, and the *Codex of All Truth* confess. In none of the books have I ever found the secret of multiplication, except in the *Great Rosary*, in the *Pandects of Mary* <note>original: "Pandectis Mariæ." Refers to Mary the Prophetess, a legendary female alchemist often cited in medieval texts.</note>, in the *Truth-Teller*, in the *Testament of Pythagoras*, in the *Turba* <note>original: "Turba." Likely the *Turba Philosophorum* (Assembly of the Philosophers), one of the oldest and most influential Latin alchemical texts.</note>, in Morienus, in Avicenna, in Bolzain, in Albugazal the brother of Bendagid, in Iefid of Constantinople—but if it is contained in others, I did not understand it, nor could I learn it from them. I knew a certain man from the March of Ancona who knew the Stone extremely well, but was ignorant of multiplication; he followed me anxiously for sixteen whole years so that he might learn it, yet he never learned it from me, for he possessed the same books I mentioned. I have therefore uncovered the entire theoretical side and the mineral principles with their explanations, by which the true can be discerned from the false; now it has seemed right to weave in the practical side, though in obscure words, just as I myself worked it out and four times composed the said Stone. Whoever, therefore, possesses and reads this little book of mine, ought to be deservedly freed from all anxiety and know the truth without fail, for I could not have written more clearly unless I were to demonstrate the thing to the eye—which all reason advises against. You yourself, when you know it, will veil it far more cautiously than I, and will be pained that I wrote so openly. The will of God has forbidden it to be made public to everyone, for it is good that it be known to very few, as is read throughout the *Turba*.

...with a pure cover, and crafted from pure gold. Therefore, eager for knowledge, I did not hesitate to take heart, and I arranged to set forth the prescribed disputations. A most learned man spurred me on to undertake this task <note>original: "calcaria... addente." Literally "adding spurs," meaning providing encouragement or incentive.</note>. It came to my mind that while those who dare are raised to sublime heights, the timid are cast down and dwell forever on the ground; thus, I passed manfully into the arena <note>original: "palestra." A reference to an ancient Greek wrestling school, here used metaphorically for a place of intellectual debate.</note>. By fate, I obtained the palm of victory in the disputation before those standing by, and a small book of the prize was offered to me quite honorably by the faculty of philosophy, so that I was respected by all.

Afterward, for the sake of refreshing my weary mind, I sought out pleasant fields and meadows. I happened upon a most limpid little fountain, enclosed and fortified by beautiful stone. It was set over an oak trunk, and the rest was surrounded by a wall, so that no beasts might enter it, nor birds bathe in it. Sitting above this fountain, I contemplated its beauty and saw that it was closed off at the top. 

As I was doing this, a man, elderly and quite venerable like a priest, came along. After I greeted him honorably, I asked why that little fountain was closed and fortified in such a manner—at the top, the bottom, and on all sides. Deigning to give me a friendly response, he said: "You should know, my friend, that this fountain is of a truly wonderful and terrifying power beyond all other fountains in the entire world. It belongs only to the King of this country, whom the fountain knows perfectly, just as he knows the fountain. If the King passes by, the fountain always draws him to itself, and it is not drawn by the King. He remains in the bath for two hundred and eighty-two days <note>In alchemical allegory, 282 days often corresponds to the period of human gestation, symbolizing the "rebirth" or perfection of the matter.</note>, by which the full strength of youth is brought to him, so that he cannot be conquered by anyone, no matter how powerful. 

Therefore, he took care to have his little fountain enclosed with a round, beautiful stone, as you see, in which the clear fountain shines like silver and the color of the heavens. To make it even stronger, so it would not be destroyed by horses or other animals, he placed an old oak tree, split through the middle, over it to protect it from the sun's rays by providing shade. Then, as you see, it is surrounded by a very thick wall: first it is closed by hard and clear stone, and finally by the hollow oak, especially because it is of a terrifying nature; once it is inflamed and irritated, it penetrates everything. Likewise, if it were to run dry, it would be the end of us."

I asked later whether he had seen the King in said fountain. He replied that he had indeed seen him entering, but from the time he was closed in by the guardians, he does not appear again until the hundred and thirtieth day <note>A common marker in the "Great Work" for the completion of a specific stage of transformation.</note>. Finally, he emerges quite splendid and shining. A primary guardian <note>original: "Custos portionarius." A specialized attendant or official.</note> constantly heats the bath so that it persists in heat, which is hidden in the water of the fountain; he heats it day and night without intermission. I asked again what color the King was. He said that his clothing was first made of golden cloth, then of an all-silk doublet <note>original: "holoferic." From the Greek 'holos' (all) and 'seric' (silk).</note>, or a black thorax <note>A breastplate or tunic; the black color signifies the *nigredo* or "blackness" stage of alchemy, representing decay and the stripping away of impurities.</note>, with a white shirt above the snow...

...flesh, however, or very red blood <note>original: "carnem... vel sanguinem rubicundissimum." This refers to the "Red Stage" or Rubedo, the final perfection of the alchemical work.</note>. I then asked whether the King, upon coming there, would bring with him a great company of foreigners and common folk? He answered kindly and with a smile: "When the King proposed to come here, leaving behind all his courtiers and foreigners, he enters alone; no one approaches the fountain except himself and his guard. A very simple man—indeed, the simplest of men—has care of it and fulfills his duties perfectly, since he does nothing else but heat the fountain." <note>The "simplest of men" is a common alchemical trope for the "vulgar" fire or the natural heat required to sustain the reaction.</note>

I asked again whether the King was a friend to the fountain, and the fountain to him? He said: "They love each other in a marvelous way; the fountain attracts the King, not the King the fountain; for she is like a mother to him." I finally asked of what race the King was? He replied that he was from the fountain, which had made him such as he is, without any other thing. I asked if he had many courtiers. He said he has only six, who await the succession; if by chance the King should die at some time, they would also possess the kingdom as he does. Hence it happens that they serve him, because they hope for great dominion and possession from him. <note>The six courtiers represent the other six metals known to alchemy: Lead (Saturn), Tin (Jupiter), Iron (Mars), Copper (Venus), Quicksilver (Mercury), and Silver (the Moon). They "hope" to become Gold (the King).</note>

Finally, I asked if he was old. He replied that he was older than the fountain, and more mature than any of his subjects. "How then," (*I asked*), "does it happen that they do not kill the King, from whose death they expect such a great succession, especially since he is so old?" He said: "Although he is of quite advanced age, nevertheless none of his subjects is as patient of cold and sweat, rain, wind, and labor as he. Likewise, none of them by themselves, nor all together, could kill him, nor could any force." <note>The King (Gold) is described as "patient" because gold does not rust or tarnish when exposed to the elements (wind, rain, etc.).</note>

"How then will they possess the kingdom if he can neither die nor be killed by anyone?" He replied: "The six subjects are from the fountain, from which they possess everything they have, just as he does; thus they are drawn to the fountain most strongly. The King is killed by the fountain itself just as they are, and he is resurrected through it. Then, from the substance of his kingdom, which is divided into the tiniest parts, each of his subjects receives a portion; and however tiny the particle any one of them has, he is equaled in wealth, strength, and power to the King, and they become equal among themselves." <note>This describes the "Multiplication" or "Projection," where the Alchemical Stone (the King) is dissolved and its power is shared to transform base metals into gold.</note>

I asked again how long he had to wait. Smiling again, he said: "Know that the King enters alone without subjects; although the fountain loves them too, they do not enter, because they have not yet earned this dignity. But as the King enters, he is stripped of his robe woven of pure gold leaves and coverings, which he gives to his first chamberlain, called **Saturn**. He keeps it for forty days—sometimes two more at most—after he has first received it. Next, the King strips off his black silk doublet <note>original: "thoracem holosericeam nigram." This refers to the *Nigredo* or blackening stage, associated with Saturn/Lead.</note>, which he gives to his second chamberlain, named **Jupiter**, who guards it for twenty-two days. Then at last, at the King’s command, Jupiter hands it to **Luna** <note>The Moon or Silver.</note>, who is the third person, beautiful and resplendent; she keeps it for twenty days."

Then at last the King appears in a **pure white shirt**, like snow or the flower of salt <note>original: "camisia alba... salis florem." The white shirt represents the *Albedo*, or white stage of the alchemical work, which follows the blackening of the "death" stage.</note>. He then takes this off and hands it to **Mars**, who keeps it for forty days—and sometimes two more. Afterward, by God’s command, **Mars** hands it over to the **yellow Sun**, though he is not yet bright; he keeps it for forty days. Then finally comes the most beautiful and **blood-red Sun**, who immediately seizes the shirt. I asked then, what becomes of all those who were present? He said: "The Fountain is then opened; the water gave them the shirt, the garment, and the breastplate. In a moment, he delivers his **bloody and red flesh** to all of them to be eaten <note>original: "carnem sanguineam & rubeam." This is a highly symbolic reference to the *Rubedo* (red stage) and the "multiplication" of the Stone, often compared to the Eucharist, where the power of the Stone is shared or "fed" to other metals.</note>; now at last they have what they desired."

I asked again whether they always waited so long, and whether they could receive any reward for their services before the end, unless they persevered until the very finish? He replied: "As soon as they have the **white shirt**, four of those courtiers could, if they wished, rejoice and enjoy great riches. However, they would only possess half of the kingdom. For this reason, they prefer to wait just a little longer for the final outcome, so that they may also be crowned with the **royal diadem** of their lord." <note>This explains that the "White Stone" (Albedo) can transmute metals into silver (half the kingdom), but the "Red Stone" (Rubedo) is required for the full perfection of gold.</note>

I asked if any doctor or anyone else ever approached during that time. He answered, "None; nor is there anything else except a **single guardian** who, from below, stirs up a continuous, circulating, and vaporous heat—nothing more." I asked whether this guardian suffered much labor? He said, "More at the beginning than toward the end, because the fire is then inflamed." I asked if many had seen this? He replied, "It is turned before the eyes of the whole world, yet no one among those in the world has recognized it." <note>A common alchemical paradox: the "Prime Matter" is common and visible to all, but its true nature is hidden from the ignorant.</note>

I asked more broadly what they might do next? He said: "If they wish, they could purge the King again in the fountain for three days, clearing the place according to the capacity of the vessel, giving first the breastplate, second the shirt, and third his bloody flesh." At this I asked, "To what purpose are these things?" But he said, "I have answered you enough so far; I am satisfied." When I realized this, I did not wish to be a nuisance, but I accompanied him some distance as he departed, giving him immortal thanks and saying farewell. He was a truly venerable and most wise old man, so much so that even the heavens obeyed him, and all things trembled in his presence.

Then a sleepiness came over me, so that returning to the fountain where I had intended to rest for a while, I could not help but take a seat above it, and I secretly unlocked all the enclosures. Meanwhile, as I was inspecting my **little book**—the prize of my debate—its splendor and beauty so increased my drowsiness that, with a certain yawn, it slipped from my hands and fell into the fountain. This distressed me greatly, for I wished to keep it in memory of the honor I had attained. As I watched, it disappeared from my sight. Thinking it had fallen to the bottom of the fountain, I began to drain the water with great industry, until only a tenth part of it remained, along with...

Concluding, I say to you: whoever reading this little book of mine has not understood the <term>stone</term> <note>The "Philosopher's Stone," the legendary substance capable of transmuting base metals into gold and granting long life.</note> through it, will never understand it, no matter what he does. Making an end therefore to my little book, I ask God, the Best and Greatest, by whose grace it was completed, that He might open the minds of men of good will, for whom, as they are ingenious, there will be little difficulty, provided they abstain from dreamed-up fantasies and the <term>subtleties of sophists</term> <note>In alchemical literature, "sophists" were those who tried to create gold through chemical trickery or false "recipes" rather than following the true laws of nature.</note>, and remain also in the way of nature, which is demonstrated through my theoretical study. ### A LITTLE TREATISE
# ON THE NATURAL
# PHILOSOPHY OF METALS BY LORD DENIS
## ZACHAIRE, A MOST NOBLE MAN
### A French Philosopher.

->TO THE KIND READER.<-

<image-desc>Large decorative initial letter Q filled with ornamental vine and leaf motifs.</image-desc>
However many learned, wise men and natural philosophers once wrote in this divine art, they forbade its profanation or its disclosure. Nonetheless, friend Reader, when I had sufficiently considered the interpretations of the contradictions, figures, comparisons, ambiguities, and various riddles occurring everywhere in their writings, I did not wish for it to remain hidden. Whatever (after many useless labors and most lengthy works—which I might better call deceptive, entirely foolish acts regarding <term>sophistication</term> <note>original: "sophisticationem." In an alchemical context, this refers to "sophistry" or the fraudulent practice of making metals look like gold or silver through surface treatments or cheap alloys rather than true transmutation.</note>) I have resolved through true insights from the books of honorable men, through continuous readings of the most approved authors, such as <term>Geber</term> <note>original: "Geberi." Referring to the Latin works attributed to the 8th-century Arabic polymath Jabir ibn Hayyan, which were the foundational textbooks for European alchemists.</note> in his *Summa* <note>The *Summa Perfectionis Magisterii* (The Sum of the Perfection of the Magistery), a famous 13th-century textbook of alchemy.</note>, and others. 

Therefore, drawing back my foot from the erroneous paths in which I had been entangled before—more so than <term>Daedalus</term> <note>The legendary Greek inventor who built a complex labyrinth for King Minos; Zachaire uses this as a metaphor for the "twisting" and confusing theories of false alchemy.</note> in his labyrinth—I wished to fix my step upon the right path. Walking in this way, I finally recognized the true and perfect <term>matter</term> <note>original: "materiam." The "First Matter" or starting substance required to begin the Great Work.</note>, prepared for us by nature in the caverns of the earth to be perfected above the earth, which generates those very metals naturally beneath it, just as experience (by God’s mercy) has taught me, as I shall declare in this little book more clearly than has ever been possible. In its first part, I will relate the manner and the progress by which I finally arrived at the true knowledge of this divine work. In the second, which authors I used in seeking out the explanations of authorities...

<meta>This page continues the preface by Denis Zachaire. The text follows a discussion of the author's decision to clarify the confusing allegories of previous alchemists. ...of terms, and other difficulties. In the third and final part, I will declare the practice in such a way that it remains hidden from the ignorant, but for the <term>sons of the art</term> <note>A traditional term for initiated alchemists who are deemed worthy of understanding the "Great Work."</note> it shall be most manifest. For their sake, I have studied to bring everything into the best possible order as diligently as I could. In this matter, I have not imitated certain men who are envious of the <term>public good</term> <note>original: "utilitatis R. P." (Rei Publicae). The author contrasts his openness with those who hoard knowledge for private gain.</note>, being too greedy for their own profit; they were unwilling to declare their subject matter except under various and diverse allegories of fables—indeed, they were scarcely willing to show their books to others. 

I once knew a certain man who had received some writings from a Venetian; he kept these hidden away as if worshipping them, so that he himself hardly dared to look inside, let alone show or share them with others. He perhaps imagined that the <term>Stone</term> <note>The Philosopher's Stone, the legendary substance capable of turning base metals into gold and granting long life.</note> would emerge from that paper alone without any labor, provided it were kept most tightly locked in a chest, like a philosophical matter under a <term>Hermetic seal</term> <note>original: "Hermetico sigillo." An airtight seal used in alchemy, named after Hermes Trismegistus; here used metaphorically for extreme secrecy.</note>. 

But these men are ignorant that such divine science is not granted to men by chance, as the Philosophers say when they rebuke those who work not at their own expense, but at the expense of others. By these men, I will undoubtedly be most harshly criticized for publishing this little work, especially in the <term>common tongue</term> <note>Though the text here is in Latin, Zachaire originally wrote his "Opuscule" in French (the vernacular) to make it accessible to his countrymen, a controversial move at the time.</note>, since in this current time no science is more hated by the common people than this. To these critics, I wish briefly to give a response they have hitherto ignored: namely, that a part of this divine philosophy is not within human power such that it can be understood by books alone, but is situated in the will of God. He reveals it to whom He wishes through His Holy Spirit, or through the medium of some man, as is told more broadly in the second part of this book; it is far from my intention to make it public to all. 

What is new if I write the art in the common tongue, when it has been described until now by all its practitioners in no other language than their own? For instance, it was written by <term>Hamech</term> the Hebrew in Hebrew; by <term>Thebit</term> and <term>Hali</term> <note>Thabit ibn Qurra and likely Hali Abenragel, influential Arabic-language scholars whose works were translated into Latin.</note>, the Chaldean philosophers, in Chaldean; by **Homer**, **Democritus**, and **Theophrastus** the Greeks in the Greek language; and by <term>Aboholy</term>, <term>Geber</term>, and **Avicenna** the Arabs in Arabic. **Morienus**, **Raymond**, and many other Latins handed down the art in Latin, so that it might be known—

<summary>Zachaire defends his decision to publish his alchemical findings in the common tongue (French), arguing that true understanding comes from God rather than mere books, while criticizing those who keep their knowledge hidden out of greed.</summary>

->### TO THE READER<-

*...[it is thought] by their successors, that this divine science was at some time granted even to men of their own nation. Regarding popular hatred, one must know that the truth of the art is not despised, but only the false <term>sophistications</term> <note>original: "sophisticationes"; in an alchemical context, this refers to deceptive techniques or "sophistry" used by fraudulent practitioners—often called "puffers"—to mimic gold through alloying or coloring without achieving a true transmutation.</note> within it, as I will relate more broadly in the first part of this little book. But if they should ask why I do not write each thing clearly and manifestly, so that anyone might be able to work safely from this little work—since by doing otherwise I would bring no benefit to the readers?*

*To answer this: who is ignorant of the countless useless expenses made daily concerning this art in France alone because of deceptions? If readers can be pulled back from these toward the right path by reading my book, then pious and honest readers may be kept on the path of truth through what I teach in the second part. For all these, the reading of the third part will not be useless, in which is told how a completely easy approach lies open to the practice of the <term>divine work</term> <note>original: "operis divini"; refers to the "Great Work" (Magnum Opus) of creating the Philosopher's Stone, so called because it was believed to require God's favor.</note>.*

*I call it "divine" for this reason: because no one can comprehend or understand it by themselves without divine inspiration, even if they are otherwise a most learned philosopher. As <term>Geber</term> <note>original: "Geber"; the Latinized name of Jabir ibn Hayyan, an 8th-century Islamic polymath. His works were the foundation of medieval European alchemy.</note> says against all those who strive to work solely by the consideration of causes and natural works, saying: "In this they err greatly, thinking they can imitate nature, when that is impossible for art in all respects."*

*Let such detractors, therefore, abstain from reading our little work: for I have not labored for them, but for the kind, teachable <term>sons of doctrine</term> <note>original: "filiis doctrinæ"; a common alchemical phrase for initiated or worthy students who possess the spiritual and intellectual character to understand the secrets of the art.</note>, and the studious lovers of this art. I friendly request them, and wish them to be forewarned before they begin to work, that once all the doubts concerning the individual operations necessary in the <term>composition</term> <note>The process of combining and preparing the alchemical materials.</note> are compared—including those that seem to contradict each other, the ambiguities of riddles, and other things of that kind—they should have a mind so resolved and free that they see and understand that these are nothing but pure agreements. They are not the sayings of different men, but the same sense expressed in various ways.*

*This is the only way of knowing the truth, especially in this art, as <term>Rhazes</term> <note>original: "Rasis"; Abu Bakr al-Razi, a 9th-century Persian physician and alchemist known for his empirical approach.</note> says. Whoever is lazy or yawning while reading our books will also be unfit for preparing the materials, when...*

<meta>Catchword: indeed (quidem)</meta>

He claims his text will reveal the underlying harmony between seemingly contradictory alchemical authorities like Geber and Rhazes.</summary>

->### TO THE READER<-

*...indeed, one thing is clarified by another, just as what is perhaps lacking in one is supplied in another. For it is impossible (so divine counsel disposes) to find all things necessary for this art written in order. Therefore, I ask all those who, through this little work of mine, arrive at such great happiness, that they do not abuse it; and above all, let them not be unmindful of the poor to their own condemnation, but let them continually give thanks to God for this and for the other gifts of His liberality, to whom alone be praise, honor, and glory forever.*

# THE FIRST PART OF THE LITTLE WORK OF DENIS ZACHAIRE, [SHOWING] BY WHAT WAY
### *the author arrived at the true knowledge of this art and of the divine work.*

<image-desc>Ornamental woodcut initial 'H' featuring floral scrollwork and stylized foliage.</image-desc>That famous **Hermes Trismegistus** <note>original: "Hermes ille Trismegistus"; the legendary Hellenistic figure regarded as the founder of alchemy, often called the "Thrice-Greatest."</note>, not undeservedly called the first prophet and father of all natural philosophers, the author of the **divine stone** <term>lapis divinus</term> <note>Another name for the Philosopher's Stone, the substance believed to transmute base metals into gold and grant longevity.</note>, and the Thrice-Great Interpreter, after he had experienced the truth of this divine philosophy, left it written to us that, had he not feared the final universal judgment of God, he never would have written anything about this divine science—so greatly did he hold it in veneration. All those who have followed him in this art have also held this opinion: for which reason they have written all their books on the subject using various arguments concluding in opposing ways, as **Geber** <note>original: "Geber"; referring to the influential 13th-century Latin alchemical author (Pseudo-Geber), whose "Summa Perfectionis" was a foundational text.</note> says in his *Summa*, so that the ignorant might be forced to wander in this manner, while on the other hand, the **sons of doctrine** <note>original: "doctrinæ filij"; a traditional term for initiated alchemists or seekers of wisdom.</note> might perceive their true meaning beneath such a variety of opinions. 

Nevertheless, it was necessary for even these seekers to wander at first, so that after they have acquired the art through the greatest labors—both of the intellect and of the body—they might value it more and keep it more hidden. This indeed is the greatest reason for concealment: for besides intolerable and painful labors, huge expenses are added, especially for those who learn from the reading of books alone, expecting inspiration from the divine spirit, just as I did for the space of ten years, as I am about to narrate, and will tell of the means through which I came to the knowledge of this secret. 

When I was about twenty years old, after I had been instructed by the care of my parents at home in the principles of **Grammar** <note>original: "Grammatices"; the first stage of the liberal arts curriculum, involving the study of Latin language and literature.</note>, and was sent off to the arts and philosophy, within the space of three years, through the diligence of my personal tutor, I progressed so much that it seemed right to my guardians (for in the meantime both my parents had died) to advance me further, namely to **jurisprudence** <term>legisprudentia</term> <note>The study of law; in the 16th century, this was a standard career path for young men of the author's social standing.</note> under the same

->## OF DENIS ZACHAIRE<-

teacher: but before I departed from the college of arts, I had formed a close familiarity and friendship with many other scholars. These students possessed various books of chemical recipes, which I transcribed with the greatest diligence when they were lent to me, with the approval of my personal tutor, who had already begun to labor in this art for some time. Thus, before I left, I had collected a very voluminous book, stuffed full of recipes of this kind. As soon as I arrived with my teacher at the place where I was supposed to apply myself to the study of law, I began to leaf through my writings. Some of them contained instructions for **projections** <term>projectiones</term> <note>The final stage of the alchemical process where the Philosopher's Stone is "projected" or cast upon base metal to transmute it into gold or silver.</note> of one part upon ten, others upon twenty, thirty, a third, or a half part; for making red gold of eighteen or twenty carats <note>original: "characterum"</note>, into the gold of crowns, ducats, and of a higher color than could ever naturally exist. One recipe was supposed to withstand melting, another the test of the **Lydian stone** <note>Also known as a touchstone, used since antiquity to test the purity of precious metals by the color of the streak they leave behind.</note>, and all other trials. Regarding the white work <note>The "albedo," or the stage of producing silver.</note> likewise, one was meant to be ten-denier silver, another eleven, another the silver used for capital coinage—a white that returns from the fire, and another that stands the rubbing of the Lydian stone. In short, I thought that if I could perform even the smallest of these, no greater happiness in this world could ever befall me.

This was especially so when I read that these recipes bore the names of great figures: one was of the **Queen of Navarre**, another of the **Cardinal of Lorraine**, of Tournon, and of countless others. Such masks and titles were used so that faith might be placed in them by the unwary; by these I was easily deceived along with the rest. Consequently, I began to build small furnaces, and moving from the smallest to the largest, I filled a large room entirely with them. I designated one for distillation, another for sublimation, and others for calcination, dissolution, the **Water-Bath** <term>balneum Maris</term> <note>original: "balneum Maris," literally "the bath of Mary"; a double boiler used for gentle, even heating.</note>, and for fusion. So much so that, for the first entry into my beginning, I had entirely consumed two hundred crowns—which we had received for the support of my studies for two years—partly on furnaces, partly on charcoal, infinite minerals, and glass vessels, as well as on gold and silver uselessly melted, mixed, and dissolved. These perished through long handling among the **dross and ashes** <note>original: "loppas & cineres"</note>, and having been so diminished, they hardly appeared at all, or left only a tiny residue that was brittle and corrupted. Before the first year had even finished, I had reduced the substance of two years (or at least the latter year just beginning) into smoke.

At this time, my teacher was seized by a very burning fever, caused by the heat excited by our charcoal (much like the heat felt by the cannon-founders in the **Arsenal of Venice**). Because he was already inflamed and glowing within, he drank cold liquid, and died—an event for which I grieved most deeply. Furthermore, my parents refused to send more money than was required for me alone. Therefore, desiring to proceed with the work I had begun, I was forced to return home so that, having been made free from guardianship and of my own legal right, I might dispose of my paternal inheritance as I wished. I immediately placed these lands under lease (as they call it)...

->### SMALL TREATISE ###<-

I spent four years writing out this recipe at a cost of four hundred crowns, which I eventually received from an Italian and decided to test. I supported this man with me until I could see the outcome of the matter; for he affirmed that he had seen its effect through experience. For this undertaking, I bought two ounces of gold and one mark of silver; once melted together, we dissolved them in **strong water** <term>aqua fortis</term> <note>Nitric acid, used by alchemists to dissolve silver and separate it from gold.</note>. Afterwards, we calcined them through evaporation, and we also attempted to dissolve them with various other waters and different distillations, until three months had passed before this powder was ready for **projection** <term>projectio</term> <note>The final stage of the alchemical process where the "Stone" is cast upon molten base metal to cause transmutation.</note>. This we performed exactly according to the prescription of the recipe, but in vain: for the expected gain was transformed into a loss, so much so that out of eight total ounces of gold and silver combined, only three ounces remained. I will say nothing for now of many other expenses, by which my four hundred crowns were reduced to two hundred and thirty. Of these, another twenty were lost when I gave them to my Italian so that he might go to the author of the recipe, who he claimed was in Milan, to be better instructed. Consequently, I waited for his return throughout the entire winter, but I might as well have stayed there until the final day of the world, for I never saw him again.

Summer finally returned, accompanied by the plague, so I had to leave that place along with other companions for half a year. During that time, I happened upon a certain old man, commonly called a **Philosopher** <term>Philosophus</term> <note>In this context, a "Philosopher" refers to a master of alchemy or the "Hermetic Philosophy."</note>, with whom I struck up a friendship. I shared my recipes with him, asking him to note the best ones according to his judgment: he pointed out ten or twelve that seemed most promising to him. When the plague ceased, I returned to my former home and began to test these shortly after my arrival. I worked through the entire subsequent winter until the Feast of St. John, with exactly as much profit as I had gained from the previous attempts: indeed, my four hundred crowns had "increased" such that I could count only seventy of them left. Yet I did not lose heart.

A certain Abbot had a recipe sent from a friend in Rome, from the court of **Cardinal Armagnac** <note>Georges d'Armagnac (c. 1501–1585), a powerful French cardinal and diplomat known for his interest in alchemy and the arts.</note>. I contributed one hundred crowns to this, and he the same amount, so that we might test it at our shared expense. Having built furnaces of different shapes than others—since we had need of a most excellent **water of life** <term>aqua vitæ</term> <note>Distilled alcohol or concentrated spirits, believed by alchemists to be a powerful solvent.</note> for the dissolution of a mark or a half-pound of gold—we bought a large vat of the most generous wine. From this, using a **pelican** <term>pellicanum</term> <note>A circulatory distillation vessel with two side-arms that feed condensed liquid back into the body, named for its resemblance to a pelican pecking its own breast.</note>, we prepared a vast quantity of that water, frequently rectified, using many glass vessels bought for this purpose. Afterwards, having first calcined our gold for an entire month, we placed one mark of it and four marks of the said water into two very thick glass **retorts** <term>retorta</term> <note>A glass vessel with a long, downward-pointing neck used for distillation.</note>, one entering into the other. Once sealed and both placed in two large round furnaces, we also bought charcoal at a price of thirty crowns in a single purchase, to maintain the fire beneath them continuously for an entire year, so that in the meantime we might test something in other recipes...

->## THE TRAVELS AND LABORS OF DENIS ZACHAIRE ##<-

# DIONYSIUS ZACHAIRE #

...[we were laboring], from which we achieved no more utility than from that first great work; namely, absolutely nothing from either. We would have tended the fire for infinite years before the **congelation** <note>The process of turning a liquid into a solid, often the final stage in creating the Stone.</note> would have occurred in the bottom of the vessels, as the recipe promised, since no **dissolution** <note>The breaking down of a solid substance into a liquid state; alchemists believed "nothing is transformed unless it is first dissolved."</note> had preceded it. However, we were not working with the proper material, nor was that the true **water of solution** <term>aqua solutionis</term> <note>A specialized solvent, often a mineral acid or "philosophical" water, intended to break down gold to its primal essence.</note> which ought to dissolve our gold, as was shown by experience. For we found the gold powder still whole, or only slightly reduced in size, which we then threw over **quicksilver** <note>Mercury, the liquid metal central to many alchemical theories.</note> as the recipe instructed, but in vain. 

We took this misfortune badly, and especially the Abbot. Like a most excellent public secretary, he had boasted before his monks that he expected nothing except the successful end of the work, after which he would liquefy the leaden fountain in the monastery and convert it into gold. He was forced to reserve those plans for another time, so that later he might recover the expenses he had meanwhile incurred through a passing German operator—an experiment he tried in vain in my absence while I was in Paris. 

The Abbot, having eventually regained his spirit, persuaded me to gather on my part three hundred or four hundred crowns, to which he would add an equal amount. Taking these funds, I was to travel to Paris, where the number of those laboring in this art is infinite. I was to dwell among them and various practitioners for a time, until I had found some perfected work to be shared between us like brothers. 

Once this pact was made, I again drew up the deeds for my possessions and, coming to Paris, I brought eight hundred crowns. My intention was not to leave there until I had either acquired or discovered what I desired. I departed not without the greatest offense to all my parents and friends; they would have gladly promoted me to a man of senatorial rank in our homeland, believing me to be a most ready legal expert. 

But I, resisting them and pretending that I would buy some state office with this money, said my farewells. I equipped myself for the journey on the day after the feast of the Nativity <note>December 26th.</note> and reached Paris three days after the feast of the Kings <note>January 9th, three days after Epiphany.</note>. For the first month, I chose to remain hidden and unknown. 

Soon after, however, I began to frequent artists, goldsmiths, founders, glass-makers, furnace-builders, and others. I established such a network that before the second month ended, more than a hundred operators had become my familiar friends. Some were working on the **tinctures of metals** <note>The "staining" or "dyeing" of base metals to look like gold or silver.</note> through **projections** <term>projectio</term>, others through **cementations** <term>cementatio</term> <note>A dry process of refining gold by heating it with powdered minerals.</note>, and some through dissolutions. Many worked through the conjunction of the essence of the stone commonly called <term>smirilli</term> <note>original: "smirilli". Likely emery or corundum, used here as a symbolic or literal alchemical agent.</note>; some through long **decoctions** <note>Prolonged heating of a substance in a liquid.</note>, some in the extraction of "Mercuries" from metals, and others in the **fixation** <note>The process of making a volatile substance stable under heat.</note> of these. 

So frequent was our gathering—sometimes in private houses, other times in the great cathedral <note>referring to Notre Dame de Paris.</note>—that even feast days and Sundays were not spared. Some said among themselves: "If only we had the means to repeat our work, we would reach perfection!" Others said: "If our vessel had remained whole, the matter...

### LITTLE WORK ###

->**THE TRAVELS AND LABORS OF DENIS ZACHAIRE**<-

# DENIS ZACHAIRE #

...seemed to be going well: some claimed that if we had possessed a copper vessel that was perfectly round, we would have achieved the **fixation** <note>The process of making a volatile substance, like mercury, stable under heat so it does not evaporate.</note> of **Mercury** <note>original: "Mercurium"</note> with **the moon** <note>original: "luna"; the alchemical name for silver.</note>. In short, not one of these men ever performed a task that lacked its own excuses, to which I still turned a deaf ear for a little while; for the useless expenses I had incurred through such persuasions kept refreshing my memory of past failures. Meanwhile, a certain Greek, who was considered learned by reputation, approached a treasurer known to me, promising him "mountains of gold" from the fixation of **cinnabar** <term>cinabaris</term> <note>A bright red mineral consisting of mercury sulfide, the most common source of elemental mercury.</note>. This news provided an opportunity for me and my friend to spend money on our own behalf to carry out this work. Since pure silver broken into filings was required for the task, we purchased three marks of it. From this, our worker formed certain nails by adding a kind of artificial paste mixed with powdered cinnabar, which he then cooked for the appropriate time in a closed potter's jar. Finally, having dried them, he "flashed" them through the **cupel** <note>original: "cupellam fulminabat"; a cupel is a small porous bowl used in assaying to separate precious metals from base metals. The "flash" or "lightning" is the bright shimmer seen when the silver becomes pure.</note>, so that we recovered the three marks of pure silver and a little bit more, which he claimed had been produced from the cinnabar: asserting that our own silver, placed there previously, had vanished into smoke. God alone could have known where the profit was, for we did not; I for my part had lost thirty **crowns** <note>original: "coronatos"; a gold coin used in France.</note> or more, or rather, spent them in vain. The rumor of these "nails" spread through the entire city of Paris, so that there was no one who had not heard of them, especially among those accustomed to the works of **sophistication** <note>In alchemy, "sophistication" refers to the art of adulterating or "stretching" precious metals with cheaper ones to make them appear more valuable than they are.</note>, just as previously a rumor had been spread about copper apples used for fixing mercury with silver. Finally, a certain nobleman arrived who was remarkably expert in these sophistications—so much so that he even turned a profit from it by selling his works to goldsmiths. I struck up a friendship with him, though not without expense, so that he would not think me a man of poor means.

I spent an entire year in his company before he declared even the smallest thing to me. At last, he finally shared his **secret** <note>original: "arcanum"</note> with me, which although he valued very highly, proved to be nothing perfect. Nevertheless, I wrote to my Abbot regarding everything that had happened, and I sent him a copy of this last work along with the "practice" of the aforementioned nobleman. He wrote back to me, urging me to remain in Paris for another year and not to fear the expenses, especially since I had stumbled upon a secret that he considered a significant beginning. However, I had already resolved in my mind not to use any material that did not persist in the same state it had first appeared—proposing to myself that I should not work, nor should anyone labor, merely to become a rogue and an impostor who grows rich through the loss of others. Nevertheless, I stayed for another year as he had written, adding to the two that had already passed. I frequented now this person, now that one, seeking out those of whom it was commonly believed they possessed something good and perfect. I had consumed almost all my money when the Abbot wrote to me again, commanding that as soon as I had seen and read his **letter** <note>original: "literas"</note>, I should come to him without delay. This I did, for I did not wish to break my promised brotherly faith. Upon my arrival...

### THE WORKS OF DENIS ZACHAIRE ###

# DENIS ZACHAIRE #

...he presented letters from the King of Navarre <note>original: "Rege Navarræ"; likely Henry II of Navarre, who was known for his interest in the occult and sciences.</note> (who seemed curious about these matters) sent to him, so that he might arrange with me—if I wished to do the King a favor—to go to the Court immediately and teach the secret of that nobleman, as well as other things he had heard I knew from reports. He promised a reward of three or four thousand **crowns** <note>original: "coronatorum"; the *écu*, a gold coin used in France.</note>. This sum so inflamed the Abbot that he could not have appeared happier if the money were already hidden in his purse; nor could he rest until I had set out for the Court. When I arrived there, I was unable to begin work for six weeks because the necessary materials had to be sought from elsewhere. 

Having finally finished the commissioned work, none of the reward I expected came to pass. For although the King had intended to reward my labors (to say nothing of the favor and friendship shown to me by the inhabitants and courtiers—though by very few of them in truth), his officials and the highest nobles nevertheless dissuaded the King from his good opinion of me. These were the very men who had been the primary cause of my coming. Thus, I was dismissed by the King empty-handed, given only a word of thanks. He promised that if I could find any **confiscations** <note>Property or assets seized by the state which the King could then grant to others.</note> in his territories over which he had power, he would grant them to me. Disturbed by this tedious response, I did not wish to trust such vain promises, which had been all too familiar to me in the past.

I returned to the Abbot quite dissatisfied, but not before visiting on my way a certain religious Doctor, most excellent in philosophy, whose reputation for singular learning was significant. This man drew me away quite strongly from **sophistications** <term>sophisticationibus</term> <note>In an alchemical context, "sophistication" refers to the fraudulent imitation or debasement of precious metals using alloys or surface treatments.</note>. After he learned that I had devoted myself to the study of philosophy to the point of receiving a Master's degree (as they call it), as I had told him, he said he grieved deeply that I had not possessed the best possible books before I had so uselessly consumed both time and wealth in such diabolical sophistications. 

I told him about this latest work, and he immediately judged that it could not withstand many tests. Therefore, he kindly urged me to abstain entirely from these errors henceforth and to read the books of the ancient Philosophers more attentively to gain knowledge of their true **matter** <note>The "First Matter" or *Prima Materia*, the fundamental, pure substance that alchemists believed was the starting point for creating the Philosopher's Stone.</note>, in which the highest perfection of this science seemed to consist. 

Therefore, I hurried my journey back to the Abbot to give an account of the expenses I had incurred in Paris and to give him his share of the reward I had supposedly received from the King of Navarre. When I had narrated everything, he was saddened, mostly because I did not want to persevere in the work; for he believed me to be an industrious operator. However, the kind words he used could not prevent me from embracing the Doctor's advice, owing to the clear reasons he had put forward. After settling the accounts with the Abbot, it was found that out of our eight hundred shared crowns, only ninety remained for each of us. Having said our goodbyes, we parted ways: I...

### THE WORKS OF DENIS ZACHAIRE ###

->OPUSCULUM.<-

...Indeed, having returned home so that I might obtain more money from my **tenants** <note>original: "arrendatoribus"; those who leased his lands.</note>, and having received those funds, I set out for Paris once again. I had made a firm resolution with myself that, once I arrived, I would not leave my lodgings until I had reached a perfect and final **understanding** <note>original: "resolutionem"; here meaning a theoretical conclusion or solution to the alchemical puzzle.</note> through the reading of various authors of our natural philosophy. This was to be done before I finally laid my hand to our **Great Work** <term>The *Magnum Opus*, the process of creating the Philosopher’s Stone.</term>, leaving behind all the **sophistries** <note>original: "sophisticationibus"; the fraudulent or deceptive methods used by "sophists" or fake alchemists.</note> of their wicked authors.

Thus, I arrived in Paris on the day after **All Saints** <note>November 2, 1546.</note> in the year 1546. I purchased several books for the price of ten **crowns** <note>original: "coronatorum"; the gold *écu*.</note> concerning this philosophy—some in print and others not—by both ancient and modern writers. These included *The Assembly of the Philosophers* <note>original: "Turba Philosophorum"; one of the oldest Latin alchemical texts.</note>, Bernard of Trevisan, *The Lament of Nature*, and many other treatises not yet printed. Having rented a room in the **Saint-Marceau suburb** <note>original: "suburbio Marceo"; the Faubourg Saint-Marceau, then a district favored by students and artisans.</note>, I remained there with the boy who served me, visiting no one in the meantime, and studying assiduously day and night for an entire year with the greatest diligence. Before the first month was even over, I began to propose one theory to myself, then another; now expanding one, now changing it entirely. I planned to do this until I finally stumbled upon one in which no variation or contradiction of philosophical opinions could be found. During these months, a good part of the second year also passed before I could elicit any stable knowledge from them.

Being situated in the midst of these perplexities, it seemed expedient to visit **honest operators** in this divine work, leaving behind the **sophists** whom I knew to be (as they say) as far off as the sky from the truth and misleading others. However, the ambiguity that kept me from my studies only increased, especially as I considered the various and diverse methods of working among them. For while one worked with gold alone, another used gold with **Mercury**, another mixed in lead—which he called "sounding" lead because it had passed through a retort with quicksilver—another likewise converted metals into quicksilver using various and diverse **simples** <term>Individual chemical or medicinal ingredients.</term> through **sublimation**. Another worked with **black ink** <note>original: "attramento nigro"; likely referring to vitriol or iron sulfate, which is black in certain states.</note>, which he asserted was the true matter that **Ramon Llull** <note>A famous Majorcan philosopher and mystic to whom many alchemical works were (often spuriously) attributed.</note> used in the composition of his Great Stone.

If one person worked with an **alembic** <term>An early chemical still used for distillation.</term>, another was found using many other different vessels of glass, some of brass, copper, lead, or silver, and even gold. Likewise, some performed their **distillations** <note>original: "decoctiones"; literally "boilings-down."</note> with a fire of large coals, others with wood, some with the **fermenting remains of grapes** <note>original: "floribus racemorum"; the pomace or marc left after pressing grapes, which provides a low, steady heat.</note>, others by the rays of the Sun, and others in **Mary’s bath** <term>The *balneum Mariae* or bain-marie; a vessel of hot water used to provide gentle, indirect heat.</term>. Such a variety of operations, combined with the contradictions in the books, brought me almost to the point of losing heart. But, raised up again by the Divine Spirit, I applied myself once more to a serious reading of the books, with even greater diligence and attention...

### Page 720 ###

...I began to reread the writings of **Raymond Lull** <note>original: "Raymundi Lullij"; a major 13th-century philosopher to whom many alchemical works were attributed.</note>, especially in the *Testament* and the *Codicil*, which I compared with a certain letter he wrote, while on the brink of death, to King Robert, and with a certain writing given to me by a teacher <note>original: "doctore"; likely a reference to his previous tutor or a scholar in Paris.</note>, which had been useless to him. This led me, contrary to all the previous notions I had seen, to finally arrive at one single conclusion. I found it to be such that it agreed with all others, and also with that resolution made by **Arnaldus de Villanova** <note>A 13th-century physician and alchemist.</note>, the teacher of Lull in this art, near the end of his *Great Rosary* <note>original: "Rosarij sui"; the *Rosarium Philosophorum*, a foundational alchemical text.</note>. 

Remaining in this opinion, I did nothing else but assiduously read and meditate upon my resolution day and night, until the time came for me to receive my income <note>original: "census"; the rents from his lands.</note>, so that I might return home to work. 

When I was finally at home, I intended to put what I had resolved into effect, having first made provision for all things that are necessary. First, I built a furnace, and I began to work on the day after **Easter** <note>Early Spring, 1547.</note>. I faced many impediments, of which I will make no mention here, aside from the frequent rebukes of my parents and friends, and of the neighbors. 

Some said to me: "Hey, what are you turning over in your mind? Have you not already spent enough useless sums on these trifles, I ask you?" Another warned me that unless I abstained from handling so much charcoal, the common people would suspect me of **counterfeiting money** <note>original: "fabricatione monetæ falsæ"</note>, as they had already begun to murmur about the matter. 

Another came, who asserted that the citizens and even the most prominent men wondered why I did not pursue the profession of **Law** <term>Jurisprudence; Zachaire had previously attained the rank of Licentiate in Law at Toulouse.</term>, especially since I was a Licentiate, so that I might reach a higher administrative office in the Commonwealth. 

Those who were more closely related and more familiar to me rebuked me daily without intermission, saying: "When will you finally put an end to these follies and the squandering of your paternal inheritance? It would be better to turn such useless expenses toward the payment of debts and the purchase of some office." Nor did that seem enough, for they even threatened me that, unless I desisted, they would ensure that the officers of Justice would rush into the house and break all my instruments along with the rest. 

"If there is no respect for us," they said, "nor for your other friends, at least have some regard for yourself. Consider that although you are thirty years old, or thereabouts, you seem to be fifty. Thus your beard is turned almost white by the great labors suffered since your youth for the sake of some **vain opinion** <note>Meaning his belief in alchemy.</note>." 

You may judge whether these words stung me most bitterly—especially since I saw my work succeeding better every day. I insisted upon it pertinaciously and most constantly, having despised even those and other intervening impediments, especially the **plague** <note>The bubonic plague was a recurring threat in 16th-century France.</note>, which raged through the whole summer, so that even all business ceased. Indeed, every day I beheld the divisions of the **three colors** <note>The *nigredo* (black), *albedo* (white), and *rubedo* (red); the traditional sequence of chemical changes indicating success in the Great Work.</note> which the Philosophers write appear before the perfection of the **Divine Work** <term>The *Opus Divinum*, or the creation of the Philosopher’s Stone.</term>. All of these, by the grace...
