# THE LITTLE WORK #

### Page 721 ###

...one after another, and then on the very day of **Easter** the following year, I saw the perfection <note>The successful completion of the "Great Work" or the creation of the Philosopher's Stone.</note>. This was proven by an experiment performed on **quicksilver** <note>original: "vivum argentum"; mercury, the primary material in many alchemical processes.</note> heated in a crucible, which was converted into **pure gold** before my eyes in less than an hour, using only a tiny amount of this **divine powder** <note>original: "pulvere divino"; the finished Alchemical Stone or projection powder.</note>. God knows with how much joy I was filled. Not that I was boastful or proud before the world because of this success, but secretly giving immortal thanks to God, who had deigned to hear my prayers through **JESUS CHRIST** His son our Lord, I prayed further that He might illuminate my heart and intellect with His grace, so that I might use it for the honor and praise of His glorious name. 

The next day, I immediately prepared myself for a journey toward my **Abbot**, so that I might fulfill the faith I had promised him; but he had died six months prior. For this reason, I was struck with the greatest grief, as well as by the death of the other **Doctor** <note>Likely the tutor Zachaire mentioned earlier in his narrative.</note>, which was reported to me on the road while passing not far from his monastery. Therefore, I went to a certain place assigned to a close relative of mine before I left my homeland, to wait for him to come to me. I had left this man at my home with power of attorney to sell all my paternal estates, so that he might satisfy my creditors and secretly distribute the remainder to the poor and needy, and so that my parents and others might become sharers in that gift with which God had willed to honor me. 

Most people, and almost all others, thought I was acting out of despair and had sold everything because of the shame of such great and useless expenses, so that I might flee to foreign lands and hide unknown—as my relative told me when he arrived on the first of **July**. Afterward we went to **Lausanne**, situated in **Savoy**, so that from there we might proceed to a certain famous trade center in **Germany**, with a very small retinue, so that I might not become known even to those who might read this little work of mine while I am still living. Indeed, I composed this only to turn good and pious men away from **deceptions** <term>original: "sophisticationibus"; in alchemy, this refers to fraudulent or superficial "recipes" that only mimic the appearance of gold without true transmutation.</term> and toward the right path of perfection in this divine work. As a conclusion to this first part, I recall to everyone's memory what the Poet sang:

> *Happy is he whom the dangers of others make cautious.* <note>original: "Felix quem faciunt aliena pericula cautum"; a common Latin proverb derived from various classical sources.</note>

So let them learn from my errors to flee from useless expenses made in deceptions. On the contrary, they should patiently and constantly read and understand good authors before setting their hand to the work, always praying to God for grace and sincere understanding. For one does not arrive here by fate or luck, but by a divine calling alone, rather than by study. To those to whom it has been given, there will also be given a way to hide it from the unworthy and reveal it to others who are upright, so that not all may understand equally. Likewise, the grace to use it well will be given, for the honor of the **Most High**, the giver of lights.

->So be it.<-

# THE SECOND PART OF THE LITTLE WORK OF DENIS ZACHAIRE #

### The part in which the author teaches the method and standard for reading the natural Philosophers according to a very easy method. ###

**I**n the first book of the *Physics*, **Aristotle** teaches that one should not argue against those who deny fundamental principles, but rather with those who admit the truth, yet through ignorance (let such ignorance be worth what it may) are incautious, failing to see the snake lurking beneath the grass <note>original: "anguem sub hac herba latentem"; a classical idiom for hidden danger or deception.</note>. Because this is placed before their eyes, they are unable to discern the false colors presented to them. But I have understood the author in this part as not being sufficiently willing to explain, so I pass on to better things, as he continues to say: "I have wished," he says, "to write this little work for good men and students of this art <note>The "art" of alchemy.</note>, by which they may be able to gain no small fruit and utility in reading the authors, understanding obscurities and veils, and the confusion spread by disordered variety." Therefore, to meet these needs and help my listeners, so that I do not divide the narrative, I will first state by whom this science was primarily discovered and passed into the successive knowledge of some; then which authors I have used in the composition of this work, and also the reason why they wrote so obscurely.

Next, we shall prove with certain arguments the truth and certainty of the art, likewise responding to the more apparent arguments brought against it. Thirdly, we will teach that our art is natural, and in what part; likewise why it is called "**divine**" because of its principal operations, therein declaring the manifest errors of those working in this time. Finally, we shall declare the works of nature beneath the earth used by her in the generations of metals, in imitation of which craftsmen must work above the earth. Afterward, we will indicate the matter <note>The "materia prima" or starting material for the alchemist's work.</note> necessary for this work; and finally, we will harmonize the principal terms used in this art, and the seemingly contradictory opinions of the ancient Philosophers, for the benefit of the **sons of the art** <note>A traditional term for alchemical initiates and dedicated students.</note>, and to the greatest disgrace, ignominy, and confusion of the detractors. We shall do each of these things through the authorities of the most ancient and learned Philosophers, lest the detractors think they are being exposed by some modern person along with their impostures.

To better teach who were the first inventors of our science, there is the doctrine of the **blessed Apostle James**, which we should recall to memory, which is held thus: "**Every good gift and every perfect gift is from above, coming down from the Father of lights**," etc. <note>James 1:17. Zachaire uses this to argue that alchemy is a gift from God, not merely a human invention.</note>. This sentence is general, and therefore it also suits our intention, especially because our science is so divine and so supernatural (specifically in the **second operation** <note>In alchemy, the "first operation" often refers to the purification of materials, while the "second operation" refers to the more complex transformation into the Elixir or Stone.</note>) that it has always been, and still is, impossible for men to understand it by any study or any industry whatsoever [without divine grace].

<page-num>723</page-num>
<header>A Little Work.</header>
<sig>Zz 2</sig>

...[even if] they are the wisest of all and the most learned Philosophers, unless it is first inspired by God. For in this area, all our natural reason and experience fail us. Wherefore it is rightly written by some that this secret is reserved by God for His own—for those who fear and honor Him—as that great prophet of ours, **Hermes**, says:

> I have it (he says) from no other, nor through any other, than from God through His divine inspiration.

**Alphidius** <note>An Arabic alchemist frequently cited in medieval Latin texts, often identified with al-Kindi or a similar figure.</note> confirms this very thing with these words:

> Know, my son, that God has reserved this art for the descendants of **Adam**, and especially for the truly poor. <note>In alchemical literature, "the poor" often refers to those who are humble in spirit or those who have exhausted their worldly wealth in search of the Stone.</note>

**Geber** <note>The Latinized name of Jabir ibn Hayyan (c. 721–815 AD), considered the father of chemistry and the most influential authority in medieval alchemy.</note> affirms the same in his *Summa* <note>Referring to the *Summa Perfectionis Magisterii*, the most famous alchemical textbook of the Middle Ages.</note> saying:

> Our science is in the power of God, who out of His mercy gives it to whom He wills.

Therefore, it is not within the power of men, nor was it devised by them. But insofar as the art itself is natural, or imitates nature in its primary operations, there are various opinions regarding the first inventor of this imitation. Some assert it was **Adam**; others **Aesculapius** <note>The Greek god of medicine and healing.</note>; some wish for **Enoch** to have had the first knowledge of it, who they say was actually **Hermes**, to whom the Greeks attributed so much honor that they called him the inventor of all occult arts. For my part, I would gladly agree with this last opinion, since it is most certain that he was a most excellent Philosopher, as appears from his writings. He most diligently scrutinized the causes of things through experiments in natural matters; once these were understood, he likewise became aware of the matter which nature uses in the hollows of the earth to generate metals. For as many as have imitated nature have all arrived at a true knowledge of this art, such as **Pythagoras**, **Plato**, **Socrates**, **Zeno**, **Haly**, **Senior Rafis**, **Geber**, **Morienus**, **Bonus**, **Arnaldus de Villanova**, **Raymundus**, and many others whom it would be tedious to enumerate. From all of these, as from the foremost authorities, we have composed this present little work of ours, not without the greatest labor, as their own books testify. For they wrote in such a manner (as they set the fear of God before their eyes) that it is impossible to reach the knowledge of this art solely by reading their books; as **Geber** says in his *Summa*:

> It is not (he says) that the son of the art <note>original: "filius artis"; a traditional term for a dedicated student or initiate of alchemy.</note> should lose heart in this divine work: for if he meditates assiduously on the causes of natural compositions, he will finally arrive where his mind tends.

On the contrary, whoever expects to find it by means of our books alone will attain the goal slowly: for the Philosophers wrote in such a way (he says in another place) that they seem to congratulate themselves alone on the true practice, mixing the method of inquiry into it. Likewise, they placed the principal operations in various ways and in different chapters. He provides the reason: because if they had observed a clear order in their treatises, this divine science could have been understood by everyone on the first day, or in a single hour, so noble and admirable is it.

Having established that the art is a gift from God, he now addresses the deliberate obscurity of alchemical texts, explaining why the ancient masters used riddles and contradictions to hide their secrets from the unworthy.</meta>

<page-num>724</page-num>
<header>OF DIONYSIUS ZACHARIUS</header>

**Alphidius** <note>original: "Alphidius"; an Arabic alchemical authority, often cited in the Middle Ages as a source of ancient wisdom.</note> says: It must be believed that the Philosophers, our predecessors, hid their primary intention under enigmatic and equivocal speech, and through innumerable figures, lest the world suffer ruin through the open manifestation of their doctrine. For all agriculture, commerce, and whatever is necessary for the preservation of human life would perish: indeed, no one would wish to labor if he saw himself filled with such great wealth, and every person would despise necessity. Wherefore **Hermes** <note>Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary Hellenistic figure regarded as the founder of alchemy.</note>, at the beginning of his book, says by way of excuse:

> Little sons, there is no reason for you to think that the Philosophers hid this secret out of envy toward the learned and studious, but only so it would not become known to the wicked and the ignorant.

**Rosinus** <note>original: "Rosinus"; a Latinization of Zosimos of Panopolis, a 3rd-century Greco-Egyptian alchemist.</note> says: By this means [of open disclosure], the ignorant would be made equal to the wise, and a malicious, wicked man would use it for the detriment, ruin, and destruction of the whole people.

**Geber** <note>The Latinized name of Jabir ibn Hayyan, the most famous authority in medieval alchemy.</note> uses similar excuses in his *Summa*, in the chapter on the *Administration of the Solar Medicine* <note>The "Solar Medicine" refers to the Elixir or Philosopher's Stone capable of turning metals into gold (the Sun).</note>, saying: 

> There is no reason for the sons of doctrine to wonder why the Philosophers wrote their books obscurely: for they did not intend it for themselves, but wished this meaning to be veiled from the ignorant and unworthy under such a great variety and confusion of diverse operations; meanwhile, however, they laid out a path for the sons of wisdom, by which they might arrive at a knowledge of the art. 

For (as it is held in another place) they did not write the art which they possessed for themselves alone, but gave the means by which it might be known and obtained by others.

This, therefore, is the cause of the difficulty in the books of the Philosophers. For what can be more difficult than to be explained out of such innumerable contrarieties and contradictions—not only among many authors and across almost all of them, but even within a single author? As **Rasis** <note>original: "Rasis"; Abu Bakr al-Razi (c. 865–925 AD), a Persian physician and chemist known for his practical laboratory manuals.</note> says:

> I have demonstrated sufficiently in my books the true **ferment** <note>A substance added to the alchemical work to "leaven" the metal and initiate its transformation.</note>, which is indeed the work for the multiplication of **tinctures** <note>The "tincture" is the concentrated essence or "color" that transforms base metal into gold.</note> for metals; [yet] because in another place I said there was no true ferment, I leave the judgment of this opinion and these sayings to those who have a sound understanding and subtle discernment. 

Likewise, if one of them says our matter is of cheap price and of no value, found everywhere—as **Zeno** says in the *Assembly of the Philosophers* <note>original: "Turba Philosophorum"; one of the oldest and most famous Latin alchemical texts, presented as a debate among pre-Socratic philosophers.</note>—against this, in the same book, **Barseus** says that what is sought is not of small price. Another says the thing is most precious, not to be found without great expense. This man teaches the preparation of the matter in diverse vessels and with diverse operations, as Geber does in his *Summa*; yet soon you find another asserting that only one vessel is necessary for the divine work to be constructed, such as **Rasis**, **Lilius**, **Alphidius**, and others. In a book of the same **Rasis**, a time of nine months is given; in another, it is read that a year is necessary to finish this work, which **Rosinus** and **Plato** <note>In alchemical texts, "Plato" often refers to pseudo-epigraphical works attributed to the philosopher.</note> assert. 

Finally, such variety appears in their terms that it is impossible for the matter to be discovered by anyone, except by the inspiration of the Most High—either immediately, or through some good and wise man...

<meta>catchword: [wise] man</meta>

<summary>Zachaire explains that alchemists intentionally used riddles and contradictions to protect society from the economic chaos that would ensue if gold-making were common knowledge. He cites authorities like Geber, Rasis, and the Turba Philosophorum to illustrate how they vary their instructions on cost, time, and materials to hide the truth from the unworthy.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Dionysius Zacharius's explanation of the "Philosophy of Nature" (alchemy). Following the previous page’s discussion on why masters hide their secrets from the unworthy, Zacharius now addresses why the art is difficult to define and argues that all true alchemists, despite their confusing terminology, are actually describing the same single process.</meta>

<header>LITTLE WORK.</header>
<page-num>725</page-num>

...[becoming] wise in this art. The most powerful reason for this is that no one appears as an expert in this matter while living, but only admits it through writings after death; for the Philosophers <note>In alchemical literature, "Philosophers" specifically refers to the master alchemists of antiquity.</note> wished to keep the art, attained through such great labors, hidden from themselves if possible, so how much more from others. We should not, therefore, marvel at this alongside the common folk, but rather alongside the wise, as to what path must be taken to reach it. 

However, before we come to the second part of our division, we must answer the objection of slanderers who are accustomed to pick apart the labors of others because their own work lacks the true light. They will say that the doctrine of Aristotle in the seventh book of the *Physics* <note>original: "Physicorum"; Aristotle's work on the principles of nature.</note> was not observed, which states: "A definition is the true form of the subject defined." They argue that since I have undertaken to treat the true method of this science, I should have begun with a definition. I will refer these and similar critics back to the ancient authors who, when they tried to give a definition of the divine science and could not find one perfect and complete, were forced to admit that it is not possible—chiefly because it lacks "familiar principles," as **Morienus** <note>A legendary 7th-century hermit said to have taught the secrets of alchemy to King Khalid ibn Yazid.</note>, **Lilius** <note>Likely referring to the alchemical works attributed to Raymond Lully.</note>, and many others say. Therefore, they were content only with various descriptions by which they might demonstrate the effects of the art. 

As for my part, I will say what I think on this matter: **It is a part of natural philosophy teaching the way to perfect metals upon the earth, by imitating natural operations as closely as possible.** We assert this definition to be true for various reasons, especially since nothing is more certain among the Philosophers than that truth is found there, particularly where no contradiction appears—as the Philosopher <note>Commonly referring to Aristotle.</note> testifies.

However many have written in this art of old, whether in Hebrew, Greek, or Latin, or any other tongue, they have agreed among themselves—even if through different modes of treatment such as figures, double meanings, and riddles—so that they seem to have written in one and the same language and at the same time, though some preceded others by a hundred, two hundred, or a thousand years. **Senior** <note>original: "Senior"; refers to Senior Zadith (Zadith ben Hamuel), a 10th-century Arabic alchemist.</note>, regarding this opinion, says: 

> Although it appears in some way that the Philosophers treat diverse things under various and different names, in truth they understand nothing but a single thing. 

**Rhazes** <note>original: "Rhasis"; Abu Bakr al-Razi, a Persian polymath and key authority in medieval alchemy.</note> asserts the same in his *Book of Lights*, saying: 

> Under diverse opinions appearing to us at first glance as contrary, the Philosophers understood only one and the same thing. 

To this, testimony is given by the distinguished professors of other schools of thought, who, likewise writing about this divine art, affirm and show that this divine science concerns itself with one single thing. The opinion of the Philosopher <note>Aristotle</note> alone would suffice for us, which he places in the second book of the *Ethics*: 

> Everything that is rightly performed is accomplished by a single means. 

It is the opinion of all, therefore, that our divine work is completed by a single path. As **Geber** <note>The Latinized name of Jabir ibn Hayyan, the most famous authority in medieval alchemy.</note> testifies in his *Summa*: 

> Our science (he says) is not perfected through diverse things, but only through a single thing, to which we add nothing and from which we take nothing away, but only remove the superfluities, pre-

# LITTLE WORK

<page-num>726</page-num>

...[we have proven], separating them by preparation alone. Likewise, **Lilius** <note>original: "Lilius"; likely referring to Raymond Lully, a Catalan polymath to whom many alchemical works were attributed.</note> says: "Our Great Work is perfected by only one thing, one regimen, and one unique means." All the Philosophers who have written on this art up to now assert the same thing, although they may seem to be pulled in different directions. But the most powerful proof of our science, by which we are confirmed that it is most true, is the **experience** <term>experience: here used in the sense of empirical testing or "experimentum"</term> we have gained from it, as **Senior** <note>original: "Senior"; refers to Senior Zadith (Zadith ben Hamuel), a 10th-century alchemist.</note> and **Rhasis** <note>original: "Rhasis"; the Latinized name for Al-Razi, a famous Persian physician and alchemist.</note> say. 

Indeed, so that we may prove it to those who rightly happen to doubt, we must admit with the other Philosophers that it is contained in that part of philosophy which they call **operative** <term>operative: the practical, experimental branch of knowledge, as opposed to the purely theoretical</term>, and under **medicine**, which can prove its truth in no other way than from experience. Just as when medicine teaches that Rhubarb purges bile, this cannot be better perceived than by the eye and by experiment through the application of the said simple remedy. 

And so we conclude in our art: if it is seen that **Mercury** <note>original: "Mercurium"; quicksilver.</note> can be coagulated by the smoke of lead alone, and that a most perfect medicine can be made and composed of **vitriols** <note>original: "atramentorum"; literally "inks," but in alchemical Latin, it refers to vitriols or metallic sulfates used for coloring and transformation.</note>, consistent with the nature and qualities of metals, by which other imperfect metals can be perfected simply by **projection** <term>projection: the final stage of the alchemical work where the "Philosopher's Stone" or "Medicine" is cast onto molten base metal to transform it into gold or silver</term> performed upon them—especially since even common minerals congeal Mercury and lead it back to its own nature. 

How much more will perfect substances, properly prepared through our art, dissolve it and lead it back with other imperfect metals, through the power and abundance of their **decoction** <term>decoction: the process of ripening or "cooking" a substance through steady heat to reach maturity</term>, which they possess through the administration of our art. To prove this intention of ours more firmly before men, so that they may more readily agree with its truth and certainty, let us cite the opinion of **Aristotle** from the fourth book of the *Meteorology* <note>original: "Meteor[ologica]"; Aristotle’s treatise on the elements and the formation of minerals, which served as a primary scientific authority for alchemists.</note>: 

"Everything (he says) that produces the same operation as some composite substance is identical in all respects, just as everything that performs the function of an eye is an eye." In the same way, since our gold, composed by our art, is similar in every respect to the mineral <note>meaning natural gold found in the earth</note> (where the whole controversy of the dispute lies: whether the gold composed by us is true gold), we seem to have sufficiently shown, based on the Philosopher’s <note>Aristotle's</note> opinion, that our art is true and most certain. 

Those who have seen its practical application admit it is sufficiently proven to them, as do others from whom we have taken the most probable authorities among the Philosophers on this matter. In the same book of the *Meteorology*, in the fourth chapter on **Digestions** <note>original: "Digestionum"; referring to the natural process of heat maturing a substance.</note>, he says thus, or similar: "Whatever is destined for perfection, and has remained as such because of a defect in digestion, can be perfected by constant digestion." 

Such are all imperfect metals, since they were directed toward gold by nature from the beginning of their composition, and would be led to that end—namely, gold—by nature itself, and they are only as they are because of imperfect digestion. Therefore, we shall hear what follows in that place where we discuss the fourth book of our division. What nature, therefore, wished to accomplish beneath the earth, we [accomplish] above the earth by imitation through our art, and by projection...

### LITTLE WORK

<page-num>727</page-num>

...we achieve, as will be heard more broadly below in the second-to-last part of our division. Again, since elements contrary to one another in their qualities—as the **Philosopher** <note>original: "Philosophus"; referring to Aristotle, the primary authority on natural philosophy in the Middle Ages.</note> says in the second book of *On Generation*—are mutually convertible into each other, how much more will the metals themselves (which are of one and the same substance and matter, and are not contrary in their qualities) be converted, this into that, most easily. For this reason **Hermes** <note>original: "Hermes"; referring to Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary founder of the alchemical tradition.</note> said that their procreation is circular, yet in a somewhat improper way, as he himself confesses; for they are not created by nature for that end—that imperfect things should come from perfect ones—but rather the opposite. Therefore, their generation is not entirely circular, except in part. 

Although these and similar reasons are sufficient by themselves for the confirmation of the art, yet because the **sophists** <term>sophists: here referring to skeptical critics who use logical arguments to deny the possibility of alchemy.</term> always bring forward arguments to the contrary which resist the truth, we shall bring them forward. We do this so that these more difficult arguments—which might disturb the soul and mind of students, holding them suspended between doubt and resolution—do not become too wordy for this little work, and so that students may learn to refute other arguments from the solutions provided here.

From the authority of the Philosopher in the fourth book of the *Meteorology* (which was also the opinion of **Avicenna** <note>original: "Avicennae"; Ibn Sina, the Persian polymath whose works on medicine and philosophy were standard texts.</note> and **Albertus Magnus** <note>original: "Alberti Magni"; a 13th-century Dominican friar and bishop who wrote extensively on nature and alchemy.</note>), they argue thus: "Alchemists work in vain trying to perfect metals unless they reduce them into **primary matter**." <term>primary matter: Latin "materia prima"; the formless, fundamental substance that underlies all physical reality.</term> Since they do not do this, they assert that the works of all alchemists are sophistical (fraudulent) by conclusion, as Albert himself says in this manner: "However many dye metals with various simple materials into different colors are impostors, unless they reduce them into primary matter."

Many very wise men have tried to solve this argument, as it is among the most apparent. Some of these say that although the imperfect metals are not reduced through **projection** <term>projection: the act of casting the Philosopher's Stone or "medicine" onto a base metal to transmute it.</term>, nonetheless in the composition of the **medicine** <note>original: "medicinae"; in alchemy, the "medicine" is another name for the Elixir or Philosopher's Stone that "heals" imperfect metals.</note> a similar reduction occurs—namely, into **sulfur** and **quicksilver** <note>original: "sulphur & argentum vivum"; the two fundamental principles of metals in alchemical theory.</note>, which are the true matter of metals, as will be discussed more broadly below in the fourth member of our division. It is sufficient, therefore, for the reduction of the active agent alone to occur, and then the highest perfection is acquired through **decoction** <term>decoction: a process of heating or "cooking" a substance in a liquid to extract its essence or mature it.</term>, even if no reduction of the **passive subject** <note>The "passive subject" refers to the base metal being acted upon by the alchemical agent.</note> occurs. In this opinion were **Arnald of Villanova** <note>original: "Arnaldus de Villanova"; a famous 13th-century physician and alchemist.</note> in his *Great Rosary*, whom **Raymond Lully** <note>original: "Raymundus Lullius"; a polymath and mystic to whom many alchemical texts were attributed.</note> followed in his *Testament*. 

With all due peace and reverence owed to these most grave authors, this opinion seems to contradict all the Philosophers too much. For since they concede that metals must be reduced to primary matter—which is a movement of **corruption** <note>original: "corruptionis"; in Aristotelian terms, "corruption" is the process of a thing losing its form so it can take on a new one.</note> according to **Aristotle**—they seem to want, by the mere fusion of our **divine stone** upon the metals, for these metals to be "corrupted" in that way and stripped of their first form. To concede this is too unworthy for any Philosopher. Many others bring forward different solutions, as can be seen in their books. I, however, shall bring forward my own solution. If indeed we were attempting to manufacture new metals, or from them stones or anything...

<meta>This page continues Zacharius's defense of alchemy, moving from theoretical arguments about the nature of metals to the practical and philosophical definitions of the "Divine Work." He specifically addresses why alchemy does not require metals to be reduced to their "primary matter" before transmutation.</meta>

-> OF DIONYSIUS ZACHARIUS <-

If anything foreign to metals were present, they would necessarily have to be led back to their **primary matter** <term>primary matter: the "prima materia," or the formless, original substance from which all things are made. Zacharius argues that since metals are already "metallic," they don't need to go all the way back to this chaotic state.</term>, and that by the means which have been spoken of. Since our only intention is to perfect imperfect metals into gold, without any transformation into substances different from their own nature, we purge and cleanse them through the **projection** <term>projection: the final stage of the alchemical process where the "Philosopher's Stone" is cast upon molten base metal to transform it into gold.</term> of our divine work, so that they arrive at an exuberant perfection. It is by no means necessary to reduce them to primary matter; for perfecting the imperfect is quite different from producing or generating something entirely new. Otherwise, one would conclude that half-cooked things must be reduced to their first form in order to be completely cooked: an idea indeed unworthy of any **Philosopher** <note>original: "Philosopho"; usually referring to Aristotle.</note>.

As for other objections usually raised against the chemical arts, I will dismiss them for now, because through the principles we have laid down, any other arguments based on the authority of **Avicenna** <note>original: "Avicennæ"; a Persian polymath whose views on alchemy were widely debated.</note> can be easily answered. I also remember the contradictions of **Aristotle** <note>original: "Aristotelis"</note> against alchemy raised in his youth. He said: "I have known the intent of those who deny our art, and of others who affirm it to be true." The former, such as Aristotle and many others, use certain arguments that are merely apparent in name only; the latter, however, say that this science cannot be proved by certain demonstrations, nor is it permitted to be, like all other sciences, since it proceeds in a manner contrary to all others. For it hides and veils the properties of its terms, while other sciences labor mostly on the declaration of their terms.

Therefore, following the order of our division, I will take up its third part, explaining the operations necessary for the execution of our divine work. First, I will explain the reason why it is called "natural" and "divine," so that the enormous errors of those working in this time may be recognized. Aristotle teaches that nature works under the earth in the procreation of metals by four qualities—or for better understanding, elements—namely fire, water, [air], and earth. Two of these contain the other two: [air] contains fire, and water contains air. Since therefore our matter consists [of water] and earth (as will be said further in the second-to-last part of our division), it is rightly called "natural," because the four elements enter into its composition. Two are manifest, under which the other two lie hidden, veiled from bodily eyes—namely fire and air—which must be perceived by the mental eyes, as **Raymond Lully** <note>original: "Raymundus Lullius"; a 13th-century philosopher and legendary figure in alchemical literature.</note> says in his *Codicil* <note>original: "Codicillo"</note>, in this manner: "Consider," he says, "the nature and property of the oil (which the sophisters call air, because they say it abounds more in its qualities); your eye does not judge its differences and properties." By these words, he sufficiently hints that the four elements in our divine work are not evident to the sight, which some have falsely thought, as will be said below where we declare our terms. This science is also called natural because in its first operation...

He defines the "Divine Work" as a natural process involving the four elements, some of which are hidden from the physical eye.</summary>

### TREATISE

...it imitates nature as diligently as it can: for it could not do so in all things, as **Geber** <note>original: "Geber"; the Latinized name of Jabir ibn Hayyan, an influential 8th-century chemist whose "Summa" was a cornerstone of medieval alchemy.</note> says in his *Summa*. The operations of the ancient **Natural Philosophers** <term>Natural Philosophers: Early scientists who studied the physical world, often blending what we now call physics, biology, and chemistry.</term> who preceded us are best confirmed in this way: after they had learned through the most diligent inquiries (as **Raymond Lully** <note>original: "Raymundus Lullius"; a 13th-century polymath and mystic.</note> says in his letter to King Albert, and **Albertus Magnus** <note>original: "Albertus Magnus"; a Dominican friar and bishop known for his works on nature.</note> in his treatise on *Simple Animals*) that nature, for the procreation of metals under the earth, works solely through continuous and assiduous **decoctions** <term>decoctions: long-term heating or "cooking" of a substance to refine and concentrate its essence.</term> of the true matter. By these, she separates the clean from the unclean, the pure from the impure, and the perfect from the imperfect, through continued evaporations. This is achieved partly by the heat of the mineral earth and partly by the heat of the Sun—which by itself does not complete that entire and perfect decoction—as they themselves confirmed.

This is declared very well by that good **Trevisan** <note>original: "Trevisanus"; referring to Bernard of Treviso, a legendary 15th-century alchemist.</note>, which experience also teaches us: for we see in the mines a diversity of metals and materials, some coarser, and others more subtle and pure, often raised up to the heights. Therefore, our science, by imitating nature, proceeds in its first operation through **sublimation** <term>sublimation: the process where a substance is heated until it turns into vapor and then solidifies again, used here to mean extreme purification.</term>, by which it may best purify our matter. For it would be impossible for us to prepare it otherwise, as Geber says in his *Summa*, and **Rhazes** <note>original: "Rasis"; a Persian physician and alchemist.</note> in his *Book of Lights* says: "The beginning of our work is to sublimate," which is why it is deservedly called natural.

For this reason, those who preceded us wrote that this work of ours is not "artificial." For whatever we do is nothing other than administering to nature, through art, the matter necessary for the composition of the work—which nature herself could not connect into this perfection because her actions are continuous, as Geber says in his *Summa*.

By reason of this so admirable conjunction of elements, our science is called **Divine**. This conjunction the Philosophers called the "second operation," and some called it "dissolution," asserting it to be the "secret of secrets," as **Pythagoras** <note>original: "Pythagoras"</note> says in the *Assembly of Philosophers* <note>original: "Turba Philosophorum"; one of the oldest and most influential Latin alchemical texts.</note>: "This is a great mystery, which God willed to be veiled from men." Likewise, Rhazes in his *Book of Lights*: "If you are ignorant of the true dissolution of our body, there is no reason for you to work; for if that is unknown, the rest will be useless." No one can learn this even from books, nor from the knowledge of natural causes; therefore it is truly called divine, as **Alexander** <note>original: "Alexander"</note> says.

Our body (which is the **Hidden Stone** <term>Hidden Stone: The Philosopher’s Stone in its unrefined or secret state.</term>) can by no means be known, nor seen, unless God Himself inspires this into us through His **Holy Spirit**, or teaches it through some living person, without which our science is nothing. This is the stone of which **Hermes** <note>original: "Hermes"; referring to Hermes Trismegistus, the mythical founder of alchemy.</note> speaks in his fourth treatise: "Our divine stone," he says, "must be known; it cries out continually: 'Defend me, and I will help you; give me what is mine, and I will in turn help you most excellently.'" About this same hidden body he speaks in his first treatise...

<meta>This page continues Dionysius Zacharius’s explanation of the alchemical process, focusing on the "conjunction" or union of substances. # DIONYSIUS ZACHARIUS
<note>original: "Dionysii Zacharii"; Denis Zacaire (1510–1556) was a French alchemist whose autobiographical account of his search for the Philosopher's Stone became a classic of the genre.</note>

...you: The Falcon, always crying from the mountain peak: "I am the white of the black, and the red of the yellow." <note>original: "Ego sum album nigri, & rubeum citrini"</note> The reason our science is useless without this **conjunction** <term>conjunction: the chemical and spiritual union of two opposing substances, often symbolized as a marriage of King and Queen.</term> is because at the time of the birth and procreation of our divine work, the volatile part carries the fixed part away with it. For otherwise, except through this marvelous and more-than-supernatural union, we could in no way bring it about that the work remains fixed in the fire: so that, as all the Philosophers command, the fixed might become volatile, and then the volatile become fixed again. This union must occur at the very hour of its birth, as **Haly** <note>original: "Haly"; likely referring to Khalid ibn Yazid or Haly Abenragel, figures central to the transmission of Arabic alchemy to the West.</note> says in his *Book of Secrets*: 

> Whoever does not find our stone at the hour of its birth, there is no reason to expect another in its place. 

For he who approaches our divine work without knowledge of its determined hour of birth will never achieve anything from his work except entirely useless labors and the pains of his own error. **Rhazes** <note>original: "Rasis"; the Latinized name of Abū Bakr al-Rāzī (c. 865–925), a Persian polymath and one of the most important figures in the history of chemistry.</note>, in his *Book of Precepts*, properly calls this same union the **weights of the Philosophers** <term>weights of the Philosophers: not necessarily physical weight, but the correct proportions and timing required for a successful reaction.</term> and the regimens, urging us to abstain from this divine work altogether if we do not know with the greatest exactitude the weights which the Philosophers have hidden above all other secrets, as is evident from their various writings. For where one might say such a divine union occurs on the seventh day, you will soon find another who asserts it is completed on the fortieth day; another on the hundredth; another toward the end of seven or nine months, as Rhazes does; another at the end of a year, like **Rosinus** <note>original: "Rosinus"; a Latinization of Zosimus of Panopolis, a 3rd-century Greco-Egyptian alchemist.</note>: you will hardly find two authors agreeing on this matter.

Yet there is only one and the same limit, one day, indeed only one and the same hour in which our union must occur for its proper **decoction** <term>decoction: the process of refining a substance through long-term, steady heat, often compared to "cooking."</term>. But because they swore a solemn oath not to reveal this greatest secret, they intentionally wrote of different timeframes, even though they agree among themselves on the single one—which, once known, the rest is nothing but "women's work and children's play," as **Socrates** <note>original: "Socrates"; often cited in alchemical texts as a legendary authority, though distinct from the historical Greek philosopher.</note> says: 

> Behold, I have shown you the true arrangement of white lead (that is, the true preparation of our matter, which first appears black like lead, and afterwards becomes white through our continuous cooking); if you have understood this well, the rest is nothing else but women's work and children's play. 

Suggesting by these words that no task is easier than ours once the union has occurred: which is indeed most true. Since there is no need for any other labor than the mere cooking of the two matters already joined: while they are cooking, the most desired rest is granted, as the **Philosopher** <note>Aristotle.</note> says in the 7th book of the *Ethics*: "Rest is far more delightful than any labor." That our final decoction is performed with rest, and without labor or torment, is testified by Rhazes in the *Book of Three Words*, saying: 

> All dissolutions, calcinations, sublimations, **whitenings** <term>whitenings: "dealbatio" in Latin; the stage where the matter turns white (the albedo).</term>, **reddenings** <term>reddenings: "rubificatio" in Latin; the final stage of the work (the rubedo).</term>, and the remaining operations which the Philosophers have written are necessary for the divine work n...

<meta>This page continues Dionysius Zacharius’s argument that the Great Work requires a singular, unified process. ### TREATISE

...our work is to be completed, occurring in the fire without ever being removed. **Pythagoras** asserts the same in the *Assembly of the Philosophers* <note>original: "Turba Philosophorum"; one of the oldest and most influential Latin alchemical texts, presented as a debate among ancient sages.</note>, saying:

> All regimes leading toward the divine work and its perfection are completed by decoction alone.

**Barseus** says the very same in that same book:

> Cooking, dyeing, and calcining <term>calcining: the process of heating a substance to high temperatures to reduce it to a powder or "calx," often to purify it.</term> must happen in this work, but truly all operations are to be perfected by decoction alone.

Lest the **Sophists** <note>In this context, "Sophists" refers to fraudulent or misguided alchemists who use complex chemical tricks rather than following the true laws of nature.</note> and detractors say that their operations are also nothing but decoctions, we shall cite other opinions of the ancient Philosophers, by which their errors may be exposed. **Alphidius** says:

> In the composition of our divine work, there is only one single matter (which they properly call water) and only one action—namely, decoction—which takes place in a single vessel without removal from the fire.

**King Solomon** <note>Solomon was often cited as an alchemical authority in the Middle Ages and Renaissance, credited with divine wisdom over nature.</note> testifies to the same thing regarding the preparation of our divine work (which he calls our sulfur):

> We have no need (he says) for anything beyond one single medium.

**Lilius** holds the same view:

> Our divine work (he says) occurs in only one vessel, by only one medium, and by a single decoction.

**Muhammad**:

> We have nothing (he says) but a single medium—namely, decoction—and one vessel, etc., by which we perfect our divine work into the white and the red. <note>The "white" and "red" refer to the two stages of the Philosopher's Stone: the "Little Magisterium" (turning metals to silver) and the "Great Magisterium" (turning metals to gold).</note>

**Avicenna** <note>Latinized name of Ibn Sina (c. 980–1037), the Persian polymath whose medical and philosophical works were foundational to Western science.</note> held the same opinion, speaking better than all others in this manner:

> All the disputations (he says)—that is, the operations—necessary for composing our divine work, take place in a single vessel, though it be a double one. <note>original: "in uno vase solo, duplici tamen"; likely referring to a "pelican" or a blind alembic where vapors circulate within a single unit.</note>

Therefore, the greatest part of those working in this time will be forced to admit their error, since there is not one of them who does not have three or four furnaces, and some have ten or twelve: this one for calcining, that one for dissolving, another for subliming <term>subliming: the process of heating a substance so it turns to vapor and then solidifies again on a cooler surface, used for purification.</term>, and innumerable vessels which they use. But truly, such men would work until the final day of the world before they reached perfection by this path, unless they correct their operations. 

I will remain silent for now regarding the "separation of elements" (as they call them) until the nature of the four elements is treated, where I shall speak about the limits of our art. It is enough for me at present to have demonstrated the method and the way of exposing and recognizing those workers who have gone astray in this art, as well as those who persist on the right path. For as I said before, and as will be said more extensively below, there is only one way of working: in a single vessel (which **Lullius** <note>Ramon Llull (c. 1232–1315); though many alchemical works were falsely attributed to him, he was considered a master of the "short way."</note> called the *Hymen*) and in a single small furnace (which **Trevisan** <note>Bernard of Trevisan (1406–1490), an Italian alchemist famous for his lifelong search for the Stone.</note> calls a closed, moist, vaporous, continuous, and digesting fire) without removal, until the decoction is completed.

There is, therefore, no need for such great instruments, nor for the expenses incurred for this purpose. I know there are many learned men, insisting upon their books, who work without any certainty; my rebuke will sit very poorly with them, since **Geber** <note>Latinized name of Jabir ibn Hayyan, the foundational figure of Islamic alchemy.</note> in his *Summa* teaches various preparations, both of sulfur and of quicksilver <term>quicksilver: the common name for Mercury, considered one of the two primary "parents" of all metals.</term>, and likewise of body and spirit. Likewise, **Rhazes**, in his book *The Perfect Magisterium*, says that bodies and spirits are by various pre-

<meta>This page continues the argument of Dionysius Zacharius, moving from the philosophical necessity of a unified process to the physical theory of how metals are formed. He transitions from debunking complex chemical "preparations" to explaining the nature of metallic humidity and the role of mercury as the base of all metals.</meta>

# OF DIONYSIUS ZACHARIUS

<page-num>732</page-num>

<warning>Text at the right margin is partially lost in the gutter fold.</warning>

...to be prepared by intermediate means, many of which he teaches. We have previously answered enough that these and similar things written by the Philosophers were written for no other reason than to veil and conceal the true preparation of our divine work in the fire. This Geber <note>original: "Geber," the Latinized name of Jabir ibn Hayyan, the foundational figure of Islamic alchemy.</note> attests to in his *Summa*, in the chapter on the differences of Medicines, saying: There is only one perfect medicine by which we are relieved of such great operations and burdens of preparation.

Now I shall set forth nature's way of working, generating metals in the hollows of the earth, which art <note>In alchemy, "Art" refers to the human practice of alchemy as an imitation of nature.</note> ought to imitate; and thereafter, I shall declare the true and necessary matter for their perfection above the earth. Since, therefore, this is the principal point in the art (as Geber says from the start of his *Summa*, and Avicenna <note>original: "Avicenna," the Latinized name of Ibn Sina, a Persian polymath who was respected for his mineralogical theories.</note>, instructing those who do not first know the true foundations of matters and minerals to abstain from the practice of this work), I will imitate the more excellent authors and those more skilled in minerals, declaring those things which are especially necessary for this matter.

It is the opinion of all the Philosophers that all things congealed by cold abound greatly in watery humidity in their first matter <term>first matter: or "materia prima," the formless base substance from which all things are made.</term>, as Aristotle <note>original: "Aristoteles," the Greek philosopher whose *Meteorologica* provided the scientific basis for medieval alchemy.</note> says in the fourth book of his *Meteorology*. Since, then, molten metals are congealed by cold, it is necessary that their first matter be rich in much aquatic humidity. 

Among these authors, Albertus Magnus <note>A 13th-century Dominican friar and bishop, one of the greatest medieval scholars of nature.</note> (who scrutinized minerals more sagaciously than all others) says that this watery humidity is not like other humidity which we commonly see in other compositions of nature. For that common humidity turns into smoke through the violence of fire. But molten metals are not reduced to vapor in this way; hence it must be concluded that their humidity is mixed with some matter that is retained in the fire and safe from its vehemence. 

Now, nothing resists fire more than a viscous <note>In the sense of "sticky" or "tenacious," referring to a substance that holds its parts together firmly.</note> humidity mixed with subtle parts of earth, as Bonus of Ferrara <note>original: "Bonus Ferrariensis," author of the *Precious Pearl*, an important 14th-century alchemical text.</note> says, and as experience teaches. Therefore, it is firmly to be believed that the humidity of metals is of this kind. 

Yet since experience teaches that certain impurities among these humidities pass away into smoke, while the metals are nonetheless not consumed, we must admit with the chief authors of our science that a twofold viscous humidity enters into the composition of metals: the extrinsic and the intrinsic. 

The first [extrinsic] is coarse and not well mixed with its subtle earthly matter, which is why it is easily burned by fire until it is consumed. But the latter [intrinsic], because it is extremely subtle and perfectly mixed with its subtle earth, causes both parts to constitute a single and simple matter; it can neither be separated from the other by fire nor consumed, unless it departs or remains in the fire as one. 

From this kind of humidity is procreated the quicksilver <term>quicksilver: or "argentum vivum," the common name for mercury, considered by alchemists to be a primary component of all metals.</term> that we see, as is also clear from experience. Arnaldus de Villanova <note>A 13th-century physician and alchemist famous for his medical and chemical writings.</note> testifies: "This," he says, "makes us more certain that both the aforementioned matters are most perfectly joined in it [quicksilver], for either the earth retains the humidity with it, or the humidity seizes the earth..."

<summary>Zacharius argues that alchemy must imitate nature's subterranean metal formation, specifically the fusion of "viscous humidity" and subtle earth. He defines mercury (quicksilver) as the perfect, fire-resistant balance of these two elements, distinguishing between impurities that burn away and the essential "intrinsic" humidity.</summary>

<keywords>Geber, Avicenna, Aristotle, Albertus Magnus, first matter, viscous humidity, quicksilver, mercury, extrinsic vs intrinsic humidity, metallic generation</keywords>

Having established that mercury (quicksilver) is the foundation, he now draws on authorities like Albertus Magnus and Geber to explain the dual nature of mercury—its fluidity and its earthy components—and introduces sulfur as the "agent" that coagulates it into solid metal.</meta>

# LITTLE TREATISE

<page-num>733</page-num>

...into the air. Albertus Magnus, most diligently investigating the causes of the composition of metals, understood this perfectly: namely, that quicksilver <note>original: "argentum vivum," literally "living silver."</note> is in constant motion and flow because each part alternately has dominion over the other; thus, the cause of the flow and motion is the rule of humidity, while the action of terrestrial dryness upon that humidity ensures that it does not stick to what it touches, nor does it make things wet. 

Hence Albert’s opinion is confirmed in his book *On Simple Minerals*: "The primary matter of metals," he says, "is a viscous, non-combustible humidity, joined by a strong mixture with a subtle earthy substance in the mineral caverns of the earth." This agrees perfectly with Geber <note>original: "Geber," the Latinized name of Jabir ibn Hayyan.</note>, who asserts in his *Summa* that the true matter of metals is quicksilver, because (he says) nature, never idle, procreated quicksilver from the aforementioned mixed matter, etc. Bonus of Ferrara <note>original: "Bonus Ferrariensis," referring to Petrus Bonus, a 14th-century alchemist.</note> says that quicksilver is the proximate matter of metals, but specifically a viscous humidity mixed with its own subtle earthy element. Geber also, in the definition of quicksilver he provides in his *Summa*, says: "It is a viscous humidity condensed by the aid of its own terrestrial part which enters into its composition."

Let us therefore diligently consider the progress of nature in the procreation of all things, into which she mixes a specific matter which the Philosophers called the "agent," because it does not produce itself, as Aristotle says: that is, it does not demonstrate its own effects. For this reason, in the procreation of metals, after nature has created the matter—that is, the quicksilver—she, being most sagacious, joins to it its own proper agent: namely, a certain kind of mineral earth, like its colostrum <note>Metaphorical use of the word for "first milk," implying a rich, primal, and nourishing substance.</note> and fatness in the mineral caverns of the earth, thickened by long decoction <note>The process of heating or boiling a substance to extract its essence or thicken it.</note>. We commonly call this "sulfur." Its relationship to quicksilver is no different than that of rennet to milk, of male to female, or of an agent to the matter subjected to it. 

The Philosophers have established two kinds of sulfur: one that melts very easily, and another that is only congealed and not fusible. Furthermore, so that nature might demonstrate the power and efficacy of the agent—that is, the sulfur—upon the matter to which it is joined, she brings about by a certain admirable composition that metals are coagulated by the action of fusible sulfur, so that they might be capable of melting. However, she composed other simple minerals by the action of non-fusible sulfur, so that they would not be meltable, such as <term>magnesia</term> <note>In alchemy, a "catch-all" term for various mineral ores, not necessarily the modern element magnesium.</note>, <term>marcasite</term> <note>Often used to refer to various metallic sulfides like pyrite or even bismuth.</note>, and others of that kind. 

Since, however, the agent cannot be the material part of the compound (as Aristotle says), nature, procreating metals beneath the earth, after she has mixed the said sulfur with quicksilver in an indeed inexpressible composition, generates therefrom the most precious metal, namely gold: separating from it its agent—that is, the sulfur—by perfect decoction. And this is the reason why it is more perfect than all other metals, since we see that nature does not transmute it any further into something better. Likewise, for this reason, it is better and more easily joined to quicksilver, because it is nothing other than...

<summary>Dionysius Zacharius explains the Mercury-Sulfur theory of metallic composition, citing Albertus Magnus and Geber to define mercury as a "viscous humidity" and sulfur as the "agent" or "rennet" that coagulates it. He distinguishes between fusible metals and non-fusible minerals like marcasite, identifying gold as the ultimate, perfect result of this natural process.</summary>

<keywords>Mercury, Sulfur, Albertus Magnus, Geber, Bonus of Ferrara, Aristotle, Decoction, Coagulation, Gold, Magnesia, Marcasite, Primary Matter</keywords>

<meta>This page continues Dionysius Zacharius’s discourse on the natural formation and artificial transmutation of metals. Following the previous page’s discussion of the origins of quicksilver, the author here shifts focus to the role of sulfur as the "agent" of change and describes the two ways nature produces gold: through immediate "perfect digestion" and through a slow, decades-long refinement of "imperfect" metals like lead and silver.</meta>

->OF DIONYSIUS ZACHARIUS<-

<page-num>734</page-num>

...than quicksilver <note>original: "argentum vivum," the metallic element mercury.</note> boiled in its own sulfur, and then separated from it by the said boiling <note>original: "decoctione." In alchemy, this refers to a specialized heating process similar to cooking.</note>. Just as the separation of sulfur is the perfection of gold, that which remains in other metals is the most powerful cause of their imperfection. From this it also happens that silver is more imperfect than gold, and copper more than silver: namely, because of a lack of complete digestion <note>original: "digestionis," the process by which raw metallic "matter" is matured into gold via heat.</note>, which alone separates the active agent from them, that is, the sulfur. 

In this is declared the greatest and most primary secret <note>original: "arcanum," a hidden or specialized mystery of the craft.</note> of our entire art. For since art ought to imitate nature in its operations, it is necessary that before this divine work of ours is perfected, the active agent—its sulfur—must be separated. All the Philosophers have hidden this fact, relegating us in their writings to natural operations, which I have sufficiently declared. 

However, so that it may be more perfectly understood in what way our science imitates the operations of nature, it is worthwhile to declare the primary and more common method she uses in the perfection of metals. Previously, we said that the perfection or imperfection of metals occurs due to the lack or mixture of the agent—that is, sulfur—and we showed the first way that nature is accustomed to use in the composition of the prince of metals and the most perfect, namely gold. 

Now it must be known that she also uses another progression; even if it seems contrary to the first, it is nonetheless very similar if one properly considers the end toward which nature’s intention tends. This end is nothing else but to refine metals, purging them thoroughly from their sulfur. For that which in the first way produces a perfect boiling, in the second way she executes through continuous and long digestions, gradually purifying the imperfect metals until they are reduced into gold. 

Indeed, experience teaches us that lead is commonly found in silver mines, and in some, both are mixed together, so that the silver appears imperfect primarily because of a defect in its boiling. For this reason, masters of metalworking advise that when the caverns are closed—so that the more subtle materials cannot evaporate <note>original: "evaporare."</note>—they should be left for thirty or forty years, or until they are perfected. 

Albertus Magnus <note>A 13th-century Dominican friar and polymath often cited as a primary authority in alchemy.</note> records that this indeed happened in his times in the kingdom of Liburnia or Sclavonia <note>Historical regions corresponding to parts of modern-day Croatia and the Balkans.</note>, and it was often reported to me by an experienced miner that such things frequently occur. According to this method which nature uses in perfecting metals, art imitates her operations to perfect the imperfect: namely, by removing its sulfur through the performance of the "divine work" upon them. After they have been melted and purified from their said sulfur, they are perfected into pure gold through their own exuberant boiling, which they acquired through the administration of our art. This is no different than the various ways nature uses in the purification of metals, which do not result in different forms of gold (I mean in its perfection), and so forth.

<summary>Dionysius Zacharius explains that gold is "perfected" by removing excess sulfur through heat, a process art can imitate to transform base metals into gold, just as nature does over decades in the earth.</summary>
<keywords>sulfur, quicksilver, decoction, digestion, alchemy, Albertus Magnus, Liburnia, Sclavonia, transmutation of metals, metallic perfection</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the argument that alchemical art and natural processes are fundamentally identical because they share the same "matter." Zacharius transitions from discussing the heat-driven "digestion" of metals to identifying the specific substance required for the Work: a refined form of mercury combined with its internal sulfur.</meta>

### A SHORT TREATISE.

...although we employ different methods of perfecting it above the earth, our gold is not rendered different from natural and mineral gold, since we use the same matter above the ground that nature itself uses beneath the ground and within its caverns. Aristotle bears witness to this very thing in the ninth book of his *Metaphysics* <note>Aristotle was a Greek philosopher whose theories on the four elements and the "soul" of things provided the foundation for medieval alchemy.</note>. "From a similar agent and matter," he says, "the operations are always similar, even though the means are different: for those two—the agent and the matter—are what count." Indeed, if the matter is one and the same in all respects with the agent, all operations which at the beginning seem dissimilar or contrary will, toward the end, achieve the same effect. To prove that our matter, which we use to perfect metals above the earth, is in every way similar to that which nature uses in the depths of the earth’s caverns for their procreation, we cite Geber <note>Geber is the Latinized name of Jabir ibn Hayyan, an 8th-century polymath considered the father of Islamic alchemy. His "Summa" (The Height of Perfection) was the most influential alchemical text in the Middle Ages.</note> as a witness in his *Summa*: "Our art," he says, "imitates nature as closely and as possibly as it can." Hermes <note>Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary "Thrice-Great" founder of the alchemical tradition.</note> says the same thing, as do Pythagoras, Senior <note>Senior Zadith, the Latin name for the 10th-century alchemist Ibn Umail.</note>, and many others. Therefore, if art imitates nature, it must necessarily be admitted that it uses a similar matter to that of nature, which in both cases can be nothing but one single thing, which we have called quicksilver <note>original: "argentum vivum," literally "living silver," the common name for the element mercury.</note>—not only by itself, but mixed together with its own proper agent, namely true sulfur. This same matter, which the Philosophers called "animated quicksilver," will be the true matter of our divine science for the completion of our divine work. Nature uses this very thing and no other in the hollows of the earth for the procreation of metals as its true matter, as we have sufficiently demonstrated above.

They called it "animated quicksilver" <note>original: "argentum vivum animatum." In alchemy, "animated" means the substance has been "enlivened" or prepared so that it is no longer chemically "dead" or inert common mercury.</note> to show the difference between it and common quicksilver; for the latter remains as it is because nature did not join its own proper agent to it. Many, therefore, have falsely believed that common quicksilver and common sulfur are the matter of metals. For at no time has it ever happened that those two were found mixed together in mines; by what reasoning, then, could they be the true matter of metals in the hollows of the earth, or of our art above the ground? As Geber speaks in his *Summa* regarding the principles of the art: "Our quicksilver," he says, "is nothing other than a viscous water, wedded by the action of its own metallic sulfur." This is our true matter, which nature has prepared for our art (as Valerandus Sylvensis <note>A 16th-century alchemist and physician.</note> says) and reduced into a certain species known to true Philosophers, without further transmutation of itself. Avicenna <note>Ibn Sina, the Persian "Prince of Physicians," whose alchemical writings explored the limits of changing one metal into another.</note> says similarly: "Nature has prepared for us one single matter, which our art is quite unable to compose by itself." It would be foolish, therefore, to believe that from all the substances we might mix together, any of them—whether metallic or otherwise—could be the true matter of our science, since nature has prepared it for us so that nothing is lacking except these two things: namely, to purify it and to perfect it...

<summary>Zacharius argues that alchemy must use the exact same "animated quicksilver" found in nature to create gold, citing authorities like Aristotle and Geber. He clarifies that alchemical matter is not common mercury and sulfur mixed together, but a specific "viscous water" pre-prepared by nature that the alchemist must only purify.</summary>
<keywords>quicksilver, mercury, sulfur, Geber, Aristotle, animated quicksilver, metallic procreation, Avicenna, natural matter, alchemical theory</keywords>

# THE WRITINGS OF DIONYSIUS ZACHARIUS

...to complete and join them together through a boiling <note>The original Latin is *decoctio*, referring to a slow, consistent heating process similar to ripening fruit or cooking food.</note> that is both proper and suitable to itself. Regarding this matter, Rhazes <note>original: "Rafis"; a famous Persian physician and alchemist (c. 865–925) whose works were foundational to European alchemy.</note> speaks in his *Book of Precepts*: "Our Mercury," he says, "is the true foundation of our science, from which the true tinctures of metals are extracted." Alphidius <note>An early, possibly Arabic or North African alchemist often cited in medieval Latin texts.</note> says of the same: "Take note, my son, that the entire work of the wise Philosophers consists in quicksilver alone <note>original: "argento vivo solo"; literally "living silver," the common name for mercury.</note>. For this reason, Hermes commands us to observe this Mercury, which he calls 'coagulated' and 'hidden in gilded hiding places.'" Geber says of this same Mercury: "Praised be the Most High," he says, "who created this quicksilver and gave it incomparable power for the sake of perfecting the true mastery of our science." In short, there was not a single one among the wise writers who was not of this same opinion.

Modern practitioners will object, judging me rash for daring to criticize so many great predecessors whose theories and practices teach the sublimation of quicksilver (which they call Mercury) with vitriol and common salt, and afterwards reviving it with hot water so that it may finally be mixed with gold (which they call the Sun), and in this manner dissolving and fixing it so that our divine work might be perfected. This is what Arnold of Villanova writes in his great *Rosary* <note>original: "Rosario"; a famous 13th-century alchemical text.</note>, as does Raymond Lully in his *Testament*.

To answer these people in a way that satisfies them, I shall use those same authors they cite, whose writings testify that all those operations—distillations, separations of elements, reductions, and others of that kind—were put there for no other reason than to veil the practice of our science under such masks <note>original: "larvis"; literally 'masks' or 'ghosts,' referring to the allegorical or "blind" instructions used to hide secrets from the uninitiated.</note>. We shall cite the same Arnold of Villanova, who, after teaching these diverse operations in his *Rosary*, bursts out near the end of his summary in these words, or something similar: "We have shown," he says, "the true practice and the true way of perfecting our divine work, but in very brief words, which will nevertheless seem long enough to those who understand." Consequently, with so many diverse and long-winded discussions of operations, he did not mean the true preparation of this divine work, nor the practice which he said he had previously treated in brief.

Raymond says this very thing at the end of his *Codicil*, where he responds to those who might perhaps ask why he described the art, when he had previously said it was impossible for anyone to arrive at this art and its true knowledge by reading books. He responds: "So that the faithful reader may be introduced and acquire a habit for himself, by which he might arrive at the true knowledge of our divine work, the preparation of which we have never sincerely set down, nor openly declared." It is certain, therefore, that the long and diverse preparations of that kind which he teaches in his books are not the one and only practice of our divine work. Those who are a little more learned will object to me, asking why I have written that our divine work is made from one single matter, namely—

<summary>Zacharius argues that "Philosophical Mercury" (quicksilver) is the sole foundation of the Great Work, dismissing the complex chemical recipes of his predecessors as intentional allegories or "masks" meant to hide the truth from the unworthy.</summary>

# TREATISE <note>original: "Opusculum"; literally "a small work."</note>

...even though it is made from the one and only animated quicksilver <note>original: "argento vivo animato"; in alchemy, "animated" mercury is quicksilver that has been "awakened" or prepared for the Work, distinguishing it from common liquid mercury.</note>, Geber says in his *Summa*, in the chapter on the *Coagulation of Mercury*, that it is extracted from metallic bodies prepared with their arsenic. Rosinus <note>A Latinized name likely referring to the alchemist Zosimos of Panopolis.</note>, on the other hand, says it is a true incombustible sulfur, from which our divine work consists. King Solomon, the son of David, attests to this same thing, saying: "God preferred our true sulfur above all things existing under heaven." Pythagoras wrote in the *Assembly of the Philosophers* <note>original: "Turba Philosophorum"; one of the oldest and most influential Latin alchemical texts, written as a transcript of a debate between ancient philosophers.</note>: "Our divine work is perfected when the sulfurs are joined in turn, one with the other; therefore, it consists of sulfurs, and not of animated quicksilver alone." 

To provide an answer that might satisfy those minds wandering from the path, we must recall what we said above regarding the matter of metals: namely, that nature, in the hollows of the earth, joins the proper active agent to the quicksilver. Furthermore, because our divine work has no name of its own, different people have given it different names. As Lilius <note>Likely referring to Raymond Lully, or a pseudo-Lullian text.</note> wrote, it is called by as many names among the Philosophers as there are created things in this world, implying by these words that it is called by infinite names—even though it always remains one and the same thing, consisting of a single, unique matter. Nevertheless, the Philosophers who came before us imposed so many and such various names upon it at their own whim, according to the variety of colors appearing during the boiling <note>original: "decoctione"; the process of slow, steady heating meant to ripen the substance.</note>.

    Those who have called it "animated quicksilver," as we do, considered our primary matter (which the ancient Philosophers called Chaos, and which takes its beginning from the very start of the work) to be truly similar in every way to the nature and matter of the quicksilver from which nature composes and perfects metals in the hollows of the earth, as we demonstrated above. Likewise, those who called our divine work the "Philosophers’ Stone" (which is its common name) did so with respect to the end of the boiling of our matter; for it remains fixed in the fire, and they are accustomed to call "stone" whatever does not flee from the fire and is not sublimated <note>Sublimation is the process where a solid turns into a gas when heated. A "fixed" substance resists this and stays solid in the furnace.</note> by it. Many others have devised many other names according to their own reasons, which would be tedious to recount individually. As Malvascindus <note>A name appearing in the *Turba Philosophorum*.</note> says: "If we say our matter is spiritual, it is true; if corporeal, we do not lie; if indeed celestial, that is its true name; if terrestrial, we do not speak improperly." By these words, it is clearly evident that the variety of names imposed on our divine work by our ancient predecessors was founded on different reasons, based on the diversity of colors and operations appearing during its boiling.

    Similarly, those who called it "sulfur" (as attested by the authorities that could be brought against me) spoke in this way with respect to the final boiling, in which the matter appears fixed. Thus, while from the beginning it demonstrated the true appearance of quicksilver because it was volatile, in the end it is fixed; then at last the hidden and internal...
