->Dionysii Zacharii<-
<meta>The text begins mid-sentence, continuing from the previous page's discussion on the nature of the "Matter."</meta>

...being [singular], it was unknown; namely, the fixed part which we call **sulfur** is made manifest as it is continued, and in the final decoction <note>original: "decoctio"; in alchemy, this refers to the process of prolonged heating or "cooking" the substance to mature it.</note> in which it dominates over the volatile part. For this reason, our matter is no longer called volatile (I speak of those who consider the final decoction) but finally **fixed sulfur**: as Arnald of Villanova <note>A famous 13th-century physician and alchemist.</note> says in his *Great Rosary*, when he speaks of the final decoction of our divine work:

> It is (he says) the true red sulfur, through which quicksilver <note>original: "argentum vivum"; literally "living silver," the common name for mercury.</note> can be perfected into gold.

Therefore, we can truly conclude and resolve every doubt that the matter from which we compose our divine work is nothing but one single thing in all respects, and in everything similar to that matter which nature uses in the hollows of the earth for the procreation of metals, notwithstanding all the authorities alleged to the contrary above, or any other similar ones. For a diversity of names (as Aristotle says) does not make the thing itself diverse. To bring our division to an end bit by bit, it remains for us to declare the terms of our science: that is, let us compare the opinions of the best and most excellent authors who put them forward. They chiefly use four terms to be understood concerning the composition of our divine work, which are: the **four elements**, the **perfect ferment**, the **true poison**, and the **perfect coagulum** <note>original: "coagulum"; refers to a substance that causes curdling or thickening, like rennet in cheesemaking.</note>, which they have elsewhere called the "male," because a comparison is made like that of rennet to simple milk. 

Therefore, to better declare what they mean by the elements, we must look at what the natural philosophers said concerning the **First Matter**, which they called **Chaos**, in which those four were confusedly contained; through their contrary natures, by demonstrating their actions, they were made manifest to us. Wherefore Alexander <note>Likely referring to Alexander the Great, to whom many medieval alchemical "Epistles" were apocryphally attributed.</note> says in his *Epistle*:

> Whatever (he says) was demonstrated to the ancients to be of a hot quality, they judged to be **fire**; what was dry and coagulated, to be **earth**; what appeared to them moist and flowing, **water**; but what was seen to be cold, subtle, and windy, they called **air**.

Two of these are hidden and enclosed within the other two, as Rhazes <note>original: "Rafis"; Abu Bakr al-Razi, a Persian polymath and one of the most important figures in the history of medicine and alchemy.</note> says in his *Book of Precepts*:

> Every compound (he says) consists of four elements, with two hidden in the other two apparent ones: namely, **air** in the hidden part of **water**, and **fire** in the interior of the **earth**, as we said before.

And because the two enclosed elements cannot demonstrate their actions except through the other two, they called them the "weak" elements, and the others the "strong." For this reason, they say compounds are perfect when the moist and the dry—that is, water and earth—are joined by the equal aid of nature with the cold and the hot—which are air and fire—through the conversion of one into the other. Wherefore Alexander says in the *Book of Secrets*:

> If you convert the elements one into another, you will find what you seek.

This opinion is well and perfectly known to us...

He then introduces the four elements as the fundamental building blocks of the alchemical Work, where hidden elements must be brought forth through conversion.</summary>

->Aaa 2<-

...shows the true matter, and indicates the perfect practice of our science: therefore, so that it can be better understood, one must speak more specifically about the four elements and their nature, since they are necessary in the composition of our divine work. Hermes <note>Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary Hellenistic figure to whom many foundational alchemical texts are attributed.</note> says: "In our earth, all other elements are created." Alphidius <note>An Arabic alchemical author often cited in medieval Latin texts.</note>, on the other hand, puts forward that water is the principal element, from which the rest of the elements required for the composition of our divine work are created: in which there is no contradiction, as it appears. For from the beginning of the procreation of our divine work, nothing else appears but water alone, which the Philosophers called **Mercurial water** <note>original: "Mercurialis aqua"; the fundamental "first matter" of the alchemists, often described as a metallic, liquid substance.</note>, from which the earth was procreated when it was thickened by a supernatural joining and decoction <note>original: "decoctio"; the process of prolonged heating or "cooking" a substance to bring it to maturity.</note>, without which it is useless to us. Hence Hermes spoke the truth when he said that the remaining elements came forth from the earth, since the earth alone demonstrates its qualities in the second operation, just as water demonstrated its qualities at the start of the work. Therefore Alphidius wrote to Valerandus and others that it [water] is the principal element in the composition of our divine work.

These are those two elements which the Philosophers say must be known before we approach the work. As Rasis <note>Rhazes (c. 865–925 AD), a Persian physician and alchemist.</note> says in his *Book of Lights*: "Before (he says) the work is begun, the nature and quality of water and earth must be known, because in these two the four elements are contained: otherwise the volatile will snatch the fixed away with it, and our science will be useless to us." For this reason, the conversion of the four elements is commanded, so that our divine work, properly qualified, may be fixed at the end, and so that it may be able to resist the violence of fire, the corruption of air, the rust <note>original: "ærugini"; referring to corrosion or oxidation.</note> of earth, and the putrefaction of water, no differently than mineral gold, because of its great perfection. This conversion of the elements (as Raymond Lull <note>A 13th-century Majorcan polymath whose name was frequently attached to alchemical treatises.</note> says) is nothing other than making the earth (which is fixed) volatile, and making the water (which is moist and volatile) dry and fixed: which is correctly done by our continued decoction in our vessel, without any removal or opening, lest perhaps our elements perish and fly off into the air as smoke.

The writings of Rasis and various other writings of Philosophers attest to this same sentiment, when they say that the true separation and joining of the four elements is done in our vessel without being touched by hands or feet in any way <note>A common alchemical phrase indicating that the process happens naturally and automatically within the sealed vessel once the heat is applied.</note>: since (as they say) our stone dissolves, coagulates, washes, purges, whitens, and reddens itself, without the addition or mixing of any external thing.

Arnald of Villanova <note>A famous 13th-century physician and alchemist.</note> is of the same opinion in his *Great Rosary*, when he says in very brief words: There <gloss>is</gloss> <note>original: "est"</note> need of no other labor than in slaying the water, that is, in fixing it: for immediately...

### DIONYSII ZACHARII
<note>Dionysius Zacharias (1510–1556) was a French alchemist known for his autobiographical account of the search for the Philosopher's Stone.</note>

...existing as [metallic], it was unknown; namely, the fixed part, which we call **sulfur** <note>original: "sulphur"; in alchemy, sulfur represents the active, masculine, and combustible principle of matter.</note>, is manifested through continued and final **decoction** <note>original: "decoctio"; the process of refined heating or "cooking" to ripen the substance.</note>, in which it dominates over the volatile part. For this reason, our **matter** <note>original: "materia"</note> is no longer called volatile (I speak of those who consider the final decoction), but is finally called **fixed sulfur**, just as Arnaldus de Villanova <note>A famous 13th-century physician and alchemist.</note> says in his *Great Rosary* when he speaks of the final decoction of our divine work: 

> "It is (he says) the **true red sulfur**, through which **quicksilver** <note>original: "argentum vivum"; mercury, the passive, feminine principle.</note> can be perfected into gold."

Therefore, we can truly conclude and resolve all doubt: the matter from which we compose our divine work is nothing but one single thing in all respects, and is entirely similar to that matter which nature uses in the cavities of the earth for the procreation of metals, notwithstanding all the contrary authorities alleged above or any others like them. For a diversity of names (as Aristotle says) does not create a diversity of things. 

To bring an end to our classification step by step, it remains for us to declare the terms of our science; that is, let us compare the opinions of the best and most prominent authors who discuss the composition of our divine work. They chiefly use four terms among others: the **four elements**, the **perfect ferment**, the **true poison**, and the **perfect curd** <note>original: "coagulum"; used here to describe how the alchemical agent "sets" the liquid matter, much like rennet curdles milk.</note> (which they have otherwise called the "male"), a comparison made to the way rennet acts upon simple milk. 

So that we may better declare what they understand by "elements," we should consider what the natural philosophers have said regarding the **first matter** <note>original: "materia prima"; the formless, original substance of the universe.</note>, which they called **Chaos**. In this Chaos, those four elements were confusedly contained, and they were made manifest to us by each demonstrating its actions through its own contrary nature. Wherefore Alexander <note>Likely referring to Pseudo-Alexander, a name attached to various medieval alchemical epistles.</note> says in his Epistle: 

> "Whatever (he says) was demonstrated to the ancients to be of a hot quality, they judged to be **fire**; what was dry and solid, they judged to be **earth**; what appeared to them moist and flowing, they called **water**; but what seemed to be cold, subtle, and windy, they called **air**." 

Two of these are hidden and enclosed within the other two, as Rhazes <note>original: "Rasis"; a celebrated 9th-century Persian physician and alchemist.</note> says in his *Book of Precepts*: 

> "Every composite consists of four elements, with two hidden within the other two apparent ones; namely, **air** is in the secret part of **water**, and **fire** is in the interior of **earth**, as we said before."

And because the two enclosed elements cannot demonstrate their actions except through the other two, they called them the "weak" elements, while the others were called the "strong." For this reason, they say that composites are perfect when the moist and the dry—that is, water and earth—are joined equally by the help of nature with the cold and the hot—which are air and fire—through the conversion of one into another. Wherefore Alexander, in his *Book of Secrets*, says: 

> "If you convert the elements one into another, you will find what you seek." 

This opinion, being well and perfectly known to us...

<summary>This page explains that the alchemical "matter" is a single substance, eventually becoming "fixed sulfur" through cooking. It defines the four elements (Fire, Earth, Water, Air) and their hidden relationships as the foundation for creating the Philosopher's Stone.</summary>

### TREATISE
<note>original: "Opusculum"; likely part of the collected works of Dionysius Zacharias.</note>

...points out the true matter, and indicates the perfect practice of our science: therefore, so that it may be better understood, we must speak more specifically about the four elements and their nature, since they are necessary in the composition of our divine work. Hermes <note>Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary Hellenistic figure and purported founder of alchemy.</note> says:
> In our earth, all other elements have been created.

Alphidius <note>An Arab alchemist often cited in medieval Latin texts.</note>, on the contrary, puts forward that water is the principal element, from which the other elements required for the composition of our divine work were created. In these views, as it appears, there is no contradiction. For from the beginning of the procreation of our divine work, nothing else appears than water alone, which the Philosophers <note>Alchemists often referred to themselves as "Philosophers" or "Sons of Art."</note> have called **Mercurial water** <note>original: "Mercurialem aquam"; the transformative, liquid essence of the matter, not common mercury.</note>, from which the earth was procreated when it was thickened by a supernatural joining and **decoction** <note>original: "decoctione"; the process of refined heating or "cooking" to ripen the substance.</note>, without which it is useless to us. Hence Hermes spoke the truth when he said the remaining elements proceeded from the earth, since the earth alone demonstrates its qualities in the **second operation**, just as the water demonstrated its own in the beginning of the work. For this reason, Alphidius wrote to Valerandus and others that water itself is the principal element in the composition of our divine work.

These are those two elements which the Philosophers say must be known before we attempt the work, as Rasis <note>Muhammad ibn Zakariya al-Razi (c. 865–925), a Persian polymath and foundational figure in alchemy.</note> says in his *Book of Lights*:
> Before the work is begun (he says), the nature and quality of water and earth must be understood, because in these two the four elements are contained; otherwise, the volatile will carry the fixed away with it, and our science will be useless to us.

For this reason, the **conversion of the four elements** is commanded, so that our divine work, being rightly qualified, may be **fixed** <note>original: "fixetur"; made stable and resistant to heat.</note> in the end, and so that it may be able to resist all the violence of fire, the corruption of air, the rust of earth, and the putrefaction of water, no differently than mineral gold, because of its great perfection. This conversion of the elements (as Raymond Lully <note>A 13th-century philosopher and mystic to whom many alchemical texts were attributed.</note> says) is nothing other than making the earth (which is fixed) volatile, and making the water (which is moist and volatile) dry and fixed: which is properly done by our continued decoction in our **vessel** <note>original: "vase"; the sealed alchemical flask.</note>, without any removal or opening, lest perhaps our elements perish and fly away into the breezes as smoke.

This same thing is attested by the writings of Rasis and various writings of other Philosophers of the same opinion, when they say the true separation and conjunction of the four elements occurs in our vessel without being touched by hands or feet <note>A common alchemical metaphor meaning the process is natural and self-contained once the initial conditions are set.</note>: because (as they say) our **Stone** dissolves, coagulates, washes, purges, whitens, and reddens itself, without the addition or mixing of any external thing.

Arnaldus de Villa Nova <note>A famous 13th-century physician and alchemist.</note> is of the same opinion in his *Great Rosary*, when he says in very brief words: The work <unclear>is done</unclear> with no other labor than in "slaughtering" the water—that is, in fixing it—for immediately

...and this will be dead, while the remaining elements are killed—that is, they are **fixed** <note>original: "fixata"; in alchemy, to 'fix' a substance means to make a volatile material solid or resistant to fire.</note>. Therefore, the sophisticated <note>In the 16th century, "sophistic" implied something deceptive or false, like a counterfeit.</note> separations of elements performed by the workers of this time are false; they are based most poorly upon the writings of such Philosophers who expressly forbid the destruction of **simples** <note>original: "simplicium"; pure, unmixed substances or medicinal ingredients.</note> in their preparations because (as they claim) it is impossible for art to give primary forms. Yet it is most certain that the four elements can by no means be composed unless they were first destroyed. For this reason, there is no need for this sophisticated and false separation of elements for the composition of the divine work.

That such a separation is false is proven by this very fact which was stated before: namely, that two elements are contained within the other two. From this it follows that we can by no means know their true separation, much less their perfect conjunction. Experience proves that the elements they claim to have separated have nothing in common with the nature of true elements. As Valerand <note>A figure often cited in alchemical texts, sometimes identified as a contemporary or an earlier authority on the "Art."</note> says: let their "oil" be an example, which they call "Air"; it moistens and wets everything it touches, which is contrary to the true nature of air. Hence it shall be enough for me to have shown the nature and quality of the elements, and their conversion which is necessary in this our science, so that the ignorance of modern workers may become manifest to the true sons of science, and so that, knowing them, they may flee from their company.

Now let us see what the Philosophers understand by this term, namely: **ferment** <note>original: "fermentum"; a substance—often compared to yeast in bread—that "leavens" or transforms a larger mass of metal into gold.</note>. They say they have used it in two ways. In the first sense, they make a comparison of our divine work to metals: just as we see a little bread ferment [yeast] convert much flour into its own nature and dough, similarly, our divine work converts metals to its own nature; and because it is gold, it also transmutes them into gold. 

But since they have rarely adopted this meaning (in which there is no difficulty), we shall come to the second, in which the greatest difficulty of our science lies. By "ferment" in the second way, they understand the true body and the true matter which perfects our divine work; this is indeed unknown to the eyes, and is something perceptible by the intellect alone. For from the beginning, our matter appears **volatile** <note>original: "volatilis"; a substance that evaporates or escapes when heated.</note> (as we have already sufficiently declared), which we must join to its own body, so that by this means it may retain the **soul**, which—by means of this already-made conjunction, and through the mediation of the **spirit**—demonstrates its divine operations. 

In our divine work it is read in the *Turba Philosophorum* <note>original: "Assembly of the Philosophers," one of the most famous and influential early Latin alchemical texts, framed as a debate between ancient sages.</note> in this very manner: 
> The Body has more power than its two brothers, which they call Spirit and Soul.

Not that they understand this in the way Aristotle or other Philosophers declared (which is very worthy of note), but they called "Body" every simple substance that by its own nature can withstand fire without any loss; otherwise, they call it "fixed." They called "Soul" every simple [that is] volatile...

...volatile, having the power to carry the body away with itself, and leading it away from the fire: they named this by another word, the **volatile**. They say that the **Spirit** is that which has the power of retaining the body and the soul, and of joining those two together so closely that they can no longer be separated, whether they are perfect or imperfect. Although in our divine work <note>original: "opere nostro divino"; a standard term for the Great Work of alchemy.</note>, nothing new enters from the beginning (I think, after the first preparation), nor in the middle of the work, nor at the end. In truth, the Philosophers, from different perspectives and considerations, called one and the same thing **Body**, **Soul**, and **Spirit**, as has been abundantly stated above.

First, when our matter was volatile, they called it the **Soul** because it carried the body away with it. Afterward, when that which was hidden was made manifest in our **decoction** <note>The process of heating or "cooking" the substance over a long period.</note>, then at last the Body made its powers known openly by means of the Spirit; that is, it retained the soul, reducing it to its own proper nature (which is Gold) and fixed it by its own power, through the help of our art. By this very thing, it is exactly declared what Hermes <note>Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary founder of alchemy.</note> wrote: that no **tincture** <note>A substance or "medicine" capable of transforming the color and nature of metals.</note> is made without the **red stone**. For as Rosinus <note>An Arabic alchemical author, likely Zosimos of Panopolis.</note> says: Our true **Sun** <note>Gold.</note> appears white and imperfect in our decoction, and is perfect in its red color. 

This is the **Ferment** <note>original: "Fermentum"; an agent that triggers the final transformation, similar to how leaven transforms dough into bread.</note> of which Arnaldus de Villanova speaks in his *Great Rosary*, which appears in those two colors, untouched and unmixed with any other matter, as might be understood through those writings. Anaxagoras <note>An ancient Greek philosopher often cited by alchemists.</note> testifies that this is true, saying: Our Sun is red and burning, which is joined to the white soul and the nature of the **Moon** <note>Silver.</note>, by means of the spirit; although in truth the whole thing is nothing else but the **Quicksilver** <note>original: "argentum vivum"; mercury.</note> of the Philosophers. 

Morienus declares: "It shall be impossible," he says, "to reach the perfection of our science until the Moon is joined to the Sun," without which our science is useless, as Hermes and all the rest of the Philosophers say. Through these things, what Rasis <note>The Persian physician and alchemist al-Razi (865–925 CE).</note> says in his *Book of Lights* can be understood: "The red servant," he says, "has married the white woman," at the end of the perfection of our divine work. Similarly, what Lilius <note>Referring to the *Lilium* (The Lily), a common title for alchemical texts.</note> holds: The true union of body and soul occurs in the white and red color, yet by the same medium, at a certain time, through the help of our decoction, governed in such a way that our matter is not destroyed. For, as it is found written in the *Turba* <note>The *Turba Philosophorum* (The Assembly of the Philosophers), one of the oldest and most famous alchemical texts.</note>, both the profit and the loss of our divine work proceed from the administration of fire.

Therefore, I would advise, along with Rasis, that no one should rashly undertake the duty of this practice in our science before he thoroughly understands all the regimes of fire (for they are diverse) that are especially necessary in the composition of our divine work. Otherwise, the end-point which they call **poison** <note>original: "venenum"; in this context, it refers to a destructive or failed state of the matter caused by excessive heat.</note> will be applied to it, which is accustomed to happen in the second operation, as was said before. No one should think because of this that something poisonous must be added to our matter, nor **Theriac** <note>A famous ancient herbal "universal" antidote.</note>, nor anything foreign (as they judge)...

<meta>This page continues the technical explanation of alchemical terminology by Dionysius Zacharius, specifically focusing on why the "ferment" is metaphorically described as "poison," "antidote," and "curd." It bridges the previous discussion of Body, Soul, and Spirit with the practical timing of the chemical marriage.</meta>

...some have estimated, considering only the literal meaning) but rather that it is necessary for the operator to be industrious and vigilant, lest he miss the limit and the hour of the activity of our **mercurial water** <note>original: *aquæ nostræ Mercurialis*; the purified solvent or "living" mercury used in the Work.</note>, so that he may join to it its own body. This body we previously called the **ferment**, but we also call it **poison** <note>original: *venenum*</note>, and this for two reasons. The first concerns us: because just as a poison can bring nothing but harm to the human body, if we do not join it at the determined hour in this stage, it will bring us nothing but loss and waste of resources, as we said above. The second reason concerns the **Mercury** (which we call the mercurial water) because this poison slays it and [coagulates] it. By this is interpreted what Hamech <note>An alchemical authority often cited in medieval texts.</note> wrote, saying: *when our matter reaches its limit, it is joined with a deadly poison.* Likewise, what Rosinus says: *This poison is of very great price.* Haly, Morienus, and all the others testify to the same. 

By the same comparison, they called it an **antidote** <note>original: *theriacam*; specifically 'Theriac,' a famous ancient poly-pharmaceutical used as a universal antidote.</note>, as Morienus says: because it performs the same work in the metallic body that an antidote performs in ours. Moreover, that which they have written can also be adapted to the joining of the perfect ferment, when the determined hour has passed, because through it our **divine work** is [perfected]. Therefore, similar authorities ought to be understood in an allegorical sense, and not by the appearance of the literal words, which many falsely believe.

Of a similar nature is the interpretation of the last term, which is more commonly used and understood: the **curd** <note>original: *coagulum*; the substance (like rennet) used to curdle milk into cheese.</note>. For the greater part of people understand by this our divine work when it is completed. They say that just as a tiny bit of curd congeals a great deal of milk, so a tiny bit of our matter, when cast upon **quicksilver** <note>original: *vivum argentum*; mercury.</note>, congeals it and brings it to its own nature. But they are deceived and far from the truth: for they conclude from this that our matter cannot be prepared from metals because they are already congealed. 

Instead, it [should be noted] that when our Mercury appears simple, it is [liquid], and the Philosophers called it **milk**. Its **curd** is what we called above the **ferment**, the **poison**, and the **antidote**. Because just as the curd does not differ from the milk except by a little boiling, so our curd also does not differ from our Mercury, [except] by the **decoction** <note>The process of steady heating or "cooking" the substance.</note> which it acquired previously. This is the great and natural secret, on account of which the Philosophers said our science was [divine]: because human reason fails in it, as we have recounted before. This is the curd that Hermes calls the **curd of gold**, by which they wish to be understood when they say: *In the [conjunction] of the spirit, the true dissolution of the body is made; and conversely, in the dissolution of the body, the true coagulation of the spirit is made.* Because by this means the whole work is perfected, as Senior <note>Zadith ben Hamuel, an influential 10th-century Arabian alchemist.</note> says: *When I saw [this] water (that is, our Mercury) coagulate by itself, I believed firmly that our science was true.* For the same reason...

<header>SHORT TREATISE</header>

...Alexander says that in our science nothing is created except that which is made from male and female. He calls our **curd** <note>original: *coagulum*; the agent that thickens or fixes the fluid</note> the male, which is that which acts; and the Philosophers attributed action to the male, and passion <note>the capacity to be acted upon</note> to the female, whom they say is our **Mercury** <note>original: *Mercurium*; here referring to the purified "philosophical" mercury, not the common metal</note>, especially because the said curd acts upon it, demonstrating its power. For this reason they said that the female has wings, because our Mercury is simple and volatile: which is nonetheless held back by its said curd. Therefore they wrote: *Make the female ascend above the male, and afterward the male above the female,* understanding this to be what is in the **Assembly of Philosophers** <note>original: *Turba Philosophorum*; one of the oldest and most influential Latin alchemical texts</note>: That our King is to be honored, and the Queen his wife, and the greatest care must be taken that they be not burned, that is, that our **decoction** <note>original: *decoctio*; the process of heating or "cooking" the substance over a long period</note> be not accelerated. For, as Arnold says in his *Great Rosary* <note>Arnold of Villanova, a celebrated 13th-century physician and alchemist</note>: The chief error in the practice of our divine work is accelerated or hurried cooking. The ancient Philosophers used similar and various terms in their writings, and because these we have explained are the principal ones, we shall put an end to the interpretation of terms: for when these are rightly known, the true matter cannot remain unknown, and thereafter the books of the Philosophers are made easy, as the good Trevisan <note>Bernard Trevisan, a 15th-century alchemist known for his clear explanations of the "One Matter"</note> says.

It must be concluded, therefore, with all the Philosophers—whose writings I have hitherto reduced into a better order than I could—that there is only one single matter from which our divine work is fulfilled. For it is composed of a single, simple Mercury (which the Philosophers, by their own term and without any ambiguity, have called **Mercurial water**) coagulated by the action of its own **sulfur** (which Hermes properly called the **flower of gold**). Through our long and continued cooking, this sulfur has acquired such great and excellent perfection that this work of ours is able to transmute all imperfect metallic bodies—to which it is joined by **projection** <note>original: *projectione*; the act of casting a small amount of the "Stone" onto molten base metal to transform it</note>—into pure and unalloyed gold similar to mineral gold. This is supported by the various reasons previously deduced and cited, by which we have amply enough declared how it happens that imperfect metals are perfected by it.

Since indeed no simple elements that are different or contrary in qualities can be joined or perfectly mixed together, our divine work likewise—because it is fashioned from **quicksilver** <note>original: *argento vivo*; common mercury</note> alone—cannot in any way suffer a union with the sulfur that remained in imperfect metals due to a defect in digestion <note>in alchemy, "digestion" refers to the slow maturation of metals within the earth or the flask</note>, as we noted above. But truly, since it is most powerful and most perfect by the highest digestion, it separates the said sulfur from the metals, and the quicksilver which remains in them, it perfects into gold. It is proven by experiment: when we perform its projection upon common quicksilver, we find the whole of it almost entirely converted into gold. We see it effect the opposite when projected upon metals:

Indeed, from half a pound <note>original: *semilibra*; in the traditional apothecary system, a pound consisted of 12 ounces</note> of some substances, barely six ounces are obtained; yet the more they are decocted <note>cooked or refined by heat</note>, the less they are diminished by this method. Thus, bringing the second part of this little work of mine to an end, I will at last embark upon the third and final part, in which I will explain the true and perfect practice of our divine science under various allegories. This, God will manifest to His faithful and to those studious lovers of the art who diligently read through these writings of mine, giving them true understanding through His Holy Spirit, to His glory and honor: to whom be praise forever.

### THIRD PART OF THE LITTLE TREATISE OF DIONYSIUS
### *Zachary, on the Practice of the divine work.*

->The whole earth has been divided by Philosophers and Cosmographers <note>scholars who described the universe and the world</note> into three principal parts: Asia, Africa, and Europe, situated under four quarters or regions—East, West, South, and North—and under the dominion of various Emperors, Kings, Princes, and powerful Lords. Each of these rulers possesses diverse and various things for their delight, both on account of their rarity and their singular value. The latter reason is not equally pleasing as the former, as I have learned through experience while traveling through various and opposing regions.<-

Indeed, where there was a great gathering of learned men, I saw (to my great misfortune) the truly wise living in misery and dejection; on the contrary, the most ignorant were extremely wealthy and held in the highest esteem. But where there was a shortage of learned and skilled men, and the greatest part were utterly ignorant and foolish, in that place the wise were especially honored by all, and I observed them to be pursued with the greatest favor and the highest respect, particularly by the great lords.

In no different a way, the scarcity of wealth and of minerals (from which gold and other metals are shared with us) in those places where they are not found, creates the highest estimation of them; just as abundance brings with it a disdain for that which is held in great supply by the wealthy. Furthermore, cheaper things of no price, having nothing of perfection besides their outward appearance, have always blinded their eyes, so that they might not recognize things that are perfect and precious. On this account, the wise are filled with indignation when they see that the ignorant are preferred; they take themselves elsewhere, deliberating how to demonstrate the strength and power of their wisdom in other places.

This was done long ago by a certain magnanimous **Governor**, who proposed never to cease until he had subjected the remaining part of the world—beyond that which he already possessed—to himself, by the protection of his troops and especially by the counsel of his faithful **steward** <note>original: *oeconomus*; here representing a key chemical agent or the alchemist's primary method</note>. Meanwhile, while he was turning these things over in his mind, he joined to himself various and diverse strangers. Because these men were not at all faithful, they thought they would be more liberally received by other Emperors, Kings, and other Princes. Therefore (as spies are accustomed to do), they defected from him and made his plans known to those others.

While in the Courts and great Palaces nothing but laughter and song occurred, and time was uselessly wasted with provocations, masks, horse exercises, fashions, and various games, and ears were kindly offered to flatterers and jesters, wise men were mockingly tossed the name of "Philosopher" <note>This reflects a common theme in alchemical literature: the "true" seekers are mocked by the decadent world, just as the hidden matter of the Stone is despised by the ignorant.</note> (a title which once great Monarchs and Potentates did not disdain, nor would they do so now, if they still possessed healthy minds and listened gladly to golden counsel). Meanwhile, that good Prince Governor, surrounded by his guards or auxiliary forces, had already besieged the most famous cities of the Empire. The Emperor, having drafted a most numerous soldiery, accompanied by many Kings and Princes, was just now preparing to bring his standards to battle, when the good Prince Governor, by the persuasion of his faithful Steward <term>oeconomus: a steward or household manager; in this allegory, he represents the Alchemist who manages the heat and the vessel</term> and others of his circle, left the siege and safely withdrew alone into a most fortified citadel, while his troops occupied the fields around it and resisted the enemy vigorously for days. The Emperor had brought fifty thousand infantry and six thousand cavalry, and countless war engines. Therefore, the Prince, leaving the city protected by an iron tower, moved his camp with his fleet in naval order, with the rear troops fighting vigorously after him against the enemy; and if they had not immediately crossed the river, broken the bridges, and looked out for themselves and their Prince, the greatest danger would have loomed over them, but they all escaped the hands of the enemies unharmed. On the next day, as the enemies pursued them manfully, the Prince was forced—assenting to the advice of his men—to withdraw into an impregnable place, and all the soldiers with him. It was fortified by a valley and ramparts, in the middle of which, on a rock surrounded by walls, sat a perfectly round citadel <note>The "round citadel" is a common metaphor for the alchemical flask (the Hermetic Vase), which must be perfectly sealed.</note> that could never be conquered. Next to it stood another very high tower, through which, by tunnels excavated underground, the Steward was able to bring in all things necessary for both food and war, without the enemies knowing—just as once happened in Nafplio <note>original: *Neapoli Romaniae*; a Venetian stronghold in Greece famous for its fortifications.</note> when Sultan Suleiman <note>original: *Solimanus Rex Turciae*; Suleiman the Magnificent (r. 1520–1566).</note> besieged it for twenty years and did not perceive from where the city received its supplies of food and other things. The Prince, however, having received his men within the walls, withdrew into the citadel and into a small, very ornate round chamber, equipped with everything worthy of such a Prince. He remained there for the duration of the siege, as he took the greatest delight in that refuge; it was crafted in the manner one may see in the Duchy of Lorraine <note>original: *Ducatu Lotharingiae*.</note>. From there, through four windows, whatever schemes the enemies might devise to intercept him were visible to him. But they could not enter, because the main door of his dwelling was closed to them in such a way that no one was able to open it except the faithful Steward, who arranged and provided for everything so prudently that throughout an entire year of siege, nothing was lacking. Because of the daily attacks made by the Emperor's soldiers, the Prince was forced to divide his army into five troops, so that each might keep watch in their own turns. The leaders of the army persuaded the Emperor in this manner not to move his camp: "If we leave the Prince (they said), he will rightly mock us, especially because he claims to have withdrawn from our ranks and from us for this reason: because he was treated with less respect than he deserved. Therefore, if he escapes our hands, he will seek every opportunity for the aforementioned revenge." These and similar words persuaded the Emperor to deliberate with a most stubborn mind to make the Prince a captive through hunger, or by whatever other way he could. As winter was pressing in, the Emperor retained a part of his camp with himself for a time, and the rest he left in the siege under the leadership of a most powerful Satrap <note>A high-ranking official or governor; here likely representing a specific chemical process or intense heat</note>, who made many attacks daily against the Prince's soldiers. 

The Emperor’s plan was that his men should not move camp before a year had passed. When the Prince understood this, he commanded his steward <term>oeconomus: the manager of the work; the alchemist</term> and his troops that each should bring back one banner seized by force of arms from the Emperor's army, under penalty of his greatest indignation if they did not fulfill his commands. He also promised an immense reward to any who succeeded; he even promised that he would go forth in his own person, accompanied by his faithful steward, and strike the enemy's hand so vigorously that he would either lose his life or bring back the Emperor's primary banner, and thus enrich all who followed him above all his enemies who were besieging him. 

Therefore, with their spirits renewed, before the appointed time could pass, as many of the Emperor's signs as he had desired were brought to him through his troops, by means of a doubled circle <note>This "doubled circle" likely refers to a specific arrangement of the furnace or the vessel's circulation</note> which a certain Prince of Italy had taught his steward. 

The first banner was of the black German knights, whom they call the Black Riders <note>original: "Reutherorum atrorum," referring to the *Schwarze Reiter*. In alchemy, this represents the *Nigredo* or the black stage of putrefaction</note>. The second was interspersed with various colors <note>This represents the *Cauda Pavonis* or Peacock's Tail stage, where many colors appear in the vessel</note>. The third was not so very different from the sign of the King of France <note>Likely the white fleur-de-lis, representing the *Albedo* or white stage</note>. The fourth was marked with a crescent Moon. The fifth, however, was like the greatest sign of the Emperor <note>The Sun or Gold, representing the final *Rubedo* or red stage</note>. This sight so increased the Prince's courage that on the following day he went to the walls with his steward and there fought vigorously beyond measure, until he obtained the greatest banner of the Emperors. 

Returning at last and exhausted, he was refreshed by the steward with the remaining food from the beginning of the siege; and with his strength revived, he and his steward manfully leaped upon the enemy again with his men. He partly threw down and partly put to flight the entire army of the Emperor, with the help of the leaders, who were all distinguished by the colors of their Prince. It happened thereafter that every Potentate—whether it be the Pope, or the Emperor, or a King, a Prince, or even the Sultan <note>original: "Solimanus," referring to Suleiman the Magnificent, the personification of worldly power</note>, as many as there are—must yield the palm to the Golden Prince <note>original: "Auro Principi," referring to the successful creation of alchemical gold</note> and grant him the victory, God thus ordering and willing it, to whom be praise, honor, and glory.

# A SHORT TREATISE #

everlasting. It remains for us to declare how the projection <note>The process of casting the Alchemical Stone onto base metals to effect transmutation</note> of our divine work upon metals, the tincture of gems, and the medicine of the human body are situated within it.

### *On the projection upon metals.* ###

Of our King <note>original: "Regis nostri"; the King is the completed Philosopher's Stone</note>, now multiplied in strength and refreshed with food, let one ounce be projected upon four ounces of pure gold, melted and purified. From this will be made a brittle material which, once pulverized, should be cooked in a "closed mountain" <note>An alchemical term for a sealed furnace or vessel</note> with the heat of the final assault, in a very narrow and well-sealed vessel for the space of three days. 

Let one ounce of this powder be projected upon twenty-five marks <note>A unit of weight for precious metals</note> of silver or copper, or upon eighteen marks of lead or tin, or upon fifteen marks of common quicksilver <term>argentum vivum: mercury</term>—either heated in a crucible or congealed with lead. The material will soon be covered with a thick foam; once the operation is complete, a crackling sound will occur, as if the crucible were breaking. Finally, let this material be melted, and it will be converted into gold. 

However, if the stated weight is not observed, or the material has not changed from its prior color, it must be refined in a large cupel <note>A shallow vessel used in assaying; "cineritio"</note> without lead, so that in the space of three hours the material which has not been transmuted may be consumed. The pure remainder at the bottom must be further purified for six hours with royal cement <note>A mixture used to refine gold</note>. In this way, all the gold will be obtained, converted by the work of our great King, similar and equal to any mineral gold. And this is the way that Raymond Lully <note>A famous 13th-century philosopher and purported alchemist</note> teaches in his *Codicil* regarding projection. He teaches the second way, for the tincture of gems, in his *Testament*.

### *On the Tincture of gems and pearls.* ###

Our great King must be washed and refreshed immediately after the white sign marked by the waxing moon is brought to him; the end of the siege should not be waited for, but rather he should be fed from his first meal of refreshment. This is the Mercury which Raymond Lully called "exuberated quicksilver." 

Let two or three ounces of it be placed upon ashes in a small, well-closed alembic <note>A distilling apparatus</note>. Let them be distilled first with a slow fire. When nothing more wishes to drip at this heat, the receiver should be changed and sealed more strongly, and finally, whatever is able to ascend should be driven up with a stronger fire. This second liquor should be distilled in a fresh alembic by means of Mary’s bath <term>balneum Mariae: a water bath used for gentle, even heating</term>, distilling the liquor three times over the viscous dregs (a process called cohobation), and the waters will be dissolved in their own short time. 

On the third time, however, let the whole be distilled through ashes, and afterwards distilled four times again in a fresh alembic via the water bath, keeping the dregs separate each time, until the distilled water is clear and shining with the white brilliance of pearls. Its use for pearls <note>original: "uniones"; refers to large, high-quality pearls</note> is as follows: Let these pearls, even if they are very small, be placed in a small cucurbit <note>A gourd-shaped chemical glass</note>, and let enough of the said water be poured over them so that it stands slightly above them. Let it be covered with a "blind head" <note>A still-head without a spout, used for digestion rather than distillation</note>, and after three hours they will be resolved into a white paste, and—

...the very clear liquor will float; let it be emptied out gently so as not to disturb <note>The sediment or dregs at the bottom</note>. Let the cucurbit <term>cucurbita: a gourd-shaped chemical flask</term> with the paste be placed, covered, into a Mary’s bath <note>original: "balneum Mariae"; a water bath used for gentle, uniform heating</note> to digest for [several] days, and afterwards let it be removed. Let a small, round silver mold be fashioned, gilded on the inside, which can be opened through the middle into two equal parts; and let a gold wire, or a silver-gilt wire, be fitted between the two cavities. Then, let each half of the gold mold be filled with the said paste; let the wire be placed through the middle in the center of its opening, and let the mold be closed. Let the wire then be pushed forward and pulled back, so that a pearl <term>unio: a large, high-quality pearl</term> is well-formed through the center. 

When the mold is opened, let the formed pearl be taken out and placed in a small gold dish covered by another similar one; do not touch it with your hand. Let it be dried in the shade, and not in the sun. When you have made many, let them all be perforated by the wire and placed in a glass channel <note>A tube</note> having a hole on one side, and on the other a hole no larger than the gold wire. Let them be placed together in a glass vessel <note>original: "bocia"; a glass flask or matrass</note> or a clean glass urinal above the liquid of the said sublimated material. Let the vessel be sealed with lute <note>A paste used to make airtight seals</note> and maintained in the air for eight days; afterwards, for three days in the sun, moving the glass every three hours so that the vapor may ascend. By this artifice, pearls of as great a quantity as you wish shall be perfected. In the same manner, it can be done with rubies and carbuncles by means of red Mercury, after its single refinement.

## *On the use of our divine work for the medicine* ##
## *of the human body.* ##

Let one grain by weight be taken after the departure of the King <note>The "King" refers to the completed Alchemical Stone</note>, and let it be dissolved in white wine in a silver vessel. The wine will be tinged with a citrine <note>Yellowish-orange</note> color. Let this be administered to the sick shortly after midnight; they will be cured in one day if the disease is of one month's duration; if it has been for one year, they will be cured within twelve days, or within a month where the disease is to be very long-lasting. To preserve health, it should be taken twice every year, at the beginning of spring and autumn. By this medicine, one lives cheerfully until the predestined term of life, God granting—to whom be praise, honor, and glory now, always, and forever. Amen.

->*The end of the short work of Dionysius Zacharius.*<-

# CERTAIN NOTES FROM NICOLAS #
## Flammel, a French Author. ##

For a true knowledge of metals, one must not be ignorant that while they still exist in their primary forms—that is, in Sulphur and in Quicksilver <term>argentum vivum: mercury</term>—they have two forms: one masculine and the other feminine. These are the two seeds of male and female. The first, Sulphur, contains two masculine elements: Fire and Air. The second [Mercury] contains two other feminine elements: Earth and Water. These two are compared in the Art to two serpents: one winged, the other... <note>Text cuts off at the margin; likely "the other wingless"</note>

### ANNOTATIONS.

...to the other, which is indeed lacking wings and is much more terrible <note>original: "alis carenti"; in alchemical imagery, "winged" often represents volatile substances, while "wingless" represents fixed substances</note>. These two seeds <term>spermata: the fundamental reproductive essences of metals</term> if they are joined through nature in the belly of Mercury—which, on account of its heat, is called the "fire of nature" <note>original: "ignis naturae"</note> and by some the "devouring lion" <note>original: "leo devorans"</note>—and although gold and silver enter its belly, they are not consumed, because they are harder and more perfect than that nature. Mercury is imperfect; nevertheless, common gold and silver originate from it. Silver is the substance of the "lower moon" <note>original: "lunae inferioris"</note>, just as gold is of the "lower sun" <note>original: "solis etiam inferioris"</note>. Mercury, therefore, the mother, must be killed and die through the aforementioned seeds; once she has been mortified by nature, she can never again return to life. For even the slightest bit [of Mercury] congealed in the veins of the earth soon contains a fixed grain of gold, which produces the true sprout of Mercury from the two seeds. This can be seen in the cavities of lead, in which there is no mineral anywhere that does not clearly contain a true fixed grain—that is, a grain of gold or silver. Indeed, the first congealing of Mercury is the ore of lead <note>original: "minera plumbi"</note>, in which it has been placed by nature. 

This can truly be multiplied to its perfection without doubt or error, yet while existing in its own Mercury and not separated from its ore. For a metal existing in its own ore is Mercury; if the grain is separated from it, it will be like an unripe apple taken from its tree, which is utterly destroyed. The fixed grain is like the fruit, and Mercury is the tree. Therefore, the fruit must not be separated from the tree, because it cannot receive nourishment from anywhere else except from its own Mercury. It is a great folly to place gold and silver into Mercury [artificially], no differently than trying to reattach a plucked apple to a tree. Therefore, so that this business may be fulfilled properly, the tree must be taken together with its fruit, so that it may be planted anew—without removing the fruit—into a more fertile and noble earth. This earth will give more nourishment in a single day than the former field would have provided in a hundred years, due to the constant agitation of the winds. 

This other earth, because it is closest to the sun, causes the tree to grow and flourish with continuous dew and the persistent sun in the **philosophical garden** <note>original: "horto philosophico"</note>. Shining without intermission morning and evening, day and night, and every single hour, the tree is sprinkled and nourished by the sweetest dew—more in one year than in ten thousand in the former earth. Therefore, when both are placed in a furnace of continuous heat day and night, its vapor, which is the dew, prevents combustion. The heat of wood or charcoal is useless, and indeed harmful. Thus, the wise Philosophers did not wish to work in any other thing than in nature itself, with the "moon" itself, in a mother suitable for Mercury. From this, they finally produced a "general Mercury," far more powerful and stronger than the natural kind. 

Ascend, therefore, the mountain, so that you may see the vegetable, royal, and mineral **saturnine herb** <note>original: "vegetabilem saturniam... herbam"; Saturnia refers to lead, but here it implies a specific stage or substance in the Great Work</note>. For its juice is smoked pure once the dregs are cast away. For from that, you will be able to perfect the greatest part of your work.

Above all, therefore, do not wash your Mercury, but join it with its own part—that is, with fire—over the ashes (which are nevertheless present) in a glass vessel alone, without any other thing. ->*The Fountain of Chemistry.*<-

The fountain and cave of all metals is the mother, from whom those seven <note>The seven metals of antiquity: Gold, Silver, Mercury, Copper, Iron, Tin, and Lead</note> are born and proceed, according to their nature. Likewise: Saturn, Jupiter, Mars, and Luna. Lead, understood intellectually, is "leprous gold" <note>original: "aurum leprosum"; alchemists believed lead was simply gold that had been "infected" by impurities or was "unripe"</note>, etc. Moreover, if the Fountain of Nature receives the Mercury placed within it, an most excellent medicine will be made from it. Mercury is born in the earth as a leaden mass; let it be liberated after it has been shut in a prison, otherwise the desired weight and measure cannot be known. However, you will be able to know the method for it. The Mercury of the Sun <term>Gold</term> is not like the Mercury of the Moon <term>Silver</term>, since the latter must always remain white so that it may procreate its own likeness, but the Mercury of the Sun must be "rubified" <note>turned red, the final stage of the alchemical Great Work</note>, and this is the first labor: and afterwards they can be gathered together. 

It must certainly be noted that the <term>fifth essence</term> <note>the "quintessence," or the pure, incorruptible spirit of a substance</note> is especially necessary to us in this art, and that this Mercury is found most of all in that place where the Sun is at its greatest heat and produces many flowers: for the fruit follows after the flowers. It is found similarly in the Moon when sought therein; in Saturn, Mars, Venus, and more safely in Mercury. But I (says Flamel) found and worked it in the Sun. Therefore, when these individual things—each of which is like the other—come together in this philosophical work, then the offspring devours the mother, and suffocates its own father in a unique lake, in which flowers, milk, fruit, and blood are found all at once. 

Therefore, this one metal must be placed in a single vessel and in a single furnace. It is Mercury of which I speak, and nothing else. To shorten the work, there is one single metal held in this world in which this Mercury of ours is found in abundance. Gold is hot and dry; the Moon <term>Silver</term> is of a cold nature; Saturn <term>Lead</term> is heavy and soft: on this account it is like the Sun, and for this reason is called "leprous gold." Venus <term>Copper</term> is like the Moon in weight and malleability; Mercury is cold and moist, similar to Jupiter <term>Tin</term> which is born from it; but Mars <term>Iron</term> is hard, heavy, and cold. 

All this business consists in two things: namely, that you make your <term>sulphur</term> <note>the active, masculine principle in alchemy</note> penetrative and attractive by fire, so that it may be able to devour its own mother; then you will have completed the work. Fix the mother in the belly of her offspring, whom she brought forth before; then at last he will be both father and son to himself, a perfected spirit from the two. After your sulphur has been devoured and its Mercury "mortified" <note>killed or chemically transformed</note>, let it be cast into a prison, in which it should remain for forty days; and you will see what you desire, according to these verses:

->*If you dissolve the fixed, and make the dissolved fly,*<-
->*And you fix the flying thing, it will make you live safely.*<-
<note>original: "Si fixum solvas, faciasque volare solutum, / Et volucrem figas, faciet te vivere tutum." This is a fundamental alchemical axiom: "Solve et Coagula" (dissolve and congeal). To "make the dissolved fly" is to volatilize a solid, and to "fix the flying" is to solidify a vapor.</note>

->**JEAN de MEUNG on the Lamentations of Nature.**<-
<note>Jean de Meung (c. 1240–1305) was a famous French poet best known for completing the *Roman de la Rose*. In the late Middle Ages and Renaissance, several alchemical treatises were attributed to him.</note>

That which is contained beneath the Moon is called "heaven" in this context, because matter desires form, not otherwise than a woman desires a man. Matter consists solely of the four elements, from which <term>Chaos</term><note>The "prime matter" or disorganized state of the elements before they are refined.</note> is made, and from that chaos the King and Queen are generated. First, indeed, fire was created by God, which He placed beneath the Moon; it is free from corruption and contains within itself the purest part of the <term>Quinta Essentia</term><note>The "Fifth Essence" or Quintessence: a celestial substance distinct from the four terrestrial elements (earth, air, fire, water), believed to be the matter of the heavenly bodies and the key to alchemical transformation.</note>. Afterward, the subtle air was made, in which God likewise placed a portion of the fifth essence—though not as much as in the fire—and a lesser amount in the water, and the least in the earth. 

Therefore, just as fire acts upon the air, so the air acts upon the water, and the water upon the earth. Earth is the mother and the nurse of all things which she conceives in her womb from the fire: she nourishes this very thing even into her center without intermission. Since, therefore, Nature alone has the power of reducing the four elements into the first matter, generally mixed from whichever elements, it would be impossible for any operator to achieve this except through Nature herself, who alone gives the matter and the life. 

For the fifth essence, which is called the <term>Golden Chain</term><note>original: "cathena aurea"; a reference to the Homeric Chain, interpreted by alchemists as the continuous link of spirit and influence between the heavens and the earth.</note>, connects and harmonizes contraries in such a way that they may never disagree again. Gold must be considered first of all, which receives its most beautiful form in heaven, and its best matter on earth, as do gemstones. Heaven, therefore, informs the fifth essence with form and matter contained within the element, through which the form is held fast: which is perfected by purification and the passing of a long time. 

Thus, gold and gems are composed by me, Nature, alone: for no one knows the proportions besides me. That which you seek is truly the highest secret of nature, descending from celestial virtue. For this reason, all science is owed to Nature, by which the simplicity of the element is drawn forth from heaven; this is called the "primitive essence" in heaven, and the "fifth essence" in the element, which Nature herself produces through reductions and long <term>circulations</term><note>A process of continuous distillation where the vapor rises and falls back into the liquid, mimicking the hydrological cycle of the earth.</note>, by turning the lower into the higher, and by preserving the cold and dry within the moist and hot; she preserves stones and metals under their "radical moisture" by the celestial motions of the stars, by which the elements are governed and obey their influences. Thus, the purer the matter is, the more excellent the work becomes through Nature. 

Therefore, celestial motion is the corresponding intelligence in lower things, in which it produces all things into being through its influences. Nature, then, uses an infallible matter in any fire, because she receives all virtue from it. Likewise, water proceeding from a dry origin, wetting nothing that it touches, neither receding nor volatile, is the <term>Incombustible Oil</term><note>original: "oleum incombustibile"; a metaphorical term for a substance that has reached a state of perfect stability, able to withstand fire without being destroyed or evaporated.</note>. No artificial fire could infuse as much heat as that which comes from heaven. Furthermore, in these matters it must not be ignored that this entire work of ours is made from a vile, homogeneous matter, closed in a single vessel, [and] in a single furnace containing... 
<meta>The text ends mid-word with the catchword "nente," completing "continente" (containing/enclosing) on the next page.</meta>

...which completes it: for it is perfected by management alone, by imitating Nature. In the generation of a human being, Nature similarly forms the body from <term>quicksilver</term><note>original: *argentum vivo*. In alchemy, "quicksilver" or Mercury represents the feminine, receptive, and volatile principle of matter.</note> and masculine <term>sulfur</term><note>Sulfur represents the masculine, active, and stabilizing principle.</note> acting within a vessel—contained, that is, within the womb—whose furnace is the belly. Although a man may assist through his own skill, while Nature burns in her own essence, he can do nothing else except pour in the appropriate matter. It is no different in our art: if someone knows how to choose the kind of matter in which Nature delights, and ensures it has been rightly prepared and enclosed in the furnace, "I," says Nature, "and he shall perfect it." This will happen without delay, provided he administers the required fire—a fire that is against nature, not natural, and without burning heat. It is a fire, she says, that is simultaneously hot, dry, moist, and cold. Consider, therefore, that it must be so: for without fire and matter, nothing is accomplished in this science. "I give you the matter," says Nature; "the form is what you yourself prepare." I do not mean the substantial or accidental form, but the melting vessel and the furnace. Next, prepare your matter, made into a powder with its own water, and enclosed in a single vessel. Rule it with a tempered fire; this will promote the action, and the coldness will promote the <term>putrefaction</term><note>The stage of "blackness" (*nigredo*), where the matter must "die" and decay before it can be reborn and purified.</note>. Indeed, because of the great coldness, the dryness could not be hindered, nor could it resist this mercury, preventing the quicksilver from being reduced into the <term>prime matter</term><note>original: *primam materiam*. The original, undifferentiated state of all things, which the alchemist seeks to recover.</note> through a complete union. 

"Before you work," says Nature, "learn to know me: I am fourfold, and without me no creature can receive essence or live, nor have a sensing soul without the heavens and the elements." There is indeed a medium between Mercury and metal which is to be made for our art: it is, I say, <term>potable gold</term><note>original: *aurum potabile*. A legendary liquid medicine made from gold, believed to grant eternal youth or health.</note>, the <term>radical moisture</term><note>original: *humidum radicale*. The fundamental life-force or "sap" believed to exist within all living things and minerals.</note>, and the highest medicine which we perfect through your skill and my knowledge. "Without me, who provides the matter, you will never accomplish anything; and without you, who ministers to it, this work could not be executed by me alone. But through me and you, it shall be concluded in a short time." Transmute the four elements, bringing forth and attracting metals under a transmutable form—this matter was considered worthy of note by the philosophers, yet was despised by the ignorant. In substance it is similar to gold, but in essence it is dissimilar. By converting its elements, you will find what you seek: by sublimating the lower things, and inverting the superior and the inferior. Therefore, take this living mercury mixed with the active vapor, and having enclosed it in a single vessel and a single furnace, bury the vessel for a third of its part, continuing the <term>philosophical fire</term><note>A gentle, consistent heat, often compared to the warmth of a brooding hen.</note> above it. Let every species be left behind, except for the matter alone from which the mineral took its origin.

this matter is confused and not diffused until it is specified and qualified by nature. Then at last it receives its <term>substantial form</term><note>In Aristotelian philosophy, the "substantial form" is the essential nature that makes a thing what it is, as opposed to "accidental" qualities like color or shape.</note>, and afterward its visible accidental form. For it transforms the prior form so that a new form may inform the matter. Indeed, the object is subject to potentiality, because it sustains a substance in <term>actuality</term><note>original: *in actu*. The transition from potential (what something could be) to actual (what it is) is a core concept in alchemical transformation.</note> which was previously in potential. Gold is known to be the treasure of all minerals; however, it does not possess a form or matter of such power that it might exceed its own perfection. For it has no greater power than that of perfecting itself, no matter what the craftsman may labor to do. To destroy it and reduce it to its essence would be a foolish task, since nothing more of virtue or power can be obtained from it than what it possesses from its own nature. No reduction occurs in those things which nature has already perfected into a species or an individual unless they are first corrupted. Even after corruption, the generation of a similar species does not occur unless there is a return to this <term>genus</term><note>The general category or "family" of matter from which specific things arise.</note>. Therefore, the destruction of gold does not pave the way for its construction, because nothing can be built through its own destruction: for when the gold itself is dead, its substance dies along with it, so that no other <term>quicksilver</term><note>original: *argentum vivum*. This suggests that once gold is "dead," you cannot extract the living, transformative mercury back out of it to start a new process.</note> or metal can ever be born from it. And because the element of fire is contained in the earth, and air in the water—of which no one knows the quantity, quality, or proportion of their perfect conjunction—the elements must not be separated, since they cannot be restored. Therefore, we must take only that which nature has generated and left for us to use in the Art. In short, the separation of elements is not effectively performed on quicksilver, nor on the <term>sun</term><note>original: *solis*. In alchemy, the Sun is the symbol for Gold and the masculine principle.</note>, who is the father of the art, imparting spirit to his own son.

Each detail is treated concisely, yet the steps necessary for this work must be most carefully considered through every period, and not passed over thoughtlessly. For the truth of this divine science is more easily grasped from such a small discourse than from the most abundant and innumerable volumes, which often hide the unity and simplicity of truth behind a multitude and variety of words.

# OTHER VARIOUS ANNOTATIONS FROM DIVERSE AUTHORS.

## *On the solution and coagulation of the matter of Chemistry.*

Since solution is the chief operation of this art, it must be spoken of first, citing the authorities of various Philosophers so that it may be more easily understood, with one interpreting the other. These, therefore, are the notes we wished to collect and weave into our notebooks. For the mind of the Philosophers must be sought out from their variety, if trust is to be placed in comparisons leading to one and the same sense. In those things where they most clearly agree, there can be no doubt that this is the very thing sought. Indeed, the entire business of the divine philosophical work consists in these two operations: namely, in <term>solution</term> and <term>congealing</term>. Solution, therefore, according to the opinion of <term>Geber</term><note>Geber is the Latinized name of Jabir ibn Hayyan (c. 721–815), a foundational figure in early chemistry and alchemy.</note>, is the reduction of a dry thing into water.

### THE LADDER OF PHILOSOPHERS.
> The solution of the stone is its reduction into mineral water.

### VILLANOVANUS.
> We dissolve (he says) when we divide bodies; we render them simple and subtle, and we resolve them into their first nature and matter.

### AVICENNA *on matter.*
> The first matter is twofold, the near and the remote: the near <meta>catchword: is</meta>

### UNKNOWN AUTHOR.

### CLANGOR.

Solution is a work of nature, and not of art; the craftsman is only the servant and helper of nature.

### VILLANOVANUS.
<note>Arnald of Villanova (c. 1240–1311), a celebrated physician and alchemist.</note>

Dissolution is the perfection of wisdom: for it is necessary that wisdom itself be sought; otherwise, it will not be found. Therefore Hermes said: Man cannot have, nor discover, dissolution except through the fire of divine genius.

The true principle of our work is the dissolution of the stone. The same author says: The first regimen of the stone is to dissolve the stone and to reduce it into its first nature.

You, whoever wishes to work, have need to labor first in the solution and sublimation of the two <term>luminaries</term><note>original: *luminarium*. ### THE PLAY OF CHILDREN.
<note>original: *Ludus Puerorum*. A title often given to alchemical texts to suggest that once the secret is known, the work is as easy as a child's game.</note>

The craftsman of our work must first dissolve the stone, then coagulate it; since our work is nothing other than to bring about a perfect solution and congealing.

### CLANGOR.

This entire art turns on this: that we join the moist with the dry—that is, that we dissolve and coagulate. The moist is the liquid spirit cleansed of all filth. The dry is the perfect body, pure and <term>calcined</term><note>original: *calcinatum*. Reduced to a fine powder through the application of high heat to remove volatile components.</note>.

## THE ASSEMBLY OF PHILOSOPHERS.
<note>original: *Congregatio Philosophorum*. Likely referring to a collection of sayings from the *Turba Philosophorum*.</note>

Nature completes that stage which it is capable of completing, but it cannot go beyond it. Another says: Nature contains within itself those things which it needs, but it does not reach completion unless it is moved by art and operation. Likewise: The first dispositions of the stone <note>The "Stone" refers to the Philosophers' Stone, the goal of the alchemical work.</note> can be induced by no art; nature alone can do this. Likewise: The matter of the stone is produced by nature. To create the matter through any artifice is impossible. For the stone is found already created by nature, and it needs nothing else except that whatever is superfluous in it—that is, in its matter—be removed.

### AVICENNA.
<note>Referring to "Pseudo-Avicenna," as the historical Persian physician Ibn Sina did not actually support alchemy, though many Latin works were attributed to him.</note>

The stone does not bear fruit until it is reduced to nothing, like running water.

### THE ASSEMBLY.
<note>original: *Turba*. Refers to the *Turba Philosophorum*, a foundational Latin alchemical text.</note>

Our whole magistery <note>The "magistery" or *magisterium* is the technical term for the entire alchemical process or "The Great Work."</note> is performed with our water; from it, and out of it, all necessary things are made. For it dissolves the bodies with a true and philosophical dissolution, so that they are converted into the water from which they originated in the beginning. Elsewhere it says: Unless every single thing is turned into water, you will in no way arrive at perfection.

### ALPHIDIUS.
<note>An Arabic alchemist often cited in medieval Latin texts, possibly Al-Kindi.</note>

Unless you refine the natures, turning them into water, you can color nothing: therefore, make the bodies become water by liquefying them, which among the Philosophers is called the "Water of Wisdom."

### THE ROSARY.
<note>original: *Rosarius*. Likely the *Rosarium Philosophorum* (The Rosary of the Philosophers), a famous 16th-century alchemical florilegium.</note>

Permanent water—also called perennial water or "burning wine"—is called the "water of the body"; that is, when the body has been reduced into Mercury. Likewise: Permanent water <note>original: *aqua permanens*. A solvent that does not evaporate when heated.</note> cannot exist without its body, with which it was dissolved. Likewise: Without permanent water, nothing is made. It is also called the "water of life" <note>original: *aqua vitæ*.</note>. Likewise: Only with burning wine can you complete the perfect elixir.

### THE LADDER.
<note>original: *Scala*. Refers to the *Scala Philosophorum* (The Ladder of the Philosophers), attributed to Guido Montanor.</note>

The Dragon is the sulfur which is extracted from the bodies through the magistery.

### AVICENNA.

He who sets out to make the white elixir will find white sulfur in silver, and red sulfur in gold. And since such sulfur is not found upon the earth except in these two bodies, the bodies must be prepared subtly, so that we may obtain their sulfur and their quicksilver <note>original: *argentum vivum*.</note> from them, just as they were the materials from which gold and silver were produced under the earth.

### THE CLANGOR.
<note>Refers to the *Clangor Buccinae* (The Clanging of the Trumpet), a well-known alchemical treatise.</note>

Dissolve the perfect body into Mercury; from this you will have the hidden virtue—that is, the philosophical sulfur, digested and decocted by...
