...no addition, except for digestion, by which means all four elements are enclosed within the gold and are matured in equal proportion.

### THE COMMON OPINION
<note>original: *Communis Sententia*. This refers to a widely accepted philosophical or alchemical maxim.</note>

The corruption of one thing is the generation of another, and this is true in artificial things as well as in natural things. Otherwise stated: According to nature, nothing is generated which is not first corrupted, and nothing rises again which has not first died.

### BERNARD
<note>Refers to Bernard of Trevisan, a 15th-century Italian alchemist known for his work on the "Great Work."</note>

If gold is boiled in quicksilver <note>original: *argentum vivo*</note>, or dissolved in the proper way and by the natural path, the quicksilver itself will obtain the natural properties of the gold. Also by the same: The solution which is made by the Water of the Philosophers <note>The "Water of the Philosophers" is a secret solvent, not common water, used to break down metals.</note> indeed corrupts the external form of the dissolved bodies, but it does not corrupt the matter.

### VILLANOVA
<note>Refers to Arnaldus de Villa Nova (c. 1240–1311), a famous physician and alchemist.</note>

That which dissolves the body is of the spirit, but that which coagulates the spirit is of the body. Elsewhere: The spirit dissolves, the body coagulates. The same: As much as the body is dissolved, so much is the spirit coagulated. For if the body were not dissolved, neither would the spirit be thickened. Elsewhere: That which comes out of the dissolved body is a radiant humidity; that which dissolves the body proceeds from the spirit, and its power is germinative. The same elsewhere: The solution of the body happens with the coagulation of the spirit, and the coagulation of the spirit with the solution of the body. Then the body is mixed with the spirit and becomes one with it, and they are never separated—no more than water mixed with water.

### THE CLANGOR
<note>original: *Clangor*. Short for *Clangor Buccinae* (The Sound of the Trumpet), a 14th-century alchemical text.</note>

When the seed <note>original: *sperma*</note> of Mercury is joined with the earth of the body, the body is dissolved into the water of the seed, and it becomes one water without division.

### VILLANOVA

Understand, moreover, that the solution of the body and the coagulation of the spirit happen at the same time.

### THE ROSARY ACCORDING TO CALID
<note>original: *Rosarius ex Calide*. Likely quoting the *Rosarium Philosophorum* citing Calid (Khalid ibn Yazid), a legendary Umayyad prince and early alchemist.</note>

The solution of the body and the coagulation of the spirit are two things, but they have a single operation. Because the spirit is not coagulated except with the solution of the body, nor is the body dissolved, except with the coagulation of the spirit. Therefore, between the solution of the body and the coagulation of the spirit there is no difference, nor any diverse work in any way; they cannot happen one without the other. Just as we see occurring when common water strives to make the earth finer and to dissolve it into its own matter: for at the same time the water becomes denser and thicker, while the earth becomes finer and more rarified.

### LULLY
<note>Refers to Ramon Lully (Raymond Lull), a 13th-century polymath to whom many alchemical works were later attributed.</note>

Many of the Philosophers dissolved the bodies of metals in common aqua fortis <note>original: *aqua forti*. Literally "strong water," a technical term for nitric acid.</note>, made from vitriol <note>original: *vitriolo*. A sulfate mineral.</note> and saltpeter <note>original: *sale nitro*.</note>, and through evaporation they drew off that water, and then the lime <note>original: *calx*. The powdery residue or "ash" of a metal after it has been heated or dissolved.</note> remained at the bottom of the vessel.

...[washed it?], which they afterwards washed with common sweet water: then they removed that water by evaporation, and dissolved the lime <note>original: *calcem*. ### ROGER BACON
<note>Roger Bacon (c. 1219–1292) was an English philosopher and friar who was later associated with many alchemical legends.</note>

Nothing adheres to metals, nor is joined to them, nor transmutates them, unless it is of their own kind.

### BERNARD OF TREVISAN
<note>A 15th-century Italian alchemist famous for his search for the Philosopher's Stone.</note>

Fools make corrosive waters from minerals by dissolution, into which they put the species of metals; and these waters corrode but do not dissolve by a natural solution, which requires the permanence of both—namely, the solvent and the dissolved.

### THE SAME
<note>Referring back to Bernard of Trevisan.</note>

No water dissolves a metallic species by natural reduction, except that which remains with the metallic species in matter and form, and which the metals themselves can re-congeal. This is not the case in strong waters <note>nitric acid</note> which do not pertain to the dissolved bodies. Indeed, bodies are corroded by strong waters, but not dissolved. But the more they are corroded, the more they are alienated from the metallic species.

### ARNALDUS DE VILLA NOVA
<note>A 13th-century physician and alchemist.</note>

Through solution, the body is mixed with the spirit, and becomes one with it, so that one is never separated from the other.

### CLANGOR BUCCINAE
<note>original: *Clangor*. Refers to the text 'Clangor Buccinae' or 'The Sound of the Trumpet,' a famous alchemical treatise.</note>

The body is dissolved into the water of the seed <note>original: *spermatis*. In this context, it refers to the 'living' metallic essence rather than biological fluid.</note>, and from that, the water becomes one without division.

### THE PHILOSOPHER
<note>Usually refers to Aristotle, though often used for any great authority.</note>

Voluntary solution is better than violent, and a tempered one is better than one that is hasty: and therefore care must be taken lest the power of the generative form be suffocated with corrosives and burning substances.

### THE ROSARY
<note>Refers to the 'Rosarium Philosophorum,' a foundational alchemical text illustrating the 'marriage' of substances.</note>

In our Stone, the Sun and Moon <note>alchemical symbols for Gold and Silver</note> are alive, and can produce other suns and moons from themselves. Other gold and other silver are dead for this purpose: for their power and potency remain in the solution made by our water. Other water would have destroyed them and rendered them sterile.

### ARNALDUS DE VILLA NOVA

Solution only occurs through quicksilver <note>original: *argentum vivum*</note>: for it alone can reduce the sun and moon to their first matter. The same: The whole benefit of this art consists in Mercury, the Sun, and the Moon.

### ARISTOTLE

If we had nothing else from Mercury except that it thinned <note>The text ends mid-word: *subti-* (likely *subtiliaret* or *subtiliat*).</note> the bodies...

...it refines to its own nature, it would offer us no small benefit.

### GEBER
<note>Geber is the Latinized name of Jabir ibn Hayyan (c. 721–815), a legendary figure considered the father of early chemistry.</note>

All perfection of solution is brought about with subtle waters, especially those that are sharp, acidic, pungent, and having no dregs, such as distilled vinegar, juice of unripe grapes, very tart pears, distilled pomegranates, and similar things.

### VILLANOVANUS
<note>Refers to Arnaldus de Villa Nova (c. 1240–1311), a famous physician and alchemist.</note>

The nature of the dissolved body and the dissolving water is one and the same, except that the nature of the body is complete, digested, and fixed; while the nature of the water is incomplete, undigested, and volatile.

### REGOR
<note>Likely a variant spelling for "Roger" (referring to Roger Bacon) or another medieval authority.</note>

Quicksilver <note>original: *argentum vivum*. Literally "living silver," the common name for mercury.</note> is a fire that burns, kills, and shatters bodies.

### ROSINUS
<note>Rosinus is the Latinized name for Zosimos of Panopolis, a 3rd-century Egyptian-Greek alchemist.</note>

Water is as much hotter than fire as fire is hotter than water.

### ROSARIUS
<note>Refers to the *Rosarium Philosophorum* (The Rose Garden of the Philosophers), a highly influential 16th-century alchemical treatise.</note>

Our water is stronger than fire, because it makes a pure spirit out of the body of gold, which fire cannot do. The same author says: The spirit is entirely fiery, dissolving and dividing bodies through its own fieriness.

### TURBA
<note>Refers to the *Turba Philosophorum* (The Assembly of the Philosophers), one of the oldest Latin alchemical texts translated from Arabic.</note>

Burn our copper <note>original: *æs*. While this can mean bronze or brass, in alchemy it often refers to the "base" matter being transformed.</note> with the strongest fire.

### CALIDIUS
<note>Refers to Khalid ibn Yazid, an Umayyad prince and early alchemist.</note>

A lesser fire wears all things down: for it works less than our water, which dissolves the body in a way that fire is unable to do.

### LULLIUS
<note>Ramon Llull (c. 1232–1315), a Majorcan polymath to whom many alchemical works were later attributed.</note>

It can be known that the "first matter" of our Stone <note>The "Philosopher's Stone," the goal of the Great Work.</note> is from the nature of quicksilver and sulfur: because it cannot be destroyed in fire, nor in water, nor in air.

### ROSARIUS

Some have said that common quicksilver adheres to bodies, which is false. For what Geber says—"We have not found in our discovery anything more befriended to the natures of bodies than quicksilver"—must be understood entirely as *philosophical* quicksilver. For it alone adheres to bodies, nor could the ancient Philosophers find any other thing—nor will the moderns find any other thing—which adheres to bodies, except philosophical quicksilver. Common quicksilver <note>original: *argentum vivum vulgare*. This refers to the liquid metal found in nature, as opposed to the "philosophical" mercury prepared by the alchemist.</note> does not adhere to bodies, and because of this, many are deceived by working with that common quicksilver.

### LULLIUS

Those who dissolve with "strong water" <note>original: *forti aqua*. Likely nitric acid.</note> are ignorant of the plant-based substances <note>original: *vegetabilia*.</note> that sharpen our solvent <note>original: *menstruum*. A specialized liquid used to dissolve solids.</note>; they are also ignorant of the water of common Mercury, which we have written of in our *Testament*.

<page-num>762</page-num>
<header>NICHOLAS FLAMEL</header>
<meta>Catchword: TUR- (Likely referring to the *Turba Philosophorum*)</meta>

->VILLANOVANUS.<-
<note>Arnaldus de Villa Nova (c. 1240–1311), a celebrated physician and alchemist who emphasized the "natural" path of alchemy.</note>

In order that nature may change and transform nature, it needs nothing but what is of its own nature. Likewise, that which dissolves and that which is dissolved are of the same kind and nature. The same author says: A solution of the body or a coagulation of the spirit is not true or philosophical if an external substance or nature is present during the dissolution.

->DASTINUS.<-
<note>John Dastin (c. 1293–1386), an influential English alchemist and member of the household of Cardinal Napoleon Orsini.</note>

It is necessary that the elements of the water be of the same nature as the elements of the metal to be transformed; otherwise, the offspring will be degenerate. For from a diversity of parts, a diversity of the whole is born. Similarity exists among those things which are of one kind and sprout from one root.

->ROSARIUS.<-
<note>Refers to the *Rosarium Philosophorum* (The Rose Garden of the Philosophers), a seminal 16th-century text.</note>

The Philosophers' Stone <term>Lapis Philosophorum; the legendary substance capable of turning base metals into gold and conferring longevity</term> is made from three: namely, the sun, the moon, and Mercury. <note>In alchemical code, "Sun" represents Gold and "Moon" represents Silver.</note> Also: Produce Mercury from the sun and moon in its own being, without common mercury, but by the philosophical way.

->LULLIUS.<-
<note>Ramon Llull (c. 1232–1315), a Majorcan polymath to whom many alchemical works were later attributed.</note>

The Stone is composed of the quicksilver of metals, not of common quicksilver.

->NOVUM LUMEN.<-
<note>Refers to *Novum Lumen Chymicum* (The New Chemical Light), published in 1604 by Michael Sendivogius.</note>

Our quicksilver is not silver in its own nature, nor is it in that nature to which it is brought by the mine, but in the nature to which our art <note>original: *artificium nostrum*; referring to the alchemical process</note> has brought it.

->RICHARDUS.<-
<note>Likely Richardus Anglicus (Richard the Englishman), a name associated with several 13th and 14th-century alchemical treatises.</note>

Raw mercury prepares bodies into their first matter, but the mercury of the bodies cannot do this. The same author says: Because through freezing <note>original: *congelationem*; the process of thickening or solidifying</note>, that raw sulfur which was previously in it (that is, before freezing) is changed in its nature, and therefore it does not corrode like the first.

->PHILOSOPHERS IN GENERAL.<-

Do not seek cleanliness from the unclean. It is foolish to seek from a thing what was never in it. Who can give what they do not have? What is this madness, to wish to make something better from something worse—that is, to make perfect things from imperfect ones?

->LULLIUS.<-

Heaven, moon-plant <note>original: *lunaria*</note>, the menstrual fluid <note>original: *menstruum*; here used as a technical term for a powerful solvent or "the mother" of the work</note>, vegetable liquor, the water of quicksilver rectified and sharpened with vegetables: it is with this that the natural dissolution of metals occurs.

->VILLANOVANUS.<-

Waters of solution made from salts, alums, and others of that kind, which have no kinship <note>original: *cognationem*</note> with metals, do not preserve the species of the metals; on the contrary, they destroy and scatter them. Opposite to these waters is the water of the Philosophers, which preserves metals, makes them more subtle, then dissolves them, and by a great agreement of nature, transfers them into their first matter <term>materia prima; the primal, undifferentiated substance from which all things are formed</term>.

<summary>This page compiles quotes from medieval alchemical masters to argue that the true "Philosophers' Stone" must be created from substances sharing the same nature as metals, rather than from harsh mineral acids or common quicksilver. It reinforces the central alchemical law that "like attracts like" and that only a "natural" solvent can reduce metals to their primal state without destroying them.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the "Annotations" regarding the chemical process of solution. The previous page established that "like dissolves like"—that the solvent and the substance to be dissolved must share a common nature. This page provides specific technical instructions and aphorisms from famous alchemical authorities (The Turba, Lull, Geber) on how to achieve this dissolution using "philosophers' water," "potable gold," and controlled heat sources like warm manure or boiling water.</meta>

<page-num>763</page-num>
<header>ANNOTATIONS.</header>
<meta>catchword: verò (meaning: "but" or "truly")</meta>

### THE ASSEMBLY OF THE PHILOSOPHERS
<note>original: "TURBA"; refers to the *Turba Philosophorum*, one of the oldest Latin alchemical texts, written as a transcript of a meeting of ancient sages.</note>

Receive the black spirit <note>likely referring to the "nigredo" or black stage of the work, representing the initial decomposition of matter</note> that does not burn, and with it dissolve the bodies, and divide them.

### THE RESOUNDING TRUMPET
<note>original: "CLANGOR"; refers to the *Clangor Buccinae*, a 15th-century alchemical treatise.</note>

In the water of the Philosophers lies hidden the spirit of the fifth essence <term>quinta essentia; the "quintessence" or purest, most refined element beyond the four physical elements</term>, whose sole task is to masterfully corrupt <note>in alchemy, "corruption" is the necessary breakdown of a substance so it can be reborn in a higher form</note> and transform [matter] into its first material.

### THE ROSE GARDEN
<note>original: "ROSARIUS"; refers to the *Rosarium Philosophorum*, a foundational 16th-century text on the chemical wedding.</note>

The juice of the lunaria <note>the "moon-plant," a symbolic name for a secret ingredient, often linked to silver or a specific lunar solvent</note> is made from our wine, which is known to few of our sons; and with it our solution is made, and our potable gold <term>aurum potabile; literally "drinkable gold," a legendary medicine made from dissolved gold</term> is made by its means, and by no means without it.

### RAYMOND LULL
<note>original: "LULLIUS"; Ramon Llull (c. 1232–1315), a Majorcan philosopher and polymath to whom many alchemical works were attributed.</note>

The solvent <term>menstruum; a technical term for a solvent, derived from the idea of a monthly cycle of renewal</term> without gold and silver cannot generate the philosophers' stone, nor vice versa. But where these are joined, the solvent moves the metals toward dissolution. And in turn, the metals move the solvent to produce fire in the stones.

### THE RESOUNDING TRUMPET

If there be one pound of twelve ounces of the imperfect body—namely, of earth—it is fixed with its own soakings for ninety days.

### RAYMOND LULL

In the singular water prepared from the red body—that is, from our prepared red earth—fitted into thin plates or reduced to the powder of filings, put two drachmas, which is the fourth part of an ounce. If you are able to dissolve more, add more, yet do not exceed one ounce. If any of the earth remains undissolved, leave it in the glass; however, set aside that which is dissolved. Afterward, let the earth which remained undissolved be placed with new material to be dissolved. But of the new earth, do not put two drachmas, but less: namely, as much as the remaining earth weighs. Understand this unless you see that the water is capable of dissolving more.

### GEBER
<note>The Latinized name of Jabir ibn Hayyan (c. 721–815), the most famous figure in Islamic alchemy, known for his systematic approach to laboratory work.</note>

The method of solution is twofold: namely, by warm manure <note>original: "fimum calidum"; a common laboratory practice of burying a flask in a heap of decomposing manure to provide a steady, gentle heat for weeks at a time</note>, and by boiling water. Both have one intention and one effect. The method by manure, therefore, is this: place the calcined material <term>calcinatum; a substance reduced to powder by heat</term> into a glass flask, and pour over it a quantity of distilled vinegar, or something similar, twice its amount. Seal the top of it well so it does not breathe <note>i.e., so no vapors escape</note>, and let it be left to dissolve under the warm manure. Afterward, remove the dissolved portion by filtering it; however, let the undissolved portion be calcined again, and after calcination, let it be dissolved again in a similar way, until through the repetition of the work upon it, the whole is dissolved. 

But the method of solution which is done by boiling water is faster, and it is this: let the calcined material be arranged in a flask with vinegar, the opening being sealed so it does not breathe. Let this flask be buried in a cauldron full of water and straw, and afterward, let a fire be lit beneath it until the water boils for an hour. After—

### THE PATH OF THE PATH
<note>original: "SEMITA SEMITÆ"</note>

Take one pound of the prize <note>original: "pretij"; likely referring to the "precious" material, such as gold or silver, used as the starting point</note>, with four pounds of water: incorporate it three times with a little salt and vinegar, until the whole becomes an amalgam <term>amalgam; a soft paste made by mixing a metal with mercury</term>. When the prize is best amalgamated, place it in a large quantity of the water of life <note>original: "aquæ vitæ"; here explicitly identified by the author as Mercury</note>, that is, Mercury. Place it over the ashes and let the heat be very slow for a natural day <note>a "natural day" refers to a full 24-hour period</note>. Let the vessel cool, and strain it through a linen cloth, so that what has been dissolved of the body passes through. What remains in the cloth, put back to the fire with new blessed water <note>original: "aqua benedicta"; a specialized alchemical solvent</note> for a natural day; strain as before. Repeat this so many times until the whole body is converted into water.

### ARNOLD OF VILLANOVA
<note>original: "VILLANOVANUS"; referring to the 13th-century physician and alchemist</note>

Grind one pound of clean filings in a mortar with four pounds of Mercury. Add to that pound twelve pounds of the water of life. Put it all in a urinal <note>a common glass laboratory vessel shaped like a flask</note>, and over a weak and steady heat of ashes, and cook for a day. When the vessel has cooled, let the water be strained, so that what has been dissolved from the body and the filings passes through; set that water aside. And what is not dissolved, put back to the fire with new blessed water for a day and a night. Strain as before what is dissolved, and put this second water with the first. Do so until the whole filing is converted into water, that is, into the first matter <term>first matter; the primordial, formless substance from which all things are made</term>.

With new menstruum, repeat the aforementioned dissolution until the menstruum is no longer colored, and at the bottom of the vessel there will remain the earth without its soul.

<header>ANNOTATIONS.</header>

### THE CLANGOR.
<note>original: "CLANGOR"; referring to the *Clangor Buccinae* or "The Sound of the Trumpet," an influential alchemical text.</note>

To dissolve is to convert the body into the nature of spirit. To coagulate is to make the spirit corporeal. Solution makes a fixed body volatile. Coagulation, on the contrary, makes a volatile body fixed. The same author says: Spirit—that is, water—is not coagulated except by means of a body which has been dissolved within it. For bodies are like the rennet <note>original: "coagulum"; the substance used to curdle milk into cheese</note> of this milk, which is Mercury. The rennet, however, is either the sun <note>alchemical symbol for gold</note> or the moon <note>alchemical symbol for silver</note>, dissolved in Mercury.

### MENABDES.

I command those who come after to make bodies non-corporeal, and incorporeal things bodies: the former is done through dissolution, the latter through gentle decoction <note>original: "decoctio"; the process of heating or boiling a substance to extract its essence</note>.

### AVICENNA.
<note>Ibn Sina (c. 980–1037), a Persian polymath whose medical and alchemical writings were foundational in Medieval Europe.</note>

Salts are the roots of the work. The same author says: Salts of whatever kind they may be are contrary to our art, except for the salt of our lunaria <note>likely referring to a "moon-like" substance or a specific alchemical plant</note>, which our lunaria leaves behind from dissolved bodies.

### GEBER.
<note>Jabir ibn Hayyan, the semi-legendary 8th-century father of chemistry/alchemy.</note>

We need nothing but one vessel, one furnace, and one arrangement. Understand this to apply after the preparation of the first stone.

### THE COUNT.
<note>original: "COMES"; likely Count Bernhard of Trevisan.</note>

When you have evaporated the water with great ingenuity and the subtle wisdom of your mind, take your salt, thus calcined <note>reduced to powder by heat</note>, and its most subtle and impalpable powder, and set it aside in a clean glass vessel until the time comes to join it to the work.

### THE ROSARY.
<note>original: "ROSARIUS"; referring to the *Rosarium Philosophorum*.</note>

There are three stones, and there are three salts, from which the entire mastery <note>original: "magisterium"; the completion of the Great Work</note> consists.

The matter of the stone is threefold: gold, silver, and philosophical water.

There are three waters: solar, lunar, and mercurial; the last of which resolves the bodies of the sun and moon into their own waters.

The Mercury of the Philosophers is threefold: the first calcinates bodies, the second dissolves and sublimes <note>the process of turning a solid into vapor and back to solid to purify it</note> them, and the third is joined to these two.

### THE SOUND OF THE TRUMPET.
<note>original: "CLANGOR BUCCINÆ".</note>

Quicksilver <note>original: "argentum vivum"; literally "living silver," mercury</note> is twofold, and the names of the "first matter" are many. The first is called the "preparing" mercury, which dissolves the body through the water of the Philosophers. The other is the "dyeing" mercury, which is extracted from perfected bodies through dissolution; and such quicksilver is called incombustible oil, the soul, the air, and the splendor of bodies, because it grants incorruptible life to dead, imperfect metallic bodies, and illuminates them.

### GEBER.

The principal natural things in the work are the "stinking spirit"—or sulfur—and living water.

### CERTAIN COLLECTIONS FROM ANCIENT WRITERS.

It is most certain that no foreign substance can perfect tainted <note>original: "infecta"; meaning "unfinished" or "impure" base metals like lead or iron.</note> metals, or perform any transmutation upon them. Wherefore, it is the opinion of insane men that animals and vegetables can accomplish anything in this art, since minerals are found to be [more] closely related to metals. However, it must be believed that the Philosophers placed the art in those things only by way of **analogy** <note>original: "similitudinem"; the author argues that when alchemists mention plants or animals, they are speaking in codes or metaphors.</note>. For from two things only—namely, sulfur and quicksilver—do any metals arise, and from no others. Nothing even adheres to them, nor transmutates them, except that which took its origin from them. It is established, therefore, that only two things which have been created are necessary for constructing the stone.

But because no metal can be generated from either one separately, but rather different metals are generated from the conjunction of both (prepared in different ways), this indeed is especially hidden: from which mineral substance it ought to be more closely made. If from vegetables, it would be necessary for sulfur and quicksilver to first be made from these by art, which would be impossible; we are therefore excused from these things, because nature itself prepares those two. But if we choose quicksilver and sulfur in their own nature, just as they are naturally created, it would be necessary for those to be joined in a **proportion** that surpasses all human ingenuity; we are therefore excused from these as well, especially since we have **bodies** <note>Refers to the "perfected" metals, Gold and Silver.</note> in which they are found proportioned by nature in the required way, in which the whole secret lies hidden. Gold is a perfect and masculine body, and silver is also perfect; if these alone, when melted, could perfect others through a mixture with imperfect ones, they would be...

# ANNOTATIONS.

...[silver] for the white, the other [gold] for the red, but they are not of that kind, because they are simply perfected by nature. If however they were ten or a hundred times more than perfect, they would perfect the imperfect by so much. But because nature simply works a simple perfection in them, they remain in that state forever, unless perhaps by art they might be reduced back to the **primary nature** <note>The "prime matter" or fundamental state before it became a solid metal.</note> of sulfur and **quicksilver** <note>original: "argenti vivi"; mercury, representing the feminine, volatile principle.</note>. Since, therefore, perfected natural bodies consist of the purest quicksilver and a similar sulfur, why would we not choose them as our material for the white and red **elixir**? <note>A substance capable of transmuting metals or prolonging life; "white" for silver and "red" for gold.</note>

**The Answer:** Because these bodies are so compact and strongly united that we find fire is hardly able to act upon them at all, nor upon their spirits. And although we are not ignorant of fire, yet through it we could not arrive at their innermost purification on account of their extremely strong natural composition. For this reason, we are also excused from choosing those two bodies, since we can find other bodies in which clean and similar quicksilver is held, upon which nature has worked only a little, so that by our **artificial fire** <note>The carefully controlled heat of the alchemist’s furnace, the athanor.</note>—through proper purification, separation, fixation, and the ingenious **decoction** <note>original: "decoctio"; a process of prolonged heating or "cooking" to mature the matter.</note> of our work continued upon them—we are able to succeed.

Therefore, a material must be chosen in which clean, pure, clear, and white quicksilver is found, not yet brought to completion, but mixed equally and proportionally, joined with such a white or red sulfur, so that by our natural ingenuity and our artificial fire, we may be able to reach their innermost purification and complete purity; and with this work finished, they may be a thousand times more perfect and stronger than the bodies in which nature has simply worked. From these things which have been said, if you are now ingenious, you will taste this **delightful nectar** <note>A poetic reference to the successful result of the Great Work, the Philosopher's Stone.</note> upon which the intention of the **Philosophers** <note>The "Philosophers" refers to the ancient and medieval alchemical authorities.</note> is founded.

Since, therefore, it is necessary to render the material revealed in the aforementioned words "more than perfect" by our artificial labor, the method must not be ignored, but rather learned from nature. Nature perfects these metals through frequent and continuous operation, using the single instrument of heat which exists within the mountains of minerals, so that the thickness of the water is cooked for a time and thickened, until finally in its own course of time or cycle it passes into quicksilver. Likewise, from the **fatness of the earth** <note>original: "pinguedine terrae"; an alchemical term for the oily, combustible principle that forms sulfur.</note>, sulfur is generated through that same continuous cooking and heat. By this same continued heat upon these two united together, either perfect or imperfect metals are generated according to their purity or impurity.

What madness holds the minds of those working in this art, that they wish to proceed by a way other than nature herself: attempting to refute or surpass her, whom they can hardly imitate by any industry. God demonstrates the right path to us through nature—namely, a simple and continuous decoction made with a slow fire. And although we always speak of a slow fire,

This page picks up with the "regime" or management of the fire and the specific operations needed to transform the matter.</meta>

# NICOLAS FLAMEL

...nonetheless, in the management of this work, the heat must be gradually increased. Therefore, there is one stone, one material, and one medicine, in which the entire **mastery** <note>The "Magisterium" or the completed alchemical process.</note> consists, to which we add no foreign thing, nor do we take anything away from it; rather, in the preparation, we remove what is superfluous. This is done during the purification, which is completed through **solution** <note>original: "solutionem"; the process of dissolving a solid into a liquid state.</note>. 

When we wish to perform our **sublimation** <note>In alchemy, sublimation often refers to the vaporization and re-solidification of a substance to purify it.</note> of the stone, we place it with its own substance into our vessel, the mouth of which we close firmly so that it cannot "breathe," and we place it in the furnace among the ashes. Finally, we stir up the fire for so long until the entire matter is dissolved into **Mercurial water** <term>Mercurial water: A liquid state of the matter, often compared to quicksilver (mercury), representing the first stage of the transformation where the solid "dies" into a fluid.</term>. 

Afterwards, manage it with a slow fire, and continue this until the greater part is turned into a black powder. In this manner, all those operations that follow are completed: namely, **Solution, Distillation, Descension, Washing, and Calcination** <note>original: "Solutio, Destillatio, Descensio, Ablutio, & Calcinatio"; these are the standard laboratory stages of the alchemical process.</note>. The Philosophers have written a specific chapter about each one so that they might hide the art. 

For when our stone is in our vessel, and our matter feels our **sun** <note>The "sun" here refers to the internal heat of the furnace or the "sulfur" acting within the chemical wedding.</note>, it is soon resolved into water, which ascends into "heaven"—that is, into the heights to the summit of the vessel—and afterwards it descends to the earth, or the bottom. Likewise, seeing such water thicken and be converted into a black earth (which stood thick upon the water at the beginning), and allowing it to thicken gradually, seeing the earth sink under the water and reside at the bottom of the vessel as something black and foul, they said that this was the operation of **putrefaction** <term>Putrefaction: Also called the "Nigredo" or blackening, it is the essential stage of decay that must precede new life and purification.</term>. 

Seeing also the yellow, somewhat black, and foul earth standing under the water for a long space of time, and seeing it lose its black color and its evil stench in our "sun," some of them called that operation **Washing** or **Ceration** <term>Ceration: From the Latin word for wax (*cera*); the process of softening a hard substance until it has the consistency of wax so it can be easily melted or combined.</term>, of which Morienus <note>Morienus Romanus, a legendary 7th-century alchemist and hermit.</note> says: "Know then that this mastery is nothing else but the extraction of water from the earth, and again the reduction of that same water into the earth, until the whole earth putrefies through its water and is purified." After it has been purified by the help of the divinity, the whole mastery will be achieved. 

The Philosopher says: the earth is waxed and imbibed through water, and by the temperate "cooking" of the sun it is dried out, and the whole matter is turned into earth, if one knows perfectly how to execute the operation. For Hermes says: "Its power is complete if it is turned into earth." <note>original: "Vis ejus integra est, si versa fuerit in terram"; a famous line from the Emerald Tablet of Hermes Trismegistus, the foundational text of alchemy.</note> 

Seeing therefore the whole matter turned into earth and reduced into a certain substance which did not flow, but stood constricted within itself, they said it was a perfect **congelation** <note>The thickening or solidifying of the liquid matter.</note>. Hence Plato says: "Dissolve our stone, and afterwards congeal it"—that is, turn it into earth—with great caution, and thus you shall have the whole mastery. This is nothing else than making a right solution and a perfect coagulation, as all the Philosophers say. 

In order, therefore, for metals to be perfected, it is necessary to reduce them to their **primary matter** <term>Primary Matter: The "Materia Prima," the fundamental, chaotic substance from which all things are made and to which they must return before they can be transformed.</term>, which is closest to the metallic genus—that is, into a **flowing gum** <note>original: "gummam fluentem"; a term for the thick, resinous state of the matter mid-process.</note>. From there, finally, such primary matter, by its innate aptitude...

...and by these disposing factors, it easily receives the true form of that metal which is intended philosophically: namely, with the nature of the **fixed ferment** <note>original: "fermenti fixi"; a stable substance added to the alchemical mix to act like yeast, "leavening" the base metal into gold.</note>, to which the already mentioned matter adheres inseparably in its depths. In this state, the matter flows, which common, crude quicksilver does not do. 

However, whoever attempts to perform **whitening** <note>Albedo: the second major stage of the work, creating silver.</note> or **yellowing** <note>Citrinitas: the third major stage, preceding the final red stage.</note> before this reduction into the **first matter** <term>First Matter: (original: "materia prima") The fundamental, formless substance that exists before it takes on the specific form of a metal like lead or iron.</term>—while the form of the previous metal still remains in the matter and is not vaporously joined or inseparably mixed into a "gum" with the matter of the fixed ferment—these people are deceivers. They produce neither true gold nor true silver. Therefore, in order for any transmutable body to be changed into any other species, it is necessary to reduce it to its first matter, since transmutation is only possible by reason of that matter. As **Aristotle** <note>Aristotle was considered the ultimate authority on the nature of matter; here Flamel cites his works on meteorology, physics, and the cycle of birth and decay.</note> says in the fourth book of his *Meteorology*, in *On Generation and Corruption*, and in the *Physics*:

> Every potential body, through the contrary operations of its nature, is reduced to its first matter—specifically through the "corruption" or breaking down of its form. This is because every contrary operation is its destruction, and the destruction of the old form is the birth of the first matter.

Demetrius, demonstrating the method of purification or "putrefaction" of both—that is, the body and the spirit—before their perfect mixture, says:

> Perfection is never obtained from that spirit until, through a perfect mixture, it has led its body (which is its brother) to a state of spirituality along with itself, so that both are made one, without separation, forever.

The **Mastery of Dissolution** <note>original: "Magisterium dissolutionis"; the high art of breaking down solids into liquid.</note>, therefore, prepares the matter of the stone so that it can be divided of its own accord into the four elements from which it was first composed. Otherwise, the elements would remain fixed in their own kind unless they were mixed in a vaporous state; neither a proportional composition nor the proper weight would be introduced as is required, nor would the perfection be reached, which is the final stage of making the transformation "stick" or remain permanent. 

In this manner, the **perfect stone** <note>The Philosopher's Stone.</note> purges and heals a man of every sickness, so that he is renewed as if by a mother. For it excites motion in bodies and "vivifies" the elements; indeed, the elements are brought to life when they are stirred into their proper action. For natural life is nothing other than the action of the elements, after which the stone does not suffer any scattering or separation due to the indivisible nature of its composition. From this, the stone has the power to delay old age through the life it infuses into the human body, just as it does with metals. By the grace of God, it increases the years of a man's life beyond his own natural proportion; having naturally received this capacity, it produces life. 

Nevertheless, effects of this kind cannot be attributed to any single one of the elements, but only to the **virtue of heaven** <note>original: "virtuti caeli"; a celestial or spiritual power that transcends the four physical elements.</note> which is contained within the stone itself. It is by this heavenly virtue that the stone is brought to its final form. Although the property of the stone comes naturally from this celestial impression, that which prepares the stone to receive such an influence is the "breadth" of its mixture or the temperament that suits its species. Therefore, the entire life of the stone and the whole mastery consist in vapor...

the matter consists, and in the refining <note>original: "subtiliatione"; the process of making a substance more spiritualized or vapor-like.</note> of its water by breathing it into the air. The life of the stone is its brilliance, and the clarity of the metal lies in an aerial refinement, fixed and meltable through fire. From the aforementioned things, it follows that **our quicksilver** <note>original: "argentum vivum nostrum"; alchemists distinguished their "Philosophical Mercury" from the common mercury found in shops.</note> can in no way be fixed for any useful purpose, unless it is bound and held by natural instruments (which are heat and cold) and by the restraints of the dry earth. And because we are not able to possess these instruments or restraints except through the power of separating nature itself into its primary parts—namely, the elemental natures—the correct coagulation cannot occur unless the separation is performed after the proper degree of refinement and **putrefaction** <term>Putrefaction: (original: "putrefactionis") The stage where the matter turns black and "dies," allowing it to be reborn in a higher form.</term>. Therefore, the universal cause of conjunction is the separation following putrefaction and the proper thinning of the body with the spirit, because things united in this way are joined correctly. Indeed, separation after putrefaction is nothing other than the reduction of a thing from its changed nature back to that same nature again. Therefore, when through mortification and putrefaction the nature has been changed from its "living" metallic species to another "dead" species—specifically into an earthy substance—it is necessary to lead it back again to that same living species closest to the metallic genus. This is done by the separation of the thing itself from the "dead" parts; then, because of the uniformity of their natures, they are joined together, and they will be glued together by a strong adherence. And this is the special form of our **dissolution** <note>original: "dissolutionis"; the process of breaking down a solid into a liquid or vaporous state.</note>: and this is the way in which the bosom of nature is revealed, by **lifting her tunic** <note>A metaphor for stripping away the external, "accidental" qualities of a substance to reveal its inner essence.</note> and manifesting what lies hidden within. Care must be taken, however, that the tunic is not lifted beyond its midpoint, so that the moisture may work within a smaller amount of dryness; whatever has been raised should be imprinted, and the whiteness of the raised vapor from the innermost caverns of things should be hidden again, so that the moisture is joined with the restraint of the dry earth, coagulated, and held fast. Lest the work become sluggish, do not be reluctant to repeat its operation, suppressing the spirit everywhere, hiding its whiteness for a long time and manifesting it again, until it reaches that most refined **whiteness** <note>Albedo: the "White Work," which produces silver.</note> which can no longer be hidden, nor altered by another, nor converted into other colors, except into **redness** <note>Rubedo: the "Red Work," the final stage producing the Philosopher's Stone.</note> once the digestion is complete. And then, finally, at that step, the conjunction of body and soul occurs—a mixing, or rather a union, which is never separated.

**Aristotle** says that quicksilver is the element of all liquefiable things: for when they are melted, they are converted into it. It is manifest, therefore, that the operation of this medicine is an operation of nature, because it is composed solely from nature. For it is certain that every thing is composed of those elements into which it is resolved—just like ice, which naturally is resolved into water by heat because it was previously frozen from water by cold. In no different a way is our stone resolved into quicksilver through our **mastery** <note>original: "magisterium"; the skilled practice of alchemy.</note>; therefore, it was itself previously quicksilver.

### ANNOTATIONES.

The first word, therefore, is the reduction of the body into <term>quicksilver</term> <note>original: "argentum vivum"; this refers to the process of breaking down a solid metal into a liquid or "mercurial" state.</note>, and this they have called solution, which is the foundation of the art. The philosopher Rosinus <note>Rosinus is a medieval corruption of the name Zosimos of Panopolis, a 3rd-century Egyptian alchemist.</note> says: **Dissolve the bodies and the spirits, and join them; then for the rest they cannot be separated by fire.** <note>original: "Solvite corpora & spiritus, & conjungite, tunc de cætero non possunt separari per ignem."</note> Hermes says: **The first body dissolved, and the perennial water, congeals Mercury with a perpetual congelation** <note>original: "Primum corpus solutum, & aqua perennis, congelat Mercurium..."</note>, which all the Philosophers also say. He who has ears to hear, let him hear: All molten metals behave like Mercury, and if they could remain in that molten state when cold, they would be Mercury itself. It must be considered that "moist" metals, such as <term>Saturn</term> <note>Alchemical code for Lead.</note> and <term>Jupiter</term> <note>Alchemical code for Tin.</note>, are easily reduced into their primitive Mercury. And Mercury, properly prepared, consumes every body and reduces it into itself. 

For heat acting on the moist first produces blackness, and acting on the dry produces whiteness, and works upon the white to produce yellowing and redness. This may be seen in lead by <term>calcining</term> it <note>original: "calcinando"; the process of heating a metal in air until it turns to a powder or ash.</note>: first it is burned into a black ash, then into white, and finally into yellow and red. Therefore, the true beginning of our work is the dissolution of the stone, because dissolved bodies are reduced into the nature of spirit—except that they are more "fixed" <note>In alchemy, "fixed" means a substance that can withstand the heat of fire without evaporating.</note> than spirits. Likewise: The solution of the body occurs with the congelation of the spirit, and conversely, the congelation of the spirit occurs with the solution of the body. Then finally the body is mixed with the spirits and becomes one with them, so that they may never be separated, no more than water mixed with water, since then all things are together reduced to their own homogeneity. 

For this reason Aristotle said: **The bodies of metals cannot be transmuted unless they are first reduced to their first matter** <note>original: "corpora metallorum transmutari non possunt, nisi ipsa prius in suam materiam primam redigantur." This is a foundational alchemical principle attributed to Aristotle's "Meteorologica."</note>; if this is done, they well receive another form, to which reason is not opposed. But a transition from one extreme to the other does not happen except through a middle state. <term>Sulphur</term> and quicksilver are the extremes of all metals; therefore, metals will be the middle between sulfur and quicksilver. Consider, therefore, if you can digest the pure substance of quicksilver without combustion; if not, your work is in vain. 

Therefore, it is necessary for the craftsman to use considerations, the certainty of which is handed down in other faculties that he presupposes. And so that his study may be directed toward the goal of experiment, he must labor and occupy himself especially with two things: first, that he diligently inquire into the elemental essence of the thing to be treated or sublimated, and its proportion; second, that he have an account of the treating thing—that is, the principal agent and transmuter. For the art must, with a very strong agent, dispose the matter so that the natural virtues of active <term>digestion</term> <note>original: "digestionis"; a slow, gentle heating process similar to biological digestion.</note> may prevail in the passive matter. For we see sometimes that through an insufficient agent every digested thing is labored—that is, it suffers imperfect digestion or rawness, which happens because of the mixture of raw, undigested matter, or because of the weakness of the digesting and terminating heat. Wherefore, the greatest care must be taken that...

### OF NICHOLAS FLAMEL <note>original: "NICOLAI FLAMELLI"</note>

The nature of the principal agent stands so strong in its own essence and is fortified in its own way, that by its own natural office it is powerful enough to digest and convert the matter into gold. And so that this nature, disposed toward that method through thinning <note>referred to here as "subtiliation," the process of making a substance more refined or spiritual</note> and raising up <note>referred to here as "sublimation," the process of purifying a substance through heat until it rises as vapor</note>, might approach the quality of its agent and of gold through its virtues acquired by art—and so that through these means, the principal agent, reigning with its sharpness, can convert it into the **Philosophers' Stone** <note>original: "lapidem Philosophorum"</note> and gold. Let the natural craftsman therefore examine his own wit, so that by means of the condition of the aforementioned nature—which he may have been ignorant of—he may find it.

Because we do not hand down to ourselves and our sons [only] the understanding of the disposition—that is, the certain and necessary mode of operating—but also the method of strengthening nature and investigating the causes. Therefore, the craftsmanship of this work would be impossible to find unless the craftsman's wit is first properly informed by his own experiences with nature. Through these, nature demonstrates how she is known, her arrangement by which she is perfected, and she teaches how to find the measure of her approach toward perfection. Each specific work requires its own arrangement, since it belongs to nature itself forming its own **quicksilver** <term>argentum vivum</term> <note>The "living silver," or mercury, considered the base of all metals.</note> and working upon its qualities: namely, heat with its tempered dryness, removing the coldness and moisture, taking away what is superfluous and adding or supplying what is absent and required, so that through this it must necessarily take the form of the complete medicine. Nor does nature possess the aforesaid power in any other way unless she is helped, namely by the art and operation of the craftsman and the arrangement proper to her, without which nothing is accomplished.

When you have found it, hide it in the garment of philosophy, just as your predecessors did, who commanded it to be most strictly concealed: for this is the entire secret and mystery of this art, which has not yet been revealed by any philosopher in their writings. It must be known, therefore, that when they say "**Dissolve the bodies into water**" <note>original: "Solvite corpora in aquam"</note>, they do not understand or care for waters that cling or moisten [wet], but they mean a permanent water which truly does not cling to what it touches, but is a moistening liquid that disperses across the surface: just as our **quicksilver** is not common quicksilver. For this matter should have nothing else added to it except what is of itself: indeed, it contains all things which it requires. This is said of our stone, and not of gold or common quicksilver, etc.

Some wrongly distill corrosive waters <note>Strong mineral acids like nitric acid.</note> from lesser minerals, in which they place metallic species and corrode them, thinking they are dissolved by a natural dissolution; but this is false. Because true **philosophical solution** <note>original: "solutio philosophica"</note> requires the persistence of both the solvent and the dissolved body together: since from the male and the female new species result. It is also certain that no water dissolves a metallic species by natural reduction except that which remains with them in matter and form, and which they...

# ANNOTATIONS.

...dissolved [substances] can congeal again, which does not happen at all in strong waters <note>original: "aquis fortibus"; these are corrosive acids like nitric acid, which destroy the metallic form rather than simply dissolving it alchemically</note>. No water, therefore, dissolves bodies except that which is of its own species, and by which bodies could be thickened; nor are bodies nourished during their creation <note>generation</note> by any other thing except a similar species. Therefore, the solvent <term>solvens|the substance that dissolves another</term> differs from the dissolved <term>solvendo|the substance being dissolved</term> only by proportion and digestion; but they do not differ in matter, because through whatever mixture, nature forms this from that—just as, in a mineral way, nature creates Gold <note>original: "Solem," literally "the Sun"</note> simply from quicksilver <note>original: "argento vivo"</note>. 

Whoever knows the art of dissolving has already reached the secret, which is to mix species and to extract the effective natures from other natures that lie hidden within them. If anyone, therefore, knows how to join and befriend our sulfur with bodies, he has found one of the greatest secrets of nature. It is as if one were to say: if someone leads a body to the point that it becomes a gum <term>gumma|in alchemy, a sticky, resinous state where the solid and liquid components of the work are perfectly balanced</term> mixable with other imperfect bodies, he has found the greatest secret of nature, etc. Because this perfected stone is a gum and a sulfur, namely from the aforementioned bodies (let it be added). 

These bodies are called the sulfurous earths. Through the thinning <note>subtiliation</note> existing in the water, the dissolution draws the stone from potential into act, because it makes it altogether subtle <note>refined, volatile, and capable of penetration</note>. And the joining of spirits with the body occurs when bodies are sublimated <note>purified by heat until they rise as vapor</note>, just like spirits, through their dissolution, grinding, and roasting <note>original: "assationem"</note> with spirits. 

The Philosophers say the water is of Mercury <note>original: "Mercurij"</note>, meaning the said stone liquefied with its own proper water, which is fixed within the stone itself, and which is then running and white like water. Likewise, the airy moisture <note>original: "humiditas aerea"</note> which is in quicksilver is one thing with the aforementioned earth and with the other elements existing in the said earth. This moisture, although it is small, is nevertheless sufficient for nourishing and perfecting the said stone in which it exists. 

Gold and Silver <note>original: "sol & luna," literally "the Sun and the Moon"</note> are present in the said composition. And yet, they are not common gold or silver, but better than in their vulgar nature; they are present there potentially, not visibly. This stone or composite is one thing only, and of one nature (as all Philosophers say), and it is a clean and clear nature from its own proper ores, which changes the rule <term>regimen|the governed stages of heat and timing in the alchemical process</term> of the fire. 

Likewise, our medicine <note>the Elixir or Stone</note> is drawn out from metals, which naturally transmute metals, and in no other way. For it is necessary that the Elixir of the Philosophers be from the Principle, root, and nature of metals, and the medicine must be nobler and more precious than the metals, etc. 

From this it is clear that when the Philosophers speak of quicksilver and other dissolving moistures, they do not mean common things simply given by nature, but only of the quicksilver separated from bodies through the artifice of putrefaction <note>the alchemical stage of "blackening" or decay, where the old form is broken down to allow for new growth</note>. This is otherwise called **Azoth** <note>a mystical name for the universal solvent or the beginning and end of all things</note>, which is interpreted in Latin as "powerful alum" <note>original: "alumen potens"</note> able to illuminate and clarify every body with its own brightness. Since, therefore, such quicksilver—or **Azoth**, or the water of life <note>original: "aqua vitae"</note> washing the latten <note>original: "latonem," a term for the impure, "bronze-like" base matter of the work</note>—cannot be extracted from bodies through generation except after putrefaction—

[The e]nd <note>Due to the tight binding, the first letters of lines on this page are obscured; reconstructions are provided in brackets where possible.</note> will be; therefore its putrefaction is its generation and preparation. The mixture and birth of vegetables is varied and distinct. For those things are said to be simply mixed which are born beyond our sight <note>likely referring to minerals formed deep within the earth</note>, or around its surface, from the mere commingling of elements composed with one another: and there are many degrees of such simple natural mixing. The first is the naked composition of the [four] elements, in which no [reduction] or alteration of one element into another has been made. To join them, the Philo[sophers] commanded that once all extrinsic matter is removed, only heat should be applied, which, [at the right time], excites the intrinsic natural heat of gold to [dissolve], and actively matures the Mercury. Since therefore its seeds <note>original: "spermata, seu femina," literally "sperms or seeds"</note> cannot be generated by art, art does not know how to set the mixture proportionally to produce seeds, neither in man nor in the earth—where the proper place of their natural generation is—these naturally made seeds are joined in another way. And in this proportional action of nature and the digestion of Mercury, the male and female natures remain closed together: the female, such as earth and water; the male, such as air and [fire]; which earth and water the Philosophers said are Mercury, while air and [fire] are like sulfur in our stone. Beyond these, nothing else enters, nor generates, nor multiplies, as is clear from the [principles]. And this dissolution is only called the liquefaction of the compound, and not properly its solution, because the parts are not dissolved into each other [as individuals]. When the compound is dissolved in the aforementioned way, the parts remain unseparated (though they are separable), so that the power of the digestive elements [is not separated] from what is to be dissolved; through dissolution, namely quicksilver <note>original: "argentum vivum"</note> is extracted, and the thick parts in such a dissolution take on the breadth of subtlety, because the body [is turned] into spirit, and vice versa.

# ANNOTATIONS

->A brilliant ground alone makes quicksilver. For nature overcomes nature.<- <note>original: *Natura enim naturam vincit*. This is one of the most famous axioms in alchemy, suggesting that the internal power of a substance is the only thing capable of transforming its own kind.</note>

If you truly wish to know the matter precisely, apply your mind to the two catalogs, because it must be known above all that Mercury is placed both in the yellow—that is, in the sun—and in the white—that is, in the moon. And in the sun, he said, Mercury comes from cinnabar <note>Mercury sulfide, the most common ore of mercury</note>; but in the white, he said Mercury comes from arsenic, or sandarac <note>an arsenic sulfide mineral</note>, or those things which follow.

I come into Egypt <note>A traditional literary device in alchemical texts; "Egypt" represents the ancestral home of Hermetic wisdom rather than a literal journey</note> bringing natural things, so that you may despise superfluous and confused matter. For nature indeed rejoices in nature, and nature overcomes nature, and nature retains nature.

Mercury, therefore, takes on all forms, just as wax receives all seals; so also the Mercury of the Philosophers whitens all things, and draws the souls of all things to itself, cooks them, and seizes them. Being adapted to the instruments, and possessing humors within itself, and even undergoing corruption, it changes all colors; it remains while they do not remain—indeed, even when it does not subsist itself, it is then contained by the governance of the bodies and subjects. I speak of the composite or composition of the four bodies and those things which are related to them, as their matters and their souls are their own matters. Just as a craftsman erecting a statue from wood, or from bronze, or stone, exhibits nothing of himself but the form upon the matter: so also Mercury, when elaborated by us through art, receives every form, and being fixed (as has been said) to the body and the four constant types, it remains strong and firm, containing and being contained; and for this reason Pibichius <note>An early alchemical authority often cited in the Greek and Latin traditions</note> said it has a great affinity. By the Mercury from cinnabar, from arsenic, vitriol <note>original: *calcantho*</note>, white lead <note>original: *cerussa*</note>, magnesia <note>In this context, a generic term for a mineral primer or "magnet" for the spirit, not modern magnesium</note>, or *Italian antimony* <note>original: *stimmi Italico*</note>, and the rest, all white or red bodies are to be understood. He also calls the body of magnesia "gold-solder" <note>original: *chrysocollam*</note> or "gold-coral." It is necessary, therefore, first to liquefy the species of things, and to convert them by meltings into one color, and to reduce the two Mercuries, the white and the red, into quicksilver, and to separate them for putrefaction.

Therefore, govern the marcasite (*which the Greeks call silver pyrites*) and prepare it according to custom so that it may be dissolved: it will flow, however, through gold or white litharge <note>lead monoxide</note>, or in *Italian antimony*: from the battle with lead. Do not understand "lead" simply, lest you wander from the path, but that which is from the fissile [ore], and our black litharge, or as you know. For nature rejoices in nature.

Govern it (I say) until it becomes incombustible, casting away the blackness. Govern it with brine, or uncorrupted urine, or sea water, or oxymel <note>A medicinal mixture of honey and vinegar</note>, as you know. Mercury, however, is white in action, but yellow in power <note>Meaning it appears silver/white but contains the "potency" of gold/yellow</note>.

They labor in vain, therefore, who explore matters and do not seek the natures of the bodies of magnesia. For the body of magnesia is a mixture of substances of four kinds, as was said before.

Three things are chief in the art: <term>Chrysolite</term> <note>original: *Chrysolitus*; literally "gold-stone," referring to a yellow-green gem or the state of the matter</note>, Mercury, and the yellow <term>honeycomb</term> <note>original: *favus*; likely referring to a porous or crystalline structure</note> or the white honeycomb, etc., in which nature rejoices. The <term>divine water</term> <note>original: *aqua divina*; the philosophical solvent</note> is a nature which overcomes and retains its own rejoicing nature; it is overcome and retained by it along with others. Is not the nature of a thicker and earthly body overcome by the nature of chrysolite, which is spiritual and airy? Is not the divine water overcome by a binding force, so that the joined Sun and Moon may retain Mercury or Venus, and so forth? Truly, when joined by themselves to these or others, they do not hold; yet when they are bound by the nature of the divine water, they are able to remain. What shall I say of you, O Magnesia, you who embrace all bodies? Who will not admire the <term>gold-coral</term> <note>original: *chrysocorallum*</note> perfected by you? For through you the whole mastery is completed. You alone command us to be good men. Within you is unfolded a similar shining cloud; you carry much within you, the image of Venus, the cup-bearer and servant of the feast. O nature above nature, overcoming all natures! You are the whole, one and the same nature, through which also every work is done. For in a superfluous number, all your adornment is skillfully declared, and the limit of that number is in a unity similar to divinity. For the One remains an unchangeable and stable center. For it shows the circular and spherical contemplation of its own numbers in the greater work. But let us return to where we began. The synonyms of Magnesia are: milk of the sea, curd, Eastern <term>moon-froth</term> <note>original: *aphroselinum*; likely selenite or a pearly mineral</note>, Magnesia of Lydia, Italian <term>antimony</term> <note>original: *stibium*</note>, pyrites of Achaia, and so forth. Its mystery is the fruit that lies hidden within it: the precious pearl. The Burning Splendor, the Garment woven with gold, the Golden Brightness, the Warrior. These can also be understood as referring to the whiteness of the Great Work.

The chemical field is threefold. The four brothers are one part; the great stone is another part—the seed sown in the purified field; the second Mercury, yellow or white, joined to the body of Magnesia, is the third part. "Taking therefore," etc.

Again, the true soot is twofold: moist and dry. The moist is the celestial vapor drawn forth through distillation. The dry is produced through the jar and the copper lid, like the white vapor from cinnabar. If, therefore, you irrigate the dry vapor with the moist vapor, you will achieve the divine work. For all substances and metals are known to be vapors; for when irrigated, vapors become moist.

The <term>Scythian comaris</term> <note>original: *Scythica comaris*; likely a symbolic name for a plant or an herbal preparation used as a metaphor for a stage of the work</note> also, when mixed with new vapor, perfects everything.

### ANNOTATIONS.

There is, to be sure, one kind of alchemy which is wordy, consisting merely of a multitude of speeches; and there is another kind which is secret, hidden, or mystical. For this latter kind proceeds solely by the reason of creation, so that man—looking toward God and created by God—may learn the correct operation through theological and mystical discourses. For this operation is primarily celestial, because it consists of celestial materials and forms.

The method of mystical alchemy is found in the figures of heaven, according to whose rule this art is directed. Thus also, metallic bodies transmuted from a contrary nature become smooth and airy.

Therefore, the seed sown in the <term>earth of the moon</term> <note>original: *terra lunae*; likely referring to silver or the "white" stage of the work</note> also perfects the sun <note>original: *solem*; refers to gold or the final "red" stage</note>, and this is achieved through a divine operation; ash and <term>zinc ore</term> <note>original: *cadmia*</note> provide the means. Likewise, the divine work and the pure <term>divine water</term> <note>original: *aqua divina*; the philosophical solvent or "mercury"</note> together with its ash, contribute to regeneration. Hear Mercury saying: "If you see all things made into ash, consider that all things have been rightly prepared." For ash possesses great power and works much. For just as wood converted into ash becomes thereafter incombustible, but is used in various wonderful works of glass and other things; so also metals converted into ash, or rather into <term>lime</term> <note>original: *calcem*; referring to calcination, the process of reducing a metal to a powder by heat</note>, return anew into a certain virtue and operation. Since their nature imitates the universal world and the elements themselves, they are generated from them again, and they possess a participation in a certain spirit, much like things produced by a material spirit. 

Thus also our <term>bronze</term> <note>original: *aes*; not common bronze, but the "matter" of the work</note>, or if you prefer the <term>body of magnesia</term> <note>The "mother" substance or prime matter of the Stone</note> (however you choose to understand it), has a soul and a spirit like a human being. For these fusible bodies and metals, after they have been turned into ash, resume their spirit while existing in the fire, as the fire supplies this to them, and they draw it from the air, which makes all these things. In the same way, humans and all things take their vital spirit and soul from there. Therefore, our burnt bronze, turned into a dry soot and undergoing all things, becomes more inspired and becomes an <term>ethereal stone</term> <note>original: *lapis aethesius*; likely from the Greek *aithesios*, meaning flashing or heavenly</note> in color, like something flashing and ethereal. 

After it is thus inspired, it is quenched in a divine manner—which they call "divine water"—as it receives a dissolved oil and the thickness of wine; and remaining there for forty days under a slow heat in a vessel that does not transmit vapors, the matter is afterward <term>putrefied</term> <note>original: *putrefacta*; the "black" stage of alchemy where the substance breaks down to be reborn</note>. The pure mystery of the divine water then perfects that which is sought: and this is the stone which performs these things. Note therefore: All things are one, through which all things are. Indeed, it begins from unity or union, and it terminates the consummation in the unity of the thing sought. For although there are many things in the nature of things, it is called one most divine water, one nature overcoming all things—not by species, but by art, with a rational science hidden from many. O celestial natures, creators of natures! By these words, the incorporeal nature is hinted at. For unless you strip the matter, and make the bodies incorporeal; unless you shake them out through corruption and dissolve them, you will not produce into birth that which is hidden and breathable; unless by this way of preparation, the incorporeal things...

# NICHOLAS FLAMEL

...you have made, you will not shape the natures, nor will the celestial natures—which are devoid of body—make bodies. Into these celestial natures, bodies infuse themselves and are shaped by the benefit of celestial wisdom; the bodies remain within these natures, and the natures subsequently embrace the bodies themselves. It is necessary, therefore, to strip the matter, and by extracting its soul, hereafter to make bodies that are not bodies, containing and shaping them. Thus, matter must be stripped so that it may reach a vaporous perfection.

The definition of this philosophy, then, is the dissolution of the body and the separation of the soul from the body, so that the <term>tincture</term> <note>original: *tinctura*; the transformative essence or "dye" capable of transmuted metals</note> may insinuate itself into the body, and the kinship of nature may delight nature—retaining, overcoming, and remaining. This occurs when the internal is pushed outward with pleasure, and the entire earthy substance is made into an incorporeal composition through elevation. Likewise, it occurs when you see the extracted <term>soot</term> <note>original: *fuligo*; refers to the volatile vapors or "smoke" produced during sublimation</note> through an inspiration, being carried as if through a cloud. For an incorporeal nature cannot thrive except among higher things; for it is accustomed to be carried upward together with that which is like and related to it. Thus, the beloved and the lover are increased together—the delighting and the delighted, the shining—the two being one thing of a natural and single matter, or rather of a united nature which overcomes everything in the whole world, hence the saying: "All things are one" <note>original: *Unum sunt omnia*</note>. Consider this to be one thing, a composite of soul and body made into a body, into a tempered "one through one." Therefore, the white moon is the lunar species; the soot is that which is wiped away and washed by <term>divine water</term> <note>original: *aqua divina*; the philosophical solvent or mercury of the philosophers</note>.

Nothing is missing then, except the elevation of the vapor of the water: the work is completed by management. First, why the clouds? Namely, the soot is elevated on high toward heaven by the divine and celestial water. Therefore, the <term>Stone</term> <note>original: *Lapis*; the Philosopher's Stone</note> known to all, cheap and precious, is joined from warlike Venus with Mercury, male and female. You should, therefore, make the red copper enter, and color it with the brilliance of gold. The battle of Venus with the battle of Mercury. Venus, through that battle, is corrupted, and the moon is fixed through Venus, being joined together—that is, Mercury is fixed through the soot and vapor of <term>magnesia</term> <note>original: *magnesia*; in alchemy, this is not the modern element magnesium, but a "mother" substance or prime matter</note>. Therefore, the body of copper must be corrupted by the moon or lunar liquor and ground down exceedingly, until the art itself can proceed. For if anyone renders this body yellow through the spirit, preparing its nature powerfully and gently according to the art, it colors every body. If anyone, destroying the body through "death" and dissolving it by the benefit of the spirit, turns it yellow through the soot, it colors every body. For in this way, a spirit is made from the body of the soot, free from impurity, the vigor and splendor of the body, by the command of its Creator. You shall take Mercury and fix it to the body of magnesia.

The whole composition is made through Mercury and the composition of magnesia, male and female. It is mixed and contained together in the body.

### ANNOTATIONS

...which is completed through the mist and the soot: if guided by reason, it calls forth the powerful nature lying hidden within, which tints every body, whitening <term>Venus</term> <note>original: *Venerem*; the alchemical name for copper</note>, and taking away the <term>hissing of Jupiter</term> <note>original: *Jovi stridorem*; a reference to the "cry of tin," a crackling sound made when bending the metal, which alchemists sought to "fix" or transform</note>. A great mystery lies hidden in these things; when you see it, praise God. Sulfurous things are contained by sulfurous things—that is, the celestial and fiery elements are contained by terrestrial ones, from which those higher elements can be obtained.

The **first key** of the work is that the fire of quicksilver—namely, of <term>Mercury</term>—is joined with the water of terrestrial <term>magnesia</term> <note>original: *magnesiæ*; here referring to the "primal matter" or a specific mineral used as a starting point</note> through its own earth. By this path, the separation of the moist from the dry is achieved; that is, the separation of the souls of copper from their bodies.

The **second key** occurs when the <term>moon</term> <note>original: *luna*; silver</note> and water are joined with the fire of the aforementioned quicksilver, through the "air of copper" during the rising of the mist. This is the reduction of cold things with moist things, and the mixing of the higher things with the lower. The earth—that is, the slag of the copper—is joined with the solar air through fire, which is to say, through quicksilver.

The **third key** occurs when, through the <term>torrefaction</term> <note>original: *torrefactionem*; a process of roasting or drying by fire</note> of the <term>putrefaction</term> <note>original: *putrefactionis*; the stage of decay or "blackening" where the matter breaks down</note>, the slag is joined with the divine water through fire. This means that through the moon, the air of the sun is also joined with the earth—that is, with the slag—by means of water, which is the moisture.

The **fourth [key]** is truly made by the union of air with earth, which has been dissolved through putrefaction and the roasting of the seven reductions, with all things forced into a single water. These exist in the <term>philosophical cinnabar</term> <note>original: *cinabari philosophica*; not the common mineral, but a symbolic "red" stage of the mercury-sulfur union</note>, which consists of the aforementioned Mercury and the sulfur of magnesia. When these things are performed in this manner, the fire becomes hot and dry again, generating the heat of the air and the dryness of the earth. Similarly, when water becomes moist and cold, it generates the moisture of the air and the coldness of the earth. Since the earth is cold and dry, it generates the coldness of the water and the dryness of the fire. The air, being hot and moist, generates the heat of the fire and the moisture of the water. Since each thing has two qualities, they become an element consisting of three elements. All collected together, they become twelve, produced from three into four, according to the twelve signs [of the Zodiac] and the four seasons: such as the airy Spring, the fiery Summer, the watery Autumn, and the earthy Winter. This is the true composition of the elements through the Art. Likewise, the seven colors appearing in the work are called the bodies of the seven planets of that same composition; they are present now, but later absent in the signs of the work, just as in the heavens they now enter their signs and later depart from them. Thus, through its seven stars, which are called planets, and through its twelve non-wandering signs, the true mystery of the Philosophers is perfected.

The **colors of the elements** in the work are: from the feet to the knees, the earthy element, which is black; from the knees to the navel, the watery element, shining and white; from the navel to the heart, the airy element, yellow or citron-colored; and from the heart to the neck, the fiery element, glowing and red.

The vapor, which is carried on high, is the matter of air; and smoke, or the smoky exhalation of dry things, is the matter of fire.
