These three, therefore, by the aforementioned triple regimen, constitute the **novenary** <note>original: *novenarium*; the number nine</note>, which is closest to the fertile unity, namely the ternary.

->**I have three times three letters, I am four-syllabled, consider me. Each of the first three syllables has two letters, the remainder has the rest; five are mutes. Of the whole number, there are two hundreds, eight, and three times ten decades with seven.**<- 

One who understands who I am will not be crude or ignorant of the wisdom that is in me. Otherwise: The hundreds of the whole number are twice eight, and three times three, and four decades. <note>These are numerological riddles (gematria) common in mystical texts. Furthermore: The **principles of science** are sense and experience. The latter is the principle of active thought, while the former provides the thought of the appearing thing, from which follows the understanding of the soul of the world and of this prudence. Since this understanding is exempt from all things, it completes the sensible world. Therefore, let the three ternaries be considered as making up the orders of immaterial substances.

Since there are also three things which pertain to the universal operation, from which a quaternary composition is afterwards made. Corrupt the bodies through Mercury, and through the **mist of magnesia** <note>original: *magnesiæ nebulam*; in this period, "magnesia" referred to a primitive mineral or a specific stage of the chemical soup, not modern magnesium</note> join the male and female; then, calling forth the hidden nature again, you shall finally make the formations of bodies through it, that is, of the colors of the planets. In this manner, therefore, bodies are rendered incorporeal, and those things become corporeal.

If all things are thinned by fire, and the soot is carried upward, various and indestructible bodies would be made. By fire, understand **Mercury** and the **fiery medicine**, because Mercury burns, corrupts, and thins by one and the same artifice. Therefore, **Venus** does not tint <note>To "tint" in alchemy means to permanently change the color and nature of a metal, usually toward gold</note>, but is tinted, and when she is tinted, she tints. For nothing can tint a body by itself, or separate itself, if the spirit that hides within does not emerge. For how can a body exist without a spirit, except through the beautiful nature which is in it—think of it as the **animal spirit**—which leads out the color of the tincture with itself, and brings it in. 

Therefore, **Venus** does not tint, but is tinted. For the earthy part of the matter, being coarse, does not tint; but that thin quality of the substance produces the tincture in the body. For when Venus—that is, the body—is rightly governed through magnesia, and brings its own thin substance into the light, then at last it assumes the power of tinting, and it tints. Moreover, **Venus** is four bodies. The species of the tinctures are called solid, and moist, and **herbs**, by way of likeness: the solid indeed from the mist even unto **gold-glue** <note>original: *chrysocollam*; a substance used in soldering or a specific stage of yellowing</note>; the moist is the **divine water**. For divine things are retained by the lemon-yellow ones <note>original: *citrinis*; referring to the *citrinitas* or yellowing stage of the Great Work</note>, etc. But this is the truth: **Nature delights in nature, and nature embraces nature.** <note>A famous ancient alchemical axiom suggesting that only related substances can work together to produce the Stone</note> 

Again, the four-fold body of **Venus** is shown through magnesia, and the **herbs** of many-colored species come forth into the light during the friction of the elements. When the friction of the bodies is done reasonably, then they bloom with greenness, though they are not truly herbs except in color alone, nor can these remain in the fire. For he says: "Solid, and moist, and herbs." He calls the **solid** the bodies—whiteness, yellowing, etc.—which penetrate and remain in the bodies, not yielding at all, but firmly retaining and overcoming them. But he spoke of the **moist**, so that he might refresh them through the moist, that is, through the **divine water**. What then is this divine water, and why do they call it divine? Certainly, this name is great above others, and more excellent, because without...

# THE WORKS OF NICHOLAS FLAMEL #

### ->784<- ###

By this [divine water] in the work, nothing is produced, nor is anything perfected. The **Divine water** <note>original: *divina aqua*; likely a reference to a powerful solvent or "mercury of the philosophers"</note> is that which makes a nature simple, most lucid, most pure, and without the shadow of bodies; it is like a substance that changes bodies, cleansing them, and it is that which extracts the hidden nature from within the bodies. For the conjunction of the form of nature produces and prepares a most beautiful work through nature. The **Sharp water** <note>original: *acuta aqua*; a corrosive or acidic solvent used to break down metals</note> is said to be elevated and called forth. For those things which lie hidden within and are extracted are Divine. Therefore, divine things are retained by divine things. The soul and spirit are extracted from divine things, and are retained by those same things, penetrating the bodies by their quality. For it is a Truth: **Nature delights in nature, nature embraces nature, and nature overcomes nature.** <note>A fundamental alchemical axiom attributed to Democritus or Ostanes, suggesting that only substances of the same "kind" can act upon one another effectively</note> For when that which lies hidden within is well-conducted and purged by the divine water, it delights itself by penetrating, overcoming, and remaining within the body’s own nature. Thus, recognizing its own nature, it rejoices in the connected and joined sequence of change.

***

But to return to the matter: the **four bodies** <note>Usually referring to the base metals: lead, tin, copper, and iron</note> are tinted, but they do not tint [other things]. For **whitened Magnesia** <note>original: *magnesia dealbata*; in alchemy, "magnesia" refers not to the modern element, but to a primitive mineral substance or a stage of the "Great Work" where the matter turns white</note> does not allow the bodies to be broken, nor the **shadow of Venus** <note>Venus represents the metal copper; its "shadow" refers to its impurities or its green/dark oxidation</note> to be introduced. But see what the Philosopher says: that the four bodies are tinted, and do not tint; nor does he say, as before, that if they are tinted, they then tint: in this way, understand the substance of the solid bodies. He says: "Whitened Magnesia," etc. What is this Magnesia if not the whole composite? How then is it whitened? It is when it is governed royally and roasted, and when, being purged with the divine thing, it brings back the hidden things of all solid bodies from the depths, so that the nature of the bodies may be tinted by them. For the composite, when irrigated by the divine water, does not allow the bodies to be broken; rather, it takes away their shadow, and the **scum of silver** <note>original: *argenti spuma*; often referring to litharge or a metallic byproduct</note> mixed with the magnesia whitens the body and others of the same kind. See the beautiful and wondrous things of Magnesia: how through a single multitude it brings in certain things from Unity, some from Duality, some from the Trinity, and even more, until its entire universe is preserved. Some indeed come from the Monad, namely the **fiery medicine**; some from Duality, as with the Magnesia and the body itself; some from the Trinity, namely the purging with the divine water; and thus it extends itself, and through others it brings back the roasting, until the whole composite work is kept cleansed, and is perfected and completed in an absolute state. For the material suitable for making **Gold** is **Mercury** itself. He says: Mercury is sometimes from **Cinnabar** <note>Mercury sulfide; the primary ore of mercury</note>, sometimes from **Venus** <note>Copper</note>, and sometimes truly from **B.** <note>This "B" likely refers to the *Balneum* (water bath) or potentially a shorthand for Borax or Bismuth in later traditions</note>. Mercury from cinnabar is magnesia; Mercury from B. is the divine water, which is extracted from a compressed instrument, and these are the things that change the matter. **Venus**, like a man, has a soul and a body. It is necessary, therefore, to strip the matter of its body, so that it may remain as a **tinting spirit**, suited to the perfection of whatever is sought. What is Venus? It is like a man, a material body. The soul is the thin part within it, which comes forth into the light through governance: that is, the spirit having the power of tinting. But the body...

[That which is] heavy, material, and terrestrial possesses its own shadow, which must be stripped away by a fiery medicine <note>original: *igneo pharmaco*; a potent chemical agent, often associated with heat or corrosive "fire"</note>. To strip away is to humble, to corrupt, to dissolve, and to mortify. Afterward, let nothing be lacking; nothing remains except the extraction of the cloud and the water. The Philosopher <note>likely referring to Zosimos of Panopolis or Hermes Trismegistus</note>, using a true figure of speech, called it the water of **copper-green** <note>original: *calcanthi*; blue vitriol or copper sulfate</note>: for in that place is the generation of copper. And this copper-green generates gold; the **flower of copper** <note>original: *flos æris*; verdigris or the fine powder that forms on copper</note>, says the Philosopher, is that very thing which consumes and perfects the work: it is also the masculine spirit. It is explained thus: Cast it forth from the substance drawn from the Highest, so that the divine power, having been effected and converted into spirit, may perform the divine work. The "divine" must be sought so that the matter may be stripped away and become soul alone; and the spirit, seeking the sublime, may take on color. Thus, being with the fire, it becomes more combative and tenacious, just like the planar body of spirits <note>original: *dæmonum*; in this context, "daemons" refers to intermediary spirits or ethereal beings</note> and those things which penetrate: for the root of a solid is the plane <note>An ancient geometric analogy: just as a 2D plane can penetrate a 3D solid, the alchemical "spirit" penetrates the "body" of the metal</note>.

Therefore, having been converted into spirit and carried upward like fire—by the reasoning of this teaching—it is in a certain way assimilated to fire, and becomes more penetrating and tenacious; these are the reasons discovered from the nature of the world. For just as the four elements are transmuted into one another—becoming what they were not, since their substance is not contrary to substance—fire becomes earth, earth becomes water, and water becomes air; and again, water becomes earth, and earth rises even to the higher things. Having been changed and dissolved within themselves, they perform all works, as it is written in the works of Hermes <note>Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary founder of alchemy</note>: for their qualities are contrary to one another, but not their substances. Thus also the composite, since it is of the earth, produces air from water, and fire from air. Therefore, just as all these things come from exhalations from the heaven which rests upon the earth like a chamber, so also within the **flask** <note>original: *olla*; literally a "pot" or "jar," used here for the boiling vessel</note> as if from the earth, and the **alembic** <note>original: *alembico*; the cap of the still used for distilling</note> placed above as if from the heaven, violent mutations occur. And just as the putrefactions of the earth are transmuted as they exhale, so also the flower of copper is transmuted as it exhales at the same time. This same thing is also observable in the human head, when a **cucurbit** <note>original: *cucurbitulæ*; a gourd-shaped vessel used in distillation</note> or a helmet-like vessel is placed upon the body. **Therefore, it is not said in vain: "grind it":** for it is not said rashly that they are cooked slowly and raised up among themselves. For by a light boiling, the hidden **tinging spirit** <note>original: *spiritus tingens*; the "elixir" or "tincture" that changes the color/nature of the metal</note> is drawn out: that which is carried upward is the spirit devoid of body, and the soul of the whole composite (that is, of the body). Just as the soul shows itself to bodies, fermenting all things—having within itself three formative substances: motion, sense, and ignition—so this spirit, having become fiery and a soul devoid of body, penetrates the body of the thing that colors all. If it is established within that body—like a plane within a solid—it is done through the injection of its medicine into silver that has been rarefied by fire. This joyful fiery spirit (he says) leaps in; it is the spirit that also lies hidden within bodies, and seeking the sublime, it retains even the body itself as its own soul. Furthermore, regarding the different cause of the extracted water, let this not terrify you: for it is the "flower" which is extracted, not only once, but twice or thrice through the **sea-vessels** <note>original: *maripetas*; likely referring to a *Bain-Marie* or "Bath of Mary," a water-bath used for gentle heating</note>. After, therefore, it has been shown...

### ->786<- ###

# [THE WRITINGS] OF NICOLAS FLAMEL #

Existence is accidental; the flower is the water of sulfur and is used as a libation <note>original: *illibationis*; a ritual pouring of a liquid as an offering</note>. For the Philosopher said: and the gum tints every body. Mary <note>Mary the Prophetess, a legendary female alchemist often cited in early hermetic texts</note> says: The restraint for those things which flee from fire is the alabaster, the whitest of all, the brain <note>original: *encephalus*; likely referring to the "spirit" or "intellectual" essence of the stone</note>, hidden in the mind, having as it were heat. The wise man grinds [it] and mixes it with vinegar, and casting it into a small vessel, at last buries it under dung <note>a common alchemical method for providing gentle, steady heat via fermentation</note>: for this is what makes the undiluted water of sulfur and the rust to be one: and here truly the hinge of the whole art turns. In this very thing, it is considered that in one composition all things are made: that which tints and that which is tinted; that which flees and that which follows; that which is healing and its contrary; male and female; bridegroom and bride; the agent and the patient. For there is one serpent, which has two dispositions and rust. The whole is one, because of which all things are; if the whole did not contain the whole, nothing would be a whole, says the greatest [philosopher]. For making things "fixed" <note>in alchemy, to make a substance "fixed" is to make it resistant to fire so that it does not evaporate</note> is not only the property of sulfur, but also of those things which have been whitened, softened, and rarefied. For when the substances undergo perfection and roasting by the white sulfur, they themselves are made into incombustible sulfur, and they remain in the form they have undergone, by giving and receiving: and then both [types of] sulfur render the substances fixed: this is what makes them not break apart from each other. 

Next, he asks: why do you search for a multitude of things, when one nature overcomes all? By weighing this nature's operation until the end, you will see the manifest sign, that is, the cymbals <note>original: *cymbalia*; likely a metaphor for the harmony or "resonance" of the completed substance</note>. O natures of celestial natures, these, when dissolved, perform all works. What then is this? Come here to the liquids and learn: Take the saffron of Cilicia <note>original: *crocum Ciliciae*; an alchemical term for a golden-colored chemical precipitate, often a metal oxide</note> joined with the flower of copper and the juice of the vine, and you will find a single solution of the liquids. Come here again to the white: and again there is dissolution, as he himself teaches you, saying: Leave the lower things. He spoke truly: some have called them "bodies," others "sulfur," and they were deceived. And for this reason, error has spread through the world because of the multitude of names. What is said of the four elements and the instruments must be referred to those. 

Consider Saturn and, opposite to it, lead at the highest peak, and after it Mars, the Sun, Venus, Mercury, and in the lowest place [the Moon]. Each is distinct among themselves, yet they are joined in one circle; one spirit serves them and governs the same, and because of one spirit they are moved, and they look at each other with mutual eyes, and they turn mutually, they dissolve mutually, and they walk in their own dwellings, just as the most high Creator made them. For similarly they are found in the earth, they are in the air, and in the water, and in the fire; they have total peace among themselves; one craftsman serves them, and rules the same, and by one law they are joined and drink one potion, from which [the Work is completed].

ANNOTATIONS. 787

<sig>Ddd 2</sig>

...they are nourished, and each of them performs its own duty, and remains in its own nature, and lies open to the Creator's will; each of them is hidden in the earth, and in its own glory. And you, O friends, when you wish to approach this most beautiful art <note>the "Art" is the standard term for Alchemy</note>, look at the nature of herbs, and from where they come: some from the mountains, others from the valleys, and others from the fields. Consider the air that serves them; consider the divine water dewing them, and bringing the mist, and the ether governing them. When these are mixed, they are one, and no one can separate them once they have come together into one nature.

O Cleopatra (said Ostanes), in this matter the whole secret <term>arcanum|A deep mystery or the "great secret" of the alchemical process</term> lies hidden; explain clearly to us about the elements, and how the higher descends to the lower, and how the middle is near to the highest and the outermost, and how the parts do not clash, though they precede and are united; what is the "middle" for them that makes them one, and how the blessed waters descend to see the dead lying there, bound and placed in darkness, and in gloom within the underworld <note>original: *inferno*; in alchemy, this refers to the "nigredo" or black stage of decay</note>, and how the medicine of life enters and rouses them, so that they wake as if from sleep, and how the new waters enter, which are generated at the head of the bed and in the bed, and how the cloud carries them, and how the watery cloud ascends from the sea. 

The Philosophers, contemplating those things which have been shown, rejoice. But Cleopatra says to them: The waters entering the bodies wake the spirits that were enclosed in them and weak, as if from sleep. Again (she said) they have suffered hardships, and again they will be shut up in the underworld, and little by little they are born, and rise, and put on diverse and glorious colors, just like flowers in spring, which rejoice and exult because of the beauty with which they are clothed. 

To you (I say), the wise, herbs, elements, and stones, when you dig them out from their places, seem quite beautiful, and yet not beautiful: since fire tests all things. But when they put on glory through fire and a green color, there are greater sights; there is the hidden glory, and accurately sought-out beauty, and the earth changed into divinity: since it is nourished in the fire. Just as an infant nourished in the womb <note>original: *sub ventre*</note> increases little by little, and when the appointed month arrives, is not prevented from coming forth into the light, such a thing is this noble matter. 

Storms and waves lash it in the underworld, and in the tomb in which it lies; but when the tomb is opened, it rises from the underworld, like an infant from the womb. The Philosophers, contemplating this beauty, are like a devoted mother contemplating the infant she has borne. Then at last they seek how, just as an infant is fed with milk, they may nourish this art with waters: since as an infant is formed, and when it is perfected in all these things, behold the secret is sealed. But now for the first time openly, where the elements and herbs lie for you, I will begin to speak in riddles: Ascend to the highest roof, onto the mountain planted with trees, and you will see a stone in...

...truth: from this stone take the arsenic, and of the white, divine <note>original: *de alba divine*; likely referring to the "white stone" or the white phase of the work, known as the Albedo</note>. Behold, nature gives back to nature, and when all things meet equally, then natures conquer natures and rejoice in turn.

Consider, O wise ones, and understand: for behold the perfection of the art, of the married groom and bride made one: behold the herbs and their differences: behold, I have told you the whole truth, and again I shall tell you: see and understand. Hear therefore, and be understanding, and judge exactly of what I speak: Take from the four elements the highest and lowest arsenic, both the white and the red, and an equal weight of the male <note>original: *maris*; the text uses the masculine to create a gendered polarity with the following term</note> and the female, so that they may be joined together. Behold the secret of the Philosophers, for which our fathers bound us by oath not to reveal it; let it have a divine form and operation. For it is divine, because when joined with divinity, it makes divine substances, in which the spirit becomes body, and the dead are brought to life, receiving the spirit proceeding from them, and they are held in turn, and they hold. Just as, on the other hand, a dark spirit, full of vanity and sadness, prevents bodies from being whitened, or from receiving the beauty and color which they had from the Creator. ...laid out in this manner, saying: Come forth from hell, and rise from the grave; awake from the darkness: for you are clothed in spirituality and divinity: since the voice of resurrection has been heard, and the medicine of life has entered into you. ->*If for the Sun, do thus.*<-
<note>original: "Sin Solis ita facito." In alchemy, the "Sun" (Sol) refers to gold.</note>

Grinding together sandarac <term>sandaracum|A red arsenic sulfide mineral used as a pigment and in alchemy</term>, blue vitriol <note>original: "calcanthum"</note>, arsenic, native sulfur, and cinnabar, and making a tenacious mixture, cast it into a pure glass vessel with a narrow mouth. Having blocked the opening with clay, let it be heated by the fire <note>original: "affato," likely referring to the breath of the furnace</note> for a day. Afterward, removing the clay, you will find a dry material similar in thickness to pitch. Grinding this again, store it in an earthenware vessel, and placing the whole in the fire and removing the cover, you will find it yellow, and so forth. And indeed, if you take white magnesia and an equal weight of well-prepared sand, and afterward, grinding both together, you cook them in radish oil, you will have that which is gold in the furnaces. If, however, it is not shining in color, let those things mentioned above be anointed with salt, and let them be ground with mysy <term>mysi|An ancient term for a yellowish, metallic mineral, likely a basic copper sulfate or vitriol</term> and saffron of iron <term>ferri croco|Iron oxide, used for its deep red/orange pigmenting properties</term>. By communicating these powers to the substances, you will produce gold more brilliant than the golden sands of the Pactolus <note>A river in Lydia famous in antiquity for its gold-bearing sands</note>. 

If you have gold and wish to double its weight without losing any of its quality, weigh out medicinal ingredients <note>original: "pharmaca"</note> twice as large as the gold: use mysy and filings of beryl so that it becomes four times the amount of gold. By mixing or tempering these two together, attach them to the gold. When you have cast them into the crucible and made them glowing hot, draw them out, and you shall find yourself twice as rich. But our intention was not to treat the brightening or increasing of gold, but its creation. This, therefore, I shall provide, although my discourse has digressed somewhat to touch upon other arts in passing.

Cinnabar, then, and the "golden flower of copper" <note>original: "aureus flos aeris"</note>, cast into lunar matter <note>Silver</note> as if they were natural forms, create a golden body. Therefore, if you temper the medicines by melting them with silver, the moon shall become the sun to you; and if you follow such a path, you will find the color and the conversion of silver into gold for every use of gold. For the moon indeed makes gold, but the sun does not make the moon: for the moon alone receives its light from the sun; yet it serves not only the moon, but also the great light. Therefore, drawing out the body of copper as much as is right, make it into something like a long tongue. Afterward, placing it upon the coals, stir up Vulcan <note>The god of fire, representing the furnace heat</note> upon it. By radiating it now with fossil salt, and now with Attic ochre continuously, or by turns adorning the shoulder and breast of the Paphian <note>Venus, representing copper</note>, she shall plainly become more beautiful; and casting away her grayish-blue color, she will appear entirely golden. When Paris perhaps saw Venus <note>original: "Venerem"</note> in such a state, he preferred her to Juno and Pallas. Since we have mentioned "governance" <term>regiminis|The sequence of heat and operations in the alchemical process</term> above, we shall interpret what that name signifies. And because we require the tincture of *chrysitis* <note>A "golden" or "gold-making" substance</note> for the works, it is first necessary to have the medicine so that we may use it in due time.

...cleansing it with sweet water, and afterward drying it with the rays of the sun, dissolve and mix it together with the flower of Scythian copper <note>original: "æris Scythici flore," likely referring to verdigris or a refined copper salt</note> and chrysolite. Afterward, taking an equal weight of split alum <term>aluminis scissilis|A naturally occurring fibrous form of alum, often used in ancient chemistry as a mordant or reagent</term> and cinnabar, and mixing them in oxymel <term>oxymel|A classical medicinal preparation made of honey and vinegar</term>, sprinkle it upon the melted lead; likewise add native sulfur (as above) so that it may then become solid, and taking the color through all its pores, it may be turned into gold because of all these things.

Shall we then briefly reveal to you the whole wisdom of Democritus of Abdera <note>A Greek philosopher often associated in the Middle Ages with secret alchemical knowledge</note>, leaving nothing behind in the inner sanctuaries? But neither those who initiate others into the sacred rites say this, nor does mystical divination. Yet set times have stirred the leader of the sacred rites, and again he has rested from his frenzy, and having been initiated into the rites, he hastened the composition. But do not take it ill if I sit before you, the first and leader of the sacred rites, as another leader of the rites myself. For more excellent things have been entrusted to you, and you bring down God from heaven, and you carry up the soul and the mind, which is in matter, and join it to the thing exempt from matter. I, however, lie upon the ground, and am a contemplator of nature, nor have I yet turned myself to the speculation of things not visible: because as of yet, a sharper light has not been made for me. Thus Psellus <note>Michael Psellus (c. 1017–1078), a Byzantine polymath and philosopher</note> wrote to the Patriarch Xiphilinus, and further. You know then what we shall do, he says? To me indeed, the depths of the earth are entrusted: but you have attained those heavenly things. Let us therefore share in turn the things we have: you to me the remarkable sights, and I to you the natural effects. But do you see what I have done for you? For when I opened the springs of gold, I neither shook Mount Athos nor moved Mount Pangaeum, nor did I reopen certain subterranean veins; but grinding stones against each other and mixing certain herbs, I have nobly and usefully labored for you a very precious gold. Devise something of this sort for me also, not stirring the air, nor lifting me on high, but by some means show me the super-celestial good upon the earth: for it is nowhere, yet everywhere, and in any part of the universe. The discovery is hidden from many, and that which is within us, we, wandering, seek in the heavens. But teach me how it is near, and how it is further away—not distant in place, but approaching nearer by disposition, that which is further away. Tell me, what is the reason for the defense of the intellect? Then, descending to such a point, how does it rise again? In short, lead me by the hand to God. If indeed it is through a narrow enough path, I shall be content, if indeed through a path capable of holding us. If you lead me to be initiated into these sacred rites, I promise you that I shall leave no work of science or nature, nor any kind of study, or ancient—

### ->SUMMARY DECLARATION OF THOSE THINGS<-
### ->which have been said thus far from Democritus, through<-
### ->enigmas.<-

What it means to strip, humble, corrupt, dissolve, and <unclear>kill</unclear> <note>likely *mortificare* (to mortify or kill), a standard alchemical term for breaking down a substance to its essence</note>, and to extract all matter, so that by the spirit entering and making it manifest, that which has the power of tinting the body <note>original: "tingendi corpus"; the power to transform or "dye" base metal into gold</note> might be known, and the response may be accommodated to the perfection of the quest. This [knowledge] is prompt and suitable for the perfect completion by ascending from observations that fall under the senses to those which are perceived by the intellect, and by beholding the great celestial ornament. When you have contemplated the ornament of these things, lifting your mind higher, and considering the great and sufficiently shining company of angels and such great joy, do not turn back hereafter to the material notion of this humble and abject science that has now been revealed: but raise yourself entirely toward higher things, lifting the wings of your mind to the splendor of the supernal substances, gazing with intent and internal eyes upon their innumerable and arduous beauties, and another light which surpasses all light, and laying down all works in the world, and thinking in your soul of the chosen [state] before death, and with you your mortal body... but furthermore denying your soul, glorifying and praising with clear hymns the King and Lord of glory: struck with trembling and fear, a contemplator of the omnipotent power in your mind, and of His goodness, which surpasses all goodness; just as all things were produced through His ineffable wisdom. The tongue grows numb, the mind also cannot bear, nor the senses investigate or recount, what great works of the Almighty God are truly laid up for the contemplating mind. Considering all these things within ourselves, let us also strive that we may be united with all as brothers through faith and delight, and let us be conformed, as much as possible, to the Word of God who loved us: and thus adoring the Lord our God, let us love Him with all our mind, and with all our heart: and let us glorify such a treasure so that at last, having been deemed worthy of the fellowship of God, through Him...

# 793 #

### ANNOTATIONS ###

...that we may be filled [with grace], and by the light of that wisdom which illustrates all nature and enlightens every mind. To Him be praise forever.

The Patriarch Xiphilinus <note>John VIII Xiphilinus, an 11th-century Patriarch of Constantinople</note> wrote these things to Michael Psellus <note>A famous Byzantine scholar and statesman known for his works on magic and alchemy</note>, who replied in return: Take one part of **chrysolite**, and three parts of **cinnabar of magnesia**: grind them until they are joined together and their substances are mixed, and no more "living sulfur" <note>original: "sulphuris vivi"; native or unrefined sulfur</note> appears. For it becomes very black, like printer's ink. After three days, casting it into a bath, add some of the liquid that is used for washing equal parts, and wash away all the tinting, receiving it, etc.

**Chrysolite** is arsenic, as you know, or the "Aethesian stone." **Cinnabar of magnesia** is chalcopyrite <note>a copper-iron sulfide mineral</note>; it is also called lead. The "liquid of the bath" is the radical vinegar of our radish root with its own salt, drawn from it by <term>cohobation</term> <note>the alchemical process of repeatedly pouring a distillate back onto its residue to concentrate its properties</note> into a solvent. Wash it, he says, until its rust comes out, and thus it goes away with no copper remaining in the lead. This is the "great solution" by evacuation, rusting, blackening, washing, and so on. Proceed as you know. Taking the mentioned "evacuation," leave it to settle in vessels; pressing out the liquid, dry what remains at the bottom. You will find this to be like printer's ink; grind this until it becomes perfectly yellow, or white first. In this way, let it be ground by drying over a continuous fire until it whitens and becomes brilliantly white. Watch, therefore, that you do not tire during the time of **whitening** <note>Latin: "dealbatio"; one of the key stages of the Great Work, representing purification</note>: for negligence often happens because that beauty is not yet seen. For through this whitening, the copper becomes without shadow, casting away all its earthly excess and thickness. If, therefore, the copper is whitened, it becomes spiritual, and finally nothing is left, nothing is missing, except for a mist and the rising of water.

Zozimus <note>Zosimos of Panopolis, a foundational Greco-Egyptian alchemist from the 3rd century</note> says: I know one order having two works: first, that it flows through resin (understand this as the "purgatory" or cleansing process); second, that the moisture of **Saturn** <note>the alchemical name for lead</note> is dried by rising into a light powder. Therefore, place an equal part of "light stone" with the purified material, and grind it by washing and "evacuating" with vinegar extracted through an <term>alembic</term> <note>a traditional distillation apparatus with a gourd-like body and a cooling beak</note> until it whitens, until it becomes brilliant white. Watch, therefore, during the time of whitening, as mentioned above, etc. 

Sweetening the medicine and drying it, put it away and level the medicine: three parts of **vitriol** <note>original: "calcanthi"; copper or iron sulfate</note>, one part of magnesia, and another part of the medicine. Grind them together, watering them in the sun with white vinegar for six days; and afterwards, drying it, place it in cow dung <note>alchemists used the gentle, steady heat of decomposing dung to maintain a constant temperature</note>, and let them be burned for two or three days. Removing it from the heat, you will find gold tinted like blood: this is the **Cinnabar of the Philosophers**, and a clear yellow copper. Why (says the Senior <note>Senior Zadith, the Latinized name for the 10th-century Arabic alchemist Ibn Umail</note>) do you concern yourselves with a forest of many things? Since there is but one natural matter, and one nature which overcomes all things. Then, therefore, dissolved by the "divine water" and fermented...

# 794 #

### ANNOTATIONS OF NICOLAS FLAMEL ###

...[fer]mented <note>original: "mentatum", likely continuing from "fermentatum" on the previous page</note>, like the leavening of bread, and thereafter also with **chrysolite** <note>In this context, chrysolite refers to yellow arsenic or orpiment, rather than the modern gemstone</note> ground in equal parts and dissolved in water; according to its nature, through <term>fluxion</term> <note>the state of being liquid or melting easily</note>, it tints every body. Zosimus <note>Zosimus of Panopolis, a major Egyptian-Greek alchemist from the 3rd century AD</note> says: The natural Sun <note>gold</note>, made spiritual through chrysolite, tints according to nature. If we also dissolve silver by means of water, and make it spiritual through chrysolite, it tints copper white. For he also said this in other words. Indeed, the two <term>tinctures</term> <note>substances capable of changing the color and nature of metals</note> differ from each other in nothing except color alone: that is, they have one and the same preparation. Because they are first ground by the **divine water**, and afterwards they become a spiritual medicine through chrysolite, each one tints according to its own nature: the sun tints gold, and the moon tints silver.

By **divine water**, understand the "visitation of hidden things" <note>This is a likely reference to the famous alchemical acronym V.I.T.R.I.O.L.: Visita Interiora Terrae Rectificando Invenies Occultum Lapidem ("Visit the interior of the earth; by rectifying you will find the hidden stone")</note>. Therefore, the **Aethesian stone** <note>another name for the arsenic used here</note> being bound with copper, and reduced with the oil of radish, this made the blessed scholars of Egypt. Therefore, by raising up that which is composed by art, and calling forth the hidden nature, you finally create the formations of bodies through it; and thus bodies are rendered incorporeal, and incorporeal things become corporeal. If all things are thinned by fire, and the soot is carried off, there will be various and unbreakable bodies.

->Praised be the Most<-
->High.<-

<page-num>794</page-num>
<header>NICOLAS FLAMEL'S ANNOTATIONS</header>

...fermented, like the leaven of bread, and thereafter also the chrysolite <note>term for "gold-stone," referring here to a yellow alchemical substance used for coloring</note> crushed in equal parts and dissolved in water; according to its nature by its flow, it tints every body. Zosimos <note>an influential 3rd-century Greco-Egyptian alchemist</note> says: The natural Sun <note>gold</note>, made spiritual through chrysolite, tints according to nature. Also, if we dissolve silver in water, and make it spiritual through chrysolite, it tints copper <note>or brass</note> white. For he also said this in other words. For the two tinctures differ in no other way among themselves except by color alone: that is, they have one and the same preparation: because they are first crushed by divine water <note>original: "aqua divina," an alchemical solvent often associated with sulfur water or "theia hydor"</note>, and afterwards through chrysolite they become a spiritual medicine; each one tints according to its own nature, the sun gold, and the moon silver. By "divine water," understand the visitation of hidden things. Therefore the Ethiopian stone <note>a mineral often associated with dark flint or hematite in ancient texts</note> bound with copper, and reduced with oil of radish, rendered the blessed students of Egypt here. Therefore, raising up that which is composed by art, and calling forth the latent nature, you finally make the formations of bodies through it, and thus bodies are rendered incorporeal, and the incorporeal become corporeal. If all things are thinned by fire, and the soot is carried, there will be various and unbreakable bodies.

->Praised be the Most High.<-
